talks.title: The Cybersecurity of Smart ‘Adult’ Toys, or Lack of It
talks.teaser: Shows how insecure connected adult toys and hookup apps leak users' location and personal data, with real case studies.
talks.summary:
Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners opens by explaining why connected adult toys are an awkward subject to examine, even though their use has grown among military personnel, long-distance couples and people during COVID lockdowns. He notes that weak security in these devices has enabled blackmail and extortion, and that one reported case ended in tragedy.

Munro then walks through a series of device case studies. An early couples toy app wrote temporary images to shared SD card storage and used fixed Bluetooth PINs. Another toy sent messages unencrypted despite privacy claims, and its vendor kept the old app live after disclosure. Broadcast Bluetooth and Wi-Fi identifiers revealed that a device was nearby, a technique the team called screwdriving. A camera endoscope toy acted as a Wi-Fi access point with a blank admin password, which gave the team a persistent root shell. Hookup apps exposed precise location through trilateration, and a chastity device's shared digital key could be used to lock a wearer in permanently. The vendor declined to fix that flaw.

The closing section argues that vendors should be held accountable and that regulation in the UK, US and EU is arriving, but it only works if consumers complain. For employers, staff use of these devices is better handled through awareness training than punishment, since hidden use creates blackmail risk. The Q&A covered revoking shared keys and the unsettled legal status of hijacking someone else's toy.

talks.title: A Walkthrough: AppSec Tool Selection, Procurement, and Implementation
talks.teaser: Walks through selecting, buying and rolling out application security tooling, from finding needs to measuring results afterward.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works on an AppSec team, walks through choosing, buying and rolling out application security tooling for a company that grew through acquisitions and many tech stacks. The talk splits the work into five stages: understanding the need and existing landscape, evaluating vendors, procurement, implementation and rollout, and operationalizing with metrics. Early on, the speaker recommends building relationships with liaisons in engineering, legal and finance, and arriving with prepared questions and answers.

Vendor work follows a familiar path of discovery calls, demos, a negotiated NDA and a proof of concept. The speaker advises scoping requirements tightly to protect the timeline and building a vendor evaluation document with a comparison matrix and a cost estimate that counts hidden costs, such as trials that drag on. Proofs of concept are measured against success criteria ranked as deal breakers or weighted priorities, and procurement then needs a business justification covering options, pricing, return on investment and engineer feedback.

For implementation, the talk stresses securing engineering leaders' buy-in, learning the platform team's systems, assigning clear ownership with a RACI breakdown, and writing runbooks for developers. Rollout starts with a cooperative pilot group, runs in a quiet mode until nothing breaks, and is tuned before wider release. Metrics such as how fast teams learn about findings and whether developers are happy with the tool guide next steps. In the Q&A, the speaker advises drawing boundaries when one vendor covers overlapping products, comparing each product separately, and questioning how mature newer offerings are.

talks.title: Unveiling the Secrets of Codesys V3: ZeroDays, Forensic Artifacts and More
talks.teaser: Reverse engineers CODESYS V3 PLC project binaries for forensic artifacts and walks through a remote code execution bug.
talks.summary:
The speakers, researchers at Microsoft, look at CODESYS V3, a widely used PLC programming SDK that runs on many CPUs and operating systems. They argue that operational technology has no shared forensics methodology, and they want a way to check the logic actually stored on a controller without relying on the engineering IDE, which an attacker could compromise.

They reverse engineered the compiled project format, using protocol tags, the symbol table and function tables to recover code sections, tasks and call relationships. Tracing how the runtime loads these structures, they built a simulator for the ARM code to recover task configuration. On a WAGO PFC controller they found a stack-based overflow in a component that handles uploaded files. The overflow could crash the device, and the team showed how it could be turned into remote code execution by bypassing ASLR and DEP with ROP gadgets and return-to-libc. They also released ICSpector, an open-source tool that reports project metadata, network capabilities, tasks, call graphs and online/offline project comparisons.

The closing guidance covers segmenting OT networks and monitoring for anomalies, patching SDK-based devices promptly, maintaining SBOMs, keeping PLC firmware current, preparing OT-specific incident response plans, and requiring vendors to follow secure development practices. Audience questions covered how to identify which SDKs are present in an environment and how offline networks delay firmware updates.

talks.title: AI, the Software Supply Chain, and Other (Not So) Puzzling Pieces
talks.teaser: Walks through securing the software supply chain using secret scanning, passkeys, AI pair programming, and build provenance.
talks.summary:
The talk treats software supply chain security as a short list of fundamentals rather than a pile of optimized tools. It sorts the basics into three pillars: software security and secrets, platform and developer security, and build systems with dependencies. To show scale, the speaker cited 10 million leaked secrets observed in 2023 and 7 million unresolved code scanning dependency alerts, and noted that AI coding tools are now widespread among developers.

A live demo covered AI-assisted code review. A pair programmer flagged an SQL injection in a Django snippet pasted from the web and suggested a fix using the framework's native constructs. Pull request scanning offered a similar AI-generated fix inline, and push protection blocked a commit containing a database credential before it reached the repository. Two-factor authentication and passkeys for contributors were also covered. The build segment generated provenance attestations in a GitHub Actions workflow, verified a Python package with the GitHub CLI, and enforced an Open Policy Agent rule allowing deploys only from approved repositories.

Closing advice included enabling secret scanning, requiring two-factor authentication and passkeys, reviewing third-party integrations, automating dependency updates, and adopting SBOMs and provenance. In the Q&A, the speaker said attestations probably would not have stopped an XZ Utils-style compromise, but would make forensics much easier.

talks.title: What Hacking the Planet Taught Us About Defending Supply Chain Attacks
talks.teaser: Walks through a product security testing method for finding hidden dependencies and vendor risk before devices join your network.
talks.summary:
The session groups supply chain attacks into vendor breaches that push tainted updates and flaws in shared libraries that products inherit. Stories from the speakers' device research illustrate the second kind. An infusion pump fell to a format string bug that a JSON library had fixed in its commit history, and a building controller gave a route into networks behind the perimeter. In a water plant test, default and hard-coded credentials were still present months later when the tester returned.

The speakers then lay out a product security testing method that mirrors an attacker's workflow but aims at defense. It moves through online product research, basic enumeration of dependencies and running processes, deeper analysis of encryption or proprietary protocols where warranted, threat modeling with attack trees, and risk scoring that selects countermeasures. Case examples include a library flaw in a 2023 Barracuda product, where the key question was which other products carried the same library, and the 2021 Codecov breach, where a popular uploader script ran downloaded code straight into a shell. A password manager's compromised update site showed why unexpected new files in an update deserve alerts.

For prioritisation, the speakers suggest starting with products that hold privileged access or talk often with vendors, and using tools such as PingCastle, flow data, Zeek and out-of-band DNS sensors. AI brainstorming tools can help generate threat ideas but only reflect the information supplied. The closing advice is to know critical assets, document dependencies, and repeat the assessment on a cadence for mission-critical systems.

talks.title: The Price is WRONG
talks.teaser: Argues that piling on point security products creates complexity attackers exploit, backed by breach data and underground sales listings.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the security industry's reliance on point products has created more complexity than defenders can manage. Breach headlines usually blame one weak spot, such as unpatched servers or stolen passwords, but a real intrusion means every layer and tool failed together. The speaker cites IBM's breach cost report, which links security system complexity to higher breach costs, and argues that falling detection times are misleading because ransomware gangs often reveal their own intrusions.

Using traffic data from about 2,200 organizations, the talk shows that many of the most-targeted vulnerabilities are years old and that a large share of outbound WAN traffic is unencrypted, with the rate varying by industry. A ransomware case at a chemical manufacturer showed a phishing email, a connection to a suspicious site and a payload download all passing undetected, with some alerts raised but ignored by the SOC. In a second case, a group returned after an earlier attack and tried to encrypt servers that had already been removed, which exposed the earlier foothold. Underground listings for domain admin access, crypting services and access brokers show attackers both exploiting basic weaknesses and defeating individual products.

The takeaway is to reduce complexity rather than add tools, and to consolidate with shared context and a unified policy rather than simply bundling products together. The talk also stresses that basics such as closing exposed ports, enforcing strong passwords and checking firewall configuration remain effective, since criminals say these simple measures still work.

talks.title: Navigating M&A Security Challenges: A Deep Dive into a Case Study
talks.teaser: Walks through a fictional M&A security case, from due diligence to post-acquisition integration, with lessons for security teams.
talks.summary:
This talk walks through a fictional M&A security case: a San Francisco accounting firm of about 15,000 employees weighs buying a smaller Barcelona accounting company. The speaker opens with real examples of acquired environments exposing buyers, then explains the standard deal stages from opportunity to integration.

With four weeks of due diligence inside a six-week exclusivity window, the target declined to answer the standard questionnaire and refused a compromise assessment. The team relied instead on a delta questionnaire, a cybersecurity rating report, a threat intelligence report, an outsourced source code review, and a recent penetration test from a reputable provider. Findings included no MFA on the VPN, end-of-life servers, high-risk issues in the code and pen test, no formal third-party risk program, and no recent security training. The compromise assessment was deferred until after closing, with price tied to its results. Deliverables were a business-language report covering scope, limits, strengths and quantified risk, plus a 30/60/90-day action plan and investment estimates.

After signing, day-one steps included engaging security stakeholders, naming a project manager, and installing monitoring agents for visibility. The first month focused on critical gaps, security training for new staff, and working with IT. Later work covered third-party assessments and the compromise assessment, with leftover items moved into the GRC program before formal project closure. The talk closes by urging early involvement in M&A, thorough diligence, transparency about limits, and a standing M&A security program.

talks.title: Agents of Chaos: Hacktivism Spreads Fear, Disinformation, and Propaganda
talks.teaser: Explains how to judge hacktivist claims for credibility, and when they hide fraud, propaganda or state-backed operations.
talks.summary:
Alexander Leslie, a threat intelligence analyst, argues that hacktivist chatter is mostly noise and that its claims are often false, misleading or exaggerated. He says the category now overlaps with financially motivated cybercrime, influence operations and state espionage. Drawing on George Lucas's three motivations (transparency, whistleblowing and vandalism), he suggests most hacktivists are vandals with personal or financial aims.

The case studies cover Ukraine and Israel and Palestine. Anonymous now works mainly as a brand that amplifies criminal affiliates. Network Battalion 65 claimed fewer than five attacks yet caused a two-week outage at a Russian broadcaster using a leaked ransomware builder, while the roughly 1,000 DDoS claims made by Killnet and allied groups showed little to no impact in 97% of cases. Groups such as FreeCivilian and CyberAv3ngers are tied to state intelligence services that use personas for plausible deniability. Cyber Toufan released databases over a fixed 30-day window before retiring, a pattern the speaker found suspicious. A database tied to a Palestinian public health institute was offered for $700 and then leaked for forum credits within about 48 hours.

The practical advice is to verify claims through third parties before acting, and to judge groups by impact and tempo rather than follower counts or claim volume. Attacks on critical infrastructure deserve more attention than routine DDoS posts. Without situational awareness and education, organizations may make hasty strategic decisions based on unverified posts.

talks.title: DPAPI and DPAPI-NG: Decrypting All Users’ Secrets and PFX Passwords
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in DPAPI and DPAPI-NG: Decrypting All Users’ Secrets and PFX Passwords.

talks.title: All You Need Is Guest
talks.teaser: Explores how Entra ID guest access enables Teams phishing, tenant enumeration, and Power Platform connection abuse.
talks.summary:
Entra ID guest invitations exist so vendors and partners can collaborate inside Microsoft 365 while conditional access and MFA still apply. In practice, ordinary users can add external addresses with a few clicks, so threat models should treat guest accounts as a realistic initial-access path.

The speaker contrasts the deny-by-default story with live abuse paths. External Teams messaging and tools such as TeamPhisher extend phishing and MFA social engineering into chat, sometimes with attachments APTs already use. Guests are not meant to map the directory, yet enumeration tooling can walk group memberships recursively. The core issue is Power Platform connections: business-built apps store credentials in API hub, often shared with the whole org or personal mail. Trial licenses from a home tenant can satisfy app licensing prompts; platform DLP blocks some apps and flows but not direct connection API calls. Abusing those calls needs an API hub token, which researchers obtain by chaining public clients through undocumented family-of-client-ID refresh-token behavior between Azure CLI and Power Apps. Connection use leaves little logging.

Microsoft’s late-2023 change blocks new connections that violate DLP but leaves existing ones usable when policies tighten. The powerpwn tool automates discovery and dumps backend data, including arbitrary SQL via generated Swagger. Practitioners are urged to tighten who may invite guests, enable Power Platform auditing where possible, run powerpwn in their own tenant for evidence, and apply application-security guardrails and OWASP low-code guidance to citizen-built apps.

talks.title: AI: Law, Policy, and Common Sense Suggestions to Stay Out of Trouble
talks.teaser: Surveys the legal risks, emerging AI regulations and governance steps organizations should take when adopting AI tools.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking what counts as AI, noting that courts and regulators still struggle to pin down a definition broad enough to cover it. The speaker argues that AI is better regulated as a set of techniques than as a single category like railroads, and raises the open question of whether AI should be judged by its outcomes or by its process. Risks are then walked through: confidential prompts that may be exposed, lawyers filing court briefs with case citations that did not exist, deliberate fake media, and biased models. One hiring example involved a model that ranked college lacrosse players named Jared as top predictors of success, reflecting a skewed workforce, and the model was dropped.

The talk then compares the legal landscape. Copyright and patent law currently require a human author or inventor, which makes ownership of AI-generated output unclear. In the United States there are state laws, such as New York City's requirement for bias audits of automated employment tools, but no federal AI statute, with federal guidance coming from the FTC and NIST's risk management framework. The EU AI Act sorts systems into prohibited, high-risk and lightly regulated tiers, with penalties of up to 7% of global annual revenue.

For practitioners, the advice is to build a cross-disciplinary governance team, write an AI responsible use policy even if no one plans to use AI, and update security, privacy and vendor-risk policies. Contracts should be checked for data use rights, liability and indemnification, and new tools should be piloted and tested before rollout. Organizations should also decide deliberately which uses need human authorship to protect ownership.

talks.title: The End of DevSecOps?
talks.teaser: Explains how a centralized SBOM inventory and generative AI can help engineers find and fix vulnerabilities faster.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from Yahoo's Paranoids security team, argues that DevSecOps is not ending but needs to change. He traces the history from siloed development, testing and operations through DevOps and the DevSecOps manifesto, and says security tools have often been bolted on as separate scanners that send findings to teams without enough context. The core theme is enriching security data so engineers can remediate issues sooner.

The middle of the talk covers a centralized software bill of materials inventory that spans code, containers, vendor software, developer endpoints and LLMs. Container images are scanned with the open-source tools Syft and Grype, and findings are mapped to image layers so the responsible team receives the ticket directly. The speaker contrasts the Heartbleed response, which relied on spreadsheets sent to team leads, with the XZ backdoor, where a database query identified affected systems in seconds. He also presents Bomber, his tool that scans SBOMs for application ecosystems and transitive dependencies using OSV and OSS Index, and describes combining EPSS scores with a decision tree for risk-based prioritization.

For the final part, he shows how generative AI can rewrite CVE details in plain language for analysts and product owners, and how the STRIDE-GPT application can generate threat models from ticket content. He cautions that AI output must be checked for accuracy. His takeaways are to start collecting SBOMs, map where vulnerabilities enter the lifecycle and where manual work happens, and shorten feedback loops between security teams and engineers.

talks.title: Detecting Website Intrusion and Account Compromise with Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Detecting Website Intrusion and Account Compromise with Machine Learning.

talks.title: Key Management 101: DEKs, KEKs, and Credentials Living Together, Oh My!
talks.teaser: Explains cryptographic key types, storage options and management decisions, from key wrapping to cloud and enterprise key managers.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a simplified view of how encryption depends on keys, separating symmetric from asymmetric keys and walking through the main key types: data encryption keys, key encryption keys that wrap them, master keys, identity credentials, signing keys and keyed hashes. The speaker argues that protecting data requires controls on the keys themselves, and that decryption keys deserve as much attention as encryption keys, since losing them makes the data unusable.

The middle section covers where keys live and how they are protected. Local key stores depend on the operating system and on whether a TPM or HSM backs them, while remote key stores and key managers can enforce policy in a way plain storage cannot. The speaker explains key wrapping and field-level encryption, which keeps sensitive values encrypted from input through the database, and compares cloud platform-managed keys, customer-managed keys, bring-your-own-key, and third-party enterprise key managers. Cost, rotation, key export and the difficulty of moving hardware-bound keys are presented as decision factors.

The closing portion looks ahead to post-quantum migration, comparing hybrid and composite approaches and the value of crypto agility. The speaker urges organizations to inventory where keys and passphrases are kept, including unmanaged keys created by developers. The main takeaway is to keep encryption, secrets and signing keys separate and to choose key management based on risk, compliance and integration needs.

talks.title: My Resilient Career: How to Do More than Just Survive in Security
talks.teaser: Two practitioners explore burnout, layoffs, and practical habits that help security professionals stay resilient through industry churn.
talks.summary:
Helen Patton and Lokesh frame the session around a July layoff cycle at their employer: Helen was eliminated while half of Lokesh’s team was cut, and they contrast personal anger and career doubt with survivor guilt and disengagement among those who remained.

They argue cybersecurity amplifies burnout through constant translation for non-practitioners, a “not today” time bias until incidents land on defenders, unbounded scope, and a mindset that chases worst cases—compounded by reorgs, acquisitions, tool churn, and layoffs. The middle of the talk maps emotional responses for both paths and emphasizes authentic leadership when teams need listening more than answers.

The closing half turns to resilience mechanics: articulate why you chose security, identify anchors, limit blast radius with finances and skills maintenance, invest in networking inside or outside the company, diversify across industries or roles, and do pre-disaster planning—updated résumés, intentional communities, and a personal board of advisors—for the next three to six months.

talks.title: How AI Is Changing the Malware Landscape
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of How AI Is Changing the Malware Landscape.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Vicente Diaz from VirusTotal presents findings from a year-long study using Large Language Models (LLMs) for malware analysis. Working with VirusTotal's database of approximately 50 billion samples, the team implemented Code Insight—an LLM-based tool to analyze suspicious scripts and binaries—and discovered both unexpected strengths and significant limitations. The talk emphasizes practical findings over speculation, addressing whether AI is meaningfully changing the malware landscape.

## Key Findings on LLM Capabilities

**Exploit Detection**: LLMs identified exploits in 100% of a test sample set, yet only 31% were detected by traditional antivirus engines. Key reasons include: exploits often referenced in variable names and comments within code, many attackers reuse public proof-of-concepts from GitHub, and antivirus engines lack incentive to flag certain behaviors (e.g., PHP scripts performing external actions on endpoints).

**Obfuscation Handling**: LLMs successfully deobfuscate code through runtime analysis in ways traditional tools cannot. Traditional detection methods show only 5% agreement with LLM identification of obfuscation.

**File Type Identification**: LLMs can identify unusual or obscure file formats by analyzing content rather than magic bytes—e.g., correctly identifying LAMMPS molecular simulation input scripts.

**Comparison with Antivirus**: Agreement rates vary by file type: Microsoft Office macros (98%), PowerShell (96%), but only 72.4% for PHP files due to differences in detection incentives and available analysis engines.

## Technical Details and Limitations

LLMs provide non-binary explanations rather than simple yes/no verdicts, helping analysts evaluate gray-area samples (installers vs. droppers). However, they face significant challenges:

- **Prompt sensitivity**: Different prompting and temperature settings yield varying results
- **False positives from code content**: Variable names or comments can mislead analysis (example: a variable named "puppies" caused an LLM to soften its assessment despite detecting malicious behavior)
- **Inconsistency between models**: Different LLMs produce slightly different answers for the same code
- **Inability to confirm AI generation**: No reliable method exists to distinguish AI-generated from human-written code

## AI-Generated Malware Findings

The team found Cobalt Strike and Meterpreter Beacon samples with artifacts suggesting LLM generation but detected no meaningful code differences from non-AI-generated equivalents. One notable example involved a ransomware script generated from a complex prompt that attempted to combine Windows and Linux operations because the LLM synthesized capabilities from both platforms to satisfy contradictory requirements. Overall, no significant new malware families or detection-evading patterns attributed to AI generation were identified.

## Observed Attack Attempts

**Prompt injection attacks**: Simple attempts (e.g., "ignore everything") were observed but remain easy to detect and control.

**Malware impersonation**: Peak in samples impersonating AI-related software and services (fake ChatGPT clients), though without significant overall impact.

**OpenAI interaction**: Unexplained peaks in malware interacting with OpenAI APIs, with no clear threat justification identified.

## Implications for the Malware Landscape

**Is AI lowering the bar?** The existing barrier to malware creation is already low. AI primarily accelerates development and enables greater agility in script creation, but does not appear necessary for technical sophistication. Greatest potential impact is in social engineering, distribution, and deep fake-enabled CEO fraud.

**Is AI changing malware?** No significant malware family transformations or patterns suggesting AI-driven evolution were detected. The fundamental challenge is that if AI-generated malware is sophisticated enough to evade detection, it would be invisible to current analysis methods—creating an unknown risk.

**Detection and monitoring implications**: LLMs provide valuable complementary analysis, moving beyond binary verdicts to offer explanations that analysts can contextualize using their own criteria. They serve as a "second opinion" signal alongside traditional detection methods.

## Takeaways

1. LLMs are useful tools for malware analysis despite limitations, particularly for exploit detection and obfuscation handling
2. Explanatory capability is the primary advantage—providing context antiviruses do not
3. The main barrier to AI-generated malware detection is indistinguishability from human code
4. Social engineering and malware distribution are the most immediate threats from AI advancement
5. Continued experimentation and knowledge-sharing across the security community is critical
6. Future expansion to binary decompilation analysis will likely reveal new capabilities

Diaz concludes that the field is in its infancy and encourages all security professionals to experiment with LLM-based analysis to discover unexpected applications and collectively improve detection and hunting capabilities.

talks.title: Public Key Cryptography
talks.teaser: Explains attribute-hiding predicate encryption, then a computational security analysis of the EDHOC IoT key exchange.
talks.summary:
The first talk, given by Olivier Blazy, introduces predicate encryption, where decryption succeeds only when a relation between the ciphertext's attribute and a user's key is satisfied. It focuses on zero and non-zero inner product encryption, and on identity-based multi-recipient encryption, which supports broadcast to a set of identities or to everyone outside a set. The speaker explains that generic transformations from inner product encryption do not preserve function privacy, and that no known non-zero inner product scheme in the standard model achieved full attribute hiding.

The proposed approach first builds a predicate-only zero inner product scheme in a group setting, shown to be fully attribute-hiding and function-private under a new assumption and also secure in the generic group model. A compiler then turns it into a non-zero inner product scheme that keeps these properties. The same route yields a first efficient identity-based revocation system. The trade-off is larger ciphertexts and a loss linear in the message length, so the construction is described as academically rather than practically efficient.

The second talk, by Loic Ferreira from Orange, presents a computational security analysis of the full EDHOC authenticated key exchange designed for constrained IoT devices. The speaker motivates it with the memory, computation and energy limits of such devices, then describes the four EDHOC authentication methods built on the SIGMA design. The analysis uses a strong security model covering entity authentication, key indistinguishability, forward secrecy and identity privacy, and derives concrete bounds from standard assumptions. The estimates favour the cipher suite based on AS-256 for high-security deployments, and the talk closes by pointing to post-quantum EDHOC as an open research direction.

talks.title: A New Era of Fraud: What Role Can Cyber Play?
talks.teaser: Explains how retail fraud rings operate and how cyber teams can detect refund abuse, skimmers, and gift card tampering.
talks.summary:
Two speakers from Target argue that organized retail crime is a business-like, cross-channel problem rather than simple shoplifting. They walk through a hypothetical in which a phone scam produces a gift card, which is loaded into an aged account bought from a service, used for an in-store purchase, and then refunded through a separate refund service. These groups sell tools and mentorship openly online, so the line between physical and digital activity blurs for attackers.

The middle of the talk covers cases where cyber defense was applied. Threat intelligence built from public social media posts exposed order numbers and buyer patterns that could be traced to accounts. Refund abuse falls into advanced refunds at carrier scan, guest-can-keep and did-not-receive claims, and a risk engine placed in guest flows blocks bad refunds while keeping the experience smooth. Skimmers have returned as custom overlays with Bluetooth and encrypted data, countered by the open-source Merry Maker tool for e-commerce scripts and EasySweep for physical overlays. Gift card tampering is tracked through balance checks and activation timing. A self-ringing case, where shoulder-surfed cashier credentials were used to load gift cards, was addressed with a handheld authentication tool. Bot attacks are handled by unifying DDoS, account takeover and reseller teams across the full lifecycle.

The closing message is that practitioners should view fraud through the adversary's whole chain, disrupt cash-out as well as initial access, bring cyber skills into retail fraud work, and share information with peers and law enforcement as the industry already does for ransomware.
