talks.title: Hiding in Plain Sight: Hunting Volt Typhoon Cyber Actors
talks.teaser: Panelists from FBI, NSA, CISA and Microsoft explain how they tracked Volt Typhoon's living-off-the-land intrusions.
talks.summary:
Officials from the FBI, NSA and CISA joined Microsoft threat intelligence to describe how they identified Volt Typhoon, a China-linked actor pre-positioning inside US critical infrastructure networks. Microsoft researchers first flagged the activity in mid-2021, and NSA tied it to edge-device exploitation around the Pulse Secure events. The panel explained that the actor leans on native Windows tools, residential proxy networks and little custom malware, so indicators of compromise often miss it.

The discussion then turned to a response on Guam, where CISA and an FBI Cyber Action Team found intrusions assessed as highly likely to be Volt Typhoon. Investigators traced the actor's use of Fast Reverse Proxy, Mimikatz and a remote execution tool, and saw movement across networks that were meant to be segmented. Later, the FBI removed the KV-Botnet from end-of-life small business and home routers, and public advisories, including a May 2023 hunt guide, shared findings with industry.

For defenders, the panel stressed keeping logs long enough to catch activity that recurs every few months, monitoring ingress and egress, centralizing logs and auditing edge devices. They urged replacing end-of-life routers, deciding in advance who responds when a government agency calls, and rehearsing manual operation during an outage. The speakers expect the campaign to last for years and warned that AI could make stolen data quick to search.

talks.title: How to Keep Your Cool and Write Powerful Incident Response Reports
talks.teaser: Shows responders how to write incident reports that inform readers, explain root causes and turn lessons into action.
talks.summary:
A famous film character who stays composed under pressure inspires this talk on writing incident response reports. Reports should inform colleagues or clients, address concerns about risk, show that the right steps were taken, and point to improvements. The core advice is to write for the reader: decide what they need, keep the details that support the main message, and cut the rest.

Covering the incident itself, the report should give the time and time zone, the affected business processes as well as systems, and why they matter, stating plainly when significance is still unknown. For root cause, it should name the specific weakness, explain the evidence and how certain the team is, and mention links to earlier incidents. Response steps can follow identification, containment, eradication and recovery. Good writing rests on five elements: information, tone, word choice, structure and look. Examples include describing a missed patch as a situation rather than blaming a team, avoiding passive voice that hides who acted, matching jargon to the reader, trimming wordy sentences, leading with the bottom line, and writing headings that carry a takeaway.

For lessons learned, the speaker recommends a table with each action, its owner and a start date, so changes get tracked. Raw data belongs in appendices. The takeaway: an accurate report must also be concise, well organized and written in a tone that keeps colleagues cooperative.

talks.title: Beginner’s Guide to Bypassing Modern Authentication Methods to SSO
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen SSO session tokens can bypass FIDO-protected sign-ins, and how token binding could help.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that hardware-backed sign-in, such as FIDO2 security keys and WebAuthn, is much stronger than passwords. The speaker argues that this protection covers only the login itself. FIDO2 binds the sign-in to the domain origin and uses public key signatures to resist phishing and replay, but the session cookie or token issued afterwards is a bearer credential that applications rarely check against the device, browser or location.

The speaker demonstrates this on a simple demo site. A session cookie captured from a decrypted TLS session was reused in another browser, which gave access to the account, and the victim's security key was then removed. A second case targets single sign-on. Because the security key only protects the identity provider's federation endpoint, an attacker who captures a session token or refresh token from the relying application can replay it. In an Azure management portal example, the refresh token was used from a different browser and the session continued without any validation of the browser or location.

As a mitigation, the talk presents token binding, which ties a session to the TLS connection using a key pair held by the device. It notes that browser support is limited and that SSL inspection products may break. Microsoft's token protection preview is mentioned as a partial step. The practical advice is not to rely on phishing-resistant sign-in alone: validate sessions, monitor authentication traffic for anomalies, and prefer direct authentication for sensitive applications.

talks.title: The Art of Cyber Insurance: What's New in Coverage and Claims
talks.teaser: Surveys cyber insurance coverages, exclusions, claims trends and underwriting expectations from insurers and breach counsel.
talks.summary:
The panel opened with the state of the cyber insurance market, which has no standard policy wording, so coverage varies between carriers. First-party coverage pays a policyholder's own costs, such as forensics, notification, crisis communications, business interruption and wire-fraud reimbursement, while third-party coverage pays for defense, settlements and judgments. Common endorsements include system failure, voluntary notification, betterment and contingent business interruption, which responds to an outage at a vendor.

Speakers then covered common exclusions and disputed areas. Criminal conduct, war-related losses and biometric privacy violations are increasingly excluded, and insurers that scan externally may deny claims over critical vulnerabilities left unpatched. Web tracking and pixel litigation was presented as a pre-breach risk that arises when marketing and legal do not coordinate. AI was described as both a threat vector and an underwriting challenge. On ransomware, payments are falling but claim costs are not, and some jurisdictions now bar public entities from paying.

For claims, business email compromise and fraudulent wire transfers make up most of the volume. Practical advice included engaging breach counsel before running forensics so that the investigation can be kept privileged, testing backups, classifying and encrypting data, and treating insurance as one part of a risk-transfer plan that must match the organization's security policy. Because premiums follow claims trends, underwriters increasingly expect controls such as MFA and EDR.

talks.title: Building AI Security In: MLSecOps in Practice
talks.teaser: Maps DevSecOps practices onto the machine learning lifecycle, focusing on supply chain risk, model scanning and AI bills of materials.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI and machine learning systems should be treated as ordinary software and secured with the same discipline teams already apply to applications, rather than approached as something mysterious. The speaker separates perceived threats, such as robot takeovers, from more immediate concerns: risky components pulled from public model repositories, a vulnerability in MLflow, a pipeline management tool, and secrets left in Jupyter notebooks.

A walkthrough of an example attack chain starts with phished credentials, followed by an inventory of the organization's systems. The attacker then uses a local file inclusion flaw in MLflow to reach SSH keys and, from there, the models themselves, where subtle tampering could go unnoticed for a long time. The talk also covers privacy leakage from trained models, where training data can be extracted, and bias in training data. It then maps the ML lifecycle of data preparation, training, deployment and monitoring onto the DevSecOps phases, adding threat modeling, model scanning, model signing and drift monitoring at each stage.

For practitioners, the speaker recommends starting with an AI bill of materials, expected to align with CycloneDX and SPDX, and using the NIST AI Risk Management Framework's map, measure, manage and govern functions as a process layer. Other advice includes working closely with ML engineers, training threat modelers and red teams on AI failure modes, keeping training data clean, and choosing vendor-neutral tooling that can detect machine learning software in the environment.

talks.title: Advancing AI Security with Insights from the World’s Largest AI Red Team
talks.teaser: Maps gen-AI prompt attacks from the Gandalf red-team platform and the dynamic defenses enterprises need as agents scale.
talks.summary:
The session frames an emerging “internet of agents,” where multimodal models with broad action spaces connect to sensitive enterprise data and expand cyber risk beyond classic application threats. Adoption is portrayed as abrupt rather than gradual, with securing generative applications described as the main barrier to rollout at scale.

The centerpiece is Gandalf, a public prompt-extraction game built to withhold embedded secrets across escalating levels. Live demos and aggregate statistics—from over a million players and tens of millions of interactions—illustrate how attackers move from direct requests to obfuscation, hinted or sequenced leakage, role-play jailbreaks, and non-English prompts that slip past naive filters. Lakera distills these patterns into a prompt-attack taxonomy with roughly fifteen categories and stresses that quiet model updates can suddenly reopen holes.

Practitioners are urged to treat AI security as continuously evolving, not a one-time control set, and to pair broad red-team exposure with defenses that match varied human-language inputs. The talk closes by inviting conference participants into a special Gandalf challenge while arguing that chatbot findings transfer to more autonomous agents that execute without a human in the loop.

talks.title: Cybersecurity’s Next Legal and Policy Frontier: Software Liability
talks.teaser: A panel explores how U.S. policy could use software liability to align incentives for more secure development practices.
talks.summary:
The session opens on the March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy, where the White House framed software liability as a lever to shift costs from users to developers and reward long-term investment in resilience. Panelists describe today’s nearly universal license terms—limitation of liability and “as is” disclaimers—that largely block suits, and they outline implementation steps since July 2023: legal homework, expert symposiums, and outreach to manufacturers before broader stakeholder engagement and possible congressional action.

Debate centers on four design problems: whether liability should flow through contracts, negligence, products liability, or regulation; how to define reasonably secure software; what safe harbors industry needs; and how open source fits. Jonathan Cedarbaum summarizes advocacy for a products-liability model focused on defects in the shipped product, with reasonableness limits rather than perfection. Jim Dempsey urges outcome-based rules tied to recurring flaws on CISA’s routinely exploited lists, while Bruce Schneider argues the core issue is market failure, separating decades-old “easy” bugs from novel hard problems and noting litigation, settlement dynamics, and insurance as practical forces.

For open source, liability would fall on large integrators—not individual contributors—mirroring automotive supply chains. Audience questions probe in-house software, insurance mandates, third-party harm from insecure devices, and tiered expectations for critical infrastructure versus consumer tooling. The close stresses that improving baseline security is fundamentally about incentives, with legal regimes as one proven way other industries learned safer defaults.

talks.title: The Art of Threat-Informed Sharing: Real-life Use Cases from NSA
talks.teaser: Officials explain how threat intelligence moves from government analysts to industry defenders through trusted, day-to-day collaboration.
talks.summary:
The session frames how the National Security Agency rebuilt its cybersecurity mission around getting nation-state insights to people who can act on them, standing up the Cybersecurity Collaboration Center alongside the cybersecurity directorate in 2019. The speakers describe scale that did not exist four years earlier: hundreds of collaboration channels, roughly a thousand partner organizations, and tens of thousands of analytic exchanges in a single year, guided by agility in tailoring data, creativity in using commercial platforms under government constraints, and trust that protects partner identities.

Josh Zaritsky walks through operational vignettes rather than abstract policy. One case involved non-public vulnerabilities in programmable logic controllers used in critical infrastructure and manufacturing; over months, government, vendor, and OT security partners aligned patching with network detection content so mitigations shipped when disclosures went public. Another traced PRC activity against a defense industrial base edge device, Citrix ADC exploitation including an in-memory backdoor artifact persisted on disk, intermediary sharing with Citrix without naming the victim company, expanded findings across other DIB firms, and coordinated public guidance when patches appeared in December 2022.

The talk closes with services aimed at smaller DIB members—protective DNS with weekly block lists and tens of millions of blocks attributed to custom indicators, attack surface management that prioritizes patches nation-state actors actually use, and cyber threat intelligence feeds tied to campaigns such as Volt Typhoon. Lessons for practitioners emphasize agreeing on outcomes first, pairing automation with analyst-to-analyst conversation, and leaning forward when one organization’s incident may affect peers.

talks.title: Redefining Threat Modeling: Security Team Goes on Vacation
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Redefining Threat Modeling: Security Team Goes on Vacation.

talks.title: Bye-Bye DIY: Frictionless Security Operations with Google
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Bye-Bye DIY: Frictionless Security Operations with Google.

talks.title: Life after the Breach: A Survivor's Guide
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn breach survival tactics: peer outreach, patching basics, executive tabletops, privileged counsel, and crisis messaging.
talks.summary:
Senior practitioners who lived through Equifax, Target, Mandiant, and high-profile government incidents discuss how organizations should prepare for and survive breaches. Early guidance centers on leaning on the security community, returning to patching and asset inventory when scanners fail, and keeping internal employees as informed as external audiences. Legal and business alignment matters before an event: risk exceptions, data on legacy systems, and SOC visibility choices should be documented so post-incident reviewers see conscious decisions rather than surprises.

The middle of the session treats communications as decisive—war games and tabletops with executives, finance, and counsel; pre-written statements for uncertain outcomes; partnerships with corporate communications; privilege when engaging responders; and planning for disinformation, extortion, and overloaded call centers. Panelists describe real twists such as simultaneous hurricanes, leadership attrition during SEC scrutiny, market impacts, and the need for backup responders who already know executives.

Afterward, remediation can last years: eroded trust, heavier audits, PCI fallout, and a chance to invalidate stale risk acceptances. Closing advice includes two- to three-hour executive tabletops with business and disclosure questions, adversary-driven scenario branches, exercises run without the CISO, appendix language for “we don’t know yet,” and depth on the bench below senior leaders.

talks.title: I Screwed Up Threat Hunting a Decade Ago and Now We're Fixing it With PEAK
talks.teaser: Explains four shortcomings in an earlier threat hunting model and introduces the PEAK framework's hunt types, structure and metrics.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a threat hunting model published around 2015 by a small security startup, Sqrrl, and walks through four things its author now considers mistakes. The speaker, who led that model and later ran a threat hunting team at a large retailer, presents PEAK, a free, vendor-agnostic framework from Splunk's research team, as the revision.

The first correction is that hypothesis-driven hunting is only one kind of hunt. PEAK adds baseline hunting, which documents what normal looks like in unfamiliar data or after a merger, and model-assisted hunting, which uses machine learning to do analysis when the hunter knows the goal but not the technique. The second correction is structure: hunts follow prepare, execute and act phases, so preparation and communication of results are planned rather than squeezed in. The framework also gives step-by-step process diagrams for each hunt type.

The third and most important correction concerns purpose. Hunting is not mainly for finding incidents that detections missed, since machines do that better. It is for driving continuous improvement across the security program, by turning new findings into detections and by reporting visibility, tooling and process gaps so others can close them. Suggested metrics count detections created or improved, incidents that later detections surface, gaps reported and closed, and techniques hunted mapped to models such as the kill chain or the pyramid of pain. Teams can adopt PEAK piece by piece, starting with baseline hunts, and the speaker pointed listeners to a free ebook and a community channel.

talks.title: Geopolitics and Cyber Risk in 2024 and Beyond
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh how Russia, China and Iran use cyber operations, and what that means for critical infrastructure and elections.
talks.summary:
A moderated panel with Bilyana Lilly and Lior Div examines how China, Russia and Iran use cyber operations as tools of foreign policy, and how much US organizations should expect over the next year. Lilly frames Russian cyber activity as part of information warfare, aimed both at damaging digital infrastructure and at shaping an adversary's decisions. She argues that large attacks on US infrastructure have been restrained by Russia's focus on Ukraine, the departure of many skilled technologists after 2022, and the loss of Western technology its tools depend on.

Div traces a drop in Russia-linked ransomware activity just before the invasion of Ukraine, later tied to state operations, and points to a recent Microsoft compromise as a sign of renewed Russian capability. He says China collects more espionage data than it can process, a gap he believes generative AI is helping close. Lilly describes Iran's use of affiliated groups and its direct attack on Israel as a possible shift in approach. Both warn that deepfakes and influence operations could target the 2024 US elections, and Lilly raises concern about poorly secured dams and water systems, citing a January incident at a Texas water facility.

The panel agrees that cyber activity often sends a message before or alongside kinetic action, and that criminal groups may become more capable with AI. Audience questions covered ransom payment tracing, response options and supply chain risk. The takeaway is that responses can target an adversary's political pressure points rather than mirror cyber attacks, and that organizations need to understand the wider geopolitical picture.

talks.title: Security Challenges in Direct Threat Environments
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Security Challenges in Direct Threat Environments.

talks.title: Navigating the AI Frontier: The Role of the CISO in GenAI Governance
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Navigating the AI Frontier: The Role of the CISO in GenAI Governance.

talks.title: How Large Language Models Are Reshaping the Cybersecurity Landscape
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in How Large Language Models Are Reshaping the Cybersecurity Landscape.

talks.title: Permissions: Centralized or Decentralized? Both!
talks.teaser: Maps centralized, local, and distributed authorization layers plus seven steps for visibility, audit, and governance at scale.
talks.summary:
Breaches often trace to authorization failures, not just stolen credentials. The speakers argue that authentication has matured faster than authorization, which still clings to application logic in heterogeneous brownfield environments. They frame three complementary models: policies administered and evaluated centrally (like validating a pilot license from a central service), policies authored and stored entirely in one application (household rules), and policies written centrally but cached and evaluated locally (device firmware that enforces safety at the edge).

Their seven-step program starts with visibility—users, groups, join-move-leave risk, workload identities they say are often unused and overprivileged, org ownership of policy decisions, and inventory of multiple legacy authorization systems. Sarah outlines when to centralize (control, consistency, compliance, analysis, sensitivity, privacy), when to decentralize for latency or offline edge cases, and when to distribute and cache typical RBAC-style rules. Pieter follows with audit logs as the control feedback loop, governance through distributed access reviews, monitoring denies and policy decision point failures, disciplined break-glass with reconciliation, and pragmatic brownfield options such as meshes or stronger observability rather than wholesale rip-and-replace.

Concrete next steps include listing sensitive capabilities that must pass a central policy choke point, finding permissions embedded in application code, and over a year layering central, application-local, and cached stores so local rules cannot bypass global constraints. Examples use the Cedar policy language; Q&A ties the model to developer adoption, moving beyond group sprawl toward policy-based access control, and using short-lived access plus edge caching so central enforcement does not fail open when disconnected.

talks.title: Protecting Machine Identities: USPTO and Certificate Automation
talks.teaser: Attendees learn how USPTO scaled certificate automation across hybrid multi-cloud after manual PKI drove eight major incidents.
talks.summary:
Modern enterprises often carry far more machine identities than human ones. At the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, roughly ten thousand servers needed certificates under federal zero-trust expectations, while manual issuance—with separation of duties across teams—could consume about ten hours per certificate and helped drive eight major incidents between 2022 and 2023, totaling hundreds of hours of downtime tied to expirations or compromise.

The organization adopted a certificate lifecycle platform with a command center in Azure, lighter footprint components in AWS and GCP, and coverage for on-premises sites. Network discovery closed much of the inventory gap versus the CMDB, while governance—not wiring—dominated the year-long rollout: roles, product-specific policies, exceptions, training, and phased adoption led by high-impact applications. Integrations touched identity tooling, IT service management, and security monitoring; adaptable patterns addressed cases such as SaaS VIPs.

Practitioners hear how shorter validity periods become affordable only with automation, with illustrative cost contrasts between all-manual renewal and automated operation. Near-term plans include broader non-person entity coverage, 90- and 30-day external certificates, per-server certs behind load balancers, and more automated incident response. Q&A covers optional human approval gates, internal versus commercial CAs, budget controls for paid certificates, and where keys and CSRs are generated.

talks.title: Bear Necessities: Ukraine's Experience Facing APTs, Building Resilience
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bear Necessities: Ukraine's Experience Facing APTs, Building Resilience.

talks.title: Leveraging MacOS's Networking Frameworks to Heuristically Detect Malware
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Leveraging MacOS's Networking Frameworks to Heuristically Detect Malware.
talks.summary:
Overview: As the majority of malware contains networking capabilities, it is well understood that detecting unauthorized network access is a powerful detection heuristic. However, while the concepts of network traffic analysis and monitoring to detect malicious code are well established and widely implemented on platforms such as Windows, there remains a dearth of such capabilities on macOS. This talk aims to remedy this situation by delving deeply into a myriad of programmatic approaches capable of enume

Key Topics: rating network state, statistics, and traffic, directly on a macOS host. We will showcase open-source implementations of relatively overlooked low-level APIs, private frameworks, and user-mode extensions that provide insight into all networking activity. And, by leveraging these techniques, you will learn how to efficiently and generically detect both known and unknown threats targeting macOS!

talks.title: Common Good Cyber
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh why internet-supporting nonprofits lack steady funding and which collective fixes could close the gap.
talks.summary:
The panel looked at why many nonprofits that keep the internet running, such as Shadowserver, struggle to find stable funding. The speakers argued that volunteer-run work supports critical infrastructure, yet money from governments often follows shifting priorities and is hard to tie to missions. Each panelist approached the gap from a different seat, including government, corporate security, philanthropy and a nonprofit.

The discussion reviewed a workshop held earlier in the year, which produced four favored directions. These were a pooled funding mechanism that governments, industry and others could contribute to, a shared narrative that explains what these groups achieve, a business case for investment, and a central resource offering fundraising and communications help. One speaker noted that the average communications budget in their consortium is around $250,000 a year, and that a large philanthropic program which had funded this work for a decade has ended.

For practitioners, the message was that each sector has a role. Companies can offer staff expertise and volunteer days alongside money, government can connect nonprofits to its infrastructure and workforce funding, and individuals can ask their employers and local officials what they are doing to protect critical services. Organizers planned a draft roadmap around July 1 and a next workshop in Europe on September 30, and the speakers encouraged attendees to contribute ideas.

talks.title: Shades of Purple: Getting Started and Making Purple Teaming Possible
talks.teaser: Shows how blue and red teams can start collaborating, from low-cost exercises to mature, repeatable purple teaming programs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing purple teaming as red and blue teams working together to test and strengthen an organization's own defenses, instead of treating a penetration test as a contest where one side's success means the other's failure. The speaker builds the approach around three questions: what the crown jewels are, what governs the organization beyond audits (legal duties, business agreements, cyber insurance), and which staff and skills are available. He argues that people outside IT, such as developers, guards and front-desk staff, can act as defenders or testers too.

The middle section walks through purple teaming in practice, ordered from low cost and staff to more advanced programs. Starting points include a gap analysis that asks the blue team about its pain points, tabletop exercises built from real IT tickets, and capture-the-flag events that mix red and blue staff. Further steps cover scanning against benchmarks and the OWASP Top 10, over-the-shoulder pen tests where defenders watch the tester, and later behavior analytics and threat intel alerting. Two semi-fictional scenarios illustrate the process: a new password policy that a tabletop showed could be brute-forced within 120 days, which also exposed a missing MFA requirement on a crown jewel, and an adversary emulation where a tester got a remote shell and the SOC struggled to see one technique because of logging levels.

The closing advice is to scope small, agree on one finding the whole group can act on, and formalize how results are shared with leadership. Purple checks should be built into engineering, change control and golden image updates so the work becomes an ongoing cycle rather than a one-time test. The speaker also stresses buy-in, communication, and avoiding a perfect score, since that can hide real gaps.

talks.title: How Sworn Enemies Found a Truce (Sort of) to Achieve NIST Compliance
talks.teaser: Security and engineering leaders at a startup recount clashing over NIST compliance and the alignment practices that eased it.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a startup's journey toward NIST 800-53 compliance, with a FedRAMP target and CMMC requirements from its customers. The two presenters describe how the security and engineering sides initially misread each other's roles. Early tool purchases, staff departures and control language handed down without explanation caused repeated rework, and a heated chat thread became a turning point.

The middle section covers what helped. The team realized it was largely aligned on its goals but talking past each other, so each side was asked to define terms like security and compliance in its own words. They separated facts, assumptions, opinions and decisions, and had people co-author the documents instead of handing down requirements. They treated compliance requirements like product requirements, set company-wide objectives tied to customer needs, and used a swimming pool analogy to explain why security changes felt like rework to engineers. The presenters also admitted they struggled to celebrate milestones, since compliance work never felt finished.

The takeaways are to write down each role's responsibilities, tailor information to different backgrounds, move DevOps toward DevSecOps, and build one shared team attitude around security. In the question period they discussed vague wording such as periodic, working with auditors on acceptable interpretations of controls, and bringing in shadow IT through executive accountability.

talks.title: Securing AI Apps with the OWASP Top Ten for Large Language Models
talks.teaser: Maps the main security risks of generative AI apps, from prompt injection to overreliance, and practical defenses.
talks.summary:
Two contributors to the OWASP project for large language models walk through the main security risks of building applications on generative AI. They use a hypothetical application as a running example: a front end, a model, logging that might feed future training, and back-end plugins that can reach databases, web services or code execution. The build stage comes first. Off-the-shelf models, downloaded weights and training data form a supply chain, and researchers reported hundreds of malicious models carrying backdoors on a public model hub.

Attack paths come next. Prompt injection is the main entry point, in a direct form where a user rewrites the assistant's role or bypasses its guardrails, and an indirect form where hidden instructions in a document or web page are read by the model. One bug bounty case involved a shared document that made an assistant render an image link carrying the user's chat history to an attacker's server. No robust fix exists, so they recommend layered defenses: strong system prompts, guardrail frameworks, AI firewalls and testing tools. They also argue that model output must be treated as untrusted, citing a library flaw that let generated code run in a Python interpreter.

The talk then covers excessive agency, sensitive information disclosure and overreliance. Models cannot reliably keep secrets, so any data they can reach may be exposed, and excessive agency is framed partly as a product-management problem. Overreliance is shown through a lawyer who filed invented case law and an airline held responsible for its chatbot's wrong refund advice. Takeaways include limiting the model's permissions, requiring human sign-off for irreversible or high-stakes actions, filtering outputs, keeping sensitive data out of prompts, and publishing a generative AI usage policy. The speakers pointed to free OWASP documents and a forthcoming second version.

talks.title: Balancing Employee Sentiment and Metrics for Successful Business Impact
talks.teaser: A panel of tech leaders shares how they measure employee sentiment and tie inclusion to leadership and business results.
talks.summary:
A panel of leaders from Cisco, Arctic Wolf and Google Cloud discusses how inclusion programs, leadership expectations and employee sentiment connect to business results. Each panelist first describes how their company launched its approach: Cisco linked its purpose to securely connecting people, Arctic Wolf let employee groups manage their own budgets, and Google Cloud stressed that senior practitioners should mentor others. The panel also notes that one company added belonging to its performance reviews, so leaders are judged on how they build inclusive teams.

On hybrid work, the panel argues that leaders should decide based on the work and the team rather than a blanket rule. Cisco reported that employees who already worked remotely before the pandemic showed promotion velocity and engagement matching their in-office peers. For measurement, Arctic Wolf runs engagement surveys twice a year with a 70% participation rate, an engagement score of 8.1 and an eNPS in the high 40s. Cisco runs a quarterly program across a subset of employees and applies sentiment analysis to chat and Q&A from monthly company meetings. Google uses a weekly survey of two or three questions to catch emerging issues faster than an annual survey allows.

Audience questions covered mentoring and workforce entry outside the United States, with the panel pointing to early exposure in high school, certification pathways and partnerships with nonprofits. The closing message was that leadership sets the direction, inclusion makes teams stronger, and organizations need to budget for these efforts as candidates increasingly look for missions that match their values.

talks.title: Controlling a Data Footprint - How to Build a Data Disposition Framework
talks.teaser: Walks through building a data disposition framework to map sensitive data, set retention schedules and pick protection controls.
talks.summary:
Toby Zimmer and Jordan present a practical method for building a data disposition framework, the structure that records what data an organization holds, how sensitive it is, how long to keep it and which controls apply. They frame the work as a governance exercise rather than only a compliance one. Retention schedules are usually set with legal and compliance teams, while security or information management teams operationalize them. They stress that legal holds must be respected before anything is purged, and that leadership buy-in and the cost of storing stale data help the effort succeed.

The middle of the session covers identifying data. Single elements such as a name or employee number may not be sensitive alone, but they become identifiable or referenceable when combined into records, so the speakers suggest mapping how elements combine. Their example framework groups business purposes, uses retention bands of under one year, one to three years and over three years, and ties classifications to controls such as encryption, tokenization, masking or anonymization. For unstructured files, they suggest using creation, access and modification dates with discovery tools, and for structured databases they recommend manually correlating column headers across systems.

The closing remarks turn to next steps: identify data owners within two weeks, document business workflows within a couple of months, and automate discovery and disposal within six months, starting with a small scope. The Q&A touched on how much choice to give data owners and on automating retention by moving aged files into a quarantine folder for validation.

talks.title: Ensuring Intelligence, National Security in a Rapidly Changing Technology World
talks.teaser: Surveys China's tech rivalry, election interference, AI deepfakes and cyber workforce gaps as threats to national security.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with Senator Mark Warner reframing national security around technology leadership rather than military strength alone, with China cast as the toughest economic and technology competitor the United States has faced. He points to the chips legislation, his committee's work on energy, critical minerals and biotechnology, and concerns about foreign control of popular platforms such as TikTok.

The middle section turns to information threats. Warner recalls a lengthy bipartisan investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and warns that influence operations are now cheaper to run and easier to scale with generative AI and deepfakes. He says voluntary commitments from AI companies on election-related watermarking have not yet shown enough real progress. He also flags radio frequency attacks, drone swarms, healthcare sector security baselines and unimplemented laws on connected devices, and argues that losing ground in technical standards bodies would be a serious strategic risk.

Audience questions cover the cyber workforce shortage, with Warner urging the country to keep high-skill immigration open and to expand broadband so training reaches more people. On possible Russia and China cooperation in cyberspace against critical infrastructure, he says the concern is justified. The session closes on the need for closer public-private collaboration and coordinated funding to meet these threats.

talks.title: The Always-On Purple Team: An Automated CI/CD for Detection Engineering
talks.teaser: Shows an automated pipeline that runs attack simulations, uses LLMs to draft detection rules, and validates them in a SIEM.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that offensive and defensive teams have long worked in isolation, and that scoped penetration tests and periodic red team exercises leave detection gaps. They present purple teaming as a way to close that gap, using adversary emulation against threat groups relevant to a given industry to check whether a SOC detects and responds to each technique. They also describe running simulations on a schedule so the detection pipeline is continuously verified.

The core demo connects a SOAR platform, the Caldera breach attack simulation tool, and Microsoft Sentinel as the SIEM. The SOAR runs a set of techniques and watches for alerts. When a technique goes undetected, it asks an LLM to draft a KQL detection rule, pushes it to the SIEM, and feeds any query errors back to the model for correction. Rules are checked against 30 days of history, and high hit counts are flagged as likely noisy. In the first run, a built-in Caldera adversary produced detections for only two of seven techniques. A second demo used agents to read an HTML threat intelligence report, extract TTPs, map them to Caldera abilities, build a new adversary profile, and deploy the generated rules without manual steps.

The speakers conclude that automated red teaming is not yet realistic, but LLMs are useful for repetitive work such as extracting techniques, mapping them to tooling, and orchestrating operations. Generated rules are often brittle, so a detection engineer must still tune them, for example by targeting handle access to LSASS rather than a specific tool name. They suggest this kind of workflow can let smaller detection teams get more done.

talks.title: Creating an AI Security and Incident Response Team
talks.teaser: Explains how a CERT team built an AI security incident response function on existing CSIRT practice, and what it has learned.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how the CERT Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon's Software Engineering Institute set up an AI security incident response team, or AISIRT, after attacks on AI systems grew quickly once generative AI tools spread. The team soft-launched in August and formally launched in October. It was modeled on the existing CSIRT framework: of roughly 200 items compared, about 80 percent carried over cleanly, and the rest needs adapting.

The speakers gave examples across the stack. One was a suffix that got large language models from several vendors to produce content they normally refuse. Another was a hardware-level memory isolation weakness that could leak data between processes sharing a processor. A third was unsafe model serialization in frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, which can allow remote code execution. Vulnerability work runs from intake and triage, using SSVC, to replication, which is often hard without the same hardware or data, and then to coordinated disclosure with vendors whose supply chains run deep. Root cause analysis asks whether a failure came from training or data, a normal model error, or a real attack.

For practitioners, the main advice was to augment an existing incident response team with data science and machine learning specialists rather than build a separate group, and to make team chiefs able to explain AI risk to executives. The speakers also said research suggested up to 10 percent of publicly shared models contained malicious code, so teams should know where their models come from. They generally advised against unplugging an AI system right away, and instead using its telemetry to scope the problem first. They noted that forensic tooling for AI is still immature.

talks.title: Smashing the Stack: Let’s Make It Less Fun And Unprofitable!
talks.teaser: Makes the case for memory-safe languages, hardware like CHERI, and published roadmaps to cut recurring memory bugs.
talks.summary:
The session argues that memory safety bugs remain a persistent source of serious software flaws, and that customers are left to cope with them. A short C program shows the problem: a string copy into an eight-character buffer overwrites an adjacent success flag. The speakers cite Microsoft and Chromium data where memory-related bugs make up around 70% of high-severity issues, and Project Zero's exploited-in-the-wild list, where about 67% were memory corruption.

They review approaches already tried, such as fuzzing, control flow integrity and ASLR, and say they have not solved the problem. Rust is presented as a memory-safe option that interoperates with C without a garbage collector, while the CHERI hardware research project aims to make the CPU reject out-of-bounds writes. Android is given as an example of incremental change: rewriting its riskiest C and C++ code in Rust each year cut memory-safety vulnerabilities from 76% to 35% of the total. An AI model's attempted translation of a linked list did not compile, so the speakers warned against trusting such output blindly.

The takeaway is that software companies should publish memory-safe roadmaps with defined phases, a date after which new projects use a safe language, training plans, dependency strategies and regular updates. Customers are urged to ask vendors for these roadmaps and to fill in CWE fields. In the Q&A, open-source dependencies were raised as a hard problem, and formal methods were named as the next step after memory safety.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from the Summer of Supply Chain Attacks
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Lessons Learned from the Summer of Supply Chain Attacks.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At this panel discussion, experts from Google Cloud, Wiley, and Mandiant examine the surge in supply chain compromises and analyze lessons learned from high-profile incidents. The session breaks supply chain attacks into two primary categories: threat actors exploiting vulnerabilities in software or appliances already embedded in digital ecosystems, and true supply chain attacks where implants are injected directly into a product's build process.

### Key Topics
- **Case Studies of Major Attacks:** Analysis of the Barracuda Email Security Gateway compromise, the MOVEit Transfer zero-day exploitation, and the 3CX cascaded software build implant.
- **Shifting Threat Actor Tactics:** The transition from traditional single-extortion ransomware to multifaceted extortion, public victim shaming sites, and aggressive harassment directed at executives, board members, and their family members.
- **Legal, Regulatory, and Contractual Landscape:** Rapidly evolving oversight and mandates from the SEC, DHS (including CISA incident reporting rules / CIRCIA NPRM), TSA, FTC, and NY DFS, alongside the necessity for robust vendor contract terms.
- **Defensive Strategies and Readiness:** The criticality of data governance, data minimization, automated detection, comprehensive tabletop exercises, and out-of-band communication plans.

### Technical Details
- **Barracuda ESG Exploitation:** Threat actors leveraged China-nexus espionage techniques, sending low-quality decoy emails to spam filters alongside malicious emails with attachments to exploit gateway vulnerabilities. Once inside, they deployed three malware families masquerading as legitimate tools, leveraged living-off-the-land techniques, staged large amounts of data in temporary files prior to exfiltration, and hid backdoor malware directly into configuration files to maintain persistence through software/hardware remediation cycles.
- **MOVEit Transfer Exploitation:** Financially motivated actors used a zero-day exploit against open file transfer instances, exfiltrating massive volumes of data affecting over 2,000 victim organizations. Due to the scale, extortion actors resorted to posting on victim shaming sites to solicit ransom payments when direct outreach was filtered by spam.
- **3CX Cascading Supply Chain Attack:** North Korean actors compromised trading software, which an employee installed on a personal laptop. This enabled attackers to pivot into 3CX's desktop application build environment, implant malware into clean software updates, and propagate downstream to 3CX customers—marking an unprecedented cascading supply chain compromise.
- **Detection and Hardening:** Edge devices (VPNs, firewalls, virtual machines) increasingly serve as initial access targets due to limited monitoring compared to mature endpoint tooling. Defenders must monitor configuration file modifications, temp file creation, and access to sensitive files (such as cyber insurance policies), while implementing zero trust, MFA, and strong data deletion policies.

### Takeaways
- **Control What You Can:** Organizations cannot dictate every third-party vendor's internal build pipeline; defense must focus on internal hygiene, rigorous data minimization/deletion, zero trust access controls, and out-of-band crisis comms.
- **Modernize Vendor Contracts:** Establish explicit notification windows, logging requirements, forensic assistance mandates, and reciprocal transparency in supplier agreements before an incident occurs.
- **Plan for Aggressive Extortion and Human Targeting:** Train workforce members against social engineering and scrub executive and employee personal identifiable information (home addresses, phone numbers) from open-source domains to mitigate direct intimidation tactics.

talks.title: Now You’re in Role: The Fearless CISO
talks.teaser: Offers CISO-level guidance on stakeholder alignment, risk appetite, governance and building a security culture from day one.
talks.summary:
The session continues an earlier talk on fearless security leadership and turns to what the CISO role looks like today. The speakers, both current or former security executives, ask the audience about career stage and aspirations, then describe the role as a business leadership position where technical skill alone is not enough. They acknowledge the burnout and personal scrutiny many security leaders now face, and share a story about preparing for a regulatory examination in which a leader had to back an unpopular decision.

The middle section covers priorities for a new cyber program. Stakeholder engagement starts with a listening tour and identifying allies among senior leaders, and disagreements can be moved to a risk committee with decisions documented. A clear RACI helps executives own their choices and shows when to engage the board. A new leader should commission an independent assessment rather than trust inherited material, then define risk appetite and tolerance. Mapping regulatory obligations to a common control framework supports governance, and security culture grows through a shared identity, educational newsletters and campaigns that tell people what to watch for.

The closing advice is to treat the role as a long-term discipline built on self-awareness and a focus on the program rather than personal reward. Candidates should interview the organisation too, checking whether the board and senior management truly support the CISO. Leaders should avoid changing their teams too quickly, expect plans to shift during incidents, and recognise that not every CISO role suits everyone.

talks.title: Regulation on the Horizon: What You Wish Your Lawyer Had Told You About
talks.teaser: A panel maps executive liability, SEC incident filings, and California’s proposed cyber audits for security leaders.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a surge of U.S. cybersecurity rulemaking and enforcement, with personal civil liability as the first theme. Panelists walk through the FTC’s Drizly order: a long-lived GitHub access path, weak authentication, AWS production exposure, and data on 2.5 million consumers, plus a decade-long CEO obligation tied to future CEO roles at firms handling large consumer datasets. They contrast that trend with SEC charges against SolarWinds’ CISO for disclosure and public statements, and note concern across the field about aligning internal honesty with outward messaging.

Attention shifts to SEC rules effective December 2023: material incidents trigger Form 8-K within four days of determination, with nature, timing, scope, and qualitative materiality; optional Attorney General delay is discussed alongside sparse early 8-K practice. Annual 10-K disclosures must describe cyber risk management and how the board and executives oversee it. A California Department of Justice representative describes state breach-notification leadership, enforcement when public claims outrun practice, and draft California Privacy Protection Agency rules that would require annual cybersecurity audits, board-facing auditor independence, and certification for qualifying businesses—with public comment still underway.

Practitioners should treat representations in policies, filings, and marketing as enforcement hooks across FTC, SEC, and state AGs; invest in mature baselines rather than panic per rule; monitor drafts and cases; and use counsel, newsletters, and integrated compliance frameworks to track fragmented U.S. and global obligations.

talks.title: Living in a Material(ity) World
talks.teaser: Walks CISOs through SEC materiality rules, prior disclosure patterns, and live scenarios for judging reportable cyber incidents.
talks.summary:
The session frames materiality as the emerging standard that sits alongside longstanding reasonableness debates, with primary focus on U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission cybersecurity disclosure obligations effective in late 2023. The speakers trace the concept from Sarbanes-Oxley and early SEC guidance through New York Department of Financial Services rules and state breach statutes, then explain triggering events, the four-day Form 8-K window after a materiality determination, and factors such as operational harm, financial loss, third-party effects, reputation, and enforcement risk.

Supreme Court benchmarks on investor-focused importance anchor a review of qualitative versus quantitative judgment. Public filings from major breaches illustrate recurring placeholder language and long-tail annual report carryover. A participatory segment presents anonymized incident vignettes—financial services access, authentication vendor customer data, SaaS misconfiguration, supplier ransomware with quarter-scale revenue hit, CEO wire fraud, and aircraft lessor data theft—so the room debates what must be disclosed.

Practitioners are urged to coordinate CISOs, counsel, CFOs, and auditors; prepare templated statements; run tabletops without over-relying on technologists first; avoid speculation in public filings; and weigh recent Supreme Court guidance on omissions versus half-truths when choosing voluntary disclosure.

talks.title: The Tie That Binds: Unique Cyber Tools in the Payments Industry
talks.teaser: Major payment processors describe peer collaboration on regulation, product security, vendor risk, cloud posture, and responsible AI use.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing card networks and processors as critical payment rails that must authorize transactions in milliseconds while facing constant targeting. Through the American Transaction Processors Coalition Cyber Council, competing firms compare notes on operational security and selective engagement with governments when new reporting categories appear.

Panelists from Fiserv, Deluxe, and Visa walk through harmonizing overlapping compliance obligations, embedding security in product development via shift-left testing and mandatory cyber sign-off before production, and tightening third-party accountability. They require software bills of materials in vendor contracts, stock hardware where needed, inventory SaaS and open source dependencies, and treat hybrid cloud with posture baselines, drift quarantine, and zero-trust extensions comparable to on-premises controls. Discussion also covers open-source governance, liability debates, vendor willingness to share after major supply-chain incidents, and frustrations negotiating transparency with large cloud providers.

The conversation closes on intelligence sharing that includes actionable timeframes, democratized threat data for smaller processors, AI and machine learning already used at scale for fraud, and cautious generative-AI governance with human review, red teaming, and ethics review of training data. A brief audience exchange touches on AI in the software lifecycle and steering committees for sensitive use cases.

talks.title: Everything Old Is New Again: Protecting Legacy Systems with Modern Security
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Everything Old Is New Again: Protecting Legacy Systems with Modern Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this panel discussion, cybersecurity and operational technology (OT) experts explore the realities of securing legacy industrial control systems (ICS). Combining nearly a century of cumulative experience across semiconductor manufacturing, food and agriculture, water and wastewater, and maritime operations, the panel examines why traditional IT security mindsets often fail in physical, plant-floor environments. They discuss practical security strategies, workforce dynamics, economics, and architectural approaches to safeguarding legacy devices without compromising human safety or halting operational production.

### Key Topics
- **IT vs. OT Mindset & Life Safety**: In IT environments, security focuses on data confidentiality and integrity. In OT, priority lies in human life safety, environmental safety, and continuous production uptime. Disruptive IT controls like standard multi-factor authentication (MFA) can impede emergency response or manufacturing workflows.
- **Economic and Accounting Barriers**: Factory managers often resist patching and upgrades due to the direct impact on product margin, yield, and factory output. The panel highlights the necessity of working with accounting guidelines (GAAP) to capitalize security investments and labor rather than absorbing disruptive in-period expenses.
- **Operational Realities & Circumvention**: When security controls slow production or fail to account for the physical environment (such as cleanroom or chemical suits requiring gloves), operators will circumvent or unplug them. Pragmatic adaptations—such as using barcode scanners instead of keyboard passwords—are necessary.
- **Workforce and Knowledge Preservation**: Securing legacy systems requires deep operational context. Decades of institutional knowledge are often held by seasoned operators. Recruiting and cross-training factory technicians into security roles builds credibility and operational alignment.
- **Patching and Vulnerability Management**: Unvetted patching in OT environments can break downstream programmable logic controllers (PLCs) or associated hardware. Rigorous testing and staged rollouts during scheduled maintenance windows are essential.

### Technical Details
- **Architectural Isolation**: Modernizing legacy OT relies heavily on network segmentation, the Purdue model, access control lists (ACLs), and VLANs. In cases where operating systems cannot be replaced (e.g., legacy systems running DOS, Windows 95, NT, or XP), virtualization and strict isolation keep systems functional while limiting exposure.
- **Physical & Boundary Controls**: Before relying on internal software tools, physical protections (e.g., dedicated badge stations and perimeter device-scanning kiosks) prevent uninspected third-party hardware from entering the plant floor.
- **Management Tool Risks**: Introducing visibility and asset-monitoring tools can inadvertently create new attack surfaces. Third-party risks and administrative access on centralized monitoring agents must be strictly governed.
- **Standards and Frameworks**: OT third-party risk assessments must remain separate from IT evaluations. The panel points to standards such as IEC 62443, semiconductor standards SEMI E187 and SEMI E188, and the Purdue model to evaluate segmentation and cybersecurity posture.

### Takeaways
Securing legacy operational systems does not require completely overhauling operational infrastructure or "boiling the ocean." Organizations should prioritize protecting life safety and environmental controls first, followed by business output. Security leaders must engage plant-floor staff, design frictionless controls tailored to physical operations, capitalize labor and security investments through financial planning, and establish robust manual failover and incident response procedures.

talks.title: Unveiling the 2024 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR)
talks.teaser: Surveys the 2024 Verizon DBIR: global breach volume, attack paths, human error, patching lag, and shifting extortion patterns.
talks.summary:
Chris Novak walks through the newly released Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report, now in its seventeenth year. The dataset spans 94 countries and reflects over 30,000 incidents and more than 10,000 confirmed breaches, assembled from Verizon consulting work and roughly one hundred partners including law enforcement, ISACs, and other responders. He distinguishes incidents from breaches and stresses that the report is a cross-sectional view meant to guide prevention and program priorities, not a universal playbook.

Headline metrics include a 180% year-over-year rise in vulnerability exploitation as an initial path, 68% of breaches involving non-malicious human factors, 15% involving third parties with sharp growth, and stolen credentials appearing in 31% of breaches over the past decade. Initial access still clusters around credentials, social engineering, and exploitation; he illustrates partial MFA coverage and lateral movement from “low risk” zones. A survival-probability view contrasts roughly five days for actor exploitation with about half of critical flaws patched at 55 days, arguing for risk-based prioritization over score alone. Ransomware trends down while separate extortion, DDoS-for-ransom, and executive targeting grow; pretexting leads social-engineering methods in business email compromise scenarios. Phishing still arrives mostly by email, with victim actions often completing in under a minute, though self-reporting rates are improving. On generative AI, public buzz far outpaces documented abuse in breach data. He closes by pointing readers to industry slices, the VERIS framework, supply-chain visibility, SEC-oriented risk quantification, and security culture.

Audience questions touch SIM swapping (rare in the aggregate data), how Verizon uses DBIR insights in awareness training, human error beyond phishing (misdelivery, misconfiguration), and industry-specific control prioritization in the full document.

talks.title: Criminal Minds: World’s Most Wanted Cybercriminals Interview Insights
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Criminal Minds: World’s Most Wanted Cybercriminals Interview Insights.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "Criminal Minds: World’s Most Wanted Cybercriminals Interview Insights," threat intelligence researcher Samantha van de Ven presents qualitative criminological research analyzing public-facing media interviews given by cybercriminals over the past decade. While malicious actors traditionally rely on operational security to stay hidden in the underground, van de Ven observed a trend where actors willingly speak to journalists and security researchers. Using the criminological "square of crime" framework—which examines the interactions between law enforcement, adversaries, victims/targets, and the public/media—the research analyzes 57 written interviews across 41 unique actors and 29 media outlets (including nine repeat interviewees) to understand actor motives, recruitment, operations, and psychology.

### Key Topics
- **Criminological Framing & Interview Typologies:** The qualitative data was categorized across 12 specific themes (demography, initiation, persistence, exiting, recruitment, professionalization, setting the record straight, the square of crime, morality/sentiment, TTPs, and security recommendations). Interviews generally fell into four lifecycle stages: post-arrest, post-retirement, post-breach, and brand building.
- **Motivations for Initiation and Persistence:** 22% of analyzed actors explicitly identified as self-taught, leveraging surface-web and dark-web tutorials, blogs, and videos. Initial drivers included economic stressors (layoffs, medical debt), curiosity, and perceived opportunities. Long-term persistence was fueled by variable reward structures akin to gaming or gambling, tangible socioeconomic mobility (transitioning from poverty to wealth), peer influence, and autonomy outside the traditional 9-to-5 economy.
- **Brand Building & Underground Economics:** Threat actors engage with the press primarily for three strategic purposes: shaping the narrative around major public security events ("setting the record straight"), promoting new services/products, and establishing brand legitimacy/trustworthiness. Underground operations mirror legitimate enterprise models through divided labor, specialization, and strict affiliate management.

### Technical Details
- **Targeting Profiles:** Operators prioritize organization size and revenue over industry verticals, choosing targets with higher capacity to pay ransoms and easier internal network navigation. Target valuations leverage stolen data, dark-web credential dumps, and insider recruitment.
- **Reconnaissance & Tooling:** Threat actors frequently deploy port and network scanners such as MASSCAN, Nmap, and RustScan. Actors also track open-source threat intelligence, zero-day research, and offensive red team tools, often customizing or adding proprietary modules to existing red-team frameworks.
- **Actor-Provided Reports:** Ransomware groups frequently provide post-intrusion security recommendations and incident summaries to victims, framing ransoms as consultation fees or corporate fines while subverting blame.

### Takeaways
- **Defensive Posture & Footprint Assessments:** Security teams should mirror attacker reconnaissance by using the same open-source scanners (MASSCAN, Nmap, RustScan) and threat intelligence sources that adversaries monitor to identify exposed assets.
- **Addressing Workforce Stressors:** Underground forums increasingly solicit corporate insiders, AI specialists, and software engineers experiencing layoffs or disenfranchisement; organizations must prioritize fair compensation, supportive workplace cultures, and talent retention to counter insider risks.
- **Actionable Awareness Training:** Security teams should incorporate real-world breach narratives and threat actor perspectives into training rather than relying on fear-based messaging, empowering staff with practical controls like password managers and multi-factor authentication (2FA).

talks.title: A World On Fire: Playing Defense in a Digitized World...and Winning
talks.teaser: A moderated panel weighs geopolitical cyber threats, secure-by-design policy, open-source risk and AI's effect on defense.
talks.summary:
Moderated by Joseph Menn of the Washington Post, this panel features CISA director Jen Easterly and her predecessor Chris Krebs discussing how geopolitical conflict now shapes business and government cyber risk. Easterly describes the scale of ransomware and China-linked actors such as Volt Typhoon, which she says are positioning inside critical infrastructure for disruptive attacks rather than espionage. Both blame much of the exposure on known flaws in technology built for speed and features.

The middle of the session covers secure by design. Easterly points to a voluntary pledge that more than sixty technology companies were expected to sign, backed by federal procurement rules and a software attestation form signed by executives. Krebs lists four levers for change: voluntary initiatives, civil litigation, regulation and legislation, and notes that European laws such as GDPR and the Cyber Resilience Act spread compliance standards worldwide. Open source gets attention too, with package manager guidance and an open-source security roadmap, and the XZ Utils backdoor is cited as a warning.

On AI, Krebs argues defenders are currently ahead, helped by private-sector tools for threat hunting and investigation, while attackers mostly use AI for social engineering and research. Easterly expects AI to amplify election threats such as spearphishing and disinformation without fundamentally changing them, pointing to secure elections in 2018, 2020 and 2022. The overall message is that progress is real but slow.

talks.title: Leading with Integrity and Resilience: Navigating Values and Adversity
talks.teaser: Offers practical guidance on authenticity, empathetic communication, and mindset when security leaders face misaligned corporate values.
talks.summary:
Lisa Plaggemier opens with her path from automotive marketing into security after a corporate spin-off, describing a C-suite culture of undocumented risk appetite and plausible deniability. She recounts how a values-driven chief security officer eventually left, how a replacement was a poor fit, and how an executive coach’s warning about misaligned values led her to file an ethics hotline complaint and resign. She frames the session around lessons from Jason Weiss’s executive coaching work with Cisco enterprise customers.

Jason Weiss structures the conversation around authenticity, communication, and mindset. He uses the 1968 Bob Beamon long jump as a metaphor for defining personal success metrics rather than chasing organizational scorecards. He recommends asking about thirty trusted contacts five reflective questions to surface strengths tied to principles, argues ethics are situational rather than binary, and urges assuming colleagues are intelligent, creative, and well-intended. Lisa plays skeptic with real security scenarios: undisclosed incidents before a business sale, pressure to delay breach disclosure until after a shareholders meeting, and an auto-manufacturer customer notification resolved through a careful client communication. Additional examples cover a Russian-owned FTP server serving inappropriate content amid decade-old shared UAT passwords, escalation habits, and finding allies such as aligned attorneys.

The close covers inspiring policy change instead of brute-force escalation, judging organizational fit with parallel reflection questions, building peer support networks at conferences, and audience questions on chronic underperformers and exhausting “lead up” dynamics with insecure managers. Weiss ends with a Japanese fishing-fleet parable about adding sharks to keep fish moving, posing what personal “sharks” might prevent stagnation.

talks.title: Cryptographers' Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists debate post-quantum cryptography after a claimed lattice attack, AI model security, and multiparty computation.
talks.summary:
The panel opened with a case from the weeks before the event. A 63-page paper posted in April claimed a quantum method against the shortest-vector problem in lattices, which underpins many of the post-quantum schemes NIST is standardising. Adi Shamir explained that researchers found a flaw in one of its pages within about a week, so the proposals survived for now. The panelists disagreed on what it meant: Craig Gentry saw a return to the status quo, while Tal Rabin felt the episode had pushed more people to attack the underlying assumptions.

The discussion then moved to migration. Speakers pointed to hybrid key exchange in TLS, and noted that encrypted traffic captured today can be decrypted later, while signing keys can be revoked once they are no longer trusted. Debbie Taylor Moore stressed building an inventory of cryptographic systems and managing third-party dependencies, and Shamir suggested that secrets needing protection for decades could rely on symmetric keys. The panel also covered AI: Shamir described a polynomial-query method for recovering the weights of a neural network from its outputs, and Moore described the governance steps organisations need around AI use. The XZ backdoor was used to illustrate the risks in open-source code, and Shamir warned that open-weight models make such tampering harder to spot.

In the final stretch, Gentry and Rabin explained multiparty computation, threshold secret sharing and fully homomorphic encryption, with Gentry estimating that FHE overhead had fallen to around 10,000 and was now usable for smaller models but not large language models. The panel closed by remembering David Kahn, Fred Piper and Ross Anderson.
