talks.title: Ending the Game of Telephone: The Future of Cyber Incident Reporting
talks.teaser: A panel examines CIRCIA’s NPRM, overlapping breach rules, and how mandated reporting is meant to strengthen the whole ecosystem.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with how CIRCIA grew from earlier incident-reporting ideas in the NDAA, momentum after SolarWinds and Colonial Pipeline, and congressional intent to give CISA visibility into attacks on mostly private critical infrastructure. Panelists describe two core goals: disrupting campaigns earlier and learning adversary tactics to prioritize investment.

CISA’s Brandon Wales walks through implementation after the 2022 authority: 27 listening sessions, roughly 140 RFI responses, and an April 2023 NPRM where the binding text is on the order of 38 pages within a much longer explanatory package, plus a comment period extended beyond 60 days. Industry voices stress scoping of covered entities and incidents, overlapping SEC and sector rules, ROI of compliance, and using JCDC-style collaboration rather than duplicating private threat intelligence. Wales notes existing report volumes on the order of 130,000 to 150,000 tickets annually, TSA and NERC forwarding models, and statutory limits on using CIRCIA submissions for regulatory enforcement against reporters.

Lawmakers and companies close on oversight, funding for implementation, single-point reporting shared across agencies, bidirectional value beyond alerts, third-party submission through counsel and IR firms, and ties to updated critical infrastructure policy documents. Practitioners should expect a evolving rule driven by comments, with ecosystem protection—not individual accountability—as the distinguishing purpose.

talks.title: Bridging Gaps in Cybersecurity for “Target-Rich, Cyber-Poor” Organizations
talks.teaser: Panelists compare volunteer programs that bring cybersecurity help to under-resourced schools, clinics and nonprofits.
talks.summary:
A CISA-led panel looks at "target rich, cyber poor" organizations: small hospitals, school districts, water utilities, local governments and nonprofits that deliver critical services with little or no dedicated security staff. The speakers note that ransomware has made these groups attractive targets, and that some nonprofits also face state-linked threats because of the people they support.

Sarah Powazek described university cyber clinics, where students give basic help such as multi-factor authentication and patching guidance to community groups. She said the consortium she coordinates includes more than 15 clinics across the country. Adrian Ogee described the Cyber Peace Builders program, which matches industry professionals with nonprofits in short, contracted engagements. He said it has supported 217 nonprofits, with over a thousand volunteers from around 50 companies. The panel named the main barriers as prioritization, leaders with limited digital literacy, talent shortages, and complex frameworks and tools that organizations cannot run. Volunteers can also act on threat intelligence from industry partners, matched against the domains and IP ranges of the nonprofits they serve.

Matt Grote said volunteering helps both under-resourced organizations and the cybersecurity talent pipeline, though funding, structure and screening volunteers remain challenges. The panelists favored a decentralized network built on local trust, with government visibility adding credibility. Their longer-term goal is systemic change, so that volunteer programs eventually matter less. The practical takeaway was that a few hours of help from a local professional can meaningfully improve basic defenses.

talks.title: A Proven Approach on Automated Security Architectural Pattern Validation
talks.teaser: Explains automated checks that compare deployed systems against security architecture blueprints to catch recurring gaps.
talks.summary:
The speakers from a health insurer's security architecture team argue that repeated security findings persist because design standards are rarely checked against what is actually deployed. Scanners and assurance programs keep reporting the same gaps, so teams end up treating symptoms. They lay out a layered model: policy-driven control libraries, domain-level reference architectures, use-case patterns, then technology and service blueprints with configuration baselines.

Their validation approach turns blueprint statements into manifest files that scripts check against live or code-defined settings, raising alerts and metrics when they drift. One case confirmed that Calico in Kubernetes accepted traffic only from defined user subnets across many clusters. Another tested that user traffic reached the internet only through the proxy, using ping, traceroute and port checks. Data came from APIs, direct logins to on-premises systems, or manual review, with mostly Python and homegrown tooling used so far.

In Q&A they said the source artifacts were still largely unstructured English and the project was about seven months in, with generative AI and standardization planned next. Their takeaway is to validate the foundation so repeated issues stop returning, while still using application-layer and posture tools alongside it.

talks.title: How to Safely Deploy AI Copilots
talks.teaser: Explains how Microsoft 365 Copilot can surface overshared sensitive data and how to fix permissions before rollout.
talks.summary:
The talk covers why many organizations have stalled Microsoft 365 Copilot rollouts and how security teams can move forward. The speaker argues that Copilot inherits whatever access a user already holds, and that years of loose sharing links, group memberships, and service accounts mean it can surface sensitive files to people who should not see them. One example was a bank that gave Copilot to its traders, which returned employee financial and identity records, prompting the CISO to switch it off. A casino case showed users getting around a confidential-label DLP rule by marking files public.

Labeling was presented as necessary but insufficient, since few organizations label more than a small share of their data and labels do not fix oversharing. The suggested approach combines three views: where sensitive data sits, who and what can reach it, including shared links and third-party apps, and how that data is actually used. Classification accuracy matters because false positives erode trust. In a readiness assessment at a financial firm, a million files were scanned, around 120,000 were highly sensitive, and 57,000 shared links exposed that data company-wide. Automated remediation finished in ten days with no help desk tickets.

The closing advice was to set a concrete outcome, automate continuous fixes such as revoking excess access and correcting labels, and monitor Copilot prompts, responses, and accessed files so alerts carry context. Restricting Copilot to a subset of SharePoint sites was described as a weak fix that reduces its value. The same problem was said to apply to Salesforce, Snowflake, and other AI platforms.

talks.title: Getting Serious: Critical Disruptions/Thinking/Responses (& Rumors of War)
talks.teaser: Examines how cyber disruptions to hospitals, utilities and supply chains become societal harm, and what organizations can do now.
talks.summary:
Josh Corman and David Etue, both speaking as volunteers, argue that cyber disruption now reaches public goods as well as private enterprise risk. They use the Change Healthcare attack and other incidents to show how one organization's outage can spread to hospitals, pharmacies and fuel supply. Corman draws on his time running the CISA Covid task force, where ransomware on hospitals was tied to delayed time-sensitive care and excess deaths.

The middle of the talk covers the threat landscape, pairing state actors such as China and North Korea with financially motivated groups. They cite Volt Typhoon pre-positioning in water and energy systems for at least five years, a 2027 window around Taiwan, and roughly 750 ransomware attacks per year on US hospitals. They argue that systemically important critical infrastructure entities should be identified in advance. For lifeline operators with little security staff, they recommend removing end-of-life systems from the internet, eliminating hardcoded default passwords and fixing known exploited vulnerabilities first.

The closing section challenges assumptions about insurance, backups and supplier diversity. The speakers suggest mapping where your organization is critical, running crisis simulations with recovery windows of weeks or months, and starting cross-functional leadership conversations. Their message is that private sector resilience supports national deterrence, so organizations should act rather than wait.

talks.title: Threat Hunting with Python and Pandas
talks.teaser: Shows how Python and Pandas can push threat hunting past SIEM limits, with URL classification and C2 beacon hunting.
talks.summary:
Matthew Dulle and Anthony Talamantes, from a university-affiliated research lab, describe reaching an analysis dead end when SIEM query languages cannot pivot across large result sets. They propose Python with Pandas, scikit-learn and Jupyter notebooks, which can work through large result sets in batches and join data from several sources.

Dulle walks through a supervised URL classifier built from a balanced set of labelled benign and malicious URLs. Features such as path segment counts and path length are checked for correlation with the classification. He compares k-nearest neighbour with a decision tree and random forest, tunes them with grid search, and judges them with a confusion matrix that prioritises cutting false negatives. The trained model is then chained into an automated enrichment step that pulls results from Splunk and writes classified output to a SQL table.

Talamantes turns to command-and-control beaconing over proxied web traffic, aiming to catch newly seen domains early in their use on the network. Unique domains are filtered by prevalence, then count and time analysis narrows over 7,500 rows to 38 hosts and about 321,000 web records. An interquartile range trims heavy byte traffic, hourly bucket counts drop hosts without beacon-like patterns, and K-means clustering with four clusters separates bytes-in and bytes-out behaviour. In an emulated Kerberoasting exercise, one host landed in three clusters. The closing advice is to start now and build skills over months, since the tools came from outside cyber.

talks.title: Accelerators in Cybersecurity: Seizing Opportunity in a Shifting Landscape
talks.teaser: Explains how cybersecurity accelerators support early-stage startups facing a shrunken investment climate and rising threats.
talks.summary:
The MACH37 leaders argue that early-stage cybersecurity startups face more strain than before. Venture investment in early-stage cyber has shrunk sharply, customers are hesitant to adopt unfamiliar vendors, and crowded markets make it harder for young companies to stand out. The speakers tie these pressures to geopolitical competition, where adversarial investors can use funding to gain access to intellectual property.

To show what accelerators do, they walk through their program: a roughly three-month cohort with workshops on business, legal and compliance basics, introductions to experts and channel partners, and support for founders' wellbeing. MACH37 reports having supported more than 85 cybersecurity startups, with over 85% still operating and over 64% having raised follow-on capital. They also describe a pre-accelerator and a growth-stage track. Case examples include a Ukrainian firm that kept growing after the 2022 invasion, and a 2014-2015 accelerator in the West Bank that paired founders from both sides of the green line. Another case involved a startup whose data room access let an investor take IP and set up a rival.

The closing argument is that accelerators de-risk ventures, help vet the teams and technology that reach the market, and give founders a clearer view of when venture capital makes sense, given the time it takes to raise. The speakers invite attendees to mentor, pilot products, or partner with startups.

talks.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once: A Guide to Alert Triage and Analysis
talks.teaser: Provides structured triage for alert floods, reporter checklists, and collection paths for communication, malware, and phishing.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from firsthand experience facing overwhelming IDS alert queues as a new security engineer, then describes how incident-response bootcamp checklist discipline became a portable framework for methodical decisions. She frames initial triage around institutional memory, Megan’s Law of Alert Triage (high volume usually means low value), and signals such as severity, scary tooling names, correlated log sources, and sudden signature spikes.

The core of the session walks through a reporter-style checklist—who, what, when, where—and routes alerts into suspicious communication, potential malware, or potential phishing tracks. For each path she outlines concrete collection steps: scope and direction of traffic, reputation, packet captures, EDR process lineage, file location and remediation outcomes, multi-vendor verdicts, emulation cautions, user interviews, and password-reset judgment calls.

Closing guidance stresses documentation loops: daily logs, tuning discipline, divide-and-conquer during incidents, root-cause and after-action reporting for management, blocking lessons learned, MFA advocacy, weekly checklist training, and using incident data to justify tooling and process investment.

talks.title: National Cyber Strategy, Roadmap for a Secure Cyber Future: Year in Review
talks.teaser: Federal officials review a year of progress on the national cybersecurity strategy and its implementation plan.
talks.summary:
Moderated by the Department of Justice's chief information officer, this RSA panel looks back a year after the National Cybersecurity Strategy was published. Panelists from the State Department, CISA, the Office of the National Cyber Director and the FBI explain how the first implementation plan's 69 initiatives were released openly, each with a lead federal agency and a due date, and note that a second version has now come out.

The discussion turns to a shift of responsibility toward technology providers, which are better placed to protect victims at scale. Examples include federal contractors attesting to secure development of their software, a planned IoT cyber trust mark, and a Secure by Design pledge from large vendors. On the FBI side, the speaker ties the strategy to disruption work: joint sequenced operations are reported up over 100 percent and threat advisories up over 30 percent. The response to Volt Typhoon combined on-site incident teams, interagency data analysis and a court-authorized operation against compromised edge routers. CISA highlighted default vendor passwords on internet-exposed operational technology as an easy entry point, and described a new national security memorandum requiring sector risk assessment cycles. Lessons from Ukraine led to the Tallinn mechanism for coordinating donor assistance and a new $50 million fund for faster response.

On workforce, panelists argued that cyber work is multidisciplinary and that people can move between public and private jobs. They noted that removing the four-year degree requirement from federal hiring made entry easier. Closing audience comments covered K-12 education and state CISO programs, with the takeaway that partnerships and sector-specific councils matter for underserved organizations.

talks.title: Why Source Code Exfiltration Is the Biggest Blind Spot in Insider Threat
talks.teaser: Shows how insider source-code theft outpaces DLP and risk scoring surfaces exfiltration while preserving developer velocity.
talks.summary:
Joe Payne frames insider risk as fundamentally different from malware: colleagues move data slowly, responses often need HR and legal, and a large share of events are accidental rather than malicious. He contrasts loud DLP-style reactions—with a financial-sector anecdote where a VP was cut off for putting files in Dropbox before a weekend trip—with education-first handling that reduces repeat behavior across teams.

Drawing on interviews with seven hundred security professionals and product telemetry, he argues that source code is among the highest-impact insider targets because leavers understand the IP they take. Personal Git remotes, unsanctioned open-source pushes, AirDrop, and cloud sync bypass conventional channels tuned for email or USB. Developers cannot tolerate endpoint drag; blocking repo movement tends to collapse within days. Payne advocates broad, lightweight monitoring that scores movement by origin, destination, actor, and data type instead of brittle allow/deny rules.

He closes with immediate and ninety-day actions: compare peer coverage for Git-based exfiltration, ask engineers how they actually sync code, and run a short proof of concept on real endpoints (including engineers and sales) rather than a lab. Education at the moment of violation—illustrated by a customer that cut related events by thirty-two percent—and onboarding watch lists for new hires round out the operational playbook.

talks.title: Getting to True Predictive Risk: Will Data Accuracy Thwart AI’s Potential?
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Getting to True Predictive Risk: Will Data Accuracy Thwart AI’s Potential?.

talks.title: The State of Venture Capital in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The State of Venture Capital in Cybersecurity.

talks.title: Cloud Security Novice to Native in 10 Steps: A CNAPP Approach
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cloud Security Novice to Native in 10 Steps: A CNAPP Approach.

talks.title: All Good Things: End of Life and End of Support in Policy and Practice
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of All Good Things: End of Life and End of Support in Policy and Practice.

talks.title: How Visibility and Segmentation Can "Improve Your Sleep"
talks.teaser: A packaging manufacturer details WAN limits, agent-based microsegmentation, and zero-trust labeling across dozens of legacy mills.
talks.summary:
Thomas Vavra from Mondi, a vertically integrated paper and packaging producer, describes securing roughly 110 production sites and on the order of 10,000 to 15,000 connected systems spanning legacy OT, Windows-heavy IT, and constant vendor maintenance access. Remote plants, decades-old machinery, and frequent acquisitions leave networks flat and fragile; a crypto incident on a paper machine that runs continuously could mean days of cleanup and weeks of downtime.

He contrasts a flat DMVPN WAN with Cisco TrustSec tagging, which removed a large share of unnecessary chatty traffic but could not scale policy matrices across 180 locations and dozens of device classes, nor stop lateral movement inside segments or in outsourced data centers. Mondi adopted host-agent microsegmentation: deploy agents broadly, map real application flows, then tighten rules from hygiene services outward in roughly three-hour working sessions per application until enforcement in production within a few weeks.

Trevor Dearing ties the deployment to zero-trust thinking—label environments, locations, and status (including quarantine) and allow only intended protocols, such as blocking RDP between IT and OT. Thomas reports simpler firewall needs, vendor acceptance because only host filters change, and a red-team exercise that reached SAP in about seventeen minutes without segmentation but stalled for a week once policies were active. Practitioners should expect imperfect rules balanced against uptime, but far tighter east-west control than VLAN-centric designs.

talks.title: Project Power Up: Fighting Electronic Warfare to Keep Ukraine's Grid Safe
talks.teaser: Explains how jammed GPS threatened Ukraine's grid sync and how holdover timing on rugged switches kept dispatch stable.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how a casual Palo Alto dinner linked U.S. grid practitioners with Ukrainian transmission operator staff who were hunting transformers and quietly struggling with unreliable GPS during full-scale war. Taras outlines Ukrenergo’s role, the 2022 isolated-grid stress test that coincided with invasion, emergency ENTSO-E synchronization, export successes, and then kinetic strikes that wrecked roughly half of transmission and generation while cyber pressure often spiked ahead of missiles.

Joe picks up the operational heart: precision time from GPS underpins frequency measurement and grid coordination worldwide, yet electronic warfare can cheaply deny that weak signal, leaving substation gear reporting lost synchronization. Project Power Up repurposed rugged industrial switches with crystal oscillators and firmware holdover so equipment keeps microsecond-accurate timestamps via precision time protocol for hours when satellites disappear, then hands back cleanly when signals return—validated by pulling GPS cables in the field and scaled through humanitarian logistics.

Practitioners hear why spoofing remains harder, how Poland’s GPS outages hint at broader EMS risk, and why substation clocks beat millisecond alternatives like NTP for wide-area grids. The close emphasizes assuming any dispatch or telemetry asset can be lost, isolating OT when bridges fall, and that cross-border cooperation under time pressure can keep hospitals and cities powered when maps and munitions both target the same fragile timing layer.

talks.title: Avoiding Legal Landmines: A Review of Recent Cyber Cases
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Avoiding Legal Landmines: A Review of Recent Cyber Cases.

talks.title: How to Take Cookies from the Cookie Monster: Genesis Market Takedown
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for How to Take Cookies from the Cookie Monster: Genesis Market Takedown.

talks.title: Backdoors & Breaches: Live Tabletop Exercise Demo
talks.teaser: Runs a live incident response card game that maps attacker techniques to defensive detections and exposes gaps in tooling.
talks.summary:
This session is a live run of Backdoors & Breaches, a free incident response card game that the presenters created to make tabletop exercises more interactive and less argumentative. Attack cards cover initial compromise, pivot and escalation, command and control with exfiltration, and persistence. Blue cards represent defensive steps such as endpoint analysis, SIEM log analysis, isolation, and cyber deception. The audience rolls a twenty-sided die with modifiers for documented procedures. A failed roll triggers a question about why a step is impossible right now, and those answers become possible findings for the organization.

The scenario begins with a user whose screen goes black and displays a war games message. Endpoint analysis succeeded and revealed application shimming, a persistence method that can hide programs from the installed-programs list. Isolating the host failed on a coin-flip roll, and SIEM log analysis also came up empty because Windows Event Forwarding had quietly stopped sending logs. Cyber deception, shown with honey user accounts and honey shares, exposed the Active Directory weaponization card and tools such as BloodHound. Firewall logs then pointed to BITS as the command and control channel, which many security products ignore. A later server analysis step revealed the initial compromise: spear phishing.

The full chain was phishing, Active Directory weaponization, BITS, and application shimming. The presenters argued that an attacker of middling skill could pull this off through patience and publicly known bypasses, and that many defenders have never encountered BITS or shimming, which can skew investigation theories. The session closed with a plausibility vote and a round where each participant named one takeaway. The presenters pointed to the free online version and the open card assets, and suggested building server checklists from hardening guides.

talks.title: Dial-A-CISO Game: 175 Leadership Issues to Choose From
talks.teaser: A game-style session that quizzes the audience on CISO leadership issues drawn from a podcast interview series.
talks.summary:
The session is a game-style talk built around 175 leadership questions from the presenter's CISO Stories podcast. Audience members joined a polling app on their phones and answered multiple-choice questions only after a numbered ball was drawn at random. After each poll, the results appeared on screen and a short clip from the guest who had covered that topic played.

The questions covered a range of leadership issues. One asked what core competency matters most for a CISO, and the answer discussed was resilience, including accepting accountability for things a CISO does not directly control. Another contrasted security awareness that is forced on staff with controls built into employee workflows. A talent-shortage question led to the view that the shortage is short term, with internships and help desk roles offered as entry paths. Other picks covered how long a deputy CISO should serve, the pressures of county government where leaders must see protecting citizen data as part of their mandate, and the need to plan now for replacing encryption as quantum computing advances.

The presenter also explained how the question set was produced. About 40 interviews of roughly 30 minutes each were transcribed and turned into multiple-choice questions with AI tools in a few hours, and the answer options were then tweaked so the right one was not obvious. The practical lesson was to translate security into terms that lawyers and executives understand, to build knowledge beyond one's own specialty, and to use AI to speed up preparation.

talks.title: They Hide, We Seek: Leveraging Global Partnerships Against Our Adversaries
talks.teaser: Allied agencies show how synchronized takedowns, sanctions, and joint alerts impose cost on criminals and nation states.
talks.summary:
Government cyber leaders from the United States, Australia, and the Netherlands frame a landscape where adversaries favor living-off-the-land access, stale CVE exploitation, edge and home-router footholds, code-signed malware, and info stealers that fuel ransomware and phishing. They stress that sophistication is often unnecessary when patching and resilience lag, while campaigns tied to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea continue to evolve from conflicts such as Ukraine.

The panel walks through how partnerships impose cost: synchronized operations that hit actors, infrastructure, tools, communications, and malware together; examples include disrupting the Snake implant, defend-forward findings shared with industry, joint advisories with many agency seals, Hafnium-related court-authorized removal of web shells alongside vendor patching, LockBit-focused Operation Cronos, and Australia’s first cyber sanctions linked to the Medibank breach. Dutch and Australian units describe standing task forces, Europol and Interpol coordination, and projects that blend prosecutors, national centers, and vendors.

Practitioners should build government and sector relationships before an incident, share early telemetry and tradecraft shifts, consume consolidated national alerts, and treat transparency and collective action as force multipliers. The closing message is that sustained global teaming—not isolated defense—offsets adversary tempo and erodes their advantage.

talks.title: AI and Democracy
talks.teaser: Surveys how AI could reshape democracy across politics, lawmaking, bureaucracy, courts and everyday citizen participation.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI will mostly change society by altering how familiar tasks are done, through shifts in speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Democracy is treated broadly, as a system for turning individual preferences into collective decisions, including bureaucratic ones. The speaker examines politicians using personalized chatbots and simulated polling, legislators sorting constituent input and drafting bills, including a Brazilian water-meter law written with ChatGPT, and AI-written laws too complex for people to follow.

The middle section covers bureaucracy and the legal system. AI could determine benefits eligibility, audit contracts, and make legal help cheap, which could flood courts with lawsuits. Automated enforcement, from camera-based checks to tax fraud detection, could make rules harder to evade, but raises concerns about false positives and about contesting software in court. Contract disputes might go to AI arbitration. For citizens, AI could explain issues, moderate discussions and watch local government.

The closing part turns to security. AI systems inherit ordinary computer risks and add new ones from how they are trained and deployed, and adversaries may try to manipulate them. Incentives, the cost of mistakes, the balance of power, and trust in specific applications all shape the outcome. The speaker argues that security experts can help make AI spread power rather than concentrate it. In the Q&A he downplays disinformation as a red herring and points to antitrust as a partial remedy.

talks.title: AI Foundations: Mitigate Risks and Boost SOC Efficiency
talks.teaser: Shows where LLM tools help or mislead SOC analysts, and how to plan AI automation with governance and risk checks.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a look at a typical day for a SOC analyst, covering monitoring and detection, incident response and threat intelligence, and uses the Log4j episode as a reference point. The presenters explain core AI concepts such as machine learning, large language models and predictive analytics, and map them to security tasks.

In a live demonstration, the presenter tested public chatbots on four network log entries from a hypothetical pharmaceutical website, including a misspelled domain and a 3:00 AM login. Answers mostly explained how IP addresses work, produced generic charts or returned a code snippet. One agent described a different CVE than the one requested, and another said an actively exploited vulnerability was not being exploited. The presenter concluded that models trained on older data and lacking organisational context can miss live threats.

The second half covers benefits and risks, with a case study that pulled threat feeds into a shared document store for querying with Gemini, and Jupyter notebooks used to automate hunts and playbooks. Risks include garbage in, garbage out, opaque models, malicious models on a public hub that got past its malware scan, model inversion, and staff pasting sensitive data into public tools. Advice: write AI policies, run a risk assessment, document processes before choosing a use case, pilot small, track metrics like mean time to detect and respond, and always review output.

talks.title: The Human Impact of Cyberattacks: Reframing the Defender Role
talks.teaser: Panelists explore CISO burnout, regulatory pressure, and why resilience must join prevention in the defender mandate.
talks.summary:
The panel opens on unsustainable expectations for security leaders: defenders must be right every time while attackers need one win, and post-breach fallout now includes regulatory action and personal liability. Rubrik Zero Lab survey results cited on stage report that 98% of security team members experienced some mental trauma after incidents and that roughly 40% of security leadership lost their jobs following a cyber event.

Discussion moves through crisis leadership, continuity planning, and evolving governance as CIO and CISO lines blur. Panelists describe election-year pressures at CISA, SolarWinds-era enforcement themes, SEC questionnaires, and growing board interest in bounce-back planning versus pure prevention. They also tie defender work to geopolitics, vendor risk, cyber insurance friction, and economic models where software providers share financial responsibility.

Practitioners hear concrete guidance: secure legal and insurance coverage, invest in executive communication coaching, maintain board access, plan leadership continuity, and treat resilience as a third pillar beside risk reduction and threat response. The closing message reframes defenders as stewards of trust and continuous operation under nation-state and criminal pressure, not guarantors of zero incidents.

talks.title: SEC Rules on Cybersecurity: Materiality, Preparedness and Board Oversight
talks.teaser: Explains how public companies can judge incident materiality and document decisions under the SEC cyber disclosure rules.
talks.summary:
The session covers the SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules that took effect in December 2023. The speakers start with the SolarWinds civil action, which named a company executive and left many security leaders feeling personally exposed. Since the rules began, many companies have filed 8-K notices early, saying they do not yet know whether an incident is material.

For materiality, they recommend a defined escalation path from the security operations center to a decision committee that reconvenes as facts change, ideally kept to a small group. Factors include whether an attack is novel or part of a campaign, which parts of the CIA triad were affected, detection and containment speed, and attribution. Financial and operational impact can be hard to predict, so they use examples such as manufacturing, e-commerce and streaming. They warn that half-truths in filings draw scrutiny, and that documenting the reasoning and missing data matters if a decision is challenged later.

For the 10-K, the speakers argue the larger risk is overstated descriptions of cyber risk management, since every statement can carry liability. They describe a line-by-line review between legal and the CISO, and suggest mapping cyber risk to enterprise risk and running tabletop exercises that include investor relations and marketing. Their practical takeaway is to review the incident response process and committee membership now, then build risk management maturity over several years.

talks.title: Keeping Up with the Algorithms: A Journey in Artificial Intelligence
talks.teaser: Panelists from industry and the FBI discuss how AI is reshaping threats, regulation and defensive priorities.
talks.summary:
This RSA panel, moderated by the chief executive of an anti-ransomware company, looks at how quickly AI is advancing and what that means for security, policy and government. Jason Clinton, CISO at Anthropic, argues that the compute used to train AI models has grown roughly 4 to 7x year over year, so organizations should plan for much more capable models within a year or two. Panelists agree that lawmakers move too slowly to keep pace, and Theresa Payton suggests building laws around ethical guardrails rather than specific technologies.

The discussion then turns to threats. Joe Szczerba describes the FBI's approach: tracking adversary use of AI, protecting American AI innovation, and ensuring ethical use under an AI Ethics Council formed in 2021. Panelists note that criminals use large language models for more convincing phishing and deepfakes, and that the same tools can help the most skilled attackers. Clinton points to models that can find software vulnerabilities and urges every enterprise to adopt a one-day patch deployment policy. Payton describes a case at a global insurance company where a chatbot pilot had elevated privileges and passed data unencrypted; incident response found no data leakage.

For executives, Payton advises presenting security as an enabler of customer experience and productivity rather than through fear, and suggests rotating passphrases for wire approvals and stronger authentication for biometrics. Clinton recommends knowing where data flows, keeping AI deployments segmented, and using independent audits and certifications. The main takeaway is that governance and fast operational response matter more while regulation catches up.

talks.title: The Cost of Innovation: Complexities of Software Regulation
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh how liability rules, attestation forms and cyber insurance could push software makers toward secure development.
talks.summary:
The panel examined how new and proposed rules are moving responsibility for cybersecurity from users and enterprises toward software manufacturers, with a focus on the United States. Nick Leiserson, from the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, described the second implementation plan for the national strategy, which adds a software liability initiative. He said officials were first consulting academics, then software makers through roundtables, to test liability frameworks that reward secure development while avoiding strict liability for every flaw. He also pointed to CISA's attestation form for federal software purchases and the EU Cyber Resilience Act as existing measures.

Mickey Bresman compared manufacturer flaws to faulty brakes in a car and user misconfiguration to skipping a seatbelt, arguing that resilience depends on both. Sam Curry said the biggest gap is poor alignment between security teams and business goals, and that an active attacker keeps probing software, so perfect code is not a realistic target. The panel also discussed the cost of compliance for smaller vendors: Curry described a startup that needed about two years and dedicated security and documentation staff before it could sell to government, while Bresman said large vendors often give government a version older than their commercial release.

On cyber insurance, the panelists saw insurers as a lever for better security, since they can trace claims back to root causes, though correlated losses make the market hard to price and officials were discussing a federal backstop. An audience member raised NIS2 and DORA as drivers of vendor audits. The session closed with a practical takeaway: ask software vendors how their products are secured, because customer demand shapes what manufacturers prioritise.

talks.title: AI in Cyber: Is the Cyber Profession Ready for Its Impact?
talks.teaser: ISC2 leaders share survey results on how AI is reshaping cybersecurity jobs, skills gaps and organizational policy.
talks.summary:
ISC2 leaders Clar Rosso and Jon France presented results from a survey of about 1,200 members collected around the turn of 2023 into 2024. 41% saw threats rise between June and December 2023, and 56% said parts of their jobs could become obsolete, while 82% expected AI to improve efficiency. They argued AI and machine learning skills must be built quickly, since these rose to second place among skills gaps in 2023.

Only 27% of respondents had a formal policy on safe and ethical AI use. Jon France described his organization's policy moving from a blanket ban to a conditional approach, keeping items such as exam content, personal data and business plans out of public language models. He also warned that AI features are appearing in familiar tools, so staff should check where their data goes.

On regulation, four in five respondents want rules for safe and ethical AI use, and 63% favour global harmonization. The speakers contrasted the US focus on federal guidance and technical risk, the EU's rights-based approach, and the UK's principle-based model. They closed with practical steps: start internal discussions, review existing AI policies, refine governance within three months, and build an AI security training plan within six months.

talks.title: So You Want to Open Source Your Project? Hold Your Horses!
talks.teaser: Explains how to weigh strategy, community and licensing before releasing a company's software as open source.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a business-minded look at whether an organisation should release its software as open source. The speaker frames the decision as a triangle of strategic fit, community and licensing. He sorts candidate code into core business software, utilities that help the wider community, and tools that grow an ecosystem around the company, and notes that APIs, helper applications and libraries are common starting points before core software.

The middle section covers how money is made and who pays for growth. Models discussed include selling subscriptions and support, as Red Hat does, building lock-in through easy-to-use tools, bundling, and running hosted services. The licence shapes which models work: a weak copyleft licence such as the LGPL can make large providers reluctant to use the code, while permissive licences such as MIT or Apache are easy to adopt. He warns against writing your own licence and says source-available licences such as the Business Source License are not open source. Community growth needs deliberate investment, and foundations can host projects, provide tooling and visibility, and give collaborators guidance on antitrust concerns.

The worked example is Enarx, a confidential computing project created at Red Hat and donated to the Confidential Computing Consortium. Its enabling code was released under Apache 2.0, while the core services were licensed under LGPL 3 with copyright kept, so the company could run a business around them. The closing advice is to talk to the business first, make a long-term strategic decision, and within six months define the product that customers will actually consume and that carries security support.

talks.title: Global Threat Overview
talks.teaser: A security leader connects geopolitical upheaval, state cyber arms races, and modern extortion to practical risks organizations face now.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by placing cyber risk inside a shifting world order: declining trade integration after decades of globalization, COVID’s exposure of supply-chain fragility, multipolar competition, armed conflicts, and a perceived rollback in democratic norms. The speaker links those trends to a accelerating cyber arms race among nations, tracing catalysts such as the Arab Spring and broad intelligence leaks, and stressing that digital weapons proliferate downward to criminals far more easily than conventional arms.

He describes cyber as cheap asymmetric power with weak escalation norms, arguing that financially motivated actors now rival historic nation-state skill and routinely prey on cash-rich, poorly defended targets like schools and hospitals. Extended attack surfaces spanning multi-cloud estates, SaaS, and unpatchable appliances receive attention, along with brief notes on generative AI as a defender force multiplier, misplaced CISO ownership of non-security AI worries, ransomware’s pivot to commercial remote tooling and hybrid identity paths, specialist criminal business models, and supply-chain cases from compromised authentication products through SolarWinds and open-source backdoors. Chinese probing of U.S. infrastructure is framed as wartime preparation rather than espionage for profit.

Practitioners are urged to assume breach, strengthen each kill-chain stage, consolidate correlated logging, and automate responses to common intrusion patterns before humans triage. Closing audience questions contrast Russia’s elite, patient intelligence operations with China’s massive parallel targeting capacity, and speculate on AI-driven mass exploitation if geopolitical constraints break down.

talks.title: Translating National Security Excellence into Private Sector Vigilance
talks.teaser: Compares how national security and corporate leaders fund cyber programs, hire talent, and adopt emerging security tools.
talks.summary:
In this fireside chat at RSA 2024, Vishal Amin speaks with Lauren Knausenberger, the former chief information officer of the US Air Force who now serves as chief innovation officer at SAIC. They compare how national security organizations and private companies plan cyber budgets. Knausenberger describes what she calls faith-based financing in the Department of Defense, where funding often arrives late and forces hard trade-offs, while corporate budgets give a clearer sense of what is sufficient.

The conversation then moves to legacy systems, data governance and workforce. Knausenberger argues that aging infrastructure is hard to justify keeping, since cloud architectures offer resilience and faster updates, and that data governance still lags behind. The speakers note that military training produces strong cyber staff, but many leave after a few years, so governments and companies increasingly lean on managed services and recruits from nontraditional backgrounds. Office 365 adoption during the pandemic is cited as an example of a platform removing burden from IT teams.

On investment, Knausenberger says organizations should partner or buy rather than build, and that a venture stake or integrator role can help a startup survive federal scrutiny. Audience questions covered sharing threat intelligence back to government, internships, and degree requirements. The main takeaway is to tie security spending to mission outcomes and a return that leaders can measure.

talks.title: Responsible AI: Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
talks.teaser: Shows how gradient-optimized suffixes can jailbreak aligned language models, and why alignment alone struggles to stop them.
talks.summary:
This session looks at attacks on aligned large language models, the chatbots whose refusals come from a fine-tuning stage applied after pre-training. The speaker argues that alignment teaches a model a content policy but does not reliably enforce it under adversarial probing. The attack treats the model as a differentiable function and searches for a suffix appended to a harmful request, combining gradient-based search with discrete token selection so the model begins with an affirmative reply rather than a refusal.

The talk then covers the universal version of the attack, which optimizes one suffix across many prompts and several open white-box models at once. Suffixes built this way were reported to transfer to closed models such as ChatGPT, Bard and Claude, with Claude needing some manual tuning. The speaker also walks through a prompt injection case in which a chatbot with web and email plugins was steered into exposing an inbox, and argues that the confused deputy problem is still unresolved. He draws a parallel to adversarial examples in vision models from 2014.

For practitioners, the main takeaways are to run continuous adversarial evaluation that matches the deployment scenario, and to re-test after every fine-tune, since changes to weights can reopen old weaknesses. Blocking known suffixes was shown to be brittle, while folding generated attacks into training showed promising results on a Llama 3 variant. The speaker stresses that no model should be treated as fully secure.

talks.title: The State of Our Cyber Is Strong: The View from the White House
talks.teaser: The discussion covers national cyber implementation plans, federal agency roles, global threats, and workforce and education reforms.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the release of National Cybersecurity Strategy Implementation Plan Version 2, framed as a public accountability document with assigned leads, deliverables, and due dates across roughly one hundred actions. The director describes two strategic shifts—moving defense responsibility toward more capable institutions and incentivizing long-term resilience—and acknowledges that measurable cybersecurity outcomes still need community-developed metrics.

The middle of the conversation maps how the Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates strategy and policy without running operations, alongside partners such as CISA, the FBI, NSA, and Cyber Command. Priorities include stronger public-private collaboration, better cyber support for sector risk management agencies and critical infrastructure, and aid for state, local, tribal, and territorial governments. The threat discussion spans PRC activity against infrastructure for potential wartime disruption, ransomware and cybercrime, supply-chain risk, and artificial intelligence as both risk and opportunity, with brief comparisons of adversary evolution and Ukraine’s resilience.

Closing themes emphasize education and talent: K-12 protections, workforce strategy, skills-based federal hiring, outreach to underserved communities and military families, and treating space systems as essential infrastructure needing minimum cybersecurity requirements. The talk ends on partnership, continuous readiness, and aligning incentives so defenders at every level can act on shared risk.

talks.title: Beyond Desktops: The Rise and Transformation of Mobile Malware
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Beyond Desktops: The Rise and Transformation of Mobile Malware.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at RSA Conference by Nicolas and Gianluca from mobile security vendor Zimperium, this talk examines the architectural differences between desktop and mobile malware, the drivers behind growing mobile threats, and the evolving mobile threat landscape. The speakers emphasize that while desktop environments traditionally offered broad file system access, admin privileges, and network propagation, mobile platforms enforce tight sandboxing, restricted file access, and lower compute resources. Despite these constraints, mobile devices have become prime targets because they store sensitive personal and corporate data, act as ubiquitous trackers, and frequently access enterprise environments via Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) policies.

### Key Topics
- **Mobile vs. Desktop Environments:** High-level architectural contrasts including limited hardware resources, strict sandboxing, hardened file systems, and the prevalence of one-to-one social engineering and smishing instead of horizontal network spreading.
- **Drivers for Mobile Attacks:** Mobile devices serve as continuous trackers (capturing location, audio, camera, and communications) and gateways to corporate networks. Attackers exploit the fact that roughly 85% of enterprises permit BYOD while mobile security awareness lags decades behind desktop awareness, with only 25% of mobile devices employing endpoint protection.
- **Threat Chains & Attack Surfaces:** Demonstration of composite mobile attack chains, such as untrusted public Wi-Fi leading to redirection, dropped encryption, malicious APK download, system tampering, and disabling SELinux.
- **Case Study: Joker Malware:** An Android consumer threat evolving since 2017 incorporating spyware, click fraud, and fleeceware (subscribing victims to premium services). Its development progressed through advanced obfuscation, multi-stage encrypted DEX dropper mechanisms, and hiding background WebViews.
- **Case Study: Banking Trojans:** Enterprise- and consumer-impacting threats that steal credentials and bypass defenses via overlay attacks, Automated Transfer System (ATS) abuse, Telephone-Oriented Attack Delivery (TOAD), screen sharing abuse, and Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) platforms such as Godfather and PixBankBot.

### Technical Details
- **Droppers and Payloads:** Malicious apps disguise themselves as legitimate utilities or games in app stores, communicate with command-and-control (C2) servers, decrypt secondary DEX payloads directly in memory, or delay secondary stage delivery by months to bypass app vetting.
- **Banking Trojan Mechanics:** Trojans inventory installed apps, notify C2 servers, and display fake UI overlays over target banking or cryptocurrency wallet apps to capture credentials. In ATS abuse, malware intercepts transactions to alter the destination account before transmission or lures users for MFA tokens. Telephone attacks (TOAD) combine phishing calls with live screen sharing to interact with the device stealthily.
- **Emerging Threat Horizons:** Cross-platform frameworks like Flutter produce serialized binary blobs that update frequently, hindering static analysis and heuristics. Emerging AI-driven threats include malware (reported by Group-IB) that exfiltrates biometrics and generates deepfake videos to circumvent facial recognition and transaction approvals on both Android and iOS.
- **Zero-Click vs. Interaction Attacks:** The speakers discussed high-profile spyware (Pegasus, Predator, Operation Triangulation, Quadream) and zero-click message parser vulnerabilities (such as historical Stagefright), noting that persistence on mobile often requires detectable indicators like disabling SELinux or remounting file systems read/write.

### Takeaways
- **Transition Beyond Heuristics:** Traditional heuristic analysis cannot keep pace with multi-stage droppers and evolving frameworks; defense requires on-device machine learning with privacy-preserving inspection.
- **Organizational Visibility:** Enterprises adopting BYOD must bridge the awareness gap by deploying Mobile Threat Defense (MTD) alongside Mobile Device Management (MDM), as MDM posture checks alone cannot detect sideloaded malware or active system compromises.
- **Application Developer Hygiene:** App developers should integrate SDK-based runtime application self-protection (RASP) to identify rooted devices, app tampering, and co-located malicious apps, while incorporating robust code obfuscation to prevent reverse engineering.

talks.title: Everything Everywhere All at Once: The European ID Wallet Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Explains the EU's eIDAS 2.0 revision and the European digital identity wallet ecosystem, from legal mandates to trust services.
talks.summary:
The panel explains the revised eIDAS regulation, known as eIDAS 2.0, which requires every EU member state to offer a European digital identity wallet. The first version treated identity as a set of separate products. The new framework is meant to work as a full ecosystem: a wallet provider issues the wallet, government sources supply personal identification data, and qualified electronic attestations add attributes such as licences or professional credentials. Qualified signatures complete the picture, and a trust list maintained by the European Commission lets components confirm they only deal with trusted parties.

Earlier signature rules left national implementations inconsistent, and the 2014 regulation mainly standardised trust services while national eID systems stayed separate. Likely use cases include identity checks in finance, health applications and general online accounts. The German approach offers two ways to present identity: an authenticated channel, or signed tokens bound to the device. German showcase projects offered lessons: public and private partners should collaborate early, municipalities understand citizen needs, and wallets need a business model if they are not funded by taxpayers.

In the audience Q&A, lost devices can be revoked, and age checks rely on selective disclosure so users share only what a service needs. Certification of secure elements was described as an open question, and third-party wallets are allowed if they meet the technical and certification requirements. For practitioners, the key point is that relying parties must check wallet attestations, while many details will arrive through implementing acts over the coming months and years.

talks.title: Ransomware Resilience: Holistic Defense for SOC Leaders
talks.teaser: Maps 2023 ransomware trends and the Scattered Spider attack chain, with prevention controls for each stage.
talks.summary:
The session opens with 2023 ransomware trends, including a rise in activity compared with 2022, affiliate programs that sell initial access, supply-chain intrusions, and a shift toward stealing data without encrypting it. The presenters connect the SEC disclosure rule that took effect in late 2023 to extortion pressure, and explain how groups rebrand after sanctions and move to newer languages such as Go and Rust.

The core of the talk walks through the Scattered Spider family across the attack chain. Initial access relies on voice phishing, SIM swapping and MFA fatigue aimed at help desks and administrators. Lateral movement uses legitimate remote-assistance tools and credential theft utilities to reach crown-jewel data and source code. Persistence comes through registering new MFA tokens and disabling endpoint protection, and exfiltration uses custom data-transfer tooling. For each stage the speakers suggest controls such as ZTNA to hide applications, Active Directory segmentation, deception decoys, FIDO-based MFA, SSL inspection and DLP.

The talk closes with two product concepts presented as possible approaches: Risk360, a risk view combining workforce, third-party, application and asset risk, and Breach Predictor, which uses machine learning over security logs to project likely next attack stages. Practical takeaways include stricter help desk verification, documented definitions of risky uploads, a response plan covering containment, eradication, recovery and communication, and regular reviews of external exposure.

Overview: Perimeter defenses are holding an important role in computer security. However, when we check the method of APT groups, a single spear-phishing usually enough to gain a foothold on the network. Therefore, red teams are mostly focused on "assume breach" type of scenarios. In these scenarios, testers need to use a post-exploitation framework. Key Topics: e's C2-Agent communication from anomaly-based intrusion detection systems. It takes a traffic capture file (pcap) of the network and tries to identify normal traffic profile. According to results, it creates an Empire HTTP listener with appropriate options.

talks.title: State of the CISO 2024: Doing More With Less
talks.teaser: Surveys CISO roles, budgets, staffing and board reporting, with advice on doing more with less.
talks.summary:
This session presents findings from a 2023 survey of CISOs and their teams, run by IANS and Artico Search with 660 respondents. The speakers describe how the role has shifted from technical leadership toward business risk ownership, with only about 20% of CISOs sitting at the C-level and many being asked to own risk outside their direct control. Scope creep is a recurring theme, and CISOs who report to the board regularly tend to feel more aligned with the organization.

The middle of the talk covers budgets and staffing. Security budgets grew on average 6% this year after years of double-digit increases, but macroeconomic pressure is tightening them, and staff costs make up about 38% of new security budgets. The speakers also cover compensation for functional leaders, how leadership roles are combined across teams, and the fact that about 65% of CISOs report into a technology function. Retention data point to management that makes people feel valued, with years four through seven as a critical stretch for keeping staff.

The speakers close with practical steps: build cross-functional relationships and internal champions, find mentors who have presented to boards, and report progress against a chosen framework using third-party maturity assessments. They also stress documenting risk ownership so that scope can be controlled.

talks.title: The Next Application Security Frontier: AI-Ready API Defense
talks.teaser: Explains why APIs now draw most attacks and how defenders can inventory, threat-model and secure them as AI adoption grows.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that application programming interfaces have become the main path into modern software, and that generative AI will add more of them. The speakers trace how APIs grew from early product integrations through cloud adoption and agile development, while security tooling and teams lagged behind. They say most attacks now target API endpoints, and that many organisations lack a complete inventory of the APIs they run.

To show the risk, they walk through a common attack chain. An attacker decompiles a mobile app to pull out embedded keys, strings and endpoint paths, then uses stolen or purchased credentials with bots. Automated abuse can escalate from credential stuffing into a denial of service once the weakness spreads. They also point to broken object and function level authorization as API-specific flaws that traditional web tools often miss, and note that generative AI lets less skilled attackers act with more capability.

The closing advice is practical. Build a threat model covering assets, actors, interfaces and actions; discover shadow and orphaned APIs across code, traffic and the edge; and keep security pace with development. Layer mobile app protection, bot defense, API monitoring and DDoS protection, and avoid trading one supply chain risk for another. The speakers encourage teams to revisit their tactics every year and to treat API governance and safe AI use as the next surface to manage.

talks.title: The Secret Life of APIs: Latest Attack Data Shows What Your APIs Are Doing
talks.teaser: Shows year-long attack data on APIs, with real fraud and abuse cases, and practical steps on discovery, posture and detection.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a year of attack data on APIs, which the presenter describes as the connections behind everyday services such as travel booking, payments, banking and healthcare. Drawing on a yearly state-of-the-internet report, he says about 29 percent of web attacks over the period targeted APIs, that EMEA had the highest share of API attacks, and that commerce and financial services were among the most affected sectors.

Three cases illustrate the patterns. At a television service, attackers used the ordering and payment-validation APIs over a few days to test tens of thousands of payment cards, a carding attack that cost the company little directly but drew in regulators. In a retail loyalty program, attackers took over accounts and moved points in small amounts that routine monitoring missed, adding up to roughly $100,000 in fraud. A SaaS notification service lacked authorization checks, so anyone with API access could send messages to its customers. Separately, an airline suffered a broken object-level authorization flaw that exposed customer data.

Common weaknesses included shadow APIs nobody tracked, unauthenticated resource access and sensitive data placed in URLs. The presenter urged organizations to discover and inventory their APIs, assign owners, prioritize the most important endpoints, and use behavioral detection and reputation data. He also argued that a web application firewall alone does not cover API-specific abuse, and that runtime findings should feed back into development.

talks.title: What Cloud Has Taught about Securing AI in the Future
talks.teaser: Maps the security questions cloud raised earlier onto generative AI and offers a shared responsibility view.
talks.summary:
This talk, given by John Yeoh of the Cloud Security Alliance, compares the security questions raised by cloud computing around 2010 with those now raised by generative AI. It traces cloud's evolution from early hosted services to cloud-native platforms, and argues that large language models inherit many of the same traits, such as running on someone else's infrastructure and concentrating data.

The middle section adapts the cloud shared responsibility model to AI, splitting it into seven elements such as identity and access, intellectual property, data control and model quality. A worked example weighs LLM data leakage against traditional data security: the risk looks low when staff use hosted public models for inference, but rises once an organization tunes its own models or agents over private data. Near-term concerns include prompt injection, data poisoning, hallucinations and attackers using AI to move faster. Resources the speaker highlights include a threat taxonomy listing over 400 AI-specific threats, a governance reference list of over 200 items, and a new AI safety benchmarking model.

The closing advice is to understand AI technologies and their risks before trying to secure them, build AI literacy across security and business teams, and check whether AI use fits business goals. Audience questions covered deleting data from trained models, how incident response may change, and whether generative models can improve anomaly detection. The speaker notes that dedicated AI control sets do not yet exist.

talks.title: Lesson Learned - General Motors Road to Modern Consumer Identity
talks.teaser: Shows how General Motors built a shared consumer identity platform on Entra, with layered fraud defenses and risk-based sign-in.
talks.summary:
Andrew Cameron, who leads technology for identity at General Motors, and Razi Rais, a Microsoft Security product manager, describe how GM built a consumer identity platform with Microsoft Entra. They argue consumer identity should be managed apart from workforce identity, since customers self-register, proofing must add little friction, and branding matters. GM replaced separate logins in each channel with one shared sign-in, MFA and account management layer, while keeping profile data in an on-premises service.

For protocols they recommend OpenID Connect with PKCE over SAML, separating the identifier step from the password step to ease a move to passwordless sign-in, and limiting federated providers to a few leading ones. Razi described layered defenses: a web application firewall at the edge against bots and DDoS, fraud checks and identity proofing at signup, and device fingerprinting. One example was a premium-rate phone number fraud that abuses phone-based MFA. The response was an alert when MFA success falls below a 95% baseline, followed by blocking the number and throttling the account. Sign-in risk scoring drives conditional MFA or blocking, and phishing-resistant methods are the default, with SMS as an opt-out.

They closed by urging teams to engage the business early, feed identity signals into the SIEM, test WAF and MFA controls hands-on, and keep improving maturity. In the Q&A, Andrew said GM is retiring the ROPC grant type and manages external entitlements through groups and attributes.

talks.title: Steering Clear of Danger: Decrypting the Realities of Remote Car Hacking
talks.teaser: Explores remote vehicle compromise from wireless entry points through fuzzing, weaponization, and cloud-exposed automotive APIs.
talks.summary:
Modern vehicles carry tens of millions of lines of code across dozens of electronic control units, yet successful remote compromise usually does not begin on the CAN bus. The presentation frames car hacking as connectivity mapping, path selection to safety-critical networks, vulnerability discovery, and reliable weaponization against real mitigations.

Using Pwn2Own 2021 against a patched Tesla as the anchor case, it walks through spoofing a service access point so the car connects willingly, then abusing DHCP and DNS handling in the connection manager to reach a stack buffer overflow in decompression logic. A live fuzzing workflow on packaged IVI-related code reproduces that class of bug, including lower-severity out-of-bounds reads that later support ASLR bypass. The talk contrasts ISO safety processes with automotive cybersecurity norms, surveys historical remote wins through telematics and infotainment, and shows how certificate transparency searches and manufacturer open-source disclosures expose backend APIs and shared GENIVI components across multiple brands.

Practitioners are steered toward undertested code and systematic fuzzing rather than replaying public exploits. Fleet operators are urged to inventory exposed APIs; OEMs to treat bundled open source as their own assurance problem. Physical CAN attacks remain relevant for theft scenarios, but drone-range compromise is portrayed as an infotainment and telematics problem first.

talks.title: From Boardrooms to Polling Places: Securing Critical Infrastructure in 2024
talks.teaser: Argues critical infrastructure defenders should move from reactive response to early warning and exposure management.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why critical infrastructure is hard to defend. Many of these environments run equipment designed decades ago, often before the internet existed in its current form, and newer internet-connected systems have been added on top. The speaker argues that cyber operations have moved from covert intelligence activity to open, disruptive attacks, and that hospitals, pipelines and power plants now face nation-state and criminal threats alike.

The middle of the talk criticises the habit of reacting once a vulnerability is publicly listed in a catalogue such as CISA KEV, by which point weaponised exploits are often already in use. The speaker contrasts a seven-day average for a zero day to be exploited with a 197-day average for an enterprise to remediate a critical vulnerability. Early-warning ideas include AI-built decoy systems that look realistic enough to study attacker techniques, weapon testing in countries with lower cybersecurity awareness, analysis of dark web chatter for intent, and human intelligence from contacts who know threat actors. The speaker also notes that EPSS is a statistical exploitation score and is less useful than real-time exploitability data tied to an organisation's own assets. A hospital case shows the cost of ignoring known issues: an unpatched edge VPN led to privilege escalation, and ransomware kept the hospital offline for two months.

The closing takeaways are to first see every asset, quantify risk, and understand which compensating controls are in place. Success should be measured by what is actually remediated, not by the number of alerts handled.

talks.title: Photographing Nature: Expanding Human Understanding
talks.teaser: Stacked nature photographs expose hidden animal rhythms, senses, and decisions operating beyond ordinary human perception.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes how pandemic lockdown led her to study local wildlife from her window and pursue photo stacking: many frames from one fixed viewpoint merged into composites with hundreds or thousands of layers. She walks through images of pelicans approaching from opposite directions, spiraling patterns in water and flight, and vultures riding thermal updrafts for hours without flapping.

The middle of the talk shifts from visible motion to senses humans lack. Bats shout at volumes comparable to jet engines; sea turtle embryos coordinate hatch timing through calls inside eggs; mice sing above human hearing. Starling flocks coordinate with lags too brief for people to notice, and falcon chase photos hint at group decisions at speeds that look chaotic from the ground.

She closes by arguing that familiar scenes still hold maps of magnetism, smell, sound, and time scaled differently than human experience. The intended takeaway is expanded curiosity: kinship with other species alongside respect for how alien their perceptions remain.

talks.title: Crush Cred Stuffing: A Method for Neutralizing Credential Stuffing Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows how to spot distributed credential stuffing through traffic frequency analysis and shut it down with blocking and alerting.
talks.summary:
The talk explains credential stuffing, in which breached username and password pairs are replayed against login pages, and how it differs from brute force guessing. The speaker argues the threat matters because reused passwords lead to account takeover, data breaches, lost customer trust and compliance penalties. The focus is on widely distributed attacks that spread requests across huge numbers of IP addresses and often begin with a sharp traffic spike that plateaus and then drops.

The core method is frequency distribution analysis over logged fields, compared against baseline traffic. One example attack came from about 1,000 IPs, with a baseline near 80 requests per second and a peak around 3000. Another came from 16,000 IPs. Low-and-slow variants evade per-IP counting rules, while a handful of autonomous system numbers can account for most of an attack, making ASN blocking possible at the cost of some false positives. TLS fingerprints and user agents help, but they can be rotated or shared by many legitimate clients. Endpoint flow checks revealed attackers imitating the visit to the login page before posting. A uniform time zone across traffic from many regions gave a quick signal for blocking.

For immediate action, the speaker recommends enforcing MFA, using password managers, cataloguing web-facing login endpoints and automating log collection when alerts fire. Over a longer horizon, he suggests building traffic and frequency analysis into security team training, alerting on rate of change rather than static thresholds, and adding challenge-response controls.

talks.title: CEO Panel: The Entrepreneur Journey to Scale
talks.teaser: Seasoned cybersecurity founders share scar-tissue lessons on narrative, fundraising, fit, culture, and scaling new security companies.
talks.summary:
A moderated CEO panel opens by comparing startup building to crossing a minefield and promising a practical map drawn from decades of founding, investing in, and running cybersecurity companies. Each executive briefly introduces their current venture and path: cloud-based cyber range simulation, industrial OT security, and AI-assisted application security, alongside an investor who has backed many cyber startups.

The middle of the session digs into how new categories get funded and sold. Panelists contrast hundreds of venture pitches with investor fit, when “I don’t get it” signals opportunity, and how authentic customer narratives beat buzzwords. They compare qualifying investors early, taking educational meetings that mature into later rounds, due diligence on partners, product-market fit via design partners or services-led delivery, listening for real customer problems, and showing fast time-to-value without hiding the cost of success.

They close on culture as competitive advantage: stated values lived in sales and customer relationships, rapid action on toxic behavior, mission-driven hiring, and candid regrets such as over-hiring under pressure or retaining excellent people who cannot scale with the company. The through-line for practitioners is that scaling security startups depends as much on narrative discipline, commercial proof, and people choices as on technology.

talks.title: Batloader or FakeBat? Unraveling Competing MaaS Operations
talks.teaser: Researchers contrast BatLoader and FakeBat malvertising loaders, underground ad abuse, and defender hunting guidance.
talks.summary:
The session opens with eSentire case data showing that more than half of traced malware intrusions in 2023 came from web browsing and social engineering, especially malicious search ads, overtaking email as the dominant delivery channel. Walkthroughs of Slack-themed campaigns illustrate how verified-looking display URLs, tracking templates, and cloaking hide imposter install pages from both users and ad reviewers.

Anna Pham outlines the underground pipeline for buying aged Google Ads accounts, farming cookies, residential proxies, URL spoofing kits, and cheap brand-themed landing pages. Spence Hutchinson then profiles BatLoader, marketed since 2022 by Afron with per-tenant themed MSIX loaders and Google ads, and the competing FakeBat (EugeneLoader) service from Eugene Fest, which mirrors the model while sourcing certificates and ads through partners such as Balamut Service.

The latter half compares infection chains, obfuscation (PyArmor versus PowerShell symbolic obfuscation), C2 check-in URL patterns, and host fingerprinting behaviors. Practitioners gain concrete hunting guidance for WindowsApps traces, PowerShell event 800, hosting and registrar patterns, JARM-based infrastructure watch lists, MSIX execution controls, and reporting abused code-signing certificates to slow operator turnaround.
