talks.title: Artificial Intelligence: The Ultimate Double-Edged Sword
talks.teaser: A panel weighs how AI both threatens and protects, from election interference to criminal misuse and society's broader risks.
talks.summary:
This RSA panel, moderated by Miriam Vogel, weighs whether AI helps attackers or defenders more. Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco lists threats her department watches: lower barriers for criminals, faster discovery and exploitation of flaws, state repression, and misinformation. Fei-Fei Li of Stanford argues every powerful tool cuts both ways, and that AI can detect fraud and spot patterns no human could.

Elections come next, with the speakers noting many national votes this year. Monaco argues that existing law already bans knowingly spreading false information about when, where or how to vote, and she cites a recent conviction of a social media influencer who told people they could vote by text. That case did not involve AI, but she warns the same scheme could be scaled with it. She also describes Justice Department uses such as triaging more than a million FBI tips a year and sifting large evidence sets, and introduces Justice AI, a series of convenings with civil society, academia and scientists. Li highlights AI-driven scientific discovery and workers augmented by the technology, and cautions that legislation fixated on existential risk can crowd out near-term harms to democracy, fairness and privacy.

Both speakers urge leaders to build trust rather than chase speed, and to widen the pipeline of talent and viewpoints. Li reminds the audience that AI should augment people. The takeaway is that existing legal tools still apply to AI-enabled crime, and guardrails should target present-day societal risks.

talks.title: Teaching Software Engineers to Threat Model: We Did It, and So Can You
talks.teaser: Explains how a large engineering org scaled self-service threat modeling through training, pilots, and embedding it in design docs.
talks.summary:
Late-stage security reviews had become bottlenecks for a company running hundreds of services with a tiny assurance team. Findings arrived after features were built, engineers rarely owned design-time risk, and splitting reviews in half did not reduce total work. The speaker frames a secure developer experience—security that protects without suffocating delivery—and describes interviewing engineering teams, securing buy-in from security reviewers, and choosing blended self-paced training with human support.

The program pairs Shostack’s four questions with STRIDE, stays low-tech on tooling, and slots threat modeling into change design documents so scope stays small. Eight voluntary pilot teams refined templates, guides, and Slack support before a voluntary adoption phase and mandatory requirement for security reviews. After roughly a year, about 200 submitted threat models averaged eight threats each; engineers filed mitigations early, and most reviews arrived with models already attached.

Practitioners hear a crawl-walk-run rollout blueprint: define DevSecOps philosophy, interview teams on real SDLC mechanics, pilot with champions, praise imperfect first attempts, and iterate. Q&A covers legacy systems via detection and compensating controls, qualitative review during security assessments, and pilot data such as training scores and threat counts. Generative AI experiments for design-stage modeling sit on the roadmap.

talks.title: Securing Sexuality: Rewiring the Most Intimate Connections
talks.teaser: Examines how surveillance is being normalized as love, and how technology is reshaping loneliness, scams and connection.
talks.summary:
Stefani Goerlich, a clinical social worker and certified sex therapist who says she has no formal security background, frames the talk as an outsider's look at technology and intimacy. She describes a shift from pull communication to push, where notifications and constant connection reach people whether they want them or not. She uses the Elf on the Shelf holiday toy to argue that families are normalizing being watched, and that this habit carries into adult relationships, where surveillance can be mistaken for love.

She then describes harms she has seen. A young woman's personal details, shared in a Reddit post, were screen-captured and targeted on another forum, which she uses to illustrate online pile-ons. She also covers romance scams, harassment as an unmet request for closeness, dating bots that chat with each other, state laws that reward reporting neighbors over healthcare, deepfakes that make it hard to tell what is real, and keyword-based moderation that blocks sexual health content. She links widespread loneliness to serious health risks and calls it a public health issue.

Her asks for builders are concrete: real authentication and deepfake detection, moderation that looks beyond keywords, data-collection reviews across a person's lifespan, and algorithms that help people connect offline rather than keeping them on screen. She urges threat modeling for intimate partner abuse and loneliness-driven harm, arguing that everything technologists build touches people.

talks.title: CloudSec Hero to Zero: Self-Obsolescing Through Prolific Efficiency
talks.teaser: Applies emergency-medicine triage to inherited cloud environments, ranking exposed credentials and misconfigurations first.
talks.summary:
The talk treats an inherited cloud environment like a mass-casualty incident, borrowing triage, prioritization and operational-period methods from paramedic and disaster response work. The presenters start with a typical scenario: a new cloud security hire takes over several providers, thousands of posture findings and unclear ownership. Their first steps are building an inventory of accounts and owners, confirming logging and telemetry, and running any simple posture scanner to get a plain list of problems.

Findings are sorted into immediate, delayed, minor and expectant groups, so the most dangerous items are fixed first. Examples include publicly writable storage buckets, unneeded root access keys, exposed remote desktop ports and leaked credentials. The speakers outline a universal cloud threat model in which most attacks follow a short sequence: exposed credentials or resources lead to automated misuse of permissions, typically for crypto mining or data extortion. They also describe dangling DNS records that let attackers claim released cloud resources, and a package whose storage bucket was taken over to deliver malware.

Later, they argue for moving from crisis response into repeating operational periods with measurable goals, then building paved roads, guardrails and fixes for systemic causes such as broad network rules and shared IAM users. Tool choices follow budget and staff time, and integration into existing ticketing matters. The takeaway is to deal with the most common, preventable problems at scale before chasing advanced threats.

talks.title: Techniques to Evolve Risk Governance and Comply with SEC Cybersecurity Rule
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Techniques to Evolve Risk Governance and Comply with SEC Cybersecurity Rule.

talks.title: RFID: Flippers and Access Control
talks.teaser: Explains how RFID badges work and how a Flipper Zero reads, emulates and brute forces common access-control cards.
talks.summary:
This introductory session explains how RFID works and how a Flipper Zero can interact with common access-control badges. The speakers start with the physics, showing how a reader powers a tag through an electromagnetic link. They cover access-control frequencies from 125 kilohertz to UHF, and the 26-bit card format with its eight-bit facility code and sixteen-bit card number. A live demo reads a low-frequency card and emulates it to open a door.

The middle section covers attack paths. Badge numbers can sometimes be read from a photo, and a short facility code can be brute forced in at most 256 tries. Sequentially issued credentials make neighbouring card numbers likely to be valid. The speakers compare the Flipper Zero with Proxmark3 and key-copier tools, and show replay of sub-gigahertz remotes. Modern car fobs use changing codes, though keyless relay attacks remain a risk. For NFC systems such as HID iCLASS and MIFARE Classic, a shared key and a weak random number generator undermined protection.

The closing section turns to defense. Suggested steps include choosing encrypted protocols that have not been broken, revoking credentials from departed staff, rotating contractor fobs, avoiding sequential numbering, and enabling brute-force alerting on controllers. Because physical attacks depend on proximity, the speakers argue that moving critical assets can be a sound risk decision.

talks.title: Private Web Search with Tiptoe
talks.teaser: Presents Tiptoe, a private web search engine that ranks results over encrypted queries without learning what users search for.
talks.summary:
Alexandra Henzinger presents Tiptoe, a prototype private web search engine. Conventional engines must read each query to answer it, so their logs reveal sensitive details about users. Tiptoe has the user encrypt the query under a locally stored key, so the server computes over ciphertexts and never learns what was asked or which page is returned.

The design has two steps. Semantic embeddings, stored on the client, turn search into a nearest-neighbour problem, and documents are grouped into clusters whose centroids the client fetches ahead of time. The client picks the closest cluster and sends an encrypted query vector; the server returns encrypted similarity scores, and the client decrypts them to find the best match. Limits include a full index scan on the server, a single-cluster check that can miss the true best match, and no hiding of query timing.

On a public crawl of about 360 million pages, Tiptoe returned results in roughly three seconds. Compared with Coeus, the earlier private system over about five million Wikipedia pages, it used about 6,000 times less server computation and 60 times less communication per query, at the cost of roughly 0.3 gigabytes of client storage. Result quality is below Google or Bing, works best on conceptual queries, and struggles with rare strings like names. The takeaway is that private web search is feasible, and the nearest-neighbour protocol could serve recommendations or advertising.

talks.title: Burnout in Cyber: The Intersection of Neuroscience, Gender, and Wellbeing
talks.teaser: Explains the neuroscience behind cybersecurity burnout, gendered pressures on women in the field, and a guided calming practice.
talks.summary:
Peter Coroneos and Kayla Williams approached burnout in cybersecurity from two directions. Williams, a CISO, described always-on expectations, staff cuts that shift responsibility onto fewer people, and a Devo survey of 200 security leaders in which 83% of IT security professionals said burnout had led to errors that caused breach incidents. She also described how women on her own team felt pressure to appear upbeat, and how she set boundaries and gave her team protected time for learning.

Coroneos explained the neuroscience. The limbic system's threat response evolved for physical danger and normally switches off once the danger passes, but virtual threats give no such signal, so stress stays switched on. He cited an ongoing baseline study that tracks emotional exhaustion, cynicism and lack of professional efficacy, and said cyber rates were worse than those of frontline healthcare workers. He then led the room through the iRest protocol, a guided practice that moves attention from thoughts to body sensations, with heart rates checked on watches before and after. Williams said hers dropped from 118 to 87.

The closing advice covered individuals setting boundaries and leaders paying attention to staff who seem tired or withdrawn. Attendees were pointed to a QR code for the baseline study and to downloadable research and program information.

talks.title: Builders and Breakers: Partnering for Secure Elections
talks.teaser: Panelists recount how voting equipment makers and researchers tested prototype machines through coordinated disclosure.
talks.summary:
Election equipment has to be trusted, yet the panel explains that researchers and vendors were once wary of each other. The IT-ISAC's election industry group set out to bridge that gap with a coordinated vulnerability disclosure program. The concept took about five years to reach a live event, held in September 2023, where manufacturers brought prototype equipment that was not yet fielded, including ballot marking devices, ballot scanners and electronic poll books.

Researchers with hardware, API, web, cloud and infrastructure skills first attended a short education session on how elections and their supply chain work, then tested the systems over three days. The scope widened as trust grew between the two groups. Most findings were rated low risk and concerned tamper resistance and routine software issues, while others involved how counties deploy the systems on election day. Three vendor reports were released alongside the event report, and the panelists described the systems as hard targets.

The discussion then turned to next steps: more testing time, involving researchers in threat modeling, wider stakeholder participation, compensating researchers, and spreading word of mouth. Panelists also noted that disclosure timelines are constrained because an election is almost always underway somewhere, and that a vulnerability does not necessarily mean it was exploited.

talks.title: Securing and Governing Generative AI: Learnings from Microsoft
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft's internal security team governs generative AI use through data labeling, inventory, review boards and controls.
talks.summary:
The talk describes how Microsoft's internal enterprise security team approached generative AI, from an early engagement with OpenAI through to employee use and product integration. Instead of treating AI as something requiring an entirely new process, the team assessed each scenario and threat model against existing enterprise requirements, such as encryption, logging and monitoring, with data protection as the central concern.

The program rests on several pillars. Data classification and labeling came first, with SharePoint coverage rising to close to 95% from roughly 20% three or four years earlier so AI tools could inherit labels. A daily crawl of about 80,000 Azure subscriptions inventoried where AI services were used and who owned them, and existing secure development and continuous assurance tooling was extended to AI. A responsible AI organization, steering committees and a deployment safety board review development and release, while an AI red team tests applications before launch.

A cautionary case came when a rapid block on external LLM sites, applied at noon, also caught OpenAI. Help desk calls rose and press coverage followed, so the block was lifted within about two hours. The speaker's takeaways are to get classification and labeling widely adopted first, build transparency into internal AI projects, apply zero trust to sensitive data, and reuse existing processes rather than inventing new ones.

talks.title: The Evolution of Industrial Cyberthreats: Year in Review Report
talks.teaser: Surveys how industrial threats and OT environments have evolved, with case studies and practical defense priorities.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how industrial control environments have changed and why that shifts the threat picture. Sites once differed so much that attackers gained little reusable know-how, while today's standardized, digitized plants share equipment and software across sectors. That efficiency concentrates expertise with contractors, making root cause analysis harder. A combined-cycle gas plant case shows the point: a turbine restarted unexpectedly, and the cause was a touchscreen HMI that insects triggered during a maintenance window.

The middle reviews the past year's threat activity. A group tracked as VOLTZITE pre-positioned inside a mid-sized US electric utility, whose IT network was breached while attempts to reach OT failed for more than 300 days until monitoring flagged it. Another group targeted an Oracle E-Business Suite supplier portal to reach manufacturing lines. Most activity relied on public proofs of concept and known vulnerabilities, and about a quarter of industrial ransomware cases involved LockBit. Vulnerability disclosures often contained errors, and most advisories lacked practical mitigations.

The closing takeaways focus on priorities. Vulnerabilities should be ranked by operational impact rather than CVSS, since only a few percent typically demand immediate action. Asset identification should come before segmentation, and detection and response need data gathered in advance. The speaker proposed five critical controls, drawn from known industrial attacks and tested against scenarios such as ransomware, Crash Override and Pipe Dream.

talks.title: Another Digital ID: Privacy-preserving Humanitarian Aid Distribution
talks.teaser: Shows how smart cards and cryptographic tags can run aid handouts while keeping recipients' data private.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how humanitarian aid such as food, blankets and hygiene items is handed out in crisis settings, based on work with the International Committee of the Red Cross. Paper lists break down at scale, registration is usually done per household, eligibility often relies on village elders, and recipients may lack identity documents. A central digital database of records and biometrics brings connectivity and privacy risks, and a biometric system run by WFP in Yemen met government pushback.

The proposed design keeps records on a smart card held by each household instead of a central server. The card generates a household key and stores the entitlement, while a biometric sample binds it to a recipient without a central biometric database. At distribution, the card produces a tag from the key and the current round, so a repeat pickup in the same round is caught. Signed outputs and commitments let auditors check totals by adding commitments, revealing far less than individual records. A smartphone version swaps in anonymous credentials and pseudonyms.

The speaker is candid about the limits. Deduplication across households is hard because households are social constructs without reliable ground truth. Other open issues include vouching by village elders, revoking lost cards, updating software in the field, aid-worker training and cost, and the gap between a prototype and a deployed system that needs funded teams. The takeaway is that careful design can cut privacy harm, and that working with NGOs and affected communities matters.

talks.title: Benchmarking Threat Resilience Metrics aka How Do We Compare to Our Peers?
talks.teaser: A compact purple team test plan produces a single threat resilience score for comparing against industry peers.
talks.summary:
Kristin Esbeck and Tim Wainwright open with a familiar problem: leadership wants a board-level story about MITRE ATT&CK, but the framework is a large matrix that does not show how well an organization detects real adversaries. Drawing on Kristin's years building ATT&CK and running purple team exercises at MITRE, they argue for a threat-informed approach that tests detection rather than vulnerability. A pen test finds weaknesses, while a purple team checks whether defenders can see an attacker once a foothold is gained.

The method they describe builds an industry index. Threat intelligence, SOC and incident response staff take part in sector workshops and pick the adversaries and techniques seen that year, producing a compact test plan of about 50 cases mapped to ATT&CK. Each result is sorted by outcome: blocked, alerted, centrally logged, local telemetry, or none. They walked through the free VECTR platform and showed how heatmaps can expose analytics that look present on paper but do not fire in practice. Scores are compared against industry distributions, with an average of 57% and a best result seen so far of about 85%. One example moved from 56% to 76% after the organization focused its limited resources on early-stage detection.

For practitioners, the takeaways were to aim for continuous improvement rather than perfection, since a lower score can still push the burden of perfection onto attackers. They recommended running the test at least twice a year, because threat techniques change faster than an annual test. Keeping red, blue, SOC, intelligence and GRC staff in the same room keeps results honest and makes them jointly owned. Tracking scores over time also shows when a tooling change, such as swapping a command and control framework, causes a dip.

talks.title: Building a Cloud Security Flywheel: Lessons from the Field
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Building a Cloud Security Flywheel: Lessons from the Field.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Shaun, a SANS instructor and former NSA security professional now at GitHub, presents a structured approach to building cloud security programs in existing deployments. Rather than prescribing technical solutions alone, he addresses the "it depends" problem by offering a three-stage flywheel strategy that balances security impact with organizational friction, applying lean startup methodology to cloud security implementation.

## Key Topics

**Stage 1: Low-Friction Foundations**
The speaker recommends three immediate priorities: (1) Activity Logs (CloudTrail in AWS, Activity Logs in Azure) deployed across all accounts and regions to capture API management events; (2) Security tooling like GuardDuty and Defender that auto-detect threats without disrupting development workflows; (3) Storage account logging for forensic capability, framed as a policy decision requiring stakeholder documentation rather than automatic implementation.

**Stage 2: Developer Engagement**
Once foundations are established, initiate conversations with development teams. First, identify and decommission unused resources (untagged VMs, orphaned storage accounts) to reduce attack surface and demonstrate cost savings. Second, audit identity access—remove unused accounts, reduce over-permissioned identities, enforce least-privilege IAM roles. Third, discover sensitive data (PII, credentials) in unexpected locations using tools like AWS Macie, establishing data classification processes.

**Stage 3: Organizational Guardrails**
Implement hard controls requiring cross-functional agreement: service control policies blocking insecure deployments, mandatory golden images and infrastructure-as-code for consistent patching, network segmentation (private endpoints, bastion hosts) removing systems from the public internet. This stage tests organizational appetite for security-first deployment processes.

## Technical Details

**AWS-specific implementations**: CloudTrail for centralized activity logging via AWS Organizations; GuardDuty for threat detection across accounts; IAM Access Analyzer to detect over-privileged roles; Macie for PII detection in S3; Service Control Policies as organizational guardrails; AWS Config with Lambda for automated remediation.

**Azure-specific implementations**: Activity Logs and subscriptions as security boundaries; Defender for Cloud; Azure Policy for cross-subscription enforcement and auto-remediation; sign-in logs for identity usage tracking; limitations in native S3-equivalent logging requiring policy-based solutions.

**Key Distinction**: AWS accounts are hard security boundaries requiring per-account management via AWS Organizations; Azure subscriptions are softer boundaries with broader federation capabilities, particularly via Azure Policy.

**Cost-Benefit Strategy**: Offset increased logging and detection costs by identifying wasteful resources (unused VMs, unpatched systems, cloud sprawl), achieving cost neutrality while improving security posture.

## Takeaways

- Begin with low-friction, high-impact changes that don't disrupt existing workflows to build organizational momentum
- Apply lean startup principles: test assumptions, obsess over metrics, iterate rapidly based on organizational feedback
- Distinguish between technical problems (solved by frameworks and tools) and organizational friction (solved through communication, process, and phased adoption)
- The flywheel effect: each successful implementation reduces friction for the next phase, accelerating security maturity
- Address the "it depends" problem by providing context-specific guidance that accounts for current deployment stage (greenfield vs. brownfield), organizational structure, and risk tolerance
- Make security operational through documentation, repeatable processes, and automation to ensure sustainability beyond individual implementers
- Investigate environment thoroughly before imposing guardrails to understand legitimate business needs and avoid blanket restrictions

talks.title: You’re Doing It Wrong! Common Security Anti Patterns
talks.teaser: Explores common security anti-patterns in strategy, SOC work and IT collaboration, and how outcome-driven thinking helps avoid them.
talks.summary:
Mark Simos and John open with the idea that security anti-patterns are recurring habits that are either ineffective or counterproductive. They frame the problem as technology-centric thinking, silver bullet expectations that a single tool or product will solve security, and a blame culture that pushes people to hide behind technical facts. The speakers stress that this is a blameless discussion aimed at improving the field, not criticising individuals.

The middle of the talk covers specific patterns. In security operations, they describe collecting every log without a strategy, buying each new tool as it appears, and repeatedly blocking the same indicators instead of closing the technique gap with IT teams. Other examples include a firewall or policy set so large that nobody can reason about it, security being brought in only to sign off late in a project, and critical systems being exempted from controls. They identify privileged access as the point where attacks usually escalate, urge teams to know their high-value assets, and argue that identity, endpoint and email deserve as much attention as the network.

The closing advice is to start from security outcomes, such as reducing the time attackers keep access, and to tackle the cheapest attacker techniques first. Teams should share technical and business summaries of attacks so IT, business and security work as one group. The speakers also point to the Pyramid of Pain as a way to aim defences at attacker behaviour that is harder to change than IP addresses or hashes.

talks.title: You Can't Measure Risk
talks.teaser: Examines why common risk scores fail to prioritize work, aggregate scenarios, and motivate security change in organizations.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a one-shot dice-wager thought experiment to show that acceptable loss depends on context and means, not tidy expected-value math. It then separates how security professionals use the word risk: hazards such as misuse, design flaws, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and broken processes; losses and incidents; adversaries; and scored environments. A complete risk is a scenario—adversary plus hazard leading to loss—not any label used alone.

Organizations measure risk mainly to communicate, compare peers, and justify change. The talk maps board, CISO, vendor, and operator incentives through discovery, scoring, prioritization, and mitigation, including nine-box models, hygiene versus severe issues, and Akamai’s incident-severity and surprise framing. It critiques CVSS 2.0’s arithmetic quirks, actuarial annualized loss expectancy justifications, and FAIR-style dollar-and-frequency estimation, plus the logical traps when merging or averaging scenario scores across assets or mergers.

Practical guidance favors fixing the easiest high-value tier-two item instead of endless ranking, recognizes risk homeostasis and perceived risk when budgets tighten, and treats posture, maturity, and compliance reporting as communication ceilings and floors. Common executive heatmaps and frameworks are read through that lens. The close urges spending less energy chasing perfect numbers, aligning language with each audience—including dollar figures for finance when that unlocks action—and investing in work that visibly reduces harm.

talks.title: Costume Jewelry: How Capital One Uses Tokenization to Protect Data
talks.teaser: Shows how Capital One uses tokenization and enterprise-wide scanning to protect sensitive data, plus the lessons from scaling it.
talks.summary:
Andy Ozment of Capital One explains the problem: the company treats data as readable whenever an application can see it, even if it is encrypted at rest, because a compromised admin account or application could expose it. Tokenization is its preferred fix after deletion, chosen over plain encryption mainly for simpler key management, resistance to brute forcing, and the ability to keep a field's format so applications need fewer changes.

The talk then walks through the program's stages. A manual inventory of existing applications turned out more valuable than expected, but an in-house scanner built from late 2018 was needed to find sensitive fields at scale. The team accepts high false positive rates on purpose so true positives are not missed. Scanning covers S3 buckets, the data lake and the Snowflake staging area, while databases are dumped to S3 for one-time scans. Findings are grouped by column, case and owner, with 10 days to triage and 120 days to fix, and the data cost is tracked at $50,000 a petabyte. Tokenization volume grew from 20 million operations a month in 2017 to 160 billion now.

Ozment closes with lessons learned. Treating the work as detection and response rather than a one-time adoption project would have served the team better from the start. Free text fields and spreadsheets remain the hardest cases, and reviewers now get a managed clean room instead of copying data into buckets. For smaller firms, he advises buying a product that meets latency and scale needs rather than building one, and he estimated the in-house build took roughly 10 to 20 developers over four or five years.

talks.title: Old McDonald Had a Server Farm—A I, A I, Oh!—A Mock Trial
talks.teaser: A mock trial weighs privacy harms when generative AI infers a public figure's secret hobby from stolen retail orders.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a nursery-rhyme titled fictional breach chain: an attacker compromises a cloud retailer holding Dolls-R-Us orders in cleartext, publishes them on the dark web, and a celebrity-gossip generative AI later ingests that material. Cage fighter Bob Flex, who buys dolls privately as Ken Carson, loses endorsements after Nosy Neighbor AI mentions doll collecting during a live broadcast, prompting a privacy suit in Moscone Federal Court.

Plaintiff and defense counsel deliver opening and closing arguments framed as a jury trial. Expert witness Dazza Greenwood explains prompts, inference, training-data rights, logging, and frameworks such as NIST AI RMF, then describes running roughly one thousand prompts that linked Ken to Flex only after dark-web purchase data was included. Nosy Neighbor CEO Hoyt Kesterson admits broad data collection, response filtering focused on defamation and racism, and deferred source logging while prioritizing speed to market.

The judge treats the audience as law clerks; opinions split on whether downstream AI users should block stolen breach data, whether inferences from public leak sites create liability, and how GDPR or CCPA might apply. The bench ruling finds no liability for Nosy Neighbor, while closing discussion stresses that inference at scale will force new expectations for data custody, provenance, and safeguards beyond gossip-style filters.

talks.title: Blackjack and Breaches: History of Ransomware on the Casino Industry
talks.teaser: Traces a decade of ransomware and data breaches at casinos, with social engineering as a recurring weak point.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that casinos are attractive ransomware targets because they hold large amounts of both money and customer data, and it walks through a timeline of attacks. It recounts a 2014 breach at the Venetian and Palazzo in Las Vegas, where hacktivists replaced website content with internal records including employee information, an incident said to have cost about $40 million. It then covers payment card malware at six Golden Nugget venues between 2014 and 2015, and malware at Hard Rock locations from 2015 to 2017 that customers noticed only when their cards were misused.

The middle section focuses on social engineering. The 2023 MGM attack began with a call to the help desk from someone posing as an employee locked out of their account. Slot machines, room keys and online booking were disrupted for about ten days, with an estimated loss of $8.4 million a day. Caesars paid roughly $15 million of an approximately $30 million demand after an outsourced IT support vendor was socially engineered, and its operations were not disrupted. The speakers also review ransomware incidents at tribal casinos from 2020 to 2022 and the growing exposure from IoT devices, RFID-enabled gaming tables and cloud or mobile platforms.

For practitioners, the speakers recommend layered defenses: separate privileged admin accounts, stronger multi-factor authentication such as authenticator apps and biometrics, and identity and access management. They also advise keeping work and personal identities apart, giving role-based social engineering training, and segmenting networks while testing response and recovery plans regularly.

talks.title: Quantum Cyber Risk: How Deep and How Wide?
talks.teaser: Panelists map post-quantum readiness after NIST standards: inventories, sector gaps, supply chain pressure, and why hygiene beats waiting.
talks.summary:
The panel treats a cryptographically relevant quantum computer as a serious future threat to asymmetric encryption, while stressing that expected NIST federal information processing standards are a starting point, not the end of migration. Speakers argue organizations should inventory cryptographic use and sensitive data now, test draft algorithms ahead of final publication, and match protection duration to real confidentiality needs, including concern about harvest-now-decrypt-later collection of traffic that must stay secret for years.

Conversation spans CISA’s critical-infrastructure guidance and federal civilian cryptography inventories, NSA’s longer validation path for national security systems, and industry movement toward crypto agility and broader crypto resiliency with stronger key governance. Panelists compare prior crypto transitions and Y2K-style preparation without a firm deadline, sector differences such as OT-heavy water utilities, international variation in how customers adopt standards, and executive messaging that frames the work as an IT upgrade rather than distant quantum hype. Supply-chain questionnaires, FedRAMP-style requirements, and secure-by-design incentives appear as practical drivers; most panelists prefer coordinated risk management over regulation as the main lever.

On technical choices, NSA’s stated position favors post-quantum cryptography over quantum key distribution for the shortest practical path, while Dell Research notes limited software performance penalty but harder embedded and IoT refresh cycles. Graham Steel suggests discovery and planning may consume most of the journey; Mike Jenkins urges protecting data in transit as early as possible. The session ends with audience questions on discovery tooling coverage, professional services needs, QKD versus hybrid models, and hardware limits before thanking the panel.

talks.title: Experts May Decide if You Are a Hero or Will Wear Orange
talks.teaser: Litigation and forensic experts explain how breach response choices and documentation get scrutinized by regulators and courts.
talks.summary:
This panel looks at how a breach response is judged after the fact by plaintiffs' attorneys, regulators and courts. The speakers, litigation consultants and forensic specialists, say that decisions get reviewed in hindsight. Materiality, they note, is weighed by data sensitivity, business interruption, whether a shared vendor touched many customers, and any effect on financial reporting.

Documentation was the recurring theme. Responders should record facts rather than opinions, since one internal message blaming earlier warnings can dominate a court record and memories fade over years of litigation. Privilege was described as covering opinions shared with counsel, not facts or business changes. For breached data, one expert noted that class membership depends on whether fields such as Social Security numbers were encrypted, and that sampling assumptions must be written down. Another said dark web listings are often misattributed when analysts misuse search tools.

The session closes with practical advice: build repeatable, defensible processes before an incident, rehearse them in tabletop exercises, and bring counsel in early. In Q&A, the panel agreed that deciding when to involve lawyers is hard because an incident's scope is unknown at the start.

talks.title: From Attribution to Accountability: Upholding International Rules Online
talks.teaser: Officials, Microsoft and the ICRC weigh how public attribution of cyber attacks supports accountability under international rules.
talks.summary:
This panel looks at how attribution of malicious cyber activity has developed over roughly eleven years, and why it matters when many attacks are not carried out by states. Speakers from the US and UK governments, Microsoft and the International Committee of the Red Cross describe their own approaches. The government speakers outline a layered process: technical attribution comes first, followed by a political decision coordinated across agencies, often with partner countries joining in. The UK describes running campaigns in response to patterns of behaviour rather than answering every incident, and says private sector reporting feeds into its assessments.

Microsoft explains that it tracks hundreds of nation-state affiliated groups, publishes technical findings to protect customers, refers information to governments and files civil court cases, where the evidence must be strong. The Red Cross says it does not attribute publicly. It needs to establish who did what and why in order to determine which international humanitarian law rules apply, and it raises open legal questions, such as whether data counts as a civilian object. The panel cites a case in which an attack on Albania was attributed to Iran and tied directly to a norm protecting critical infrastructure. It also describes the UK's attribution of a 2021 attack on its electoral commission to China as aimed at building resilience, shaping norms and imposing reputational costs. The speakers note that China responded by demanding evidence and then did not follow up.

On criminal groups, the panel discusses naming individuals. Microsoft has named individual defendants in recent civil cases, and the UK's National Crime Agency coordinated a LockBit takedown with sanctions against a named person. The main takeaway is that attribution is most effective as part of a sustained, coalition-based campaign, combined with sanctions, law enforcement and resilience measures, and that more work remains on how international law applies online.

talks.title: Tech Diplomacy: Building Cyber Resilience Together
talks.teaser: Panelists from five governments discuss cyber diplomacy, UN cybercrime talks, and resilience support for Ukraine.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with moderator Tarah Wheeler asking five diplomats how they came to represent their governments on cyber policy. Germany's cyber ambassador describes the post's revival after the Snowden revelations, while Ukraine's deputy foreign minister, who comes from an IT background, explains how the war has pushed cyber resilience onto the diplomatic agenda.

Much of the discussion centres on the Tallinn Mechanism, a coalition that coordinates civilian cyber emergency support for Ukraine. Estonia's ambassador says the name came from a vote, and Poland describes taking the coordinating back-office role while donors work through different legal systems. The panel also covers public attribution of state actors, with the US ambassador arguing it should rest on forensically verifiable technical evidence and be backed by multiple countries. Germany outlines its China strategy as a mix of partner, competitor and strategic rival. On the UN cybercrime treaty, speakers debate whether talks with Russia are worthwhile, with several arguing that diplomacy must continue even when it is hard.

The closing message is that cyber security cuts across government, military and society, so no single country can secure itself alone. Capacity building for countries in the middle ground is presented as a way to strengthen shared security. Audience questions on AI policy and the balance between security and free expression lead panelists to stress that technology can be used for good or harm.

talks.title: Avoid Being Accidentally Offensive (Guys Guide to Being An Ally)
talks.teaser: Offers workplace guidance for men on avoiding accidental exclusion and becoming better allies to underrepresented colleagues.
talks.summary:
Forrester analysts Jeff Pollard and Joseph Blankenship frame this session as a guide for men who want to be allies to underrepresented colleagues in security. Their premise is that most people support inclusion yet still act in exclusive ways, usually without meaning to. They stress that educating peers should not always fall on the people being excluded, and that deliberate harassment is a separate matter outside the scope of their advice.

They walk through accidental exclusion: unwanted hugs and touching, remarks about smiling more, assumptions about who the expert in a room is, interrupting colleagues, blocking someone's exit in a cubicle, and defaulting women to note-taking or party planning. Their advice centers on basic etiquette, letting people finish their thoughts, inviting quiet colleagues in, complimenting accomplishments rather than appearance, volunteering for tasks before they get assigned by gender, and praising colleagues when they are absent. On mentorship, they note that mentees must choose their mentor and need guidance suited to their own circumstances.

In the audience questions, attendees described being mistaken for event staff at vendor booths and being told a presenter could not be a hacker because of her shoes. Suggested responses included calling out interruptions politely, thanking someone for a view without engaging, and separating a mistake from one's character. The closing message is that allyship takes ongoing effort, and a sincere apology includes a commitment to change.

talks.title: Operation Cookie Monster & Genesis Market: An International Cyber Takedown
talks.teaser: FBI investigators explain how a multinational operation dismantled the Genesis Market credential marketplace.
talks.summary:
Genesis Market was an invite-only marketplace that opened around 2017 and grew in 2018. It sold stolen credentials, cookies and device fingerprints, and its Chromium plugin and custom browser let buyers emulate a victim's machine closely enough to get past multifactor checks. The speakers cited roughly half a million infected machines and about 80 million stolen credentials, with victims in nearly every country.

The FBI's Milwaukee cyber squad opened its investigation in 2018 and imaged the marketplace's backend servers twice, in late 2020 and early 2021. User counts rose from about 33,000 to 59,000 over that period. Rather than focusing only on administrators and infrastructure, the team targeted the users. They narrowed the list using location, money flows and operational security levels, working through a sprint with Europol and private sector partners.

The coordinated action on April 4 and 5, 2023 involved 424 law enforcement actions across several time zones, domain seizures and a concurrent Treasury sanction. Afterwards, bot ingestion fell to 128 in a month, users openly doubted the market, and Genesis offered the whole platform for sale before its Tor site vanished. The speakers urged organisations to enforce multifactor authentication, patch systems, avoid pirated software, prepare incident response plans and report incidents to IC3.

talks.title: Apocalypse Avoided: The Future According to the Four Horsemen of Cyber
talks.teaser: Officials deliver Buckshot Yankee origins, Iraq fusion lessons, and Pentagon briefings that launched U.S. Cyber Command.
talks.summary:
The session reunites four senior officials who helped conceive U.S. Cyber Command, framed as their first joint public appearance since those early years. The arc opens with Buckshot Yankee in 2008, when Defense Department leaders discovered malware on warfighting networks—including classified systems—and faced daily crisis meetings while struggling even to inventory machines on the network.

Panelists tie that shock to parallel lessons from Iraq, where NSA teams supported brigades and built real-time regional gateway capabilities to fuse insurgent communications and accelerate targeting. They describe a short “implementation team” assignment that stretched into roughly fifteen months: merging global network defense with network warfare, educating senior leaders who barely used email, and road-testing a visual “cyber storyboard” narrative across the Pentagon, industry storytellers, skeptics in policy offices, tabletop exercises, and eventually Congress—with memorable logistics around portable screens, classified lock bags, and keys.

They emphasize the dual-hatted NSA–Cyber Command model, fast iteration under General Alexander’s mentorship, and tensions among agencies that later eased as CISA matured. Closing reflections highlight unforeseen growth of private-sector ownership of infrastructure, interagency collaboration on elections and critical infrastructure, integrating authorities across commands, and treating cyber risk as executive accountability—from combatant commanders then to corporate boards now.

talks.title: Risk Profiles: Why Some Employees Attract Danger and Others Dodge It
talks.teaser: Research on over 67,000 employees explains who faces more attacks and who is likelier to click phishing links.
talks.summary:
The presentation asks why some people in an organization draw more successful attacks than others, rejecting the idea that employees are simply the dumbest link. Risk is defined as vulnerability: how often someone is targeted and how likely they are to fall for phishing, malware, or risky browsing.

Findings draw mainly on Elevate Security customer telemetry spanning more than ten companies and about 67,000 employees. Managers see more phishing than individual contributors, with higher monthly volumes; U.S. staff rank among the most attacked geographies; and attack rates rise with tenure as addresses spread. Likelihood to fail ties to cognitive load, inbox density, deadlines, neutralization of policies, hostile workplaces, department norms such as customer service, prior clicks, and diminishing returns from repeated training or roughly ten simulations. A RAND-style view separates factors that are ethical and repeatable to measure from those that are not.

Practitioners are urged to mine email, endpoint, identity, and related logs; segment people into low, medium, and high risk without discriminatory profiling; and protect high-risk users with stronger controls, lighter training where enough, and motivations aligned to what employees already value.
