talks.title: Director's Cut: A Dummies Guide to Leading a Global Cybercrime Program
talks.teaser: Maps Interpol's global cybercrime program via regional capacity building, secure collaboration, and industry data partnerships.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by describing his path from local UK policing and naval communications to directing Interpol’s Global Cybercrime Program from Singapore. He outlines how Interpol operates across 196 member countries as a neutral body with a mandate to reduce—not eliminate—cybercrime harm, and why program management with clear objectives matters when local trust-based policing meets borderless online crime.

He walks through a tiered view of national capability, Interpol’s three workstreams (threat response, operations, and strategy without tying only to “crime” labels), and practical delivery in Africa since 2019: regional desks, vetted platforms instead of ad hoc messaging, working groups scaling from small Nairobi meetings to dozens of countries planning ISP and infrastructure disruptions. He contrasts capacity with capability, cites Nigeria’s unit growth and project-funded support, Americas alignment with Ameripol and a Buenos Aires hub, and shifting strategy toward docking with existing regional bodies amid geopolitical friction. He covers UN negotiations on a new cybercrime convention, Interpol’s four law-enforcement priorities there, data-sharing rules with member states and vendors, LockBit and ransomware coordination, Atlas and Counter Ransomware Initiative partnerships, and major-event operational support.

Practitioners hear that underreporting hides scale, enterprises should engage national law enforcement first and consider expert attachments, and industry datasets can feed global operations when trust and processing rules are respected. He closes by ranking cybercrime as Interpol’s top priority while noting core funding has not kept pace, then answers questions on public-private incentives, prioritization across competing harms, and engagement with difficult jurisdictions.

talks.title: Cloud and Platform Agnostic Security Posture Management (xSPM)
talks.teaser: Explains security posture management terms and shows how a homegrown cloud checker cut detection time to under two minutes.
talks.summary:
The talk sets out to demystify the crowded vocabulary around security posture management, covering CSPM, SSPM, ASPM, DSPM, ISPM, CASB, CWPP and CNAPP. The presenters compare how each category differs in scope, data collection and the cloud, SaaS, application or identity settings it watches, and they point out where tools overlap. They suggest that enterprise buyers can also build their own tooling instead of purchasing a product for every gap.

The middle of the session covers guiding principles that apply whatever the product: shift left, zero trust, a defined standard, simplicity, automation, risk-based prioritization, actionable remediation and open integration. The workflow runs from defining a standard and a short list of top checks, through collecting configuration data and logs, analysis, reporting and remediation. Two examples are shown. The first checks that every Azure Active Directory user has MFA enabled, using a PowerShell script to pull the data. The second checks that databases meet an AES 256 encryption standard, with results split into deviating and compliant resources.

The presenters describe their homegrown cloud posture platform, which reacts to resource changes through event triggers. They say it detects and responds in under two minutes, compared with nine to 10 minutes for commercial tools that poll APIs under throttling limits. They stress that a custom tool covers a few dozen high-value checks rather than hundreds. The takeaways are to match tooling to organizational size and capability, and to keep blueprints current through governance reviews. An audience question about versioning reports when new policies arrive was left as an open gap.

talks.title: Inside Payback: Using Metrics to Demonstrate Insider Risk Program Value
talks.teaser: Shows how to build goal-question-indicator-metric sets that show an insider risk program delivers value to executives and boards.
talks.summary:
Presented by two researchers from the Software Engineering Institute, this session explains how leaders of insider risk programs can show that their work delivers value. The presenters argue that decision makers need information rather than raw data, and they introduce the goal, question, indicator, metric (GQIM) process for linking metrics to organizational objectives. Metrics are built through iterative stakeholder interviews, with indicators that carry defined bounds and benchmarks drawn from peers or regulation.

Randy Trzeciak then covers insider threat specifics. An insider is anyone with authorized access, including contractors and partners, and accidental harm counts as well. Programs can be assessed by whether each component is not, partially or fully implemented, and training results can be measured through pass rates and pre- and post-test scores. For return on investment, security rarely earns revenue, so the speakers suggest weighing avoided losses against staffing, tool and consultant costs, and starting narrowly, as one manufacturer did by focusing only on departing employees.

Audience questions raised privilege accumulation, the effort needed to collect data from spreadsheets, and works council objections in Europe. The closing advice was to treat metrics as a marathon, set expectations that early metrics will evolve, and revisit them as the program matures.

talks.title: Living with Chronic CFIUS: Foreign Investment Review Security Imperatives
talks.teaser: Explains how foreign investment reviews by CFIUS affect cybersecurity companies and what mitigation agreements demand of them.
talks.summary:
This session gives an update on CFIUS, the interagency committee that reviews foreign investment in US businesses for national security risk, and explains why cybersecurity companies draw particular attention. The presenters recap the difference between elective filings, which the committee can review on its own initiative, and mandatory filings, which the law requires for certain technology businesses and government-backed investors. They note that many security vendors count as critical technology businesses because of how they use encryption, and that a license exception can avoid a mandatory filing without removing the committee's elective reach.

Recent changes were a central theme. A 2022 executive order told the committee to weigh supply chains, advanced technologies, cyber risks and sensitive data, and enforcement has since widened to investors from allied countries and sovereign wealth funds. Similar review regimes are spreading abroad, including in France and several European countries. New US rules are planned for outbound investment and for data transactions that involve no investment at all. Proposed enforcement changes would raise the minimum fine from 250k to $5 million.

On mitigation, the second presenter describes national security agreements as deal-specific contracts that often require established cybersecurity frameworks and physical controls, and sometimes a third-party monitor who is paid by the company but answers to the government. The agreements can be vague about purpose and method, and a proposed rule would require a response to a mitigation request within three days. The takeaways: assess foreign investors early, prepare for mitigation before it is requested, bring in counsel experienced with these agreements, and treat monitors as partners. For security vendors, the government's focus on data access, auditability and data location is an opening for services.

talks.title: Building a Safer Future: Navigating Digital Currencies in the Modern World
talks.teaser: A panel surveys crypto crime trends, enforcement priorities, and industry-government collaboration for safer finance.
talks.summary:
The session opens with how programmable money fits into the shift from centralized web services to distributed trust, and how a major bank pursues regulated payment and settlement pilots while watching public-private currency networks. The exchange chief argues blockchain transparency can aid tracing compared with cash, while stressing that criminals follow money into the growing ecosystem.

Discussion then turns to threats facing institutions and victims: darknet-era evolution toward business compromise, pig-butchering and confidence scams, exchange hacks linked to nation-state funding, ransomware, and mixer takedowns such as Sinbad alongside recent prosecutions. Panelists contrast aggregate illicit-volume statistics between fiat and crypto while emphasizing human harm, underreporting, DeFi growth, and fraud amplified by AI and deepfakes. Consumer education, transaction finality, and jurisdictional gaps for programmable assets receive sustained attention.

The close focuses on collaboration: DOJ cryptocurrency enforcement coordination, DAC networks, rapid fund freezes with industry partners, screening for sanctioned flows, and early dialogue with Web3 builders. Speakers urge supervised markets, data-sharing models akin to ISACs, victim reporting, and practical audience education—including slowing rushed financial decisions—to build a safer future.

talks.title: Quantum Safe Computing for Telecommunications
talks.teaser: A telecom panel explores post-quantum readiness, crypto inventories, standards timing, and pragmatic migration paths for carriers.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing post-quantum cryptography as a present-day planning problem rather than distant theory, citing recent EU migration guidance, the U.S. Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act, sector working groups, and expected NIST standard releases. Panelists argue that overhauling RSA- and ECC-based trust is a multiyear effort comparable to replacing structural parts on a ship still at sea, and that procrastination leaves operators facing rushed rip-and-replace cycles across radio access, backhaul, core, and interconnect paths.

Discussion centers on crypto agility—switching algorithms with minimal operational disruption—and on where to begin: map sensitive use cases, run small-scale algorithm trials to understand customer impact, and automate cryptographic discovery instead of manual one-off reviews. Vodafone, IBM, and GSMA’s Post Quantum Telecommunications Network Task Force illustrate a heat-map prioritization model and a deep dive on eNodeB-to-secure-gateway links involving Nokia. NIST finalists such as Kyber and Dilithium are described as shifting work from theory to hands-on labs covering PKI, VPNs, and code signing, while regulation threads through CNSA timelines, EU coordinated roadmaps, and industry standards bodies.

Audience questions bring harvest-now-decrypt-later risk into focus, especially long-lived secrets and live TLS key exposure, versus shorter-lived payment data. Practitioners are urged to iterate on a handful of applications, illuminate leadership, build inventory and crown-jewel prioritization, engage sector consortia, and press vendors on readiness and cryptography bill-of-materials—without expecting instant flips the day standards publish.

talks.title: Navigating Third-Party Risk in OT Environments
talks.teaser: Explains how to manage vendor risk in operational technology through segmentation, remote access limits and contract terms.
talks.summary:
The talk explains operational technology as computers that control physical equipment, from a smart thermostat up to power grids, water valves and factory lines. It argues that vendors and partners with remote access create third-party risk, and that OT systems can run for decades, so security often has to be wrapped around legacy devices that cannot protect themselves.

Much of the middle focuses on controls. Remote access should be granular and recorded, with individual accounts instead of shared logins, and contracts should require vendors to disclose vulnerabilities early rather than after a fix exists. Segmentation comes up repeatedly because OT networks are often flat, so teams may need new VLANs or managed switches to see east-west traffic and build a baseline of normal flows. Case examples include a vulnerability scan that knocked control servers offline and a metering penetration test that reached a control center through a device on a utility pole, both showing how fragile these environments are.

The closing portion covers the people side: bringing procurement and legal teams into vendor negotiations, training SOC staff on OT, building runbooks and running tabletop exercises. Audience questions touched on limited vendor choice, contractors who may not go through procurement and where to find OT-focused communities. The takeaway is to inventory what each third party does, limit and log their access, and treat vendor management as part of business continuity.

talks.title: From Chatbot to Destroyer of Endpoints: Can ChatGPT Automate EDR Bypasses?
talks.teaser: Shows LLM agents hunting EDR telemetry gaps, escalating privileges and dumping credentials in a recorded Caldera demo.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with how endpoint detection and response products gather telemetry. The speakers outline three common sources: user-land API hooks, kernel callbacks that Microsoft offers as the supported alternative to kernel hooking, and Event Tracing for Windows providers. They then cover ways to find telemetry gaps, including parent-child process spoofing and direct system calls that avoid hooked APIs.

The second part presents Caldera GPT, a research system built on the Caldera emulation platform and Microsoft AutoGen. A coordination agent delegates work to a Caldera API agent that runs commands on endpoints, and to a browsing agent that reads tool documentation and public repositories. In the recorded demo, the agents confirm standard user privileges, identify Elastic as the running EDR by comparing services against a list of EDR products, and pick a PowerShell download technique they expect to go unflagged. They then abuse an unquoted service path to gain elevated access after a restart, and use nanodump to dump credentials and exfiltrate the output. The speakers admit they disabled Elastic's automatic flagging of nanodump for the demo and sometimes had to steer the agents.

The takeaway is that language model agents can produce working system commands when paired with a human operator, but they lacked creativity without outside guidance. The speakers suggest that junior red teams could lean on public research the same way, while defenders should map their own telemetry gaps and explore AI for detection rule creation. They also warn that relying on attackers not knowing these techniques is a risky strategy.

talks.title: Beyond the Hype: Research on How Cybercriminals Are Really Using GenAI
talks.teaser: Examines what criminals are actually doing with generative AI, from jailbreak services to deepfake fraud, versus the hype.
talks.summary:
The speakers ask whether criminals are really using generative AI as much as the media claims. They surveyed offerings in the criminal underground and found that earlier AI use in crime centered on tasks like prediction and classification. Newer cases were mostly existing criminal tools with AI features added, such as a phishing tool that connected to GPT-3 to write better emails.

Criminal large language models drew the most attention. The speakers described WormGPT as the only credible attempt at training a model on criminal data. Its developer sold a subscription for a few months and then shut the project down in August 2023 after heavy media exposure. Other branded models, such as FraudGPT and DarkBERT, appeared briefly and their listings vanished within a week, so many were likely scams. A more common pattern was jailbreak as a service, where sellers maintain working prompts that bypass a provider's restrictions and wrap them around requests. Deepfakes are also being sold, including identity-verification bypass for crypto exchanges and video impersonation services. Audio deepfakes were shown to be the more effective tool for targeted fraud and extortion calls.

The speakers argue that criminals adopt technology gradually and only when it beats their current methods. Social engineering, which dominates the most lucrative cybercrime categories in the FBI's internet crime report, is where language models help most. Their practical advice was to stop trusting voice or video alone for high-value transfers, to build verification steps into business processes, and to require live movement on video for identity checks instead of a single photo. They also flagged prompt injection through external content as a near-term risk.

talks.title: The First Decade of Corporate Ransomware
talks.teaser: Traces corporate ransomware from 1989 floppy-disk extortion to today's brand-driven gangs, with lessons for defenders.
talks.summary:
Mikko Hyppönen opens with his decades of analyzing malware, starting with the 1989 AIDS Information Trojan, which he presents as the first ransom trojan. He follows the early DOS-era families and the police-themed lockers of the early 2010s. He explains that CryptoLocker's use of Bitcoin for payment changed the criminal business model, and that early ransomware mostly hit home users and their photos before gangs moved toward bigger corporate targets.

The middle of the talk focuses on 2017, which he treats as the outlier year. WannaCry spread as a worm using an SMB exploit, and the North Korean group behind it failed to collect money because its operator shut down the email channel. NotPetya looked like ransomware but was a wiper written by Russian military intelligence, and it reached Maersk through a Ukrainian financial software update. He then traces ransomware-as-a-service, double extortion, and negotiations in which gangs knew victims' finances, along with law enforcement actions against Hive and LockBit.

He closes by arguing that ransomware will persist as long as victims pay, and that the rise of new entrants makes the threat last for years. His practical advice covers multifactor authentication, patching, timed backup restores, considering devices that are harder to infect, network visibility, and rehearsing how to work during a shock.

talks.title: Harnessing the Strengths of Neurodivergent Staff for Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how neurodivergent traits can strengthen security teams and how managers can support them.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames neurodiversity as differences in how the brain is wired rather than as behavior, and argues that cybersecurity has many people with these traits. Drawing on years of managing ethical hacking, incident response, forensics and development teams, the talk links traits such as pattern spotting, questioning everything and deep focus on special interests to the strengths they bring. It explains how executive function, including impulse control, emotional regulation, planning and sense of time, shapes how people work, and contrasts multi-threaded and single-threaded working styles.

The middle section offers practical guidance. Some roles suit certain styles better, such as operations or penetration testing for one group and forensics or project management for another. Meltdowns are described as nervous-system responses that call for a calm, focused reset rather than discipline. Useful strategies include managing energy across the day, using timers, visible reminders and transition routines, pairing dull tasks with engaging ones, and body doubling. Several tools are shown, including a task-breakdown assistant and a headband that tracks brain activity for focus training. The speaker also argues that rigid interview formats hide candidates' skills and recommends letting people talk through real work.

The closing notes that diagnosis often looks different in women, who may be given an anxiety label instead, and that a poor fit with a workplace is not a character flaw. The main takeaways are to give yourself and others grace, accept different working styles, manage energy and find peer groups where people are accepted as they are.

talks.title: Data-Driven Cyber Policy: From Dream to Reality
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how measurable cyber data could shape US policy, from incident reporting rules to insurance and patching outcomes.
talks.summary:
The panel, guided by a moderator from a Washington think tank, asked whether the United States is getting better or worse at cybersecurity and how that could be measured. Former congressman James Langevin pointed to new institutions and strategies, including CISA, a national cyber director and recent incident reporting legislation, while noting that outcome measurement still lags behind. Eric Goldstein argued that no one can empirically answer the question today, and compared the gap with highway safety and public health programs that track causes and outcomes over time.

Goldstein said the field has good data on exposed internet assets and on reported incidents, but little on the attacker steps in between, and that victims are discouraged from sharing what failed. Jake Olcott described cyber insurers as holders of largely unpublished incident and telemetry data, and discussed a BitSight study finding that government agencies patch known exploited vulnerabilities faster than the private sector. Langevin proposed a Bureau of Cyber Statistics to collect anonymized data, while Goldstein described a nascent CISA working group on cyber insurance data and a proposal to tag incident reports with MITRE ATT&CK techniques.

The panelists linked slow patching to business and change-management constraints and to the sheer volume of vulnerabilities, so secure-by-design efforts that remove whole bug classes were presented as a necessary direction. Market pressure, liability and regulation were named as levers, with labeling regimes emerging abroad. The main takeaway was that data-driven policy needs agreed outcome measures and broad data sharing from the community before it can reliably guide spending decisions.

talks.title: Moving Security Architecture from Art to Engineering
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn security architecture from ad hoc artistry into a repeatable method of artifacts, layers and data-flow analysis.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security architecture is improvised, with every organisation drawing its own diagrams and documents in inconsistent formats. The speaker wants consistent techniques and artifacts that scale from single products to systems of systems. He describes architecture as the significant design decisions that shape a system, where significance is judged by the cost of change, and treats communicating those decisions as the core job. Secure design, data-centric protection, zero trust principles and compliance are presented as four areas to integrate rather than handle separately.

The method begins by establishing context: external drivers such as regulation, the threat landscape and consumer privacy expectations, alongside internal policies and enterprise architecture. A reference enterprise architecture of about 20 models groups domains into categories and services that can serve as a heat map or coverage checklist. The core technique is layered design, shown through a worked case study: a system context diagram of actors and boundaries, a component diagram of functional parts, and a deployment diagram placing those parts on infrastructure. Following data flows through these layers drives threat modelling, and shared responsibility differs by cloud service model.

The closing advice is that security thinking belongs to every architect, with security architects acting as subject-matter experts who also own the security applications they run. Organisations can use the artifact dependency diagram as a maturity heat map, record architectural decisions, and practise the techniques on case studies. Architecture boards gate releases and track cross-programme issues. Even bought products have interfaces and actors that need the same questions, and vendors can be pressed to supply the missing diagrams.

talks.title: A Step-by-Step Guide to Securing Large Language Models (LLMs)
talks.teaser: Presents a layered framework for securing enterprise LLM apps across data, prompts and responses.
talks.summary:
Ravi Ithal opens by noting that large enterprises run hundreds of custom applications, many of which are now being given LLM features. He explains that an LLM app has the same overall shape as a traditional three-tier app, with an added runtime step where private data is pulled in and folded into prompts. Data privacy is the central concern, since a model's learned content cannot be inspected the way a database can. He cites a shopping-site review summary that was steered into producing reverse-shell code.

He maps the OSI model onto LLM security and argues that the language and data layer sits above the application layer, where firewalls, proxies and DLP tools fall short. Risks are grouped by confidentiality, integrity and availability, with availability described as the hardest to control. The proposed method has four steps: inventory LLM apps through cloud provider APIs, protect the lower layers as usual, scan training and retrieval data, then check prompts and responses. Building blocks include data store scanners, on-demand document and text scanners, and an AI policy matcher that uses a second model to enforce plain-language rules.

He closes by warning that using an LLM as a guardrail can cost far more than generating the response itself, and recommends a phased rollout over the coming weeks, months and six months. In audience questions he addressed input filtering, independent enforcement models and alignment with the OWASP LLM Top 10.

talks.title: Cybersecurity for “Have Nots”
talks.teaser: Offers budget-friendly security controls for small teams and explains why common enterprise advice often fails them.
talks.summary:
The talk is aimed at organizations with limited budgets and small security teams, and argues that they cannot simply copy controls recommended for large enterprises. Security is framed as choosing the best use of scarce headcount and budget, and losing one key person hurts a small team far more than a large one. Common advice such as just deploying network access control or disabling NTLM domain-wide is shown to be hard to carry out without substantial resources.

For a low-budget stack, the speaker recommends an affordable EDR agent, moving off on-premises Exchange with help from a managed provider, and keeping file storage in online cloud services with version history. Free built-in features such as larger event log sizes set through group policy, print monitoring, and USB write restrictions are also suggested. For network visibility he points to Security Onion, cheap network taps, and Wazuh as an agent for offline environments, alongside periodic offline backups on inexpensive storage.

The talk closes by urging attendees to report to boards with data rather than feelings and to accept that some attacks will get through, so detection and recovery matter. Practical next steps are a gap assessment, discussing candidate recommendations with management within three months, and reviewing supplier relationships.

talks.title: Data-Driven Cyber Indicators of Malicious Insider Threat
talks.teaser: Three analyses from 150-employee network studies show which exfiltration routes and evasion combos matter most for insider risk detection.
talks.summary:
Organizations running insider risk programs often recycle external-threat detection ideas that poorly fit employees who already know internal workflows. The speaker outlines MITRE’s long-running applied behavioral experiments, emphasizing a 2021 study at a large U.S. defense-industrial base firm where 150 real staff searched internal networks for anti–money laundering material, then collected and removed it under benign, malicious, or super-malicious intent, with the last group drawn from deeply cyber-trained roles.

Sensors on organization-furnished systems captured more than 10 terabytes of activity, supplemented by interviews where visibility ended. The first analysis cataloged 24 exfiltration methods and dozens of evasion behaviors, highlighting nine removal paths rarely seen in benign participants, from phone photos and USB use to draft-email staging and everyday collaboration tools. Many evasions are unsophisticated yet purposeful; after-hours workload showed no meaningful split between groups. A remote-versus-on-premises comparison surfaced roughly 32 potential risk indicators with limited environment-specific drift, while sequence mining across millions of ordered activity chains yielded only 13 useful patterns—suggesting combinations outweigh strict ordering.

Practitioners should prioritize risky search and collection before exfiltration, weight indicator bundles over single events, and avoid assuming remote staff need wholly different rules. The talk closes on MITRE’s emerging Insider Threat Framework, which rejects one-size-fits-all APT models and depends on voluntary, air-gapped sharing of real case data across sectors and organization sizes.

talks.title: Progress in Standardizing Cryptography Extensions for RISC-V Processors
talks.teaser: A panel maps ratified and emerging RISC-V crypto ISA extensions, post-quantum acceleration plans, and how vendors deploy them in silicon.
talks.summary:
The session blends prepared updates with audience Q&A on RISC-V cryptographic instruction extensions. Andrew frames RISC-V as an open, clean-slate ISA where horizontal security governance and task groups specify protections from hardware root of trust through side-channel-aware instructions, memory isolation, and confidential computing building blocks. He surveys near-completion work such as scalar and vector cryptography, shadow stacks, pointer masking, and supervisor-domain isolation, alongside newer efforts including high-assurance crypto, post-quantum support, and capability-oriented memory safety.

Richard details what scalar extensions already deliver: lightweight byte-oriented primitives for AES, SHA2, SHA3, SM3, SM4, and GHASH, grouped profiles for different algorithm sets, data-independent timing rules for heterogeneous implementers, and a portable entropy interface. Vector crypto adds element groups for wide-register acceleration with similar timing guarantees, often aimed at server-class profiles. In progress, high-assurance features emphasize hardware key handles, Wrap-V key wrapping that can preserve masked shares, and full-round AES opcodes intended to reduce register-level leakage during multi-round execution.

Nicola covers the post-quantum task group in active development for Kyber and Dilithium, using instruction profiling to confirm bottlenecks in Keccak, modular arithmetic, and NTT, and proposing dedicated instructions—including fused Keccak rounds and fixed-modulus accelerators targeting large speedups. Graham describes industrial use from low-area secure subsystems with scalar extensions on small cores to vector-backed throughput for communications and HSM-class products. The closing discussion compares crypto ISA extensions with pure software and dedicated accelerators, flexibility as algorithms evolve, RISC-V versus ARM and FPGA from a security standpoint, and expected open-source library support after ratification.

talks.title: Phishing LLMs: Reeling in the Machine
talks.teaser: Compares LLM stacks to three-tier web apps and maps prompt injection, rate limits, and governance to practical defender controls.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by arguing that generative AI applications are not a wholly new security domain. Their runtime paths—gateways, orchestration with plugins, vector data stores—mirror familiar three-tier and microservice designs, which helps explain why MITRE and OWASP already catalog many tactics against them.

A central distinction is that LLMs collapse the control plane and data plane into plain text, making prompt injection akin to injection flaws where malicious instructions are indistinguishable from legitimate ones. Through a customer-success agent scenario, the talk shows how attackers can skip elaborate email phishing and instead use natural language to reveal system prompts, expose plugin scope, or request sensitive resets. Tokenization, embeddings, and context framing are explained as the mechanism behind predictable completions and manipulated outcomes.

Mitigations emphasize controls security teams already know: egress output filtering over weak WAF rules, rate and prompt-size limits against context-window stuffing, role tagging in conversation formats, least privilege for plugins, data governance for poisoning, and STRIDE-style threat modeling. Q&A extends the same lens to agent tool use and vendor due diligence on data residency, retention, and third-party risk.

talks.title: Changing from Probability to Prioritization Method in Risk Measurement
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Changing from Probability to Prioritization Method in Risk Measurement.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Glauco Sampaio, Chief Information Security Officer at Brazilian payment systems company Cielo, discusses how the company transitioned away from traditional vulnerability scoring and probability models toward a context-driven prioritization framework. Faced with thousands of vulnerability findings from scans, penetration tests, war games, threat intelligence, and pipeline code scanning, technical and product teams were overwhelmed by standard 30-day remediation mandates based purely on CVSS. To address this, Cielo aligned cybersecurity with product risk and business appetite by adopting Protection Level Agreements (PLAs), moving from static reports to a dynamic, prioritized risk management model.

### Key Topics
- **Reframing Security as Product Risk**: Shifting the responsibility of remediation to product and technical owners rather than treating security as purely a cybersecurity team problem.
- **Protection Level Agreements (PLAs)**: Introducing Gartner's concept of PLAs (analogous to SLAs) to establish an agreed baseline of protection aligned with organizational risk appetite and budget.
- **Deprecating Probability**: Abandoning traditional probability calculations (e.g., dismissing low-likelihood edge cases like 0.0001% that could still cause severe business impact) in favor of asset criticality and exposure.
- **Culture and Collaboration**: Partnering with business stakeholders and "security champions" across product and infrastructure teams rather than imposing rigid, top-down mandates.

### Technical Details
Cielo established a five-level classification model complemented by dynamic modifiers to determine remediation urgency:
1. **Product / Asset Criticality**: Distinguishing core transaction and revenue-generating systems from lower-impact assets (e.g., public marketing sites).
2. **Level of Exposure**: Assessing whether a system is externally accessible via the Internet or isolated internally via microsegmentation.
3. **Access Control Level**: Factoring in authentication requirements and whether privileged internal access is required to reach a flaw.
4. **Public Exploitation**: Checking whether active public exploits exist for the vulnerability.
5. **CVSS Severity**: Utilizing CVSS ratings as an input rather than the sole driver of remediation timelines.

To reflect internal controls, the framework applies **positive modifiers** (e.g., web application firewalls, virtual patching, workarounds, or active monitoring architecture that grant extended remediation windows) and **negative modifiers** (e.g., regulatory compliance mandates like PCI DSS requiring 30-day fixes, or real-time threat intelligence confirming active exploitation). In practice, this narrowed a backlog of 8,000 high/critical issues down to 35 immediately exploitable, externally facing issues requiring urgent "war room" remediation, while the remainder were prioritized into standard team backlogs.

During implementation, Cielo managed these vulnerability databases using Microsoft Excel, Power BI, and Power Apps before publishing official dashboards to their GRC system. Furthermore, because Cielo does not accept permanent risk, unaddressed vulnerabilities without valid justification carry financial penalties affecting annual bonuses.

### Takeaways
- **Start with Champions**: Begin rollout with supportive product and infrastructure teams who already implement secure architectures to demonstrate clear benefits (such as extended remediation timelines) before expanding company-wide.
- **Treat Risk as a Movie, Not a Picture**: Integrate real-time threat intelligence and incident response data so vulnerability prioritization adapts as threat landscapes change.
- **Formalize Governance**: Update internal policies, involve auditors and risk teams early, and embed security remediation allocations directly into regular engineering backlogs.

talks.title: Seeing Sounds and Hearing Colors: The Vibrant World of Synesthesia
talks.teaser: Explores synesthesia, cross-sensory perception, and a LED violin that visualizes note colors in real time.
talks.summary:
Kaitlyn Hova opens by tracing how a music-theory comment in college revealed that she perceives sounds visually, a trait she later learned is called synesthesia: stimulation in one sense triggering automatic experience in another. She outlines grapheme-color synesthesia, shares personal examples such as colored letters shaping grade-school binder preferences, and cites research suggesting roughly one in twenty-three people may have some form, often unnoticed.

The talk describes how multiple synesthesia types can overlap and produce everyday cognitive quirks, including mismatches between a person’s appearance and the color of their name. She introduces the mild kiki/bouba effect as a window onto how cross-sensory mapping may sit on a spectrum within normal human perception.

To show note-to-color mapping live, she describes the Hovalin, a 3D-printed violin with LEDs programmed to mirror the hues she associates with each pitch while music plays. Listeners leave with a clearer picture of synesthesia’s varieties, its prevalence, and one concrete way technology can make invisible perceptual differences visible.

talks.title: Kubernetes Security: Attacking and Defending Modern Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Maps Kubernetes attack techniques, then covers built-in defenses such as security contexts and network policies.
talks.summary:
The talk, presented by two speakers from Google and Semgrep, starts by explaining containers as ordinary processes isolated with kernel namespaces, cgroups and capabilities. It then introduces Kubernetes as an orchestration layer and breaks down its control plane and node components. A threat model follows, showing how control of a pod, a node or the control plane widens what an attacker can reach.

The middle section maps attack techniques onto a threat matrix for containers, modelled on the MITRE ATT&CK approach. Examples include exposed management dashboards, kubeconfig files found in public code, malicious images in registries, sidecar containers used to hide activity, and scheduled jobs used for persistence. Privilege escalation is shown through privileged containers and over-permissive cluster-admin roles, while credential theft and discovery target secrets, service account tokens and the unauthenticated read-only kubelet API.

The defensive part covers resource limits that curb crypto miners, security contexts, network policies enforced by a CNI plugin, and encryption in transit and at rest. It compares deprecated pod security policies with pod security admission and admission controllers such as OPA Gatekeeper and jsPolicy. The talk closes with audit logging, kubelet hardening and ten practical recommendations, including GitOps workflows that stop single users making unilateral cluster changes.

talks.title: Secret to a Healthier Life? Fun!
talks.teaser: Evidence-backed habits frame fun as playfulness, connection, and flow—and show how delight practices boost mood and resilience.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by challenging the shallow dictionary idea of fun and arguing that peak fun is the feeling of being most alive—visible as an inner radiance in shared moments across everyday life and public life alike. Research from collected stories yields a tighter definition: fun is a feeling built from three overlapping states—playfulness as lighthearted attitude, connection as shared experience with others, and flow as deep presence where time slips away. When all three align, the result is what the speaker labels true fun.

That state is framed as more than pleasant; it boosts energy, resilience, presence, creativity, and social unity while easing burnout and stress, with physical and emotional upsides. Happiness is linked to stacking ordinary fun rather than treating it as optional fluff.

Practical guidance warns against forcing fun and instead cultivating its ingredients. A delight practice—noticing small joys, signaling them aloud, and trading phone reflexes for sharing delights with nearby people—is offered as a mood-lifting exercise drawn from poet Ross Gay’s approach. The close urges deliberately prioritizing fun despite fatigue and busyness, treating it as essential fuel for relationships and sustained wellbeing.

talks.title: A National Initiative for Cybersecurity Advancement
talks.teaser: Gives a progress report on a research agenda for a more trustworthy cyber ecosystem and asks the audience to contribute.
talks.summary:
Greg Touhill, a professor at Carnegie Mellon's Heinz College and director of CERT at the Software Engineering Institute, gives a progress update on a research project he calls a National Initiative for Cybersecurity Advancement. The project aims to build a research agenda that produces measurable gains in the trustworthiness of the cyber ecosystem. He says the work has taken longer than planned because the problems proved deeper than expected, and it is structured using the Heilmeier Catechism.

Touhill outlines planning assumptions: the ecosystem reaches beyond enterprise IT into telephone, satellite and AI systems, and cybersecurity is ultimately a risk management function where risk can be managed but never reduced to zero. The team has not yet found good measures for systemic risk; as one example, he pointed to UEFI firmware, where a few vendors reuse code from questionable sources and no marketplace tooling scans it quickly. The findings were binned into seven areas: awareness, usability, capability, flexibility, visibility, comprehension and consilience. Awareness, for instance, means empowering people to thrive in a cyber-enabled society, and one-and-done annual training is judged ineffective.

For practitioners, his lessons include treating usability as a procurement requirement, weighing how long a workforce needs to reach full effect, considering open source to avoid vendor lock-in, and recognizing that memory-safe languages do not make code safe by themselves. He also urged attention to API security and to AI that enhances rather than replaces people. He closed by asking listeners to send feedback on the research agenda and taxonomy over the coming months.

talks.title: Hacker’s Perspective on Your Infrastructure: Lessons from the Field
talks.teaser: Shows how weak passwords and misconfigurations let attackers reach domain admin, and how defenders can hunt for them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a retail incident the speaker was pulled into, where a USB stick carried ransomware into a store and a global firewall blocked its outbound traffic before encryption could spread. Responders struggled because nobody knew what had happened in a very large environment. The post-incident gaps included weak monitoring, one local administrator password reused across machines, no network segmentation, missing updates and limited staff training.

The middle walks through live attack demos. A password spray with seasonal and company-themed guesses found one valid domain account, and its logon events included a network logon type that people rarely use. Service accounts were then targeted by requesting Kerberos service tickets and cracking them offline with a common wordlist. Another demo ran a scheduled task under a disconnected administrator session, and a certificate enrollment web page was abused to obtain a domain controller ticket. Defensive checks followed: hiding Microsoft entries in AutoRuns can conceal a suspicious item, and a service can be hidden by changing its security descriptor.

The closing section covers detection and readiness. Detection often fails because of understaffing, alert fatigue, unclear procedures and budget cuts, so the speaker recommends hypothesis-based hunting built on team knowledge and less obvious data sources. A memory example showed injected code with read-write-execute permissions and an MZ header, which process memory scanning can reveal. An AI assistant can draft a Sentinel KQL query, but the output needs checking. The final advice is to test incident response readiness against a prepared checklist for a compromised Active Directory.

talks.title: Thwarting the Adversary: Bending the Zero Trust Curve to Defense
talks.teaser: Two federal officials explain how the US zero trust strategy is being rolled out, measured, and funded across agencies.
talks.summary:
The conversation, held by two government leaders, opens with the SolarWinds intrusion and how it pushed federal agencies toward zero trust. The speakers describe how the executive order and the 2022 strategy, which set a three-year plan, shifted the federal approach from implicit trust toward verifying every user, device and system before granting access. They explain that agencies wrote their own implementation plans, so timelines could fit each organization's procurement cycles.

They describe tracking spending against strategy pillars to justify budget requests, and the metrics leaders use as proxies for progress: phishing-resistant MFA coverage measured per system rather than per user, endpoint detection rollout, vulnerability disclosure programs, and remediation speed for known exploited vulnerabilities. They stress that data discovery and asset inventory are often culture problems more than technology problems. A risk-based approach, starting from the outcomes an organization most wants to prevent and applied to the electric grid, is also discussed, along with software bills of materials and vendor attestations to secure development practices.

The closing discussion covers how quickly disclosed flaws are now weaponized, as the Log4j review showed, and why the speakers want government to lead by example. Their call to action is to stop letting business exceptions keep the status quo, to explain risk to executives in plain terms, and to ask for outside help on hard migrations.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: Next-Generation Tactics, Techniques and Procedures
talks.teaser: Traces a real Cozy Bear intrusion from a supplier into a target's Entra ID environment, with matching defenses.
talks.summary:
This session walks through a real incident response case attributed to Cozy Bear, also known as APT29 and linked to Russia's foreign intelligence service. The presenters describe a patient group that targets smaller supplier organizations, then pivots through trust relationships into the primary target. Alongside custom malware, the group mixes in common utilities such as PsExec and Mimikatz, which makes attribution harder.

The demo follows the intrusion step by step. Attackers sprayed passwords slowly, alternating timing to avoid lockouts, and an RDP login that one client rejected succeeded from a client without network-level authentication. Posing as Microsoft support over Teams, they persuaded a help desk user to enter an MFA code, then reset the password, returned a new one, and registered a device for persistence. From an Entra Connect sync server they dumped synchronized credentials and reached cloud resources without extra factors. A privileged app with mailbox access was abused through PowerShell to pull executive email, and a permissive AD CS certificate template produced a certificate that opened an S3 bucket.

The countermeasures focus on reducing exposure and hardening identity. Turn off Teams features that let outside users contact staff, limit publicly reachable RDP and Exchange servers, and right-size user and application permissions. Protect sync servers and their accounts, require extra authentication for service accounts, and avoid default configurations. Conditional access, cloud log collection and automated response are also emphasized, since identity-based attacks now account for most of what the presenters investigate.

talks.title: The Five Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques You Need to Know About
talks.teaser: Panelists survey emerging attacks, from aging code and deepfake identity fraud to AI-accelerated exploit discovery.
talks.summary:
A SANS-led panel reviewed emerging attack trends and the defenses that match them. Johannes Ullrich opened with technical debt, examining two security products with code dating to 1998 and 2002, where aging Perl, Java and Python stacks had few remaining developers who understood them. He urged incremental patching and asking vendors how they handle old code. He then covered identity: fake audio and video now cost little to produce, so he suggested strong initial identity proofing followed by risk-based re-authentication.

Heather Mahalik Barnhart described sextortion as a fast-growing threat in which images are used to coerce victims, including teenagers, and noted that AI can fabricate material even when nothing was ever shared. She covered grooming and romance-scam patterns and recommended talking with children, checking privacy settings, and using the NCMEC Take It Down service for removal. Terrence Williams argued that generative AI makes election messaging cheaper, and that repeated breaches and deepfakes erode trust, calling for accountability from companies, politicians and researchers.

Stephen Sims focused on offense, saying AI speeds vulnerability discovery and exploitation. He pointed to a paper claiming language model agents could exploit one-day vulnerabilities, and described automating patch diffing to weaponize flaws faster. He expects skilled humans to remain necessary for complex exploits and proposed automated purple-team loops for defenders. The panel closed with career advice to start in general IT first.

talks.title: Remaining Resilient in the Supply Chainpocalypse
talks.teaser: Explores how organizations build resilience against software supply chain attacks across vendors, monitoring, and zero-trust controls.
talks.summary:
Software supply chain risk reaches far past an enterprise's own patching because imported libraries, SaaS plugins, and fourth-party vendors can bring compromise inside the perimeter. The session opens by contrasting isolated data-center firewalls with today's interconnected cloud and SaaS stacks, then explains why enterprises cannot deeply assess every upstream party. Industry figures highlight third-party roles tied to account takeover and the share of 2023 breaches linked to third parties, with MOVEit used as a prolonged discovery story across CMDB checks, scanning, legal outreach, and vendor cascades.

The speaker catalogs common supply-chain attack paths such as dependency confusion, upstream build injection, developer-environment compromise, CI/CD tampering, and malicious open-source contributions. A five-part resilience model covers vendor and open-source assessment, risk classification, ongoing advisory monitoring, third-party code oversight, and protecting the home environment through surface reduction, compromise prevention, lateral-movement limits, controlled egress, zero-trust identity policies, homogenous automated controls, rapid secrets rotation, and running major disclosures as full incident-response programs rather than slow vulnerability queues alone.

A facilitated discussion with a Genentech and Roche security leader describes scale across thousands of contracts and vendors, post-SolarWinds centralization of vendor management, tougher contractual security questions, decision-maker education, privileged-access hardening, and extending zero trust outward while improving user experience via cloud application delivery, SSO, and MFA. The talk also touches on early AI adoption guardrails and closes on realistic expectations: future large campaigns remain possible, but narrower blast radius, detection, and recovery capacity improve readiness.

talks.title: Coordinated Disclosure for ML: What's Different and What's the Same
talks.teaser: Compares CVE-style disclosure with a proposed coordinated flaw process grounded in model cards, datasets, and public ML red-teaming.
talks.summary:
Machine learning systems are predictable in aggregate yet impossible to verify like traditional software: small input changes, adversarial examples, dataset imbalance, and open-ended generative outputs mean in-house benchmarks are never enough. The speaker argues vendors must invite public testing and build observability, because failures range from catastrophic one-shot harms to subtle statistical bias that a single prompt cannot prove.

He describes organizing public red-team events, including warmups that surfaced severe safety failures on ostensibly aligned open models and a Defcon capture-the-flag exercise across eight major vendors, with challenges tied to the White House AI Bill of Rights themes. Random model assignment was meant to support coordinated disclosure rather than drive-by tweeting. The exercise highlighted tension between rare “not-even-once” harms and bias findings that need resume-style counterfactual datasets and vendor-specific safety tradeoffs.

For disclosure, he contrasts CVE-style “vulnerabilities” with “flaws” judged against each model card’s stated scope, backed by archivable datasets and statistical arguments rather than one-off proofs. Adjudication remains unsolved, as both reporters and vendors can cherry-pick samples. He closes with buyer guidance: demand verifiable performance and scope in contracts, study model-card practices, and aim for embargoed, collaborative fixes instead of PR-driven knee-jerk changes.

talks.title: How the Cookie Crumbles: What OSINT Tells Us About Dark Web Cookie Sales
talks.teaser: Explores how stolen session cookies bypass multifactor login and what OSINT reveals about their sale on dark web markets.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by an Australian OSINT practitioner, starts with the basics of HTTP sessions and cookies, covering persistent and session cookies and first- and third-party cookies. It explains why attackers value session cookies: a cookie that already carries an authenticated session can get past multifactor authentication. The speaker describes the EA hack, where a group reportedly used stolen authentication cookies to enter a Slack channel and then persuaded support to issue a new MFA token, and mentions a later BeyondTrust breach as another example.

The middle section demonstrates Evilginx, an open-source reverse proxy tool that serves a lure page, captures credentials and two-factor input, and saves the session cookie, which is then loaded into a browser add-on. The speaker then moves to dark web research over Tor, using onion directory sites that track which marketplaces are online, and search engines such as Torch and Ahmia. A forum case shows information slippage: a seller of Italian medical records reused a distinctive username, which led to a linked Skype account and then to a Russian social media profile with photos and location details. Repeated searches found cookie sales consistently available but still niche compared with other compromise methods.

The closing part connects the findings to GDPR and ePrivacy rules and to browser vendors phasing out third-party cookies, which may push more reliance on first-party cookies. The speaker recommends an OSINT strategy approved by management, with clear policy, ethical limits and training before anyone researches the dark web. Defensive advice includes email gateway filtering, conditional access, device management, automated network monitoring and robust authentication such as FIDO2.

talks.title: A Blueprint for Detection Engineering: Tools, Processes, and Metrics
talks.teaser: Walks through a detection engineering workflow, from attack hypothesis to tested SIEM rules, using open-source tooling and metrics.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a practical question: can an organization show it detects a given attack, and prove it within about fifteen minutes? The Splunk threat research presenters explain how shipping detections as plain searches led to slow escalations from services staff, which pushed the team toward a structured process. Their cycle moves from understanding a threat and forming a hypothesis to generating attack data, writing a detection, testing it and packaging it for deployment.

The middle section covers the tooling. Version control and CI/CD pipelines keep detection logic, documentation and history together. Automated validation catches missing fields and invalid search syntax within seconds. Simulations use Atomic Red Team on Attack Range, an open-source lab that collects logs, and the resulting data is published to a shared attack data repository for replay. A testing tool called contentctl then replays that data to confirm searches run and return the expected results. Aggregated metrics, such as MITRE ATT&CK coverage diagrams, coverage by asset type and pass rates over time, help teams spot gaps and decide where to invest next.

The final part covers deployment and upkeep. Teams must decide whether passing tests should trigger automatic release or whether a person should review changes first. Analyst feedback, both explicit labels and signals such as whether alerts are enabled, guides tuning, and detections should be retested in fresh environments as software and logs change. A falling pass rate can reflect added checks rather than worse content. The presenters describe moving from ad hoc tracking to automated releases, and their takeaway is that the process takes effort but makes coverage questions far faster to answer.

talks.title: Building Your Quantum-safe Future with Crypto-agility
talks.teaser: Outlines quantum threats to asymmetric cryptography and shows enterprise discovery, observability, and remediation for crypto agility.
talks.summary:
IBM Quantum Safe presenters frame their work as protecting digital trust while advancing quantum computing. They explain how Shor’s algorithm threatens factoring-based public-key schemes such as RSA 2048, how Grover’s algorithm raises brute-force risk for symmetric cryptography, and why harvest-now-decrypt-later makes today’s non-quantum-safe data worth protecting even before a capable machine exists. They cite a common industry view of meaningful quantum risk within about a decade, note that migrating algorithms historically takes seven to ten years, and argue for calm, early planning.

They summarize NIST’s post-quantum competition, lattice finalists including Kyber, Dilithium, and Falcon, expected certification timing, and U.S. legislation pushing critical federal infrastructure and supply chains toward quantum-safe cryptography by 2033. Industry bodies spanning telecommunications, payments, and vendor consortia are positioned as coordination points for interoperable migration.

The operational core is crypto agility: quickly updating, monitoring, and retiring cryptography under architecture, automation, and governance. Practitioners should start with discovery of libraries, methods, algorithms, and key sizes; add network visibility into TLS handshakes and cipher strength; merge static cryptography bills of material with dynamic monitoring; prioritize by regulation and business impact; then remediate dependencies, not isolated algorithm swaps. Demonstrations cover large-scale repository scanning, endpoint inventory, policy violations, and generative models that explain crypto weaknesses and suggest code fixes, while Q&A acknowledges hardware and firmware lag behind software agility.

talks.title: Art of Possible: Transforming How We Develop the Next-Gen Cyber Workforce
talks.teaser: Panelists from government, academia and industry explore how to grow cyber talent through apprenticeships and upskilling.
talks.summary:
The panel starts from workforce gaps: too few qualified cybersecurity instructors, curriculum that cannot keep pace with technology, and degree requirements that keep experienced practitioners out of classrooms. Panelists from government, a university and a training provider argue that these problems need solutions across government, academia, nonprofits and industry rather than from any single sector.

Several approaches came up. Federal changes now let agencies hire for skills regardless of background, and some schools are adding cyber to non-computing courses such as manufacturing, healthcare and law enforcement. One university described pairing cybersecurity students with aerospace engineering students to work on employer-set problems. Speakers also pointed to adjunct teaching by working practitioners, early exposure for high school students, and upskilling programs that move service desk or systems administrators into security roles. Apprenticeships were acknowledged as costly for employers, which makes buy-in hard to win. AI was described as a training aid and as a way to remove routine tasks, leaving people to do the judgment work.

The closing advice was practical. Attendees were urged to volunteer with local schools, offer talks or workshops, and raise entry-level hiring and experience requirements with their own employers. Speakers also suggested training recruiters and bringing cyber into infrastructure projects early rather than adding it later.

talks.title: Don't Worry About Your Toilet...I'm Just Hacking It
talks.teaser: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi hacks on consumer gadgets frame IoT trust, shadow devices, patching gaps, and practical risk management.
talks.summary:
Ben Schmerler of Independent Security Evaluators recounts how his team turned a conference gimmick—a hacked smart toilet seat dubbed for demos—into a broader story about connected devices. Using black-box reverse engineering over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, they built apps to command the seat (heating, lights), a robotic vacuum, and Bluetooth bulbs, often with modest effort compared with the scale of IoT deployment worldwide.

He argues the stunt mirrors serious targets: leak sensors, clinical monitors, and solar gear share similar radios and weak assurance. The talk walks through trust in manufacturers, what devices do on your network, patching and abandonment, shadow IoT, and the limits of “fully secured” products. He ties past work on medical gear to the idea that false readings and remote manipulation are realistic, not theoretical.

Closing sections translate lessons for consumers (inventory, research, threat modeling, layered home security), IT integrators (security-first rollout, visibility, isolation, candid user dialogue), and product builders (design-time security, recurring assessment, independent review, vetted libraries). Audience questions explore verifying devices before join, home segmentation, and mitigating unpatchable legacy systems in healthcare through monitoring and network controls.

talks.title: Bridging the Talent Gap: How Certifications, Upskilling, and AI Can Help
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh certifications, skills-based hiring, and AI tools as ways to close the cybersecurity workforce gap.
talks.summary:
Ron Culler and Keatron Evans open by asking whether the cybersecurity talent gap is real. They cite CyberSeek data showing about 500,000 open cyber jobs in the US, and an ISC2 estimate of about five million open jobs globally. They argue that many openings are already filled by staff who also carry other duties, and that entry-level postings still ask for degrees and two to three years of experience, which screens out capable candidates.

The speakers present certifications as proof of job-ready skills without a degree. Vendor-specific credentials suit shops built on a given platform, while vendor-neutral ones build foundations. They argue that upskilling existing support, network and server staff is faster than hiring outsiders, who can take months to learn an organization. In one case, a company turned a compliance-scanning role into an upskill path, which then let it hire a true entry-level analyst. Gamified training platforms were described as good for engagement but weak at producing hireable skills. Generative AI was presented as shortening the learning curve, with a two-hour lab in which people with no malware analysis background found hidden malware in captured traffic using prompts.

Audience questions covered skills-based pay, shadowing for people at small firms, physical security staff moving into cyber, and the federal government's move to drop degree requirements. Takeaways include verifying skills rather than degrees, building apprenticeships and partnerships with local employers, using certifications as a map of skills to learn, and keeping private data out of public AI tools.

talks.title: AI Governance: The Security Perspective
talks.teaser: Explains where security teams fit within AI governance, from organizational structure to emerging regulation.
talks.summary:
The session examined AI governance from a security perspective, drawing on a global survey of more than 500 professionals in over 50 countries. Over half of the companies surveyed had already deployed AI, and about 20% planned to do so within the following year. The top concerns organizations named included inaccuracy, intellectual property, explainability, security and regulatory compliance.

Governance leadership in the survey usually sat with privacy teams, often under a committee, while security contributed in over half of cases. The panelist said the CISO frequently drove the operational side, and that a cross-functional group was the practical way to see which models and AI tools were in use. He described unsanctioned adoption, such as an AI co-pilot that 5,000 people began using within a week at one financial firm. He also noted that AI red-teaming differs from classic testing because providers' terms of service can forbid it, and pointed to MITRE ATLAS as a reference for adversarial AI risks.

Practical takeaways were to inventory AI use first, set up a regular governance structure with clear owners, and build shared vocabulary so leaders can discuss risk. Existing privacy impact assessments and security tools can be repurposed for AI risk reviews. Data governance, including access controls and deletion requests, was presented as a prerequisite for using models safely.

talks.title: Outpacing the Pacing Challenge: Cyber Command's Strategic Scaling
talks.teaser: A military cyber leader explains how the command scales partnerships, talent, and new technology to stay ahead of the pacing adversary.
talks.summary:
The briefing opens with the strategic landscape U.S. Cyber Command faces: China as the pacing challenge, rapid technological change that favors speed over size, and non-state actors empowered by commercial technology. The speaker describes CYBERCOM’s relationship with NSA under dual leadership, the need for agility in acquisition and operations, and why dominance in cyberspace erodes without deliberate change.

He walks through four mission lines—defending Defense Department networks, supporting combatant commands, national defense with interagency and industry partners, and building partner capacity—including Hunt Forward deployments since 2018 across dozens of allied networks. Future scaling covers the DARPA Constellation pipeline, an internal AI task force supporting hunt teams with translation and alert triage on GPU kits, Lock Shields participation with NATO allies and universities, and academic programs such as NSIN capstones that surfaced North Korean IT worker fronts.

Practitioners hear how legislative authorities for innovator awards, civilian pay supplements, and limited eminent expert hires aim to recruit scarce skill, plus Army support for headquarters hiring. The close emphasizes CYBERCOM 2.0 planning, Constellation bridging research to operators, and coalition exercise as the model for matching global adversaries.

talks.title: A Constitutional Quagmire: Ethical Minefields of AI, Cyber, and Privacy
talks.teaser: Surveys the legal and ethical risks of AI, from patient privacy and biased hiring tools to liability after a breach.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the legal and ethical questions raised by AI, contrasting how the United States, Europe and China approach them. The speaker frames the issues around privacy, transparency, accountability, intellectual property, bias and liability. He compares AI oversight to aviation regulation, arguing that the field still lacks the standards and auditing practice that aircraft have.

Working through scenarios, the healthcare case covers an AI tool that gathers patient data without proper consent. The recommended steps are privacy by design, specific consent captured in writing rather than a click-through, audits of what engineers actually built, and a breach response plan that explains how affected individuals will be notified. A cybersecurity case looks at a zero-day that compromises an AI security product. Here the advice is a documented assessment framework, a rapid response plan for AI incidents, prompt patching, and bringing in lawyers for breach notification. A trade secret case covers departing engineers, with granular access controls, encryption and policies that are reviewed regularly. A hiring bias case recommends routine algorithm audits, contract terms that secure audit results, more representative training data and a feedback channel for applicants.

The closing message is that the law trails technology by years, so the realistic goal is a defensible, reasonable process rather than perfection. Organisations should document their decisions, consult qualified counsel instead of improvising legal answers, and expect auditing standards for AI to mature over time.

talks.title: Breaking the Cloud to Rebuild It: A Tale of 3 ☁️ Breaches!
talks.teaser: Replays a leaked-credential AWS breach and argues for threat modeling, data perimeters and incident response readiness.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a recorded walkthrough of a breach against a training environment the speaker's company ran. A security researcher had shared a private video showing an attacker starting from a Terraform credentials file in a private GitHub repository. The IAM user it held had no MFA and read-only permissions, yet the attacker used SSM to reach an instance, copied an S3 bucket onto an attached volume, and exposed that volume publicly. CloudTrail was not enabled, so the activity left little trace.

The speaker then sets this case beside three public incidents. In one, an access key exposed on GitHub had excessive permissions to an S3 bucket. In another, lost IAM user credentials without MFA and with shared passwords led to loss of AWS accounts and the crypto wallets stored in a secrets manager. In the third, an EC2 instance role had S3 access and the instance used IMDSv1. He argues that cloud incidents now span many accounts, identities and pipelines, so CSPM findings alone do not show the attack path, and he points to valid accounts, trusted relationships and public-facing applications as common entry points.

For practitioners, the talk recommends three practices. Threat modeling should include cloud engineers, who understand how their systems can be broken. A data perimeter built from identity, resource and network controls should limit who can reach trusted resources. Incident response readiness means confirming logging is on and that responders can quickly access every cloud account. The speaker closes by asking when the last cloud incident in the audience's environment was raised and where it came from.

talks.title: The Good, the Bad, and the Bounty: 10 Years of Buying Bugs at Microsoft
talks.teaser: A decade at Microsoft shows how paid bounties shifted reporting, scaled global research, and hardened triage-to-release workflows.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with coordinated vulnerability disclosure at scale and why external researchers matter as products and AI expand the attack surface. Katie Moussouris walks from Don Knuth and early Mozilla rewards through Google Chrome’s program to starting Microsoft’s bounties in 2013, including internal pushback, the Internet Explorer 10 beta reporting cliff, and how modest cash and credit encouraged earlier submissions.

Anusha Gupta shares roughly five years of program data: on the order of $60 million paid, more than a thousand researchers across dozens of countries, and many product-specific programs with tiered awards for high-impact classes. She contrasts a hard-to-reproduce race condition that stalled communication and ended in a public proof-of-concept with a well-written report that triggered a grant and surfaced many related issues. Hyper-V and other critical findings illustrate risk-based payouts.

The speakers outline Microsoft’s intake pipeline: bidirectional updates, fast detection deployment, kill-chain mitigations, upfront payments under coordinated disclosure, engineering fixes, variant hunting, validation programs, and broad AV guidance before patch Tuesday. They warn against treating bounties as researcher control or vanity spend—“bug bounty botox”—and urge goals, signal-oriented metrics, internal process investment, and feeding findings into the security development lifecycle. Q&A covers scope disputes, spam triage, automation, and spinning up programs when new products draw reports.

talks.title: Countering Cyber Threats, Digital Fraud and Theft in the Retail Sector
talks.teaser: Panelists detail how retail fraud ranks among top member threats and how intelligence sharing plus merged teams counter omnichannel abuse.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the Retail and Hospitality ISAC describing decade-long maturity in sector cybersecurity while member reporting still elevates fraud to the second spot among top trends, just behind phishing. Ryan Miller argues that industry labels separating fraud from cybercrime matter less than attacker behavior: omnichannel shopping, generous return flows, and aged customer accounts invite refund schemes, label manipulation, and account takeover used to bypass controls rather than steal cards alone.

Christian Beckner adds organized retail crime and transnational gift-card tampering—shelf theft, alteration, and rapid draining at activation—as national-scale economic harm drawing federal law enforcement and marketplace accountability rules. He and Miller describe years-long work at Target to unite threat intelligence, fraud abuse engineering, and loss prevention through shared data, proof of stopped losses, leadership backing, and product changes. Policy partners cite Homeland Security Investigations case work, proposed interagency coordination, and the need for shared fraud vocabulary comparable to cyber indicator standards.

Practitioners should prioritize external visibility into schemes targeting their brands, map fraud tactics to legitimate checkout and return flows, and sustain cross-functional product owners so collaboration does not revert to silos. Smaller retailers can lean on ISAC and trade-association working groups for taxonomy, benchmarks, and peer alerting while measuring financial impact to fund defenses.
