talks.title: Inside the Making of a Zero Trust Architecture
talks.teaser: Walks through NIST's zero trust guidance and a lab demo project, with lessons for building a zero trust architecture.
talks.summary:
This session by two NIST staff members traces how federal zero trust work grew from a 2018 steering group into the SP 800-207 guide, published in August 2020. The presenters describe it as descriptive rather than a single standard, and explain its core parts: a policy engine that decides, a policy administrator that carries out the decision, and an enforcement point in the data plane. They also outline three deployment approaches, enhanced identity governance, micro-segmentation and software-defined perimeter, which real environments often blend.

The NCCoE demonstration project, launched in July 2021 after a call for vendor participation, builds example architectures in a lab with several clouds, a branch site and on-premises networks. The team started with enhanced identity governance because identity underpins every approach, and plans micro-segmentation, software-defined perimeter and blended builds next. Its practice guide, SP 1800-35, comes in three volumes: a leadership overview, a technical volume on technologies and requirements, and a hands-on engineering volume. Answering questions, they said confidence levels matter mainly when changes grant or remove access.

For organizations starting out, the advice is to inventory assets, identities, workflows and traffic flows first, then write access policies and identify technology, policy and process gaps. Progress comes in small steps over 6 to 12 months, since zero trust is a journey.

talks.title: State of the Hacks: NSA’s Perspectives
talks.teaser: Offers defenders a strategic view of hybrid-war cyber ops, state router attacks, ransomware economics, and cloud identity abuse.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how a combat-support and foreign-intelligence mission shapes what gets shared with industry as attacks spill across borders. On Russia and Ukraine, it walks through pre-invasion defacements, wiper families, DDoS, hacktivist friction with norms, Ukrainian resilience, and the Viasat terminal disruption that bricked European gear and cut communications—with a practical warning to encrypt satellite backhaul for OT links.

China is framed as the long-term pacing threat: brazen IP theft, cost-imposing integrated deterrence, published CVE lists used by state actors, the Exchange exploitation surge after discovery, coordinated advisories with TTP mappings, and router-and-ISP tradecraft that outpaces typical network instrumentation. Ransomware is treated as criminal and national-security risk, with specialization in initial access, Treasury and sanctions effects on cash-out, war-driven reuse worries, and faster weaponization of public proof-of-concepts.

The closing arc centers on cloud adoption, trust abuses in SolarWinds-style SAML forgery, managed-provider and CI/CD supply-chain cases, Chinese vulnerability research and disclosure law, and calls to reassess third-party risk, rehearse cloud incident response, fix misconfigurations, engage standards bodies, and pursue aggressive cloud security testing sandboxes.

talks.title: Sigstore, the Open Source Software Signing Service
talks.teaser: Explains why open source signing stays rare and how Sigstore aims to make it free and easy.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the software supply chain and the ways it gets attacked. Examples include a website that served a swapped ISO image while visitors skipped the hash check, compromised build systems, and typosquatted package names that differ by one letter. The speaker also points to maintainers of unfunded hobby projects who burn out, and cites a 50% increase in attacks, mostly around open source projects.

Next the speaker asks why so few open source developers sign their releases. Private key handling is hard for them: rotating keys, a lost laptop, choosing an algorithm. Hardware tokens cost money that a student or a developer in an emerging country may struggle to justify. PGP and key-signing parties, the speaker argues, no longer scale to globally distributed teams. The HTTPS story offers a model: after 2015, free certificates from Let's Encrypt drove adoption upward.

The project presented is Sigstore, a free public service for software signing. Its code-signing service issues short-lived certificates based on an OpenID Connect sign-in. Signed material is recorded in a transparency log that lets anyone verify later that an artifact was signed at a given moment. Integrations with GitHub Actions and Maven Central were covered, and enterprises can use an existing key management system such as Vault. Policy decisions, such as requiring several signers before production, are left to tools built on top. The goal is to make ingesting unsigned software socially unacceptable.

talks.title: CI/CD: Top 10 Security Risks
talks.teaser: Walks through real CI/CD breaches like PHP, Stack Overflow and CodeCov to map the top 10 pipeline security risks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the SolarWinds build-system compromise and asks how an organization can avoid becoming the next victim of a supply chain attack. The presenters describe the engineering ecosystem as a fast-changing mix of source control, CI and CD systems, secrets, human users and third parties, and they argue that attackers now focus on these environments. They introduce a Top 10 CI/CD security risks list, built from their own client work, expert feedback and published incidents.

The middle of the talk goes through five case studies and ties each one to the risks that enabled it. The PHP Git infrastructure breach let an attacker push a malicious release, with forged maintainer signatures, because no review was required and signed commits were not enforced. The Stack Overflow breach began with a service account password stored in clear text, which led to admin access on a TeamCity instance and then to a GitHub SSH key that bypassed 2FA. In the Codecov case, a tampered script exfiltrated CI environment variables from many organizations, exposing production credentials. A Travis CI flaw exposed encrypted secrets through forked pull requests for about a week. Dependency confusion showed how a public package with a higher version could replace an internal one during installation.

The closing section gives practitioners a path forward. Defenders should treat the engineering pipeline as part of the attack surface, build a detailed map of assets and third-party connections, and continuously review that map from an attacker's point of view. Logging and visibility are presented as a base layer for detecting and investigating any pipeline incident.

talks.title: Importance of Cybersecurity Mesh Platform in Securing Digital Acceleration
talks.teaser: Argues that enterprises should consolidate security tools into use-case platforms that share threat intelligence and policy.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why security tools bought as separate point products struggle to keep pace with a growing attack surface. The speaker describes organisations running dozens of vendors that work in silos, and presents a cybersecurity mesh, also called a fabric or platform, that spans endpoint, network, cloud and security operations. The speaker separates convergence, which merges functions into one product, from consolidation, which keeps several products but makes them share policy and threat intelligence.

Rather than one vendor for everything, the proposed approach builds a platform around specific use cases such as work from anywhere, multi-cloud, the zero trust edge and operational technology. Examples included an endpoint posture change being passed to a zero trust policy engine, and a vendor that had built about 25 connectors by reverse engineering APIs because many large vendors did not publish open ones. For OT, the talk argued for microsegmentation enforced at switch ports, since agents cannot run on controllers. External attack surface monitoring and brand protection were presented as front-end parts of the kill chain, and the Log4j response was cited as an example of pushing updates to many control points quickly.

The takeaway is that buyers should choose a small number of platforms per use case and insist that they integrate through open APIs and shared intelligence, with automation keeping pace with faster attacks. Zero trust was described as a multi-year journey rather than a single purchase.

talks.title: The Road to Adversary Engagement: Get Your Organization from 0 to 88 MPH
talks.teaser: A panel maps denial, deception, and adversary engagement, with legal guardrails and a practical maturity path from one laptop.
talks.summary:
Panelists from MITRE, HSBC, and the FBI unpack cyber denial, deception, and adversary engagement as distinct ideas. Denial blocks adversary operations; deception shapes what attackers see so their actions benefit the defender; engagement reduces the payoff of intrusions by surfacing TTPs in controlled conditions—not hack-back. They stress deception as planning and mindset rather than a product category, and cite DOJ guidance that activity on your own network is generally permissible, with caveats for insider misuse.

Operational lessons emphasize isolated, kill-switch-equipped environments, malware hypotheses, and careful bait so adversaries are not trained on production secrets. MITRE’s path began with a single decoy laptop and PCAP collection and grew into richer faux offices; HSBC iterated after an early exit when no Active Directory was present, later holding actors for days. Cross-sector sharing— including an EDR blind spot that fed a new ATT&CK sub-technique—shows how joint detonations improve detections. The FBI frames counterintelligence overlap and urges relationships before incidents.

Closing advice: assume breach, master basics first, and treat engagement as a late maturity capability requiring skilled malware handlers. Practitioners are pointed to MITRE Engage for structure, community feedback, and stepwise growth toward safer, intelligence-rich operations.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Spoken Word #3 with Poet, Rives
talks.teaser: The segment answers playful questions about RSAC, from a Wordle sponsorship to sci-fi blog posts and sponsor anagrams.
talks.summary:
This short comedic segment has the presenter answer questions the conference supposedly received from its website, social media and attendees. Rather than a technical presentation, it is a light-hearted look at the conference's own quirks. The questions cover a sourdough baking contest planned for a hotel roof, an offer to sponsor a word-guessing game on the website, and whether the blog's science fiction and cryptography themes amount to a lazy stereotype.

The middle of the segment moves through the blog's upcoming post schedule, teasing future articles that tie well-known science fiction franchises to topics such as denial-of-service attacks, retinal and palm scanning, and biometrics for users without those traits. The presenter then addresses whether sponsor names and logos hide subliminal messages. Playing with anagrams of the names Google Cloud and Microsoft, the presenter offers joke readings and then builds up a list of sponsor anagrams, each paired with a quip about the vendor's product.

The closing portion presents the final three sponsor anagrams of the year and wraps up the session with a playful sign-off. There are no technical findings or defensive controls to apply here. The takeaway is a lighter view of how the conference organizers and sponsors are perceived by the people who attend.

talks.title: Strengthening Security in the Era of Digital Transformation
talks.teaser: Shows how a data-centric approach to security operations improves visibility, detection and response across hybrid environments.
talks.summary:
Gary Steele, CEO of Splunk, opens with a run on Hawk Hill in San Francisco where a false summit made him turn back. He uses that as a metaphor for security teams that feel they have not reached their goal. He names three persistent challenges: a threat landscape that keeps shifting, complexity from adding tool after tool across cloud and hybrid environments, and silos that separate security operations from application monitoring.

His proposed remedy is a data-centric approach that he says brings end-to-end visibility, faster detection and response, and stronger cyber resilience. A large US health system used a data-centric SIM platform to ingest data from any source, which also helped it spot possible diversion of controlled substances. When COVID arrived, wire-diversion attempts, fake credentials and supply chain attacks rose, and the team used orchestration to automate routine work. Transurban, an Australian road operator, reported cuts of 87% in detection time, 94% in response time and 70% in remediation time. In a video segment, REI's CISO, Mike Hughes, describes security as a journey and explains how a cloud platform now feeds SIM and SOAR.

Steele closes by restating the three outcomes and stressing that teams should reach their data from a central console without moving it between environments. He ties the story back: he reached the Hawk Hill summit by studying maps, understanding the risks ahead and preparing properly. For practitioners, the takeaway is to prioritize visibility and automation over adding yet another tool.

talks.title: Security’s Dirty Little Secret: The Conservation of Complexity
talks.teaser: Argues that growing security complexity calls for zero trust and cloud-delivered SASE architectures.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the argument that security has become too complex even as work has grown faster and more distributed. The speaker points to a projected $10.5 trillion annual cost of cybercrime by 2025 and to millions of unfilled security jobs. He describes how perimeter-based designs, which hairpin traffic back to corporate sites, no longer fit how people and applications now operate.

The proposed fix combines zero trust, which grants explicit access only to approved applications and keeps verifying each connection, with secure access service edge (SASE) delivered from the cloud. Inspection services such as antivirus, sandboxing, content disarmament and reconstruction, and remote browser isolation sit in that cloud layer. The speaker explains that endpoints can send traffic for inspection, block it, or bypass inspection for low-risk traffic such as web conferencing. He gives examples: browsing a suspicious site through a remote browser that is reset afterward, sanitising file downloads, and giving contractors access only to specific applications.

He closes with business benefits. Moving from implicit trust to zero trust, sending only appropriate traffic for inspection, and removing on-premises equipment that needs upgrades and patches all improve security and user experience. His takeaway is that organisations must adopt these architectures quickly, because standing still leaves them behind.

talks.title: Staying Secure in Today’s High-stakes World
talks.teaser: Shows how ransomware now targets supply chains and critical infrastructure, and why security must be shared across the whole business.
talks.summary:
Chris McCurdy, general manager of IBM Security Services, opens by arguing that cyberattacks now cause real-world harm. He cites the ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline, which he says pushed fuel prices up, and the rising cost of data breaches during the pandemic. Attackers, he says, have shifted from stealing data to disrupting supply chains, where pressure on manufacturers and their customers drives ransom payments. Using IBM X-Force data, he notes that manufacturing became the most attacked industry, with ransomware making up 23% of those attacks.

He urges organizations to assume attackers are already inside and to focus on detecting and stopping them. In his framing, zero trust is a set of principles for building a strategy rather than a product. He also proposes opening every meeting with a "security moment," adapted from the safety briefings used in industrial settings, so that cybersecurity becomes a shared responsibility across departments instead of sitting only with the CISO.

Two CISOs then joined the discussion. Fernando Madureira of Cosan described central information security and cyber defense teams that set minimum standards across group companies, with business security officers embedded in operations. He involves smaller suppliers in training, phishing tests and crisis exercises, and says OT security is hard because operations staff must learn why patches and shutdowns matter across more than 100,000 connected devices. Charles Tango of Sysco Foods said ransomware has replaced data theft and compliance as his top risk, shifting focus toward the interconnected supply chain. He recommends segmentation, including OT in incident response playbooks, and relying on peer CISO networks.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Spoken Word #2 with Poet, Rives
talks.teaser: Short on-camera interviews with RSA Conference attendees capture how the past two years have changed them.
talks.summary:
Filmmakers Rives spent the previous day at the RSA Conference asking attendees two questions on camera. The first asked for one adjective to describe the last two years, and answers ranged from weird and chaotic to adaptive and transformational. The second asked how those years had changed each person, which drew a wider spread of replies.

The middle of the piece plays short clips from attendees. One woman said her work now centers on getting women into cybersecurity and technology, pointing to a large gender gap in the industry. A mother said having a baby in 2020 made her better at handling security challenges, since crises tend to arrive at inconvenient hours. Others described becoming a parent, walking more for fun, paying more for housing, slowing down to value family, and feeling more adaptable and human overall.

The session closes with the filmmakers asking the audience how they would like the coming year to transform them. The result is a light, human snapshot of how attendees were coping with change over the past two years.

talks.summary:
This segment opens the RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox with a short on-stage recognition of the 2021 contest winner. The host notes that the previous year's sandbox ran as a virtual event and encourages attendees to think about how they can contribute to security.

The winner, Apiiro's founder, joins the host for a brief interview about the company. He describes Apiiro as securing the software supply chain from design through development and delivery, helping security teams and developers fix risks in cloud-native applications before they reach the cloud. Since the win, he reports the company grew its team from about 20 people to 90 across the globe, with customers ranging from small shops of around 50 developers to organizations with 25,000. He also says the company contributed to NIST's secure software development framework and to software bill of materials standards.

He mentions a zero-day software supply chain vulnerability the team found, which was disclosed responsibly and fixed with the affected vendor. The company also launched a partner program the previous week with Google, HashiCorp, NetSPI and other vendors. The segment is mostly a progress update and celebration rather than a technical presentation, with the practical takeaway being how an early-stage security startup can grow by addressing supply chain risk.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Explains why asset inventories from multiple tools are incomplete and how continuous asset telemetry keeps device records current.
talks.summary:
The pitch starts from a familiar gap: organizations pass audits for asset inventory controls, yet many cannot say how many devices they own. Each existing tool reports a different subset of the environment, so none gives a complete picture on its own. The proposed fix is to connect those existing inventory sources through APIs and pass the records through a correlation engine that merges them into a single view of devices.

The second half argues that a merged inventory is still a snapshot. Staff are hired, leave, and work from different locations, so device records change constantly. The platform described streams and correlates inventory data in real time and records asset telemetry that captures changes over time. The presenter compares this to endpoint detection and response, which moved incident response from disk and memory snapshots to continuous endpoint telemetry.

The closing point is that asset data underpins most IT and security processes. When the platform is deployed, it is expected to surface problems, and the presenter argues that teams struggling with those problems are usually working from bad data rather than being ineffective. Giving them accurate, current inventory should improve their results with little change to existing processes. The takeaway is to fix the underlying data system rather than patch individual symptoms.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Presents an API detection and response approach that baselines user behavior to spot API abuse without relying on signatures.
talks.summary:
The presenter, chief executive of Neosec, argues that API security has a growing blind spot. Business-to-business APIs are built in-house, connect machines together, and are often assumed safe simply because they require authentication, yet many security teams do not even keep an inventory of them. The talk identifies three main problems: shadow APIs that are poorly documented, badly written APIs that attackers exploit, and API abuse by attackers using stolen credentials, which the presenter calls the bigger issue.

Drawing on earlier work in network and extended detection and response, the presenter proposes applying behavioral analytics to APIs instead of depending on signatures and inline inspection of single requests. The described cloud platform first discovers APIs and their posture from activity data, then profiles normal behavior for each user to flag abnormal activity without signatures. It automates response through direct integrations and open APIs.

The final part covers investigation and threat hunting. The platform keeps 30 days of API activity so teams can reconstruct a timeline of events for each API user. The takeaway is that teams should inventory their APIs and monitor authenticated machine-to-machine traffic for unusual behavior rather than trusting it by default.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Presents a graph-based cloud security platform that ranks exploitable risks by attack path to cut alert noise.
talks.summary:
Lightspin's CEO, Vladi Sandler, opens by describing the strain on cloud security engineers: a flood of low-value alerts, tools that overpromise, and blame after breaches. He argues the problem is growing with multi-cloud setups and several flavors of Kubernetes, while skilled staff remain hard to hire.

He proposes a cloud security platform built on graph theory. A proprietary algorithm maps the topology and attack surface of a cloud environment, then connects risky routes, CVEs and malware into attack paths specific to each customer. The company claims this reduces alert noise by about 94.6 percent. Its code analysis step says one underlying issue can account for 15 to 20 alerts, and its remediation step generates infrastructure-as-code fixes for quick deployment.

Sandler closes with company traction: more than 100 tenants in just over a year on the market, a team with prior experience at large technology and security firms, and $20 million raised from investors. The practical takeaway is the approach itself, ranking exploitable risk by context and attack path rather than by raw alert count, as a way for small teams to keep up.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Explains how a continuous context layer links cloud data inventory, access and sensitivity to automated risk alerts.
talks.summary:
The pitch starts from a familiar tension: data must be protected, yet businesses depend on it more than ever and need speed. The speaker says security, data and compliance teams often work in silos, which leads to manual processes, false positives, intrusive tools that teams avoid, and unreliable attestations. The proposed answer is a continuous context layer that builds security and compliance into everyday workflows, an approach framed as DataGovOps.

The platform works by connecting to several sources. It keeps a near real-time inventory of databases across cloud providers, then reads each data store's schemas, privileges, usage and sensitivity. It also links to identity services to see who uses the data and where they sit, and to data catalogs to learn which team owns each asset. All of this is correlated, enriched, classified and tagged, which supports live data maps and questions such as who can reach a given sensitive dataset.

The main value claimed is automated routing of findings. Security risks go to existing security tooling, tasks for data teams become Jira tickets, and catalog metadata is updated automatically when needed. The stated goal is to detect risk earlier, shift from inspection toward prevention, and let the business use data more freely. The talk closed by noting the company has about 30 staff and customers across major industry verticals.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Shows how Cycode maps CI/CD tools and infrastructure into one knowledge graph to secure software supply chains end to end.
talks.summary:
Lior Levy, CEO of Cycode, opens by arguing that software supply chain attacks are rising and that attackers are shifting away from hardened production applications toward the developer tools and infrastructure that build them. He cites a Gartner projection that these attacks will triple by 2025 and affect 45% of companies. He gives three reasons: many modern SDLC tools are owned and run by developers, where security teams lack visibility; the SDLC offers many attack vectors for a foothold and lateral movement between phases; and application security has focused on code and production rather than on securing the CI/CD pipeline.

He then presents Cycode as a platform providing visibility, security and integrity across the pipeline. At its core is a Knowledge Graph that ingests data from DevOps tools and infrastructure and analyzes their metadata, configurations and security issues. Levy describes three parts of the approach: organizing tools and data for visibility across the SDLC, centralizing security policy to harden those tools, and verifying where, when and how software artifacts are produced. The platform also finds issues in code, third-party dependencies and Infrastructure-as-Code templates, and weighs deployment paths and exploitability so that real issues are blocked before production.

Finally, he describes a workflow automation engine that orchestrates third-party tools, modifies infrastructure configurations and helps developers with code fixes inside existing workflows. He closes by citing a $43 billion market spanning application security, DevSecOps and cloud security, and by stating that securing software supply chains is the biggest unmet need in cybersecurity. The practical takeaway for defenders is that the build pipeline deserves the same scrutiny as the production applications it produces.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2022 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Presents a cryptography-based approach to zero-trust remote access for servers, containers, clusters, and databases in cloud environments.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that engineers and build pipelines need access to production cloud infrastructure, which makes that access a weak spot in an organization's defenses. Long-lived credentials are easy to steal, as the Colonial Pipeline incident showed. Many zero-trust designs replace them with authentication at every login, but the speaker contends that these designs still put all trust in one authentication system, creating a single point of compromise.

The proposed alternative uses cryptography with two independent roots of trust: the vendor's cloud service and the customer's single sign-on provider. Users see only single sign-on and multifactor authentication. Administrators get a cloud-agnostic, lightweight access system that discovers targets automatically and removes stored database and server passwords. If one root of trust is compromised, the other still protects access.

The closing portion places the product across cloud security, DevOps productivity, privileged access management and VPN markets, and cites use in health tech, fintech and e-commerce. The takeaway for practitioners is to check whether a remote access design actually removes single points of trust, rather than only adding authentication steps on top of one system.

talks.title: The Only Constant
talks.teaser: Global shocks frame lessons on identity, information integrity, and rejecting convenience-over-security dogma.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by distinguishing disruption from transformation and walking through recent shocks—from a pandemic absent from earlier risk forecasts to war-driven cyber mobilization, ransomware, supply chain attacks, and disinformation that also reverberate physically, such as fuel shortages after pipeline incidents. In a hyperconnected world, local operators remain exposed to distant events, and the sector’s reactive chase after each new threat is unsustainable.

Three lessons structure the middle of the talk. Constants matter: while technology and vulnerabilities shift rapidly, human identity stays comparatively stable, so most breaches trace to compromised credentials and MFA remains under-adopted despite decades of recommendation, passwordless standards, and insurer demands; zero trust and unified identity platforms are framed as the durable anchor. Imperatives matter: protecting critical infrastructure and information integrity is not enough when tampered or false information can outdamage compromised systems, so verifying creators and fighting disinformation joins classic confidentiality goals. Dogmas must go: convenience has too often trumped security even as digitization raises risk, while regulation advances and innovators can pair security with new benefits rather than zero-sum tradeoffs.

The close urges deliberate transformation before a “cyber pandemic” spreads at network speed, reorienting practice from infrastructure-centric firefighting to identity-centric and information-centric resilience, and acting as authors of that change rather than waiting for crisis.

talks.title: Webcast: The Metaverse of Vulnerability
talks.teaser: Surveys metaverse security risks, from avatar impersonation and account takeover to moderation gaps, with proactive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that metaverse platforms, loosely defined as any shared online space with social interaction and transactions, inherit security problems that earlier virtual worlds already exposed. Tracing examples from IRC and Second Life to Pokemon Go, the speaker separates virtual reality, where the host controls the whole environment, from augmented reality, where real-world location data and map errors can put players at risk.

The middle section catalogues concrete risks. Account takeovers often leave victims unable to reach platform owners, and proprietary currencies or decentralized finance offer little recourse after theft. Avatar appearance makes impersonation easy, and telemedicine credentialing is hard to verify. Client software on user devices can be altered, and moderation of harassment is costly yet essential.

The advice is to assume not every vulnerability can be known, and to brainstorm what could go wrong. Organizations should negotiate contracts that guarantee direct administrator contact and the power to remove users, actively moderate their own venues, and build security into the platform from the start. He also notes that users seeking anonymity must work hard to protect it, since activity can often be traced.

talks.title: Webcast: RSA Conference 2022 Know Before You Go
talks.teaser: Covers RSA Conference 2022 logistics, including campus layout, registration, sessions, the expo floor and networking events.
talks.summary:
The webcast opened with RSA Conference vice president Linda Gray Martin, who framed the 2022 event around its transformed theme and the return to in-person gathering in San Francisco. Michelle Adam-Sixen then outlined health and safety measures for the Moscone Center, including proof of vaccination or a negative test, verification through an app or an on-site desk, and testing windows that depend on the test type. Attendees were directed to the health and safety hub on the website for the latest updates.

Amy Hubbard walked through the three Moscone buildings and how they connect, along with registration hours, the government ID requirement, the mobile experience for building a schedule and reserving seats, and food and transport options. Official hotel shuttles ran every 15 minutes at peak times, ride share drivers were directed to a pickup point in front of Moscone West, and a parking discount was offered for pre-booked garages. The content segment covered tracks, keynotes, the difference between favoriting a session and reserving a seat, session viewing points, paid trainings, learning labs, and the innovation sandbox, with recordings posted about 24 hours after each live session.

Networking highlights included the Monday welcome reception, a women's networking event, and an expo crawl, while the expo floor held over 400 exhibitors and the early-stage area featured 35 startups. The practical advice was to schedule meetings early, reserve seats in advance, keep backup sessions in mind, pace yourself across a long week, and watch for the post-conference attendance report needed for continuing education credits.

talks.title: Webcast: Intro to Purple Team: Cyber Threat Intelligence, Attack, Detect, Respond
talks.teaser: Shows how red, blue and threat intel teams can run a purple team exercise using MITRE ATT&CK as shared language.
talks.summary:
The webcast, presented by Jorge Orchilles, CTO of SCYTHE, introduces purple teaming as a virtual team in which threat intelligence, offensive and defensive staff work together to test and improve an organization's defenses across people, process and technology. The speaker traces the idea to his time at a large financial institution, where repeated stealth red team engagements produced little improvement until red and blue teams ran a joint exercise.

The middle section walks through the four-phase Purple Team Exercise Framework. Threat intelligence should focus on the adversaries likely to target a given sector, and the talk contrasts tactics, techniques and procedures using the Pyramid of Pain and a TTP pyramid. A procedure-level example of credential dumping from LSASS shows why exercises need concrete detail rather than a coverage claim. Preparation covers in-person logistics, production target systems with working security tools, and the data sources, logging and alerts needed to detect each behavior. During the exercise, the red team runs each technique, the blue team checks whether it was logged or alerted, and gaps are tracked.

The closing part covers detection engineering, noise tuning, and operationalizing purple testing when new techniques appear rather than waiting for scheduled exercises. Attendees are pointed to free resources, including the framework, community threat files and SANS purple team material. The takeaway is to build the program around MITRE ATT&CK as a shared language and to measure what is actually detected.

talks.title: RSAC 365 Virtual Seminar: Zero Trust (Part 2)
talks.teaser: Walks through zero trust basics, asset visibility, gap analysis and CISA's maturity model for planning incremental adoption.
talks.summary:
This session, part of a 2022 RSAC virtual seminar, is aimed at teams who find zero trust material either too conceptual or tied to one product. The first presenter defines the core terms, such as policy decision points and policy enforcement points, and shows how a zero trust deployment can start by swapping a VPN client for a new agent while policy is tightened behind the scenes. The model also covers service-to-service and microservice access, not only people reaching applications.

The practical method begins with visibility: listing users and groups, their privilege levels, whether endpoints are fully, partially or unmanaged, the networks they connect from, and the resources they reach. Those facts go into simple tables with conditions such as multifactor authentication and posture checks, and a gap analysis ranks the holes by priority. Low-hanging fruit includes third-party and remote privileged access, while refresh cycles such as VPN replacement and protection for regulated data are natural next steps. The presenter also separates cloud-routed products from on-premises ones and warns that many vendors simply relabel existing tools.

The second presenter, from CISA, explains the Zero Trust Maturity Model, which is organized into five pillars (identity, device, network environment, application workloads and data) and three cross-cutting capabilities. Each function is graded from traditional to advanced to optimal. A forged-token attack in the style of Golden SAML, drawn from the SolarWinds intrusion, illustrates why identity controls alone are not enough. Federal guidance such as the OMB strategy and NIST SP 800-207 is noted as further reading. The takeaway is to build visibility first, pick a small initial project, and treat zero trust as a long, incremental effort.

talks.title: Webcast: How to Avoid Being a Scam Victim When Your Phone Rings
talks.teaser: Walks through the top phone scam pitches, from fake Amazon fraud calls to Social Security threats, and how to avoid them.
talks.summary:
This talk explains why phone scams keep working and how to spot them before money is lost. The speaker argues that scammers earn large sums per victim while rarely being caught, and that older adults are a prime target. Legitimate companies seldom cold-call, caller ID can be spoofed, and urgency is a standard pressure tactic.

He walks through ten phone scams he received over about a year and a half. An Amazon fraud call asks for remote access and moves money out of bank accounts, with one victim losing $120,000. A Social Security impersonation claims a warrant exists and demands money or gift cards. Debt-elimination calls create new, costlier debt, and vehicle service contracts offer coverage that cannot be used. Medicare callers hunt for identifiers, energy callers obscure rates, and vacation offers hide large fees. Solar, political committee and cable upsell pitches round out the list.

Suggested defenses include hanging up, assuming unsolicited calls are scams, and contacting organizations through numbers you find yourself. Never share financial details or let anyone install software on your computer. Call-blocking tools catch only some calls, so the speaker argues carriers and regulators should act. Wasting a scammer's time is considered low risk.

talks.title: Calling All Students! Start Planning Your Cybersecurity Career
talks.teaser: Hiring leaders advise students on internships, networking, and building soft skills to land a first cybersecurity job.
talks.summary:
Three professionals who work on hiring and intern programs discuss how to narrow the cybersecurity skills gap and connect students with employers. They tie National Cybersecurity Awareness Month to workplace habits, noting that staff often face attacks such as malicious email and that the same lessons protect people's personal devices and accounts at home.

For students, the main advice is to pursue internships through many channels, including job fairs, conferences, professional groups, university clubs, and social media. An internship shows which kind of organization fits a student and gives a head start on a first full-time role. The panel stressed that the market remains competitive, so candidates who take part in capture-the-flag events, sponsored challenges, and other activities outside coursework stand out. Students can also enter through adjacent teams and build broader skills in areas such as risk management or privacy. For those whose internship search fails, the panel suggested volunteering with a local nonprofit on basic tasks like changing default passwords to gain experience and a reference.

Networking came up repeatedly, with speakers describing contacts as a circle that helps in both directions. They suggested that quieter students treat the interview process as a two-way evaluation of the employer. They also warned that early industry certifications, which often require years of work experience, matter less than communication and problem-solving skills.

talks.title: Experts Take On Hacker Burner Phones
talks.teaser: Practical guidance covers sourcing, pickup tradecraft, and daily habits for a modern burner phone kept apart from a real identity.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting classic disposable flip phones with modern smartphones that pack multiple transmitting radios. As long as the device has power, brokers, advertisers, and government entities can collect location and behavioral data from apps and radios, so compromising the number is less important than compromising the person behind the phone. The stated goal is to pair data separation with operational discipline to build a distinct digital identity.

Use cases span human-rights work under hostile governments, protest coordination where stingray-style capture should only touch the burner, fictional tight-knit conspirator groups that rotate hardware together, and security conference travel where foreign intelligence or other attendees might surveil primary devices. Hardware choice balances memory, customization, footprint, and budget; the presenter cites a Motorola Moto G7 while noting a primary iPhone elsewhere. Acquisition runs through Proton Mail created over VPN in a private browser, a new Amazon account on that mail, cash-bought Visa gift cards under typical U.S. reporting thresholds, locker delivery to an unfamiliar site, and pickup wearing mask and gloves, parking away from cameras, unboxing off-site, stripping serials, and stashing the powered device in a quality Faraday bag.

Initial setup favors distant free Wi-Fi, Wi-Fi-only mode, tightened privacy settings, VPN, minimal apps, privacy-oriented browsers, and DuckDuckGo search. Closing guidance stresses keeping the burner bagged away from home, office, and the everyday phone; minimizing powered time; separate bags for swaps; avoiding wearables that phone home; and never signing into personal accounts from the burner.

talks.title: The Future of Hardware Security
talks.teaser: Explains DARPA's SIFT program, which builds processors meant to block exploitation even when software is flawed.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that software patches often arrive too late or are never fully deployed, a gap that is especially hard to close for embedded and IoT devices. The speaker argues that attackers succeed by making hardware perform actions the programmer never intended, and that current hardware has no way to tell an intended memory access from one an attacker uses to exploit a system.

From there the talk presents DARPA's SIFT program, which aims to close whole classes of weaknesses so that systems resist exploitation even when the software running on them is flawed. Performers developed techniques such as memory tagging, limited capabilities, runtime analysis of hardware operations, and encryption with compartmentalization. These were demonstrated on processors ranging from 32-bit microcontrollers to 64-bit out-of-order high-performance CPUs, validated with formal methods and synthetic security benchmarks, with minimal impact on performance, power and area.

The first DARPA bug bounty, held midway through the program against emulated systems built on SIFT technologies, drew more than 500 researchers who spent over 10,000 hours attacking them. The processors prevented exploitation of the vulnerabilities in the provided software stacks. An independent review by the Microsoft Security Response Center of one SIFT architecture concluded that over two thirds of the 2019 vulnerabilities reported to it would have been mitigated without a security update. The program is now moving toward transition, including hardware and software co-design and zero-trust protections against malicious hardware. The takeaway is that hardware design can provide protections that previously could only come from software patches.

talks.title: Webcast: Struggling to Manage Your Cybersecurity Workforce? The NICE Framework Can Help
talks.teaser: Shows how the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity can shape hiring, skills growth and staff assessment.
talks.summary:
The session introduces the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity, a resource maintained by the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education at NIST. The speaker traces its origins to a 1998 federal initiative, its first publication in 2017 and its 2020 revision, and explains why it was built to be agile, flexible, interoperable and modular. Its building blocks are task, knowledge and skill statements, which are grouped into work roles and competencies. The material covers seven categories, 52 work roles, 55 draft competencies, more than 1,000 task statements, over 600 knowledge statements and nearly 400 skill statements.

Several uses are covered. Employers can write job descriptions and screen candidates, educators can align courses with the statements, and learners can compare their strengths against a role. Three composite scenarios follow a program lead checking team gaps, an HR partner writing a job posting, and an employee planning a career move. Two success stories are then discussed. JPMorgan Chase set baseline proficiency expectations for staff and built them into its employee assessment platform, which improved visibility of strengths and guided training. Lynx Technology Partners, a consulting firm, built a competency program for clients, using the statements to assess teams and work roles to shape career paths.

The closing part points to supporting resources, including a resource center, a success story series and a users group, and notes a planned revision process. In the question period the speaker said the framework is not regulatory and that proficiency levels are still being developed. The main takeaway is to start from organizational needs, then use the shared vocabulary to find gaps in hiring and training.

talks.title: 7 Steps of Setting Up a C-SCRM Program
talks.teaser: Outlines seven steps for setting up a supply chain risk management program, from tracking purchases to sharing incident information.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces cyber supply chain risk management and argues that, for information and communication technology, the main concern is integrity and provenance: whether what was bought or built contains what it should. Traditional supply chain thinking focuses more on availability and logistics. The speaker describes planning at three layers, executive, organizational and system, and notes that these layers often do not talk to each other.

A central idea is deciding what is critical and what is disposable. Every organization has a limited budget, so protection should match mission importance, while components that connect to critical systems must also be protected. The speaker stresses knowing what you have bought and keeping track of it after purchase, because things change and shadow IT exists, so teams can react quickly when a supply chain threat appears. Threat planning is suggested through scenario-building games, chaos engineering and role-play exercises, weighing likelihood and consequences and deciding which risks are acceptable.

The talk closes with incident communication and countermeasures. Executives and business owners need a clear, digestible path from analysts' findings, and that path should be defined before an incident rather than during one. Existing countermeasures often explain why an attack does not affect the organization, and sharing information with others leads to faster resolution.

talks.title: Webcast: Fighting New Era Bandits Who Are Plundering Your AI/ML Application
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can copy AI models through query access alone, and how detection and active defenses respond.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at model extraction attacks, in which an adversary who can only send inputs to a deployed AI model and read its outputs rebuilds a functionally similar copy without breaching the surrounding system. The speaker, who works on AI security at Bosch, frames this as a threat to the value of AI investments and walks through a taxonomy of attacks based on how much the attacker knows, from black-box to white-box access.

Case examples follow. An early real-world case involved spam filtering: researchers queried an email security product, used the returned scores to build a substitute classifier, and then crafted messages that evaded it. Other experiments covered a handwritten digit classifier, an audio classifier for vehicle-related sounds, and a model offered as a cloud service. A kill chain was shown against a security camera's person detection, where an extracted model supported adversarial patches that evaded detection. For defense, the speaker described training a "don't know" class so the model flags suspected attack queries, a separate binary detector that runs alongside the original model, and an active defense that alters outputs so extraction fails while the attacker keeps receiving answers. A tool called AIShield was demonstrated for assessing model vulnerability, generating defenses and providing runtime protection.

The closing section covered organizational impact. The speaker recommended ranking AI assets by their value and by how easily they could be attacked, engaging vendors, and contributing to the MITRE ATLAS framework, which was described as still a work in progress. Defenses were noted to carry compute cost and some accuracy trade-offs.

talks.teaser: A million-dollar grant ceremony spotlights nonprofits advancing public cybersecurity awareness through the data care message.
talks.summary:
Ron and Cyndi Gula of the Gula Tech Foundation host an RSA award session for competitive Data Care grants totaling one million dollars. They frame “data care” as everyday personal and organizational responsibility for protecting information, tied to workforce gaps and broad public engagement rather than industry jargon alone.

Foundation advisors narrowed a large applicant pool using impact lenses: target demographics, delivery medium, and reach scale. Four runner-ups each receive one hundred thousand dollars: National Cybersecurity Center, One In Tech, Partners In Care, and Theorem Media. Third place goes to the National Cryptologic Foundation for K–20 education and a middle-school data care booklet expanded via focus groups. Second place goes to Cybercrime Support Network for victim support portals, scam spotting tools, veteran and romance-fraud programs, and hands-on SecureTogether posture help. First place goes to UTSA’s Center for Infrastructure Assurance and Security for free K–12 card and digital games such as Cyber Threat Defender, with decks in many countries and an estimated two hundred fifty thousand students touched yearly.

Representatives from the top three organizations describe how funding will amplify outreach. The hosts close by inviting collaboration among winners, pointing volunteers to gula.tech, and treating data care as open language anyone may adopt.

talks.teaser: A student-focused workshop on personal branding, tailored resumes, networking, and interview preparation for cybersecurity hires.
talks.summary:
The session opens with guidance on owning a professional narrative in an era where employers and peers look candidates up online. The presenter frames career positioning as an iterative cycle of introspection, validation, and consistent self-presentation, including exercises to mine past roles for transferable skills, distill a few defining themes, and align public profiles and elevator pitches with that story without exaggerating experience.

Human resources specialists then walk through reading job descriptions like a matching game: diagramming requirements, tailoring each resume to specific roles while keeping prior versions, and emphasizing clarity, scannable skills, action verbs, and concise summaries over fluff or long page counts. They discuss biases candidates bring to qualification lists, cover letters and LinkedIn as part of one package, and networking through community events, mentors, and treating applications as two-way fit checks.

Dell hiring leaders close with interview mechanics: practicing behavioral answers, researching the company, preparing achievement stories in short past-tense bullets, virtual interview setup, thoughtful questions for interviewers, and follow-up thanks. The event ends with breakout rooms advertised for resume feedback and direct Q&A with panelists.

talks.title: Managing Privacy and Cyber In A Pandemic: Lessons Learned For 2021 & Beyond
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Managing Privacy and Cyber In A Pandemic: Lessons Learned For 2021 & Beyond.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at RSA Conference by Aaron Charfoos (Partner at Paul Hastings) and Ericka Johnson (Senior Associate at Squire Patton Boggs), this session examines the privacy and cybersecurity implications brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic and remote work. The talk focuses on the operational and legal complexities of collecting employee health data during workplace reopenings, the surge in cyber incidents and double-extortion ransomware attacks, the necessity of Written Information Security Plans (WISPs), and legal strategies to protect post-breach forensic reports from discovery in litigation.

### Key Topics
- **Workplace Health Data Collection**: As organizations reopen, employers increasingly gather health data. Data presented indicates 76% of surveyed organizations ask employees to report positive diagnoses, 53% ask about personal travel, 35% inquire about household members, and 23% take physical temperatures. Additionally, about 50% adopted new work-from-home technologies, with nearly 60% bypassing or expediting privacy and security reviews.
- **Legal & Regulatory Frameworks**: HIPAA generally does not apply to employer-collected workplace monitoring data, which is instead regulated under state unfair/deceptive practices acts, personal data laws, and guidance from agencies like the EEOC. Internationally, regulations such as the EU's GDPR and Canada's PIPEDA impose stricter obligations. U.S. state statutes (e.g., in Kansas, New York, South Carolina) and proposed federal bills (e.g., COVID Consumer Data Protection Act, Public Health Emergency Privacy Act) establish varying requirements for consent, transparency, and retention.
- **Evolving Cyber Threat Landscape**: The pandemic exacerbated cyber attacks, particularly phishing and social engineering in remote environments. Threat actors have shifted towards double-extortion schemes—exfiltrating sensitive corporate, customer, or partner data before encrypting systems—increasing litigation risk and pressure to pay ransoms.
- **Written Information Security Plans (WISPs)**: WISPs serve as an organization's playbook for controls, incident response, and disaster recovery. Regulators increasingly scrutinize them, and maintaining a recognized security program can provide legal benefits or affirmative defenses under state statutes such as Ohio Chapter 1354.
- **OFAC/FinCEN Sanctions Guidance**: On October 1, 2020, OFAC and FinCEN issued parallel advisories regarding ransomware payments and sanctions violations under the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list. Organizations must conduct rigorous, documented OFAC checks and coordinate closely with cyber insurance carriers.
- **Discoverability of Forensic Reports**: Drawing from the *Capital One* and *Clark Hill* rulings, courts have deemed third-party forensic breach reports discoverable when prepared for business or remediation purposes rather than strictly in anticipation of litigation.

### Technical Details & Best Practices
- **Data Minimization**: Organizations should assess whether data (such as temperature logs or detailed test results) truly needs to be stored, establish clear retention/deletion timelines, and consider delegating physical checks to third parties (e.g., building management) to limit exposure.
- **Contracting with Testing Providers**: Ensure agreements with COVID-19 testing or vaccine clinic vendors do not mistakenly classify data under HIPAA if HIPAA compliance is not required, as misclassification incurs stricter disclosure and security liabilities.
- **Ransomware & Sanctions Compliance**: Involve legal counsel on the incident response team to document due diligence through an OFAC check memo, review insurance policies for payment pre-approval and indemnification, and leverage threat intelligence or dark web monitoring to check actor leak sites.
- **Protecting Privilege on Forensic Reports**:
  - Avoid relying on pre-existing Master Services Agreements (MSAs) or statements of work with existing IT vendors; retain a new, independent forensic firm solely for legal defense.
  - Draft statements of work specifying that the work is prepared exclusively at the direction of counsel in anticipation of litigation.
  - Pay for forensic engagements directly out of litigation budgets.
  - Strictly restrict dissemination of forensic reports, avoiding distribution to general business leadership, broad employee groups, or outside regulators/investigators.
  - Exclude forward-looking business or remediation recommendations from litigation forensic reports.

### Takeaways
Organizations must proactively align pandemic-era health data collection with data minimization and state-level breach laws. When handling ransomware, entities must balance legal sanctions risks with cyber insurance requirements and comprehensive OFAC vetting. Finally, when investigating incidents, companies should structure IT forensic engagements deliberately through legal counsel to avoid producing self-incriminating technical reports that become discoverable to plaintiffs in subsequent litigation.

talks.title: It's Been a Privilege to Serve You–a Mock Hearing
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning It's Been a Privilege to Serve You–a Mock Hearing.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session presents a mock evidentiary hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler in the hypothetical case of *Who I Want To Grow Up To Be v. Dolls-R-Us*. The dispute centers on a motion to compel discovery of a post-incident forensic investigation report and related interview records generated by a third-party cybersecurity firm, Technotronic. Dolls-R-Us had contracted with the plaintiff to manufacture Ruth Bader Ginsburg action figures, requiring commercial security assessments and penetration testing. Prior to delivery, threat actors penetrated Dolls-R-Us, compromised credentials, manipulated backup encryption keys, and executed a ransomware attack over Labor Day weekend. Production was halted for six weeks, causing the plaintiff to miss the holiday season and incur severe financial and contract losses. Dolls-R-Us asserted that the forensic investigation was privileged work product directed by outside legal counsel in anticipation of litigation.

### Key Topics
- **Attorney-Client Privilege and Work Product Doctrine**: Whether a technical forensic investigation directed by outside counsel following a ransomware incident is shielded from civil discovery, or constitutes an ordinary business practice required under an incident response plan (IRP).
- **Dual-Purpose Investigations and Preexisting Vendor Relationships**: The legal complications that arise when the same security firm performs both pre-incident risk assessments and post-breach forensics, including team collaboration across internal Chinese walls.
- **Case Law Standards in Incident Response**: Judicial analysis stemming from cases such as *Premera*, *Dominion Dental*, and *Capital One*, specifically evaluating statement-of-work (SOW) scopes and whether investigations would have occurred in substantially similar form "but for" the prospect of litigation.

### Technical Details
- **Hypothetical Intrusion Mechanics**: Attackers established persistence, escalated privileges, surveilled management, manufacturing, and development systems, and altered the encryption keys of an automated backup utility service, rendering backups unusable because they were never tested.
- **Pre-Incident vs. Post-Incident Scopes**: In June, Technotronic executed a commercial security assessment and penetration test contracted directly by Dolls-R-Us. In September, after the ransomware deployment, outside counsel (α, β, and γ) retained Technotronic under a separate agreement funded via a legal contingency budget to determine the scope of unauthorized access, examine data exfiltration, evaluate regulatory breach notice triggers (PI/PHI), and assess exposure to OFAC sanctions.
- **Information Isolation and Collaboration**: Inside Dolls-R-Us, technical findings were restricted to three individuals (the VP of Information Systems, assistant/system director, and architect). However, testimony revealed that Technotronic's forensic team reviewed the prior June assessment report and consulted with the assessment team to investigate whether unremediated vulnerabilities facilitated the ransomware intrusion.

### Takeaways
- **Separation of Scope and Vendors**: Courts closely scrutinize statements of work, retainer timelines, and previous engagements. Reusing the same vendor for both baseline IT security assessments and privileged breach investigations risks eroding work product claims if the scopes overlap or if the work would be conducted under routine IRP business operations.
- **Fact Product vs. Work Product Reality**: True underlying factual information regarding an incident cannot easily be hidden simply by routing technical investigations through outside counsel.
- **Two-Track Investigations**: While maintaining separate tracks—one internal technical investigation for business remediation and one strictly counsel-directed investigation for litigation—can better insulate legal reports, conducting two comprehensive parallel investigations is expensive and may still require disclosing underlying technical facts during litigation.

talks.title: An Existential Crisis for Global Data Flows: Privacy and Security Issues
talks.teaser: Examines how the Schrems II ruling changes EU-to-US personal data transfers and the assessments companies now need.
talks.summary:
The panel looks at personal data flowing from Europe to the United States after the Court of Justice of the EU invalidated the Privacy Shield framework, building on the earlier Safe Harbor ruling. The speakers trace the story from Snowden's 2013 revelations through the Schrems cases. Standard contractual clauses remain usable, but only when a company assesses whether the receiving country's surveillance laws still give essentially equivalent protection.

They show why this reaches everyday business: a single online purchase involves card issuers, banks and fraud checks across jurisdictions, and under the GDPR even remote access to European data from abroad counts as a transfer. Regulators are now acting. Portugal's data protection authority ordered a national statistics institute to stop using a US cloud provider, a first-instance French court found AWS's technical safeguards sufficient, and Spain fined Vodafone for a transfer with no safeguard at all.

For practitioners, the advice centers on knowing your data flows and vendors, benchmarking supplementary measures against public transparency reports, and writing a policy for government access requests backed by a standard set of responses. On technology, the EDPB guidance says encryption works for storage and backup but generally not for cloud providers that must process data in the clear, with caveats for pseudonymization and multi-party computation. The speakers conclude that a political solution is needed.

talks.title: Defend Forward: Moving Toward Coordinated Active Cyber Response
talks.teaser: Maps defend forward, threat sharing, and legal limits on coordinated private-sector active cyber response.
talks.summary:
The session opens by distinguishing Department of Defense defend forward from hack-back and related slogans, citing the 2018 cyber strategy and Cyber Solarium’s proactive framing. Panelists trace how public-private information sharing evolved from early national strategies through ISACs, ISAOs, and recent executive orders, and why many companies still hesitate to share with government despite occasional high-value cooperation.

Randy Sabett frames private-sector defend forward as imposing costs on adversaries and collective defense, walking a spectrum from honeypots and intelligence handoff to actions only government may take legally. Shane McGee argues liability reform—especially around the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and models like the SAFETY Act—must pair with trust mechanisms, attribution rules, deconfliction, and proportionality before companies lean forward. Andrew Epstein stresses balanced roles, real-time sharing, and structures akin to ISACs or ISAOs.

Practitioners should treat active cyber response as coordinated and lawful, not vigilante hack-back; invest in government relationships and sharing channels; and watch mandatory cyber incident reporting as distinct from state breach notices. The panel closes cautiously optimistic on momentum but skeptical that timely public-private sharing will mature quickly without clearer metrics and sustained policy follow-through.

talks.title: So You Want to Be an Expert Witness
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of So You Want to Be an Expert Witness.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "So You Want to Be an Expert Witness," technologist Hoyt Kesterson and attorney Lauren Topelsohn share practical insights on how technical and cybersecurity professionals can become effective expert witnesses in legal proceedings. Kesterson reflects on his real-world experiences across multiple trials, patent disputes, and regulatory lawsuits—such as testifying for the State of Arizona regarding Dealer Management System open APIs—while Topelsohn provides legal context on witness qualifications, evidentiary standards, and attorney expectations.

### Key Topics
- **Fact Witnesses vs. Expert Witnesses**: A fact (or lay) witness testifies strictly based on firsthand direct observation of events without being paid for testimony or relying on hearsay. In contrast, an expert witness is not involved in the case events and is retained to explain complex technical concepts or provide formal opinions to the judge and jury.
- **Legal Standards and Gatekeeping**: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 702, an expert opinion is admissible if scientific or specialized knowledge assists the trier of fact. Topelsohn details the five *Daubert* factors established by the U.S. Supreme Court (*Daubert v. Merrell Dow*): general acceptance in the scientific community, empirical testability, known error rate, peer review/publication, and repeatable standards/controls. Judges act as gatekeepers, deciding whether an expert and their opinion are admissible.
- **Discovery, Privilege, and Work Product**: Discovery requires exchanging case-relevant information, interrogatories, documents, software, and expert reports to avoid surprise at trial. The speakers discuss attorney-client privilege, work product protection, the risks of discoverable draft reports, and maintaining strict confidentiality under non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).
- **Spoliation of Evidence**: Spoliation involves failing to preserve evidence once a reasonable expectation of litigation arises (citing Judge Shira Scheindlin and the *Zubulake* cases). Failing to halt scheduled data destruction or properly handle forensic disk dumps can result in severe sanctions, such as adverse inference jury instructions, default judgments, or case dismissals.

### Technical Details
- **Forensic Acquisition & Handling**: The speakers discuss a software liability case involving accounting software where evidence was mishandled by taking a Linux data dump and converting it to Windows, destroying critical filesystem metadata. Proper forensic disk imaging must be forensically sound rather than informal copies.
- **Code Analysis & Intellectual Property**: Experts are often called to analyze source code for copyright infringement or backdoors, identifying stylistic signatures, function call patterns, and API usage even when variable names or tags are altered.
- **Security and Cryptography Concepts**: Technical subject matters highlighted include cryptographic key escrow failures, hash chains and timestamping in patent disputes (Markman hearings), X.509 directory services, and network protocol layers.

### Takeaways
- **Courtroom Demeanor and Delivery**: Resumes and degrees alone do not suffice; experts must be likable, professional, non-condescending, and articulate. They must strictly answer only the question asked, pause before answering on cross-examination to give counsel time to object, and maintain equanimity in high-pressure adversarial settings.
- **Compensation Rules**: Expert compensation is fully discoverable and must be disclosed to opposing counsel; it cannot be contingent on case outcomes.
- **Building Visibility**: Technologists can enter the field by publishing, speaking at local and industry conferences, engaging on LinkedIn, and participating in cross-disciplinary groups such as the American Bar Association (ABA) Section of Science and Technology Law (via Associate Memberships) and InfraGard.

talks.title: What Was I Thinking?: Bungled Breach Responses
talks.teaser: Explains how loose chat messages, weak incident report privilege and missteps with regulators can make a breach far costlier.
talks.summary:
Two data breach litigators and a transactions cybersecurity lead examine the ways companies make a breach worse than it needs to be. They start with communications: plaintiffs routinely seek every message, including chats and texts sent during an incident, and casual or negative remarks can later be read as proof of what the company knew. Tone matters as well, and the panel notes that an attacker may be reading company email during a ransomware negotiation.

Next come incident response reports, which courts often do not shield when they would have been written for business reasons anyway. The speakers suggest keeping reports to facts, separating remediation into a later assessment, having counsel direct the responders, and sometimes skipping a written report altogether. They also cover standing and damages defenses in data breach suits, where the type of exposed data matters, and they say an incident response plan only counts once it has been tested in tabletop exercises and kept in a copy that survives ransomware.

The final section covers conduct that can turn a breach into criminal or regulatory trouble. A former Uber security chief was indicted after an earlier breach was under FTC investigation and a later hack was allegedly not disclosed. Other risks include paying ransomware groups sanctioned by OFAC, which can create strict liability, and hacking back, which can violate federal law. The practical advice is to prepare in advance, build relationships with FBI cyber agents, escalate early to counsel, and disclose rather than guess when unsure.

talks.title: Internal AppSec Awareness and Education
talks.teaser: Three AppSec leaders share advice on building developer training, security champion programs and teaching secure coding.
talks.summary:
This session brought together three AppSec practitioners to talk about bringing the rest of an organisation into application security work. Marisa Fagan, head of security awareness at Atlassian, argued for a verifiable training program. She advised choosing a platform with basic learning management features such as enrolment, reminders and manager reports, tailoring courses to the flaws an organisation actually sees, and making one baseline course mandatory for developers. Optional deeper paths and hands-on challenges could follow.

Nikki Brandt, who leads part of Slack's product security organisation, covered starting a security champions program. Her advice was to recruit volunteers first, define a narrow set of tasks with a stated time commitment (two hours a week at Slack), offer incentives that appeal to both managers and engineers, and teach champions to think about threats rather than become security experts. She said Slack has roughly 35 champions for about 800 engineers and judges them on whether they complete the agreed tasks, not on vulnerability counts.

Tom Hudson, a security researcher at Detectify, described teaching secure coding to recent graduates with no prior background. He found that rules without reasons are quickly forgotten, so he explained how the web and databases work, told the story of how SQL injection emerged, and taught both attack and defence. Once the boundary between client and server was clear, prepared statements made sense. In the Q&A, the panel favoured measuring adoption and quiz results over year-on-year vulnerability counts, and suggested free hands-on labs for small budgets. The main lesson: start small, keep training practical, and be clear about what you expect from people.

talks.title: Pandemic & Peril: 3 Experts Unpack Challenges Faced in Healthcare Security
talks.teaser: Three experts examine how economics, regulation and patient data protection shape security in healthcare.
talks.summary:
The session at the Biohacking Village Sandbox at RSA featured three speakers, each given seven minutes followed by questions. Vidya Murthy argued that healthcare security is shaped by economics: attacks are cheap, attacker budgets are generous, and security spending has grown about 10% a year. Device buyers rarely make security a core purchasing criterion, which leaves one-off fixes and security debt. She urged regulators and buyers to push manufacturers toward secure-by-design development.

Caleb Barlow focused on patient genomic and health data, which cannot be changed once lost. He described DNA as able to reveal relatives and be re-identified through genealogy matches. Using BGI Genomics' COVID-19 work, which included 35 million rapid test kits sold in 180 countries, he raised concerns about nation-state access to genomic data. He also noted that 66% of American hospitals cannot meet a level three NIST score, and framed attacks on hospitals as a bridge between cyber and kinetic harm.

Sharka spoke about misinformation during the pandemic, describing an infodemic as an overabundance of information, some accurate and some not. She cited research estimating at least 800 deaths in the first three months linked to coronavirus misinformation. Her guidance was to check the source, read beyond the headline, verify authors and data, check dates and images, and consult fact-checkers. Across the session, the speakers agreed that healthcare is under attack and that industry, hackers and patients must work together.

talks.title: The Value of CyberSec Certifications: A Holistic View
talks.teaser: Three industry speakers weigh how security certifications matter at each career stage, from entry-level hiring to senior roles.
talks.summary:
Three speakers joined this RSA Conference lightning session to discuss how security certifications fit into different stages of a career. They agreed there is no single certification path that suits everyone, and that people should evaluate each credential against their own goals. Early on, a certification can help a resume stand out to applicant tracking filters, and the speakers suggested checking which credentials recur in job postings before choosing one.

As careers advance, the speakers said the value shifts. Entry-level candidates benefit from foundational networking and security credentials, while mid-level and senior roles place more weight on practical, hands-on exams and on explaining why a technique was used. One speaker described an early government-focused role that required a specific compliance certification, and noted that some employers still use certifications as a screening tool even though many hiring managers care more about demonstrated skill. Senior professionals may see diminishing returns, so management or business credentials can be more useful at that point.

The question-and-answer segment covered whether CISSP is really a requirement, whether online-only degrees carry weight, and how to know when enough certifications is enough. The main takeaways were to pick credentials deliberately, combine them with practical work such as CTFs, bug bounties, write-ups or volunteering, and not to be discouraged by job postings that list more requirements than a role truly needs.

talks.title: Are Pentests Relevant with Bug Bounties
talks.teaser: A Red Team village panel weighs when pen tests still matter alongside bug bounties, compliance, and continuous delivery.
talks.summary:
The session frames penetration testing as a broad spectrum, from compliance-mandated third-party assessments and commodity scanning to boutique manual work and open-book hunts for serious flaws. Panelists contrast that model with bug bounties, where many researchers test within a published scope and are rewarded only for accepted findings, often running continuously on public web and cloud targets.

Neither option is presented as a replacement for secure development practices, threat modeling, risk assessment, or recurring vulnerability scanning. Bug bounties multiply eyes on exposed services and can surface issues pen tests miss at scale, while pen tests retain value for regulated industries, internal and network assessments, OT and ICS environments without dedicated test beds, and tradecraft such as social engineering and insider simulation that typical bounties exclude. Fast-changing container and DevOps deployments make any point-in-time report age quickly, so testing in UAT, after-hours windows, and layered programs matters.

Questions from the audience cover outsourcing programs to platforms, vulnerability disclosure policies and contacts, fitting breach and attack simulation and adversary emulation into the budget, persuading leadership when pen tests already satisfy checkboxes, and limits on crowdsourced internal network testing. The panel closes on a blended strategy that keeps red teaming, pen testing, and bug bounties in play together.
