talks.teaser: Panelists explain why state, local and small business organizations struggle with security and which basic controls help most.
talks.summary:
This RSA panel looks at how state, local, tribal and territorial governments and small and medium businesses handle cybersecurity. The first speaker, from the Center for Internet Security, argues that these groups share one problem: they lack the staff, funding and time to build defenses the way larger enterprises do. He pointed to yearly survey results from members of the multi-state information sharing center that keep showing the same issues, including tight budgets, difficulty keeping up with technology and attackers, and a shortage of skilled people. Programs matured faster where there was dedicated security staff, a recognized framework and executive involvement.

The second speaker, who assesses risk for smaller clients, described benchmarking data from small businesses, smaller government clients and managed service providers. Weaknesses clustered in the same set of controls across all three groups. Because one managed provider can administer many small clients, compromising it can expose a large number of organizations at once. He stressed that attackers mostly exploit basic gaps, such as exposed and unpatched remote desktop services, missing multifactor authentication and legacy systems that cannot be patched, rather than novel zero-day flaws. Ransom demands against smaller organizations can still be very large, and attackers may already know how much cash a victim holds.

The third speaker focused on low-cost steps. He recommended building a security culture where staff can raise questions without penalty, using education and the NICE workforce framework for job descriptions, giving everyone a password manager, turning on multifactor authentication everywhere, and keeping tested backups in both online and offline copies, starting with the most critical data. Across the panel, the advice was to inventory data, ask operations staff and executives separately which assets matter most, and avoid assuming an organization is too small to be targeted. The closing message was to start now using available guidance.

talks.title: Taking Flight
talks.teaser: 3 Experts Discuss Aerospace Cybersecurity explores Taking Flight.

talks.title: Colorful AppSec - Red, Blue, or Purple?
talks.teaser: Contrasts red, blue and purple team views on application security and how they can work with developers.
talks.summary:
This short lightning talk from the AppSec Village at RSA Conference had three speakers, each giving a red, blue or purple team perspective on application security, with Erez Yalon moderating. Pedro Umbelino opened from the red side. He argued that offensive exercises are among the most realistic tests an organisation can run, because real attackers ignore scope limits and rules of engagement. He said red teamers learn what the business does and what it stands to lose, which can surface risks that a severity score or bug bounty payout would miss.

Luis spoke for the blue team. He described defensive monitoring moving from basic log collection toward correlated, orchestrated and increasingly AI-assisted detection. He stressed that defenders need their own creativity, and that someone who understands how the product should behave can spot unusual activity, as customer support staff sometimes do, even without deep development experience. Tanya Janka presented purple teaming as collaborative security that bridges developers and security staff. She covered empathy, advocacy, practical tooling, workable processes and continuous learning. She described security champion programs and a weekly report that tracks the vulnerabilities developers introduced and the training that would have prevented them.

In the Q&A, the panel discussed phishing ethics and agreed that exercises should educate staff rather than blame them. They also said organisations should start red team exercises early instead of waiting until they feel mature. The session closed with the point that most people carry some red, blue and purple thinking.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Invisible War to Hijack Minds, Distort the Truth, and Impact Elections
talks.teaser: Explains how manipulation campaigns mix truth and lies, and traces a COVID-19 vaccine misinformation network with free tools.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how manipulation campaigns mix truth, half-truths and outright falsehoods to push people to act, or to hold back, and why technology alone will not solve the problem. Examples range from fabricated videos after the 2020 Beirut explosion and a false claim that a presidential candidate was ineligible, to a Russian troll campaign that falsely linked a Pennsylvania family farm's turkeys to poisonings. A harassment case against an Indian investigative journalist, whose likeness was edited into a pornographic video, shows the personal cost.

A common pattern: a story is seeded on state-sponsored and seemingly independent sites, then spread through hashtags, fake personas and bots until it gains a foothold. Red flags include sensational headlines, topics missing from mainstream media and memes aimed at younger audiences. In the central case, a 48-hour NodeXL search on COVID vaccine and hoax, checked with CrowdTangle and Botometer, found accounts that looked small but linked into large affinity groups. By the researchers' estimate, about 30 people reached at least 94,000 people, and a blog tied to a parent organization asked readers for donations.

Practical steps include keeping three trusted sources at local, national and international levels, and using Botometer and CrowdTangle in daily routines. Companies should build incident response playbooks for false claims about their industry or executives, prepare prebunking talking points and monitor for misinformation. For policymakers, the speaker calls for an international framework and for media firms to avoid knowingly circulating false news.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Coming AI Hackers
talks.teaser: Explains how AI systems could find and exploit loopholes in tax codes, finance and software, and why that is hard to notice.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that AI systems will increasingly find hacks, meaning unintended ways of obeying a system's rules that defeat its goals. The speaker widens the term beyond computers, using the tax code, frequent flyer programmes and the filibuster as examples. Reward hacking is illustrated with simulations in which agents exploited poorly specified goals, such as a soccer agent kicking the ball out of bounds and a robot vacuum that learned to drive backwards to use its rear sensors. The Volkswagen emissions cheat shows how a hidden hack in software can go unnoticed for years.

The main worry is explainability: modern AI systems are close to black boxes, so a harmful outcome may never be traced back to its cause. Hacking is easiest where rules are formal, such as games, simulations and financial regulation, which is named as a likely first target. Ambiguous human systems such as legislation are harder for AI to exploit, a gap the speaker presents as a near-term defence. Speed, scale and scope would change the picture, with AI finding loopholes quickly and bots flooding social media, and AI decisions in bail, loans and hiring would make hacks more damaging.

On the defensive side, the speaker suggests vulnerability-finding AI could let software makers patch code before release and let legislators or journalists test bills for loopholes, though legacy code and the transition period remain risky. The conclusion is that laws and governing structures must be patchable and able to respond at the speed of technology, and that society should decide technology's role in advance.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: What (Actually, Measurably) Makes a Security Program More Successful?
talks.teaser: Survey data ranks which security program practices correlate with better outcomes, and which ones matter least.
talks.summary:
This RSAC 2021 keynote presented a data-driven study of what makes a security program succeed. Wendy Nather and Wade Baker described a survey of about 4,800 IT and security professionals, narrowed to roughly 150 well-qualified responses from organizations in 25 countries. Respondents reported on 11 program outcomes, such as keeping up with the business, minimizing unplanned work and recruiting and retaining talent, and on 25 security practices. The speakers then ran statistical analysis to find where practices and outcomes were significantly correlated.

The analysis found that 23 of the 25 practices were linked to a better chance of success in at least one outcome, and that every outcome benefited from at least nine practices. Proactive tech refresh and well-integrated technology ranked as the strongest correlates, followed by timely incident response, prompt disaster recovery and accurate threat detection. Among the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions, protect was least correlated with success, which the presenters read as a call for more diverse programs rather than less protection. Results shifted by organization size, industry and geography. Identifying top cyber risks, for example, had no overall correlation but mattered mainly for large enterprises. No single practice stood out as a quick win.

The speakers closed with practical steps: read the report's outcomes matrix, which can be scanned by row to choose practices for a target outcome or by column to see what a practice supports, check the industry and size-specific follow-up reports, and consider how to measure progress toward each outcome. Their overall message was that governance, people, money, strategy and technology work together, so no single investment is likely to guarantee success.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Cryptographers' Panel
talks.teaser: Esteemed cryptographers debate NFTs, RSA factoring scares, quantum hype, fragile ML, supply-chain risk, and systemic resilience.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a familiar RSA Conference panel on trustworthy digital systems, quickly turning to non-fungible tokens. Ron Rivest frames NFTs as tokens pointing at copyable images, likening the value chain to homeopathic dilution, while Adi Shamir treats them as a benign collectible game and proposes minting the signed 1977 MIT RSA technical report for charity.

Discussion then centers on Claus Schnorr’s recent factorization paper and its claim to break RSA. Rivest emphasizes skepticism until large moduli are actually factored; Shamir cites independent implementation work suggesting relation counts fall far below what the paper needs. The group explores responsible disclosure when a flaw affects everyone, parallels with COVID tracing apps, and whether factoring breaks could be signaled without immediately publishing methods. Quantum computing draws mixed views: retracted topological-qubit claims, contested supremacy demonstrations, and doubt that scaled machines will soon threaten Bitcoin or replace ordinary key agreement. Machine learning is portrayed as opaque, adversarially brittle, and at odds with simplicity in security, with Ross Anderson highlighting NLP systems derailed by odd character injections.

SolarWinds underscores supplier concentration and outsourced engineering cultures; Intel’s fab strategy raises process-tampering fears for on-chip randomness. On COVID technology, Carmela Troncoso and others argue that mobile-platform gatekeeping and strict privacy engineering shaped global tracing choices, sometimes clashing with effectiveness and adoption, while Ross Anderson favors low-tech tracing and paper vaccine records over sprawling PKI passport schemes. The panel closes by grading cryptography versus deployment on resilience, warning that cloud and platform centralization magnify failure impact.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Five Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques
talks.teaser: Surveys dangerous new attacks, from supply chain tampering and token session abuse to machine learning evasion and extortion.
talks.summary:
Four presenters, Ed Skoudis, Heather Mahalik, Johannes Ullrich and Katie Nickels, walked through the attack techniques they considered the most dangerous new ones at the time. Skoudis started with software integrity, citing the SolarWinds intrusion and a dependency confusion case that gave a researcher code execution inside large companies' development environments. He urged software inventories, software bills of materials, file integrity monitoring, threat hunting and assumed-breach red team exercises.

Mahalik focused on session and token handling, walking through how a single sign-on login plus a one-time code could open cloud, email and storage access. She urged expiring tokens, logging out and reviewing app permissions. Ullrich covered attacks on machine learning malware classifiers, including poisoning training data with a second stream of malware and probing a model to find evasions. Nickels explained that ransomware now steals data before encrypting it, that renamed file-sharing tools such as RClone offer a detection clue, and that paying extortionists gives no guarantee of deletion.

The closing advice was to verify vendor models instead of accepting black boxes, to start with stronger detections, and to keep fundamentals like networking and operating systems solid.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Hugh Thompson Show: Backyard Edition
talks.teaser: Stories of remote-work chaos, personal resilience, and hands-on invention cover color home gaming and the Apple II floppy disk drive.
talks.summary:
The closing session frames the conference’s resilience theme through pandemic-era video meetings, where pets, children, and unexpected interruptions turned sterile calls into more human connections—and sometimes full-blown chaos before the host could mute the camera.

The conversation shifts to sustaining optimism and grit. The guest describes building color, software-driven arcade-style games into the Apple II, then needing a floppy disk demo to earn a trip to CES when only marketing staff were originally slated to attend. With no prior disk experience, he studied a Shugart drive schematic, simplified the electronics, and used a Berkeley state-machine approach so the machine could read and write data with minimal chips, finishing a working checkbook demo after an all-night push in Las Vegas.

The segment closes with encouragement that novel, demanding projects—often startups rather than classrooms—can be the most meaningful and enjoyable work, and with a brief farewell until an in-person return.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Spanning the Globe: The State of the Industry from the People Who Run It
talks.teaser: Global security leaders share how pandemic-era digital shifts, empathy, and trust reshaped enterprise protection and CISO priorities.
talks.summary:
A keynote host gathers short interviews with senior security executives from retail, healthcare, finance, technology, telecommunications, and energy, framed as globe-spanning vignettes on what changed during the pandemic and how leaders plan ahead.

Ahold Delhaize’s security chief describes scaling a 74 billion Euro grocery footprint while onboarding 45,000 people remotely, and introduces daily “vitamin shot” meetings where leaders share personal struggles to rebuild trust across countries. Johnson & Johnson’s CISO recalls roughly 30% more cyber crime as vaccine work made the company a hotter target, and stresses coordinating physical, brand, and supply chain risk while partnering with government. A former Goldman Sachs officer now at Google Cloud argues cloud scale can deliver usable security, cut false-positive fatigue, and multiply defender productivity through better design. Another leader ties conference resilience themes to empathetic leadership, public-private coordination, and threat-informed defense.

Australia’s national broadband CSO recounts chairing crisis response as millions shifted home over the network, elevating connectivity, people, and a shift toward trust and business continuity. Kuwait Oil’s former CISO describes 2020 as survival against burnout and human-targeted phishing, then moving into digital transformation leadership with security embedded from the start.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Global Threat Brief: Hacks and Adversaries Unveiled
talks.teaser: A joint briefing contrasts SolarWinds and Exchange intrusions, then surveys nation-state activity and ransomware trends.
talks.summary:
The keynote frames 2020 as a year when defenders faced pandemic stress while adversaries adapted. Two headline incidents anchor the discussion: the SolarWinds operation attributed to Russian SVR intelligence, characterized as traditional espionage against government and related targets, with malware that included a kill switch used to shut down access at most victims while preserving stealth on high-value networks; and the Exchange activity linked to HAFNIUM, which began with familiar intelligence targeting but escalated into mass exploitation ahead of patching, leaving widespread web shells and collateral risk from follow-on actors including ransomware groups.

The speakers then survey major nation-state players. China pursues strategic targets such as healthcare and biotech, shows restraint on destructive operations while reorganizing civilian and military intelligence capabilities, and aggressively targets dissidents and mobile users. Iran mixes espionage with information operations, including voter-intimidation email campaigns, LinkedIn targeting, and renewed DNS hijacking, alongside regional wiper activity. North Korea blends destruction, hack-and-leak, financial crime, custom tooling, supply-chain compromise, and attacks on researchers and cryptocurrency ecosystems. Russia complements SolarWinds with VPN exploitation, Golden SAML against federated identity, stealth infrastructure choices, cloud focus, and interest in transportation and airport-related critical infrastructure.

Ransomware is presented as the broadest civilian threat, with rising payments, public extortion tactics, hospital targeting, and sanctions complications. Looking forward, they expect Olympic targeting, ransomware evolution toward firmware or pure extortion without encryption, China's growing zero-day use, and increased targeting of security researchers. They close on worsening geopolitical relationships and actors who appear less deterred by public attribution.

talks.title: A Primer: Getting Started with MITRE Shield
talks.teaser: A primer on MITRE Shield explains deception maturity, adversary engagement, and defender techniques mapped to ATT&CK for stronger detection.
talks.summary:
Bill Hill and Stan Barr frame MITRE Shield as a defender-oriented companion to ATT&CK, rooted in years of deception and adversary-engagement work at MITRE. They walk a maturity path from passive logging and honeypots through active deception to deliberate engagement, stressing that defenders should learn from adversaries instead of disconnecting at the first sign of compromise. Hack-back and offensive active defense sit outside Shield’s scope.

Hands-on examples cover detonating malware in pseudo-realistic environments, collecting C2 and operator activity, and quantifying how engagement yields far more indicators, files, and signatures than static analysis alone. They share operational lessons—start simpler than a full enterprise clone, avoid tells that blow the engagement, and plan objectives like a chess game rather than checkers—and caution against gold images that leak real organizational detail.

Shield organizes defender actions around finding, understanding, and affecting threats, mapping adversary ATT&CK techniques to opportunity spaces and columns such as detect, legitimize, test, and collect. The speakers preview Shield 2.0 with clearer planning, analysis, and disrupt-focused taxonomy, and urge practitioners to review the framework, provide feedback, and only run malware when isolation and safety are well understood.

talks.title: MDR: Making Sense of the Veg-o-Matic Buzzword Blender
talks.teaser: Compares managed detection and response offerings and the trade-offs buyers should weigh before choosing one.
talks.summary:
Diana Kelley and Lisa Lee frame the talk around the confusion created by overlapping acronyms in managed security services. They break down what endpoint, network, threat and extended managed detection and response each cover, and note that MSSPs often stop at alerting while MDR providers add human threat hunting and hands-on response. The speakers also describe a response spectrum, from alerts-only to full remediation, and urge buyers to define where the handoff to the provider sits.

The middle section weighs decision points: whether to bring your own security stack, use a vendor-supplied stack, accept a vendor-built stack, or blend these. Each model is weighed for lock-in, integration gaps and staff workload. The talk also raises visibility and data access, how much to trust a provider's vetting, the value of correlating threat intelligence, how far automation should act without a human in the loop, and whether audit trails and forensic evidence will hold up.

To close, they suggest defining the problem and current capabilities first, then comparing vendors with normalized questions, and measuring results over time with metrics such as mean time to identify and contain, citing Ponemon's cost of data breach report. Attendees are pointed to NIST detection mappings, the Ponemon report and a CIS response plan template as starting resources.

talks.title: AppSec’s Future and the Rise of the Chief Product Security Officer
talks.teaser: Explains why software risk is pushing organizations toward a chief product security officer role and what that job covers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software now runs safety-critical products, connected devices and critical infrastructure, so its trustworthiness has become a leadership concern. The speakers contrast the chief product security officer with a traditional CISO, since products expose their own attack surface: internet-connected devices, APIs, social media links and legacy systems that never get retired. Many applications also depend heavily on open source and third-party APIs.

The middle covers practical shifts. Scanning infrastructure-as-code alongside application code gives context that can remove false positives, and policies such as whether a defect should break a build can live in the pipeline as code. A software bill of materials records components so they can be traced through the supply chain. One example showed a flaw first assumed to affect one vendor's operating system that actually sat in a deeper networking component used by many embedded systems. The speakers also recommend threat modeling, security architects and disclosure programs that welcome good-faith researchers.

To close, they advise practitioners to get fluent in SBOMs, supply chain risk and everything-is-code tooling. Longer term, they suggest defining objective criteria to rank applications by potential loss of life or regulated data, securing executive sponsorship, and starting with pilots on top-tier or new projects. The role is presented as a path to redefine a security career.

talks.title: Serverless Architecture Security Patterns for Securing the Unseen
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Serverless Architecture Security Patterns for Securing the Unseen.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Jabez Abraham, a Cloud Security Architect at Asurion (referred to phonetically as Osurion), examines the security challenges and architectural design patterns essential for securing serverless environments. While serverless technologies abstract away infrastructure management and patching, Abraham emphasizes that ephemeral compute functions are not inherently secure. Organizations must shift their security mindset from traditional infrastructure-centric controls to a data-centric model focused on protecting what matters most throughout its entire lifecycle.

### Key Topics
- **The Data Lifecycle and Threat Actors:** Understanding data creation, storage, and consumption across producers, consumers, protection boundaries, and perpetrators.
- **The Serverless Threat Landscape:** The "invisible" threat model of the cloud (the iceberg metaphor) where cloud providers manage the underlying physical layers, but application weaknesses, configuration, and ephemeral runtime permissions remain customer responsibilities.
- **Demonstration of Ephemeral Vulnerability:** A live demonstration using an interactive Lambda shell environment (lambdashell.com) showing how an attacker can extract runtime AWS environment variables (access key, secret key, session token) and interact with cloud resources externally.
- **Layered Architectural Patterns:** Applying defense in depth across the Edge, Compute, Middleware, and Back-End layers.
- **DevSecOps and Shared Responsibility:** Integrating security directly into developer sprint cycles and balancing user experience with compensating controls under the cloud shared responsibility model.

### Technical Details
Abraham illustrates security requirements by breaking serverless architectures down into distinct architectural tiers:
- **Front-End / Edge Layer:** Implement edge protections such as Web Application Firewalls (WAF), geographic and IP restrictions, CDN caching, enforcement of TLS/HTTPS redirects, security headers, and rate-based rules. Access to storage like Amazon S3 should be restricted using tight bucket policies that enforce least privilege (e.g., restricting specific source IPs and limiting actions strictly to `s3:GetObject`).
- **Middleware Layer:** Protect APIs through token validation, strong input sanitization, and standardized input validation to prevent injection or unexpected execution. When using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication and authorization, best practices include validating issuers, audiences, signatures, and expiration times while minimizing token scope.
- **Compute Layer & Lateral Movement:** The demonstration highlighted that even with a default minimal execution role (`AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole`), exposed temporary session credentials allow attackers to execute AWS CLI calls remotely. While privilege restriction prevents unauthorized role listing, an attacker could still create log groups and streams to generate garbage events and drive up billing costs. Overprivileged roles (such as admin privileges) create critical risks of lateral movement and account takeover. Additionally, developers must be mindful of shared global context across Lambda function warm invocations.
- **Back-End Layer:** Isolate databases (such as Amazon DynamoDB) within VPCs, use VPC endpoints and granular database resource policies (e.g., restricting queries strictly to designated source VPCs and specific actions like `GetItem`). Abraham emphasizes that while cloud providers protect physical data centers, data-level encryption and strict IAM policies prevent exfiltration. He also recommends automated containment strategies, where compromised or anomalous instances are tagged, snapshot for external forensic analysis, and isolated without disrupting business availability.

### Takeaways
Securing serverless architectures requires moving away from one-size-fits-all tooling toward layered, tower-specific controls. Abraham advises organizations not to "boil the ocean" but instead structure planning into immediate, short-term (e.g., 3–4 months), and long-term (e.g., 4–6 months) phases. Security teams must actively participate in DevOps sprint cycles from the ground up to educate developers and implement guardrails collaboratively. Ultimately, serverless security is not a fixed destination, but an ongoing journey of continuous iteration and adaptation as cloud services evolve.

talks.title: Security-as-Code to Accelerate DevSecOps, a Practical Guide to Get Started
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn security policy into automated checks across code, infrastructure and the software factory.
talks.summary:
Cindy Blake frames security as code as the next step after infrastructure as code. She traces provisioning from hand-requested hardware to templates and then to machine-readable definitions, and notes that a central configuration point is also an attractive target for malicious changes.

The core of the talk is a six-part framework. It covers testing source code with SAST, dependency, secrets and fuzz scanning; testing running applications with dynamic and API testing; scanning containers, packages and configurations; checking infrastructure-as-code files such as Helm charts and Terraform; controlling traffic between pods and applications inside Kubernetes; and securing the software factory through access control, code signing and push rules. For each area, teams must define processes and policies, including who may grant exceptions. She recommends running scans at commit and before merge, and uses the SolarWinds build compromise to show that a signed component can still carry a backdoor.

Her practical advice includes applying common controls, such as keeping the person who changes code separate from the one who pushes it to production. She also suggests applying least-privilege and zero trust principles across the DevOps toolchain, inventorying admin access to registries, package managers and Kubernetes, limiting alert noise, and keeping audit trails of who changed what and when. Her suggested starting point is to identify access to application infrastructure, then define processes and policies over the following months.

talks.title: How Digitizing the Workers Advances the CISO's Goals
talks.teaser: Shows how a wearable-based worker identity service can unify access, privacy and contact tracing for enterprises.
talks.summary:
Chris Sullivan of Nymi and Tim Callahan, global CSO at Aflac, open by tracing how security programs moved from compliance to maturity models, then to defensibility, and now to cyber resiliency. They describe the idea that resilient firms suffer little damage when breached, and Aflac's all-hazards crisis approach, adopted in 2017, which let the company shift quickly to remote work during the pandemic. Planned technology, a paperless workflow and existing logging and badge data also helped it monitor building occupancy and remote logins.

The middle of the talk argues that access controls such as badges, terminal locks and multifactor prompts are separate point solutions that burden workers and are hard to change. Sullivan proposes a single worker-centric service that verifies identity and uses signals such as location and activity to adjust controls without adding friction. Aflac applied this with a wearable that screens people at building entry instead of relying on guards with thermometers, supports contact tracing, replaces a keypad step with biometric multifactor, logs staff into computers, and enables secure printing. A pilot with roughly 80 to 100 people addressed early privacy worries, since the device only works for its wearer.

The closing section connects the approach to privacy by design and to digital transformation teams, who could use curated worker data without collecting it directly. The speakers recommend that attendees first decide whether the direction suits their organisation, then build a business case, and consider whether badges and passwords can eventually be retired.

talks.title: The Rise of the BISO Role
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Rise of the BISO Role.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Manuel Chowrimootoo, Business Information Security Officer (BISO) at Cogeco Communications, discusses the emergence and practical implementation of the BISO role. After joining a newly formed 15-person corporate cybersecurity team in January 2020 under the CISO's leadership, Chowrimootoo was tasked with building awareness, establishing a service catalog, and operationalizing cybersecurity as a service across disparate business units and corporate departments. The session outlines the mandate, operating structure, procedural developments, and lessons learned from establishing the BISO function from the ground up.

### Key Topics
- **Understanding the BISO Mandate**: Defining the BISO as an enabler and operational bridge between centralized security and business units, contrasting with the CISO's strategic focus.
- **The Cyber Roadshow**: Launching introductory tours across corporate functions (legal, procurement, internal audit, project management) to understand people, processes, and tools.
- **Operationalizing Cybersecurity as a Service**: Evolving from informal spreadsheets and shared mailboxes to formalized request forms, structured intake workflows, and resource allocation tracking.
- **Risk Management Integration**: Partnering directly with internal audit, enterprise risk, and governance teams to identify critical findings and prioritize remediation.
- **Demonstrating Value**: Generating qualitative and quantitative reporting, such as tracking effort hours, maintaining status dashboards, and setting formal delivery timelines.

### Technical Details & Operational Mechanics
- **CISO vs. BISO Division**: The CISO operates at a strategic tier, collaborating with executive committees (e.g., Audit Committee, VP of Internal Audit, CIO, CTO). In contrast, the BISO operates at the tactical and operational layer, working directly with audit directors, individual auditors, and business unit IT architecture and operations teams to close specific findings.
- **Service Request Evolution**: Initial intake relied on a general mailbox, phone numbers, and an Excel template. As volume grew and services stabilized, this was decommissioned in favor of user-friendly electronic forms featuring prebuilt drop-down menus tailored to known service offerings.
- **Service Offerings**: Core delivered services included architectural reviews, scans for PCI compliance, third-party vendor reviews, and log monitoring.
- **KPIs and Metrics**: To avoid the early pitfall of "best efforts" SLAs, the team formalized timelines once sufficient operational data was captured. For example, security opinions were benchmarked to an average delivery turnaround of two weeks.
- **Reporting Structure**: Reporting was tailored by audience—executive-level views used red/yellow/green indicators for red flags, while business unit managers received weekly or twice-weekly updates covering open project statuses, effort hours, and deadlines.

### Takeaways
- **Interpersonal Over Technical Skills**: The BISO role requires wearing multiple hats (negotiator, project manager, security advocate) and communicating effectively across different domains, from corporate attorneys to infrastructure engineers.
- **Avoid Over-Promising**: Relying on unmeasured commitments leads to dissatisfaction; teams should capture performance metrics before cementing firm delivery timelines.
- **Senior Leadership Backing**: Explicit alignment with CISO and CTO strategic plans, paired with executive sponsorship, ensures the BISO is accepted onto critical decision-making committees.
- **Actionable Steps for Organizations**: Within the first few weeks, identify designated cybersecurity contacts and obtain the cybersecurity service catalog and policy documentation. Within three months, review policies, address gaps, and confirm formal communication channels for requesting security engagements.

talks.title: Your Breached Controls May Have Been Reasonable After All
talks.teaser: A legal panel applies a proposed reasonableness test to a hypothetical health app breach, weighing security costs against benefits.
talks.summary:
A panel from the Sedona Conference presents a proposed test for deciding whether an organization's data security controls were reasonable under the law. The test grew out of a working group that found courts, regulators and industry all relied on reasonableness without agreeing on its meaning. The group adapted an old cost-benefit formula from a judge, adding the benefits a risky activity provides to others, such as the public, to the burden side of the calculation.

To test it, the panelists walk through a hypothetical health app for senior citizens whose users' data was sold after credentials were phished and multi-factor authentication was absent. The consultant explains that a soft certificate approach slowed sign-ins and was bypassed in a red team test, and the replacement gesture check drove many senior users away. The CIS representative argues most organizations can implement multi-factor authentication and suggests risk-based authentication as an alternative. The FTC attorney says regulators would ask why the control was skipped, whether it was industry custom, and how the soft certificate weakness was handled instead of simply turning it off. The defense lawyer stresses that benefits should not be overstated and that lost utility, labor and support costs must be counted.

The panelists agree the test gives companies and regulators a shared framework, though they disagree on how much weight lost utility deserves. Their closing takeaway is that reasonableness depends on the specific company, the sensitivity of its data and the costs to the company, consumers and the public, since no security measure is costless.

talks.title: ComPriSec: A Weird Word for a New World
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning ComPriSec: A Weird Word for a New World.

talks.title: Attack & Defend: Protecting Modern Distributed Applications and Components
talks.teaser: Demonstrates bypassing an API gateway with a captured JWT, then shows defenses like private endpoint policies and SRI hashes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at modern single page web applications built from distributed parts: static file storage, an API gateway, back-end APIs and an identity provider. The demo app uses Keycloak for identity and Kong as its gateway. One presenter attacks while the other defends, with each attack followed by a fix.

The first attack copies a browser request as a curl command, uses certificate transparency logs to find other hostnames, and sends the same request straight to a back-end port, skipping the gateway. The gateway's rate limit, which returns 429 errors, never applies on that path. The suggested defense is a private endpoint policy that accepts requests only from the gateway's source VPC rather than relying on IP addresses. The second attack decodes the JSON web token from the request to read its claims and roles, then calls an operation the web interface never exposed. The proposed fix hands the browser an opaque ticket that the gateway exchanges for the full token, using the token signature as a cache lookup key.

The final scenario swaps a JavaScript library loaded from a third-party CDN for a script that captures keystrokes and sends them to an outside domain. Subresource integrity hashes stop the browser from running a modified file. The presenters close by urging teams to review the architecture and configuration of each component, understand how credentials flow and what tokens contain, and agree on shared credential handling guidelines across development teams.

talks.title: Cloud Threat Modeling - from Architecture Design to Application Development
talks.teaser: Shows how to apply threat modeling to cloud architecture, using attack trees and the CSA threat cards.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why threat modeling matters when applications move to the cloud. The speakers frame it around three questions: what to protect, who it needs protecting from, and how much defense is worth spending. They point to the NIST SP 800 series, the Cloud Controls Matrix, Microsoft's process and STRIDE categories as reference points. A playful attack tree built on the film Home Alone shows how each attack step meets a countermeasure, and how analysis can stop once an attacker's path stops being useful.

The middle covers the Cloud Security Alliance's Top Threats Working Group work. It presents threat modeling cards that link threats, vulnerabilities, assets and controls, and a case study based on a Dow Jones scenario. Two Elasticsearch deployments show the same product carrying different vulnerabilities depending on where each asset came from and who maintains it: a CIS-hardened AWS image versus a self-managed build. The speaker also proposes a consistent threat naming pattern of actor, verb and object.

The closing advice is practical. Pick a system that is moving to the cloud, build a threat model around what it protects and from whom, and use the Cloud Controls Matrix to plan mitigations. Revisit the model roughly six months later to confirm it still matches the environment. The presenters also flag upcoming Top Threats output, including a survey to replace the Egregious 11, and work on gamified threat modeling scorecards.

talks.title: Due to Less Pollution, Secrets Stored on the Cloud are Now Clearly Visible
talks.teaser: Shows how credentials leaked to public GitHub repos can enable cloud compromise, backed by months of collected leak data.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how secrets such as SSH keys, API keys, OAuth tokens and SAML tokens move through DevOps and IT operations pipelines that now span cloud platforms. The presenters argue that the old network perimeter has blurred with cloud services, so reused or federated credentials let an attacker pivot between environments. They point to hard-coded credentials, unvetted public container images and federated credentials as common routes, and mention recent post-exploitation methods such as cookie passing and Golden SAML.

The second half turns to a tool the researchers built, which runs GitHub advanced searches, parses the matching results and checks file contents against roughly 30 credential patterns. In a live demo, a search for AWS credential files returned about 350 results, and the tool flagged keys inside them and wrote the findings to a JSON file. Over eight months of running the tool and indexing its output in Splunk, most leaks were passwords embedded in URLs, followed by GCP service account data and API keys. The average time a secret stayed exposed was about 52 days, and the number of leaks trended downward over the monitoring period.

For defenders, the takeaway is that exposure does not end when code is published. The speakers recommend knowing what developers download and publish, scanning and inventorying containers and libraries, and asking IT and development leads which cloud services and images are in use. They also note that GitHub offers a tool to help prevent this kind of leak, and suggest checking whether an organization's own secrets are already public.

talks.title: Multi-Cloud Anomaly Detection: Finding Threats Among Us in the Big 3 Clouds
talks.teaser: Shows how to spot hidden cloud intrusions in AWS, Azure and GCP using network flow and API audit logs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why malicious activity hides well in public cloud networks, since attacker traffic and API calls can look just like normal use. It argues that the audit logs the big three providers already offer, covering network flow logs and cloud API activity, can expose indicators of compromise if teams enable them, retain them and query them. Flow logs record metadata about who talks to whom and how much data moves, not packet contents, and none of AWS, Azure or GCP turns them on by default.

The speaker compares how each provider handles flow logs. AWS can be set per VPC, subnet or network interface and captures rejected traffic. Azure logs accepted and rejected packets at the network security group level but aggregates records, so one row may stand for many messages. GCP logs from the VM's point of view, so blocked inbound traffic is invisible unless firewall rule logging is enabled. In one demo, a malicious npm package made unusual outbound connections on port 9999, and a packet capture showed DNS queries carrying encoded host identifiers, a sign of exfiltration. A separate demo covered API logs, where repeated key decryption events traced back to a data scientist decrypting database backups from a workstation outside the network. The Capital One breach was used to show how stolen instance credentials can reach storage far beyond what a server needs.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to turn on flow and API logging everywhere, keep logs for at least a year as the CIS guidance suggests, and set alarms on log-based metrics, such as a spike in decryption events within a short window. Teams should baseline normal behaviour before writing queries, tighten permissions with least privilege, and combine cloud-native tools with any third-party monitoring they already run. Machine learning can help scale the search for anomalies.

talks.title: Multi-Cloud Security Monitoring and CIS Benchmarks Evaluation at Scale
talks.teaser: Explains a plugin-based framework for monitoring multiple clouds and auditing them against CIS benchmarks, with Azure examples.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses why security monitoring across several cloud providers is hard: each provider has its own APIs, data formats and terminology, and auditing very large estates takes a long time. The presenters describe a plugin-based framework. Cloud plugins pull resource records, store plugins write them to systems such as Splunk, Elasticsearch or MongoDB, event plugins check each record for one type of issue, and alert plugins send the resulting events onward. Plugins never interact directly; the framework runs each one as a separate process and connects them with queues.

Each record is split into three buckets. The raw bucket keeps the provider's original object, the ext bucket adds context such as the source cloud plus derived fields like power state or disk encryption under uniform names, and the common bucket holds metadata shared by all plugins. This normalisation lets one query work across providers. The presenters then map CIS benchmarks onto the design. One example flags Azure virtual machines whose OS disk is not encrypted; another flags Azure web apps that accept a TLS version below the configured minimum. Each event carries a description of the problem and a remediation note for the administrator, and a new event plugin takes only about 30 to 40 lines of code.

To close, the speakers outline a practical process: list the cloud resources in use, rank them by business importance, identify which standards and compliance frameworks apply, and name the team responsible for acting on audit findings. Because CIS benchmarks cover only common misconfigurations, they recommend adding guidance from NIST, PCI or ISO. They also point to an open-source Python reference implementation that can be used as is or extended with new plugins.

talks.title: Knowledge Glaciers in the Age of Automation and Cloud Native
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Knowledge Glaciers in the Age of Automation and Cloud Native.

talks.title: MITRE ATT&CK® as a Framework for Cloud Threat Investigation
talks.teaser: Presents survey results on using MITRE ATT&CK to investigate threats across hybrid cloud, network and endpoint environments.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how security operations teams investigate threats in cloud environments and why the MITRE ATT&CK framework is being applied to that work. The presenters outline the enterprise and cloud matrices, then summarize how responsibility is split between provider and customer across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. Under IaaS the customer keeps the operating system and everything above it, while under SaaS the provider covers almost the whole service. In every model the customer still configures the service, manages user accounts and protects its own data.

The presenters report a survey of 325 large and medium-sized enterprises in the UK, US and Australia, with interviews of 10 cybersecurity experts. Only about 39% of respondents correlate events from network, endpoint and cloud sources together, even though hybrid deployment is the most common architecture and attackers can move from on-premises workstations into cloud accounts. Eighty-one percent of respondents use ATT&CK in some form. The most cited challenges were lack of interoperability with security products (45%), difficulty mapping events to tactics and techniques (43%) and too many false positives (36%).

For practitioners, the recommendations are to adopt ATT&CK as a common taxonomy for investigations, to investigate threats across all data sources, and to automate tagging of events so that high-priority tactics such as exfiltration are reviewed before lower-risk ones. The presenters also stress continuous testing of security products to confirm they tag and alert on techniques and sub-techniques, not only the top-level tactics.

talks.title: Attacking Kubernetes Clusters Through Your Network Plumbing
talks.teaser: Shows how pod network plumbing enables ARP spoofing, VXLAN packet forgery and BGP session hijacking in Kubernetes clusters.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how the networking layers of Kubernetes clusters, including pod network namespaces, bridges, virtual ethernet links, kube-proxy iptables rules and overlay devices, can be abused by an attacker. It splits the attacks by plugin type. For layer two plugins, using Flannel as the example, the speaker shows ARP spoofing that lets an attacker sit between two pods and redirect DNS replies to a fake service.

Next the speaker covers two common mitigations: an iptables allow rule and removing the NET_RAW capability from pods. Both are shown to be insufficient in a demo. A pod without raw packet rights can still craft VXLAN-formatted payloads sent to a node's UDP port 8472, and the receiving overlay device unwraps them as legitimate pod traffic, letting the attacker spoof a source address past a block rule. For layer three plugins, using Calico, routing daemons run as host processes, so a low-privileged foothold on a node or a pod in the root network namespace can threaten the whole cluster's data flow. The speaker hijacks a BGP session and describes a new issue in the BGP RFC: a crafted notification that removes Graceful Restart support keeps the attacker's session persistent. The issue was disclosed to the Calico project, with the fix tied to version 3.17. A final demo injects a route that sends traffic meant for a database pod through an attacker's machine.

The takeaways are to know which network plugin and overlay type your cluster uses, drop NET_RAW from pods unless it is needed, block encapsulated packets from pods, and protect routing protocol sessions with passwords.

talks.title: Telehealth Cybersecurity: Secure Remote Patient Monitoring Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Telehealth Cybersecurity: Secure Remote Patient Monitoring Ecosystem.

talks.title: What’s Old is New: Hybrid Security for Microsoft Azure and On-Premises Tech
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers pivot between on-prem Active Directory and Azure AD, and how to harden hybrid identities.
talks.summary:
This talk examines why attackers still target on-premises Active Directory while organizations move identity and data to Microsoft Azure Active Directory. The presenters, from Mandiant's security transformation services team, point to privileged groups and delegated permissions that are often overlooked on-prem, such as accounts that can replicate directory changes or edit group policy. They also show that Azure AD directory roles and Azure RBAC resource permissions operate as distinct systems, and that some roles stay hidden in the portal but can still be listed with PowerShell.

Recon and privilege escalation come next. Techniques include Kerberoasting, re-enabled WDigest to capture clear text passwords, and cached Kerberos credentials on laptops used away from the VPN. In the cloud, a non-privileged account can still enumerate users and resources if the portal restriction is off, and a global administrator who elevates into user access administrator can reach a cloud virtual machine that acts as a domain controller. The presenters also describe adding a certificate to a service principal so an attacker keeps access after passwords are reset, since service principal sign-ins are not governed by conditional access.

The defenses include separate cloud-only admin accounts with MFA, two monitored break-glass global admins, sign-in frequency policies, blocking legacy authentication, limiting device joins because joining users become local administrators, and treating identity providers as tier zero. The main takeaway is to baseline and alert on service principal sign-ins and on role assignments in Azure AD, which many organizations do not yet monitor.

talks.title: Visible Figures: Bridging the Skills Gap With Inclusion and Equal Opportunity
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Visible Figures: Bridging the Skills Gap With Inclusion and Equal Opportunity.

talks.title: Implementation
talks.teaser: A framework unifies matrix linear-layer heuristics and reduction rules to shrink XOR costs for cipher implementations.
talks.summary:
The presentation addresses how to implement linear layers in block ciphers as binary matrices while minimizing XOR gate count, a problem distinct from heavily tool-supported S-box optimization. The speaker defines D-xor, G-xor, and S-xor cost models that trade direct evaluation, register use, and in-place updates, then surveys established heuristics including Paar's column-pair method and Boyer-Peyrin-style BP variants with distance factors and preemptive choices.

The core contribution is a modular framework that can start from a partial implementation, recover an equivalent submatrix from real inputs and outputs, re-optimize segments with embedded heuristics, and apply post-processing reduction rules. Rules nine through eleven eliminate single-use intermediates when algebraically redundant, saving XORs without changing behavior. The workflow supports plugging in future heuristics rather than fixing one construction path.

Empirical comparisons show the composed approach beating standalone heuristics on benchmark matrices. For cipher use, the framework yields a notably compact XOR implementation for AES column mixing, presented as the shortest known mix-column construction in this metric. Practitioners gain a flexible recipe for shrinking linear-layer cost on constrained devices.

talks.title: Authentication and Key Exchange
talks.teaser: Surveys group key exchange models, revisits EPID signature security, and proves a tighter bound for signed Diffie-Hellman.
talks.summary:
The session covers three cryptography papers on key exchange and authentication. Paul Rosler opens with group key exchange, where members agree on a shared key that encrypts group messages. Reviewing 12 papers among more than 30 security definitions, the authors find no generic standard model: definitions were informal, over-fitted to single constructions, or ignored environment properties. Their compact model handles asynchronous communication and several authentication methods.

Jacques Poway then revisits the security model of EPID, an anonymous signature scheme standardized by ISO and embedded in many devices. Existing unforgeability proofs extract corrupt signing keys in joint sessions, limiting concurrency or slowing the protocol. The proposed model instead requires N+1 valid signatures from N corrupt keys, and gives the adversary control over revocation lists in the anonymity game. Without this, a malicious revocation manager could break anonymity by inserting randomized revocation tags. Two new EPID schemes meet these stronger requirements.

Magnus Ringerud presents a tight security proof for signed Diffie-Hellman, a core part of TLS. The earlier bound lost a factor quadratic in the session count, so 128-bit security could fall to 68 bits with two to the 30 sessions. The reduction uses a strong computational Diffie-Hellman assumption and a verifiable key exchange technique to answer key reveal queries. The loss becomes constant, and existing implementations are argued to remain secure. State reveals are not modelled, and extending the work to group key exchange is future work.

talks.title: Shuffling and Friends
talks.teaser: Explores lattice shuffles for e-voting, two-challenge shuffle arguments, and accumulator cryptanalysis.
talks.summary:
The session strings together three research presentations on verifiable shuffling and closely related cryptography. The opening work targets electronic voting where a shuffle server must decrypt ballots, reorder them, and convince outsiders that no ciphertext was swapped for an attacker-chosen vote. That design leans on lattice commitments, verifiable encryption, and a shuffle proof built from polynomial techniques, with explicit discussion of integrity via zero-knowledge checks, ballot privacy when ballot box and shuffle server do not collude, and voter verifiability through return codes. An implementation over a cyclotomic ring is quoted at about 32 milliseconds and 17 kilobytes per vote for decrypt-plus-shuffle, compared favorably to an earlier lattice voting scheme that only supported binary choices.

The middle segment reframes the classical problem: ciphertext order can deanonymize voters even when encryption is otherwise sound, so shuffling must be accompanied by a proof that only permutation and rerandomization occurred. Building on earlier verificatum-style arguments, the speakers introduce PM-evidential polynomial families so a verifier need not send one challenge per ballot; their concrete family uses only two challenges while preserving the permutation-matrix logic.

The closing segment is offensive cryptanalysis of a dynamic universal accumulator from 2009. Witness constructions leak structure in the non-membership case, enabling recovery of the secret accumulator parameter and, in a CRS-held-private model, reconstruction of secret CRS material from batches of witnesses. Practitioners should treat witness formulas and initialization as part of the threat model, not accessory details.

talks.title: Symmetric Design
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Symmetric Design.

talks.title: Cryptanalysis II
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cryptanalysis II.

talks.title: Post-Quantum
talks.teaser: A survey maps post-quantum design paradigms to implementation flaws, side channels, masking, and NIST-style benchmarks.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames post-quantum cryptography through a process-oriented lens—assumption, design, implementation, and deployment—while concentrating on scheme design and coding practice. Classical signatures and key establishment map to four recurring paradigms (Fiat–Shamir, hash-then-sign, Diffie–Hellman, and public-key encryption), and most post-quantum proposals still fit that skeleton. Experience shows that copying constructions naively tends toward broken assumptions or poor efficiency; the more reliable path tweaks problems and paradigms while keeping meaningful security proofs. A detailed thread walks from full-domain hash signatures and trapdoor permutations to trapdoor preimage sampleable functions and their average-case variant, motivating lattice schemes such as Falcon and code-based schemes such as Wave.

The second half stresses that deploying post-quantum algorithms introduces operations and failure modes uncommon in classical stacks—Gaussian sampling, rejection sampling, decryption failures, and data-dependent branches that invite leakage unless constant-time discipline is enforced. Recent implementation attacks target Fujisaki–Okamoto transforms via timing and domain-separation mistakes. Side-channel work spans power analysis on family-specific linear algebra, fault and cold-boot threats, and how physical hints feed cryptanalytic estimates for lattice and code attacks. Masking and hiding are surveyed as prerequisites for real-world use, with early masking proposals for leading candidates and fresh evidence that masked designs remain fragile.

Practitioners should treat post-quantum migration as an engineering program, not a algorithm pick: align paradigm choice with provable assumptions, harden implementations against microarchitectural and transform-level flaws, and measure honestly on reference platforms. Benchmarking efforts collated for NIST-style evaluation highlight how seed expansion dominates cycle counts on embedded ARM targets and how FPGA implementations vary across candidates. A hedging technique for Fiat–Shamir signatures illustrates ongoing fault-mitigation research. Fuller treatment of assumptions and deployment appear in the associated CT-RSA and e-print write-ups.

talks.title: Applied MPC
talks.teaser: Explores multiparty PageRank for fraud graphs, secure function compilation for MPC, and oblivious TLS for split servers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with collaborative graph analysis on transaction networks, where banks each see only their clients’ edges but want PageRank-style reputation scores without exposing raw data. A multiparty computation protocol built on linear secret sharing is described for iteratively evaluating the stationary distribution, including fixed-point encoding of rational matrix entries, early stopping when convergence is within a fixed error bound, and an analysis of what leaking the iteration count reveals about the second-largest eigenvalue in PageRank-style matrices.

A second segment shifts from protocol mechanics to how functions are prepared for secure evaluation. It contrasts idealized arithmetic-circuit inputs with practical compilation paths that exploit protocol gadgets such as Beaver triples, parallel secret-sharing rounds, and deliberate declassification steps. It introduces M-Circuits and STEM-Circuit classes, argues that compilation can introduce statistical insecurity or outright insecure declassification even when the high-level function is correct, and extends the same compilation viewpoint to MPC-in-the-Head zero-knowledge constructions.

The closing presentation describes oblivious TLS, in which multiple parties jointly act as a TLS server while Internet clients use ordinary TLS. Secret-shared symmetric keys support multiparty decrypt and encrypt steps, and a multiparty elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman construction with mask points and cut-and-choose preprocessing yields shared key material without any party learning the full key. Reported LAN experiments cite about one second for the handshake and roughly three megabytes per second AES-GCM throughput for the online phase, with threshold EdDSA for authentication and an MPC-oriented AEAD discussed in the paper.

talks.title: Cryptanalysis I
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Cryptanalysis I.

talks.title: Cryptography in Distributed Systems
talks.teaser: Explores distributed-trust accumulators, accountable blockchain anonymity, and half-aggregation of Schnorr and EdDSA signatures.
talks.summary:
Roman Walch starts with cryptographic accumulators, which compactly represent a set with witnesses for members. Merkle-tree witnesses grow with the set, while q-SDH accumulators have constant-size witnesses but need a secret trapdoor that must be discarded, making updates slow. It splits the trapdoor across several accumulator managers, as in Sovrin, and uses multi-party computation so updates and witness creation run in constant time. MPC benchmarks in the MP-SPDZ library beat the non-MPC baseline, which exceeded 100 seconds at 2^14 elements.

Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh addresses the tension between privacy and accountability for blockchain identity. Bitcoin-style systems expose balances and transaction graphs, while fully anonymous systems fall short of know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering rules. The design uses account holders, identity providers and anonymity revokers: a blind signature caps how many accounts a user can open, zero-knowledge proofs validate each account, and a threshold of revokers can unmask a suspicious account and link its siblings.

Yashvanth Kondi closes with a non-interactive scheme that half-aggregates EdDSA and Schnorr signatures, using only black-box access to the hash and group. Sigma-protocol reasoning shows that proving knowledge of n Schnorr signatures can be compressed to the nonces plus one combined response, roughly 50% smaller. This rate is essentially optimal for black-box approaches, since going further needs costly non-black-box techniques. Implemented with the Dalek library, Fiat-Shamir aggregates over 1000 signatures in under a millisecond, while the Fischlin transformation gives tight security. Takeaway: if exact bit representations of signature batches do not matter, aggregation can save up to 50% bandwidth.

talks.title: One Step Ahead: Keeping Security at the Forefront
talks.teaser: Panelists explain how pandemic remote work shifted security focus, human risk, and sector responses in healthcare and nonprofits.
talks.summary:
The session opens on how the sudden move online during COVID changed whether security led or lagged behind accessibility and continuity. Panelists from nonprofit services, security awareness, and healthcare IT describe rushed remote pivots, stretched business continuity plans, and new worries about home networks, personal devices, and blended work-life boundaries on endpoints.

The middle turns to people as the control point: event-themed phishing, distraction at home, data leakage on unmanaged networks, and the need to communicate threats under stress. One speaker cites survey results where nearly half of users believed technology alone could stop social engineering. Healthcare receives extended treatment—ransomware resurging around May 2020, double extortion against protected health data, industry threat coalitions, and patient-safety research tying breaches to delayed care and higher mortality.

Nonprofit leaders report sharper phishing exposure, mission-driven shame after incidents, and harder questions about cloud vendors and donor privacy in living rooms. The close covers hybrid workforce futures, celebrating small security wins, and a health-sector note that breach counts rose while individuals affected fell from 2019 to 2020. Practitioners should treat remote work as permanent attack-surface change, invest in awareness without blaming users, and align sector-specific trust and compliance with realistic third-party and telehealth risk.

talks.title: Upskilling, Credentials and Soft Skills: Closing the Cyber Workforce Gap
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Upskilling, Credentials and Soft Skills: Closing the Cyber Workforce Gap.

talks.title: Protecting What Matters Most - Tools for Managing Risk
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss aligning cybersecurity risk with enterprise risk management, business goals and compliance requirements.
talks.summary:
The panel explores how security teams can connect cybersecurity risk to enterprise risk management and business objectives. Panelists with backgrounds in federal standards work, higher education and professional certification bodies argue that practitioners should first learn what leadership and stakeholders consider important, instead of building programs around their own priorities. They point to NIST interagency report 8286 as a way to tie system-level cyber risk work back to enterprise strategy, with risk appetite and tolerance recorded in a risk register.

Compliance was a major thread. Panelists noted that compliance requirements can feel like box-checking and can slow research or operations, so teams should ask what each control is meant to achieve. One speaker described a structured, repeatable process for communicating major vulnerabilities and attacks, so leadership hears about incidents in a consistent way. The panel agreed that compliance should be an outcome of a well-run program rather than the end goal.

For reporting, the panel favored board-level enterprise risk formats and heat maps of the top risks showing change over time, along with audience-specific metrics such as scorecards for vulnerability management and training. Security leaders were urged to learn business terms, including operating and capital expense impacts, so their messages land. The closing advice was to speak the language of the business and present security as an enabler.

talks.title: Why Resilience Has Become A Cybersecurity Superpower
talks.teaser: Explores how cyber risk programs can grow organizational resilience through identification, ecosystem thinking, and diverse teams.
talks.summary:
The session argues that mature security organizations should shift from treating cyber mainly as a technology or controls problem toward holistic cyber risk management and resilience. It opens by framing cyber as a modifier for digital and cyber-physical exposure, then maps how missions, business processes, and assets connect to risk management activities such as vulnerability handling, threat inputs, and control prioritization tied to appetite and mission context.

Resilience is presented as an emergent organizational capability—not something purchased like a product and broader than classic business continuity and disaster recovery alone. The speaker describes anticipating disruption through robust risk identification, preparing without expecting perfection, adapting under uneven incidents, and recovering while linking practices such as coordinated incident response and vulnerability management. A ransomware-style outage example illustrates unifying continuity, incident, and situational awareness work.

The closing sections emphasize multidisciplinary teams, workforce diversity, and closing large talent gaps through skills like cloud security, risk analysis, and critical thinking. Recruiters are urged to hire for attitude and aptitude, broaden hiring pools, invest in mentorship and rotation, and take concrete steps over the next week, month, and quarter to strengthen personal and program resilience muscles.

talks.title: How to Guide: Using ISSA/ESG Research Data For Your Benefit
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning How to Guide: Using ISSA/ESG Research Data For Your Benefit.

talks.title: Reducing Payment Fraud with SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework
talks.teaser: Explains how SWIFT's Customer Security Controls Framework and industry collaboration aim to curb payment fraud across banks.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with background on SWIFT, a member-owned cooperative that carries large bank-to-bank payment messages for institutions in about 220 countries. A 2016 attack on the Bank of Bangladesh, attributed to a North Korean group, showed how attackers who get into the back office through a malicious link can steal operator credentials and inject fraudulent payment messages. In response, SWIFT launched the Customer Security Program, a set of controls based on NIST, ISO 27001 and PCI DSS, split into mandatory and advisory tiers across seven themes, with yearly attestation. Average compliance per control rose from about 77 percent in the first year to roughly 97 percent by early 2021.

The panelists, from Deutsche Bank, JP Morgan Chase and SWIFT, said the program has brought cybersecurity, fraud and business teams onto a shared vocabulary, and that its outcome-based design lets controls keep pace with APIs and cloud. They reported that the value lost to fraudulent transfers has dropped since members adopted the controls, though attempts continue. The hardest open problem is counterparty risk: members can now see peers' control status, but turning that data into decisions and extending oversight to unregulated third-party vendors remains a work in progress.

Looking ahead, the panel favored aligning overlapping frameworks, including the financial sector cybersecurity profile, so that demonstrating compliance costs less and more effort goes into control design and continuous monitoring. Practical takeaways include involving security early in new business initiatives, treating availability as part of resilience, and using available data to assess counterparties and suppliers.

talks.title: Pinata Time: Why We Should All Start Bashing Mules!
talks.teaser: Senior bank fraud executives outline mule typologies, COVID-driven account-opening surges, and practical detection tactics.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a typology that separates mule activity tied to new account opening from abuse of existing customer relationships, and within that landscape distinguishes unwitting recruits from professional operators. Panelists from large US and Australian banks describe how COVID-era government relief—unemployment insurance, disaster loans, and similar fast-disbursement programs—reshaped the threat: stolen identity data fed industrial-scale openings aimed at stimulus and loan proceeds, often cashed out through peer-to-peer apps and debit rails before dispute workflows could claw funds back.

Midway through, the discussion stacks operational case studies without blurring them together: rental-market double fraud, a digital bank drowned by hundreds of manual applications per day, micro-deposit validation abuse through a major online platform generating tens of thousands of inbound transfers daily, cross-institution mule hopping, and enduring romance and family-impersonation recruitment. Faster payments, especially instant transfer schemes, are framed as amplifying risk when review-and-release and inbound monitoring lag behind outbound speed.

The close turns to defense and organizational buy-in. Practitioners highlight layered account-opening controls—behavioral biometrics, cut-and-paste signals, device and network link analysis, and incoming-payment patterns that diverge from normal consumer use—plus industry collaboration to trace shared attributes across banks. A simulated budget conversation argues for near-term blocking at the door and longer-term cleanup on the books, citing material fraud-reduction potential and regulatory and reputational pressure to treat mule receipt as a first-class control problem.

talks.title: Get Rich or Get Hunted Trying: Uncovering Large Scale Fraud Operations
talks.teaser: Dissects account takeover campaigns, from reverse proxy phishing to emulator device spoofing, and outlines defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
The session covers how the shift to remote work during COVID widened the target pool, as people logged in from personal, unmanaged devices and organizations launched new online services. The presenters walk through phishing trends their lab tracked, including new top-level domains, phishing sites that carry SSL certificates, and per-visitor randomized URL folders. They also show anti-research filters that redirect visitors based on geolocation, proxy use, or IP blocklists.

A live demo reconstructs a reverse proxy phishing kit built on Evilginx and aimed at Instagram. The proxy relays the genuine login page, so victims see their real account while the operator captures the password and session cookies. The stolen cookies then open the live session, and the password is changed to lock the owner out. In a separate case against a global financial institution, each phishing email carried a unique token, and victims were steered into updating their two-factor phone number to one the attacker controlled. The mobile emulator section covers fraud crews that spoof device attributes, route traffic through proxies or VPNs, and script logins. One emulator produced more than 8,000 compromised sessions, and one-time codes were harvested through smishing, malware or robocalls.

The closing advice is to hunt for blind spots in current processes and tooling. The presenters suggest machine learning for phishing detection, such as comparing page structure against the legitimate site and detecting brand logos. They stress that AI should be paired with rules and heuristics, since false positives remain, and that organizations should keep assessing their threat landscape.

talks.title: Super Apps and Digital Wallets: Securing the Unstoppable Force
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how super apps and digital wallets reshape fraud, identity, privacy and consumer trust.
talks.summary:
A panel examined super apps, the hubs that bundle messaging, payments, banking and commerce into one mobile platform. Panelists said the pandemic accelerated digital payments and contactless use, and that people who already rely on their phones for high-value transactions are likely to extend that trust to more services.

The discussion then covered adoption barriers and risk. Panelists argued that lasting adoption depends on real customer utility, noting that early digital wallets which solved a genuine pain point survived while others faded. They also flagged the need for shared standards and portability, balanced against antitrust limits. On security, they stressed that consumers must understand who bears fraud losses, that a breach in one integration can damage trust in an entire platform, and that the attack surface grows with mobile point-of-sale and connected devices.

For trust, the speakers outlined a sequence: assess fraud, verify users and devices, register and pair devices, strongly authenticate, authorize access, then continuously monitor under a zero trust model. They said static knowledge questions fail because attackers often hold the answers, so machine learning on device signals, behavioral biometrics and email reputation should drive risk decisions. Friction should match what each market expects. The takeaway was that convenience and protection have to be designed together.
