talks.title: Your Metrics Suck! 5 SecOps Metrics That Are Better Than MTTR
talks.teaser: Explains why MTTR and activity reports mislead SOC teams, and offers metrics that build confidence and drive real change.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that many security metrics fail because they only report activity instead of driving change. In their view, useful metrics give the business confidence that a service works, or point to a specific next step. A personal story about a house cleaning service that went unmeasured shows how unchecked work can breed false confidence. They single out mean time to resolution as a poor measure for analysts, since it rewards rushing and cherry-picking easy tickets, though it still helps check whether automation is working.

They sort metrics into configuration confidence, which asks whether the right tools are set up and tuned, and operational confidence, which asks whether people and processes can use them. For analyst activity, events per analyst per hour shows overload: 10 incidents per hour suggests a well-staffed team, while 100 suggests one that will miss alerts. Other measures include handling time by alert stage and analyst, and incidents by severity. Hygiene checks cover unused and duplicate rules, the top and bottom ten alerts, and tuning counts per technology. For realized value, they look at unused features, the share of traffic actually visible given that 85% is now encrypted, and deployment backlogs.

The talk also covers process deviation, such as missed steps in the SOC process, automation failures, and training completion time. Analyst distribution looks at rotating alerts so work does not depend on a few experts, and at splitting time across response, hunting and project work. The closing advice is to separate reporting from metrics, explain the so-what for each metric, audit how fully tools are used, and tie metrics to the service the business expects.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Operations Center Technology Taxonomy
talks.teaser: Lays out a broad taxonomy of technology categories a security operations center may need, and how to select them.
talks.summary:
Christopher Crowley presents a technology taxonomy for security operations centers, drawn from his consulting and teaching work. He argues that organizations rarely buy a complete SOC package and should instead start from a full list of capabilities, then select tools that fit their functions, budget and constraints. He limits the scope to SOC tooling rather than general IT, so the list covers monitoring the systems a SOC relies on rather than running them.

He walks through the categories: visibility into external threats, the wider news and internet conditions that affect operations, communications, and operational tools such as orchestration, automation and ticketing. Detection and protection are organized by what they watch, including endpoints, networks, cloud environments and logs. He also covers long-term data storage and protection, deception techniques such as honeytokens and honeypots, analysis workstations, vulnerability management, and the glue of scripting and SOAR integration. He draws on a 2020 survey finding that many organizations buy tools but never fully implement them.

For takeaways, he suggests a practical path: hunt your own tools to confirm the whole team knows the stack, compare the list against what you already have, and use MITRE ATT&CK and its evaluations to choose tools that address real gaps. He also stresses planning how a tool will be deployed before buying it. Finally, he warns that the SOC itself must have the same confidentiality, integrity and availability protections as the systems it defends.

talks.title: Displacing the Dollar: Is Crypto Robust Enough to be the New Reserve Currency?
talks.teaser: Maps how reserve currencies work, how cryptocurrencies operate, and which security failures still block replacing the dollar.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the central question of whether cryptocurrency could displace the United States dollar as the world’s reserve currency. It walks through how money functions as a medium of exchange, unit of account, and store of value, then traces the Bretton Woods peg to gold, the shift to fiat dollars in 1971, and why many countries still hold dollars for stability and sanctions exposure. Examples such as wartime gold shipments, dollarization in volatile economies, and state moves toward gold or de-dollarization illustrate how trust and policy shape what nations treat as reserves.

The discussion then covers peer-to-peer digital ledgers, proof-of-work mining, and why miners compete to validate blocks. Operational abuse appears when miners harvest free continuous-integration capacity on hosted code platforms, evade detection with low-and-slow resource use, and deploy cryptojacking campaigns such as WannaMine. Wallet theft remains the highest-impact target; custom multi-platform malware like ElectroRAT has lured users through blockchain-themed sites while capturing keys and files.

The speakers conclude that in the near term cryptocurrency is unlikely to replace the dollar because of volatility, throughput limits compared with card networks, and unresolved trust and custody risks such as lost passwords and weak exchange controls. Longer-term adoption may grow, but governments may resist transparency that undercuts monetary authority. Practitioners should treat mining fraud, wallet compromise, and detection of unauthorized hash activity as ongoing defensive problems alongside the macroeconomic debate.

talks.title: Traveler’s Protection Guide: Low Tech Physical OPSEC for a High Tech Job
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Traveler’s Protection Guide: Low Tech Physical OPSEC for a High Tech Job.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at the RSA Conference by Dan and Marco from Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), this talk outlines operational security (OPSEC) best practices derived from over a decade of travel and threat investigations. The presenters stress the core asymmetric defense principle: while an attacker can make numerous attempts, a defender needs only a single mistake to be compromised. To counter risks such as border device seizures, intercepted network traffic, and hotel room burglaries, the session details practical safeguards across both digital and physical realms.

### Key Topics
- **Digital OPSEC Foundations**: Defending operating systems, encrypted storage, and secure messaging channels against eavesdropping and data extraction.
- **Authentication and Key Management**: Protecting cryptographic keys and accounts using hardware security tokens and two-factor authentication.
- **Physical Device Security**: Countering unauthorized physical access, malicious hardware implants, and untrusted peripherals while in transit.
- **Hotel and Room Security**: Identifying and neutralizing hidden audio bugs, two-way mirrors, and concealed cameras using accessible techniques.

### Technical Details
- **Storage Encryption**: Emphasizes using software-level full-disk encryption rather than relying solely on SSD hardware options. Recommended solutions include BitLocker for Windows, FileVault for macOS, LUKS for Linux, and VeraCrypt for open-source cross-platform usage and plausible deniability via hidden containers.
- **Secure Communication**: Recommends GPG email encryption with minimum 4096-bit RSA keys (noting smaller 1024-bit or 2048-bit keys may be susceptible to cracking), storing private keys on hardware tokens. For instant messaging and calls, recommended tools include Signal, Threema (which does not mandate a phone number), Session, Wire, Ricochet (routing over Tor), and self-hosted Jitsi Meet servers. Paid VPN services are recommended over free providers when connecting to public networks.
- **Hardware Security Tokens**: Highlights hardware authenticators (such as YubiKeys and nano models) with physical touch confirmation enabled for two-factor authentication and SSH/account administration.
- **Physical Countermeasures & Implants**: Cautions against USB/keystroke injection tools (like USB Rubber Ducky), malicious cables (such as O.MG cables), and RF-manipulated adapters. Recommends using USB condoms to physically sever data lines and allow power only, checking device SMART data to detect unauthorized power-on events (evil maid attacks), and shielding RFID/NFC cards.
- **Surveillance Countermeasures**: Demonstrates techniques to spot two-way mirrors (fingertip and knock tests), mask acoustic eavesdropping with white noise (e.g., running bathroom water or radio noise), detect spy cameras using reflected lens light or smartphone cameras without infrared filters, locate hidden electronics using portable thermal imagers, and inspect local Wi-Fi MAC addresses and SSIDs using standalone Wi-Fi tools.

### Takeaways
- Never leave operational equipment unattended while traveling, even briefly.
- Ensure reciprocal security: transmitting data over a hardened channel is ineffective if the receiving endpoint is compromised.
- Establish proactive response plans for compromised accounts or lost credentials before embarking on travel.
- Implement layered, low-cost physical checks—such as "Do Not Disturb" door signs, stickers over lenses, and power-only charging adapters—to substantially raise the bar for potential adversaries.

talks.title: Picking Winners: How the Pandemic Changed Cybersecurity Investing
talks.teaser: Panel of venture investors discuss how the pandemic reshaped cybersecurity funding, deal activity and remote due diligence.
talks.summary:
Three venture investors look back at how the 2020 pandemic affected cybersecurity investing. They say their firms had not planned for a global health crisis, but their software-focused portfolios, many already built on cloud delivery and flexible work, held up. One panelist recalls a brief slowdown in March and April, when deals were delayed and customers rushed to secure home working, before activity picked up again.

The discussion turns to market figures. One speaker reports about 540 cybersecurity investments tracked in 2020, up from 420 the year before, and about $11 billion invested against about nine billion in 2019. Another describes a sharp rise in deal velocity, with a small team closing six transactions in 60 days, and more pitch meetings in late 2020 than the previous year. Investors now often back founders they have never met in person, although the panel agrees that in-person meetings still matter for building trust in new partnerships.

Looking ahead, the panelists name cloud security, policy-as-code pipelines, zero trust network access, data security, identity, shift-left tooling and security services as areas of interest. Their main takeaway is that remote work pushed digital transformation forward faster and opened the door to new vendors, while investors still judge companies by the same core criteria as before.

talks.title: Jill and the BeenSTALKed
talks.teaser: A panel explains stalkerware abuse, commodity spy markets, and OSINT overlap, then outlines device hygiene and victim support paths.
talks.summary:
The session opens with personal stakes around intimate partner surveillance and frames stalkerware as software used to facilitate intimate partner violence, spanning commodity spyware, dual-use tools like Find My Phone, mobile remote access trojans, shared accounts, and passive collection via open sources.

Panelists describe who deploys it, how cheap subscriptions work, and that most kits need brief physical access to a phone. They cite survey and vendor-report figures on prevalence and pandemic-era growth, walk through named commercial products and their advertised capabilities without directing listeners to sources, and explain how password reuse, breach data, and image lookups amplify monitoring. Enterprise angles include breached stalkerware vendors, MDM compromise scenarios, mapping to familiar attack chains, and weak antivirus detection of stalkerware.

The close focuses on practical prevention—unique credentials, multifactor authentication, permission reviews, and never leaving devices unattended—and on advocacy to remove non-consensual tracking apps from stores and strengthen policy. Victims are pointed to nonprofits, coalition sites, corporate programs, and network inspection tools, with emphasis that survivors often struggle to get credible help.

talks.title: Purple Team Auth: Hacking & Bypassing MFA Systems, and How to Armor Up
talks.teaser: Walks through how multi-factor authentication gets bypassed through human, phone and account-recovery weaknesses, and what to harden.
talks.summary:
Dan Houser opens by arguing that multi-factor authentication is not a complete answer. Factors designed for narrow uses, such as ATM cards or chip-and-PIN payments, become fragile when they are stretched across an enterprise with many integration points and entry points. He urges defenders to map every path into a system rather than hardening only the intended login flow. He also flags weak factors such as SMS, email, static tokens and secret questions, noting that NIST has decertified some of them.

The middle of the talk covers attacks that go around the technology. In one demonstration, an attacker who already has a password triggers repeated approval calls to the target at odd hours, using a spoofed caller ID, until the target presses the confirmation key. A second example describes a smishing scheme in which the attacker learns a bank's fraud-center numbers by opening an account, then texts a victim who is persuaded to read out a one-time code. He also describes cloned or stolen phones, and mobile carrier help desks being pretexted into moving a number to a new SIM. He cautions that approving logins on the same phone used for browsing may not count as out-of-band verification.

He closes with practical steps. Account reset is the weakest point, so resetting an MFA credential should require two factors. He suggests video-based identity proofing, with a live face check against the employee record and a random question to defeat replay. Organizations should inventory every credential, treat changes to phone numbers or addresses as security events, and correlate failed logins across VPN, email, Wi-Fi and voicemail in the SIEM. He also proposes a credential firewall so that crown-jewel access uses credentials separate from everyday ones, and recommends keeping a backup MFA system because cryptographic controls can fail quickly.

talks.title: Weak Links in Cloud IAM - Never Trust. Always Verify!
talks.teaser: Shows how overly permissive IAM passrole and trust policies let attackers escalate privileges and reach sensitive AWS data.
talks.summary:
The talk examines weak points in identity and access management on AWS, drawing on a 2020 red team engagement the presenters ran against a customer's cloud account. They first explain how IAM principals, service roles and the iam:PassRole permission fit together. In the first misconfiguration, a developer-level account held a PassRole grant with a wildcard resource, so it could attach admin-level service roles to new EC2 instances and reach full administrator access. In the second, a role trust policy that named everyone as a principal let an outside tester with no account access obtain short-term credentials, then move through EC2 metadata and S3 buckets to find secrets and decrypt data with KMS.

After the exercise, the team searched public GitHub code for AWS account IDs and guessed likely role names. They reported that a subset of the roles they tested were misconfigured, exposing snapshots, buckets and keys across many accounts. The second half covers evidence from internal cloud datasets: many organizations ran virtual machines with admin-level service accounts on Google Cloud, many access keys were older than 90 days, and about three quarters had not enabled MFA on group accounts. The presenters also described cryptomining groups such as Kinsing and TeamTNT, which scan for exposed systems, harvest AWS credential files and send them to their command servers to reach the wider cloud environment.

The closing section offers practical guidance: avoid root and admin credentials, manage users through groups and roles, rotate access keys automatically, enforce MFA, remove stale accounts and unneeded admin rights, apply least privilege, monitor IAM API activity, restrict firewall rules, and deploy only vetted container images.

talks.title: Are You Really You? Higher Assurance Identity Proofing to the Rescue!
talks.teaser: Maps NIST higher-assurance identity proofing, IAL selection, and fraud detection for remote digital enrollment.
talks.summary:
Remote work and pandemic-era benefit programs expanded online enrollment, while breach-leaked data and dark-web PII made static knowledge-based checks unreliable for trusting digital applicants. The session frames identity proofing as binding a digital identity to a real person through validated evidence, sometimes repeatedly across the identity lifecycle as risk rises.

It walks through NIST Special Publication 800-63, especially volume 63A: Identity Assurance Levels one through three, the decision tree for picking an IAL, and the enrollment flow of resolution, validation, and verification. A remote IAL2 example covers collecting core attributes, strong and fair identity documents, authoritative-source checks, document forensics, selfie biometric matching, liveness, and enrollment codes. The talk contrasts certified credential service providers such as ID.me and Login.gov, including state unemployment programs where large volumes of fraudulent claims were blocked, and surveys fraud types—synthetic identities, stolen PII, forged documents, consortium watch lists, and emerging deepfake spoofing of liveness prompts.

Practitioners are pointed to NIST implementation resources, MITRE practice-statement templates, and planned 800-63 revision four. Takeaways include minimizing static KBV, using dynamic out-of-wallet questions only where needed, varying liveness challenges, querying authoritative and vital-records sources, and documenting enrollment policy before selecting a provider.

talks.title: WebAuthn 201: How to FIDO
talks.teaser: Shows how WebAuthn and FIDO2 resist phishing and enable passwordless login, from platform biometrics to security keys.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the case for stronger login, noting that phishing has been the leading attack vector on the internet since 2015. Christiaan Brand introduces the two standards behind FIDO2: the W3C WebAuthn API used between web servers and browsers, and the CTAP protocol between the client and authenticators. The core mechanism is a server-issued challenge that the authenticator signs together with the relying party ID, so the signature binds the login to the real web origin and a look-alike domain fails.

The middle section walks through use cases from the How to FIDO guide. Re-authentication uses a platform biometric, checked with a feature-detection call before offering a passwordless opt-in. Second-factor registration uses a cross-platform security key with an exclude list to prevent duplicate registrations. Roaming user-verifying keys store account data so users can sign in without a username or password, with a PIN or fingerprint unlocking the key locally. The phone-as-authenticator case, using Bluetooth and a cloud-assisted pairing protocol, is presented as work still in progress.

The talk closes with guidance to keep sessions long where possible, to limit password and MFA prompts, and to treat account bootstrapping on new devices as the point where attackers are most likely to succeed. Suggested next steps include an IBM FIDO server, an open-source FIDO server from Google, and Android codelabs.

talks.title: Hot Topics in Misinformation: Election 2020, COVID 19, and More
talks.teaser: Three misinformation researchers compare lessons from the 2020 election with COVID-19 vaccine narratives and what tooling comes next.
talks.summary:
A panel of three misinformation researchers reviews what the 2020 election revealed about false and misleading content. They found that much of the activity came from domestic sources, although at least 12 foreign information operations were also identified. One crowdsourced reporting program showed how small incidents, such as a few misplaced ballots, were distorted and merged into larger false stories. The researchers also found that a small set of repeat offenders produced much of the disinformation.

The discussion then turned to COVID-19, where the panelists described separate conspiracy communities, including anti-vaccine, technophobic and political groups, merging around shared narratives. Vaccine stories crossed borders quickly, which made context and certainty hard to establish. Responders struggled to decide when to issue counter-narratives and what to say. Misleading content often moved to smaller platforms, some of which have weak or no policies. The panelists also separated misinformation from influence, noting that true facts can be framed to shape what people believe and do.

For the next phase, the panelists called for a common language and shared data across tools, cross-platform analysis that reduces the manual effort analysts face, and analysts with social science training who can read how communities receive content. They also urged sustainable funding for the people protecting election and public health infrastructure, while protecting free speech and treating commercial manipulation as fraud.

talks.title: We’re All in this Together: Technology Abuse and Design
talks.teaser: Panelists explain how technology abuse in intimate partner violence shapes survivor safety and what designers should change.
talks.summary:
This panel brings together advocates, a university safety specialist and a computer science researcher to examine technology abuse within intimate partner violence. The speakers explain that abusers misuse both everyday tools, such as device location features, and purpose-built stalkerware to monitor, harass and isolate survivors. They describe how opting out of a shared account can raise the risk of harm, and how survivors often meet disbelief or dead ends from phone companies, police and courts when they ask for help.

Using a campus case, one speaker described a former partner who sent intimate images through spoofed emails to a student's department and to conferences she had joined. The response path that left her isolated was contrasted with one that connected her to victim advocates and a platform team trained for these cases. The researcher argued that threat models for intimate partner abuse differ from standard security models, which is part of why antivirus tools long ignored stalkerware. He recommended design reviews that ask how an interface could be abused by someone who already knows a victim's passwords. The panel also covered legal gaps, including misdemeanor cases that rarely get investigators and court filings that expose intimate images.

For companies, the speakers urged a move from compliance to culture change, with trust and safety work and advisory councils that include gender-based violence experts. For people supporting survivors, they advised listening, respecting privacy, avoiding advice to simply stop using technology, and being careful with hands-on fixes that could escalate danger. They pointed people toward specialist support and to options that let survivors make their own safety decisions.

talks.title: Are Password Managers Improving our Password Habits?
talks.teaser: Surveys real password manager users to test whether they choose strong master passwords and fix weak or breached logins.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the long-predicted end of passwords, which never arrived, and the password managers that filled the gap. The presenters question whether the security benefits usually recommended for these tools rest on real data. They name three assumptions: that users pick a strong master password, let the manager generate strong passwords, and replace weak, reused and breached logins. Earlier lab work showed that memorizing random passwords took many training sessions, so the team turned to field data.

The researchers ran a two-stage study with paid participants. A screening survey found that about two thirds of respondents used a password manager, most often Chrome's built-in one. Participants whose desktop manager had a dashboard, and who had used it for at least two months, were invited to a longer study where they uploaded dashboard screenshots. After removing unverified submissions, 109 participants remained. Only a few third-party users had randomly generated master passwords, and many reused their master password. About half of other third-party users let their manager create passwords, while 79% of Chrome users did not. Between two thirds and three quarters held weak or reused passwords they should replace.

The team also found that roughly half of participants had not known the dashboard existed before the study, and most said they would probably use it again. The presenters caution that this is self-reported intent, and a follow-up study would be needed to show whether habits change. Their takeaway is that the three assumptions should not be taken for granted.

talks.title: As Worlds Collide: Responding to Cyber Events in a Converged IT/OT Universe
talks.teaser: Shows how gamified tabletop exercises can help IT and OT teams prepare for cyber incidents in converged environments.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that IT and OT are merging in industrial plants, which widens the attack surface and makes incident response harder. The speakers trace the convergence from early mechanisation through Industry 4.0, then walk through ICS malware cases: Stuxnet, Shamoon, Havex, BlackEnergy, Industroyer and Triton. They tie these to real costs, from an exposed water treatment system in Florida to the NotPetya losses at Merck and the Lockergoga attack on Norsk Hydro, which forced a switch to manual operations.

The second part makes the case for gamification as preparation. The speakers compare game-based learning with tabletop exercises, war games, capture the flag events and cyber ranges. They explain how IT and OT teams differ in goals, language, timelines and room to respond, and how a scenario can be built around a chosen use case, with budget decisions, runbooks and a repeatable sandbox. The aim is to find gaps in people, process and technology rather than only to identify an attacker.

The closing advice is to start cross-team conversations quickly, design and rerun tabletop exercises within the first three months, and within six months test governance policies and stress test runbooks, so that mistakes happen in practice rather than during a real incident.

talks.title: Understanding Impact of Foreign Influence Activities on Research Programs
talks.teaser: Explains how nation-state talent recruitment targets research programs and which governance practices reduce foreign influence insider risk.
talks.summary:
Organizations with proprietary research face foreign influence activities: formal or covert government-backed initiatives that assess, recruit, and exploit insiders to reach trade secrets and intellectual property. Drawing on thousands of insider threat investigations, the speaker frames scale with a “5% rule”—not implying malice across that slice, but suggesting how large the insider-risk population may be when people prioritize other interests, with state-directed talent recruitment at the severe end.

The session defines global talent recruitment programs as a major foreign influence vector, motivated by nation-state desire to leapfrog technology gaps. It outlines a recurring lifecycle: identify capability gaps, attach financial incentives, hunt organizations across academia, industry, and government supply chains, then profile and contact individuals through social media and associations. Finding one recruit often signals a wider network; recruits consistently mishandle employer data. Targeted technology areas largely mirror critical infrastructure sectors, and operational patterns differ among major sponsoring countries.

Impacts span IP theft, damaged researcher trust, and broken security and compliance obligations under grants and partnerships. Mitigation centers on a dedicated research security or insider threat management program integrated with existing controls: clear policies, contractor and partner education on conflict of interest and undisclosed funding, awareness of recruitment tactics, and shortening time from detection through assessment and remediation. The closing message is that foreign influence is manageable when organizations treat it as part of the threat landscape and prepare people not to participate.

talks.title: Leveraging Human Risk Data to Strengthen Cyber Resiliency
talks.teaser: Shows how measuring employee security decisions can guide targeted training, controls and phishing simulations.
talks.summary:
The talk treats employee decisions as central to cyber resilience, since risky choices such as clicking phishing links feed incidents that response teams must clean up. The speakers cite a Verizon breach report finding that nearly two-thirds of breaches tie back to human factors. They argue organizations should measure human risk, the likelihood of a risky decision multiplied by its impact, instead of relying on training quiz scores alone.

Using 4.5 million security decisions from about 114,000 employees, the speakers reported several patterns. Non-contractors clicked phishing links more than contractors, and managers more than non-managers, with middle and first-line managers the riskiest group. Simulated phishing clicks peaked around 9 a.m., while real-world phishing was clicked most often early in the morning and late in the day. Department culture mattered more than size, and employees often late on training were less likely to report phishing and almost 5% more likely to click.

For practitioners, the speakers recommended tuning phishing simulations to reflect real campaigns shared through industry groups and timing guidance to high-risk hours. They also suggested personalized, positive feedback such as congratulation messages and recognition. Controls like social media restrictions could be applied only to individuals showing risky behavior, reducing friction for everyone else. The session closed with advice to invest in fundamentals, measure risk specific to your environment, and build a network of security champions.
