talks.title: Ransomware: Creation, Detection, and Response
talks.teaser: Shows how a training ransomware sample was detected, evaded with small changes, and traced during incident response.
talks.summary:
Aaron Rosenmund explains how a ransomware sample he built for a training exercise was leaked and then spread across malware sites. He uses the episode to test whether antivirus detection for ransomware is as reliable as vendors claim. The sample encrypted files with AES, dropped a spoofed ransom note, planted backdoors through batch scripts, and cleared logs and shadow copies. Analysis engines flagged it mostly through file hashes, an auto-generated YARA rule, ransom note strings and a Tor address, while many missed the batch drops, log clearing and shadow copy deletion.

The middle of the talk covers evasion. Renaming the file or changing its target folder shifted the detection results. Changing the note text, removing the Tor string, dropping the registry backdoor and renaming functions produced a version with zero detections from the engines tested and from Windows Defender. Defender's behavioral alert appeared only after encryption had already started, which showed that signature checks alone were not enough. Rosenmund argues that defenders should prioritize command-line logging, EDR, JA3 hashes and full packet capture.

For response, he shows that the modified times on encrypted files help order events, that the local Windows firewall log in System32 survives event log clearing, and that RDP session logs (event ID 24) can reveal the attacker's address after the logs were wiped. He also presents Revenant, a tool that aggregates firewall logs into Elastic to map lateral movement. His takeaway is to test detections through emulation rather than trust antivirus alone.

talks.title: New Face, Who Dis? Protecting Privacy in a World of Surveillance
talks.teaser: Surveys adversarial tools that disrupt facial recognition, then demos an open-source iOS app that alters photos before upload.
talks.summary:
The speaker starts from the idea that facial recognition is accurate and effortless when it works, which makes it useful but also easy to misuse. They point to bias against minority groups, government and police use of face matching, and companies that scrape public photos into databases that can be breached. Laws such as Illinois's biometric statute react after harm, so the talk argues for proactive adversarial research that lets people control how their photos are matched.

The speaker traces adversarial methods in order. Pixel-level changes from 2001 worked but were static and were quickly countered. GAN-based approaches created synthetic faces but were fixed and computationally costly. Camera Adversaria, an Android camera app, injects procedural noise to disrupt classifiers. Fawkes, from the University of Chicago, cloaks photos toward a target identity so recognition systems learn the wrong face, and its strongest setting took about five minutes per image in the demo. Lowkey, from the University of Maryland, is a hosted service judged by top-N suspect results.

The main part is an open-source iOS proof of concept built with TensorFlow Lite. It applies one of 32 onboard styles through arbitrary style transfer, lets the user blend the style with the original, adds simplex noise, and checks the result with Google ML Kit face detection. In a small test of 50 PubFig individuals, stronger styling evaded detection and affected classification, which the speaker framed as proof of life rather than rigorous evidence. Next steps include formal testing on FaceScrub, on-device classification checks, and higher resolution. The closing advice is that organizations should audit their facial recognition use and protect stored biometric data.

talks.title: Windows Kernel Patch Protection - Achilles Heel: PatchGuard
talks.teaser: Shows how hooking memset via CPU debug registers can block PatchGuard’s bug-check path and suppress its crash response.
talks.summary:
Kernel Patch Protection (PatchGuard) periodically verifies critical kernel structures and triggers a bug check when tampering is detected, rewriting call stacks and saved routines so the root cause is hard to recover. The presentation walks through that response chain—from corruption capture through KeBugCheckEx and KeBugCheck2—and argues that running entirely in ring 0 leaves no strong isolation between PatchGuard and attacker-controlled kernel code.

The core flaw emphasized is reliance on saved routines such as memset during the crash path. Because memset is invoked constantly across the system, the speaker avoids patching it directly and instead uses hardware debug registers and a temporary IDT hook on all processors to gain a controlled window for rewriting the kernel’s memset implementation. The reroute checks whether execution originated from KeBugCheck2 with bug-check code 0x109 (PatchGuard); if so, a stall routine logs details, reverses partial bug-check side effects, and waits forever—preventing the BSOD. Addresses for KeBugCheck2, KiHardwareTrigger, memset, and KPRCB context offsets are recovered by scanning KeBugCheckEx without private symbols. A demo loads an unsigned driver (after DSE bypass), runs the chain, and shows DbgView output plus a log entry while the simulated PatchGuard trigger hangs instead of rebooting.

Remaining issues include DPC timeouts if the stall runs in the wrong context, and FsRtl/MdlReadCompleteDevEx verification appearing in crash analysis. The speaker reports prior disclosure attempts without vendor action, and urges patching KPP, stronger hardware-assisted integrity monitoring, and eventual extension of such controls to cloud-hosted Windows workloads.

talks.title: Android Rootkits: Analysis from Userland and Kernelland
talks.teaser: Covers how Android rootkits hide processes and modules, and how to expose them from userland and kernel memory.
talks.summary:
The session looks at Android rootkits in the traditional malware sense, where software hides its own artifacts, rather than jailbreaking or rooting a device. The speakers cover userland techniques, using LD_PRELOAD to hide an app from the Settings list, and kernel-side techniques such as ptrace abuse, system call table hooks and direct manipulation of kernel task structures. A live demo shows an app vanishing from the apps and notifications screen after a preload library is injected.

For userland samples, the method captures the state of every running process and its loaded modules before infection, repeats the capture afterward, and compares the two snapshots. Differences in new processes, module paths, sizes and memory protections point to changes. A Frida-based tool called Smart Alec automates the capture and comparison. In the example, it flagged a module loaded from the data partition into the email app, and the speakers dumped that shared object for reverse engineering. For kernel-side work, they acquire memory with LiME, build a Volatility profile, and run plugins to find LD_PRELOAD variables, ptrace flags on tasks, hooked system call table entries, and processes unlinked from the kernel task list. Findings are written to a knowledge graph as the plugins run, so an analyst can navigate relationships between processes and files.

The takeaway is that these techniques can form an instrumentation layer that feeds sandboxes and automated behavior extraction, not only for rootkits but for other malware. The speakers point to an open source project on GitHub that packages the tooling.

talks.title: Malware Reverse Engineering with PE Tree—OSS Inspired by COVID
talks.teaser: Shows the open-source PE Tree tool for exploring, dumping and rebuilding portable executables during malware reverse engineering.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces PE Tree, an open-source Python tool for navigating and reverse engineering Windows PE files. It started as an internal IDA Pro plugin, and its rainbow view maps a file's sections by size so analysts can compare samples visually. The speaker walks through the PE format, covering the DOS stub and rich header, the NT and optional headers, the data directories and the sections, and explains how entropy and timestamps can hint at packing, tampering or related samples.

Case studies follow. In an APT32 sideloading sample, a multi-stage shellcode chain was captured by attaching IDA as a debugger and taking a memory snapshot. PE Tree's IDB search then found a hidden DLL, whose export descriptor revealed its compile-time name and whose resource section held the final payload. A second sample, packed with MPRESS, was dumped from memory, and its import table was rebuilt by scanning code references for calls into loaded modules. Rekall integration was shown for listing processes and drivers from a memory dump and reconstructing their imports.

The talk closes with Ghidra support for browsing file structures, with dumping to follow once a debugger is released. The tool runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, can be installed with pip, and is hosted on GitHub, where the speaker invites contributions and issue reports.

talks.title: Sherlock and Watson Fight Deep Social Engineering
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Sherlock and Watson Fight Deep Social Engineering.

talks.title: WarezTheRemote? Under the Couch, and Listening to You
talks.teaser: Researchers show how a Comcast XR11 voice remote becomes a distant listening device via malicious RF firmware updates.
talks.summary:
The session examines the XR11 voice remote bundled with Comcast X1 cable boxes—widely deployed units that pair long-range RF links with a push-to-talk microphone. The presenters from Guardicore Labs open the hardware, trace microphone control through a Texas Instruments CC2530 processor, and reverse engineer 8051 firmware pulled from the paired set-top box. They anchor analysis on LED-handling routines from vendor sample code, then follow the blue-record-indicator path to microphone initialization code that otherwise runs only when someone holds the record button.

Building on earlier findings that the remote accepts unsigned over-the-air firmware with only a weak integrity check, the team impersonates the trusted box without owning it. They briefly knock out the box’s Control Manager with simple packet fuzzing, exploit per-packet RF4CE encryption so plaintext replies are accepted, and blind-guess encrypted chunk requests to deliver roughly fifteen hundred packets of chosen firmware. A thirty-six-byte patch speeds daily upgrade polls, adds a “start recording” response, and streams audio for about ten minutes per trigger. Outdoor tests reportedly succeed through a wall at roughly sixty-five feet; decoded capture stays intelligible for conversation tens of feet from the remote.

After responsible disclosure, Comcast shipped fixes including signed firmware, stricter handling of unencrypted traffic, and hardening against the denial-of-service helper on the box (mitigated around version 1.1.0.4). The closing message is that mundane living-room remotes now carry IoT-class RF administration surfaces that security reviews rarely stress, with work-from-home blurring home gadget risk and enterprise privacy.

talks.title: Tales from the Underground: The Vulnerability Weaponization Lifecycle
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Tales from the Underground: The Vulnerability Weaponization Lifecycle.

talks.title: Beyond Living-Off-the-Land: Why XP Exploits Still Matter
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers abuse old vulnerable Windows binaries for stealthy persistence, and how defenders can spot them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attackers who already have a foothold go beyond living-off-the-land by bringing their own older, vulnerable but legitimate programs and exploiting them. The speakers call these VULNBins. Even in an environment with no Windows XP machines, such binaries can be signed and allowlisted, and newer mitigations like ASLR may not protect them.

A case study covers InvisiMole, a targeted espionage group. Depending on whether it had admin rights, it chose among four persistence strategies. The simpler chain abused an outdated video player scheduled to run at startup, using a malicious configuration file. The preferred chain on newer systems loaded a Windows XP library through a legitimate component and reused its code fragments in a shellcode loader to keep the footprint small. Payloads were encrypted per victim with DPAPI and kept in the registry, so the researchers could decrypt them only with help from the affected parties.

For defenders, the speakers note there is little guidance on VULNBins compared with LOLBins, and EDR rules rarely cover them. Suggested steps include WDAC or AppLocker block rules keyed to patched versions, monitoring vulnerable binaries that cannot be blocked, and flagging unsigned older Windows binaries, since catalog-signed files can appear unsigned on newer systems. Teams can also compare file versions and compile dates against vendor releases. The talk closes by asking researchers to share known VULNBin cases to start a community list.

talks.title: ISE-Skating: Lessons Learned in Bypassing Network Access Control
talks.teaser: Demonstrates bypassing network access control by inserting a hidden device between an authenticated endpoint and its switch port.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how network access control works. Under 802.1X, a supplicant on an endpoint authenticates over EAP to an authenticator, usually a switch, which consults an authentication server. Devices that cannot run a supplicant fall back to MAC authentication bypass, which trusts a MAC address. The speaker reviews traditional attacks on these mechanisms, including MAC cloning and abuse of permissive profiling rules, along with their mitigations and indicators of compromise.

The core of the talk is ISE-Skating, in which an attacker sits between a legitimate endpoint and its switch port. Hubs and unmanaged switches are useful because they do not emit BPDUs, so spanning tree protections do not flag them. The attack device, built into a modified power strip with a Raspberry Pi and an LTE link, waits for the victim's EAPOL start, copies the victim's MAC address, and lets normal authentication finish. It then spoofs the victim's IP address, applies unused addresses found on the network, and blocks its own outbound traffic so it does not trigger error-disabled mode. In a live demo against a Cisco switch, the port reauthenticated with the attacker box, which then reached a domain controller it should not have accessed, in under a minute.

For defenders, the indicators include a device briefly disappearing, one MAC address holding several IP addresses, and atypical traffic such as port scans from endpoints. Recommended steps are physical security for switches and edge ports, consistent NAC configuration across every port including unused ones, ACL isolation of MAB devices, and validation testing of the design. The speaker stresses that NAC is one layer of defense, not a complete solution.

talks.title: The Game of Cyber Threat Hunting: The Return of the Fun
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Game of Cyber Threat Hunting: The Return of the Fun.

talks.title: Inside the Mind of the SUNBURST Adversary
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Inside the Mind of the SUNBURST Adversary.

talks.title: Biohacking: The Invisible Threat
talks.teaser: Shows how implanted NFC and RFID chips can clone access badges and push malicious payloads to nearby phones unseen.
talks.summary:
Len Noe opens by framing implanted technology as an emerging attack vector for enterprises. He traces implants from 1950s pacemakers to today's smart devices, then describes commercial chips such as NFC tags, RFID inserts and a small single-board computer. Because these implants use the same technologies as door badges and phone payments, a compromise may leave no visible trace.

The demonstrations come next. In the first, a door badge is read with a Proxmark-style tool, its data is saved and written to an implanted tag, and the copy is checked against the original. In the next two, an implanted NFC tag directs a nearby Android phone to a malicious APK built with Metasploit, which gives shell and data access once installed. A second tag sends a phone browser to a page hooked with BeEF, enabling a location lookup and a ping sweep of the local network. Both rely on social engineering to get close to the victim.

Noe then turns to law and ethics. There is no federal law on microchip implants, though some states restrict employer mandates or ban implants outright. Implants also stay active with no off switch, unlike a badge left at home. He closes with a short, medium and long term timeline for defenders and mitigations, including RFID switches with lock passwords, mutual authentication, turning off NFC when unused, patching, staff education and blocking shields.

talks.title: Discord, Generation Z’s Hacking University
talks.teaser: Explores how Generation Z uses Discord to learn hacking, coordinate ransomware, and harden defenses against platform-born attacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames Discord less as a single attack vector than as the social and technical hub where a younger cohort learns offense and defense. The speaker describes field interviews with ransomware actors including HILDACRYPT, contrasting how small modern crews used chat platforms, purchased components, and peer troubleshooting to produce serious ransomware in months where older malware operations once took most of a year.

On Discord the talk catalogs dual-use scripting, criminal marketplaces, credential spraying, CDN and command-and-control abuse, cryptocurrency cash-out patterns, and collaboration spanning Discord and Telegram. Attacker profiles emphasize pessimism and personal grievance tipping learners toward crime, while defenders often cite early recognition through bug bounties and mentoring. Citing Discord transparency reporting, the speaker argues malware and cybercrime reports rise yet enforcement actions lag spam and reputational priorities, with VirusTotal illustrating CDN-hosted payloads.

Practitioners are urged to treat Discord and Telegram like hostile infrastructure where policy allows, enforce hygiene the interviewed attackers themselves say stops most incidents, harden email and memory-aware sandboxing, and close exposed services. Longer term, bug bounties, transparent corporate response, mentoring teenagers, broader hiring—including skilled contributors from regions with weak legitimate wages—are presented as ways to redirect the same community drive toward defense.

talks.title: How I Hacked Your Website and You Didn’t Even Know
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of How I Hacked Your Website and You Didn’t Even Know.

talks.title: Blockchain Security Guarantees and Exploits
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Blockchain Security Guarantees and Exploits.

talks.title: Flying to DevSecOps with a USAF Cyber Weapon System
talks.teaser: A case study maps how one contractor merged Agile DevSecOps with Air Force compliance while operating the CVAH defensive cyber platform.
talks.summary:
Dr. Mark Peters describes the first operational year after Technica Corporation assumed a consolidated contract to sustain the Air Force CVAH (Cyber Vulnerability Analysis and Hunt) defensive weapon system in late 2019. The program inherited waterfall acquisition habits, three fragmented prior contracts, unfinished software, weak documentation, more than 900 open POA&M items on the previous authority to operate, and no shared DevSecOps infrastructure.

The team adopted Scaled Agile, stood up GitLab pipelines with automated testing and static analysis, centralized infrastructure as code, embedded security engineers in daily standups, and paired technical writers with developers so audit evidence lived alongside the code. Despite moves through temporary facilities, they closed most POA&M findings, re-enabled logging such as Winlogbeat via Ansible, shifted from Jenkins to GitLab, and published Tenable ACAS and SonarQube results for team visibility. Release cadence accelerated from years between versions to roughly quarterly drops (3.2.1 through 3.5), including Kubernetes options and Windows Server 2019 upgrades.

Practitioners should treat cultural, process, and technical debt as jointly managed, prioritize transparency over siloed compliance work, and set explicit goals for secure test integration and continuous compliance. Peters closes with a phased roadmap: define intent within a week, run meaningful retrospectives over 90 days, and adjust team structure over six months while pursuing continuous monitoring, hybrid cloud, and pipeline automation toward a continuous ATO.

talks.title: The State of the Union of DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The State of the Union of DevSecOps.

talks.title: The Scientific Method: Security Chaos Experimentation & Attacker Math
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Scientific Method: Security Chaos Experimentation & Attacker Math.

talks.title: Building Secure and Reliable Systems at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how zero trust access, microservice boundaries and zero-touch production help make systems both reliable and secure.
talks.summary:
Heather Adkins, a Google security leader, argues that a system cannot be truly secure without being reliable, and the reverse. Citing supply chain attacks on the tools engineers depend on, she urges teams to design reliability and security together from the start rather than as separate concerns.

She walks through three examples. For enterprise networks, she contrasts the castle model of corporate VPNs, which scale poorly and let a compromised roaming laptop reach sensitive systems, with Google's BeyondCorp approach, which verifies each device and user before granting access to web services over SSL. For application development, she recommends splitting monolithic stacks such as LAMP into containerized microservices with authenticated APIs, so one compromised component cannot reach everything and recovery is faster. For infrastructure, she describes Zero Touch Prod, where engineers send requests through a proxy that authenticates each action with security keys, requires peer approval for sensitive changes, validates requests and logs them. Red teams can bypass the proxy, but it slows attackers down.

For practical next steps, she suggests reviewing past outages and intrusions to see where such controls would have helped, workshopping a redesign of one monolithic service, and sharing these ideas with teams through training. She closes by recommending a book written with about a hundred Googlers as a group reading resource.

talks.title: Nurture vs. Nature in AppSec: Data-Driven Measurement of DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Presents data on application flaws across languages, open-source libraries, and what speeds up or slows down remediation.
talks.summary:
Jay Jacobs and Ben Edwards of Cyentia Institute analyze roughly 130,000 applications from Veracode customers, using each application's full scan history. Because these organizations already invest in security, the results may look better than the wider world. About three in four applications carry at least one flaw, and roughly one in four has a high or critical one. The flaw mix shifts sharply by language: cross-site scripting dominates PHP, while buffer management stands out in C++.

Ben Edwards turns to third-party code. Many Java applications are almost entirely third-party code, while C++ and PHP code is mostly written in house. Transitive dependencies add exposure, so a flaw in a library a team never imported directly can still reach it. Only about 1% of library flaws are both exploited in the wild and reachable by attackers, and more than 80% can be fixed by a minor or patch version update.

Jay Jacobs then covers remediation speed. Simple medians mislead, since closed flaws have a median of 86 days while open findings already sit at 216 days and climbing, so the team used survival analysis. Half of flaws are fixed within about six months, and a quarter remain after a year and a half. Frequent scanning, dynamic testing and composition analysis go with faster fixes, while high flaw density and large legacy applications slow them. Practitioners should split up big applications, reduce flaw density, and build scanning into the pipeline rather than adding it later.

talks.title: Security Champions: Drive Innovation by Creating Future Cyber Workforce
talks.teaser: Shows how a security champions program built on people, not tools, can scale application security across engineering teams.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's own history as a developer whose release was halted by a security review hours before deployment. She later moved into application security in 2016, doing code reviews for hundreds of teams, and found there were not enough people to keep pace with delivery. She frames the underlying problem as one of people and process rather than tooling, since remediation depends on engineers who have little security training.

The middle section describes a champions program extended beyond awareness. Champions hold defined accountabilities such as secure code review, secure design, architecture or offensive testing, with one champion placed in each delivery team and linked to security staff as a virtual talent pool. Learning follows a 70-20-10 split of on-the-job work, peer and expert learning, and formal training, with the NIST NICE framework guiding role transitions. The strategy also replaces engagement reviews with guardrails and guidelines, is shaped bottom-up by the teams themselves, and includes recognition, a goal of half of nominations being women, and a maturity model tied to metrics. Across five pilot teams, the speaker reported optimization of more than 50 percent.

The closing advice is to start from a people-centred approach, define champion roles and responsibilities, and examine the engagement models that create bottlenecks. Practitioners are encouraged to review the roles within three months, extend the model to roles such as scrum masters, release engineers and testers, and reassess after six months. Executive buy-in is named as the hardest challenge, and the speaker suggests mapping the program to business goals to make it easier to secure.

talks.title: Security: The Hidden Cost of Android Stalkerware
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Security: The Hidden Cost of Android Stalkerware.

talks.title: Project 2030: Scenarios for the Future of Cybercrime
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Project 2030: Scenarios for the Future of Cybercrime.

talks.title: Uncovering Covert Channels in Your IoT Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how covert channels hide in IoT and Modbus traffic, and how a Python analyzer flags them.
talks.summary:
Mike Raggo and Chet Hosmer open by framing the problem as poor visibility and weak supply chains across IoT, industrial IoT and OT networks. Many devices run unfamiliar operating systems and protocols, standards are fragmented and rarely adopted, and security updates often never arrive. They point to a water utility intrusion that started through a remote access tool on an old Windows laptop, and to the SolarWinds campaign, as cases where covert command and control and data exfiltration can go unseen.

The research covered several device examples. Older RTSP video cameras sent traffic in clear text, with encryption often disabled by default and web interfaces lacking authentication. A covert spy camera exposed its UID, MAC address and passwords in clear text and uploaded video to a cloud service abroad. A week after that research was disclosed, the US banned the same camera models. Chet Hosmer then explained Modbus, a serial-era protocol with no built-in security, showing how requests are matched to responses by transaction, protocol and unit identifiers. Their Python 3 analyzer, demonstrated on captured PCAP files, flags requests with no reply as warnings and unsolicited responses as critical.

The closing advice was practical: capture traffic on a test network, run the analyzer against Modbus flows, and forward results to Grafana with InfluxDB or to Splunk, including on modest hardware such as a Raspberry Pi. The speakers stressed that encryption, integrity checks and timely patching are often missing from these devices, so monitoring and deliberate network placement matter.

talks.title: Building Trust in Supply Chains
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Building Trust in Supply Chains.

talks.title: Monitoring Strategy for the Coming Space 5G Network
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Monitoring Strategy for the Coming Space 5G Network.

talks.title: Research on New Vectors of UDP-Based DDoS Amplification Attacks of IoT
talks.teaser: Research maps new UDP reflection vectors in IoT protocols and shares exposure scans, honeypot telemetry, and vendor guidance.
talks.summary:
Internet-facing IoT gear increasingly fuels UDP reflection and amplification floods. The presentation ties that rise to IT–IoT–OT convergence, weak device design, and the long shadow of large botnet-driven attacks, then focuses on discovery and control protocols whose small probes can yield outsized replies when source addresses are spoofed.

The core walkthrough covers WS-Discovery, DHDiscover, ADDP, flawed OpenVPN retransmission behavior, CoAP, and Ubiquiti-style discovery, using bandwidth amplification factor measurements and honeypot captures. Internet-wide scanning shows tens of thousands of exposed services per major protocol class. NSFOCUS telemetry from 2020 reports IoT sources in a growing share of DDoS and reflection traffic, with WS-Discovery leading, CoAP second, and DHDiscover rising; ONVIF’s variable source ports complicate mitigation. ADDP exposure is flagged as a pivot toward Ripple20-affected devices. The speaker briefly notes brute-force credentials, DNS hijack demos, and abused UPnP port mapping without dwelling on UPnP amplification details.

Practitioners are urged to treat discovery services as dangerous by default: restrict unicast replies, segment assets, inventory managed and unmanaged IoT, harden configs and passwords, monitor exposure with intelligence tools, automate IoT in endpoint programs, apply zero trust across home-to-enterprise paths, and use cloud DDoS protection where on-prem capacity is thin.

talks.title: All Your LAN are Belong to Us. Managing the Real Threats to Remote Workers.
talks.teaser: Shows how a compromised home router or captive portal can threaten remote workers, and how VPNs fare against it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shift to home and public Wi-Fi during the pandemic. The speakers argue that consumer routers are often insecure and rarely patched, so a remote worker's access point should be treated as untrusted or fully compromised. They point to a well-known botnet and a DNS-hijacking campaign that infected large numbers of routers as evidence that these devices are actively targeted.

Next come live demonstrations. A rogue DHCP server pushes a route that diverts an RDP session, even while a VPN is up, to a service that captures credentials, unless the VPN enforces route precedence. A compromised router serving PXE boot files boots a modified operating system on the victim's machine, exposing an unencrypted disk and a remote shell. A tampered captive portal prompts the user to run an application, and control of name resolution lets a Responder-style attack collect Windows authentication hashes.

The speakers then tested six traditional and zero trust products against six threats, in standard and lockdown configurations, across captured and online states. Results were inconsistent, and without special configuration most threats still worked once the tunnel was established. Their advice includes enabling route precedence, limiting split tunneling with a forced tunnel and carefully chosen exceptions, flushing DNS and serving it from corporate resources, and considering company-controlled connectivity. They stress that zero trust is a mindset rather than a product.

talks.title: Measuring the Ethical Behavior of Technology
talks.teaser: Explains a method for scoring whether websites and apps treat people respectfully, and the lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The session introduces the Me2B Alliance, a standards development group building a measurable standard for respectful technology. The speakers liken the work to crash testing for connected products, judging how a product treats the people who use it rather than how the company builds it. Their ethical foundation draws on healthy interpersonal relationships rather than a single universal ethic, and they frame each user's interaction with a product as a relationship that unfolds over time. Visible first-party links and hidden third-party affiliates run in parallel within that relationship.

The team explained that its specification started as a planned sequence but became iterative in practice, after ethnographic research showed that people most worried about getting a fair deal and about security lapses. Testing of websites and mobile apps uses a scale from minus three to plus one, where zero means no harm detected and plus one reflects extra care for users. Lessons included that clear, measurable criteria are hard to write, that nearly all digital technology carries some risk, and that third-party data flows can cause more harm than the visible experience. The passing threshold is still unclear and is likely to vary by industry.

For practitioners, the recommendations were to build respect in from the start, make products private by default, ask only for the data that is needed, and make sign-up and removal easy. Teams should also know what third-party services do with user information and reflect that in supplier agreements. The speakers argued that software complexity makes it hard for any single person to know all of a product's behavior, so teams should move slowly and understand their dependencies.

talks.title: Smart IoT: IoT Botnet Attacks on Power Grids Exploiting Their Weak Points
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Smart IoT: IoT Botnet Attacks on Power Grids Exploiting Their Weak Points.

talks.title: Strengthening Resilience of Positioning, Navigation, and Timing Services
talks.teaser: Outlines GPS dependency risks for critical infrastructure and NIST voluntary guidance to detect disruption and design safer PNT use.
talks.summary:
Two federal presenters frame position, navigation, and timing as a hidden backbone of digitized critical infrastructure, tied to Executive Order 13905 and a Commerce estimate of roughly $1 billion per day economic impact if GPS fails. The first segment explains weak open GNSS signals, inexpensive jamming and spoofing, and “responsible use”: never trusting unauthenticated PNT without validity checks and defined fail-safe behavior.

Real-world illustrations include Black Sea maritime spoofing, the April 2019 GPS week-number rollover disrupting receivers and grounding airliners in China for about seven to ten days, and a motorist following bad dashboard GPS into a canal. The discussion ties those cases to power-grid phasor measurement, agriculture, telecom synchronization degrading within hours without GPS, and markets plus other sectors.

The second segment introduces NISTIR 8323, the Foundational PNT Profile mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework through an open collaboration with dozens of stakeholders. It is voluntary guidance to inventory PNT-dependent assets and sources, detect disturbance or manipulation, and manage risk, with suggested timelines for inventory, source identification, alternatives such as time over fiber, threat analysis, procedures, and policy updates.

talks.title: Public Health Cyber War Games: How Hackers are Exploiting Healthcare
talks.teaser: Examines how ransomware is disrupting hospitals and what healthcare teams and security leaders can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how ransomware has shifted from stealing patient data to disrupting hospital operations, using incidents from 2019 and 2020. Examples include an IT provider serving nursing homes, a system-wide outage at UHS that hit about 250 locations, a German clinic where a patient death was reported after emergency patients were diverted, and the University of Vermont Health Network outage that needed a National Guard deployment. The speakers argue healthcare is an appealing target because many providers fall short of a maturity level of three on the NIST framework.

Robin Ford then describes what an outage looks like inside a hospital. Paper order processing, staff fatigue, delayed claims and a recovery stretching for months come up, along with a revenue drop of $2 million at one organization. She outlines regulatory exposure and lawsuits that can follow even when a third party is breached, and notes that organizations that paid ransoms were frequently attacked again. Caleb Barlow then covers emerging risks: pressure on vaccine producers and the cold chain, contact tracing data that reveals who people associate with, genomic testing tied to a foreign supplier, and altered medical records.

The closing advice turns these points into a checklist for executives: compromise assessments, network segmentation, endpoint detection and response, multi-factor authentication, privileged access management, security validation in production, and a tested ransomware playbook. The talk ends with supply chain security, using the US CMMC model as an example of third-party assessment for government contractors.

talks.title: Trusted Internet of Things Device Onboarding and Lifecycle Management
talks.teaser: Outlines trusted IoT network onboarding, lifecycle credential flows, and how DPP, BRSKI, and FDO compare in practice.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the scale problem: tens of billions of connected devices make manual, shared-password provisioning unsafe for both devices and networks. Trusted network-layer onboarding is framed as deploy-time assignment of unique credentials, mutual authentication before provisioning, encryption, no human exposure to secrets, and the ability to repeat the process across a long lifecycle—from manufacturing and integrator networks through operational use, credential refresh after incidents, decommissioning, resale, and moves to new owners.

The first segment walks through a generic flow: bootstrapping credentials from the factory, introduction of trust (sometimes via a human trusted onboarder), authenticated secure channel delivery of network credentials, then optional extensions such as attestation tokens, device intent (for example MUD-style communication rules), and bundled application-layer bootstrapping. It maps onboarding to supply-chain versus use-phase responsibilities, highlights security and usability traits (network selection, proof of ownership, bulk zero-touch for enterprises), and describes MITRE documentation plus an NCCoE initiative to demonstrate repeatable trusted onboarding with attestation, intent, and lifecycle management.

The second segment compares three recent standards. Wi-Fi Device Provisioning Protocol (Easy Connect) uses out-of-band public-key material (often via QR) for minimalist one-step wireless provisioning, with enterprise paths toward certificate-based join. BRSKI uses manufacturer-issued vouchers and registrar paths toward EST and enterprise AAA for zero-touch first onboarding, with tradeoffs around online manufacturer services and ownership transfer. FIDO Device Onboard focuses on application onboarding and late binding to reduce custom SKUs, with certificate-based anti-counterfeiting but limited network-layer onboarding. Practitioners are urged to inventory connected devices, strengthen post-onboard authentication infrastructure, and press vendors on zero-touch versus one-touch needs and connectivity constraints.

talks.title: Burnout—The Greatest Threat to Your Organization’s Security
talks.teaser: Shows how burnout erodes security teams and offers leaders concrete steps on planning, time off and respecting boundaries.
talks.summary:
Chloe Messdaghi argues that burnout is a security risk in its own right, not only a wellbeing concern. She describes warning signs seen in colleagues, such as slower replies, withdrawal, frequent sick days and missed deadlines, and links prolonged stress to physical and mental health harm. Remote work during the pandemic, with the office and home now in the same space and messages arriving after hours, is presented as a major driver of the cycle.

She then turns to industry figures, citing research collected by Dark Reading that she notes likely understates the current situation. Among CISOs, 21% had taken a leave of absence because of job stress, 48% said work stress affected their mental health, and 94% of American CISOs reported working more than their contracted hours. Response planning is weak as well: 74% of surveyed organizations had ad hoc plans or none, and 52% of those with a plan had never reviewed it. Tools are often added without updating plans, leaving teams unprepared when a breach happens.

To close, she offers four investments for leaders: listen to the team and act on what they say, plan together and keep response plans current, encourage real time off, and respect boundaries by avoiding after-hours contact. Practical steps include a 15-minute weekly one-on-one, a no-meetings day each week, anonymous surveys, and a monthly day off for mental health.

talks.title: Rebels & Resilience—Why It Pays Off to Break Your Patterns!
talks.teaser: Small steps, curiosity, and varied perspectives can help security teams move from stalled projects to remediation.
talks.summary: The speakers describe how teams working on vulnerability and patch management can get stuck because they lack a clear view of their systems, lose trust, or fear failure. Drawing on a model of four rebel types—the pirate, traveler, climber, and guard—and five team talents, they discuss how curiosity, varied perspectives, novelty, and supportive leadership can help teams make progress. Attendees are encouraged to start with small steps, keep teams motivated, and make room for different ways of solving problems.

talks.title: CISO Leadership: Building Your Personal Action Plan
talks.teaser: Offers a practical plan for security leaders to build teams, transform their programs and advance their own careers.
talks.summary:
The session addresses a common problem for security leaders: getting pulled into everyday emergencies and losing sight of the bigger priorities. The speaker frames a personal action plan around three areas: developing the team, transforming the security program and advancing one's own career. He introduces a CISO mind map of daily leadership duties and a leadership matrix that separates boss, manager and leader behaviours.

For the team, the talk walks through Patrick Lencioni's five dysfunctions of a team, starting with inattention to results and ending with the absence of trust at the base. A trust circle of integrity, empathy, contribution, consistency and transparency follows, and Kim Scott's Radical Candor grid guides feedback, with facts first and listening before any response. For the program, the speaker urges a shared vision in the style of Jim Collins' big, hairy, audacious goal, links security work to business outcomes, compares maturity against NIST functions, and repeats strategic messages often. BJ Fogg's behaviour model of motivation, ability and prompts is used to drive secure habits.

For personal growth, the talk separates coaching, mentoring and sponsorship, cites Harvey Coleman's view that performance is only a small share of career advancement, and reviews Steve Katz's six career considerations. The closing plan lists steps for the first week, three months and six months, such as learning team goals, writing a mission, finding a mentor and seeking a sponsor.

talks.title: Analyst View: How To Manage Info/Cybersec Careers in a Pandemic Recession
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Analyst View: How To Manage Info/Cybersec Careers in a Pandemic Recession.

talks.title: Your Cyber Journey
talks.teaser: A veteran panel revisits a 2013 session to compare eras and deliver lessons on careers, peers, and long security journeys.
talks.summary:
Four cybersecurity leaders reunite a decade after a 2013 conference panel to trace how the profession and their own roles evolved. They set the scene in an earlier era—before sweeping privacy laws, headline supply-chain crises, and today’s ransomware waves—while noting where each of them worked then, from federal banking oversight and major security vendors to nonprofit alliance work.

Guided by rapid-fire prompts, they trade unfiltered stories about discrimination, betrayed expectations, advocacy intimidation, and conference hostility, then unpack why “dream jobs” often sour: undisclosed incidents, hollow mandates, or personal patterns that recreate toxic workplaces. They emphasize documenting what you want from a move, refusing backward steps on base pay, and acting as your own advocate when reality diverges from the pitch.

The conversation pivots toward sustaining a long career: trimming low-value habits, leaning on trusted peers, mentoring in both directions, and accepting loneliness and sharper impact as seniority grows. They highlight standout wins such as standing up new federal security programs, privacy engineering outreach, and awareness campaigns that reached national scale. They close uncertain about the next industry shock but aligned on staying curious, uncomfortable, and connected as the journey continues.

talks.title: Breaking the Box: How Emerging Technology Can Close the Cyber Skills Gap
talks.teaser: Maps workforce myths, education paths, and creative hiring tactics practitioners can use to shrink the cybersecurity skills gap.
talks.summary:
The presenters open by contrasting headline claims about endless cybersecurity jobs with real stories of graduates who hold degrees and certifications yet still struggle to land roles. They trace disconnects such as unclear career ladders compared with older professions, organizational confusion about where security leaders sit, and tension between security as a business brake versus an enabler.

The middle of the session reframes the “box” metaphor around breaking early stereotypes, diversity, and hands-on curiosity from K–12 through programs like Code.org, Khan Academy, Chick Tech, and Girls Who Code. They cover certifications versus degrees as intersecting paths, scholarships including CyberCorps, Women in CyberSecurity, and related funds, plus internships, externships, virtual options such as Forage, boot camps, reskilling, CTFs, and bug bounty programs as résumé builders. Interdisciplinary majors—from criminology to engineering—are positioned as legitimate entry routes.

They close on recruiting friction from applicant tracking systems and bloated job posts, inclusive wording, networking, mentorship, advocacy, and creative examples such as novel billboards. Hiring managers are urged to redesign descriptions, internship design, and measurement; job seekers are encouraged to apply below full checklist match and build three- and six-month plans.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from Diverse Paths to Successful Cybersecurity Careers
talks.teaser: Veterans of varied backgrounds share how they entered security and what newcomers should prioritize for lasting careers.
talks.summary:
A moderator opens a career panel by describing his own hopscotch path through government crypto work, early internet incident response, analyst roles, and training. He stresses how fast the field changes, the satisfaction of defensive work, and advice to learn how to build systems first, chase interesting roles over salary jumps, recognize recurring patterns, and contribute locally while networking widely.

Another panelist explains growing up during the dot-com era, earning a computer science degree without wanting to code, discovering digital forensics through night school, and later blending investigative work, vendor value roles, teaching, and policy programs. She highlights careers she never imagined as a student, mentorship that lasted decades, combining technical depth with business and policy views, and continuous education when the linear college-to-job plan fails.

A founder describes immigrating for education, early firewall and government engineering work, founding a consulting company, and lessons that hands-on breaking and building matter more than credentials alone. A fourth voice covers pivoting from small business and biochemistry through an academy into blue-team and threat-intelligence community work, with emphasis on managers, ethics, learning priorities, and giving value when networking. The session closes with tips on virtual and local events, associations, curated social feeds, open repositories, and mentoring the next generation.

talks.title: A Sustainable Security Workforce Starts at the Local Coffee Shop
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning A Sustainable Security Workforce Starts at the Local Coffee Shop.

talks.title: Election Security: Lessons from the Front Lines
talks.teaser: Election officials and federal agencies review 2020 threats, from social media disinformation to coordinated foreign influence.
talks.summary:
Three officials from Maricopa County, the FBI Cyber Division and CISA reflect on the 2020 US election cycles. Maricopa's security lead says the attacks his office saw were limited, including port scanning and DDoS, while misinformation on social media proved the biggest challenge. An FBI section chief summarizes the joint reports: no evidence that foreign actors manipulated results, but Russia and Iran tried to shape voter opinion through amplified content and intimidation.

The panel credits closer collaboration across federal, state and local partners. CISA describes its election-focused information sharing center, which all 50 states joined, and tailored services for thousands of local jurisdictions, including incident response planning and scenario exercises. The FBI points to a policy that notifies chief state election officials of any local incident. Maricopa County shares its playbooks, reported hourly on election day, and its social media monitoring uncovered a planned caravan following election staff and bot-driven account registrations on a popular platform.

Looking ahead, the speakers stress regular tabletop exercises, since reading a playbook for the first time on election day is too late. They also call for transparency about security practices so voters can find trusted sources, public attribution to raise the cost for adversaries, securing the vendor supply chain, auditable paper records and steady funding. For security professionals, the advice is to report suspicious activity to the FBI and CISA and to talk with election officials before pitching services.

talks.title: Operational Collaboration: Enhancing Cyber Readiness
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Operational Collaboration: Enhancing Cyber Readiness.

talks.title: Creating the Next Cyber Generation - Lessons Learned from the NSA and UWF
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Creating the Next Cyber Generation - Lessons Learned from the NSA and UWF.

talks.title: How Governments Can Promote a Secure 5G Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Industryents discuss how governments can weigh supply chain, virtualized network and operational risks in 5G security.
talks.summary:
Panelists from ITI member companies discuss how governments can encourage a secure 5G ecosystem. They note that policy has often focused on which vendors build network equipment, while 5G moves networks toward virtualized, containerized and software-defined functions from many suppliers. Network slicing is raised as a new risk, since shared underlying services could let an attack move between slices, and integrity and availability are described as more important than confidentiality.

Much of the talk concerns scale and sourcing. Educating every developer to write secure code will not scale, so the speakers favor security tools built into development platforms and automated operations. Country of origin is judged important for critical functions and easier to assess for hardware than for software, where open-source and international development make origin hard to trace. Software and hardware bills of materials and certification are proposed to manage residual risk, and the Mirai botnet illustrates how weak device practices can affect the wider internet.

Recommendations include using machine learning for anomaly detection, involving industry in policy design, and rewarding good supply chain and secure development practices through procurement. One speaker suggests placing more responsibility on mobile service providers for edge infrastructure, comparing this to how card issuers took on fraud liability. The panel closes by urging engagement on international norms, since industry often detects nation-state attacks first.

talks.title: Who You Gonna Call: The Quest for a National Data Breach Reporting Law
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Who You Gonna Call: The Quest for a National Data Breach Reporting Law.

talks.title: The Cyber Solarium Commission: What is Left to Be Done?
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh which Solarium Commission cyber recommendations were enacted and which still need funding and new legislation.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the Cyberspace Solarium Commission’s 2019 mandate, its March 2020 report, and layered cyber deterrence strategy, noting that roughly 27 initial recommendations were written into law while follow-on work continues under later authorization. Former commissioner Frank Cilluffo stresses that enactment is not completion: agencies must carry out the intent, Congress must fund initiatives, and about thirty priorities remain for the current fiscal year, spanning a Joint Collaborative Environment for operational public-private defense, designation of systemically critical infrastructure, continuity-of-economy planning with a cyber response fund, elevation of State Department cyber diplomacy, federal data breach notification, a National Supply Chain Intelligence Center, and a National Security Investment Corporation.

Paul Rosenzweig argues the largest gap is measurable cybersecurity. He urges a Bureau of Cyber Statistics to produce transparent metrics for breach trends, network-wide hygiene signals, and enterprise security posture so leaders can prioritize spending instead of relying on qualitative judgment alone. Tom Corcoran, drawing on insurance sector experience, favors a single national data protection and breach standard to replace fragmented state rules, plus a JCE weighted toward timely, tool-ready threat intelligence flowing to ordinary enterprises through channels such as the Cyber Threat Alliance rather than opaque vendor black boxes.

The panel debates whether JCE demands new authorities, a purpose-built agile entity, or faster pipes from CISA into existing alliances, using SolarWinds as a lens on who held actionable information first. Closing reflections return to implementing deterrence across instruments of national power, victim assistance for state and local communities, expanded FBI cyber liaison capacity, counter-ransomware effort comparable to counterterrorism, and adjacent challenges such as social disinformation that the commission did not fully address.

talks.title: Ticking ‘Cyber Bomb’: Is There a Global Response to Fix Value-Chain Risks?
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Ticking ‘Cyber Bomb’: Is There a Global Response to Fix Value-Chain Risks?.

talks.title: Building Resilience Standards, Resiliently
talks.teaser: Examines how openness, membership rules, and stakeholder mix in standards forums shape adoptable cyber resilience outcomes.
talks.summary:
Cyber resilience depends on standards that can protect, detect, and recover across changing threats, yet the path from early BIOS protection work to broader firmware resilience shows that technical requirements alone do not guarantee usable outcomes. The presenters frame resilience at psychological, organizational, and technological levels, then argue that standards development organizations must balance openness, membership types, decision processes, and the mix of customer versus implementer voices.

They anchor the discussion in NIST platform resilience work evolving from SP 800-147 toward SP 800-183 and implementations spanning servers, network gear, IoT, and 5G. Three case studies illustrate how culture shapes results: Trusted Computing Group TPM work that moved quickly but saw slow adoption until usability improved; IETF remote attestation procedures that emphasize rough consensus and running code; and 3GPP use of attestation for connectivity and analytics decisions, including trustworthy data for machine learning on the network.

The talk closes by contrasting those models with ITU-T-driven 6G planning, warning that customer-heavy, consensus-bound processes without enough vendor input can slow implementable networks. Practitioners are urged to diversify thought locally, map cannot-fail systems, review resilience standards for gaps, and participate in relevant forums so future wireless and cloud requirements reflect real operational needs.

talks.title: Municipal Cybersecurity: Building the "Last Mile" of Resiliency
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Municipal Cybersecurity: Building the "Last Mile" of Resiliency.

talks.title: Cyber Risk Management Programs: Bringing Clarity to Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Government and finance panelists discuss measuring cyber risk, weighing insurance and managing third-party exposure.
talks.summary:
Three cybersecurity leaders joined a panel led by an official from CISA to discuss what makes cyber risk management work and where it falls short. The panelists were Lisa Donnan of a cybersecurity-focused private equity fund, Alma Cole, a CISO at US Customs and Border Protection, and Shaun Khalfan, a CISO at Discover Financial. Donnan said her portfolio companies treat cyber risk as a business matter, and that investors now weigh it during acquisitions. Khalfan argued that cyber risk is harder to quantify than credit or market risk, and described blending the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and threat models with key risk indicators.

Cole explained that federal law requires controls to be based on risk, yet applying them system by system can hide the enterprise-wide picture. The agency feeds an enterprise risk register from certification work, vulnerability management, penetration tests, bug bounty programs and incident lessons, then ranks the results. Insurance came up as well: Donnan said insurers now require policyholders to show a practiced risk framework, while Khalfan called coverage a risk-transfer tool, not a substitute for controls. Cole added that attackers increasingly target suppliers and partners, so DHS is exploring third-party risk scoring and attestation similar to CMMC.

Looking ahead, Donnan expects cyber to become part of every company's value proposition, Cole anticipates more outsourcing and zero trust with disposable services, and Khalfan warns the threat environment will worsen before it improves. The takeaway across the panel: measure risk in business terms, anchor on proven frameworks, and rely on peers for shared intelligence.

talks.title: Liberal Democratic Values and the Geopolitics of Technology
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Liberal Democratic Values and the Geopolitics of Technology.

talks.title: Leveraging Suricata in the Enterprise: Shifting from Events to Insights
talks.teaser: Shows how Suricata network metadata and filter sets can cut alert noise and turn events into asset-focused investigations.
talks.summary:
Peter Manev and Eric Leblond, both from Stamus Networks and contributors to the Suricata project, explain how the open-source engine goes beyond raw intrusion alerts. Suricata records application-layer metadata for protocols such as TLS, HTTP, SMB and FTP, giving investigators context around each transaction. Signature metadata, such as a malware family or the date a rule was created, adds further context. The session also introduces SELKS, a Debian-based live distribution that bundles Suricata with Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana and a management interface.

The demo walks through filter sets in the Scirius hunting interface. One query surfaces TLS sessions that use outdated protocol versions, and another finds HTTP responses that claim to be images but are actually executables. A Kibana dashboard of file transactions highlights executables with unusually long names seen over SMB, which the presenters check against VirusTotal. They argue for tagging events rather than suppressing them, so context is kept for later correlation. They also cover building asset-oriented views using the source and target keywords added to signatures, so that internal hosts and the malware families touching them can be seen in one query.

The closing advice is to find queries that give useful results in your own environment, learn the baseline before tuning, and hunt proactively rather than only reacting to alerts. Automate only the steps that repeat, because signature sources change daily and rule maintenance is an ongoing task.

talks.title: Analyzing Windows Malware on Linux: Getting Started Tips and Examples
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Linux tools for triaging a suspicious Windows executable, from static properties to string deobfuscation and emulation.
talks.summary:
The session tackles a practical question: how to begin examining a suspicious Windows executable when your analysis workstation runs Linux. The speaker, who created and maintains the REMnux toolkit, uses a real-world sample as a running example and argues that cheap first steps often reveal the most. He starts with file-type identification and signature scanning, then uses static tools to pull out hashes, an appended overlay, and API references that hint at file, registry and network behavior.

Next, the walkthrough covers recovering hidden strings. Simple XOR obfuscation concealed lookalike domain names, which were found by trying single-byte keys, and a broader decoder called FLOSS recovered dozens of strings, including a registry run-key persistence command and a hard-coded user agent that could serve as a network indicator. Emulators such as binee and qltool showed timing and foreground-window checks, a sign of sandbox evasion, and capa mapped those behaviors to anti-debugging and anti-analysis techniques with code addresses. The decompiler RetDec and Ghidra were offered for deeper code reading.

The closing takeaway is that sandbox-style analysis may fall short against evasive samples, so hands-on static and emulated analysis is worth learning. Suggested follow-up steps include installing REMnux, reading its documentation, and simulating fake DNS and web services in a lab, which were covered only in the slides rather than demonstrated live.

talks.title: My Phishing Kit Burnbook
talks.teaser: Shows how phishing kits operate as a criminal ecosystem and how to analyze them in a containerized sandbox.
talks.summary:
Zack Allen, Senior Director of Threat Intelligence at ZeroFOX, argues that phishing is more than a fake login page. He describes a criminal economy of operators, kit developers, infrastructure brokers and open marketplaces, and walks through how a kit moves from purchase to deployment to victim data collection. He also shows that many kits harvest far more than credentials, including personal details and identity documents that can be used to get past know-your-customer checks.

The case study covers 16Shop, an Indonesian phishing-as-a-service operation sold on the open web through a storefront with user guides, licensing limits and an admin dashboard. Allen ties its growth to the geopolitics of fraud and notes that the developer's name was signed into the kits, which helped attribution. He then reviews public data sources such as the Anti-Phishing Working Group and urlscan, and explains that kit-level data is scarce and few kits are labeled by brand.

He introduces phishpond, an open-source Docker project that detonates phishing kits using a man-in-the-middle proxy, a containerized browser and a web server with PHP shims that neutralize the kit. Demos show finding exfiltration points in text files, pausing and inspecting requests, redirecting a Telegram API call to a logged response, and stepping through obfuscated PHP in a Visual Studio Code debugger. The takeaway is that kits hold unused intelligence, such as exfiltration endpoints and Telegram keys that support pivoting, and that the community needs more shared samples.

talks.title: Evolution of AppSec: Perspectives from a Decade of Building OWASP ZAP
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Evolution of AppSec: Perspectives from a Decade of Building OWASP ZAP.

talks.title: Open Source as Your Career Catapult
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Open Source as Your Career Catapult.
talks.summary: Overview: With words like community bandied about, what can the individual gain in professional terms from getting involved in extra-curricular activities?  Come and hear tales from someone who has almost accidentally benefitted from her community activities about what drives her to get involved and how this has crossed over into her day job.  Everyone will take home from this session some new ideas about how giving can actually be receiving, and strategies for situations where everyone wins.

talks.title: Confidential Computing Across Multiple Clouds and Platforms: Project Enarx
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Confidential Computing Across Multiple Clouds and Platforms: Project Enarx.
talks.summary:
Overview: Confidential computing systems involve computation over private inputs held by mutually distrusting parties while producing public, cryptographically verifiable evidence of what was computed. Trusted execution environments (TEEs) are a practical building block for these systems, enabling code to run inside hardware-encrypted enclaves that emit attestations binding a measurement of the loaded code to genuine hardware. We present Cove, a framework that composes attested computations into multi-sta

Key Topics: ge, multi-party workflows structured as directed acyclic graphs. Each node runs in its own enclave, decrypts private inputs only under attestation-gated key release, and emits a certificate that downstream nodes can require as a cryptographic precondition before consuming upstream artifacts; anyone holding the workflow bytes and the TEE vendor's attestation roots can verify the whole chain non-interactively. We show that a small set of reusable primitives - confidential artifact provisioning, encrypted dynamic outputs, attested ephemeral-key channels (RA-TLS), and certificate-gated preconditions - compose into systems that lift attestation fr

Takeaways: erties, and use this to express practical applications in secure AI systems including confidential AI inference, attested AI benchmarks, and training-code verification. We give an open-source reference implementation on Intel TDX via Phala Cloud's dstack and demonstrate end-to-end feasibility with an attested benchmark workflow.

talks.title: Evasion, Poisoning, Extraction, and Inference: Tools to Defend and Evaluate
talks.teaser: Shows membership and attribute inference attacks on machine learning models, and differential privacy as a defense.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces four adversarial threats to machine learning: evasion, which alters inputs to change a model's output; poisoning, which tampers with training data to plant backdoors; extraction, which steals a model; and inference, which recovers sensitive training data from a model's outputs. The speakers, maintainers of the open-source Adversarial Robustness Toolbox from IBM Research, present it as a library for evaluating and defending models against these threats.

The privacy demos cover two attacks. Attribute inference predicts a hidden sensitive feature, such as a social health rating in a nursery dataset, for a record known to be in training; the black-box attack reached about 70 percent, against a 66 percent baseline from the most common value. Membership inference asks whether a specific record was used in training; on a small logistic regression model the black-box attack reached about 54 percent.

For defense, the speakers trained differentially private models with the Diffprivlib library, where a lower epsilon means stronger privacy. At epsilon around 25 they found a workable balance, keeping reasonable accuracy while lowering membership attack accuracy. Their closing advice: inventory models trained on personal data, start with ART, reduce sensitive features, and consider alternative architectures.

talks.title: Who Stole My 100,000 Dollars’ Worth Bitcoin Wallets
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Who Stole My 100,000 Dollars’ Worth Bitcoin Wallets - Story of HoneyTokens.

talks.title: Making Sense of the Landscape of Attacks and Defenses Against AI
talks.teaser: Surveys adversarial machine learning attacks and defenses, and presents a modular testbed for measuring AI security.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with NIST's view of trustworthy AI, arguing that the field still lacks a shared taxonomy and vocabulary for risks such as accuracy, robustness and security. Principles must become measurable requirements before they can support testing and policy.

The security section groups adversarial machine learning attacks into poisoning, which tampers with training data; evasion, which alters inputs at inference time; and oracle attacks, which query a model to copy it or leak training data. Examples include a patch that makes any input classify as a toaster, low-level noise that turns a sports car into a purse, and a blended apple-currant image that poisons training. Defenses such as data sanitization, adversarial training and feature squeezing each carry trade-offs, and results shift with dataset, model and attack, so they are hard to generalize.

To address this, the presenters describe a modular testbed with a REST API, Redis job queue, worker containers and MLflow tracking, organised into experiment, entry point and task levels so users with different skills can run or extend experiments. The talk warns that robustness bounds may not match human perception and that deployment context, from controlled facial recognition to open road signs, changes the threat. Attendees are urged to try the testbed, review their ML-dependent processes and give feedback.

talks.title: AI vs AI: Creating Novel Spam and Catching it with Text Generating AI
talks.teaser: Shows how a GPT-2 model generates new spam samples to augment small datasets and strengthen spam detection.
talks.summary:
Younghoo Lee, a senior data scientist at Sophos AI, starts from the problem of building a spam detector when labeled data is small and expensive to produce. He reviews the usual options in order: exact-match signatures, which miss anything new and need constant rewriting, classical machine learning on TF-IDF features with Naive Bayes and Random Forest, and neural models such as LSTM, CNN and transformer-based networks. Pre-trained language models are presented as the approach that needs little labeled data and still catches similar or unseen messages.

The talk then turns to GPT-2. The language-modeling head is replaced with a two-class classification head, so the model can label messages as spam or ham. Experiments used the UCI SMS spam collection, with training sets of 200 and 1000 messages. Across the tested models, the fine-tuned GPT-2 variant performed best, and the speaker notes that data size matters most for deep networks. To generate new samples, the team applied a PPLM-style controlled generation method, steering GPT-2 with a small attribute model toward spam or ham, seeded with the first five words of each original message. LIME was used to show which tokens pushed generated spam toward the spam label.

The takeaway is that high-quality augmentation can stand in for expensive hand labeling. Adding 1000 generated samples to 200 originals, with originals weighted higher, gave performance comparable to a model trained on 1000 hand-labeled messages. The speaker suggests a staged plan: identify a small but important dataset, fine-tune a pre-trained model within three months, then refresh augmentation and monitor performance within six months.

talks.title: Ethical AI: Addressing Bias & Algorithmic Fairness
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Ethical AI: Addressing Bias & Algorithmic Fairness.

talks.title: AI: Legal and Policy Considerations and Landmines to Avoid
talks.teaser: Outlines U.S. and international AI policy, pending bills, and practical governance pillars for organizations deploying automated decisions.
talks.summary:
Automated decisions now touch credit, employment, transport, and other high-stakes domains, yet many organizations still treat AI mainly as an engineering problem. The session opens by contrasting narrow and general AI, and by asking whether society expects models to mimic humans or to outperform them, using autonomous vehicles and MIT’s Moral Machine dilemmas to show how “better” hides unresolved value choices.

Federal activity is surveyed from FTC guidance through executive orders, departmental AV guidance, and competitiveness-focused commissions, alongside OECD, G20, and bipartisan but advisory federal legislation. Failed federal algorithmic accountability proposals and pending state bills in California, Washington, and Maryland illustrate a patchwork where ethics often runs ahead of binding law.

Practitioners are offered four governance pillars—fairness and effectiveness, competence, transparency, and accountability—with concrete practices such as bias review, diverse teams, defined override rules, whistleblower protections, human appeal paths, and AI impact assessments modeled on privacy programs. The closing message is to design narrow-AI deployments with inclusive stakeholders, plain explanations, and accessible human review before trust and adoption can scale.

talks.title: Securing Tesla and Mobileye from Split-Second Phantom Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows how split-second projected phantoms fool Tesla and Mobileye driver-assist systems, and how a committee of experts can reject them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines split-second phantoms, fake objects shown to a car for a fraction of a second, that can trigger driver-assistance systems. Object detectors accept an object only after it persists past an appearance threshold, and a flash too brief for a human to notice can still clear it. Phantoms can be sent remotely by a drone-mounted projector or by hacking an internet-connected billboard. In tests, a Mobileye 630 PRO detected a projected speed-limit sign shown for 125 milliseconds, while a Tesla needed 416 milliseconds; a Tesla also stopped mid-road for a stop sign hidden in a billboard advertisement.

Detectors act as feature matchers that ignore context, color and texture, so phantoms expose a scientific gap rather than a coding bug. The defense scores each detection on seven aspects, including size, angle, focus, light and depth. The Ghostbuster prototype uses four of them (context, surface, light, depth) as expert networks feeding a combiner of about 1 million parameters. Across seven object detectors, phantom attacks succeeded 92 to 99% of the time; with the guard, success fell below 1%, even at zero false alarms.

Practitioners should consider redundancy for safety-critical AI, test models on edge cases missing from training data, and retrain with features that separate real from fake objects.
