talks.title: The Road to End-to-End Encryption
talks.teaser: Maps how Zoom rolled out meeting E2EE, from TLS-era server risks through key rotation, leader security codes, and planned identity layers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames why typical video conferencing trusts a central server with plaintext meeting keys, and why TLS alone, cloud compromise, insider access, and on-prem deployments still leave high-value virtual meetings exposed to silent exfiltration.

It contrasts Zoom’s earlier enhanced encryption—where the server generates an AES-GCM meeting key for features such as PSTN dial-in—with phase-one end-to-end encryption, where the leader creates the key and distributes it via signed Diffie-Hellman exchanges so ciphertext transits the server but the key does not. It covers key rotation when participants leave, ten-second leader heartbeats that expose who holds the key, mitigations for meddler-in-the-middle via out-of-band security codes and locking the meeting, and acknowledged UX limits.

Looking ahead, it describes trust-on-first-use across personal device clouds, encrypted contact-history sync, signature chains with transparency-tree and VRF ideas to resist malicious servers, and identity-provider attestations via OAuth2 so organizations—not the conferencing vendor—vouch for participants, with a white paper cited for deeper detail.

talks.title: Death to CIA! Long live DIE! How the DIE Triad Helps Us Achieve Resiliency
talks.teaser: A framework talk maps distributed, immutable, and ephemeral design to resilience beyond classic confidentiality goals.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that decades of security thinking tracked evolving challenges—from asset management through assume breach—and that the 2020s demand recovery-oriented resilience against irreversible, destructive attacks. He contrasts the familiar confidentiality-integrity-availability model with the DIE triad: distributed, immutable, and ephemeral systems that aim to make many compromises irrelevant rather than relying solely on preventive controls after breach.

Using the pets-versus-cattle analogy, he reframes security roles toward limiting long-lived “pets” while treating replaceable infrastructure as cattle. He shows practical measurement ideas: uptime distributions to separate pets from cattle, power-law beta exponents tied to fault tolerance research, network topology graphs, server security grades from changeability, and code churn as ephemerality. Examples draw on volunteer organization inventory data, CNCF projects, supply-chain integrity tools, ephemeral privileged access, and AWS shared-responsibility patterns.

Practitioners are urged to measure DIE characteristics, track how policy shifts their pets-versus-cattle curve, catalog design patterns for assembling cloud-native building blocks, and deliberately gate new pets. Privacy-enhancing technologies are framed as a path to treat sensitive data more like cattle. The closing position favors designing for DIE first, using traditional controls mainly where DIE cannot fully apply.

talks.title: Why 5G Demands a New Approach to Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how 5G changes the risks organizations face and why security should join business planning early.
talks.summary:
David Grady, chief security evangelist at Verizon, frames 5G security around the questions businesses and security teams ask about new technology. Business leaders ask what a technology can do for them, while security and risk staff ask what it could do to them. He compares earlier industrial revolutions to 5G, then describes 5G as a new networking technology with low latency, high throughput, dense device support and fast tracking of moving assets, alongside edge computing.

Grady walks through use cases in retail, manufacturing and healthcare, and uses a fleet of self-driving cars to show why security should work backward from worst-case outcomes such as a hijacked vehicle. He outlines 5G security across physical, transport, edge and infrastructure layers, citing network slicing and continuous authentication from the 3GPP standard. He notes that breaches often involve only a few attacker steps, so faster detection and automated response at the edge can help.

He argues that 5G mainly amplifies existing program weaknesses rather than creating entirely new ones. His takeaways include involving security early in planning, requiring assessments before deployment, keeping an accurate asset registry as IoT devices multiply, and checking whether visibility across the attack surface can scale. He closes with suggested steps over one week, three months and six months.

talks.title: Optimizing Operations: Simplification, Visibility, Response and Automation
talks.teaser: Explains how extended detection and response unifies security telemetry to cut alert overload and speed investigation.
talks.summary:
Security operations teams face alert fatigue, staffing gaps, and sprawling vendor stacks that analyze and prioritize threats in isolation. The speaker cites widespread skills shortages, averages of dozens of tools per organization, and difficulty orchestrating alerts across products, noting that long dwell times persisted even as SIEM and SOAR adoption grew because many teams lacked the people and budget to use those platforms fully.

The middle of the session frames extended detection and response as unified incident detection that ingests and correlates telemetry from proprietary controls, with centralized historic and real-time data, machine learning over combined signals, and automation for response. It situates endpoint and network detection as foundations and argues that email, cloud, firewall, and web controls should feed the same analytics and playbooks.

Practitioners evaluating offerings are urged to verify true cross-vendor data unification, analytics across attack vectors, endpoint depth, and automation fit against their KPIs. The close warns that not every product labeled XDR delivers integrated partnerships or normalization without expensive data lakes, and ties success to simpler operations, cross-domain visibility, and automated remediation that does not overtax lean teams.

talks.title: Identity Resilience: What Doesn’t Kill You Makes You Stronger
talks.teaser: Argues that digital identity underpins trust and outlines identity, access and activity assurance as pillars of resilience.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that digital identity is the foundation of trust in modern society, and that today's identity models give individuals little control over their own credentials. The speaker traces the history of the idea, from the RSA public-key work of the late 1970s, which drew on earlier Diffie-Hellman and Merkle research, through certificate authorities, federated identity and user-centric models. He describes the move toward decentralized identity built on verifiable claims, which lets people share only what a transaction needs. He credits mobile secure enclaves, password fatigue, decentralized storage and privacy concerns with making this shift practical now, while stating that blockchain is not a required part of it.

The middle of the talk organizes identity around three pillars. Identity assurance covers proving who someone is and weighing context, such as location, time and device signals, against the sensitivity of what is being accessed. Access assurance asks what a user should be allowed to reach as roles, partners and hybrid work change. Activity assurance asks whether people do the right things once they have access. The speaker then walks through zero trust, tracing the principle of least privilege to 1976 and the idea of treating trust as a liability, and points to NIST SP 800-207 as a reference. He closes the passwordless discussion with caveats about accessibility and fallback paths that often still depend on passwords.

For practitioners, the closing advice is to review identity strategy against the three pillars soon after the conference, check gaps against the NIST zero trust tenets within three months, and connect identity with integrated risk management and the security operations center. Programs to close the remaining gaps should follow after that, with spending tied to the largest expected reduction in risk.

talks.title: Ransomware: New Recipe For An Old Dish
talks.teaser: Explains how ransomware-as-a-service affiliates, entry vectors, and double extortion reshaped enterprise attacks.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting early consumer ransomware with today's enterprise-focused operations. Speakers trace evolution from spray-and-pray campaigns through SamSam, GandCrab, and Ryuk to modern ransomware-as-a-service models built on developers, admins, and skilled affiliates who behave more like penetration testers than bulk spammers.

They compare historical and current underground job postings for groups such as CTB-Locker and REvil, showing demand for Active Directory, backup, and exploitation skills. Press headlines that name only malware brands are challenged as misleading about who actually targets victims. Affiliate recruitment, branding, and extortion platforms—not encryption novelty—drive major family success. Initial access commonly involves exposed RDP, infostealer credential markets, phishing, commodity loaders, vulnerable public-facing apps, initial access brokers, and ransom sizing informed by business intelligence tools.

The talk closes on double extortion leak sites, optional denial-of-service pressure, CEO direct outreach, affiliate earnings, and payment fueling wider crime. Defenders are urged to scan for port 3389, enforce MFA, maintain backups, patch-facing services, treat commodity malware seriously, use No More Ransom decryptors when possible, and follow practical first-response steps if infected.

talks.title: Fighting Where They Aren't: How Attackers Avoid Endpoints in Modern Attacks
talks.teaser: Follow how attackers reach sensitive data through exposed systems, cloud app permissions, and insider access.
talks.summary: The speakers describe attack paths that can avoid endpoint defenses, including gateway and supply chain compromises, malicious cloud applications, and insider access. They explain how attackers can use exposed systems, application permissions, and legitimate accounts to reach or remove data. Attendees learn to assess exposure, monitor data and identity activity, and enrich alerts with context about users, devices, and sensitive files to support faster investigation.

talks.title: A Data Protection Problem: Insider Risk
talks.teaser: Reframes insider risk as a data protection problem and lays out a five-step contextual approach to prioritizing and responding.
talks.summary:
The talk treats insider risk as a data protection problem rather than only a question of malicious insiders. The speaker separates insider threat, which centres on a small group of users acting with harmful intent, from insider risk, which covers everyday data movement across all users, files and channels. He cites survey findings that many security teams cannot separate ordinary collaboration from real exfiltration and feel they lack purpose-built tooling for it.

The core of the session is a five-part framework: identify where data is exposed, decide which exposures each department can tolerate, define the indicators worth alerting on, match the response to severity, and measure posture over time. He illustrates indicator chaining with an example where a resignation notice, an earlier zip file and a later upload to an unsanctioned cloud service combine into a case that needs investigation. Responses range from doing nothing or sending a nudge, to extra training or a watch list, up to escalation to HR, legal or incident response.

The closing part covers outcomes. Measurement should show gains in security team productivity, shifting analysts from maintaining tools toward maturity, along with business results such as policy compliance and a risk-aware culture. Risk tolerance changes during events like IPOs, mergers or restructuring. He recommends starting with people, then processes, then technology, and reassessing posture at set intervals.

talks.title: CVSS Scores Are Dead. Let’s Explore 4 Alternatives
talks.teaser: Argues CVSS falls short for patch prioritization and compares EPSS, SSVC, VPR and other risk-based scoring alternatives.
talks.summary:
Allan Liska of Recorded Future starts with the volume problem. Figures from the United States National Vulnerability Database rose from about 6,000 vulnerabilities a year in 2016 to almost 18,000 in 2020, and Microsoft's Patch Tuesday totals went from about 400 to almost 1,500 over the same span. He argues that CVSS, first released in 2005, measures severity rather than real-world risk, so a 10 on a little-used product scores the same as a 10 on Exchange. Low-scored flaws also matter when attackers chain them after gaining access.

He then compares alternatives. EPSS, maintained by the same group as CVSS, estimates exploitation likelihood using exploit ecosystem activity. SSVC uses a decision tree that developers and vulnerability teams can both apply without numeric scores, though he doubts it scales to organizations with thousands of software packages. Tenable's VPR blends technical severity with exploitation likelihood and how widely a flaw is deployed. Recorded Future's approach adds real-time threat-based scores, early reporting before NVD publication, matching against uploaded software inventories, and details on which actors used a flaw.

The main takeaway is that a score alone rarely moves other teams to patch quickly. Liska says a message that a flaw is being used by a ransomware group prompts faster change approval than a bare severity rating. He recommends scores that plug into existing scanners and ticketing tools, and that combine external threat data with internal exposure and the sensitivity of data on affected systems. Teams need not replace everything at once; they can start adding risk context to their current process.

talks.title: Lessons From Our Zero Trust Journey: Successes, Failures & Dodging Pitfalls
talks.teaser: Shows how a 600-person security firm phased in zero trust over four years, with its wins, missteps and budgeting lessons.
talks.summary:
James Carder, chief security officer at a security company of about 600 employees, describes how his organization built a zero trust model over roughly four years, starting in 2017. He frames the concept as splitting workflows into separate identity perimeters, and says the Google BeyondCorp design was the loose model they followed. The journey started with GDPR data mapping, which the team extended to business-critical and toxic data. They then wrote a business plan, budget and ROI case from scratch to win board and executive approval.

Implementation began in early 2018 by loading roles and access rights into the identity platform, with the HR system as the source of truth for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning. Multifactor authentication, single sign-on, behavioral baselines and threat intelligence checks followed, and micro-segmentation separated medical device networks from finance systems, with unusual access used as a trust signal. The team had not planned for custom integration work, so 2019 became a reevaluation year. In 2020, device management enforced device trust and cleaned up personal laptops, and privileged access management arrived in 2021. A SaaS-based access broker then replaced most on-premises firewalls, saving 30 to 40% in costs.

The lessons were that zero trust need not be deployed all at once, that architecture should be revisited as technology matures, and that budgets need room for unplanned costs. He also urged framing benefits for the business beyond security alone. He closed by offering project plans, board decks and budgets to attendees as a starting point.

talks.title: Beyond Endpoints: A Case for Open XDR
talks.teaser: Explains how open XDR unifies dispersed security stacks via vendor integrations, open standards, and SOC automation.
talks.summary:
Enterprise security grew scattered as users, applications, and workloads spread across cloud and remote access, leaving teams juggling many disconnected products. Analysts routinely pivot among numerous consoles while related alerts stay hard to connect, which drives alert fatigue, integration overhead, and weak return on security spending.

The presentation frames extended detection and response around centralized normalized data, meaningful correlation, and focused response actions rather than a full SOC replacement. It advocates open XDR: keep investments that already work, integrate across vendors instead of rip-and-replace, lean on prebuilt correlation for common incidents, and automate enrichment and containment. Openness extends to shared rule formats, common query taxonomies such as STIX, MITRE ATT&CK alignment for coverage gaps, and composable integrations across endpoint, network, cloud, and SIEM tools.

Practitioners are urged to map integration silos and manual response steps, prioritize high-frequency automation, demand vendor-built interoperability, and consolidate tools that resist connection. Citing Ponemon survey figures, the speaker ties stronger outcomes to interoperable stacks and end-to-end automation in detection, investigation, and response.

talks.title: Into the Mind of an IoT Hacker | How to Protect IoT Networks & Devices
talks.teaser: Shows why unmanaged IoT devices expose enterprise, hospital and factory networks, and outlines layered defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why internet-connected IoT devices widen the attack surface of corporate, hospital and factory networks. Many of these devices are unmanaged, hard to patch, and often run old operating systems or default credentials. They estimate about 20,000 IoT devices in a typical enterprise of 5,000 employees, roughly 10,000 in a 500-bed hospital, and around 5,000 industrial devices in a 2,000-worker factory. Internet search tools for exposed devices returned more than 25,000 printers and almost 300,000 cameras in two queries.

Researchers showed that a ZigBee smart-lighting gateway could be taken over from within wireless range, and a group of ethical hackers found 28,000 exposed printers and printed a warning page on them. A building management controller carried a backdoor on port 22 and received a score of 10, a critical rating. A hospital ultrasound unit running Windows 2000 without patches was compromised in minutes. Among more than 1,800 internet-connected water pump controllers, default passwords made access straightforward.

The recommended response is layered. Teams should discover every device, isolate devices from the rest of the network and from each other, and use intrusion prevention as virtual patching where updates must wait. The talk also describes a lightweight firmware-level agent that watches for control-flow hijacking and memory corruption, tuned to each device because constrained hardware cannot carry a large security footprint.

talks.title: New Normal, New Security? Five Security Trends to Watch in 2021 and Beyond
talks.teaser: Covers five security trends for 2021, from user experience and remote work to disinformation, insider threats and data location.
talks.summary:
Forcepoint CTO Nicolas Fischbach opens a session on security trends the company's research group expects to shape 2021. He is joined by a fellow CTO from a Middle East systems integrator, who describes how clients act on them. The talk covers five themes: user experience, people, disinformation, insider threats and data location. Security is framed as a business differentiator, with tools bought more like consumer subscriptions.

On remote work, the speakers argue that users should be trusted and that blanket DLP blocking drives staff toward workarounds. Real-time, in-the-moment coaching and risk-adaptive access are presented as better options. The integrator gives a case from the start of the pandemic, when data loss rose mainly because staff sent large files to personal email after hitting a size limit. On disinformation, deepfake audio and video are described as an emerging phishing aid, and supplier bank-detail changes still succeed where processes are weak. Awareness should be continuous rather than a one-time programme.

For insider threat, the talk says most incidents stem from mistakes rather than malice, and cites a large volume of COVID-themed phishing seen early in the pandemic. The goal is to stay left of loss by spotting risky data movement before a breach. The closing discussion asks where data sits, recommends assessing endpoints against normal attack scenarios and building visibility across distributed workers.

talks.title: The Skeptic's Guide to Using XDR to Get Zero Trust
talks.teaser: Weighs the hype around XDR and Zero Trust, asking which claims hold up for SOC teams and what real visibility requires.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a skeptical look at pairing extended detection and response (XDR) with Zero Trust. The speaker argues that security operations teams have long had to connect breadcrumbs across siloed tools, and that attackers exploit the gaps between those silos through slow, multi-step campaigns that can run for months. Earlier promises of integration through vendor APIs and single-vendor suites have fallen short, and SIEM alerts often arrive without the context needed to act on them.

He describes what a genuine XDR should include: a data layer spanning endpoints, networks, email and cloud workloads, machine learning that narrows alerts rather than multiplying them, and a response function. Cloud provider telemetry beyond security APIs, plus unmanaged devices and shadow IT, are highlighted as blind spots. Remote work expanded the attack surface, and Zero Trust is framed as verifying before trusting, built on pillars such as strong identity, restricted network access and application control. The speaker notes that Zero Trust is a concept rather than a standard, and that SASE is one implementation within it, combining ZTNA and CASB capabilities.

The takeaway is that Zero Trust decisions depend on continuous posture and historical security data, so XDR needs to supply that depth. Buyers should question vendors who relabel EDR as XDR or sell Zero Trust as a single product, since no one currently offers a complete solution. Practitioners should test such claims against concrete capabilities rather than marketing terms.

talks.title: Your Fraud Metrics Suck, Losing Money and C-Suite Ignoring You - Now What?
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Your Fraud Metrics Suck, Losing Money and C-Suite Ignoring You - Now What?.

talks.title: Escalation from Heist to Hostage: Modern Bank Heists 4.0
talks.teaser: Survey findings from 126 financial CISOs explain how bank attacks shifted from heists to punitive, destructive hostage scenarios.
talks.summary:
The presentation draws on four years of Modern Bank Heist reporting and structured interviews with 126 chief information security officers worldwide, weighted toward North America and Europe. Kellermann frames finance as heavily defended yet preyed on by the most capable cybercrime cartels and state-tied actors, especially as stimulus-driven payment flows, remote work, and a surge in zero-day trading on criminal markets erode perimeter assumptions.

Survey results quantify the shift from theft to coercion. Wire transfer fraud, brokerage account takeover, and theft of non-public trading or strategy information appear at high rates, alongside island hopping, watering holes in mobile and payment apps, and reverse business email compromise that weaponizes trusted executive communications. More than half of respondents reported destructive activity, with a sharp year-over-year rise, while most intrusions involved active counter–incident response such as log tampering, security tool disablement, and timestamp manipulation. Russian-linked groups rank as the top concern, followed by China, domestic underground actors, North Korea, and Brazil.

Practitioners should treat offense as informing defense: prioritize contextual threat intelligence, XDR, workload and container security, and weekly threat hunting. Response discussions should stay off monitored collaboration tools; defenders should assume dormant secondary command channels and pursue clandestine eradication before adversaries punish victims by attacking customers or wiping data. The closing model compares financial architectures to supermax-style containment—limiting lateral movement, integrating network detection with endpoint protection, and using deception where paths cannot be fully hardened.

talks.title: From Zero to Hero - How Cisco Deployed Zero Trust in Five Months
talks.teaser: Explains how Cisco rolled out a zero trust architecture for its workforce in five months, from design to stakeholder management.
talks.summary:
Brad Arkin, Cisco's Chief Security and Trust Officer, walks through how the company rolled out a zero trust architecture in about five months. He starts by defining zero trust as a model that moves away from passwords and relies on user and device certificates, with posture checks and multifactor authentication before access is granted. The user experience should be identical for SaaS and on-premise apps, whether the person is on the corporate network or working from a coffee shop.

The middle of the talk covers the building blocks. Beyond the existing enterprise single sign-on, directory and identity provider, Cisco added a network gateway so external endpoints could reach on-premise apps, a cloud certificate authority with multifactor authentication, and certificate management to track which certificates belong to which users and devices. The rollout covered well over a hundred thousand endpoints, with a pilot of 35,000 users and about 20 applications at first. The hardest part, he notes, was getting every team to see the change as a transformation rather than an incremental upgrade.

He closes with the outcome and lessons. Once live, most users needed no training because links simply opened in the browser without VPN, and posture checks let the company catch misconfigurations and prompt corrective action before access to sensitive resources. Weekly stakeholder emails with a countdown and a list of blockers helped the project get unstuck quickly. Practitioners should take away a checklist of components, a firm commitment to an aggressive schedule, and steady stakeholder communication.

talks.title: Work Smarter Not Harder: Tips to Approach Cloud Security the Easier Way
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Work Smarter Not Harder: Tips to Approach Cloud Security the Easier Way.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented at RSA Conference 2021 by Trend Micro researcher Erin Sindelar, this talk explores strategies for approaching cloud security more effectively by addressing both organizational culture and technology. Rather than traditional security threats like zero-days or ransomware, the primary cause of cloud breaches is simple misconfigurations. Sindelar argues that security teams can overcome friction with developers by reframing security controls from restrictive roadblocks into operational enablers that accelerate cloud innovation and ensure systems work as intended and only as intended.

### Key Topics
- **The People Problem and the Four-Box Model**: Historically, developers and security have had seemingly contrasting goals. As DevOps and dedicated CloudOps teams emerged, security was often pushed around rather than truly integrated. Developers focus on making things work fast, while security focuses on making sure they work only as intended.
- **Misconfigurations as the Primary Cloud Threat**: Trend Micro research indicates that 65% to 70% of cloud security issues originate from misconfigurations. Filtering public records shows that over 2 billion sensitive records have been leaked due to single misconfigurations. A notable exception was the 2019 Capital One breach, which resulted from two misconfigurations and an inconsequential bug, exposing 100 million user records.
- **Cloud Service Provider (CSP) Reliability**: Addressing the misconception that CSPs represent major security risks, Sindelar notes only two breaches occurred across the top four CSPs in five years. However, high platform velocity (over 5,000 features released in 2020 by the big four, equaling at least two updates daily per cloud) makes manual oversight impossible.
- **Shared Responsibility Model**: Under the cloud shared responsibility model, configurations are always the customer's operational responsibility across IaaS, PaaS, and managed services.

### Technical Details & Security Controls
To bridge the gap with developers, security professionals should ask two core builder questions: "What else can this do?" and "Are you sure?"
- **Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)**: The cornerstone tool for continuous auditing. Trend Micro's CSPM identifies over 840 million misconfigurations per day. For builders, CSPM automates checks across hundreds of daily deployments, assists with cost optimization, and streamlines audit compliance.
- **Network & Application Controls**: Network controls prevent unwanted traffic from impacting code execution. Automated security testing integrated into CI/CD pipelines eliminates late rollbacks or post-release hotfixes.
- **Containers & Open Source Security**: Container admission controls and image scanning prevent vulnerable images from deploying (referencing Snyk's State of Open-Source Security report highlighting vulnerabilities in official base images). Open source dependency scanning catches third-party security vulnerabilities and licensing compliance issues early.

### Takeaways
1. **Shift Messaging from Prevention to Enablement**: Security teams must stop focusing solely on what security stops and explain what it enables for developers.
2. **Inventory Cloud Footprint and Controls**: Map all active cloud services and consult CSPs and cloud-native security partners to identify non-disruptive controls.
3. **Automate and Maintain Continuous Visibility**: Deploy CSPM and CI/CD security controls continuously to handle the rapid release cadence of cloud platforms.

talks.title: How to Build a Long-term XDR Architecture Strategy
talks.teaser: A panel outlines how extended detection and response tackles alert overload, tool sprawl, and faster orchestrated security operations.
talks.summary:
Security leaders frame extended detection and response as a way to ease alert fatigue and the sprawl of point products, while shifting operations from pure log collection toward orchestrated, automated response. Panelists argue digital transformation and cloud have widened the attack surface, making unified visibility and faster handoffs between teams more urgent than in the era of defense-in-depth buying alone.

Architecturally, many organizations combine a top-down SIEM view with bottom-up endpoint detection, seeking shared context instead of siloed investigations. They recommend gap analysis across people, process, and technology, informed by red team work, knowledge of critical assets, compliance needs, and business goals. Pitfalls include vendor fatigue, single-vendor lock-in, and overlooking prevention plus recovery alongside detection; one speaker urges pursuing paths from detection to recovery in under 10 minutes.

For staffing, teams can inventory skills, plan analyst development to reduce burnout, and weigh in-house tier-one work against managed security providers. Getting started means defining security and business outcomes first, aligning partners and culture fit, and using trusted advisors rather than diving straight into product comparisons.

talks.title: Ditching Run-To-Failure as Part of a Winning ICS Strategy
talks.teaser: Argues OT security should be predictive, not run-to-failure, using active device querying and continuous monitoring.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that industrial control environments are often maintained the way a car is driven until something breaks. Reactive, run-to-failure maintenance is costly and stressful for staff, and in cybersecurity it amounts to ignoring defenses until a ransomware incident forces an expensive response. The speaker contrasts this with schedule-based checks such as periodic compliance assessments, which give only a point-in-time snapshot, and with predictive approaches that watch equipment condition continuously.

The middle of the talk maps those maintenance ideas onto OT security. Thermal imaging of a running motor serves as an analogy for inspecting systems without stopping production. Passive network monitoring alone is presented as insufficient, because many industrial devices are quiet and only answer requests. The speaker describes active querying that uses vendor-native protocols to ask a controller for its firmware level, whether it is in run or program mode, and a copy of its logic. Three detection layers are outlined: a policy engine with allow and deny lists, anomaly detection for new, missing or unexpected devices and protocols, and signature matching using Suricata. Comparing a controller's running configuration against a known good baseline is shown to help both troubleshooting and forensic investigation.

The closing argument is that organizations should build asset inventories, detection and skilled staff before an incident, and combine OT data with enterprise data so leaders can assess risk across both. The speaker stresses that people, process and technology are all needed, and says a proactive approach costs less over time, though it cannot prevent every bad outcome.

talks.title: Multi-Front War: Mitigating Cyber Risk and Maximizing Security
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss ransomware response, supply chain risk and what the 2020 shift to remote work means for security teams.
talks.summary:
The panel opened by asking what organizations would have done differently had they foreseen 2020. Panelists agreed the pandemic forced fast moves to remote access and cloud services that many firms had postponed, and argued that deliberate strategy beats reacting to outside pressure. The lesson they drew was a change in mindset rather than a single product rollout.

On ransomware, speakers stressed a written, rehearsed incident plan aligned with recognised frameworks, including guidance on not paying sanctioned entities, with forensic firms, insurers and counsel lined up in advance. One panelist said the first hours are key for understanding scope and limiting lateral movement, and noted that data theft alongside encryption adds regulatory exposure. Non-technical roles such as finance, communications and legal must join the response, and a printed copy of the plan is worth keeping because laptops may be unavailable.

On supply chains, the discussion centred on SolarWinds and the view that digital supply chains reach cloud providers, open-source libraries, firmware and private keys. Panelists said familiar concentration-risk techniques from physical procurement still apply, and that testing overlapping security tools regularly helps avoid both complacency and paranoia. The session closed with a call for more public-private dialogue on issues such as 5G hardware suppliers.

talks.title: What is New in California Privacy and What Does it Mean for the Company?
talks.teaser: Explains what the CPRA changes for California privacy law, covering who is in scope, selling data, opt-outs and penalties.
talks.summary:
Two speakers, one in-house privacy counsel and one outside lawyer, walk through the California Privacy Rights Act, which amends the CCPA and becomes fully effective January 1, 2023. They place it among hundreds of California privacy laws, noting that federal legislation remains stalled over preemption and private lawsuits.

The law reaches any California resident, including employees and contractors, though some business-to-business and employee provisions are delayed. A company falls in scope through revenue above 25 million, a records threshold that rises from 50,000 to 100,000 in 2023, or half of revenue from selling personal information. Selling is defined so broadly that sharing data for any valuable consideration, even with some service providers, can count. Companies must decide whether to sell, post opt-out links, avoid penalizing people who opt out, and seek opt-in consent for under-16s. The speakers recommend a separate California privacy notice and privileged assessments of security, while noting audit reports can help or hurt.

Penalties reach 7,500 per intentional violation, and a narrow private right of action applies after breaches when reasonable security cannot be shown. The right to cure has effectively been removed for breaches, since harm has already occurred by then. Practical steps include keeping data inventories current, updating vendor contracts, securing consumer login credentials, training staff on consumer requests, and working toward data minimization, while balancing the needs of data science teams.

talks.title: Who Owns Your Data?
talks.teaser: Outlines privacy statutes' property framing of personal data, stickiness, mutuality, and breach liability for collectors.
talks.summary:
Steve Black opens with two questions his law students and executive clients raise: why property law matters, and how organizations navigate liability after breaches. He places today's wave of data-protection legislation—spanning well over a hundred jurisdictions—on a map of compliance, market entry, and advocacy pressures, and suggests that when statutes grant individuals control over information, they quietly transform data from mere bits into a new kind of property.

The core of the session retraces legal history from Blackstone and Hohfeld through the "bundle of rights," using Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council to show how regulation can create property interests. He compares the right to exclude on land with GDPR and CCPA-style rights over personal data, introduces "stickiness" when copies persist after sale or disclosure, and walks through mutuality (social security numbers, paparazzi and celebrity photo disputes), classic capture-and-finding doctrines, household data and children's privacy, erasure of shared records, and humorous hypotheticals about AI cars earning income from collected imagery.

He closes on breach response: thieves often sit beyond extradition, so victims assert rights against the company that held the data—even when that company never truly "owned" it either. Legislatures, he argues, boxed an unfamiliar asset into familiar property language. Practitioners should expect ongoing legal wrangling while still collecting data, and prioritize trust so customers keep handing over access.

talks.title: Protests, Pandemics, and Privacy: The Rise of Surveillance States
talks.teaser: Contrasts how China and the US used surveillance during unrest and the pandemic, and where sensors and AI are heading.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts how China and the United States have used surveillance during recent crises. It starts with the treatment of Uyghurs in Xinjiang after the 2009 unrest, describing phone monitoring apps, checkpoints and facial recognition aimed at that minority. It then turns to the January 2021 Capitol riot, where advertising, phone and social media data were used to rebuild one rioter's movements, and to China's COVID-19 response, including a color-coded health code app and camera-based contact tracing. By comparison, the US left contact tracing largely to states, companies and individuals.

The speaker traces the roots of privacy from the telegraph era and the 1890 essay by Louis Brandeis up to modern sensors. Surveillance is framed as three linked parts: sensors such as cameras, phones and satellites; the signal they produce; and AI, especially deep learning facial recognition that makes identification possible at scale. Examples include commercial satellite imagery that can be bought cheaply and a commercial facial recognition service used by police, where the talk argues that the gap between responsible use and abuse can come down to a company's usage policy.

The closing section looks at China's global data reach through telecom equipment, payment apps and its Belt and Road initiative, and argues that democracies must decide which future they want. The speaker also points to positive uses of the same tools, such as monitoring police conduct, wearable health sensors, and drones for wildfires and search and rescue, and urges policymakers, businesses, journalists and technologists to take part.

talks.title: Lessons Drawn From Cybersecurity In The Rise of Privacy Tech
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Lessons Drawn From Cybersecurity In The Rise of Privacy Tech.

talks.title: A Year Spent Virtually: The Lasting Effect of the COVID Pandemic on Privacy
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh whether the pandemic eroded privacy, how legal harms should be defined, and what guardrails data use needs.
talks.summary:
The panel looks at how the pandemic shifted people's relationship with technology, as work, school, and socializing moved online. The speakers argue that consumers now expect more say over how their data is used, and that individuals are carrying too much of the privacy burden alone. They also question whether privacy law can carry every societal problem, comparing the patchwork of US state laws with the GDPR model in Europe.

Much of the discussion centers on harms. One speaker notes that privacy torts were built for mass publication, and that courts tend to demand financial or physical injury, so a taxonomy covering thwarted expectations, autonomy, relationships, trust, and discrimination was proposed. The other describes a rise in non-consensual intimate imagery during the pandemic, citing a 250% increase in complaints in Australia over the first six months, and argues that Section 230 immunity should be conditioned on good-faith moderation.

The panel then turns to data for public health and equity. Companies lacked clear guardrails for using health data during COVID, and sensitive data is needed to detect discrimination, which creates a tension. Skepticism is raised about AI products offered without proof of concept. The closing exchange covers browser and platform moves away from third-party cookies, and the need for an advertising model that lets small players and publishers compete without making people feel creeped out.

talks.title: Personal Threat Models and, Speculatively, Privacy Governance
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Personal Threat Models and, Speculatively, Privacy Governance.

talks.title: Compliance Made Easy—Simplify Your Approach to Privacy
talks.teaser: Walks through the NIST Privacy Framework and shows how to map regulations into one profile to document current privacy gaps.
talks.summary:
Organizations facing overlapping privacy rules, such as CCPA, ISO standards and NIST guidance, often struggle to see where their requirements align. The presenters propose gathering those requirements in one place using the NIST Privacy Framework, published in January 2020. Its core has five functions broken into categories and subcategories, implementation tiers describe how mature a practice should be without requiring the top tier, and profiles record current and target state.

The talk separates privacy risk, which concerns unintended consequences of data processing, from cybersecurity risk, which centres on confidentiality, integrity and availability. A worked example maps the inventory subcategories of the identify function against regulations and frameworks in a spreadsheet, with notes and gaps columns. The example organization's critical systems appear in a configuration management database but not all systems do, owner roles are undefined, legacy systems lack documented data actions, and cloud data locations are unknown. The advice is to start from what is known and prioritise gaps from there.

Attendees were encouraged to identify relevant regulations first, map them to the framework, document current practice over the following months, and then extend across all subcategories. Community crosswalks and templates were pointed to as starting material. The main takeaway is that writing down "none" is still useful, since it shows where work must begin.

talks.title: Extreme Makeover: Privacy Edition
talks.teaser: Panelists share practical advice on building, funding, and measuring a privacy program and working with security teams.
talks.summary:
Speakers focus on how privacy leaders can win support inside their organizations. They stress executive sponsorship, translating legal duties into product benefits through stories and peer benchmarks, and using a crisis to secure budget. Programs should not be copied wholesale; they should be sized to jurisdictions, data collected, team size and risk appetite, starting with the basics.

On working with security, the panel recommends close alliances, since security teams are usually larger and already run data inventories, incident response plans and review workflows that privacy can extend. One speaker described adding privacy checkpoints to an existing development lifecycle at a chipmaker. Another urged reusing the collaboration tools engineers already use. Formal titles such as privacy champion, backed by incentives, helped build a volunteer network of nearly 300. For measurement, speakers suggested counting assessments and turnaround times, and charting simple desk checks over time.

To sustain a program, the panel noted that compliance is ongoing as new laws arrive, so leaders should keep learning from peers. When building teams, they advised hiring diverse voices and people who already know the systems, and considering a privacy operations manager with program-management skills alongside lawyers.

talks.title: Taking Back Your Brand: New Techniques to Stop Robocallers
talks.teaser: Explains how tracebacks and call fingerprinting help trace illegal robocalls that impersonate trusted brands.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of robocalls in the United States, as counted by a call analytics company. Unwanted calls reached nearly 60 billion in 2019 and dipped in 2020 when pandemic-disrupted call centers went quiet, then passed 6 billion in March 2021 alone. Federal Trade Commission complaint data names phone calls as the top first contact for identity theft and fraud victims. Scams such as car warranty offers and COVID test-kit pitches show how fraudsters exploit news events.

The middle section explains detection and tracing. The company runs a sensor network built from its answering service users and carrier-integrated call data, tracks call volume per brand, and uses machine learning to cluster suspicious calls without listening to them. Audio fingerprints then match new calls against known fraud. The Industry Traceback Group, started by US Telecom, explains why spoofed caller ID is hard to trace: each call crosses many providers, and an automated process asks each one for its upstream source. Investigations that once took law enforcement two to three months now take roughly 24 to 48 hours. A new rule makes cooperation mandatory, and COVID-era campaigns led to more than 300 tracebacks and warning letters to gateway providers.

The closing advice targets brands. Organizations should check call-center complaints and the public directory for calls using their name, trace campaigns while volumes are still low, and have a monitoring plan within about six months. Consumers can install free call-blocking apps, and providers that cooperate with tracebacks often cut off the customers involved.

talks.title: Building a Global Cyber Rating - How to Objectively Rate Cyber Capabilities
talks.teaser: Outlines a blended methodology that merges five assessment styles into an ordinal global cyber rating for boards and risk leaders.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that no single cybersecurity assessment gives boards and risk officers a consistent, financially grounded view of enterprise posture. They walk through five existing approaches—outside-in scanning, management and maturity frameworks, inside-out technical posture, probabilistic loss models, and scenario stress testing—and explain why each is useful yet incomplete on its own.

They propose blending those views with validated data: external intelligence and scanning, self-attestation, API-driven control signals, and empirical tests that simulate adverse events. Jack Freund lays out a parsimonious modeling hierarchy from top-level methodology through rubrics, scaled scores, and raw metrics, emphasizing backtesting, documented assumptions, and model risk management discipline. Derek Vadala describes an eight-notch ordinal scale akin to credit ratings, supported by four rubrics—threat, governance, fortitude, and risk—with deeper decomposition tying business interruption, disclosure, and fraud scenarios to frameworks such as Basel II and MITRE ATT&CK, plus peer cohort benchmarking for loss materiality.

Practitioners are urged to contextualize vendor scores before board reporting, involve model validation specialists, and seek third-party review of risk models as the field matures beyond pure technical dashboards toward economic, benchmarked cyber ratings.

talks.title: A Case Study of the Capital One Data Breach
talks.teaser: Examines whether compliance controls and cybersecurity regulation could have prevented the 2019 Capital One data breach.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a research paper that asks whether compliance controls and cybersecurity legislation are enough to prevent a breach like the 2019 Capital One incident. The authors used MITRE ATT&CK to lay out each step of the intrusion, then mapped those steps to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework to find applicable controls at each stage. They describe a former Amazon employee who exploited a misconfigured web application firewall, used a server-side request forgery to reach internal credentials, and copied data from more than 700 S3 buckets.

Across the attack, the authors identified 61 potential NIST controls that could have prevented or detected it, and one stage alone had seven. Common gaps included weak vulnerability management, excessive privileges, and missing logging and monitoring. The regulator's review reached similar conclusions, citing weak risk assessment, internal audit failures, and poor reporting of known vulnerabilities to technical staff.

The speakers argue that regulatory flexibility can lead companies to drop important controls, and that risk management must stay consistent across the three lines of defense and extend to cloud environments. They also link the failure partly to human factors, including a leadership change and high staff turnover of 130 employees in 2018. Recommendations include reviewing audit and vulnerability processes, applying defense in depth and least privilege, monitoring compliance continuously, and aligning HR with security leadership.

talks.title: Using Threat Modeling to Improve Compliance
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Using Threat Modeling to Improve Compliance.

talks.title: Getting Cybersecurity Funding from Your CEO: the 5 Critical Steps
talks.teaser: Walks security leaders through five steps for winning budget approval from a CEO, from framing risk to ROI-ranked proposals.
talks.summary:
This session covers how security staff can secure funding from a chief executive. The speaker breaks the process into five steps: tailoring the message to the person who approves the budget, making two specific asks, running a risk tolerance meeting, ranking solutions by return on investment, and presenting the proposal. A central point is that cyber risk never reaches zero, so the goal is to agree with leadership on an acceptable level of risk and to transfer the remainder, for example through cyber insurance. Executives are encouraged to treat cyber risk like financial or legal risk.

The middle of the talk covers persuasion and preparation. The speaker suggests finding a colleague who already wins budget approvals, tying the request to a realistic breach example from the industry, and choosing timing carefully, such as after a scary incident in the sector rather than during downsizing. The first ask is to present a strategy for improving the security posture, and the second is to meet with peers in legal, finance, HR and operations to align on risk. In the risk meeting, the speaker recommends using scoring dashboards and framework comparisons, and presenting three options. Solutions are ranked by cost, necessity or urgency, overlapping or redundant controls, and estimated impact, with the lowest combined score ranked highest. Quick wins such as least privilege and removing unneeded sensitive data are presented as low-cost ways to cut risk.

The talk closes with a practical sequence: prepare the message, meet the CEO, meet other executives, test the pitch with a reviewer who thinks like the decision-maker, then present and follow up over the following months. The main takeaway is to speak in business terms, keep requests realistic, and show progress over time.

talks.title: FAIR Controls: A New Kind of Controls Framework
talks.teaser: Introduces FAIR-CAM to quantify control value by mapping anatomy-style frameworks to systemic control physiology and dependencies.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by asking which controls matter most and least, noting that security teams rarely agree or can justify those choices. Spending on risk reduction does not always buy proportional benefit because practitioners lack a shared way to see which levers to pull and in what order. Control value is defined as how much risk a control reduces, directly or indirectly, yet familiar catalogs from ISO, NIST, PCI, and CIS describe structure without explaining how controls work together.

A medical analogy separates anatomy (control lists) from physiology (how parts interact). Awareness training illustrates upstream dependencies on policy and risk appetite and downstream effects on authentication and phishing outcomes, including compensating controls. FAIR-CAM is presented as a model for reliable measurement and empirical validation, with loss event, decision, and variance control types and finer-grained functions such as avoidance, deterrence, resistance, visibility, monitoring, resilience, and loss reduction. Anti-phishing training is reframed as variance management that improves human resistive controls rather than a primary loss event control.

Practitioners are urged to map dependencies, accept mapping pain when legacy frameworks blend functions, and await a fuller white paper on ontologies, defense-in-depth measurement, human behavior, and framework alignment. The takeaway is that investment and retirement decisions need systemic physiology, not intuition alone.

talks.title: Ten Things to Include in Remote Work IT Risk Assessments
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Ten Things to Include in Remote Work IT Risk Assessments.

talks.title: When Your Dashboard Explodes - Do You Care Enough to Send the Very Best?
talks.teaser: A security leader recounts dashboard failures, patching fallout, and restoring trustworthy phishing metrics after vendor and cloud issues.
talks.summary:
The presentation uses a real program turnaround rather than generic metric theory. After a NIST Cybersecurity Framework self-assessment framed a multi-year roadmap, the speaker rebuilt neglected foundations—SIEM, outsourced SOC accountability, EDR currency, and authenticated vulnerability scanning—before tying executive attention to business-relevant risk and trust-building moves such as tailored awareness, insurance conversations, and ISAC peer sharing.

Dashboard design followed audit and framework pillars for board audiences, including a cyber-versus-human health narrative to avoid jargon. A first publication of patching metrics damaged collaboration with infrastructure until reports were shared early and rollouts were staged. Phishing visibility expanded to directors and bonuses hinged on a 3% peer benchmark, yet failure rates kept climbing until internal testing showed Microsoft 365 sandboxing and vendor integration problems skewing results.

The program paused reporting and testing for two months, adopted an email-gateway-aligned phishing platform, led with short interactive training, and saw sub-1% failures on the first campaign. Practitioners are urged to validate dashboard inputs, review safelisting and blocking rules monthly as SaaS changes, confirm executive understanding of security value, align dashboards to their chosen framework within six months, and balance awareness incentives beyond failure reporting.

talks.title: DBOM and SBOM: New Options For Better Supply Chain Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Panelists explain how SBOMs and Digital Bills of Materials can help teams track software supply chain risk.
talks.summary:
Moderator Mark Weatherford led a panel with Jennifer Bisceglie, Chris Blask and Tom Alrich on how supply chain risk management has changed, and how software bills of materials relate to a Digital Bill of Materials. The panelists tied the shift to recent disruptions, including the pandemic, the SolarWinds attack and shipping blockages, which pushed supply chain exposure into board-level discussion. Bisceglie cited a survey of about 500 professionals in which only 2% looked beyond their tier-one suppliers.

Alrich described an SBOM as a machine-readable list of the components in a software product, noting that an average product contains over a hundred components. He said adoption is stalled by a chicken-and-egg problem, since developers already generate SBOMs but customers rarely request them. He pointed to NTIA proofs of concept in healthcare, with electric power and other industries following, and argued that the fear that SBOMs help attackers is weak because attackers can build their own inventories. Blask presented the Digital Bill of Materials as a set of attestations about a product or artifact, shared through defined channels, and described an open-source node code project under a Linux Foundation consortium.

Bisceglie explained how AI-driven mapping can surface risk in lower-tier suppliers in near real time, and the panel expected upcoming executive orders to address breach notification and software transparency. For practitioners, the message was to inventory components and suppliers, move from emailed spreadsheets to automated and shared attestations, and consider joining NTIA's software transparency work groups, which meet weekly.

talks.title: How Risky Is Cybersecurity Insurance?
talks.teaser: Examines how cyber insurance pricing, ransomware coverage and underwriting questions shape security spending and incident response.
talks.summary:
The session treats cyber insurance as a business risk decision that security teams should help shape. The speakers explain that policy prices move like a market, that costs differ widely by company size, and that buying coverage never reduces the security work a program still has to do. They also note that after NotPetya many insurers stopped covering ransomware under traditional property and casualty policies, so it now often needs a separate rider.

The middle of the talk covers the practical traps. Answers given during underwriting must be accurate, because an inaccurate answer can lead to denied coverage or denied payment after an incident. During a ransomware event, insurer investigators and payment compliance experts join the response, and their priorities, including sanctions checks with the Treasury's OFAC, may differ from the company's.

Two cases are walked through. A small company with a phishing-driven exposure of 28,000 customer records chose not to claim on its $2 million policy, estimating a fix of about 125K for a mailbox forwarding gap and about 250K for two-factor authentication. Baltimore's 2019 ransomware attack, which the city estimated cost about $20 million, led it to buy a policy, and its premium rose to $950,000 the following year. The closing advice is to learn existing coverages early, run tabletop exercises with executives and the insurer's team, and make payback arguments for preventive controls, since insurance fits uncommon events rather than everyday gaps.

talks.title: Through the Zoom Dimly: A Year of Remote Audits
talks.teaser: Explores how independent auditors adapted PCI, ISO, and FedRAMP assessments for remote work and which lessons persist post-pandemic.
talks.summary:
Jacob Ansari, CISO at an independent audit firm, describes how COVID-19 forced continued security assessments without onsite travel. Standards bodies such as PCI SSC, ISO frameworks, and A2LA largely issued remote-work guidance, often requiring documented exceptions or equivalent assurance to onsite visits.

Remote practice shifted interviews to web conferencing, made some PCI cryptographic and PIN workflows nearly impossible on video, and often reduced efficiency despite travel savings. Teams saw Zoom fatigue, scheduling pain across time zones, and unprepared clients delaying evidence. Physical controls sometimes worked well via mobile walkthroughs or pre-recorded facility tours, though a minority of colocation sites refused video and left gaps in reports. Rare onsite visits targeted key-injection facilities with careful risk selection for staff.

The speaker frames durable evidence needs around authenticity, currency, and completeness, warning against incremental patchwork submissions and stale screenshots. Pilots before large evidence pulls, explicit scheduling strategies, and tracking how long artifacts remain valid matter more when projects stretch. Most frameworks may return onsite, but shorter visits plus more remote technical review align with distributed work and cloud operations. Clients and auditors should plan early, maintain ongoing compliance cadence instead of pre-audit cramming, and negotiate what truly requires physical presence.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Controls: It Isn't Just Technical Controls That Need Testing
talks.teaser: Shows how to test whether security controls and their response workflows still work as designed.
talks.summary:
Glauco Sampaio argues that security teams run many tests, such as application scans, vulnerability scans and penetration tests, but these do not show whether controls keep working over time. Environments and attacks keep changing, and audits often flag controls that were fixed long ago but have quietly stopped working. Change management cannot catch every disabled control.

He illustrates the approach with five tests that check the full response process, not just the control. A data loss prevention rule blocking card numbers in email should block the message, open a ticket, get analyst action within four hours and notify the sender's manager. Creating an Active Directory account outside the identity team should lead to blocking, creator notification and handling within eight hours. Adding a user to Domain Admins should disable that user and open a ticket. VPN use from a non-corporate machine should block the user and IP address, and disabling endpoint protection should make the SOAR quarantine the machine. Each test also confirms that logs reach the SIEM.

For a start, he suggests a two-week plan. In week one, map controls protecting the crown jewels, favoring ones that are easy to test, drawing on red team input and past audit reports. In week two, choose three to five scenarios, define the expected end-to-end response, run the tests, fix gaps and retest. Share results with the technical team before management, then formalize a prioritized, recurring routine, automated where possible. He notes staff time is scarce and that breach-and-attack simulation tools help but do not fully cover process testing.

talks.title: Three’s Company: Unpacking and Settling in with Three NIST Frameworks
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Three’s Company: Unpacking and Settling in with Three NIST Frameworks.

talks.title: Empowering Hybrid Workforce With Security-driven Networking For All Edges
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Empowering Hybrid Workforce With Security-driven Networking For All Edges.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Nirav Shah, Vice President of Product and Solution at Fortinet, addresses the networking and cybersecurity challenges created by the expansion of the hybrid workforce, multi-cloud adoption, and edge computing. As users shift between remote environments and office locations, traditional hub-and-spoke network architectures—which route traffic back through central data centers via VPNs—introduce security gaps and degrade user experience. Shah advocates for Security-driven Networking and the convergence of security and networking through a unified Secure Access Services Edge (SASE) platform to secure all edges without compromising application performance.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Workforce and Infrastructure Shifts**: The widespread adoption of multi-cloud strategies (over 93% of surveyed customers) and enduring remote work models (IDC reporting over 72% maintaining a hybrid workforce) demand a departure from legacy centralized data center backhauling.
- **Limitations of Legacy Architecture**: Routing remote traffic through legacy VPNs into a data center causes latency, poor user experience (reported by over 70% of organizations), and prompts users to bypass corporate controls to access SaaS applications directly.
- **Explosion of Edges**: The definition of the network edge has transformed from traditional branches and campuses to home offices, mobile environments, IoT devices, and 5G connectivity, resulting in fragmented point products and operational silos.
- **Three Pillars of Security Posture**: Organizations must converge networking and security around three core foundations: Security-driven Networking (incorporating SD-WAN and SD-branch), Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA), and Adaptive Cloud Security.
- **Convergence via SASE and Platform Approach**: Shifting from disconnected point tools to an integrated cybersecurity mesh platform (such as Fortinet's Security Fabric) delivering cloud-delivered security services alongside organically developed SD-WAN.

### Technical Details
- **Threat Landscape and Performance**: Threat actors are executing increasingly sophisticated campaigns (e.g., SolarWinds, deep delivery mechanisms, and command-and-control infrastructures). Shah notes FortiGuard Labs blocks over five million web attacks every minute. Defending against these threats requires purpose-built security processors capable of deep packet and security inspection without creating network bottlenecks.
- **Cloud-Delivered SASE and Edge Controls**: SASE consolidates Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW), Secure Web Gateway (SWG), Intrusion Prevention Systems (IPS), Application Control, Sandboxing, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP) into cloud-delivered security as a service.
- **Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)**: ZTNA replaces the broad, implicit network access granted by traditional VPNs with explicit, per-session, application-level verification managed by edge- or cloud-based access proxies. Access decisions factor in user role and context (e.g., preventing an HR employee in Singapore from accessing finance systems without appropriate permissions).
- **Thin Edge Deployment and AIOps**: Branch offices can deploy "thin edges" using SD-WAN and 5G connectivity to offload heavy security inspection to the cloud while maintaining local segmentation on the LAN. Artificial Intelligence for Network Operations (AIOps) provides event correlation, predictive analytics, and Digital Experience Monitoring (DEM) to evaluate end-to-end performance.

### Takeaways
Shah recommends an actionable timeline for enterprise transformation:
1. **Immediate (Next Week)**: Establish cross-functional teams unifying networking and security personnel to dismantle operational silos.
2. **Months 1–3**: Define a comprehensive SASE strategy with measurable milestones and begin replacing legacy VPN connections with ZTNA access proxies.
3. **12+ Months**: Consolidate branch and remote architectures using unified SD-WAN and cloud-delivered security, maintaining open integrations (such as APIs, cloud connectors, and ITSM tools) to preserve existing infrastructure investments while continuously monitoring end-to-end user experience.

talks.title: OODA Looping in a Turbulent World
talks.teaser: Applies Boyd's OODA loop to cyber defense, using COVID-themed threats and SolarWinds to show why orient and decide must precede action.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes Colonel John Boyd's observe-orient-dececide-act cycle, originally developed for fighter pilots, as a practical mental model for network defenders. Ryan Kovar argues that many blue teams rush from alerts or headlines straight to action, and that slowing down to orient and decide yields better outcomes. He maps observe to telemetry, news, and peer reporting; orient to exposure analysis, tooling pivots, and risk conversations; decide to IOC strategy, user education, and leadership buy-in; and act to concrete technical and procedural changes.

Two headline-driven case studies illustrate the loop. For early COVID-era abuse, he traces malicious domains and coronavirus-themed lures, DNS and domain-intelligence research, email hunting ideas, and balancing blocks with business risk appetite. For the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, he covers learning from public blogs and government alerts, hunting with shared indicators in internal data, assessing software dependencies, questioning vendors, aligning with compliance mandates, and iterating after initial response.

The closing theme ties defender improvement to adversary cost: share intelligence, burn infrastructure, and accept daily failure while documenting 30-, 60-, and 90-day reviews so each cycle fails a little less. He encourages combining OODA with frameworks such as the Lockheed Martin kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK only where context fits, and using past incidents as repeatable practice rather than one-off heroics.

talks.title: Zero Trust and Privacy: Moving Security Closer to the Target
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Zero Trust and Privacy: Moving Security Closer to the Target.

talks.title: Enemy Inside the Gates: Securing the New Battleground
talks.teaser: Explains how segmentation, behavior-based network detection and endpoint context can catch attackers moving inside a data center.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the assumption that attackers will eventually get past the perimeter, so the damage depends on what they can do inside. It cites a credit rating agency breach in which attackers made 48 lateral movements over nine months, and argues that east-west controls within the data center matter more than a strong perimeter alone. Traditional firewalls were built for a physical perimeter and have little context for internal traffic that has to pass through them.

The speakers describe a layered approach: segmentation to block obviously bad paths, distributed layer-7 aware signature inspection of traffic, and behavior-based network detection. The detection portion uses unsupervised learning to establish a baseline and supervised models trained on large volumes of analyzed threats to separate harmful anomalies from benign ones. Individual suspicious events are then correlated over time and across hosts into intrusions mapped to the kill chain, which sharply reduces what analysts must review. For encrypted traffic, they outline metadata-based analysis, decryption, and guest introspection that pulls decrypted files out of virtual machines for malware analysis, arguing this works regardless of protocol.

The closing takeaway is to combine endpoint and network context. A sensor inserted from the hypervisor can tell the network layer which processes are running, so an unexpected process requesting bulk data from an app server stands out. The speakers present this combined approach as XDR and stress that machine learning needs enough high-quality data to be effective.

talks.title: Zero Trust, Zero Pain: A Practical Implementation with Intrinsic Security
talks.teaser: Lays out how device posture, user identity, network transport and cloud workloads combine into one end-to-end zero trust design.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue the traditional perimeter has dissolved. Applications have moved from single three-tier servers to microservices, containers and several public clouds, while staff use corporate and personal devices from many locations. That spread adds openings for phishing, credential theft, endpoint compromise and misconfigured cloud storage, and remote access VPNs have drawn more attacks since remote work grew. Their answer is to stop trusting devices, networks or users by default and verify each one.

The middle section treats user identity and device posture as inputs to access policy. Device checks can include how recent the operating system is, missing patches for actively exploited flaws, host firewall status and disk encryption. Identity controls cover multifactor authentication, single sign-on, federation and hardware security keys, with stricter rules for sensitive systems such as HR or finance. Decisions may also weigh group membership, role, location and country, and signals like repeated failed logins can raise a user's risk level. Responses range from notifying users to automatically enabling a firewall or applying patches on managed devices. On the network side, per-application tunnels replace device-wide VPNs, east-west segmentation limits lateral movement, and layer 7 inspection and endpoint telemetry feed a shared analytics plane.

The closing point is that no single vendor delivers zero trust, so components must share threat data and standard interfaces to drive automated responses. Practitioners should correlate signals across identity, device, network and application layers rather than manage each separately, and expect the move to take time.

talks.title: How to Ruin your SOC in 5 Easy Steps
talks.teaser: Lays out five common ways security operations centers fall short, from SIEM-only visibility to analyst burnout.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out five ways a security operations center can be weakened, framed as pitfalls that even well-funded, mature teams fall into. The first is stopping at the SIEM. Logs show only the past, so the speaker argues for network traffic monitoring, covering north-south and east-west flows, plus endpoint data showing which processes are running. Together these sources underpin extended detection and response.

The next pitfalls concern people and process. Analysts lose working memory during an incident, and a story about a CISO with thick binders of response steps shows why runbooks should be online and kept current. Orchestration and SOAR tie these together. Automation helps with timed escalation, but automated infrastructure changes such as firewall updates or privilege removal need dependency mapping first, and earlier robotic process automation projects offer useful lessons. Threat intelligence platforms should be built into this workflow. Machine learning analytics, ideally delivered as SaaS so models stay current, can surface outliers in large data volumes. One bank had stopped monitoring part of its network because the data flood overwhelmed it.

The final pitfalls involve staffing. Job rotations let promising junior analysts shadow senior ones, senior staff can be recognized as mentors, and regular reviews with an MSSP help transfer skills. Security awareness should treat all employees as extended team members. The closing advice is to inventory existing visibility tools, verify runbooks, define metrics, adopt analytics, and watch for gradual burnout.

talks.title: Transformation of the Digital Leader
talks.teaser: Traces how CIO and CISO roles have shifted and offers case studies on linking technology transformation to business value.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of the CIO and CISO roles, from the 1980s, when the CIO title was new and often tied to mainframe work, to the first CISO at Citibank in 1994, hired after a major breach. The speaker argues that the CISO was often a compliance function buried in infrastructure, and that organizations now add roles such as chief data officer alongside the CIO. Security budgets, which grew freely after a wave of breaches, are shrinking as companies look for measurable business value. The walled-garden data center is giving way to cloud and zero-trust tools, and security teams need people skilled in cloud and container work.

The middle of the talk is a case study of Tencent and WeChat. Tencent moved its PC messaging product to mobile, reached 100 million users in one year, and then used virtual red envelopes to launch payments, reporting 16 million transactions and 5 million new bank accounts. The app then grew into a platform for ride-hailing, doctor bookings, news, and wealth management. The speaker links failed transformations to treating cloud migration as the goal rather than a business outcome, and draws on a Gartner model of systems of record, differentiation and innovation. Remote work during the pandemic, IoT risk, and supply chain disruption, including the SolarWinds attack and overloaded third-party VPNs, are also covered.

For practitioners, the talk recommends getting the technology organization in order first, retraining staff, and expecting early failures on the way to cloud-native operations. Vulnerability management can shrink when cloud images are patched and replaced rather than repaired in place. Leaders should frame security work in business terms, understand P&L and cash flow, and focus on speed and flexibility.

talks.title: Getting Started With SASE: Connect, Control and Converge With Confidence
talks.teaser: A crash course on secure access service edge covers workforce trends, architecture building blocks, and practical rollout guidance.
talks.summary:
Distributed work and multi-cloud adoption have shifted the network edge from the data center to the user, breaking the old model of MPLS backhaul and centralized security stacks. Direct internet access improves performance but opens policy gaps, inconsistent controls, and weaker identity assurance when protection no longer sits in one place.

The presentation defines Secure Access Service Edge as Gartner’s cloud-delivered blend of SD-WAN, firewall-as-a-service, secure web gateway, CASB, and ZTNA, framed around connect, control, and converge. It walks through cloud-edge placement, security layers from DNS and SWG through DLP and workload protection, continuous zero-trust session checks, and observability from user to application. Two anchor use cases are secure remote workers and securing WAN edge locations at scale.

Practitioners hear five adoption tips—integrated architecture, flexible consumption, cloud quality, security efficacy including threat intelligence and XDR ties, and phased “your way” migration with hybrid and investment protection—plus pitfalls such as shallow multi-vendor stitching.
