Closing steps urge cross-team scoping, complexity review, vendor research, and a realistic project timeline.

talks.title: Web Attacks and Fraud: Lessons Learned from the Deep End of the Pool
talks.teaser: Panelists trace the shift from web flaws to credential stuffing and bot attacks, and what defenders can do.
talks.summary:
The panel, moderated by Lori MacVittie, features Sara Boddy and Dan woods discussing how web attacks have shifted. They separate inadvertent vulnerabilities, such as misconfigurations and classic injection bugs that can be patched, from inherent ones, where attackers abuse legitimate features like login and account recovery. The panelists say breaches moved from web application flaws to access attacks around 2018, with credential stuffing now the leading attack type.

Woods describes automated attackers evolving from simple tools that replay browser network traffic, which a JavaScript challenge can stop, to headless browsers and finally human click farms. Blocking on attributes such as IP address or user agent only pushes attackers to retool. On two-factor authentication, he argues that SMS and email codes add friction and can be bypassed through SIM swaps, and that differing login error messages can reveal valid credentials before the second factor appears. Captchas are presented as solvable by paid human workers, so the panel favors continuous authentication based on device, network and behavioral signals.

For defenders, Woods recommends a real-time first stage using rich signals, plus a retrospective second stage that analyzes aggregate transactions to catch retooled attacks. Mitigations should not signal detection to the attacker. Organizations should map which public applications, including employee and partner logins, face unwanted automation, and recognize that much traffic comes from a long tail of addresses. Boddy urges zero trust, automation at scale and secure coding, and both close by recommending password managers.

talks.title: Learning from the Enemy: A Look Inside the Techniques of Ocean Lotus /APT32
talks.teaser: Shows how OceanLotus-style Office documents run fileless command and control on both Windows and macOS.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at fileless attacks, which avoid writing new executables to disk and so tend to slip past antivirus scanning. The speaker frames them as document-based intrusions that begin with social engineering: a user is persuaded to open an attachment and click past the application's security warning, after which an embedded script sets up command and control. The talk then focuses on techniques attributed to the OceanLotus group, also known as APT32.

The first demonstration uses Microsoft Word's Dynamic Data Exchange feature. A field in a resume-style document launches a PowerShell command that downloads a client from a web server and runs it in memory, while a built-in error dialog is edited so the prompt looks legitimate. The second uses a macro-enabled document whose malicious commands are base64 encoded and stored in the document's company and comments properties, so the macro itself contains no obvious URLs or suspicious strings. The same file is shown targeting both Windows and macOS, with a Python client on the Mac, and a disguised iTunes sign-in prompt is used to collect a user's password.

The closing section argues that defenders should run fileless attack simulations, use policy to restrict macros and DDE, and watch PowerShell and script activity rather than relying only on on-disk malware detection. Ongoing user education and regular retesting of controls are presented as the practical takeaways.

talks.title: Better Call Brussels - News on European Cyber Security and eID Regulation
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Better Call Brussels - News on European Cyber Security and eID Regulation.

talks.title: Blind Spots: Two Cloud Threats You Didn’t Even Know You Had
talks.teaser: Covers cloud IAM and infrastructure-as-code misconfigurations that hide risk, using a red team case and template survey data.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that two cloud areas are often overlooked: identity and access management, and the infrastructure-as-code templates that provision cloud environments. The speaker explains that once an organization has hundreds of roles and policies across several accounts, it becomes hard to know what a given user can actually do. He then describes a red team engagement against a large SaaS provider's cloud environment. Starting from a separate account and publicly available information found through search engines and code repositories, the team enumerated configurations for several days until it obtained a temporary access token. A misconfigured role trust policy then exposed instance metadata and internal storage buckets, and a key management call let the team decrypt credentials that could have enabled a supply chain attack.

To test how widespread such problems are, the team gathered public files and repositories from GitHub, extracted role names and cloud account identifiers, validated the accounts, and tried a shortlist of 500 frequent role names. A separate survey of almost a million infrastructure-as-code templates reported that 42% of CloudFormation templates had at least one insecure configuration, 76% exposed sensitive ports such as SSH, and 60% had storage logging disabled. About 22% of the surveyed Terraform files contained at least one insecure setting.

The speaker's recommendations span the whole lifecycle. Teams should first build deep, multi-cloud visibility, then add automated guardrails that detect anti-patterns and correct them without waiting for a ticket. Security should be scanned in templates, containers and registries before deployment, with builds broken for critical or high findings. Runtime protection through workload agents and cloud APIs was presented as the remaining necessary layer.

talks.title: Zero Trust in a Post-pandemic World
talks.teaser: Two Microsoft executives discuss Zero Trust, remote-work security, and how automation can ease SOC workloads.
talks.summary:
Microsoft executives Rob Lefferts and Bret Arsenault talk through how Zero Trust shapes their security strategy and how the shift to remote work tested it. Zero Trust starts from an assumed-breach position and rests on healthy devices, strong identity and persistent telemetry, with identity treated as the new perimeter. Arsenault describes cutting the number of suppliers to reduce complexity, and consolidating a sprawl of more than six tools into a smaller set his team values most.

They recall that an early smart-card two-factor rollout met resistance, while moving toward passwordless sign-in with facial recognition and telemetry feedback worked better. Giving staff choices, such as bring-your-own devices or virtualized access on unmanaged home PCs, helped enforce device health without an uprising. When the company went from roughly 10% to 97% remote within 72 hours, VPN capacity needed to grow by less than 5%. They expect people to work from more distant locations, which will complicate what counts as normal behavior for anomaly detection.

The closing advice is to automate the find and then the fix, while expecting early automation to produce benign positives that need tuning. They describe augmented intelligence in the SOC as a way to keep analysts effective rather than replacing them. For basics, they point out that under 20% of enterprises have full multi-factor authentication and that more than 60% of breaches involve patches that were available but never applied, so progress matters more than perfection.

talks.title: Total Security: Investigative Perspectives from Public to Private Sector
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Total Security: Investigative Perspectives from Public to Private Sector.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this panel session, three former federal investigators—Shawn Henry (President of CrowdStrike Services and CSO of CrowdStrike), CJ Moses (Deputy CISO at AWS), and Mary Galligan (Managing Director at Deloitte)—discuss the evolution of the cybersecurity landscape and how their public-sector investigative experience applies to private-sector security practices. They reflect on the transition from handling website defacements and denial-of-service attacks in the early 2000s to managing modern threats like ransomware, destructive malware (such as NotPetya), critical infrastructure intrusions, and software supply chain attacks. The discussion highlights the necessity of viewing security through a comprehensive 'total security' model covering physical, personnel, and operational attack surfaces.

### Key Topics
- **Cultural Differences and Actionable Threat Intelligence**: In the federal government, awareness of nation-state adversaries and cross-agency intelligence sharing were standard operational procedure. In the private sector, organizations historically struggled to acknowledge nation-state threats or view intelligence as directly actionable. Translating threat intelligence into operational actions—such as dynamic patching and business risk prioritization—fosters an organizational culture where business owners take active ownership of security.
- **Risk Communication and Business Impact**: Communicating security risk to boards and C-suite executives requires translating threats into business impact. Emphasizing resilience and operational disruption (e.g., inability to produce products or service clients) engages leadership more effectively than purely technical metrics.
- **Attribution as a Defensive Strategy**: While some in the private sector historically questioned the necessity of threat actor attribution, understanding the human adversary behind an attack provides vital context regarding motivation, capabilities, and toolsets. Attribution enables organizations to be proactive rather than merely reactive, illustrated by historical patterns such as Iranian DDoS campaigns against the financial services sector following U.S. sanctions.
- **The Total Security Framework and the 360-Degree Attack Surface**: The role of a CISO extends beyond traditional IT boundaries. True security governance requires stewarding across data center physical security, operational technologies, personnel, and the software supply chain.
- **Managing Insider Threats**: Employees typically fall into three insider risk profiles: ignorant (unaware of policies), indifferent (circumventing rules for convenience or speed), and malicious (willfully exfiltrating data or tampering with systems). Addressing these risks requires holistic organizational coordination across Human Resources, legal, and operational leadership beyond standard phishing training.

### Technical Details
- **Software Supply Chain Defense**: To counter self-upgrading threats and third-party code risks within CI/CD and DevOps pipelines, organizations must employ defense-in-depth mechanisms, including structured code reviews, fuzz testing, and behavioral monitoring. CJ Moses highlights that AWS deploys CrowdStrike Falcon on edge devices to monitor for communication aberrations between systems.
- **Least Privilege and Access Controls**: Limiting exposure across both insider and supply chain attack vectors involves moving toward continuous authorization and just-in-time (JIT) access, granting minimal access based on strict parameter sets for limited durations before revoking them.

### Takeaways
- Organizations must dismantle silos across business, legal, HR, and technical teams to manage risks effectively.
- Collaboration and intelligence sharing across industry peers (such as ISACs and ISAOs) and with government entities remain essential to counter common advanced persistent threats, as demonstrated historically by multi-agency efforts like the Moonlight Maze investigation.

talks.title: Adapt to the New, Unstable Normal: How to Secure the Roaring 2020s
talks.teaser: Maps five pandemic-driven shifts across the decade and the security work each one will demand from practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk looks ahead across the 2020s, arguing that changes forced by the pandemic, such as remote work and digital-first services, will persist and reshape business and technology. The speaker organizes the argument around five shifts, each assessed over three timeframes: the next 18 months, the period through about five years, and the longer remainder of the decade.

The shifts cover customer expectations that balance safety and convenience, hybrid digital-physical experiences, the future of work, retiring technical debt, and business resilience becoming a competitive advantage. For each one, the speaker outlines how it is likely to develop and what security and privacy teams should do. Examples include securing contactless experiences such as car keys delivered by drone, adjusting fraud controls for customers new to digital channels, rebuilding insider threat detection models for hybrid staff, replacing ad hoc remote access tools with permanent ones, and widening risk management to cover supply chain visibility and business continuity.

The closing recommendations are short-term actions: secure no-touch experiences, review QR code payment risks, align return-to-office plans with privacy rules, harden remote work tooling so it can fall back to fully remote, retire redundant security products, and invest in cloud security. The talk ends by urging attendees to use the disruption as a chance to fix gaps that were neglected for years.

talks.title: A Year of Living Dangerously: Resilience After COVID & Killer Hornets
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning A Year of Living Dangerously: Resilience After COVID & Killer Hornets.

talks.title: COVID Contact Tracing Apps: Balancing Privacy, Security, and Health
talks.teaser: Examines legal, ethical and technical trade-offs of COVID-19 contact tracing apps, with Switzerland's app as a case study.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why digital contact tracing became a tool during the COVID-19 pandemic, since the virus often spread before symptoms appeared and no proven treatments existed. The speakers recall that manual contact tracing in the US dates back to the 1920s and that confidentiality mattered in earlier outbreaks such as syphilis and HIV, where stigma and prosecution were real risks. They frame the ethical questions a deployer must weigh: public health impact, less invasive alternatives, uptake, access for people without smartphones, discrimination, transparency and data minimization.

The legal section covers GDPR principles such as data minimization, purpose limitation and retention limits, and contrasts them with the US patchwork of sector laws, state privacy laws and biometric statutes. It also raises workplace and anti-discrimination issues for employers. On the technical side, location data is described as highly sensitive, while Bluetooth proximity tracking is presented as easier to anonymize. The talk compares centralized and decentralized storage, mandatory and voluntary participation, and the shared Google and Apple API.

The Swiss case study reports 2.36 million downloads between May 25 and September 10, with active users estimated at 18.9% of the population. Of 12,000 confirmed cases, 7,800 people who disclosed their testing reason cited the app, and 41 of them tested positive. The speakers conclude that effectiveness depends on testing, accurate quarantine and rapid notification, and that privacy protections help build trust and uptake. They note that published data on effectiveness and real-world uptake remains limited.

talks.title: A "Great Equalizer", Until it Isn't: Regional Security in a Global Pandemic
talks.teaser: Explores how infrastructure and resources in different regions shaped enterprise security during the 2020 pandemic.
talks.summary:
Allie Mellen of Forrester and Kerissa Varma, group chief information security officer at a large African insurer, argue that the same pandemic was lived very differently depending on where an organisation and its staff sat. Varma opens with a contrast between fibre-connected homes and crowded informal settlements in South Africa, where remote work, home quarantine and schooling were far harder for some families. Mellen notes that 40% of enterprises surveyed had no business continuity plan before the pandemic, and describes security teams in the US and UK being pulled into IT work such as admin privilege decisions.

Varma describes African teams watching the outbreak elsewhere, learning from it and acting early. Kenya and South Africa imposed full lockdowns before their first deaths. She cites Zimbabwe, which faced 680% annual inflation in March 2020 and two to three days without power in homes, as a case where several crises overlapped. Supply strain followed, since many technology partners sat abroad, so teams bought laptops in Kenya to send to Zimbabwe. Varma also noted that remote incident response, once chaotic, may become the model that sticks.

The closing takeaways are that crises can coincide, so teams should consider combined scenarios such as a breach during a power outage; that supplier risk reaches suppliers' own suppliers; and that no plan covers everything, so resilience depends on adaptable people. The speakers also flag a skills gap, citing a 40% drop since 2015 in secondary pupils taking IT subjects at GCSE.

talks.title: End the Battle Between Security and Productivity
talks.teaser: Explains how Zero Trust choices can cut employee friction and strengthen security, with survey data and practical next steps.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how security controls can slow employees down and how a Zero Trust approach can reduce that friction while protecting enterprise data. The presenters, both Forrester researchers, define employee experience as the sum of an employee's perceptions at work. Their Employee Experience Index research found that about 30% of engagement drivers were technology-related, and that data was gathered before the pandemic.

Survey results link security to engagement. 89% of the most engaged employees were satisfied with company security policies, versus 25% of the least engaged. Reasons for bypassing policies included outside collaboration (34%), efficiency (33%) and strict or unreasonable policies (31%), and 10% said they would bypass a policy if they knew how. Security policies ranked tenth among predictors of burnout. The speakers recapped the 2009 Zero Trust principles: trust identity rather than network location, enforce least privilege, and assume breach.

Practical examples included replacing full VPN tunnels for remote staff with zero trust network access and a cloud secure web gateway, and moving toward passwordless authentication to cut password fatigue. For endpoints, the speakers suggested managing devices through cloud APIs instead of domain joins and VPN patching, and reducing overlapping security agents that slow workstations. First steps over the next 60 to 90 days include inventorying device agents and collecting employee feedback on controls that block work.

talks.title: Hacker’s Paradise: Top 10 Biggest Threats When Working From Home
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Hacker’s Paradise: Top 10 Biggest Threats When Working From Home.

talks.title: Lessons Learned From Taking Justice Remote During the COVID Pandemic
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Lessons Learned From Taking Justice Remote During the COVID Pandemic.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Jack McCarthy (CIO of the New Jersey Courts) and Sajed discuss how the New Jersey Judiciary transitioned from an almost entirely in-person court system across roughly 700 sites to a remote virtual court system on just three days of notice during the COVID-19 pandemic. Operating under a unified statewide judiciary serving 7 million residents, 13,000 staff, 100,000 attorneys, and 40,000 police officers, the IT department drew on years of prior technical planning and security policies to support remote judicial proceedings securely and rapidly.

### Key Topics
- **Threat Trends During the Pandemic:** As remote operations escalated, the team tracked surging threats communicated via MS-ISAC and Homeland Security, such as Zoom bombing, phishing campaigns weaponizing COVID-19 lures (showing up to a 4,000% increase in related domains), targeted regional lures, and major supply-chain events like SolarWinds.
- **Rapid Operational Pivot:** Moving from 1% remote work in February 2020 to near 100% remote within days. Because the judiciary only had 2,500 laptops and iPads for 13,000 staff, they allowed employees to take pre-encrypted desktop PCs home as large portable machines.
- **Application Continuity:** To maintain courthouse filings and payments, IT launched the Judiciary Electronic Document Submission (JEDS) system in three days to handle filings and fee collections electronically.
- **Scaling Remote Infrastructure:** Upgrading remote access from a few hundred concurrent connections to thousands via physical servers and cloud bursting into AWS. Transitioning from Skype to Microsoft Teams for 10,000 users in one day, and expanding Zoom to host over 400 court sessions concurrently.
- **Security Posture & Enforcement:** Upholding pre-existing baseline policies—such as mandatory two-factor authentication, device full-disk encryption, and network access control (NAC)—rather than compromising controls during the crisis.

### Technical Details
- **Data Center & Network Topology:** The court operates a hub-and-spoke model terminating in Trenton, reinforced with triangular redundancy across multiple platforms and quarterly disaster recovery failover exercises. Legacy infrastructure spans mainframes, COBOL, .NET, Java, and Pega BPM software.
- **Remote Access Architecture:**
  - **VDI:** Scaled VMware VDI from 100 concurrent sessions to 1,500 (averaging ~1,450 daily), while also utilizing VDI for secure public access terminals.
  - **VPN Capacity:** Scaled on-premises VPN appliances up to 7,500 connections before establishing a secure VPN infrastructure directly in AWS within a week.
  - **Posture & Access Controls:** Implemented Zscaler for endpoint posture assessment prior to connection, blocked risky ports (such as RDP and SMB) exposed to threats like BlueKeep and DejaBlue, and enforced network access controls to automatically patch delinquent systems and block unauthorized external Windows PCs or untrusted IoT devices.
- **Platform Migrations:** Migrated 10,000 staff to Microsoft Teams in a single weekend to offload roughly 10,000 weekly administrative meetings away from the core on-prem data center.

### Takeaways
- **Security Must Precede the Crisis:** Quick emergency response was only possible because essential controls—full-disk encryption, MFA, and asset visibility—were already established before the pandemic.
- **Virtual Court Viability:** The judiciary conducted over 250,000 remote court events with 2.5 million participants in a single year, proving that routine dockets, conferences, and uncontested matters can be resolved remotely without demanding in-person courthouse appearances.
- **Future Model:** The judiciary expects a lasting hybrid model (approximately 60% in-office and 40% remote), moving toward a Zero Trust security architecture and reimagining traditional court procedures permanently.

talks.title: A Punch to the Supply Chain: Fighting Back to Resilience
talks.teaser: Executives discuss mapping fourth- and fifth-party supply chain risk and using scenario planning to build operational resilience.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with how resilience relates to security. The panelists argue that reliance on cloud platforms and layered third-party ecosystems adds opacity, and that operational resilience, keeping business running through major disruptions, should become the central goal. They point to challenges such as converging IT and OT, and to the need for flexible controls instead of one monolithic approach.

Discussion then turns to visibility beyond direct suppliers. The moderator cited a study in which only 2% of 450 executives asked about second- or third-tier suppliers. Suggested practices include mapping business processes and multi-tier relationships, monitoring them over time, modeling scenarios and running tabletop exercises, with operational tests reserved for critical risks. Controls should follow activities rather than people or locations, and the same framework should be applied internally as well as to suppliers.

On the cloud, one panelist described a shift from a shared responsibility model toward shared fate, where providers supply secure defaults and blueprints. Panelists also stressed spreading workloads across multiple platforms built on open standards to reduce concentration risk, and efforts to score open-source projects. Looking back at the Sunburst incident, they concluded that one event can reach many organizations through partners. Government's role was framed as existing regulation plus information sharing across industry and governments.

talks.title: Supply Chain Resilience in a Time of Techtonic Geopolitical Shifts
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Supply Chain Resilience in a Time of Techtonic Geopolitical Shifts.

talks.title: Culture Matters—Put People at the Heart of Security
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how to build stakeholder support, handle toxic team behaviour, and run awareness programs that engage people.
talks.summary:
Budge, a security and risk research analyst, argues that leaders should put people and culture at the centre of their programmes. The talk draws parallels between the speaker's experience as a teenage migrant and security professionals who struggle to speak the language of the business, avoid politics and are seen as obstacles. Survey data cited shows leaders spend little time on technical work and far more on stakeholders, awareness, business cases and strategy.

Budge recommends mapping stakeholders across executives, business and technology leaders, end users and external parties, then listening before proposing change. Persuasion is presented as an ethical process built on momentum from engaged sponsors, executive influence, relationships and reciprocal favours. A major focus is toxicity inside security teams. Responses to a LinkedIn question, about 200 contributions, pointed to lack of organisational support as the top cause, followed by the hero complex or "brilliant jerk" archetype. Budge also predicted that a CISO at a global 500 firm would be fired for instilling a toxic culture, and cited research finding 53% of employees say their firm does not address toxicity.

The talk outlines a four-step human-centric programme: identify key stakeholders, define the behaviours to change, build awareness and training initiatives, then measure and keep improving. Examples include a gamified breach simulation where executives play attackers, a client who researched executives' personal digital footprints, a rangoli display for computer security day, and a comedian addressing identity theft. Budge closes by urging leaders to protect their mental health, lead with purpose and be open about challenges.

talks.title: How CISA Is Charting a Path Toward Defensible Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of How CISA Is Charting a Path Toward Defensible Infrastructure.

talks.title: How You Can Ask the Right Questions to Succeed with Your Security Projects
talks.teaser: Shows how wording security questions carefully builds rapport, uncovers risks and gets stakeholders to support security projects.
talks.summary:
Lenny Zeltser opens by arguing that security professionals succeed on projects largely through the questions they ask, and through the wording and timing they choose. He organizes the talk around three kinds of activity: discovery, planning and persuasion. For discovery, he stresses that the audience's familiarity with terms matters, so a question about a compliance control should match what the listener knows. When unsure, an open-ended question lets the answers reveal the vocabulary to mirror in follow-up questions.

He contrasts opening with a blunt, intrusive question against easing into a conversation with a colleague you will work with for years, where light questions that gradually grow more sensitive tend to build a lasting relationship. Accusatory wording that centres on "you" should be replaced with a description of the situation and the desired outcome. During an urgent incident, he suggests guiding stressed responders with specific, prepared questions instead of open-ended ones. For planning, collaborative framing such as "how might we" invites others to help, and the scope of a question should be neither too narrow nor too broad. A question about training people not to click links is reframed around mitigating phishing risk, which opens up more controls.

For persuasion, he recommends asking questions that help others see the security perspective, such as asking how a request can be approved while staying consistent with the organization's risk approach. Tying a budget request to shared business objectives, such as customer expectations, works better than citing threats and vulnerabilities. He also suggests phrasing questions so that the easy answer is no, since people hesitate to commit to a yes. His takeaway is to listen closely, adapt follow-up questions to the answers, and rehearse the questions that fit your current projects.

talks.title: Thank You, Next! Protecting Next-Generation OT Networks
talks.teaser: A practitioner-oriented tour of how modern OT networks evolve and which defenses beyond the Purdue Model organizations should adopt.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing operational technology as everyday IP and wireless plant networks that now carry far more sensors, actuators, and compute than they did twenty years ago—often an order of magnitude or more. Use cases span access control, HVAC, healthcare, manufacturing, and SCADA, with familiar breach patterns such as vendor-mediated HVAC access illustrating why connectivity growth enlarges the attack surface.

The middle section argues that the Purdue Model’s DMZ between industrial and enterprise tiers remains useful but is under pressure from embedded Linux devices, Raspberry Pi controllers, vendor telemetry requirements, on-prem OT clouds, and analytics in public clouds. Seven converging trends are outlined, followed by eight defense themes: IT–OT convergence, MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, selective zero trust, shared identity services that fail safely, monitoring for privileged activity and IOCs, early SOAR on OT, protection of PLC configurations, and segmented third-party connectivity.

The close proposes enhanced Purdue zoning with industrial security and shared service layers, then urges practical steps today—joint IT and OT planning, stronger logging, port-scan checks on plant switches, and ATT&CK-for-ICS–guided detections—before larger budgeted roadmaps over the next few years.

talks.title: Is Your Organization’s Confidential Data Really Confidential?
talks.teaser: The session maps NCCoE identify-protect and detect-respond stacks to demos of exfiltration, ARP spoofing, and data-theft ransomware.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking whether sensitive organizational data stays confidential during an active breach, and contrasts average breach costs with operational disruption and eroded customer trust. Speakers frame data confidentiality events as both malicious attacks and honest mistakes, then describe MITRE’s work with the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence on NIST’s data security challenge.

Anne Townsend outlines paired Special Publication 1800 guides—identify and protect versus detect, respond, and recover—each mapped to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework across executive and technical volumes. Michael Ekstrom walks through reference architectures built in the NCCoE lab: browser isolation, zero-trust-style network controls, encryption, strong access management with multi-factor authentication, data inventory, policy enforcement, and centralized logging that feeds detection and response.

Recorded use cases stress how architectures interact when defenses fail. A backdoored laptop silently exfiltrates unencrypted files; an intruder ARP-spoofs to capture uploads; a phishing flow steals admin credentials and deploys ransomware that also claims stolen data. Additional planned scenarios cover spear phishing, misdirected email, lost devices, and privileged misuse. The close urges reassessing controls, adopting publication guidance, joining the Data Security Community of Interest, and phasing mitigations over weeks and months.

talks.title: Top Seven AI Breaches: Learning to Protect Against Unsafe Learning
talks.teaser: Surveys seven documented AI failures, from gender-biased translation to self-driving cars, and argues for testing and oversight.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts what was promised for AI with what has actually been delivered. Opening with historical comparisons, including a 1977 remark about collaboration versus competition, the speaker frames AI limits around incompleteness, imitation and efficiency. Machines, the argument goes, need outside oversight, and promised fairness and efficiency tend to break once they are tested.

The middle section walks through seven categories of failure. Translation tools flipped gender when a single word or phrase was altered, in examples from Hungarian, Finnish, Persian and Turkish. Text tools produced abusive output, and one sentence describing a gay Black woman was scored 87% toxic. Emotion recognition could be fooled into reporting high happiness, and a Facebook software engineering ad reached 63% men and 36% women, while LinkedIn was roughly even. Facial recognition changed results after a simple crop, and self-driving systems were shown missing signs and obstacles.

The closing takeaways are practical. Teams should test systems for fairness, impact and transparency, keep an off switch and a reset that can undo learned behaviour, and set up an ethics review board with threat modelling. Releases should be gated through tests and audits, backed by executive enforcement, because regulation depends on being able to prove a system is broken. The speaker urges collaboration over competition.

talks.title: Patterns for Encryption in Hybrid Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows encryption and key management patterns for moving workloads from on-premise to multiple clouds without exposing keys or data.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why encryption matters when workloads span on-premise data centres and several clouds. Consolidating data in the cloud raises its value and attracts attackers willing to stay inside for months, as in the SolarWinds intrusion the speaker cites. The talk frames protection as needing to be effective, trusted and resilient, and sets out five risks, from storage loss and insider access to key loss and vendor concentration in financial services.

Two architectural principles follow. Encrypting low and broad at the block layer is fast and transparent, and covers storage loss. Encrypting selectively, limited to sensitive files, folders and databases, keeps key counts manageable while blocking privileged users. The on-premise HSM, key manager and encryption components are rebuilt for cloud. A single-tenant cloud key manager on a FIPS 140-2 level 4 HSM partition, loaded through split smartcard ceremonies, avoids trusting a shared service. An encryption manager adds file, folder and database protection, letting encrypted data move between clouds without decryption.

Resilience comes from synchronised key stores across zones, smartcard reloads after a regional failure, and offline key backups taken on a schedule or after re-keying. The speaker closes by asking attendees to test their current setup against the five risks, build a roadmap, and plan staffing for rarely performed key ceremonies. Security, in this framing, should enable cloud adoption rather than delay it.

talks.title: The Resilience Business Case: Three Case Studies
talks.teaser: Three composite case studies show how organizations fund IT resiliency and turn continuity programs into broader security gains.
talks.summary:
The session argues that many organizations write continuity, disaster recovery, and incident response plans yet still miss the outcomes leaders expect. It scopes resiliency to IT—recovery, continuity, problem management, and technology availability—not broader organizational, supply chain, or personal resilience, and presents three composite case studies drawn from common market patterns.

The first case is a financial services firm pushed by a third-party audit and SEC expectations: a thin call-tree plan, misplaced ownership, and annual fire drills give way to a compliance-led business case, scenario mapping, and business impact analysis that prioritizes trading and reconciliation systems. That prioritization is meant to flow into vulnerability management and monitoring. The second is a SaaS provider where an outage reframes DevOps reliability as governance: automated rebuilds and immutable infrastructure help contain adversaries staging on a zero-day before lateral movement. The third is a manufacturer answering a major customer’s certification demand; business impact work surfaces redundant applications, and instrumented network paths isolate suspicious traffic and later aid investigation when a fast-moving worm hits legacy plant systems.

The talk closes with patterns from reviewing many plans—wrong owners, recovery at the wrong layer, and exercises that do not match real threats—and urges integrating asset context into security operations, testing that matches declared metrics, and treating funded resiliency as a brake that enables digital business rather than paperwork alone.

talks.title: Tool Time: Building Your Cybersecurity Architecture Planning Toolbox
talks.teaser: Surveys analytical, informational and design tools that help teams plan security architecture in a more repeatable way.
talks.summary:
Security architecture work is often manual, slow and hard to repeat, and teams struggle to get everyone on the same page. The speakers frame the architecture process as three stages: understanding the current state, examining the threat environment, and documenting the intended future state. They argue that tools can add repeatability and capture the tribal knowledge that otherwise gets lost.

For current-state analysis, they look at effectiveness, maturity and efficiency, and point out that total cost of ownership can far exceed license fees. Examples include Eramba as a GRC platform, a total cost of ownership model, OWASP Threat Dragon and Trike for threat modeling, and the Open Group's FAIR tool, which is only available on a 90-day evaluation license rather than as open source. For informational work, they cover Grafana dashboards, an inventory tool that goes beyond spreadsheets, OpenNMS for network visibility, and a CSF reference for cross-mapping controls.

For design, they stress documenting scope, goals and principles, pointing to the architecture description in TOGAF. Modeling options include Archi for ArchiMate, Modelio for UML, mind mapping for gathering stakeholder requirements, and OSATE2 for embedded systems. The takeaway is to review your current planning process for inefficiencies, automate where possible, and track how long the architecture process itself takes.

talks.title: From Zero to Hero at the Edge
talks.teaser: Describes building edge security programs with SASE, separating strategy from frameworks, and prioritizing zero trust and DDoS controls.
talks.summary:
Organizations no longer fit the old picture of an outward-facing network edge plus internal endpoints; for many customers, almost everything sits at the edge across data centers, multi-cloud, private cloud, and distributed compute. The presentation argues that security leaders need a clear strategy first—what resiliency or access means for the business—and then use frameworks such as NIST, ISO business continuity guidance, MITRE for SOC maturity, or analyst models as tools rather than substitutes for strategy, so auditors do not lock the program into checklist compliance alone.

The middle of the talk centers on Secure Access Service Edge and related edge models as a way to cut vendor sprawl, staffing load, and latency by unifying networking capabilities like SD-WAN and CDN with security services including CASB, secure web gateway, zero trust network access, DNS, and web application firewalls. It walks through defining what “edge” means internally, sample architectures for web and API delivery, DDoS and DNS concerns, crosswalking threats to design, and matching controls to business models from branch-heavy banks to location-agnostic remote work and IoT touchpoints such as dealer tablets tied to vehicles.

Practitioners are steered through dense reference material on situational awareness, resiliency versus mere redundancy, segmentation with audit evidence, vendor geography and privacy rules, gaps the SASE framing may miss such as JavaScript at the edge, and an as-is versus to-be review tied to business transformation. Implementation is explicitly gradual: prioritize zero trust access and identity risk, then infrastructure and DNS resilience against denial-of-service trends, then CASB or SWG depth depending on SaaS reliance, while keeping network and security teams aligned and stakeholders from legal, privacy, and the board engaged.

talks.title: Doing the Safety Dance: Will Trusted Execution Environments Protect Us?
talks.teaser: Panelists debate whether trusted execution environments can keep data protected in use, and where cloud providers still need trust.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the Confidential Computing Consortium's working definition: protecting data in use with hardware-based trusted execution environments. The speakers argue that anyone who handles sensitive data, from security leaders and architects to developers and cloud teams, should understand the technology. They stress that open source matters because code has to be auditable before anyone can trust it.

On trust, the panelists differ in emphasis. One argues that cloud providers should open-source what they run, while another wants the provider removed from the trust path entirely, so that no one at the provider can see a customer's workload or data. All agree that a TEE protects a whole application and its memory, unlike TPMs and HSMs, which guard specific components or keys. Trust agreements between businesses could eventually be encoded in enforceable policy. Attestation is singled out as the concept newcomers should learn first, since it shows what is actually running and where.

Looking ahead, the panel expects confidential computing to become a default, comparing it to the spread of HTTPS, though performance, usability and scale must improve first. They also caution that it will not fix human error or the software supply chain, and that it is one more layer rather than a silver bullet. The session closes with an invitation to the consortium's open meetings.

talks.title: Critical DNS & Domain Name Security Intelligence to Thwart Cyberattacks
talks.teaser: Maps weaknesses across the DNS ecosystem and tracks COVID-themed domain registrations used in phishing and fraud.
talks.summary:
David Conrad, speaking for ICANN, first walks through the DNS ecosystem and its weak points. He covers protocol issues such as missing data integrity, which DNSSEC addresses, and missing confidentiality, which encrypted transports like DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS aim to fix. He also covers look-alike internationalized domain names, redirection of name server records, resolver hijacking through compromised routers, amplified denial-of-service traffic, and transitive trust across name servers in other zones. Provisioning attacks on registrar and registry accounts are highlighted, where registrar lock and registry lock help but can be defeated through social engineering.

Ihab Shraim, CTO of CSC, presents research on domain abuse during the COVID-19 pandemic. His team counted about 325,000 new COVID-related domain registrations, with .com holding about 64 percent and the United States the most targeted country. Registration spikes tracked events such as the US reaching 2,000 deaths, pandemic stimulus payments and vaccine availability, with drops in registrations trailing each spike. Themes included treatment and testing names, e-commerce and counterfeit stores, and a scam chain that lures older people to fake sites that install malware and join botnets.

The main takeaways are to monitor authoritative name server changes, validate DNSSEC where possible, limit out-of-zone name servers, use registrar and registry locks, watch for look-alike characters in names, and monitor brand abuse in near real time.

talks.title: WAF Made Easy
talks.teaser: An IT security practitioner covers WAF build-tune-support staffing, phased rollout, and on-prem and cloud architecture.
talks.summary:
Micah K. Brown frames a web application firewall as compute sitting between users and web applications, terminating TLS, inspecting traffic against policy, and permitting, denying, or alerting before traffic reaches front-end servers. He promotes a build, tune, and support lifecycle so networking-oriented staff own deployment while application-security-minded colleagues own policy tuning, then operations carries steady-state care.

The build phase centers on per-environment implementation guides, collaboration with application owners and developers via network and data-flow diagrams, cold builds with hosts-file testing, and DNS cutovers guarded by bridge calls, ACL restrictions so servers accept only WAF-origin HTTPS, and about an hour of functional testing. Tuning stays in learning or alert mode with daily developer review; he warns that ranking alerts by frequency missed rare monthly features and broke niche behavior despite 99.998 percent of traffic passing. Blocking mode follows go/no-go checks, a one-week hypercare window, and ongoing support procedures including patching and documentation.

Architecture guidance covers virtual WAFs, DNS-based interception, management VLAN isolation, optional TLS offload, and cloud layouts that separate a security-controlled container from developer-controlled infrastructure. Policy sections address unequal test versus stage environments, promotion paths for learning suggestions, and parent-child policies instead of one monolithic rule set. Closing challenges urge inventorying web apps, piloting a non-production WAF within three months, reaching blocking mode within six, and standing up a trained support team.

talks.title: DHS CISA Strategy to Fix Vulnerabilities Below the OS Among Worst Offenders
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of DHS CISA Strategy to Fix Vulnerabilities Below the OS Among Worst Offenders.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Boyden Rohner and Tom Ruoff from the Cyber Security Division at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) examine an emerging class of threats: vulnerabilities below the operating system (VBOS). Comparing software security to an iceberg, they emphasize that while the cybersecurity industry traditionally focuses on the visible tip—the operating system and application layers—critical risks lurk beneath in firmware, BIOS, and UEFI layers. As commercial threat actors increasingly repurpose sophisticated rootkits once restricted to nation-states, addressing firmware-level vulnerabilities has become an urgent priority for national critical infrastructure resilience.

### Key Topics
- **Vulnerabilities Below the Operating System (VBOS):** Defining the security gap in code that connects hardware to the operating system, particularly firmware and UEFI.
- **The Worst Offender Concept:** Rather than naming specific commercial vendors, the speakers identify UEFI as the "worst offender" due to its ubiquity, core architectural role, and chronic lack of enforced memory protections.
- **The Nutrition Label / Twinkie Analogy:** A conceptual framework comparing software transparency to FDA food labeling: Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) show the "ingredients," but testing reports and designer intent are essential to evaluate actual risk.
- **Discrepancy Between Software Intent vs. Capability:** Formulating risk indicator scoring by evaluating whether purpose-built devices perform only their intended functions or exhibit unintended, exploitable capabilities.

### Technical Details
To ground the threat, the speakers highlight real-world historical attacks exploiting VBOS:
- **2015 Ukrainian Power Grid Attack:** Adversaries installed malicious firmware onto serial-to-internet gateway devices, severing remote operator access and preventing substations from being brought back online after opening circuit breakers.
- **2018 LoJax Campaign:** Threat actors deployed a UEFI rootkit that compromised legitimate anti-theft software (LoJack), utilizing phishing drop vectors and command-and-control channels to maintain persistence across OS reinstallation and hard drive replacement.

Rohner and Ruoff contrast above-the-OS defenses with below-the-OS realities. While above-the-OS code heavily deploys mitigations like Data Execution Prevention (DEP) and Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)—approaching 90% implementation in commercial products—these mitigations are rarely applied to UEFI code. Furthermore, vendors often disable hardware and memory protections (such as NX / No-Execute) by default to save cycle time or due to perceived lack of operational necessity.

To tackle software analysis at scale without "boiling the ocean," CISA advocates starting with constrained, purpose-built devices such as programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and medical devices. Because these devices have tightly scoped expected behaviors, automated testing can compare vendor design claims against actual capabilities (e.g., whether a device designed for 5 behaviors unexpectedly exhibits 25).

### Takeaways
CISA outlines several paths forward for industry, government, and procurement officials:
- **Leverage Policy and Executive Orders:** Organizations should review the federal Executive Order guidance on SBOMs and participate in multi-stakeholder initiatives like NTIA/SBOM.
- **Shift Procurement from "Faith-Based" to "Risk-Based":** Buyers must actively ask vendors for SBOMs, lists of known CVEs and their remediations, designer intent notes, and documentation of firmware vulnerability mitigations applied (such as NX enforcement).
- **Implement Compensating Controls:** Until vendors incorporate standardized mitigations below the OS, organizations should apply systems-engineering compensating controls around vulnerable firmware and devices.
- **Community Collaboration:** CISA plans to convene stakeholders across critical infrastructure sectors, collaborate with code researchers on automated capability verification, and establish data-driven risk indicators to steer procurement away from the worst offenders.

talks.title: Modern Identity Hacking: Have Hackers Really Adjusted to Constant Remote?
talks.teaser: Live demos expose VPN pivoting, MFA phishing, and Windows Hello persistence in remote identity setups.
talks.summary:
Organizations accelerated remote work during the pandemic, often by extending VPN access without strong multi-factor authentication. The speaker ties that shift to a familiar intrusion pattern: phishing harvests credentials, VPN login follows when MFA is absent, lateral movement and privilege escalation unfold inside the network, and ransomware often closes the loop.

The middle of the session contrasts legacy perimeter thinking with zero-trust ideas—never trust, always verify; least privilege; assume breach—while arguing that identity has become the real boundary. Statistics on personal devices and weak management of non-corporate endpoints frame why trusted-device policies matter. Three demonstrations follow: Metasploit meterpreter and SOCKS4a proxy chains on a VPN-connected Windows host to scan and reach internal servers without VPN credentials; Evilginx-style phishing that proxies real Microsoft login and captures tokens after MFA; and abuse of Windows Hello for Business by planting NGC key material in Active Directory and using Kekeo to obtain Kerberos tickets and NTLM hashes from a non-domain account.

Practitioners should treat VPN as a critical monitoring surface, keep MFA despite bypass research, favor modern credentials over passwords where possible, plan patching for always-on VPN, and fold remote-access scenarios into incident response. Longer term, partial zero trust, conditional access, passwordless options, and visibility into remote worker behavior are presented as the durable counter to attackers who pivot through compromised identities.

talks.title: What's New with the CIS Controls v8
talks.teaser: Outlines CIS Critical Security Controls version eight, from eighteen controls through cloud service management and elevated data inventory.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame the CIS Controls as a prioritized, measurable alternative to endless security checklists, emphasizing metrics, alignment with compliance frameworks, and offense-informed defense drawn from breach lessons. After this foundation, they contrast version 7.1 with version 8.0: the set shrinks from twenty items to eighteen through retirements and merges, while data discovery and protection move up as the third inventory pillar alongside hardware and software. New material includes a dedicated cloud and service-provider control, companion guides for cloud and mobile use, international framework mappings, and implementation groups sized for small, medium, and large enterprises.

Russell Eubanks walks through a five-step adoption path—choosing frameworks, mapping to controls, risk management, current-state assessment against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and targeted maturity gains—with repeated emphasis on demonstrating progress to leadership. Randy Marchany details each control area at a high level and stresses supplemental resources such as AuditScripts mapping tools.

Closing guidance urges practitioners to adopt version eight deliberately rather than overnight, concentrating on two or three controls at a time over multi-year programs, securing an executive champion, and using free gap-analysis tooling. Both speakers highlight inventory work as the hinge that scopes later tasks like vulnerability scanning, secure baselines, and malware defenses, while warning that political and data-gathering hurdles across business and IT units often dominate real-world rollouts.

talks.title: Cyberspace Solarium Commission
talks.teaser: Two congressional commissioners review which Cyberspace Solarium recommendations became law and what remains for the next Congress.
talks.summary:
Representatives Mike Gallagher and Jim Langevin, both members of the Cyberspace Solarium Commission, look back at how the group's work turned into law. Gallagher describes the choice to write recommendations as draft legislation instead of a report that would gather dust. Gallagher put the number enacted at about 25, while Langevin said about 27 of roughly 80 recommendations were passed through the National Defense Authorization Act. Highlights include a Senate-confirmed National Cyber Director, expanded CISA powers such as administrative subpoena authority and proactive threat hunting on federal networks, and a joint cyber planning office.

On SolarWinds, Gallagher notes that the first warning came from FireEye, a private company, and uses that to argue for stronger public-private collaboration. He also says criticism of defend forward misses the point, because the intrusions exploited blind spots in blue space, so intelligence from blue, gray and red space needs to be fused. Langevin says the administration must decide whether the intrusion was traditional espionage or crossed a line, warning of blowback that could put US operatives at risk. Gallagher expects the National Cyber Director to coordinate existing incident response groups rather than displace CISA or the FBI.

On election security, Langevin urges sustained federal investment in modern equipment, paper ballots, risk-limiting audits and voter registration systems, and notes that adversary efforts are shifting toward misinformation. Both members see parts of the cyber agenda as bipartisan, including intelligence sharing with state and local officials. The takeaway is that election gains must be locked in and societal resilience built, not treated as finished.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Explains how behavioral anomaly detection on Microsoft 365 mail catches impersonation and vendor-compromise phishing that gateways miss.
talks.summary:
Evan Reiser, CEO of Abnormal Security, argues that socially engineered email is the largest security threat facing companies. He cites an FBI figure of more than $2 billion a year in losses and says impersonation attacks pose a greater risk to organizations than widely publicized incidents such as ransomware. He also notes that the Colonial Pipeline attack traced back to a single spear phishing email.

He walks through a case from a Fortune 100 customer in which an attacker compromised a known vendor and used that trusted relationship to steal money. Such messages evade conventional controls because they carry no known bad signals, such as reputation problems, malicious links or dangerous attachments, so reputation analysis and file sandboxing have little to act on. His product instead connects directly to Microsoft 365 through cloud APIs, rather than sitting in the network path, and builds behavioral profiles of each organization from identity, relationships and content. In the vendor example, the message was flagged because it came from an unusual location, was sent to a person with no known relationship to the sender, and differed from the vendor's normal patterns, which were compared against a shared supply chain intelligence network.

He says the same approach extends to phishing, malware, internal account takeover and supply chain compromise, and claims roughly 10 times higher accuracy than conventional email systems. The practical takeaway is to model how trusted senders normally behave, rather than relying only on known-bad indicators.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Apiiro explores RSAC 2021 Innovation Sandbox.
talks.summary:
## Overview

Idan Plotnik, CEO of Apiiro, presents the company's approach to reimagining the security development lifecycle for agile and cloud-native environments. The core problem: existing DevSecOps, cloud security, and risk management tools lack visibility and understanding of risk across the complete application lifecycle, from design through code to cloud deployment.

## Key Problems

The talk identifies several critical gaps in current security practices:

- **Multidimensional Risk**: Risk assessment requires understanding developer expertise, code logic changes, pull request discussions, cloud infrastructure modifications, and authorization controls—information typically scattered across disconnected tools.
- **Scale Mismatch**: Organizations operate with approximately one security architect per 159 developers, yet each developer generates multiple changes daily. Manual review processes (threat modeling, security reviews, pen-tests, alert triage) are impossible to scale.
- **Fragmentation**: No single view exists connecting design decisions to code changes to cloud deployment, resulting in late decision-making and process inefficiency.

## The Apiiro Solution

Apiiro's Code Risk Platform addresses these gaps through:

- **Multi-source Analysis**: Uses NLP and machine learning to analyze application code, open-source components, infrastructure-as-code, user stories, developer knowledge, third-party tool data, and business impact.
- **Core Capabilities**:
  - Real-time application inventory
  - Remediation work plan generation
  - Adaptive governance engine
  - Automated remediation workflows
  - CACD attack prevention (with anomalous developer behavior detection, similar to detection of Solar Winds-style attacks)

## Market Position

Apiiro targets the intersection of DevSecOps, cloud security, and risk management, addressing a $100 billion market opportunity. The company launched in October and had already acquired over 40 customers at the time of this pitch. The fundamental thesis: DevSecOps and cloud security must evolve from fragmented point solutions into multidimensional risk management platforms that act as business enablers rather than blockers.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Innovation Sandbox
talks.teaser: Pitches a cloud unified access platform that replaces VPNs with per-session, policy-based application access.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the argument that remote access has become fragmented. Organizations began with VPNs that granted broad network access, then added secure web gateways, cloud access security brokers, and other appliances such as jump boxes and application delivery controllers. As described, the result is complexity, excessive access, many policies to maintain, little visibility into user activity, and a large attack surface that grows as networks extend. Moving these legacy tools to the cloud is presented as not solving the underlying problem.

The speaker presents a unified access cloud, built from the ground up, as the alternative. Every user session is routed through the platform, where it is authenticated, monitored and continuously authorized, so a single policy governs access whether users are on-premises or going to SaaS applications. In one example, a user connects from an unmanaged device without an agent and sees only the applications they are authorized to reach. Those applications have no public IP address and are not exposed to direct internet access. In a second example, two colleagues on managed devices place a peer-to-peer voice call routed through the platform, and neither device touches the corporate network.

The talk closes by describing the visibility this model provides, including queries about a user's access to a database table or a file download, plus reporting on activity. The speaker says the platform already handles millions of connections daily for large enterprises and ends by pitching simpler, more secure access as the goal. The takeaway for practitioners is to consider consolidating access policy and limiting network-level exposure instead of layering more appliances.

talks.summary:
Eldad Chai, CEO and co-founder of Satori, presented the company's data SecOps platform in this Innovation Sandbox pitch. He argued that modern data infrastructure, spread across multiple clouds, data lakes and warehouses, has outpaced security. Access is still handled manually through ad hoc configurations, which makes IT and database admins a bottleneck and leaves teams struggling to answer who can act as what, which data is sensitive, and where controls should go.

Satori sits as a transparent data proxy between data users and data stores. Connecting takes minutes by changing the data store URL, and people keep their existing way of working. The platform analyzes queries and results in real time to provide full data flow visibility, and its workflow and policy engine can mask data or start an off-band authorization step. Policies can be enforced without writing code, and users can request just-in-time self-service access. In the example given, a head of data analytics building a machine learning model requests access, gets approval from an owner, and starts work without waiting weeks for reviews, while customer data is anonymized and security teams get monitoring and reporting.

The closing portion covered the team's background in security and the investors and advisors backing its goal of enabling secure data democratization. The main takeaway is that access to sensitive data can be governed continuously through automated workflows instead of manual permission changes.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: SolarWinds: What Really Happened?
talks.teaser: An executive interview traces the Sunburst crisis timeline, customer remediation support, and lessons on transparency and accountability.
talks.summary:
The conversation begins with a dated recap of public disclosures from December 2020 through early 2021: FireEye’s breach and stolen toolkit, linkage to a backdoor in Orion called Sunburst, urgent customer notifications, widely reported federal impacts, and evolving attribution narratives. The incoming chief executive describes learning of the incident on December 12 during a birthday dinner call from the general counsel, and explains why he pressed forward with the transition rather than stepping away, emphasizing continuity during crisis.

Discussion then moves to customer impact and response. Leadership cites prior product security and incident response routines, the strain of answering “what does this mean for me,” and an initial estimate that as many as 18,000 customers might have received the affected update. Months later, support continued through the Orion Assistant Program, funding partner-led help for upgrades and rebuilds. He ties those choices to earlier breach-handling experience at another vendor, stressing humility, vigilance, and transparent progress updates even without full facts. On tradecraft, he characterizes the attackers as sophisticated and notes investigative scale involving hundreds of terabytes and thousands of virtual build systems, with possible presence from January 2019 recon activity.

The close covers organizational choices: retaining the existing CISO, rejecting scapegoating after nation-state tradecraft, correcting congressional messaging that blamed an intern, and recruiting university talent. Asked what he would change after taking office, he points to stronger, more proactive media and outreach capacity than the company’s historically low public profile had prepared.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Securing Today’s Unbound Enterprise
talks.teaser: Forcepoint's CEO explains the unbound enterprise, unified hybrid policy, and reading user intent to get ahead of breaches.
talks.summary:
In this fireside chat, Forcepoint CEO Manny Rivelo describes how the pandemic accelerated a shift that was already under way. Users, applications and data now sit everywhere, so the old office perimeter no longer protects much. He points to the scale of the threat, citing about 46,000 phishing sites brought up per week against organizations last year, and a $50 million ransomware attack on Acer. He also says the problem reaches small specialist businesses, not only large enterprises.

He argues that defenders need to act before a breach or data exfiltration happens. He cites over 100 million lines of new code produced annually by enterprises, over 120 million malware variants, and a forecast of three times as many endpoints by 2023. Customers often juggle 50 to 100 security vendors, so he favors a unified platform with open APIs that partners can build on. He describes SASE, secure access service edge, as an architecture rather than a product. For hybrid environments, he says one shared policy should cover staff on-premises and in the cloud, instead of separate management systems that must be kept in sync.

He also says that traditional allow and block lists are not enough, and that systems should model a user's behavior and intent. In his example, an executive who captures thousands of customer records, bundles them into a folder and encrypts it would see a rising risk score and could be stopped from moving the file to a cloud storage folder, with a notice shown on screen. He closes by urging the industry to work together, warning that organizations that do not adopt security alongside digital and AI-driven change risk being left behind.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: It’s Time for Data Contact Tracing
talks.teaser: Argues that security teams should unify all their data sources to speed detection and response.
talks.summary:
Doug Merritt, CEO of Splunk, opens this RSA Conference keynote by arguing that security is fundamentally a data problem. He draws a parallel to COVID-19 contact tracing and describes the anxiety many leaders feel about whether they hold a complete, trustworthy picture of their environment, while managing a growing number of data sources and exhausted analysts.

The middle of the talk gives examples of organizations that pulled their data together. The University of Arizona combined VPN, single sign-on, wireless and Zoom traffic on one analytics platform to shift 60,000 students, faculty and staff away from campus safely. Intel's InfoSec team built a defense-in-depth strategy on a unified data foundation to automate prevention and detection across perimeter, network, endpoints and applications, and said this let it handle 99% of threats targeting its environment. Slack described verifying its zero trust network through visibility into activity across its many cloud services. Merritt also cited survey results, with 78% of companies expecting another SolarWinds-style supply chain attack, and Mandiant figures showing median dwell time falling from 78 days in 2018 to 17 days in 2020.

He closes with practical advice: collect data from every source, apply automation and machine learning to speed detection, remodel existing zero trust and SOC programs instead of rebuilding them, and favor open integrations over closed ecosystems.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: The Internet is Small: Own Your Attack Surface Before Somebody Else
talks.teaser: Explains why attackers scan the public internet faster than defenders can inventory exposed assets, using Fortune 500 exposure data.
talks.summary:
Tim Junio, head of engineering for Palo Alto Networks Cortex and former CEO of Expanse, opens by arguing that internet-wide scanning has become fast enough for attackers to sweep a single protocol across the public internet in minutes. Defenders, by contrast, often need days or weeks to find all of their own internet-facing assets. He points to the Microsoft Exchange zero-day publication, after which scanning for vulnerable servers rose within minutes, while defenders took much longer to locate and patch their exposed systems.

He then reviews common defensive approaches, including penetration testing, red teaming and vulnerability management, and argues that each runs more slowly than attacker tempo. He recommends an inventory-first approach and measuring mean time to inventory, meaning how long it takes to find and register a new asset that was set up outside central provisioning. The research covered a subset of Fortune 500 companies and found a serious exposure on average every 12 hours. Exposed Remote Desktop Protocol was the most common category, often from Windows machines that fall back to the public internet when a VPN drops. Most exposures sat in cloud environments, and roughly one in five were on premises. Other findings included exposed database servers and misconfigured IoT and operational technology devices.

He closes by saying the attack surface problem is solvable, pointing to top organizations that automate asset discovery and resolution. He directs viewers to the published white paper and best-practice guidance at asmtop10.com.
