talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Safeguarding Privacy with Purpose and Passion
talks.teaser: Argues that organizations must pair security controls with privacy practices to earn and keep customer trust.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the shift to remote and hybrid work, which has spread personal and sensitive data across more devices and clouds while attacks grow harder to detect. It separates data protection, which keeps unauthorized parties away from information, from data privacy, which governs how personal information is handled, stored and used. The speaker notes that security teams increasingly share responsibility for that second area with privacy staff.

The middle of the talk cites a survey in which most respondents worried about sharing their information, and an analyst estimate that about two-thirds of the world's population would have personal data covered by modern privacy rules by 2023. The speaker argues that placing most privacy responsibility on individuals is unrealistic. Three areas are offered for organizations: giving users control over and transparency about their data, encrypting and protecting data at every stage while guarding against insider as well as outside loss, and defending users' privacy choices and pushing for stronger protections.

The closing section recommends a zero trust approach applied from outside in and inside out, supported by identity, data governance, insider risk and data loss prevention tools. The speaker frames trust as a business differentiator and suggests organization-wide privacy training for staff who handle sensitive information.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Reshaping Security to Power Business Growth
talks.teaser: A CISO explains how Dow Chemical applies zero trust in practice, from roadmaps and partners to workforce retraining.
talks.summary:
Mary O'Brien, general manager for IBM Security, argues that trust and community should guide how businesses secure themselves after the disruption of the past 18 months. She frames zero trust as a response to the old perimeter model, which worked when most assets sat behind a firewall, and to a world of mobile users, cloud applications, IoT devices and data spread across many environments.

Mauricio Guerra, CISO at Dow Chemical, lays out three duties: compliance with IT controls and regulations such as Sarbanes-Oxley and GDPR, managing cybersecurity risk from threat identification to mitigation, and delivering digital capabilities securely. He describes zero trust at Dow as a concept, architecture and framework, and began with zero trust network access so employees could reach the internet, cloud services and email securely. Later deliverables covered secure access to Dow's sites, an SD-LAN and SD-WAN solution replacing its telecommunications network, secure management of manufacturing IoT sensors, and conditional access with authentication.

On challenges, Guerra pointed to retraining an IT workforce used to firewall thinking and to selecting the right partners for a technology area that is still maturing. His advice to other leaders is to work closely with IT and business teams and build a roadmap, perhaps covering three years and revisited about every six months. O'Brien closes by arguing that open, collaborative security, with shared standards and APIs, lowers barriers to innovation and makes zero trust actionable.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Bathtubs, Snakes and WannaCry, Oh My! Risk in the Physical and Cyber World
talks.teaser: Uses micromorts and threat data to recalibrate physical and cyber risk perceptions so defense investments match real likelihood and impact.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting instinctive fears—such as snakes—with statistics showing where harm actually occurs in daily life, including driving and ladder falls. It introduces the micromort, a unit expressing a one-in-a-million chance of sudden death, and applies it to activities from routine driving to Everest climbs to show how quantified risk challenges intuition.

That framing shifts to cybersecurity, arguing that media and emotion similarly distort what organizations fear versus what data shows. A three-vector model weighs how lethal an incident is to one company, how many organizations could be affected, and how often similar events occur. Examples span single-victim breaches, globe-spanning worms like WannaCry, supply-chain compromises, widespread malware loaders, and human-operated ransomware, noting that attention and actual organizational risk do not always align.

The closing emphasis is practical prioritization under limited budgets: hygiene and user education for everyday threats, detection and machine learning for broad malware, and skilled operators alongside technology against active human adversaries. The speaker urges measuring trade-offs with evidence—for instance comparing multifactor authentication to other controls—rather than defending primarily from headlines or hype.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Cybersecurity as a National Imperative
talks.teaser: Outlines a national approach to cyber defense, covering software security, critical infrastructure, ransomware and emerging technology.
talks.summary:
The keynote frames cybersecurity as a matter of national and economic security. It points to the SolarWinds and Microsoft Exchange incidents as lessons that prevention should take priority over responding to one breach after another. It cites breach cost estimates and notes that small businesses, schools, hospitals and local governments often bear the heaviest burden.

The speech lays out three lines of effort. The first is modernizing federal defenses, including basic controls such as MFA, encryption, logging and endpoint detection, along with a push for secure development and build environments in federal software purchasing. It argues that buyers cannot see which vendors build securely, so trust in vendors is largely blind, and it describes a pilot with electric sector leaders to add detection and blocking capabilities to critical infrastructure. The second line covers international partnership, including the Quad Security Dialogue, a coalition of countries supporting attribution of the SolarWinds intrusion to the SVR, and a cooperative effort against ransomware, which the speaker describes as growing more sophisticated through fileless variants, big game hunting, ransomware cartels and double extortion. The third covers investment in emerging technology, including a proposed $180 billion in R&D, and warns that quantum computing could disrupt asymmetric encryption.

The closing message is that secure development and visibility into vendor practices should be rewarded economically, and that continued partnership between government and the private sector is essential to meet these goals.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2021 Day Two with Poet, Rives
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning RSA Conference 2021 Day Two with Poet, Rives.
talks.summary:
## Overview

This is a community-focused address by spoken word artist Poet Rives, delivered from his backyard in New York state during RSA Conference 2021. As he notes, this is his fifth consecutive year speaking at the conference. Rather than a technical cybersecurity talk, it reflects on the human connections within the cybersecurity community and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on conference culture and collaboration.

## Rives' Interactive Conference Traditions

Rives shares his history of engaging attendees through participatory activities. In 2019, he circulated a cardboard box labeled "more betterer" where attendees wrote index cards describing their strengths. In 2020, he stationed himself at conference escalators with blank buttons and gel pens, inviting attendees to customize identity buttons. He expresses deep nostalgia for bringing these collected items backstage for the broader community to experience together.

## Community Message

The core of the talk features a video segment with multiple members of the RSA Conference community—attendees, advocates, advisors, speakers, and one of the conference founders—collectively expressing what they miss about in-person gatherings. Their message emphasizes face-to-face collaboration on security challenges, spirited debates during keynotes, informal networking ("the Bash"), and lifelong friendships. They frame the cybersecurity community as "one family" united by shared commitment, noting that while attendees and speakers may be competitors and colleagues, their "fates are intertwined" and they "rise and fall together."

## Key Themes

The speakers acknowledge that the pandemic year has fundamentally changed how people work, think, and live. They frame the community's response as one of adaptation, perseverance, and collective survival. Central messages include calls for unity in facing "the 21st century's biggest threat to humankind" and emphasis on human resilience. The repeated refrain "we miss you" underscores the emotional and professional value of in-person connection.

## Takeaways

The overarching message stresses resilience, community cohesion, and hope for future in-person reconnection. Rives urges the audience to "hold on, to hang on, and to hang in." The talk closes with calls for bravery and unity as the community faces challenges ahead, expressed through collective gratitude and acknowledgment that next year they hope to meet in person again.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: Telling Hard Truths to Impact Change in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Telling Hard Truths to Impact Change in Cybersecurity.
talks.summary:
This RSA Conference 2021 keynote conversation features Angela Weinman (Head of Global Governance Risk and Compliance for VMware) and Jimmy Sanders (Information Security for Netflix) discussing three fundamental truths about cybersecurity that require immediate attention to drive meaningful change and improve organizational resilience.

**First Hard Truth: Security Risk Picture is Out of Focus**
Research shows less than half of top executives are satisfied with how their resiliency risk plans were executed, reflecting that security professionals tend to be overly conservative when predicting risks and impacts. The speakers advocate shifting from narrowly defined risk scenarios to a broader spectrum-of-impact approach. Using the pandemic as a case study, most organizations planned for a small subset of employees working remotely temporarily, but reality required virtually everyone to have remote access for extended periods. Those organizations that pivoted fastest either had broader contingency plans or were further along their digital transformation journey. The recommendation is to present spectrum-based risk views across the organization—to CISOs, risk committees, executives, audit committees, and boards—allowing business stakeholders to participate in determining acceptable risk levels. Additionally, security teams should avoid treating all assets and environments uniformly; instead, environments should be prioritized so that loss of less critical systems doesn't cascade into organizational failure.

**Second Hard Truth: Legacy Security Practices are Slowing Us Down**
Both speakers emphasize abandoning outdated security processes that have accumulated like geological layers—inflexible and heavy, constraining security teams and business units. They advocate challenging the "how" and "why" behind every security process, questioning whether box-checking activities still serve genuine security goals. Jimmy Sanders highlights that diversity means bringing various perspectives into the conversation, while inclusion means actively ensuring those voices are heard and valued. Organizations can build resilience by conducting monthly proof-of-concept evaluations of new tools and techniques. New team members often identify redundant work because they lack ingrained assumptions about standard practices. The speakers recommend mapping security efforts back to cyber hygiene fundamentals and business objectives, eliminating practices that don't align, and continuously challenging legacy approaches—necessary to scale and move faster in the modern threat landscape.

**Third Hard Truth: Security is Not a Solo Sport**
No single company, regardless of sophistication, can unilaterally reduce industry-wide security breaches. Security professionals function as "superheroes" whose collective power achieves what no single entity can. Knowledge-sharing within the security community is essential; the most rapid growth in security practices occurs when organizations share both successes and failures. Relationships and connections are foundational to security success at all career stages. Jimmy Sanders leads the ISSA International emerging technology group, which aims to explore, document, and distribute information to the security community. Both speakers stress that peer support is a two-way street and emphasize that "we need each other now, more than ever."

**Takeaways:**
The speakers distill their message into three actionable steps: (1) **Zoom Out** by adopting a wide-angle perspective on risk and letting business stakeholders help define acceptable risk levels; (2) **Throw Out** legacy security processes that no longer provide value; and (3) **Reach Out** to leverage professional relationships, join communities of practice, and share knowledge. They conclude that shared accountability, increased diversity, and a commitment to scientifically effective techniques—paired with genuine collaboration—are essential for driving meaningful progress in cybersecurity.

talks.title: RSAC 2021 Keynote: A Resilient Journey
talks.teaser: Frames cyber resilience around chaos engineering, risk-based prioritization and community, using Netflix, WWII and SEWA stories.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that the security field should stop trying to secure chaos and instead get good at resilience, which the speaker defines as falling less often, withstanding falls better, and rising stronger. It opens with Netflix's Chaos Monkey, a tool that shut down production instances and cables so the streaming service could degrade gracefully, and notes that this idea inspired a wider set of simulation tools.

The middle section covers preparing for chaos and limiting damage. Teams should attack their own networks to check whether they record those attacks, then use threat intelligence to model likely adversaries plus a few unlikely ones. Zero trust is presented as a mindset that limits trust to what is absolutely required, and third-party sprawl is highlighted, with segmentation and least privilege suggested for northbound traffic as well. Drawing on Abraham Wald's WWII analysis of returning aircraft, the speaker argues that armor belongs where risk is greatest rather than where damage is most visible. He recommends risk-based prioritization and AI-assisted incident triage.

The closing section turns to recovery through community. It describes the Self Employed Women's Association, whose members sewed masks during India's lockdown, and the story of Marcus Hutchins, presented as an argument for recruiting talented people rather than shutting them out. The takeaways are to prepare for chaos, prioritize smartly and lean on the community, ending with the kintsugi metaphor of repair that highlights breaks rather than hiding them.

talks.title: Paula Januszkiewicz Shares her Story of Resilience, the RSAC 2021 Theme
talks.teaser: Outlines three factors that reshaped cybersecurity during the pandemic, from remote work to incident response.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at three factors that shaped the cybersecurity market during the pandemic, framed around the resilience theme of the RSA Conference. The first is the loss of personal contact. The speaker notes that people missed community meetings and conferences, yet her own team and customers became more inventive when devising security solutions, and security development moved forward in those organisations.

The second factor is readiness for incident response. Citing 2020 summaries, the speaker says phishing was the main route for delivering ransomware and other malware. Her firm handled more incident response projects during the pandemic than ever before, and some companies were unprepared. Even when systems were restored from backups, recovery consumed time that could have gone elsewhere.

The third factor is secure remote work, which the speaker expects to persist in some form. Questions to address include whether staff use personal or corporate devices, whether family members could reach work equipment, the risks of public or insecure Wi-Fi, and shadow IT left unmanaged in the infrastructure. The talk closes by noting these challenges will likely keep arising over the coming months.

talks.title: Webcast: My Threat Model is Your Threat Model
talks.teaser: Explains how threats below the operating system, from firmware to supply chain, shape PC security and what defenders can do.
talks.summary:
Rick Martinez of Dell Technologies argues that a PC maker's threat model must cover what happens before a device ships and below the operating system. He cites figures tying 70% of breaches to the endpoint and finding that 63% of surveyed customers believed they had faced an exploited hardware or silicon flaw. Weak firmware, boot chain or supply chain links undermine every security tool built above them.

Shark films serve as a framing device. Jaws represents the visibility gap below the OS, Mike Brody's perimeter gate stands for physical access, The Meg for firmware tampering, and Deep Blue Sea for insider threats. A brief timeline runs from the Hacking Team leak and a 2017 proof of concept mixing boot-path tampering with ransomware, to the first in-the-wild UEFI rootkit in 2018 and firmware and supply chain campaigns in 2019 and 2020. The SolarWinds build-system compromise is singled out as the most telling case. A bottom cover can come off in about 30 seconds with no tools.

Mitigations are split into today and tomorrow. Today that means UEFI scanning, TPM-based boot measurements, chassis intrusion detection, replay-protected flash and feeding firmware alerts into existing monitoring tools. Looking ahead, he wants firmware resilience frameworks adopted widely, attestation extended beyond boot, and reference measurements and SBOMs published. His closing requests: developers should add below-OS threats to their threat models, customers should press vendors to publish their assumptions, and firmware belongs in patch management.

talks.title: Critical Infrastructure Network Attacks: Code Red, Alert Network Operators
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Critical Infrastructure Network Attacks: Code Red, Alert Network Operators.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Israel Barak, CISO at Cybereason, presents findings from a honeypot study designed to emulate an electric transmission substation network. Using internal and external network identifiers closely mirroring a major electricity provider, the research aimed to track evolving adversary tactics, techniques, and practices (TTPs) across combined IT and operational technology (OT) environments. The findings revealed that industrial control system (ICS) environments are no longer targeted solely by advanced persistent threat (APT) or nation-state groups; cybercrime threat actors are actively targeting critical infrastructure using multi-stage ransomware playbooks.

### Key Topics
- **Ransomware Evolution**: Contrasting traditional single-stage ("shotgun") ransomware—which detonates immediately upon impact with low customization and blunt tools—with multi-stage ransomware operations. Multi-stage attacks function as comprehensive post-breach hacking campaigns aimed at high extortion payouts by executing credential theft, data exfiltration, lateral movement, and simultaneous detonation across critical enterprise systems.
- **Honeypot Architecture**: Modeled after a typical electrical transmission substation featuring an external DMZ with remote technician interfaces, firewall segregation between IT and OT segments, Windows and Linux hosts, openSCADA-based Human-Machine Interface (HMI) systems, and ICS controllers, all monitored via Cybereason endpoint sensors.
- **IT-to-OT Traversal**: The observation of cybercrime actors possessing ready playbooks to pivot across firewalled segmentation from corporate IT networks into OT networks.

### Technical Details
- **Initial Access & Persistence (Days 0–2)**: Two days after connecting the honeypot to the internet, automated scanning brute-forced the local administrator password on an external Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) remote technician interface. The actor performed active directory and reverse DNS discovery, used PowerShell to deploy first-stage tooling and initiate data theft, and created a backup local administrator account for persistence.
- **Lateral Movement & Tool Staging (Days 4–23)**: Following an apparent handoff between threat actors, the secondary operator dumped credentials from memory using Mimikatz and moved laterally through the IT environment using SMB and PsExec. The actor staged commodity ransomware into temporary folders on compromised hosts without detonating it, while stealing data files.
- **OT Pivot (Day 23)**: After 19 days of navigating the IT environment, the attacker discovered an IT service with access to the HMI data stream. The adversary exploited a web service vulnerability in the openSCADA HMI to pivot across the firewall into the Linux-based OT segment.
- **OT Lateral Movement & Detonation (Days 23–24)**: Inside the OT network, the actor utilized the pass-the-ticket technique and SMB to propagate across hosts, exfiltrating data via command-and-control channels and staging ransomware. On day 24, after exhausting lateral movement opportunities, the ransomware was detonated simultaneously across both IT and OT environments, shutting down systems and issuing a ransom demand.

### Takeaways
- **Broadening Threat Landscape**: The attacker exhibited commodity tooling (Mimikatz, PsExec, standard discovery utilities) indicative of cybercrime groups rather than stealth-focused APTs, yet possessed a dedicated playbook for pivoting from IT to OT.
- **Adversary Risk in Fragile Environments**: Untrained or profit-motivated cybercrime actors operating in fragile legacy ICS environments are prone to causing unintended, severe operational disruptions and physical failures out of ignorance.
- **Unified IT/OT SOC Visibility**: Organizations must unify security operations center (SOC) monitoring across IT and OT rather than isolating OT to a network operations center (NOC), ensuring visibility across IT-to-OT transit points.
- **Proactive Threat Hunting**: Relying solely on static alerts or immediate detonation indicators is insufficient against multi-stage operations that dwell for weeks. Proactive threat hunting and behavioral endpoint detection are essential to detect and remediate intrusions before payload detonation.

talks.title: Scaling Your Defenses: Next Level Security Automation for Enterprise
talks.teaser: Explains how to move a SOC from manual alert handling to scored, staged automation, up to machine learning.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how security operations teams can shift from hand-running every alert to automated workflows, freeing analysts for more complex threats. The speaker places automation on a five-level scale, starting with fully manual handling and single-request orchestration, moving through automated analysis, and ending with end-to-end SOAR. He argues that alert volumes keep rising faster than the number of skilled staff available.

The end-to-end incident response workflow spans alert ingestion, data collection, analysis, remediation and reporting. Ingestion favours endpoint and proxy or firewall alerts over raw feeds. Analysis builds in stages: scoring a single indicator, such as a VirusTotal detection count; a heuristic that sums scores against a threshold with source trust weighting; and a machine learning model trained on past alerts and metadata like ASN and geolocation, able to score new domains without external lookups.

The closing section covers tuning automation to the organisation's risk and disruption tolerance, keeping manual checks, and collecting statistics. A rollout example grows from about five playbooks handling 50 to 100 events a day in 2017, to about 25 playbooks and 25,000 events a day in 2019, and roughly 41 playbooks aiming for 100,000 events a day by late 2021. The suggested starting plan runs over 30 days: validate manual steps, build a first scoring algorithm, compare it with manual results, then back-test any model.

talks.title: A Primer: Getting Started with MITRE Shield
talks.teaser: Introduces the MITRE Shield knowledge base of active defense tactics, techniques and use cases, linked to ATT&CK.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces MITRE Shield, a newly published knowledge base of active defense ideas with a focus on defensive adversary engagement. The presenters say the approach comes from more than ten years of MITRE applying these methods to defend its own corporate network. They trace it to an earlier APT intrusion, where the team knew little about the adversary and decided to study it inside a synthetic, instrumented network instead of hacking back.

The walkthrough explains the Shield website, which mirrors the layout of ATT&CK with a matrix of eight tactics and techniques in the cells. Each entry links an ATT&CK technique to an opportunity space, a use case and the techniques a defender can apply, summarised as what you can gain, your goal, your plan and how you carry it out. A single technique can allow or block adversary behaviour depending on how it is applied. One example uses decoy credentials that are monitored for use to detect an intruder. A SolarWinds case shows where decoy processes, decoy data and decoy credentials could have influenced or revealed an attacker's actions.

For getting started, the presenters say there is no single path. Teams new to this can begin with threat sharing, threat-based defense and community connections, then move toward simple adversary engagement on a limited budget. They suggest starting with the first five tactic columns. Their practical warnings are to secure management and legal support before deploying deception, and to treat engagement as a way to build team skills and retention.

talks.title: Managing Privacy and Cyber In A Pandemic: Lessons Learned For 2021 & Beyond
talks.teaser: Explains pandemic privacy duties, HIPAA gaps, forensic report privilege and ransomware payment limits for employers.
talks.summary:
A privacy and cybersecurity lawyer explains how the pandemic has both sped up remote work and changed what employers ask staff to disclose. He urges teams to challenge whether reopening checks really need to record individual temperatures or the names of infected employees. Citing a survey, he notes that 76% of organizations asked employees to report COVID diagnoses, and that many shared data externally or skipped privacy review when adopting remote-work tools. He recommends deciding in advance how long test results are kept, how positive cases are communicated without naming the person, and how the data is securely disposed of.

He points out that HIPAA usually does not cover employee testing, so generic HIPAA clauses in vendor contracts give little protection and breach terms need to be spelled out. Remote work has also raised phishing, web application breaches and ransomware, which makes reasonableness, measured against current industry practice, a moving target. Security teams should join new business processes early and refresh data maps, training, continuity plans and incident response procedures. After a Virginia court ordered Capital One to disclose its forensic report, he argues that forensic work should be retained through counsel under a separate statement of work, with counsel actively directing it and the report kept to what is necessary.

On ransomware, he reviews an OFAC advisory that treats payments to sanctioned parties as strict liability and presumes denial of licenses, so organizations should set a payment policy before an attack. He also flags Hong Kong data centers as a concern now that Chinese national security authority extends there, prompting some companies to move assets to locations such as Tokyo and to write escalation procedures for staff served with government demands. He closes by urging teams to review reopening protocols, ransomware playbooks and security programs against peer practice.

talks.title: Lessons Learned Developing an AI Cyber Immune System: The Good, Bad & Ugly
talks.teaser: Reviews AI cyber defense lessons for critical infrastructure, covering human-data needs, adversarial limits, and physics-based detection.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames development of an early AI-driven industrial immune system meant to protect aviation, power grids, defense platforms, and healthcare. It argues that effective AI cyber defense still depends on human domain experts paired with data scientists, and on high-quality training data, while advances in storage, compute, and math enable better pattern recognition without removing analysts from the loop.

The middle section diagnoses converged IT and OT challenges: legacy industrial systems with weak authentication, enormous telemetry volume, and adversaries who can cause physical harm through legitimate control protocols once they reach human-machine interfaces. Signature and heuristic tools fall short; attackers also adopt machine learning, poisoning, and evasion. Pandemic-era remote connectivity illustrates how brittle baselines produce crippling false positives. The speaker contrasts those limits with research directions such as explainable, humble, and trust-oriented AI.

The closing focus is Digital Ghost, built around a high-fidelity digital twin and physics-aware monitoring using dozens of machine learning algorithms to detect, localize, and neutralize abnormal sensor behavior, with reported live plant testing at 99% detection accuracy. Practitioners are urged to judge investments by false-positive rates, OT protocol coverage, resilience after compromise, and the people and processes around the technology rather than treating AI as a replacement for cyber staff.

talks.title: Sweeping the Area: Cleaning out Cloud Risk to Maintain Business Continuity
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh shared responsibility, provider transparency, and cloud-specific incident response for business continuity.
talks.summary:
A closing panel for a half-day cloud risk seminar brought together four presenters to discuss how organizations can keep business running when cloud risk is not fully understood. The moderator opened by asking what a comprehensive cloud risk program should include. The speakers described shared responsibility models, checking provider frameworks and certifications, weighing the sensitivity of the data being moved, and using automated governance to keep an asset inventory current as usage grows.

Discussion then turned to what providers can do to help customers. Panelists asked for greater transparency and digestible documentation, and pointed to blueprints, recommendation services and self-service audit reports as useful tools. Examples of costly mistakes included storage buckets shared with all authenticated accounts, which the speaker said actually means any account on the provider, and one-off resource spin-ups that bypass policy. The advice was to combine policy, training, internal detective controls and segmentation, and to test cloud-specific incident response plans through tabletop exercises and hands-on game days.

Closing points covered vendor questions on physical access, staff access approvals, key management and monitoring, plus planning for regional or provider outages, including multicloud designs. Logging was framed as a tuning problem, with teams defining use cases to cut noise and learning each provider's log formats before an incident. The panel stressed that readiness has to be practiced in advance.

talks.title: Cloud Configuration: Mitigate Risks from Cloud Security Failures
talks.teaser: Walks through common cloud misconfigurations in IAM, security groups and storage, and how to reduce them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that cloud misconfiguration is a leading cause of cloud security problems, citing industry research on how common it is and what breaches cost. Moving from a traditional data center to the cloud expands the attack surface. The shared responsibility model splits duties: the provider secures hardware, networking, storage and facilities, while the customer secures its data, applications, identity and access management, and operating system and firewall settings.

Common mistakes are covered next. Identity and access management is often over-permissioned, with one account holding full control, shared credentials and no multi-factor authentication. Security groups are misused by attaching the wrong group to a service, reusing defaults and opening all ports to all sources. Public storage is easy to overlook, and the "authenticated users" option in AWS grants access to any AWS customer. Missing logging and object versioning hinder audits and rollback. Causes include unclear responsibility, default settings, quick spin-ups that skip security steps, missing templates and limited training.

For mitigation, the speaker recommends a security baseline beyond compliance requirements, continuous discovery of misconfigurations, least-privilege reviews, and automated deployments from approved templates. The speaker describes Cisco Secure Cloud Analytics as a tool the speaker's team uses for visibility into entities, traffic and threats. The takeaway is to know which controls fall to your team under the shared responsibility model.

talks.title: Enhancing Visibility for Cloud Security Operations
talks.teaser: Shows how to regain visibility into cloud environments through native logging, configuration monitoring and automated remediation.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with why cloud adoption erodes security teams' view of their environments. Citing a cloud security survey, the presenter notes that most respondents are concerned about public cloud security, with data loss and privacy at the top, and that a lack of qualified staff and visibility gaps rank highly. He compares on-premises, private and public cloud models, explaining that multi-cloud adds differences between providers, and that short-lived scaling resources and microservices make data movement harder to track.

The middle section lays out a framework: inventory cloud assets, study cloud-specific attacks using MITRE ATT&CK's cloud content and Cloud Security Alliance guidance, plan the visibility strategy, centralize and correlate logs, and automate remediation. He then walks through provider tools. A CloudWatch filter traces one user's activity after a suspicious access key is created. Security Hub scores the account against CIS and AWS best practices and flags a root account without multi-factor authentication. GuardDuty surfaces SSH brute force attempts and root credential use. AWS Config shows a security group's changes over time, and Macie flags confidential content in a bucket meant for public files. He notes that provider tools leave gaps, so third-party products may be needed, particularly for serverless and container workloads.

The closing part covers posture management tools for a single view across environments, automatic remediation of obvious mistakes such as public buckets, and staff training through hands-on exercises and game days. The main takeaway is to plan first, make logs actionable, fill tooling gaps where they exist, and invest in people.

talks.title: Protecting Privacy In The Cloud: Key Considerations and How to Implement
talks.teaser: Maps the privacy challenges of cloud adoption, from data sovereignty and compliance to governance, encryption and policy as code.
talks.summary:
Michee Smith, a product manager on a data protection and privacy team at a major cloud provider, sorts business privacy concerns into three groups: data access and sovereignty, compliance with laws and frameworks, and user privacy. Customers ask whether their data stays confidential, who at the provider can reach it, what happens to encryption keys when a service lacks customer-managed key support, and whether foreign government requests could expose it. Compliance questions center on overlapping regulations and on evidencing controls under shared responsibility, since many standards were written for on-premises environments.

The middle of the talk surveys market responses. For data governance, she points to provider inventory systems used to build data maps and retention rules, classification at collection time, and policy as code, which lets teams preview policy changes before production. For data protection, she covers externally held keys, confidential computing for encryption in memory, field-level encryption tied to identity, and de-identification such as differential privacy for research sharing. She also notes recommender services that use usage metadata, and continuous compliance monitoring that is starting to extend into privacy.

She closes with practical steps: build privacy policies around data classification so controls apply automatically, use proxies to keep unapproved data from leaving on-premises systems in hybrid setups, and reduce regulatory scope by anonymizing data where possible. Teams should fold provider audit reports and access logs into their own compliance processes and assess which frameworks fit cloud-native or lift-and-shift designs now, not later.

talks.title: Insights on Modern Day Cyberwarfare: Considerations from the SolarWinds Breach
talks.teaser: Weighs whether the SolarWinds intrusion counts as cyber warfare, and how layered deterrence and collective defense apply.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a question about whether the SolarWinds breach counts as cyber warfare. The speaker explains that cyber warfare is usually framed as an armed attack under international law, one that destroys or corrupts something, and that espionage typically falls outside that definition. The intrusion is described as large-scale intelligence collection against government bodies and other companies, with access lasting months, and no evidence yet of data being destroyed or manipulated.

The speaker argues the picture could shift if intruders start threatening to use their access, which would edge toward warfare. Responses to pure intelligence collection could include closing embassies, expelling spies, or exposing collection methods, while more offensive measures or preemptive self-defense might follow if an attack looked imminent. He says the US has not clearly stated its red lines or what it would do if they were crossed, partly because cyber capabilities are classified. A figure cited from just after the breach says 50% of CEOs now express concern about nation-state attacks.

On layered deterrence, the Solarium Commission's idea of collective defense is central. Organizations currently defend themselves individually, while the threat is a national-scale campaign. The speaker urges every company and agency to assume it could be targeted, to hunt inside its networks and watch traffic in and out, and to share data across companies, industries and government initiatives. The closing point is that the nation must defend as one, with government and industry working toward a shared mission.

talks.title: SolarWinds Breach: An RSAC Interview with Dmitri Alperovitch About Who, How and Why
talks.teaser: Covers scale and mechanics of the SolarWinds Orion supply-chain intrusion, SVR-linked espionage motives, and assume-breach hunting guidance.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens amid active exploitation alerts affecting Orion customers, including reported compromises at major U.S. agencies. The guest frames the incident as potentially one of the most consequential cyber-espionage campaigns to date, because SolarWinds Orion reaches over three hundred thousand organizations worldwide, including large enterprises and sensitive government users. Attackers reportedly compromised build infrastructure, implanted a backdoor in software updates, and thereby gained access across a vast customer base, though operational limits mean truly exploited victims likely number in the hundreds rather than everyone who could have been reached.

Attribution discussion centers on SVR, described as a Russian civilian intelligence service focused on espionage rather than destructive operations, with parallels drawn to earlier DNC and government intrusions. The exchange covers immediate response: disabling affected Orion versions pending a patch, following federal binding guidance, and investigating using compromise indicators publicized after FireEye’s disclosure. SolarWinds’ own estimate that fewer than eighteen thousand customers received the malicious build is noted alongside the broader population still at risk.

Closing guidance stresses that even top-tier defenders can be hit, so organizations should plan around likely compromise, hunt continuously for adversary presence, and evict intruders quickly. While supply-chain attacks are unusually difficult to prevent, the speaker highlights softer network clues—such as abnormal service creation and callbacks to new domains—that diligent hunting can surface, crediting FireEye’s detection and transparency with revealing the campaign’s true breadth.

talks.title: Interview: What does the ransomware attack on Universal Health Services mean for the future?
talks.teaser: Examines how a hospital ransomware attack can delay care and endanger patients, and what that means for healthcare security.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with Cecilia Marinier of RSA Conference asking Beau Woods, of the Biohacking Village, what is known about a ransomware attack on Universal Health Services, one of the largest hospital systems in the United States. According to Woods, the attack hit over a weekend and several systems went offline. Some were shut down deliberately by the operator to stop the malware from spreading.

Woods then describes a German case in which a hospital was disabled by ransomware and a stroke patient was redirected to another facility and died en route. He stresses that the attack did not itself cause the death; the underlying medical emergency did. He points to research on delayed care, where an average delay of 4.4 minutes was linked to significantly higher mortality, to argue that even small disruptions can matter. He notes that losing electronic health records, lab systems and radiology imaging slows rapid decisions, and that diversion is a routine practice that can add far more than four minutes. He argues that healthcare security must prioritise availability and integrity over the confidentiality focus of most past defences, and calls for studies measuring how often ransomware or device attacks cause harm.

The closing turns to positive trends. Woods points to the rapid growth of telehealth during the pandemic, now reimbursed by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers, which brings earlier care, fewer trips and shorter waits, and he hopes these changes leave healthcare better off afterwards.
