talks.title: Through the Eyes of the Adversary: How to Build a Threat Intel Program
talks.teaser: Shows how to see conflicts through the adversary's eyes and structure a threat intel program around stakeholders.
talks.summary:
## Overview
This CrowdStrike presentation, delivered by Jason Rivera (Director of Strategic Threat Advisory Group) with Scott Jarkoff available for questions, teaches threat intelligence professionals how to build effective programs by understanding conflicts from an adversary's perspective. The core principle is that better understanding of adversary motivations, capabilities, and tactics enables organizations to communicate actionable intelligence to stakeholders and improve defenses.

## Key Topics
The presentation structures threat intelligence around a strategic-operational-tactical framework applied to both defender and adversary sides. It identifies three fundamental conflict types: security (nation-state threats), economic (financial crime), and ideological (hacktivism). Organizations are engaged with adversaries across three spaces: your environment, the adversary's environment, and contested space (the internet).

Adversary analysis focuses on motive (why attack), intent (extortion, espionage, destruction), capability (malware, DDoS, social engineering), infrastructure (botnets, C2, proxies), and TTPs (techniques, tactics, procedures). The model emphasizes understanding how adversaries target people, processes, and technologies across three access vectors: digital (exploits), physical (USB/supply chain), and psychological (social engineering, bribery).

## Technical Details
Three threat intelligence capability areas form the operational backbone:

**Intelligence Enrichment:** Consumes indicators of compromise and signatures to empower defensive systems. Includes IOC ingestion, sensor tuning, malware analysis, and automated sandbox analysis for timely, attack-telemetry-derived content.

**Threat Monitoring:** Monitors the internet (surface, social media, dark web, digital footprint) for leaked credentials, PII, brand infringement, malware, and malicious mentions. Critical to understanding adversary infrastructure and capabilities, though dark web should not be overemphasized—smart actors don't announce intent there.

**Threat Reporting:** Uses a "What, So What, What Next" model—describing what's happening, why it matters, and what actions stakeholders should take. Reports should be actionable and implications-focused rather than sector or geography-specific, since malware affects all industries.

Three stakeholder types require different intelligence products: strategic stakeholders (CSO, CIO, CTO) need decision-support intelligence; operational stakeholders (SOC analysts, threat hunters, vulnerability managers) need job-focused intelligence; tactical stakeholders (SIEM, firewall, EDR, IDS/IPS) need indicators and rules for automated blocking.

The presentation debunks common myths: more indicators cause false positives and false confidence; not all intelligence can be automated; dark web chatter is rare from sophisticated actors; and threats apply universally across sectors and geographies.

## Takeaways
Effective threat intelligence programs require: (1) adopting an adversary perspective to understand motive, intent, capabilities, infrastructure, and TTPs; (2) collecting intelligence across enrichment, monitoring, and reporting areas; (3) designing teams with strategic analysts (presenters), operational analysts (SOC-aware), and tactical analysts (malware experts); and (4) ensuring all intelligence activities serve defined stakeholders. Two detailed scenarios—financially motivated ransomware targeting domain admins and nation-state intellectual property theft—illustrate how to map these frameworks and identify appropriate defenses. The underlying principle remains: understanding conflict through the eyes of the adversary enables better strategic decisions, operational effectiveness, and tactical system tuning.

talks.title: Recent Trends in Information Operations and Predictions for 2020
talks.teaser: Surveys 2020 information operation trends, including fake news sites, deepfakes and Singapore's anti-falsehood law.
talks.summary:
Yao Lim, presenting from Singapore, defines information operations as deliberate distortion of news by actors with political, financial or trolling motives. He points to the 2016 US presidential election as a turning point and says the tactic has spread to more states and to subjects beyond elections, including the COVID-19 pandemic, where fake messages were used to harvest personal data or push conspiracy theories.

The middle of the talk walks through examples. A fabricated letter attributed to the Lithuanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs claimed the US would build a nuclear weapons base there. A compromised Kuwaiti state news agency reported that American forces would withdraw immediately. A Myanmar military Facebook post reused images from the 1971 Bangladesh independence war. He describes Iranian-origin news sites linked by registration data to a marketing firm in India, and a non-state website tied to the Falun Gong. He covers AI-generated profile photos, a news clip demonstrating deepfake video, and how the same concern applies to ordinary people. He then outlines Singapore's POFMA law, prompted by a hoax about a collapsed roof at a private apartment, and what it means for businesses publishing content there.

He closes by predicting that governments will keep using these tools, including against rivals, and that AI-generated media will grow. His practical advice is to cross-check social media claims against official government sources, stay skeptical even of established news outlets, and help friends and family question what they receive in messaging groups.

talks.title: Threat Hunting
talks.teaser: Lays out a five-phase, hypothesis-driven model for proactively hunting attackers who have slipped past automated defenses.
talks.summary:
The session presents threat hunting as a hypothesis-driven, iterative practice for finding attackers who are already inside an environment after evading automated defenses. Breach statistics frame the problem: many breaches are found by outside researchers, and some take months or longer to uncover. The speaker also notes the volume of events a typical mid-sized organization produces, which makes useful signals hard to pick out.

A five-phase model runs through baselining and objectives, including sponsorship and a framework such as MITRE ATT&CK; setting targets by choosing data sources such as NetFlow, proxy, DNS and endpoint logs while cutting noise; building an arsenal of threat intelligence, SIEM and EDR platforms and Sysmon; execution, starting with crown jewels, forming a hypothesis and applying searching, clustering and stacking; and improvising, where results and visibility gaps feed back into the first phase. The worked example hunts for command-and-control channels using proxy, DNS, SMTP and NetFlow data, frequency analysis of queries, and fields such as bytes in, bytes out and session time to spot regular beaconing.

The speaker stresses that hunting does not replace preventive or signature-based controls, and that tools only help when they are well configured and supported by process. Recommended next steps include gauging maturity, identifying critical assets and studying adversary TTPs, then running short sprints before moving to periodic hunting campaigns.

talks.title: You See Honey, I See Beehive: Developing Honey Networks
talks.teaser: Explains scalable breach detection through NetFlow phantom tripwires, simple honeypots, and SIEM dashboards centered on reconnaissance.
talks.summary:
Joseph Muniz frames defense as a moving target: edge blocking with firewalls and antivirus still fails against packed malware and changing attacker paths, so organizations need breach detection that scales across branch, data center, and cloud. He argues the real risk is post-exploitation outcomes such as ransomware and remote access tools, and that dwell-time measured in weeks or months is unacceptable; the goal is response in hours.

The core method pairs two scalable layers. Phantom networks use rich NetFlow (he recommends NetFlow 9, not sampled flow) to baseline normal traffic and stand up fake network segments that should never be touched; reconnaissance against those segments becomes a tripwire, with customer examples including unauthorized port scanning from an X-ray system in a DISA-style environment. Honeypots fill gaps when attackers scan narrowly: he favors low or medium interaction decoys, often with IoT-style personas, warns against misconfigured internet-exposed honeypots, and notes attackers can probe for honeypots with tools such as Kali and Metasploit detectors.

Anomaly and behavior detection reinforce each other—stealthy insiders look abnormal on NetFlow while noisy recon trips honeypots or phantoms. Logs should flow into a centralized SIEM, SOAR, or XDR platform with simple widgets and alarms tuned to reconnaissance, whitelist expected vulnerability scanners, and optional integrations to packet capture or network access control for quarantine-style isolation rather than hard disconnects.

talks.title: Reality Under Attack: Just How Serious Is the Deep Fake Threat?
talks.teaser: Surveys how deepfakes are built, where they threaten businesses, and how organizations can respond to fake media.
talks.summary:
The talk frames deepfakes as an attack on human perception rather than on systems. It traces their spread from a 2017 research release and early misuse on Reddit for fabricated pornography, through a 2018 political fake of Barack Obama made with Jordan Peele, to business cases. These include a suspected 2019 deepfake audio call that reportedly preceded a €220 million transfer at a UK energy company, extortion risks from fabricated images, and a hypothetical fake video used to move a company's stock price.

The speaker explains how generative adversarial networks produce fakes: a generator creates frames while a discriminator scores their realism until the output is acceptable. Consumer options range from the open-source Faceswap to a paid hosted service, and an app that was pulled quickly is noted as a warning. A personal attempt after lengthy training still showed visible flaws. Detection methods are reviewed in turn: facial warping, which generators have largely overcome; eye blinking, which was soon reproduced; and behavioral analysis, which is still emerging. Single-image real-time tools such as Avatarify remain visibly flawed, and adversarial noise that disrupts facial recognition is described.

The closing argument is that deepfakes are a human problem, because false beliefs are hard to remove once they fit existing views, so rebuttals must offer facts that fit the same beliefs. For organizations, the practical steps are to keep official channels as the sources of record, to fold fake-media response into the incident response plan, to monitor for fabricated content about the company, and to follow legislation and detection research while avoiding overhyped products.

talks.title: Cyberespionage: Targeted Attacks Abusing Third-Party Cloud Services
talks.teaser: Shows how APT groups abuse legitimate cloud storage, chat and publishing services for malware command and control and theft.
talks.summary:
The talk compares custom malware infrastructure, where attackers register domains and run their own command servers, with malware that relies on popular third-party cloud services for configuration, command and control, and data upload. The speaker argues that these services are cheap, reliable and hard to block without disrupting ordinary users.

Several espionage groups are walked through. A South Asia-linked group's BadNews backdoor fetched encrypted configuration from GitHub, WordPress and Feed43, and searching GitHub for a shared file name surfaced many similar configurations. Confucius used Dropbox and pCloud to store stolen files, with API keys and credentials recovered from decompiled Python code. Even when a storage account looked empty, the Dropbox listing call revealed victim folders and file names. A Middle Eastern group, MuddyWater, used Dropbox as a command channel in a PowerShell backdoor and used a Telegram bot API in an Android app to send bulk device data. A group with North Korea-related interests used GitHub gists for commands, Slack for results and file.io for exfiltration, and later moved commands into pinned Slack messages with fallback tokens published on a micro-blogging site.

The speaker stresses that cloud traffic is encrypted, so blocking IP addresses or domains has limits. Service APIs and stored history, however, let researchers track victims, campaigns and commands using the tokens found in malware. Reporting abused tokens to providers can cut off attacker access, giving defenders a way to monitor actors without hacking back.

talks.title: Getting the Security and Flexibility Balance Right in a COVID-19 World
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Getting the Security and Flexibility Balance Right in a COVID-19 World.

talks.title: Taking Control of Cyber-Supply Chain Security
talks.teaser: Shows how hidden software dependencies spread vulnerabilities across supply chains and how software bills of materials help expose them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a hospital MRI and an Airbus A380 to show how one flaw can travel through a supply chain. The Urgent/11 vulnerabilities in the VxWorks real-time operating system were traced back to the Interpeak IPNet TCP/IP stack, which had been licensed to Green Hills Software and then ended up in devices and aircraft far downstream. The speakers argue that modern software is built on layers of other software, so these chains keep getting longer and harder to see.

The speakers sort supply chain risk into four groups: supplier-facilitated risk, counterfeit or unlicensed components, malicious taint by well-resourced adversaries, and unintended taint from known but unmitigated vulnerabilities. They then look at the problem from three roles: software producers who need to know what they ship, buyers who evaluate the components they select, and operators who must check whether a newly disclosed issue affects them. A software bill of materials, described as an ingredient label, records components, suppliers, versions and hashes. The talk points to existing formats such as SPDX and SWID, and to a proof of concept in which hospitals and device makers exchanged this data.

For practitioners, the talk recommends asking vendors whether they provide SBOMs and how long they will support security updates. It also suggests using model procurement language, such as the Mayo Clinic's, to clarify accountability in contracts, and running tabletop exercises with and without an SBOM to compare response times and costs. Monitoring components for new vulnerabilities or backdoors and joining NTIA working group discussions were also suggested as next steps.

talks.title: Securing Your M&A Activity with Cybersecurity Due Diligence
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Securing Your M&A Activity with Cybersecurity Due Diligence.

talks.title: Explore Adventures in the Underland: Forensic Techniques against Hackers
talks.teaser: Walks through Windows memory and disk forensics, from recovering corrupted event logs to tracing an SMB relay intrusion.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through Windows forensics, beginning with memory. Using Volatility on a memory dump, the presenter finds the svchost process that hosts the Windows event log service by checking loaded DLLs. Its file handles are then dumped, which yields EVTX logs, and a free recovery tool repairs a corrupted log so it can be opened and read.

Next comes a demonstration of an SMB relay attack, which works where SMB signing is absent and NTLMv2 is used. After a reverse shell reaches SYSTEM and migrates into another svchost, the attacker's original process disappears from the process list. Netstat still reports that vanished process ID, so its output cannot be trusted. Prefetch files instead record what ran, including run counts and loaded DLLs, although administrators can delete them. On disk, PowerShell with the Power Forensics module lists deleted MFT records, reads data runs and carves a deleted executable from its cluster offsets, then checks whether the file is digitally signed.

The closing advice is to write a solid incident response plan and prepare a toolkit for collecting evidence before an incident, since responders work under stress. The tools shown are free and are described on the presenter's blog.

talks.title: How Protocol Gateways May Introduce More Problems than They Solve
talks.teaser: Shows how Modbus protocol gateways add flaws, including translation errors that let crafted packets slip past ICS firewalls.
talks.summary:
Philippe Lin, a researcher on Trend Micro's forward-looking research team, examined protocol gateways, small devices that translate between industrial protocols such as Modbus TCP and Modbus RTU. The talk separated two types: real-time gateways that translate each packet as it arrives, and data stations that translate asynchronously through I/O mapping tables. The team tested three real-time gateways and two data stations, priced from $200 to $650, using a heavily modified boofuzz fuzzing framework on a Raspberry Pi based test rig.

Findings covered several classes. Some gateways ran out of resources under heavy traffic, one stopping after roughly 400 packets, and one rebooted under stress. A crafted read request crashed one data station, and another exposed a built-in Modbus command that could reboot it. Legacy flaws ranged from a low-privilege ping page that opened a root Telnet session without credentials, to an encrypted configuration database that could be decrypted, and a random number generator without a seed that enabled replay of admin password data. The most novel issue was translation error: one gateway stripped headers without checking payloads, and another turned error responses into valid write commands that an ICS firewall would pass. A one-to-one I/O mapping let an attacker overwrite internal memory. Cloud links over MQTT lacked encryption and input validation.

For practitioners, the talk urged listing gateways as critical assets, reviewing their rules, whitelisting access, asking vendors for patches, scheduling firmware upgrades, and choosing firewalls that inspect packet content rather than just format. Detailed technical findings were withheld until vendors fix the issues, with release planned for mid-August.

talks.title: Detection as Code: Detection Development Using CI/CD
talks.teaser: The session maps CI/CD onto detection engineering, from schema-based rules through lab tests to packaged SIEM deployment.
talks.summary:
Defenders face a shifting threat landscape, and detections that worked months ago may miss changed command-and-control or tooling. The presenters frame detection engineering like software delivery: commit rules, build and convert them for each platform, validate structure, test against realistic telemetry, then deploy. They contrast broad anomaly products with schema-driven rule libraries such as Sigma and Splunk Security Content, which stay readable, product-agnostic, and enforceable in pipelines while still feeding machine-learning stacks.

Version control enables branching so large SOCs can work in parallel, tag releases, and share packages across business units. Conversion turns shared YAML into SIEM-specific searches and scheduling metadata. Continuous integration runs checks—for example via CircleCI—on field correctness, successful packaging, and vendor-specific app validation before anything reaches production. Continuous testing belongs in a detection lab that mirrors logging and tooling, not on domain controllers in production; adversary simulation with Atomic Red Team or Caldera generates logs to develop or verify rules, with pass-or-fail reporting wired into the pipeline.

They highlight Mordor labs and Mordor datasets for Azure lab templates and prerecorded events, and Attack Range for local Vagrant or AWS Terraform builds with Ansible, attack simulation by MITRE technique ID, and search-based detection checks suitable for CI jobs. Deployment paths include SIEM apps, forked Git projects with local tuning, or API releases enriched with metadata. Practitioners are urged to stand up a lab, adopt a detection CI/CD workflow within months, test continuously, automate further, and contribute rules openly.

talks.title: Beyond Penetration Testing: Developing a Defensive Cyber-Workforce
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Beyond Penetration Testing: Developing a Defensive Cyber-Workforce.

talks.title: How to Tell the Right Cyber-Story to Executives and Board Members
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how to turn technical findings into business risk language that executives and board members can act on.
talks.summary:
Ian Yip explains why security teams often fail to win over executives and boards. Practitioners tend to report technical measures such as alert counts and vulnerability totals, which are hard for non-specialists to interpret. Drawing on more than 100 conversations and a study of what leaders care about, he argues that executives focus on risk, controls, organisational measures and financial impact. He points to a costly NotPetya incident and a prediction that boards will question cyber risk at least once a year.

The core of the talk is a balanced-scorecard style structure: an objective, the current position, the target, and the measures and actions to reach it. Each technical finding should be tested with the question "so what". Five hundred cloud vulnerabilities become a risk of sensitive data exposure and regulatory fines, while unpatched servers become a risk to system availability that could halt financial transactions. Preparation means defining risk tolerance levels, rating current risk from red to green, costing risks where possible, and scoring capabilities against a framework with target numbers.

For delivery, speak plainly, start high level and go into detail only when asked, and make slides look polished. A one-page scorecard can show a headline figure, such as a resilience score moving from 25 to a target of 42, with red items flagged for discussion. The talk closes with three actions: confirm you can articulate risks, tolerance levels and capabilities next week, set target outcomes within three months, and make reporting repeatable within six months.

talks.title: Forced Digital Transformation and the Realities to ICS/OT Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains why rapid remote connectivity in industrial plants raises risk, and how to prioritize critical sites and controls.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the rapid move toward remote and hyper-connected industrial operations that the pandemic accelerated, and why it brings both opportunity and risk for control systems. The speaker notes that industrial control systems predate networking and that IT and OT convergence began about a decade ago. Two cases make the business argument: a utility that remotely monitored transformers and estimated about $8 million saved through predictive work, and a petrochemical operator whose analytics project was credited with $17 million a year and a 36% reduction in unplanned downtime.

On the threat side, the speaker says the state groups tracked against industrial environments depend heavily on remote access, and cites Crash Override, Trisis and Ekans ransomware as examples. He argues that enterprise security playbooks copied into plants often fail because the mission involves physical processes, and urges security leaders not to become the blocker to remote operations.

The practical part is a phased strategy. Start by identifying digital transformation stakeholders and ranking physical sites by criticality with a formula agreed with business leaders. Build risk scenarios from past incidents, geopolitical awareness and consequence thinking, map each attack step, then choose architecture, passive and active defenses. Protect the top 10 percent of assets first, report against scenarios instead of raw scan counts, and follow a timeline from post-conference rest through a 180-day rollout.

talks.title: Authentication and Beyond Using FIDO and Push Notifications
talks.teaser: Shows how eBay pairs FIDO keys with push notification approvals to add secure sign-in across web and mobile.
talks.summary:
eBay runs a large global login service with many existing sign-in methods, from passwords and email or SMS codes to knowledge-based checks and third-party identity providers. Any new option has to balance security, usability and maintainability, because legacy options are hard to retire. FIDO fit those needs: the server keeps only a public key, so a server-side breach exposes no secret, and nothing secret crosses the wire.

For web and other platforms, eBay pairs its existing FIDO deployment from the mobile apps with push notifications. A signed-in user registers a key pair, and the private key stays on the device. At web sign-in, a push reaches the registered device carrying only a short-lived, single-use transaction identifier. The app asks the user to approve or deny, signs the data with the private key, and the server verifies it against the stored public key. Because the payload is useless on its own, the team avoided a full TLS session for it. The same mechanism covers step-up checks, account recovery, trusted device management and session extension.

The speaker described hard problems: devices vary in local security, so the protocol uses whatever is available instead of requiring biometrics; backup access for users without their device remains open; and key rotation was handled by asking users for a gesture. WebAuthn was offered as an alternative primary method on ebay.com only, because the protocol does not span multiple top-level domains, and behaviour differs across Windows, Mac and Android. The talk concludes the system is not yet truly passwordless.

talks.title: Does Artificial Intelligence Need a General Counsel?
talks.teaser: Explains why AI projects need legal and compliance experts involved early to avoid biased or unlawful outcomes.
talks.summary:
This talk surveys where artificial intelligence is used in business, from customer experience and research to trading and insider threat detection. The speakers argue that systems predicting human behavior raise the sharpest legal and ethical concerns.

Several cases show how things go wrong. A naval close-in weapon system set to automatic fired at a test missile, and the rounds that missed kept flying and struck another ship's bridge, because its design only considered hitting the target. A loan-approval model trained on 250,000 past loans found that postal code predicted repayment, so it effectively reintroduced redlining. A police facial recognition system was 99% accurate only for white male faces because its training images were mostly of them. A résumé screening tool penalized résumés that mentioned women's activities and downgraded graduates of two all-women's colleges, and it was never deployed.

The speakers recommend bringing compliance, legal and regulatory experts into design, so they can define what a system must not do, such as geographic redlining, and what evidence would show it worked correctly. They also stress training and testing data that reflect the full population, since a test set split from the same source inherits the same bias, and early ethical review of fairness. Their closing point is that AI brings real benefits, but legal and regulatory problems found late can cost an organization far more than the system did to build.

talks.title: A Simplified and Practical Approach to Pursuing a Zero Trust Architecture
talks.teaser: Presents a phased, budget-aware Zero Trust model built around identity consolidation, confined trust boundaries and people risk scoring.
talks.summary:
The talk presents the CARE model (Conditional Access Responsible Enforcement), a Zero Trust approach meant to fit real constraints such as budget, staffing, timelines and legacy systems. The presenters name the references they drew on, including NIST SP 800-207, Gartner CARTA, Google BeyondCorp and Netflix's Lisa model. They walk through an access request from a user on a coffee shop network: a policy enforcement point asks a central decision point to weigh device health, a behavior-based user trust score and threat feedback before deciding between adaptive MFA and standard sign-in.

The middle section covers the building blocks. Identity comes first, so fragmented directories and HR or LDAP stores should be consolidated, legacy Active Directory groups normalized, and authentication and authorization, network access and admin policies managed centrally. Privileged access management is folded into the same workflow with credential vaulting and session recording. Trust boundaries are drawn as logical segments tied to workloads, with enforcement points placed close to the resource instead of at a single perimeter firewall. For people, a central data lake feeds an engagement portal and a confidence score that reflects each employee's security behavior and informs access decisions.

The rollout follows a walk, crawl and run sequence: map critical assets, data flows and identity stores first, then start small with segmentation and identity unification, and finally scale risk-based access across the enterprise with continuous logging and monitoring. The speakers suggest concrete early steps, such as understanding the current network topology in the first week and blocking insecure protocols and building a trust score within the first few months.

talks.title: Countering Persistent Threat Actors in APAC and Globally
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers regain access after cleanup through backdoors, password filters and web shells, and how to spot them.
talks.summary:
Mandiant responders Steven D'sa and Vincent Wong describe persistent threat actors in APAC and globally who return after being removed. They report attackers re-attempting access in about one in three cases over the past year, and nine in ten times in APJ a year earlier. These actors stay quiet, live off the land with built-in tools, and exploit gaps in visibility and budget. After a 2014 public report, APT1 changed its tools and parked domains to survive cleanup.

Attackers often return using prior knowledge such as network diagrams, internal portals and architecture documents. Backdoors covered include RDP tunnels built with Plink for full graphical access, web shells on internet-facing servers, and a scheduled task launching a PowerShell reverse shell. In a Citrix NetScaler case, a flaw led to a backdoor called NOTROBIN. A malicious password filter DLL captured about 800 to 1000 reset passwords in clear text. In a SharePoint case with a two to three day patch window, attackers used certutil to decode Base64 and drop web shells.

Defenders should widen investigations beyond infected hosts, iterate indicators and live response until scope is clear, and hunt for unexpected password filters, odd domain controller reboots and unsigned DLLs. The speakers also recommended reviewing IIS ISAPI filters, enabling command-line logging, blocking macros from internet files, and enforcing two-factor authentication on internet-exposed VPN, Citrix and OWA services.

talks.title: Effective Software Supply Chain Monitoring
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Effective Software Supply Chain Monitoring.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Michael Angelo discusses the persistent challenge of software supply chain security, drawing on a decade of experience building internal tooling. Drawing an analogy to bottled water—which seems pure until foreign additives are introduced—he explains that organizational security models can be weakened not by the overall brand or origin of software (whether commercial, homegrown, or open source), but by the third-party components nested inside it. Because commercial binary analysis tools can be cost-prohibitive, Angelo presents a blueprint and architectural lessons for creating an internal monitoring system to track components and correlate them with known vulnerabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Software Component Visibility**: Organizations rarely have full visibility into the software downloads, third-party libraries, and specific versions deployed in their environments.
- **Widespread Component Exposure**: A single vulnerable library can have massive reach. For example, Angelo cites statistics showing 324 OpenSSL vulnerabilities across 3,208 products, noting how widespread OpenSSL has been across hundreds of millions of websites and web-facing servers.
- **Data Collection and Identification**: Strategies for discovering components include inspecting product headers, copyright statements, license files, generating hashes to look up against the NIST Software Reference Library, or using free tools like the OWASP Dependency Checker.
- **Software Bills of Materials (SBOM)**: Requiring internal developers to declare components and asking external vendors for software bills of materials according to emerging standards.

### Technical Details & Tool Architecture
Angelo outlines how to design an internal tracking tool and relational database:
- **Database Schema & Nested Relationships**: The database must map products to components and subcomponents across multiple nested levels (e.g., Product 1 contains Component 2, which contains Component 3). It must link component IDs and specific version enumerations directly to CVE records.
- **Daily CVE Synchronization**: Because 20 to 30 new CVEs typically arrive daily, the system must update its CVE database regularly (allowing users to specify release years, such as catching 2019 updates during 2020) and run checks against both existing inventories and newly discovered products or machine portfolios.
- **User Interface and Querying Capabilities**: Helpful tool features include progress bars for network-transferred databases, displayed SQL/Access command strings for debugging, portfolio scanning (e.g., scanning an entire HR machine group), and specialized query views (e.g., listing all CVEs by component, listing components within a product, or finding component/CVE matches on specific machines).

### Takeaways & Triage Strategy
- **Triage and Status Tracking**: Finding a vulnerability in a component does not automatically indicate exploitability, as the affected functionality may not be enabled (such as unused modules in Tomcat). Teams must classify findings by relevance (Relevant, Not Relevant, Under Investigation) and mitigation status (Mitigated, Not Mitigated, No mitigation necessary).
- **Handling Data Inaccuracies**: The National Vulnerability Database (NVD) occasionally lacks complete information or contains errors; tracking systems must be resilient to missing fields and database errors.
- **Continuous Monitoring**: Effective supply chain security requires ongoing vigilance and triage rather than a one-time scan, ensuring newly published vulnerabilities against older software are flagged promptly.

talks.title: Inside the Mind of a Hacker: How a Light Bulb Almost Stopped Christmas
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Inside the Mind of a Hacker: How a Light Bulb Almost Stopped Christmas.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this RSA presentation, Joseph Carson, Chief Security Scientist at Thycotic, walks through a real-world ethical penetration testing engagement against a global shipping management company. The engagement was prompted by a surge in piracy attacks off the coast of Somalia and the Gulf of Aden targeting vessels scheduled to deliver holiday goods from Asia to Europe. Carson shares how his red team pivoted away from planned social engineering when physical reconnaissance uncovered an unexpected entry point: smart light bulbs.

### Key Topics
- **Evolving Attack Surfaces and IoT Risks**: How single-purpose connected devices (IoT) function as full-fledged networked computers that introduce overlooked entry points into enterprise environments.
- **The Failure of Traditional Perimeter Security**: Why static network perimeters, firewalls, and DMZs fail against stolen credentials and mobility, especially when attackers mimic trusted insiders.
- **Reconnaissance and Social Engineering**: Techniques used to build digital blueprints from public footprints, alongside common phishing lure themes (urgency, speeding fines, delivery notices).
- **RF and Physical Reconnaissance**: Using software-defined radios (SDR), antennas, and Raspberry Pis to identify radio frequencies, MAC addresses, and wireless assets around a facility perimeter.
- **Living off the Land and Lateral Movement**: Bypassing detection by utilizing native administration tools and customer software rather than noisy off-the-shelf exploitation toolkits.

### Technical Details
- **Reconnaissance**: While preparing a phishing campaign from a rented apartment near the target's headquarters, a red team member conducted a perimeter walk equipped with a backpack, antennas, Raspberry Pis, and software-defined radios (SDR) to analyze Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and GPS signals.
- **IoT Discovery**: Analysis of captured RF traffic revealed a recurring MAC address that mapped back to an IoT smart light bulb vendor. The team purchased identical units, tested known vulnerabilities, extracted the Wi-Fi credentials, and configured a Raspberry Pi to masquerade as a light bulb.
- **Initial Access**: The hijacked light bulb credentials provided initial access to the organization's guest Wi-Fi network rather than the corporate LAN.
- **Privilege Escalation and Lateral Movement**: Exploring the guest network in promiscuous mode revealed an unpatched conference room presentation PC containing four years of vendor presentations and financial files. The machine shared its local administrator password with employee corporate laptops. Employees routinely connected corporate laptops to the guest Wi-Fi during meetings to bypass corporate filtering. The red team compromised an employee laptop, installed a remote access tool, and maintained persistent access when the user reconnected to the internal domain network.

### Takeaways
- **Risk Assessments for IoT**: Every IoT device introduced to an organization must undergo a formal risk assessment addressing functionality, maintenance, and patching.
- **Rigorous Network Segmentation**: IoT devices, guest access, and internal corporate assets must be isolated so that compromise of a peripheral device does not expose client machines.
- **Patch Management Beyond Core Servers**: Peripheral systems like conference room PCs must be patched and maintained just as strictly as production servers.
- **Eliminating Password Reuse**: Unique local administrator credentials must be enforced to prevent immediate lateral movement across disparate machines.
- **Security Culture**: Organizations must treat employees as frontline detectors rather than security liabilities.

talks.title: Building Safety, Security and Resilience through Chaos
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Building Safety, Security and Resilience through Chaos.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show with Special Guest, George Takei
talks.teaser: An actor links Star Trek's themes of diversity and problem-solving to the human side of security.
talks.summary:
This closing session of RSA Conference 2020 Asia Pacific and Japan, held virtually, opened with host Hugh Thompson, the conference's Program Committee Chair. He described how video calls have become a daily part of work and how people's home lives show through them, and he argued that security professionals thrive on change. He stressed that people come before their job titles.

The conversation then turned to Star Trek. George Takei described how creator Gene Roddenberry used science fiction as a metaphor to comment on the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War. In that framing, the starship represented a diverse Earth, and its crew's differing perspectives were a strength. He also recalled a Star Trek IV plot that solved a problem through human ingenuity rather than technology alone. The two discussed how a leader makes bold decisions on incomplete information while relying on a group of voices that offer different views.

The discussion closed on a lighter note, with Takei's remarks on longevity and a hope that the conference would develop the shields he had called for in Star Trek VI. The main takeaway was that human problem-solving, including diverse viewpoints and calculated risk-taking, drives progress in security as much as technology does.

talks.title: It Hurt Itself in Confusion: No Distribute Scanners and Stealthy Malware
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in It Hurt Itself in Confusion: No Distribute Scanners and Stealthy Malware.
talks.summary:
This presentation examines No Distribute Scanners (NDSs)—also known as "counter AV"—and their critical role in facilitating cybercrime. NDSs are standalone websites that allow attackers to scan malicious files against dozens of antivirus products without sending detection reports back to the vendors, keeping malware stealthy. The speakers emphasize the severity of these services by opening with the case of Scan4You, run by Ruslan Bondars, which operated for eight years with 30,000 registered users before Bondars received a 14-year US prison sentence.

**Key NDS Services and Features:**
The presentation surveys approximately nine different NDS platforms. DynCheck emerged as the dominant service after Scan4You's takedown in 2016, serving both Russian and English-speaking criminal communities. All examined NDSs offered API access and static analysis; only two provided dynamic scanning capabilities. Static analysis inspects file format, string patterns, and entropy without execution, while dynamic analysis executes samples in isolated environments and monitors behavior, requiring significantly more computational resources (potentially 50+ virtual machines to test against 50+ AV products daily).

**Pricing Models:**
Three distinct pricing structures emerged: free models (static scanners only, supported by advertising), single/bundle scan pricing (DynCheck's static scan against one AV product cost approximately one cent), and subscriptions ($50–$300 USD monthly for DynCheck, depending on features). Subscription models typically bundle static and dynamic scans with API access.

**Malware Developer Workflow:**
The speakers outline how attackers exploit NDSs throughout the malware lifecycle: (1) Development—submitting code to identify which AV signatures trigger, then modifying to evade detection; (2) Advertising—displaying scan results as proof of quality (e.g., "only detected by 3 of 45 vendors"); and (3) Exploitation—using periodic scans every 5 days to monitor detection status and using domain-check features to verify command-and-control servers aren't blacklisted before launching campaigns.

**Advanced Integration:**
The research reveals deeper integration of NDSs into the criminal ecosystem. Crypters like Cyber Seal embed NDS functionality (CyberScan) to automatically verify encrypted malware against AV vendors. NDSs also offer API access for automation and integration into third-party tools, and some platforms (notably DynCheck) operate as back-end infrastructure for other NDS services, creating a tiered ecosystem.

**Architecture Insights:**
The speakers explain why dynamic scanners are rare: static analysis requires only command-line AV execution—simple and scalable. Dynamic scanning demands isolated virtual machines, daily AV database updates across all instances, snapshots for system reversion, and continuous infrastructure maintenance. This complexity increases operational costs and explains why most freely available NDSs offer only static scanning.

**Key Takeaways:**
Antivirus is not a comprehensive solution; threat actors actively monitor vendor responses and adapt accordingly. Researchers should identify major players in cybercriminal ecosystems, particularly high-impact services like DynCheck. Malware authors inadvertently provide intelligence by sharing NDS scan results, allowing defenders to identify emergent threats and determine which malware variants successfully evade detection.

talks.title: Third-Party Risk Management: Preventing the Next Stuxnet
talks.teaser: Shows how vendor access becomes an attack path, using Stuxnet as the example, and outlines a third-party risk program.
talks.summary:
Rafael Garcia opens by framing cyber risk as uncertainty multiplied by exposure, and argues that every organization is a possible target regardless of size. He points to attacks on financial, healthcare and energy organizations, including the 2015 grid attack in Ukraine, to show that third parties are part of that exposure.

The central case is Stuxnet. Malware targeting Siemens S7 PLCs changed the speeds of centrifuges at an Iranian nuclear plant, and the speaker explains that the attackers researched the plant's suppliers and delivered the code through a third-party vendor on a USB drive. The drives were not scanned before they reached the control network. He notes that industrial systems are often built without security in mind and that air-gapped networks are rarely truly isolated. He also summarizes the Carnegie Mellon Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model, which covers ten domains and treats IT and operational technology together.

The talk then lays out a third-party risk management lifecycle: planning, due diligence, contract negotiation, transition, continuous monitoring and termination. Practical steps include tiering vendors by criticality, using automated tools and questionnaires, scoring vendor security posture, tracking vendor locations, and reassessing vendors yearly or semi-yearly. The action plan asks organizations to identify critical assets and vendors immediately, select tools within three months, and be ready to replace vendors that fail security standards within six months.

talks.title: The Accountability Game: Streamlining Data Privacy across APAC and the Globe
talks.teaser: Shows how a fintech used ISO 27701 to build privacy governance across Asia Pacific rules.
talks.summary:
The session is a conversation between Rob Roe of OneTrust and Jason Lau, chief information security officer at Crypto.com, a fintech. The problem: privacy rules across Asia Pacific keep changing, many are modelled on the GDPR, and running a separate strategy for each region is hard. Jason explains why his company built an overall privacy governance model on a standard rather than chasing individual laws, and why ISO 27001 has to be in place before ISO 27701 can extend it.

Jason walks through the rollout. ISO 27001 took about eight to nine months, depending on company size, regions and staff. The privacy scope was set enterprise-wide, backed by management buy-in, a privacy policy and a privacy notice. Assets were ranked by risk, and privacy impact assessments were applied at the design stage so product teams could check what personal data they collect, whether it is sensitive, and how long it is kept. Standard templates for privacy notices and consent policies, adapted per region, were easier to maintain. Cross-border transfers were described as an early, ongoing project, with binding contracts as the current approach. Rob notes that many customers still track this work in spreadsheets and email, and that mapping third-party and fourth-party vendors is a growing difficulty.

The takeaway is that privacy depends on management commitment and cross-department process rather than any single system. Jason said his company believes it is among the first in the region to hold the 27701 certification for its sector. Rob closed by pointing to a white paper and a comparison of regional laws against the GDPR as follow-up material.

talks.title: Continuous Security by Design
talks.teaser: Shows how to scan container images for known vulnerabilities in build pipelines and gate Kubernetes deployments on the results.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Kubernetes handles scheduling and traffic routing but does not secure the processes running inside each container. By default, any container in a cluster can reach any other, so a compromised container can expose secrets or pivot to its neighbours. The speaker treats a container as a short-lived, mostly read-only Linux machine that should be hardened like any server.

Build-time checks come first: unit and integration tests, static analysis, a check for vulnerable packages, license compliance, and a policy gate that decides whether an image ships. Container scanning can run during the build, against a registry, against running production workloads, or through a Kubernetes admission webhook. Scanning in the build pipeline is preferred, since production scans only find problems after a vulnerable container is already running. The demo uses Anchore, an open source tool that inventories operating system and library packages and matches them against vulnerability data. It does not inspect individual files, so a manually added file would not be flagged. The speaker found the initial setup and feed sync slow, and showed a GitHub Actions workflow that fails the build when vulnerabilities are found.

The closing advice is that Kubernetes only protects the cluster itself, so teams must secure their containers. Save each image's package inventory so it can be rechecked against new vulnerability data later, and expire containers that become vulnerable.

talks.title: The Wolves Among Us… A Tale of APT’s Thievery
talks.teaser: Traces an incident response case in a Middle East government network where two APT groups overlapped.
talks.summary:
A Middle East government agency asked for help after finding evidence of an intrusion dating back to August 2018, including sensitive archives on a DMZ server. The archives were RAR files disguised as image files. Forensic review of the file system showed a credential-dumping tool dropped months earlier, followed by a temp file full of domain credentials. Logs led the team to an administrator workstation and a laptop used for SMB lateral movement, and persistence was a VBS script hidden in a scheduled task named after an Nvidia updater. The initial access came through a weaponized Excel macro sent to five internal users, and the tooling matched the OilRig group.

Remediation covered rebuilding compromised machines, a full domain password reset, removal of local authentication, and two-factor authentication for VPN access. A separate workstation held a Turla Gazer package and a legacy VirtualBox driver, which the team treated as a leftover from a 2016 Turla infection. Later, machines that had used OilRig's DNS channel began contacting the same command servers over BITS, revealing a new Turla implant. The implant ran through rundll32 processes, and Turla also planted a backdoor in the Outlook Web Access server that captured new logons into a hidden file.

The main lessons were not to assume a customer's remediation succeeded, not to assume an unrelated infection can wait, and not to assume a sophisticated attacker uses only its own infrastructure. Blocking the command server's full address range pushed the implant to a second C2, which exposed more indicators.

talks.title: Drone Penetration Testing and Vulnerability Analysis Framework
talks.teaser: Presents DRAT, an open-source Kali Linux framework that launches and reports on known attacks against consumer drones.
talks.summary:
Many drones communicate over WiFi or radio links and run IP-based software, so they inherit weaknesses that attackers can exploit. Manufacturers may not disclose product risks, and there is no central, open platform for drone penetration testing. The talk introduces DRAT, a drone attack tool built for Kali Linux. It has a local attack database with search and report generation, a user mode for launching existing attacks, and an admin mode for adding drones and attack modules.

Attacks were shown across several platforms. Against the DJI Tello, flooding its open UDP port disrupted the live video feed, a dictionary-based WPA2 passphrase crack was run with Aircrack-ng, and disrupting control commands left the controller without control of the drone. ARP poisoning cut the video while control remained, forcing a pilot to fly by line of sight. Against Hubsan drones, the same WPA attack applied, and MAC-spoofed authentication flooding disconnected the controller. For the DJI Mavic models, a HackRF was used to spoof GPS so the drone believed it was in a no-fly zone and landed automatically. Changing firmware configuration values, such as brake sensitivity, made flight behave erratically, and a repackaged DJI Android app bypassed login.

Work in progress targets the DJI Mavic Mini and Phantom, including USB sniffing between controller and phone and RTSP video streaming attacks. Public release on GitHub was pending review by funders and a government partner. The takeaway for practitioners is that controller links, default settings and companion apps all form part of a drone's attack surface.

talks.title: Don’t Worry, Be API: Addressing AppSec’s Newest Challenge
talks.teaser: Explains why API-based apps face different risks and walks through the OWASP API Security Top 10, focusing on access control.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that APIs now sit at the center of nearly every modern application, from microservices to IoT devices. Compared with traditional web applications, clients are more varied, servers return raw data for the client to assemble, and business logic shifts to the client side. The speaker names three sources of risk: a much larger attack surface, raw data moving between components without clear control over where it ends up, and fast DevOps pipelines that leave forgotten endpoints running.

The speaker explains that the OWASP API Security Top 10 was created to fill a gap left by web-focused guidance. Injection still appears but is less common, while access control is presented as the biggest challenge, covering object-level and function-level authorization and broken authentication. Excessive data exposure and mass assignment are illustrated with a mobile app that hid sensitive location data in the interface but still sent it to the client, and with a smart vacuum whose access control flaw exposed video feeds from many users. A misconfigured cloud database also exposed data from many Android apps.

The closing advice is to educate developers, keep an up-to-date API inventory because you cannot protect what you do not know exists, and build access control in from the start. Turning access rules into concrete developer requirements, such as letting each user read only their own document, is suggested as a practical step.

talks.title: The AppSec Error Loop: How We Can Stop Repeating Common Security Mistakes
talks.teaser: Explains why common application security flaws keep recurring and how developer training and in-tool guidance can break the cycle.
talks.summary:
Peter Danhiex, CEO and co-founder of Secure Code Warrior, argues that software security keeps repeating the same basic mistakes and that the approach of the last two decades is not working. He compares patching flaws again and again to repairing a tent with duct tape, and notes that software engineering is still a young profession. He cites estimates of the growing developer population and the volume of code written each year, and points to breach reports showing that many incidents involve old web flaws such as cross-site scripting and SQL injection.

He then reviews the tools and team model. In his view, static, dynamic and interactive scanners need specialist knowledge, produce false positives or negatives, run slowly and cover too few languages. Penetration testers often report generic fixes that developers cannot act on, and with roughly one AppSec specialist for every 200 developers, the central team becomes a bottleneck. Drawing on about a million secure coding challenges completed by developers at around 400 enterprises, he reports that developers answered SQL injection questions correctly about 60% of the time, while insecure direct object reference questions were answered incorrectly about 80% of the time.

His recommendations focus on people. Security should be built into engineering, with framework-specific microlearning delivered inside IDEs, ticketing systems and pull requests at the moment developers need it. Teams should find security champions, start with the top three weaknesses in their main languages, and measure whether those issues return after six months.

talks.title: The Four Horsemen of DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Four pillars address how teams secure pipelines when delivery speed, open-source dependencies, and weak controls outpace security.
talks.summary:
Organizations often accelerate DevSecOps with new stacks and CI/CD components while security teams struggle to keep pace, and delivery pressure can push security to the sidelines. The speaker outlines recurring pain points: unfamiliar pipeline tooling for cyber teams, neglected controls in fast releases, risky free and open-source dependencies, weak maker-checker and compliance habits in regulated settings, and solution architects who are not consistently threat-aware.

The core framework groups mitigation into four areas presented as the “good horsemen” of DevSecOps. Secure architecture design spans campus and branch networking, data centers, internet-facing services, edge devices such as ATMs and mobile apps, and WAN/LAN paths to SaaS— with examples like VDI for vendors and encrypted transit for core banking users. Secure code and binary review covers SAST, DAST, and IAST in the IDE and repository, vendor binaries, third-party libraries gated through scanning (e.g., Nexus firewall), and standardized, reviewed open-source tooling. Container and cloud security emphasizes image and runtime scanning, blue-green recovery for vulnerable workloads, MFA, VPC and IAM layering, encryption for burst cloud processing, and AI-assisted DDoS handling.

Continuous compliance closes the loop: automated policy checks (such as multi-reviewer rules), measurable thresholds like zero critical findings, auto-healing or rollback on breach, and near real-time validation with SLAs. The speaker argues that covering these four domains can secure roughly 75–80% of a DevSecOps journey, with the remainder requiring organization-specific gap analysis as the program matures.

talks.title: Implementing Critical Cybersecurity Controls in a DevOps Environment
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Implementing Critical Cybersecurity Controls in a DevOps Environment.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by the Vice President of the ISACA Singapore Chapter, this talk examines the integration of critical cybersecurity controls within DevOps environments. Against the backdrop of increased remote work, heightened cloud adoption, and a rise in sophisticated cyber attacks, the presentation emphasizes moving past the mindset of "if, but when" toward an explicit "assume breach" principle. The speaker outlines why standardizing security into continuous delivery pipelines (DevSecOps) through robust governance, cultural alignment, and automation is essential to protect modern cloud infrastructures without impeding delivery velocity.

### Key Topics
- **DevOps and Cloud Integration Risks**: While DevOps and cloud computing bring high-velocity deployment, elasticity, and infrastructure as code (IaC), they also introduce distinct risks. Automated workflows can rapidly replicate human errors, reduce visibility into low-level network and hardware layers, obscure patch deployment timelines, and blend traditional developer and operator duties, challenging classic segregation of duties.
- **Mindset and the 3 C's**: Effective DevSecOps requires an ingrained culture based on Collaboration, Communication, and Cohesiveness. The goal is to follow the spirit of security rather than treating it as a superficial compliance or checklist exercise, ensuring shared ownership across the software development life cycle.
- **Risk Optimization vs. Minimization**: Risk cannot be reduced to zero, making "minimizing risk" an endless resource sink. Instead, organizations must focus on optimizing risk to acceptable business thresholds, keeping risk ownership tied to decision-makers who control budgets.
- **Threat Modeling and Governance Frameworks**: Structured governance involves adopting recognized IT risk frameworks, performing threat modeling via the MITRE ATT&CK framework and Cyber Kill Chain tactics, and aligning controls with standards such as COBIT, CMMI, ISO, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (focusing heavily on detect, respond, and recover pillars).

### Technical Details
- **Tooling and Infrastructure as Code**: Configuration assurance and continuous integration/continuous deployment rely on tools like Jenkins, Docker, Kubernetes, Chef, Puppet, SaltStack, Ansible, and Terraform. The speaker notes threats such as cryptomining malware distributed via Docker Hub and guest-escape vulnerabilities like Meltdown and Spectre.
- **Pre-deployment and In-deployment Cloud Controls**: Key operational considerations include coordinating tabletop incident drills with cloud providers, evaluating asset criticality, planning for forensics (ensuring de-provisioned or breached instances are preserved before returning to the resource pool), and establishing clear RACI charts.
- **Baking Security into the Toolchain**: Practical measures include using Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP), CIS benchmarks to scan Docker images, secure code scanners, and tools like Qualys for asset tracking and vulnerability scanning. Security configurations should trigger automated application scans whenever infrastructure code updates.
- **Active Cyber Defense and OODA**: Emphasizing rapid incident detection and response via SIEM and SOAR platforms, incorporating threat intelligence, network security monitoring, and active threat hunting using the OODA loop.
- **Deployment and Remediation Strategies**: Vulnerability fixes can be rolled out via A-B testing or blue/green-style replacement, spinning up newly patched VM images and scaling down unpatched systems. For segregation of duties, the speaker recommends restricting developer access and maintaining detailed, auditable change control logs with a detection-centric approach.

### Takeaways
- Shift security left by designing and automating "security as code" into deployment pipelines, but balance it by maintaining robust monitoring and incident response capabilities on the right side of the lifecycle.
- Plan explicitly for cloud-specific incident response challenges, such as forensic image preservation and risk-based vulnerability remediation timelines with cloud service providers.
- DevSecOps succeeds only when cultural alignment (collaboration, communication, cohesiveness) is paired with measurable governance and automated assurance.

talks.title: Creating a Culture That Thrives with Disruption
talks.teaser: Maps openness, agency, and bias for action so leaders can build cultures that grow through disruption instead of freezing.
talks.summary:
Leaders face relentless crises and market shocks, yet many teams still cling to familiar routines because past success feels like a guarantee for the future. The speaker contrasts stuck cultures with flux cultures that constantly test ideas, share power, and treat disruption as fuel for growth rather than something to dodge.

Flux cultures rest on three beliefs. Openness builds trust through transparency, surfaces weak commitment, and makes failure visible so peers can help. Agency means everyone acts like an owner without waiting for permission, while leaders resist highest-paid-person opinion and adopt disciplined disagree-and-commit execution. A bias for action favors minimally viable data, reversible choices, short cycle times, and deadlines that force progress over perfection, illustrated with examples from large retailers, universities, and banks.

Sustaining change requires a cultural operating system: structure encodes values in org design, process strips waste through open crowd-sourced input, and lore uses rituals, symbols, and stories to reinforce belonging. Practitioners should audit formal and informal beliefs, align purpose statements, tune structure and process, and place cultural review on leadership agendas, treating culture as the engine that sets pace on the strategy road.

talks.title: Can Policing Prevent Cybercrime?
talks.teaser: Explores how global law enforcement coordinates with industry to reduce cybercrime through shared intelligence and prevention campaigns.
talks.summary:
Craig Jones, Interpol’s director of cybercrime, frames policing’s purpose as protecting communities in both physical and online spaces. He argues cybercrime is unlike commodity crimes because offenders abuse the same digital infrastructure legitimate users rely on, and that no single actor can shrink the playing field alone. The talk situates Interpol among 194 member countries and three global crime programs, with cybercrime work headquartered in Singapore.

The middle focuses on the COVID-19 shift: remote work, healthcare scams, phishing, ransomware against hospitals, malicious domains, VPN and teleconferencing risk, and slack-formed volunteer coalitions. Jones describes collecting partner data under strict processing rules, Project Gateway, fusion-center work with thirteen public-private partners, CERT coordination via FIRST, and operational outputs such as a malicious-domain taskforce (roughly 200,000 domains reviewed), Purple Notices on healthcare ransomware and COVID-themed malware, fifteen targeted cyber activity reports, and the four-week “Wash Your Cyber Hands” campaign reaching millions.

The close summarizes Interpol’s three pillars—threat intelligence, operations support without arrest powers, and capability building—including regional router remediation, new secure knowledge and operational platforms, and merging national victim data with private-sector feeds. Practitioners should treat prevention as continuous threat understanding, monitoring, business continuity clarity, remote-work policy, stronger partnerships, and hygiene awareness—not policing alone.

talks.title: 3rd-Party Cyber-Risk Mitigation by Using ISO Standards
talks.teaser: Explains how ISO 31000, 27001 and 22301 help organizations manage risks from their suppliers and wider third-party relationships.
talks.summary:
The speaker, presenting for BSI, begins by explaining ISO as an international federation of national standards bodies headquartered in Geneva, whose name is treated as a word rather than an abbreviation. Third-party risk is framed as wider than direct customers and suppliers, since organisations also connect to investors, contractors, regulators and interest groups, and risk at deeper supplier tiers can flow back to the organisation.

The middle of the talk walks through several standards. ISO 31000 is described as neutral guidance on risk management that cannot be certified and must be repeated regularly. ISO 27001 covers information security around confidentiality, integrity and availability, and its supplier clause calls for documented agreements, monitoring and audits of suppliers' information security, cascading down the supply chain. ISO 22301 addresses business continuity, using business impact analysis and risk assessment to keep operations running through disruptions such as earthquakes, terrorist attacks or pandemics, with partners and suppliers counted as dependencies. Organisational resilience is presented as the capacity to adapt and recover while keeping an acceptable level of function.

The closing section notes that ISO 31000 and 22316 are guidance documents, while 27001 and 22301 are certification standards. The speaker recommends reviewing these standards, identifying the risks that third parties pose, and within six months putting in place a process for proactive review of all third parties.

talks.title: Your Application is Mostly Written by Strangers
talks.teaser: Argues that most application code comes from outside developers, then walks through recent package breaches and how to respond.
talks.summary:
Edwin Kwan argues that most application code is written by outside parties through open-source libraries. In one Java Maven application he analyzed, 12 components were in-house and 268 were open-source, roughly 98% by count and by file size (504 kilobytes of internal code versus 86 megabytes of open-source libraries). He also cites a 2019 report stating that 85% of modern applications contain open-source components.

He then reviews recent incidents. The event-stream npm package changed hands, and the new owner added a malicious dependency that stole cryptocurrency wallet data, forcing npm to contact nearly 4,000 maintainers to clean up copies. A RubyGems library, strong_password, was found to contain remote code execution code that never appeared in its source repository. A developer reviewing changes line by line discovered it, and the cause was a compromised maintainer account protected by an old reused password, on an account created before two-factor authentication existed. A typo-named gem for atlas-client took close to 30% of downloads and, on Windows, swapped cryptocurrency addresses on the clipboard. British Airways was later fined $229 million over a breach of more than 380,000 credit cards, traced to 22 lines of malicious code in a common JavaScript library.

For practitioners, he recommends keeping a dependency list or bill of materials so exposure can be assessed quickly, and applying a lightweight review to new open-source additions based on need, active development, popularity, license and known vulnerabilities. Dependencies should stay current through policy, a monthly maintenance slot or automated pull requests. He also suggests a local cache repository that build agents pull from exclusively, with pipelines that report CVEs against severity-based deadlines: two weeks for high, three months for medium and six months for low.

talks.title: Hackers Going to Hack
talks.teaser: Links gamification history and brain science to CTFs, bug bounties, and stronger security team training and retention.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing security work as already playful—CTFs, hackathons, and bug bounties—and argues that formal gamification can address burnout, staffing gaps, and training that certificates alone do not fix. A long historical timeline runs from ancient games through loyalty programs and the coining of “gamification,” then shifts to an infosec-specific chronology highlighting Netscape’s 1995 paid bug finding, the first DEF CON CTF in 1996, and later platform-driven bounty programs.

Audience participation through Slido pop quizzes and memory drills illustrates how the temporal lobe, hippocampus, and amygdala support short-term recall, emotional encoding, and stress-driven performance. The speaker ties those mechanisms to why interactive exercises outperform passive reading, and shows how vivid or emotional storytelling can improve ordered recall.

Cited workplace statistics emphasize widespread reported benefits where gamification is used, manager belief that security would improve with more of it, and preference for game-based training over textbooks. The closing guidance urges individual practitioners to pursue CTFs and bounties for skill growth, while leaders invest in gamified development to surface talent beyond résumé filters, ease bias in hiring and promotion, and build more resilient teams.

talks.title: The New CISO: What Got You Here, Won’t Get You There
talks.teaser: Explains how CISOs can shift from technical roles to business enablement using business-focused KPIs and executive relationships.
talks.summary:
Stan Lowe argues that the technical expertise which earned many CISOs their jobs no longer defines the role. Security leaders were often promoted as strong technologists guarding IT infrastructure, yet work now spreads across remote staff, cloud services and connected devices, and security has become a business problem. He presents the modern CISO as a business enabler who helps the organization use needed technology while staying within its agreed risk tolerance, instead of saying no and getting bypassed.

The middle of the talk covers how to make that shift. He suggests learning how each business unit operates at a macro level rather than mastering its details, and building relationships with the leaders who run those units. Because boards often tune out technical jargon, he advises reporting in business terms. Rather than counting attacks blocked, a CISO can estimate incident costs, express avoided incidents as cost avoidance, and compare that figure with program spending. He also recommends asking questions openly, keeping notes on business priorities, and delivering quick wins.

To close, Lowe proposes a six-month cycle of recurring sessions with business leaders, revisiting KPIs at each review while balancing short-term deliverables with longer 18 to 24 month goals. His key question for any new tool or control is whether it helps, harms or has no effect on the business. The takeaway is that cybersecurity is now a business problem, and CISOs should leave their comfort zone to become trusted business partners.
