talks.title: Building Cybersecurity as a Shared Service
talks.teaser: Explains how a regional headquarters runs shared cybersecurity services for group companies using a three-tier responsibility model.
talks.summary:
Erwin Eimers, general manager of a regional headquarters in the Americas for a chemical group, sets out the problem. The group spans five sectors and about 33,000 employees, and its subsidiaries differ widely in size and business model. Many have only a handful of IT staff and little security expertise. Earlier shared services, hosted in a privately owned data center, were inflexible, costly for small companies and poorly adopted, and a gap analysis showed they focused on availability rather than confidentiality and integrity.

The response was a set of common services delivered under a three-tier responsibility model shared by subsidiaries, the regional headquarters and corporate IT. A joint Microsoft 365 rollout set rules of engagement and escalation paths. A managed SIEM service sends alerts through a portal to subsidiaries and the regional team. The regional team also set security standards for internet-facing systems, runs localized awareness training and phishing campaigns whose results stay with each subsidiary, and is building pen testing and an incident response plan. That plan is rolled out one subsidiary at a time through tabletop exercises. Headquarters funds implementation and uses global pricing agreements so subsidiaries can benefit from them.

The main lessons were that outsourcing did not suit the group's culture, that plans must be realistic for each company's size, and that the regional layer must carry communication up and down. The talk closes with questions for listeners about which pieces to keep at subsidiary level, how to price services and how to agree on success measures with leadership.

talks.title: Two Weeks with a Russian Ransomware Cell
talks.teaser: Shares months of direct contact with a Russian ransomware crew, covering its motives, intrusion methods and the defenses that stop them.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a security strategist, explains how a retweet from a Russian ransomware crew led to a private channel and months of conversations. He frames ransomware as shifting from broad spray attacks toward targeted campaigns against companies and government bodies. The group, called Hildecrypt, is a small team of young men based in Russia that has grown from two ransomware families to five, combining tools it built, stole and bought.

The talk sorts attacker goals into theft, data sale and harm, and argues this crew wants visibility, since victims who see them as capable are more likely to pay. Described tactics include Discord scripts that ping servers and guess passwords, bulletproof command-and-control hosting behind VPNs, spearphishing, and attacks on non-standard ports and common vulnerabilities. Weak administrator passwords come up repeatedly, and proceeds are reportedly moved from Bitcoin into privacy coins. Trend figures show ransomware down 9% year over year, while malware attacks on customer systems, roughly 3.7 million, rose 27%.

For defense, the speaker recommends closing unused ports, enforcing strong passwords, patching, segmenting networks and keeping backups. He also advises layering email security, sandboxing and behavior-based endpoint protection that can roll back infected devices. He ends by arguing that hiring talent from the former Soviet Union could shrink the pool of attackers over time.

talks.title: Hack Your Cybersecurity Career: Your Role in the Ecosystem
talks.teaser: It ties workforce shortages, pentest research, and team culture types to concrete habits for advancing in security careers.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that cybersecurity remains essential because the internet and software now carry business value the original networks were never meant to protect. Citing workforce studies, it describes a widening global talent gap and stresses that people, process, and technology must stay balanced—tools and machine learning cannot replace judgment, especially for business-logic flaws that automated checks miss.

A large middle section draws on aggregated pentest data and practitioner surveys from a published industry report. Machines reliably surface many vulnerability classes when configured well, while humans dominate findings such as business-logic bypasses, race conditions, and chain exploits; some flaw types need both. Survey figures touch on release cadence, pentest frequency, agile and DevOps adoption, and cloud testing scope, with the point that scanners only help when skilled practitioners interpret results and prioritize real risk.

The close shifts to team culture—checklist, engineering-driven, money-driven, and collaborative models—and offers timed actions: reflect on preferred culture, build cross-functional relationships inside the organization, study aspirational job postings, and widen external networks for long-term career direction.

talks.title: Intelligence Sharing for Critical Infrastructure Resiliency
talks.teaser: Explains how OT-ISAC intelligence sharing and maturity assessments can strengthen critical infrastructure against cyber threats.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that operators of operational technology need to share intelligence to make critical infrastructure more resilient. It opens by defining OT, covering ICS and SCADA, and explains how linking IT and OT networks has opened new attack paths. Incidents are walked through: a 2014 spear-phishing intrusion that shut down a German steel mill's blast furnace, a 2012 attack that hit 30,000 workstations at a Saudi oil company, and a 2015 attack that left more than 200,000 Ukrainian homes without power.

Next comes the C2M2 maturity model from the Department of Energy, which assesses OT security across ten domains such as risk management and incident response. Comparing current practice with a target state reveals gaps, and benchmarking against sector peers helps set priorities. The talk also covers zoning networks into enterprise, control and field zones, and frames threat intelligence through the intelligence cycle and F3EAD. The Pyramid of Pain shows why sharing TTPs hurts adversaries most.

The talk closes with the OT-ISAC incident sharing process, where submissions are vetted, anonymised and passed on under the Traffic Light Protocol. A case of a server beaconing to a command-and-control host shows how indicators were gathered, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and turned into a community alert. Takeaways: understand where OT sits in your organisation, build an asset inventory and use a maturity framework to remediate high-priority risks.

talks.title: Getting Engagement in the Midst of Chaos
talks.teaser: Surveys pandemic phishing waves, remote-work attack surfaces, and marketing-style awareness that drives lasting employee behavior change.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting quieter streets and surging online traffic during early pandemic disruption, then charts how COVID-themed phishing moved from scattered lures to bank and relief spoofs and finally into dark-web kits. Speakers tie uncertainty, weak remote-work guidance, and anxiety to spikes in abuse targeting people at home, citing exposed RDP, collaboration tools, credential stuffing, and emotion-driven social engineering amplified by bots and fatigue.

The middle shifts to defense framed as engagement rather than policy lectures. They argue awareness must change behavior, not recite rules, and draw parallels to repeated public-health messaging, executive modeling, peer champions, baselines from simulated phishing, gamified click-rate competition, and multi-channel campaigns that repeat one message.

Practitioners should plan for chaos while setting modest habit goals, use nudges and relatable content instead of bland mandates, measure clicks over time, and partner with HR and marketing. Cited outcomes include roughly 38% initial phishing clicks falling toward 5% after a year of sustained programs, with immediate, mid-term, and long-term actions offered as examples.

talks.title: Cloud Safeguarding: View from Cloud Providers
talks.teaser: Cloud provider panelists advise CISOs on shared responsibility, identity, automation and staffing for public cloud moves.
talks.summary:
Three security leaders from AWS, Google and Microsoft answer questions that RSA Conference gathered from its CISO community about moving to public cloud. The opening segment covers the benefits: providers absorb the work of patching underlying infrastructure, supply hyperscale defenses and multi-region resilience, and offer native logging that is hard to build on premises. Abbas Kudrati describes how roles shift, with network-focused staff moving toward identity and cloud-specific analysis.

Shared responsibility runs through much of the discussion. The customer's share shifts with the service model, from IaaS to SaaS, but identity, data classification, encryption choices and key protection stay with the customer. Independent third-party audits give assurance, and providers publish them in trust portals. Myles Hosford recommends a platform-agnostic control framework of objectives, such as encrypting data at rest and in transit, mapped to regulations and to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework's 98 control objectives. For identity, the panel favours a central identity provider, strong authentication, least privilege and vaulted privileged credentials.

Automation and visibility come next, with guardrails preferred over approval gates because no human team can review every change. Examples include flagging virtual machines not built from approved images and automatically fixing a firewall rule that exposes a service to the internet. Mark Johnston points to native flow analysis and benchmark checks. The closing takeaways: train staff, name a single owner for cloud security, embed controls in delivery pipelines, and define clear responsibilities across teams.

talks.title: Breaking Bad (Passwords)
talks.teaser: Shows what real password data from years of penetration tests reveals about weak policies and user habits.
talks.summary:
The talk examines three years of penetration test data on password policies and the passwords people choose. The speakers drew on compromised Active Directory environments and measured settings against NIST, CIS, Microsoft, PCI DSS and the Australian ISM. Most organisations stayed at the bare minimum: about 41% required an eight-character minimum, and around 63% required seven or eight. Nearly a quarter set a lockout threshold of zero, and almost half used at least 30 minutes lockout duration, which gives attackers short windows.

To analyse the passwords, the team cracked recovered hashes on a PC with four GPUs, usually within two to five hours. Nearly half of the cracked passwords were eight characters long, and most fell between eight and nine. Common patterns appeared, such as company names followed by the current year, and Welcome1 or Password1, which appeared in most engagements. The speakers also flagged weak history settings that let users cycle passwords, and MFA that covers web logins but not PowerShell for Exchange or legacy mail endpoints.

The takeaways centred on length over complexity, blocking breached passwords, dictionary words, repetitive sequences and company-specific words, and applying MFA to every entry point. They also recommended protecting service and machine accounts, encouraging users to avoid corporate credentials on public sites and to use password managers, and running identity audits roughly every six months. A quick first step is checking whether company passwords appear in current breach data.

talks.title: PKI Well Revised: Common Mistakes Which Lead to Huge Compromise of Identity
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PKI Well Revised: Common Mistakes Which Lead to Huge Compromise of Identity.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Dr. Mike Jankowski Lorek, Director of Consulting and cybersecurity expert at CQURE, examines how misconfigurations in Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) can allow attackers to escalate privileges and fully compromise identity across an organization. Using an opening analogy about an abandoned mine in Joshua Tree, he emphasizes that PKI is intended to boost security but can become an attack vector if improperly configured. The session covers fundamental cryptographic mechanisms, the function of certificates, and an end-to-end live demonstration showing how an Active Directory environment can be compromised using a flawed certificate template.

### Key Topics
- **Cryptographic Fundamentals**: Distinction between encoding (data transformation for systems without secrecy, e.g., Base64, URL encoding), encryption (confidentiality via symmetric ciphers like AES or asymmetric pairs like RSA), hashing (one-way message integrity via MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256), and digital signatures (author verification using private keys and algorithms such as SHA-256 RSA).
- **Certificates and PKI Architecture**: Role of X.509 certificates in binding public keys to identities; Certificate Signing Requests (CSRs); Certificate Authorities (CAs) as trusted third parties; Certification Practice Statements (CPS); revocation methods (CRLs and OCSP); Certificate Transparency logs; and operating system/browser trust lists (e.g., Windows vs. Mozilla Firefox).
- **Cross-Certification Risks**: Dangers of blindly adding third-party root CAs into trusted stores versus utilizing constrained cross-certification (name constraints restricting DNS suffixes or email domains).
- **PKI Exploitation Vectors**: Risks arising from client authentication Extended Key Usage (EKU), user-supplied Subject Alternative Names (SAN), automatic CSR approval, and permissive certificate template permissions.

### Technical Details
During the live demonstration, the speaker logged into a Windows Server member machine as a local administrator account (`CQURE\Bob`). He demonstrated that properly secured templates (such as the default user template) automatically populate identity attributes from Active Directory and ignore arbitrary subject inputs. However, inspecting computer certificate templates using `certlm.msc` revealed a misconfigured template named `CQWeb_bad`.

This vulnerable template exhibited two critical flaws:
1. It allowed the enrollee to supply the subject and Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the request.
2. In addition to Server Authentication, it included Client Authentication in its Extended Key Usage (EKU) and lacked manager approval requirements.

The speaker submitted a certificate request using `site3.cqure.lab` as the common name and DNS name, while injecting an alternative name of `admin@cqure.lab`. Upon automatic issuance, the certificate and private key were exported to a password-protected PFX file (`FC5.pfx`), which bypassed default export protections using the Data Protection API (DPAPI). 

To leverage this certificate for identity impersonation without native smart card hardware, the speaker created a virtual smart card tied to the machine's TPM chip. Utilizing `certutil` with the Microsoft Base Smart Card Crypto Provider, the exported PFX was imported into the virtual smart card using the default PIN (`12345678`). With the client-authentication certificate loaded:
- A connection to the domain controller's hidden administrative share (`net use Z: \\dc01\c$ /smartcard`) succeeded, exposing Active Directory database files in `Windows\NTDS`.
- Executing `runas /user:admin@cqure.lab /smartcard cmd` spawned an elevated command prompt. Checking `whoami /all` confirmed the session had Domain Admin privileges, and `klist` showed active Kerberos tickets that could be captured and reused for pass-the-ticket attacks.

### Takeaways
The speaker outlined essential practices to avoid PKI-driven identity compromise:
- **Restrict Subject Name Supply**: Do not allow requesters to define arbitrary SAN values in templates that also permit client authentication.
- **Limit Extended Key Usage (EKU)**: Avoid issuing multipurpose certificates or granting client authentication capabilities when only server authentication is required.
- **Enforce Approval Workflows**: High-value or sensitive certificate requests should require manual review and approval by certificate managers rather than automatic issuance.
- **Lock Down Template ACLs**: Restrict template editing and enrollment permissions strictly to domain administrators to prevent unauthorized modifications.
- **Use Constrained Cross-Certification**: Restrict external CA trust using specific naming and domain constraints to avoid domain-wide impersonation.
- **Secure Key Storage**: Be mindful that software-based key storage providers can often be exported despite administrative export flags.

talks.title: The DevSecOps Journey at Prudential Asia
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The DevSecOps Journey at Prudential Asia.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Mohan Yelnuda discusses the DevSecOps journey at Prudential Asia, reflecting on the guiding question, "Did we cover enough ground?" He defines DevSecOps as the integration of security across both development and operations to facilitate early and frequent automated feedback across the entire application attack surface. The presentation outlines the four primary DevSecOps tracks established at Prudential—Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), Software Composition Analysis (SCA), and Container Security (CSec)—exploring the distinct challenges, integration points, triage processes, and operational lessons learned along the way.

### Key Topics
- **DevSecOps Implementation Strategy**: Requirements must be tailored to an organization's specific technology landscape rather than generic vendor or analyst guidance. Key steps include conducting proof-of-concept evaluations, placing automated build-breaker gates in pipelines, and establishing triage workflows to differentiate between false positives and non-applicable vulnerabilities.
- **Tool Lifecycle and Stakeholder Enablement**: Security tools must be reevaluated or replaced every two to three years as risk profiles, exploitation techniques, and application frameworks evolve. Because security teams are heavily outnumbered (around one security consultant for every 200 developers), Prudential scaled enablement by producing self-service resources, including FAQs, false-positive guides, and 3-to-5-minute video tutorials.
- **Progress Metrics**: Measuring track maturity begins with onboarding metrics (tracking how many applications are integrated into scanning pipelines) and shifts over time to remediation metrics prioritized by risk (starting with critical findings, followed by high, medium, and low).

### Technical Details across Tracks
- **SAST**: Ingests custom developer source code and outputs code vulnerabilities. It integrates into developer environments via IDE plugins (e.g., Eclipse, IntelliJ, Visual Studio, VS Code) and CI pipelines (Jenkins, Bamboo, CircleCI, Azure DevOps). The primary challenges are high rates of false positives and tools lagging behind modern language versions. A recommended practice is having developers review findings first before escalating edge cases to security.
- **DAST**: Requires a stable running pre-production application or API endpoint as input and integrates into CD pipelines. Automated DAST tools (such as Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP) excel at detecting low-hanging fruit like missing input validation and injection flaws, but manual penetration testing remains essential for application logic vulnerabilities.
- **SCA / Open Source Security**: Scans third-party library dependencies by computing version hashes and matching them against vulnerability databases. Integration covers IDEs, CI pipelines, and artifact repositories. Triage focuses on determining whether an impacted library is actually applicable based on specific API usage. Yelnuda emphasizes enabling production monitoring on artifact folders to detect newly disclosed vulnerabilities in already deployed code (citing the 2017 Equifax breach as a cautionary tale).
- **Container Security**: Analyzes Docker images, base OS layers, and container orchestration platforms (such as AKS, OpenShift, or Kubernetes). Scans are embedded into IDEs, CI pipelines, container registries, and runtime environments via sidecars, daemonsets, or micro-scanners that can alert or quarantine compromised pods.

### Takeaways
DevSecOps is an ongoing process rather than a static goal. Organizations cannot rely on a single silver bullet tool across all layers of the attack surface. Sustainable adoption requires automating gate checks, building self-service educational content, enabling continuous production monitoring, and continually reassessing both tooling and architecture as new technologies and threats emerge.

talks.title: Hacking the Cybersecurity Job Market: A Primer for Students & Grads
talks.teaser: Industry panelists offer career advice for students and graduates entering the cybersecurity job market.
talks.summary:
This recorded career panel targets students and recent graduates considering cybersecurity. Four panelists from government, industry, policy and technology described how they entered the field, from cryptography research and financial services fraud work to policy roles. They argued the field needs varied backgrounds. On openings, they agreed demand has held up during the pandemic and that policy, legal, marketing and training roles often need security knowledge even when the job title does not say so.

Day-to-day work was described as meeting-heavy and cross-functional, with translation between technical, legal and business teams. For a first role, the advice was to network through conferences and social media, research the employer before interviews, and craft a clear account of how past experience applies. Panelists also mentioned mentoring new hires without prior jobs and smaller firms that offer faster responsibility. An audience question on moving into management got the answer that empathy for technical staff, plus a strong personal narrative, matters most.

The closing advice centred on burnout, scheduling demanding tasks for peak energy hours and protecting self-care time. Panelists also urged newcomers to shadow colleagues, keep learning as tools change, and ask for help without fear of looking unskilled.

talks.title: Understanding Human Genomic Data Privacy and Security | RSAC 2020
talks.teaser: Covers consumer control of genomic and health data, research sandboxes, re-identification risk, and fairness beyond cryptography.
talks.summary:
Growing interest in direct-to-consumer and clinical genetics has sharpened tension between protecting individuals and enabling research. The discussion describes a consumer-centered model where people deposit genomes, medical records, and patient-reported outcomes, decide who may access them, and queries run in sandboxed compute against data that stays in controlled repositories. Participants tie that vision to faster clinical–research integration at large health systems and to rewarding sharers, including a platform approach overseen with SEC-qualified shares so contributors are treated as partners rather than passive subjects.

The middle of the conversation compares academic federally funded studies, which pass institutional review, with corporate or non-federally funded work that may lack the same credible vetting. On scale, speakers note that genomes are largely shared across humanity, with only a small uniquely identifying fraction, yet that fraction still matters on billions of records and when combined with other identifiers. They cite cases where one person’s shared DNA helped investigators identify someone who never consented, and warn that one person’s genome implicates relatives across generations.

Technical options such as cryptographic queries against clinical data are acknowledged as powerful but not always aligned with what people want when “privacy” also means fairness—for example, insurers inferring pricing without seeing plaintext genotypes. The close emphasizes messy, unsettled policy questions about discrimination, consent, and cross-border norms, and urges practitioners to pair strong controls with governance that matches public expectations.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show with Penn & Teller | RSAC 2020
talks.teaser: Magic performers explore how deliberate deception, deep fakes, and information overload reshape trust in what people see and hear.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with Penn and Teller explaining why audiences rarely stay amazed by endless similar magic tricks, and how entertainment still works when secrets are known. They describe their television format where they recognize methods yet still feel wonder, and how explaining a classic sleight in the same performance targets both intellect and gut feeling.

The conversation turns to public anxiety over deep fakes. They argue that trustworthy reproduction of reality through photos, audio, or video was a brief modern exception, while societies long relied on judging authors and publishers rather than treating media as self-proving. They welcome synthetic media as a push back toward skepticism, note the shift from scarce to overwhelming information, and express comfort that more speech answers bad speech.

They close by contrasting honest magicians, who announce deception, with ordinary liars, and by describing a password-themed illusion built from nineteenth-century spiritualist techniques, reframed around modern surveillance paranoia rather than afterlife claims.

talks.title: Dr. Peggy Whitson: Breaking Records and Life at NASA | RSAC 2020
talks.teaser: A NASA astronaut recounts her path to record-setting spaceflight and shares lessons on diverse teams and facing failure.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a childhood fascination with the Moon landing, which turned from a private dream into a concrete goal once female astronauts were selected in the year the speaker finished high school. She describes the long stretch of applications that followed as some of the most important years of her life, and argues that making the most of a situation, even when it falls short of what you want, can take you further than you expect.

The middle of the talk covers her leadership career. She recalls leading the Astronaut Office as its first woman and first chief without a military background, which she calls among the most meaningful parts of her career, and later commanding the space station after an earlier flight. She argues that NASA's strength comes from mixing different ways of thinking, and points to the station as proof: its pressurized section is longer than a football field and bigger than a 747, and it was assembled in orbit from parts made across the world. Crews on board, she says, deliberately encouraged those differences too, since the human element makes every group stronger.

The closing section turns to perspective. She shows a time-lapse image of the Milky Way taken on her last mission and notes that our galaxy is one of billions, which puts Earth in scale. She ends by urging listeners to step outside their comfort zones, take on challenges that feel hard, and treat failure as something that builds strength for the next attempt.

talks.title: My Botnet Always Beats Yours: A Honeypot to Massive Bot Fight Scenes
talks.teaser: Shows how one home honeypot exposed IoT botnet operators who fought over devices, cloned scripts, and wiped rivals' networks.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a single home honeypot, running since 2017, that caught IoT botnet traffic. It starts with Mirai, whose leaked source code let anyone build variants. Its chain runs from a scanner that finds devices with default credentials, to a loader, to a command-and-control server. The speaker then introduces the Glutton honeypot, which listens on every port and routes traffic to the right handler. After a maintenance restart in September 2019, an attacker reached the honeypot and dropped payloads within minutes.

Log analysis centred on download and execution commands. Some carried hard-coded strings that act as birthmarks, revealing the variant and target architecture. Instagram searches turned up several C2 dashboards, showing roughly 5,200, 10,000 and 20,000 bots under different operators. One 2018 seller advertised access at around $15 for 1,000 bots.

The later part covers turf wars. A recorded session showed an attacker entering a rival's botnet panel, adding users and wiping the network. Free tutorial scripts bundled a root account and sent victims' IPs through a link tracker. The takeaway: small log traces and cheap honeypots reveal operator behaviour, so defenders should keep watching them.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show, featuring Dr. Lorrie Cranor
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding The Hugh Thompson Show, featuring Dr. Lorrie Cranor.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this concluding session of RSA Conference 2020, Program Committee Chair Hugh Thompson hosts a discussion centered on the conference's overarching theme: the "human element." Thompson explores human vulnerabilities through personal anecdotes and social engineering parallels before inviting Dr. Lorrie Cranor, a leading researcher on security and privacy from Carnegie Mellon University, to discuss human behavior, password choices, IoT security labels, and modern deception.

### Key Topics
- **Human Factors and Social Engineering:** Thompson discusses human cognitive traits as inherent "zero days" that attackers exploit. He references Dale Carnegie's *How to Win Friends and Influence People* as an early handbook for social engineering principles, noting that sincere compliments and personalization parallel tactics used in phishing.
- **Personal Exploits and Heuristics:** Thompson shares an anecdote regarding his obsession with puzzles and extreme couponing, explaining how deep-seated personal traits can be manipulated to trigger targeted actions like phishing clicks.
- **Password Strength and Mental Models:** Dr. Lorrie Cranor discusses a decade of research at Carnegie Mellon examining how users assess and select passwords versus their empirical strength.
- **IoT Security and Privacy Nutrition Labels:** Research on consumer comprehension of IoT privacy/security risks and how perceived inconvenience affects purchasing behavior.
- **Deception, Deep Fakes, and Phishing Resilience:** The challenges humans face evaluating synthetic media and social engineering.

### Technical Details & Research Findings
- **Password Predictability:** Cranor highlighted audience experiments demonstrating the disconnect between user perception and actual password entropy. Users typically judged `I love you 88` and `I eat kale 88` as equally secure due to identical character lengths and number patterns; however, Cranor stated that `I eat kale 88` is "four trillion times better" because `I love you` is among the most commonly chosen phrases.
- **Character Positioning:** Similarly, comparing `SpongeBob01` and `Sponge01Bob`, moving digits or special characters into the middle of a string dramatically increases strength compared to standard trailing numbers, which follow common user habits and automated cracking dictionaries.
- **IoT Security Labels:** Cranor described an initiative (IoTSecurityPrivacy.org) designing nutrition-style security and privacy labels for smart devices. User studies showed consumers accurately grasp risk indicators (identifying what increases or decreases risk). However, purchasing intent did not always align with risk reduction: features like multi-factor authentication on a smart speaker were perceived as inconvenient, reducing likelihood to buy. Concerns varied by device type, with smart speakers prompting more concern than smart light bulbs, while smart toothbrushes raised unexpected privacy issues around data transmission (e.g., brushing habits sent to insurers).
- **Phishing and Media Authentication:** Discussing threats from deepfakes generated using tools like GANs, Cranor noted that despite advanced synthetic media, users still frequently fall for simple plain-text email attacks, though general awareness of routine phishing has modestly improved.

### Takeaways
- Security controls cannot evaluate human risk purely on rigid rule-checklists (e.g., character length and symbol inclusion) without accounting for human predictability and common patterns.
- Usability remains a dominant hurdle: users frequently reject proven security enhancements (like MFA on IoT devices) when perceived convenience is degraded.
- While users have developed moderate resilience against basic phishing attacks over time, mitigating social engineering and synthetic deception remains an ongoing challenge.

talks.title: Hacking Society
talks.teaser: Treats tax loopholes, gerrymandering and market distortions as security vulnerabilities, asking how society could patch them.
talks.summary:
Bruce Schneier argues that security thinking can be applied beyond software, to sociotechnical systems such as the tax code, elections and markets. He defines a hack as something a system permits that its designers did not intend, and he treats tax loopholes as vulnerabilities that specialists search for. He cites a 2017 drafting error that taxed military death benefits as earned income, leaving surviving families with unexpected bills, and the cum-ex trading scheme that is being prosecuted mainly in Germany.

He then sets out concepts he wants to carry over from IT security. These include changes in the threat model, class breaks where one discovered technique becomes available to everyone, the blurred roles of attackers and defenders in political systems, and "too big to fail" as an emergent vulnerability. He also looks at hacks of cognitive systems such as advertising, attention-driven social media and trust heuristics. Drawing on joint work with a political scientist, he compares how autocracies and democracies are exposed to information attacks, and he presents the work as preliminary.

To close, Schneier suggests transparency, defense in depth, resilience and iteration as possible tools for policy, while warning that technologists should not assume they can solve problems outside their field. Audience questions covered whether broken social structures can be replaced rather than patched, how to handle disputed definitions of a hack, and how to involve technologists in policy. He asked listeners to send examples and rebuttals.

talks.title: You Can Stop Stupid
talks.teaser: Argues that user-caused losses are system failures and maps prevention and response controls around them using a boom-based model.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that when a person triggers a loss, it is usually labeled an awareness failure, when the real issue is a system that let one action cause harm. They open with a conference anecdote about an administrator who ordered stickers telling staff not to click on stuff, showing that the environment shaped the outcome. They then test the dictionary meaning of stupid against hiring and training, asking whether people are given the knowledge they need before being expected to act correctly.

Drawing on safety science, scuba instruction and workplace injury data, they describe three phases: left of boom (prevention), boom (the user-triggered event) and right of boom (response). Examples include warehouse lanes that separated people from forklifts and cut most injuries, and the 737 MAX crashes, where faulty sensors, an unfamiliar software system, brief training and a rushed certification combined against the pilots. A senior executive recalled from around 2013 clicked a link that seemed to come from a colleague, and an awareness program followed. Awareness is one tactic alongside governance, written processes, filtering, least privilege and detection.

A W2 fraud example shows how anti-spam and anti-phishing filters should stop the email, how a rule routing PII requests through HR leadership and legal approval should guide the employee, and how data loss prevention should block any file still leaving the company. The takeaway is to review governance for common user-triggered losses, define the processes clearly, and build preventive and response controls around them, using awareness to teach staff how to do their jobs correctly.

talks.title: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure: You’ve Come a Long Way, Baby
talks.teaser: Traces how vulnerability disclosure and bug bounties evolved, mixing survey data with firsthand stories from vendors and researchers.
talks.summary:
Katie Moussouris and Chris Wysopal start by separating vulnerability disclosure from penetration testing and bug bounty programs. They then trace how coordinated disclosure emerged, from researchers publicly posting bugs in the 1990s to a 1997 Internet Explorer report that led Microsoft to request advance notice, and a deadline-based policy from Rain Forest Puppy. They also explain why the word "responsible" became a pressure tool against researchers.

Survey data from Veracode and 451 Research anchors the middle of the talk. Most researchers report privately, and most respondents considered 30 to 60 days a reasonable window to fix a flaw. The speakers recount cases: a Lexar USB drive whose stored password was exposed after the vendor ignored contact attempts; an Uber bounty that paid extortionists under an NDA and led to charges against researchers; and a Facebook messaging flaw that showed why a separate test instance matters. Microsoft's IE11 bounty drew many bugs for a modest spend.

The closing advice is practical: confirm your organization has a contact address, build an internal process for handling unsolicited reports, and test your own software before release. The speakers argue that disclosure has improved, though bounty terms and slow vendors still cause friction.

talks.teaser: Privacy leaders explain how data ethics and company values can shape privacy engineering and better security products.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with a question many attendees have not answered for themselves: what data ethics actually means. The speakers draw on bioethics, contrasting treating people as ends in themselves, with autonomy and consent, against weighing benefits and harms for the greatest number. They argue that law tends to trail technology, so compliance alone is a weak guide, and that teams should ask whether they ought to act, not just whether they can.

Moving to practice, the panelists describe a balancing test in which teams list benefits for the company, third parties, society and individuals, weigh them against possible harms, then add safeguards for the risks that remain. For hard cases they suggest scenario testing, starting with absurd examples and narrowing to realistic ones. For engineers, one speaker advises working within existing development processes and using scoping workshops to turn policy statements into business rules, while privacy failures that could harm users or the brand should be treated as bugs.

The closing segment covers review boards that include stakeholders beyond the project team, such as an external advisory board drawn from several countries. The main pitfalls are that ethics processes slow delivery and lose support without a clear business rationale and efficient procedures. The takeaway is to start from why a product is built and design safeguards around the people whose data it uses.

talks.title: Mercedes-Benz and 360 Group: Defending a Luxury Fleet with the Community
talks.teaser: Explains defending a connected car fleet, with a test-bench study of Mercedes-Benz attack chains and the resulting fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Mercedes-Benz product security leadership with a researcher from 360 Group, starts from the problem of defending a whole fleet of connected cars rather than one vehicle. The speakers outline a fleet security operations approach borrowed from enterprise and IoT practice: assess posture, detect abnormal activity, respond, and keep protecting through ongoing patching. Scale, slow remediation and software diversity across models are named as the main difficulties.

The 360 researcher then describes building a low-cost test bench from parts sourced through second-hand markets, including a telematics control unit and an infotainment head unit. Replaying recorded signals was not enough, because anti-theft checks raised warnings, so the team isolated a wake-up signal and an anti-theft signal from a running car. The attack chains covered far-field routes through backend servers and over-the-air reflashing, and near-field routes through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.

After about ten months of work, the team reported 19 findings to Mercedes-Benz in August 2019. The manufacturer shut down the affected services within two days, fixed the vulnerabilities by September, and set up a joint workshop in October. The researcher estimated that around two million vehicles in China could be affected, with no customer impact. The takeaway is to treat a fleet as ongoing operations and to bring the security community in.

talks.title: Breaking Password Dependencies: Challenges in the Final Mile at Microsoft
talks.teaser: Explains how Microsoft tackled blocking legacy authentication, why its first attempt failed, and what the rollout taught about people.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Microsoft's identity security team arguing that password defenses still fail while legacy authentication protocols remain enabled. The speakers said most password spray attacks used older protocols such as IMAP and SMTP, which cannot enforce multifactor authentication, and replay attacks followed the same pattern, with 97% using legacy authentication. In their analysis, turning off legacy authentication in tenants was associated with a 67% reduction in compromises.

The middle of the talk covers Microsoft's own rollout. A policy blocking legacy authentication was tested on about 2,000 users, then applied to a 60,000-person sales organization. There, a single back-end service account used by a sales application was blocked, the application was down for effectively a full day, and the policy was rolled back. The team then kept 90 days of sign-in data, added a report-only mode to test policies, and traced each legacy client to its application owner so the code could move to modern authentication. Remaining exceptions were granted only with a dated commitment signed off by a vice president or general manager.

The rollout restarted in January 2019, and about 94% of users had legacy authentication disabled within two months. Microsoft was blocking roughly 1.5 million legacy requests a day in the live data shown. The speakers concluded that switching off the protocol is the easy step; the hard part is working with people across the business. Practitioners should start capturing sign-in logs early, pilot with low-impact groups, and plan for exception handling. They also flagged Exchange's removal of basic authentication support in October.

talks.title: SIMs, eSIMs and Secure Elements: Dynamic Security for Connected Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how SIM and eSIM hardware can run security functions and secure links for connected devices.
talks.summary:
The talk contrasts today's phones, where contacts live on the handset or in the cloud, with earlier years when a SIM swap restored everything. The speaker, from the Trusted Connectivity Alliance, presents SIM and eSIM hardware as small secure computers that can manage security functions on connected devices, not only attach them to a network. Attacks are split into remote ones that reach many devices at once and physical ones that clone or read a single device, with examples drawn from connected cars, smart meters and wearables.

Security by design and penetration testing before launch are presented as steps that should be mandatory, supported by regulation such as the EU certification framework and GDPR. The main worked example is a temperature sensor in a power plant: readings are handled inside the eSIM, which encrypts them and sends them to the operator over a channel the device itself cannot read. For devices without cellular connectivity, an embedded secure element is described as a smaller option. The IoT SAFE applet, developed with GSMA, standardises mutual authentication between device applications and the cloud, and interoperability work aims to let profiles load on SIMs from any vendor.

Audience questions covered whether application code can fit inside a SIM, how the element relates to TPMs, carrier control over SIM space, and whether eSIM contents can be audited. The speaker deferred several of these to working group contacts. The takeaway is that SIM-based hardware can take cryptographic work off constrained devices, though practical use depends on operator cooperation and common standards.

talks.teaser: General Motors' executive outlines how the company builds cybersecurity into connected and self-driving vehicles.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short video and framing from General Motors' leadership on how cars have reshaped daily life for a century. The company's goals of eliminating crashes, emissions and congestion depend on electrification, autonomous driving and connectivity. The speaker argues that consumer trust will decide whether self-driving vehicles succeed, and that one serious breach at a single manufacturer could damage confidence across the whole sector.

The middle of the talk covers what GM is doing about it. The company spends over $100 million a year on automotive security and employs close to 500 specialists, building protections in from the earliest design stages. Its new vehicle platform supports over-the-air updates, 5G and built-in protections, and the Cruise Origin autonomous vehicle, which has no pedals or steering wheel, has its own layered defenses. Other measures include a HackerOne bug bounty, secure coding training for thousands of developers, supplier oversight, the NIST cyber framework, a research agreement with the US Army Ground Vehicle Systems Center, and shared standards work with SAE.

The closing section turns to workforce. Estimates of unfilled cybersecurity jobs run from 1.8 million to nearly 4 million, so the speaker calls for recruiting more women and minorities, starting outreach as early as middle school. GM says its programs reached nearly 300,000 students and teachers last year. The takeaway is that the industry has to share practices and develop people as well as technology.

talks.teaser: Maps how authoritarian regimes use disinformation, intimidation and internet shutdowns, and what defenders can do about them.
talks.summary:
The panel, with Brittan Heller and Ben Nimmo, opens with three trends in digital authoritarianism: stoking domestic fear through existing social divisions, silencing critics with harassment and internet shutdowns, and bending human rights language through copied laws. Heller recounts a study of anti-immigrant hate speech on Reddit, after which a white nationalist site posted guidance on threatening people while staying within legal limits. She also cites a Senate committee finding that the Internet Research Agency aimed racially charged posts at African-American voters before the 2016 US election.

Heller then turns to Uganda's 2016 election, where a four-day internet shutdown left opposition candidates unable to post while the government kept publishing. Nimmo focuses on how messages are shaped, using four tactics: dismiss, distort, distract and dismay. He points to a Russian Embassy post that mocked actor Morgan Freeman's personal habits instead of the evidence in his video. He also described an Internet Research Agency operation that staged rival protests in Houston in 2016 and told participants to bring arms.

The closing advice centers on defense: aim regulation at conduct rather than content, run human rights impact assessments to spot risks early, shift from one-off product fixes toward systemic change, and invest in citizen education, which Heller links to results in Scandinavia. Both speakers argue that attribution must come first, because knowing who runs a campaign is what makes a response possible.

talks.title: The Age of Economic Warfare: What to Expect in This New Reality
talks.teaser: Explores how nation-state attacks on OT networks enable economic warfare and what defenders can do now.
talks.summary:
Geopolitical conflict increasingly uses cyber operations against industrial and operational technology environments to pressure economies without crossing into open war. The presentation frames critical infrastructure broadly—utilities, manufacturing, and everyday building systems—and revisits Ukrainian grid incidents, NotPetya spillover into global OT, and public UK–US attribution tying activity to Russian military intelligence. It argues adversaries favor subtle outcomes such as loss of view, process manipulation, or reputational harm over dramatic blackout narratives.

For organizations, accidental IT-to-OT propagation shows that weak OT posture amplifies weapons aimed elsewhere. The speaker urges defenders to map terrain, avoid IT-style over-engineering, and start incremental controls rather than multi-year perfection plans. Common failure modes include excessive complexity from IT consultants, split ownership between engineering and security, and running OT security as an isolated program that starves the SOC of context.

Practical guidance centers on the Purdue model, compensating controls where endpoint agents or active scanning are unsafe, virtual zoning when physical segmentation lags, and early integration of OT telemetry into existing governance and playbooks. Recommendations emphasize near-term risk reduction over lengthy roadmaps.

talks.title: Advanced Persistence Threats: The Future of Kubernetes Attacks
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Kubernetes persistence tactics that abuse admission webhooks, audit logging, and a rogue k3s control plane.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how attacks on Kubernetes may evolve as the project grows more complex and ships new releases about every 90 days. The speakers note that attackers now need a deeper grasp of Kubernetes components and Linux internals, while defenders struggle to track every moving part. Their goal is to keep access to cluster state and secrets while staying out of view of the audit trail.

Several demonstrations followed. A validating admission webhook configured to fail open and time out after one second quietly received a copy of each secret as it was created. Oversized requests with padded annotations pushed audit entries past the logging parser's field limit, so only request metadata was recorded. A shadow API server ran on the control plane node with anonymous access and an always-allow authorization mode. Finally, k3s agents were rolled out as daemon sets across nodes in three clouds, joining an attacker-run control plane that collected secrets and instance metadata credentials. A later section showed that reconfiguring the kubelet through dynamic configuration could restore command execution inside a kube-proxy pod.

The defensive advice centres on alerting for changes to webhooks, dynamic configuration and RBAC, reviewing audit logs and feature gates, and testing upcoming features in a development environment. The speakers also stress planning upgrades, since in-place upgrades may not bring newer security features into a cluster.

talks.title: Test or Be Tested: Adversary Emulation with Atomic Red Team
talks.teaser: Shows how Red Canary's open-source Atomic Red Team tests map to ATT&CK techniques for checking security controls.
talks.summary:
Chris Rathi of Red Canary explains why the company releases open-source work and how Atomic Red Team began in 2017. Customers often tested detections by running batches of malware samples on one virtual machine, which taught them little. The team combined its internal test library with MITRE ATT&CK techniques to make tests quick to run.

Each ATT&CK technique has a YAML file with its ID, name and one or more atomic tests. A test specifies a name, description, platform, configurable arguments with defaults, and the commands to run. Markdown documentation is generated from these files automatically. Contributors fork the repo, create a template with a Ruby helper, write a test with a harmless payload such as opening Calculator, validate it, and open a pull request that maintainers review before merging.

Adoption came from a Slack workspace where users request tests, small rewards such as shirts and stickers for first contributions, and a monthly webinar called Atomic Friday. Companion projects Chain Reactor and Invoke Atomic Red Team, a PowerShell framework, were split out to keep the core project focused. The speaker said the project does not map tests to specific adversary groups; that mapping comes from MITRE ATT&CK, and Navigator layers can track coverage over time. Practitioners should use the tests to check their defenses and contribute missing ones.

talks.teaser: Shows how compliance teams and engineers can calibrate controls like separation of duties so audits and DevOps work together.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the friction between GRC and DevOps, arguing that the two sides often pursue their goals in isolation. The speaker, a technology compliance manager, opens with a story about a change-management conversation in which an engineer suggested peer review in place of a formal approval meeting. She frames the problem as the gap between work as imagined, meaning how policies and controls are written, and work as done, where operators adapt procedures to keep systems stable.

Using separation of duties as the main example, she explains that a rule built for financial fraud, where the person requesting a payment should not approve it, does not translate cleanly to software delivery, where developers write code and operations deploys it. She describes checkbox compliance and malicious compliance as traps that leave teams unable to say why a control exists. She suggests auditing for transparency and visibility through logs, evidence and smart notifications, and using CI/CD pipelines, automated configuration management, pre-approved access matrices and single sign-on for account termination.

The closing advice is practical. Ask engineers what risk a control mitigates, invite auditors into planning and engineering meetings, share the controls matrix early, and whiteboard the actual deployment process together rather than the diagram on file. She ends by arguing that people's ability to adapt is the strongest control an organization has.

talks.title: The Industrial Cyberthreat Landscape: 2019 Year in Review
talks.teaser: A review synthesizes Dragos 2019 ICS data on threats, vulnerabilities, incident lessons, and prioritized defensive controls.
talks.summary:
Industrial cyber risk is framed as distinct from enterprise IT: operations combine digital systems with physical processes, hyperconnected homogenous platforms increase adversary scale, and copying IT controls into plants often adds little real protection or can worsen outages.

The core of the session is Dragos’s 2019 year-in-review findings. Vulnerability research showed many advisories are not weaponizable, heavy reliance on patching with weak compensating options, and frequent vendor patch errors. Eleven state-linked activity groups now target industrial victims at scale, including newly tracked Parisite and Wassonite campaigns using edge and VPN flaws, living-off-the-land movement, and tailored network knowledge. Incident lessons highlight Xenotime’s safety-system focus and Trisis, EKANS as ICS-aware ransomware, and patterns such as logic modification and safety-system compromise. Response data cited total internet reachability to control systems in handled cases, outdated asset documentation, and no effective monitoring in any engagement.

Practitioners are urged to prioritize ICS-specific incident response and tabletops, behavior-focused detection aligned with MITRE ATT&CK for ICS, segmentation and vendor-access choke points, on-premises MFA where cloud dependency is risky, and risk-based patching instead of score-driven programs. OEMs are asked to remove warranty barriers to hardening, with a phased post-conference plan to select scenarios, map controls, and execute a small set of improvements.

talks.teaser: Two former officials survey nation-state cyber threats, election security and the policy gaps around critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
This fireside conversation looks at how nation-state cyber threats map onto US national security and homeland security. The speakers go country by country. They describe Russia's offensive cyber capabilities, its tolerance of criminal groups that act on its behalf, and its interference in US elections. They describe China's campaigns against intellectual property and defense technology, North Korea's use of cyber operations to raise revenue and to retaliate, as in the Sony Pictures attack, and Iran's growing interest in banks, dams and water utilities. The Sony case is used to show how a company that does not see itself as a security target can fall to a single weak administrator password.

The middle of the talk turns to election security. The speakers separate disinformation on social media from technical risk. They cite the Iowa caucus app failure as an example of avoidable technology problems. They argue that attackers are more likely to disrupt the systems around voting, such as communications, polling access and local infrastructure, than to change vote totals, and that the real goal is to erode public confidence. They also cover the defense industrial base. They describe the Pentagon's Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification, with five levels and outside certification, and the challenge of bringing hundreds of thousands of smaller suppliers up to standard. They also discuss how industries such as banking and the electric grid are starting to self-regulate.

The closing section covers education and governance. The speakers argue that policy experts need technical skills and that boards need members with real cyber expertise. They name polarization as the largest threat to the country and argue that cybersecurity work is a form of public service. The takeaway for practitioners is that defending critical systems, supply chains and elections depends on both technical rigor and institutional trust.

talks.title: Hunting Linux Malware for Fun and Flags
talks.teaser: Shows sysadmins how built-in Linux tools reveal malware on compromised servers, from file timestamps to process memory.
talks.summary:
The ESET malware researcher argues that server-side Linux malware is a real threat that many sysadmins are poorly trained to analyze. He recalls an operation that used an OpenSSH backdoor on more than 40,000 compromised servers to redirect web traffic for monetization, and a spam botnet taken down with Ukrainian law enforcement. Servers attract attackers for their bandwidth, long uptime and usefulness as relays.

The middle section covers artifacts that standard Linux tools expose. Timestamps and file type checks can flag tampering, though attackers can forge timestamps. Package verification can be defeated by forged metadata, as in one backdoored RPM that differed only in its key ID. Auditd and logs reveal executed commands and connecting addresses. On live hosts, the procfs exe link recovers deleted binaries, SIGSTOP freezes a process for gcore memory dumps, and NAT rules can relay traffic with no listening process. Large packet captures are better handled by Bro than Wireshark.

For analysis, script-based malware can be cleaned with code beautifiers and its eval calls replaced with print statements to expose later stages, while compiled binaries call for strings, disassemblers, strace, ltrace and gdb. Dynamic work should happen in an isolated environment. The closing advice: inventory Linux assets and who can reach them, and enable two-factor authentication on SSH to limit credential reuse. A hands-on sandbox workshop with root access to three servers accompanied the talk.

talks.title: What’s in Your Risk Assessment?
talks.teaser: Explains how quantitative ranges, loss scenarios and trade studies can replace heat maps in risk assessments.
talks.summary:
The session argues that many risk assessments satisfy regulations yet fail to support business decisions. The speakers say heat maps squeeze ranges into single points, which creates false precision, and they propose a probabilistic method instead. Their approach rests on five visible artifacts: assets, loss event scenarios, data, probability distributions and trade studies. Audience polling during the talk checked how many attendees' assessments already included industry cost data, probability distributions and trade studies.

The middle of the talk walks through a case study about a regional bank with a large customer database. The team modeled nine loss scenarios, estimating threat event frequency, resistance strength informed by a red team exercise, and secondary loss magnitude, then ran Monte Carlo simulations. The top scenario showed a 10% chance of losses above 160 million, well beyond the stated risk appetite. The speakers then compared mitigations such as encryption, insurance, tokenization, faster recovery and awareness training by risk reduction against cost.

The closing advice is to start with numeric ranges rather than red, yellow and green labels, and to accept uncertainty when perfect data is missing. Calibrating subject matter experts and documenting the source and method behind every input makes estimates easier to defend. Mapping the assessment to regulatory wording and to the company's loss taxonomy helps with compliance. Attendees were pointed to Fair Institute resources and books by Doug Hubbard and Jack Jones for further study.

talks.title: Same Thing We Do Every Few Minutes, Pinky - Try to Take Over All Your Subdomains!
talks.teaser: Shows how Starbucks tackled dangling DNS records that let attackers take over subdomains, and the automated scanner it built.
talks.summary:
Alun Jones, an application security engineer at Starbucks, explains subdomain takeover. A DNS CNAME still points to a cloud resource the company has deleted, so an attacker can claim that resource and serve content under the company's own domain. He outlines the risks: cookies scoped to a parent domain can be read by the attacker's site, trusted embeds can be abused, and employees can be phished through a convincing lookalike login page. He also describes a takeover that happened within an hour of a live developer training session.

The first response was a script that checked CNAME targets for NXDOMAIN errors and reported matches to teams, followed by a PowerShell check that queried the Azure graph to see whether the company still owned a resource. That was more accurate, but it still relied on manual steps. Bug bounty reports rose after the payouts were disclosed, many were false positives such as traffic managers whose endpoints were all disabled, and teams often took most of a day to find who owned a page. The team moved to automated scans that run every couple of minutes, using DNS zone data it already holds rather than waiting for caches to expire.

The resulting tool, submon-cli, runs as Azure Functions, queues any name whose target no longer belongs to the company, and recreates that resource so it can be held. The speaker also covers other takeover types: A records reassigned by cloud providers, leftover NS delegations on AWS, and abandoned hard-coded resource names in page source. He closes by asking cloud providers to delay releasing DNS names in enterprise subscriptions and to send faster deletion notices, and urges organisations to audit their own environments and automate the checks.

talks.title: Rives: Buttons Now
talks.teaser: Shares a collection of self-written conference buttons, showing how attendees choose to describe themselves.
talks.summary:
Rives opened day two of the RSA Conference with a short session tied to the event's human element theme, centred on magnetic buttons placed around the venue. Attendees could pick pre-printed descriptors such as MacGyver or Nurturer, or take a blank button and fill it in with a white gel pen.

Rives then collected write-in designs digitally: blank button templates were loaded onto a tablet, and attendees around the grounds were asked to design a button that showed something people might not guess from looking at them. The results were shown on screen and grouped into recurring themes. Some were about self-image and humour, such as a proud chubby hubby or a dad of nine. Others were nerd references, including Star Trek, Star Wars and Street Fighter, along with jokes aimed at the RSA crowd, such as blockchain for president and a firewall. A few were personal announcements, and some were playful takes on being tired or humble.

The session closed with an invitation for attendees to come up and make their own button, with a closing question about what design they would pick for 2025. The talk is a light, art-focused look at identity and self-expression, with no technical security content for practitioners to take away.

talks.title: You, Me and FIPS 140-3: A Guide to the New Standard and Transition
talks.teaser: Maps FIPS 140-3 against 140-2, key transition dates, and vendor guidance for surviving the cryptographic module validation shift.
talks.summary:
Federal Information Processing Standard 140-2 has anchored cryptographic module assurance since 2001, but its reliance on ever-growing implementation guidance makes modern products—SoCs, virtual HSMs, and cloud stacks—hard to validate. Ryan Thomas outlines why the program stalled, how the U.S. chose ISO 19790 (with ISO 24759 testing requirements) as FIPS 140-3, and how NIST’s SP 800-140A–F series reshapes documentation, approved algorithms, authentication, and non-invasive attack mitigation.

The middle of the session walks through terminology and requirement shifts: degraded versus normal operation, sensitive and public security parameters, renamed self-tests, conditional algorithm checks before first use, stricter bypass integrity using MACs or signatures, stronger role and authentication rules, physical-security updates at levels 3 and 4, software modules at level 2 without Common Criteria, and removed legacy items such as CRNGT and formal modeling at level 4.

Practitioners should track publication of the slimmer implementation guidance and 800-140 set (targeted around March 2020), September 2020 as the opening for 140-3 submissions, and September 2021 as the cutoff for new 140-2 submissions. Existing 140-2 certificates remain valid for five years and are not mass-revoked. Parallel 140-2 and 140-3 validations may be feasible at levels 1–2. Near-term actions include static analysis, default-credential changes, optional pre-operational self-tests, and business-driven timing amid parallel NIST algorithm transitions (ACVP, RSA key generation, entropy, and key-agreement updates).

talks.title: Women Hacker Boss
talks.teaser: Explores how Offensive Security's CEO balances operational leadership with deep technical teams and workforce diversity goals.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with Offensive Security as a global training and certification provider behind OSCP and Kali Linux, serving students in more than 130 countries through mostly online programs plus selective live offerings such as Black Hat sessions. Ning Wang describes her path from a China-U.S. physics exchange scholarship and Berkeley PhD into executive finance and operations roles at Lynda.com, HackerOne, and elsewhere, then into the CEO seat without being the room's deepest hacker.

She argues that product direction in security training should come from listening to certified offensive practitioners on a nine-person executive team, admitting gaps openly, and asking learning-oriented questions rather than pretending to own every technical decision. She recounts seeking candid buy-in before accepting the role and building mutual respect by leaning on team strengths while covering weaknesses.

The discussion closes on market demand for hacking skills, the "try harder" lab mindset behind long hands-on exams, recent refreshes such as expanded PWK with Active Directory content, and plans for streaming and broader curricula. She acknowledges limited proactive outreach to women and diverse learners, describes personal welcomes at advanced classes, and outlines an internal women empowerment initiative plus ideas like diverse training voices.

talks.title: Insights from Kara Swisher
talks.teaser: A journalist maps how social platforms, weak oversight, and new tech trends amplify hacking, disinformation, and election gaps.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames technology as leaving an early euphoric internet era for a harder phase where inventions must be judged by their real-world harm. Cybersecurity sits inside that shift because widely deployed products affect consumer, business, and national safety alongside opportunity.

The speaker walks through a running list of trends: artificial intelligence, quantum and robotics, mobility and drones, algorithmic endless choice, and privacy erosion through both theft and voluntary data sharing. She argues platforms reward attention through outrage, citing engagement architecture and a statistic that each added word of moral outrage raises retweet rates by 17%. Founder-controlled giants lack accountability; Tristan Harris’s “human downgrading” idea ties addiction, civility, and democracy to one attention economy. On security, she describes continuous partial hacking as devices multiply, notes interference campaigns that used social products as designed rather than breaking in, and laments stalled election-protection legislation amid weakened political will. Bot-driven pile-ons on opposing public figures illustrate discord as the goal.

Analog shocks—climate change and novel coronavirus—are framed as existential backdrops, with telework raising new exposure. She closes that outcomes remain changeable: a handful of large companies could alter deployment, regulation and citizens still matter, and practitioners should steer emerging systems toward tools rather than weapons.

talks.title: Why Your People Are Still Your Best Cyber-Defense
talks.teaser: Uses ransomware responses at Hydro and Nunavut to argue that people remain the strongest element of cyber defense.
talks.summary:
Ann Johnson opens with the 1982 Elk Cloner virus, a prank by a teenager that exploited ordinary people as well as the machine. She argues that human weaknesses have shaped cyber incidents ever since, from that early virus to a 1998 hacker testimony before the US Senate.

The core of the talk is two ransomware responses shown in a video. Aluminum producer Hydro, with about 36,000 staff, began its attack when one employee opened an infected email. Executives hand-wrote notices, photographed them on their phones and had managers post printed copies around the buildings to keep staff informed. In Canada's Nunavut territory, an attack knocked out financial, health and emergency services across 25 communities. Officials refused to pay, reverted to paper forms and fax machines, and rebuilt with help from Microsoft's DART team.

Johnson advises never paying ransoms, since criminals return to places where they have succeeded. She says AI and machine learning help but will not be a perfect answer. Her takeaway is to invest in people alongside technology, hire candidates others might overlook, such as a blind cybersecurity intern, and stay patient with human mistakes during an incident.

talks.title: How to Reduce Supply Chain Risk: Lessons from Efforts to Block Huawei
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how to judge supply chain risk in 5G, weighing national security against trade and testing standards.
talks.summary:
This RSA panel looked at how to manage supply chain risk in telecom and government systems, with the U.S. effort to remove Huawei equipment as the central case. The moderator framed the discussion around whether the issue is a trade dispute or a matter of critical infrastructure, and the panelists questioned whether a vendor's country of origin is a sound basis for judging its risk.

Bruce Schneier argued that supply chain security is extremely hard because hardware, software, assembly and shipping span many countries and many engineers, so a backdoor can be hidden almost anywhere. He added that much of 5G's exposure comes from inherited protocols rather than from vendor choice alone. Katie Arrington, speaking for the Department of Defense, said the department reduces risk using its own data and by requiring contractors to meet the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification, which she described as built on NIST and ISO 27001 controls. Andy Purdy proposed a three-legged approach covering products, carrier operations and supplier access to customer networks, backed by transparency measures. Kathryn Waldron warned that checklist-based audits can create a false sense of compliance.

The panel agreed that testing catches bugs and default passwords but is weak at finding deliberate backdoors. A software bill of materials was presented as useful for tracking vulnerable libraries, though not as a defence against nation-state threats. The main takeaway was that carriers often lack objective criteria for assessing vendors, and the discussion ended without agreement on how to balance security and trade concerns.

talks.title: Navigating Privacy in a Data-Driven World: Treating Privacy as a Human Right
talks.teaser: Argues that privacy should be treated as a human right, drawing on cookies, GDPR and emerging biometric data.
talks.summary:
Jules Polonetsky, a longtime privacy leader, argues that privacy and security teams should be partners rather than adversaries. Security staff guard against outside attackers, while privacy staff ask whether those who hold data use it legally, fairly and ethically. He recalls his early years as chief privacy officer at DoubleClick, where linking offline records to web browsing triggered regulatory investigations, and a government anti-drug website that quietly carried third-party tracking pixels.

He then reviews the limits of current approaches. U.S. privacy rests largely on consumer protection law, and tools such as the AdChoices icon and Do Not Track never shifted public expectations. Biometrics, brain-computer interfaces and health data drawn from social media often fall outside HIPAA. He urges treating privacy as a civil rights and power issue, pointing to California's access and deletion rights and the GDPR's broader rights framing. Technical options include differential privacy, federated learning and synthetic data, alongside independent academic access to corporate data and ethical testing of algorithms for discriminatory outcomes.

In the question period he explained that GDPR data protection officers currently have no formal certification, and he expects U.S. firms to rely on certified privacy professionals. He also flagged concerns about police use of open genetic databases. He closed by arguing that balancing innovation and rights is messy, and that policymakers need translators who understand the technology.

talks.title: Kr00k: How KRACKing Amazon Echo Exposed a Billion+ Vulnerable WiFi Devices
talks.teaser: Researchers explain Kr00k, a Wi-Fi chipset flaw that exposes buffered packets encrypted with an all-zero key after disassociation events.
talks.summary:
The presenters open with why consumer IoT expands enterprise attack surface, then position Kr00k as broader than gadget bugs: a flaw in widespread FullMAC Wi-Fi silicon that can undermine WPA2 link-layer confidentiality even when applications do not add TLS or a VPN.

They walk through association, unauthenticated management frames, and the four-way handshake, then describe how CCMP encryption relies on a temporal session key implemented in hardware for speed. After a disassociation, vulnerable chips zero the key as expected but still transmit leftover transmit-buffer data encrypted with all zeros. Attackers can trigger dissociations repeatedly, try all-zero decryption, and recognize leaked plaintext by management-frame patterns. Live capture in a workplace setting exposed DNS, TCP, and cleartext HTTP; a demo recovered a smart-hub web session ID and hijacked the session. Affected lab-tested devices span phones, laptops, and some access points using Broadcom or Cypress chips; the work began when first-generation Amazon Echo proved KRACK-vulnerable and a modified variant led to the chipset root cause.

Kr00k differs from KRACK as a bug rather than a handshake key-reinstall attack, and mitigation is firmware on clients and often-neglected routers. Vendors received coordinated disclosure with extended patching timelines; practitioners should apply current security updates and manufacturers should confirm chipset fixes.

talks.title: RSAC Launch Pad
talks.teaser: A startup pitches automated network access policies that contain attackers, then takes questions from security investors.
talks.summary:
Zero Networks, one of three early-stage companies in this Launch Pad segment, pitched to security venture investors. Its premise is that attacks spread because users and machines hold far more network access than they need. Segmenting networks and applying zero-trust controls everywhere is hard at scale, so the company generates network access policies automatically for each user and machine. It likened this to Gmail challenging logins from new devices rather than requiring a ticket for every exception.

The product observes normal communication, then simulates and visualizes the policies it would create before the administrator switches to prevention. Blocked users can be cleared with two-factor authentication on their phone, without IT stepping in. The pitch cited design partners in retail, manufacturing, energy and the public sector, plus a blocked penetration test at one of them. Sales are direct for now, with MSSP and reseller partnerships planned.

In the questions, the founder said an early agent-based design was dropped after talking with CISOs, reusing existing infrastructure to reduce friction. The service runs in the cloud, with an on-premises virtual machine acting as a proxy rather than sitting on every endpoint. Customers often start with a small set of machines, and vendor integrations can flag the most exposed ones. The judges showed interest, and the takeaway is that a small, low-friction proof of value helps a cautious buyer say yes.
