talks.title: ICS OSINT: An Attacker’s Perspective
talks.teaser: Shows how public filings, vendor press releases and job postings aid ICS attack planning, and how defenders can cut exposure.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces open source intelligence (OSINT) for industrial control system (ICS) environments from an attacker's point of view. The speakers, both from Dragos, note that destructive ICS attacks need specialized skills, while the early reconnaissance needed to plan one takes little advanced capability. They define OSINT and operational security, place collection in the reconnaissance stage of the ICS kill chain, and describe passive and active methods. They also outline the kinds of information adversaries look for, including personnel, accessibility, recoverability and vulnerability details.

Several cases show how public material can become targeting data. A manufacturer's SEC filing revealed legal proceedings, acquisition history, an ERP update and its accounting firm. After a 2019 New York City blackout, which was not a cyber event, public utility documentation showed decades-old equipment and a protection relay link that required an engineer on site to change settings. Vendor press releases named specific control systems and software at a plant, and RFPs on a procurement site exposed schematics and contractor details. Job postings listed the devices and software a role required, and a public energy map showed plant locations and fuel types. In a Dragos case, an activity group gathered generation station lists and engineering diagrams while planning an attack on a Western energy company. A separate LinkedIn lure impersonating oil, gas and mining firms led victims to a credential capture site.

For defenders, the speakers recommend regular OSINT assessments of their own organization, limiting public detail about vendors and partners, and reviewing job ads and public data dumps. They also suggest multi-factor authentication, password-protected sharing of sensitive documents, and checks for services exposed to the internet. A collection risk and vulnerability matrix was presented to rate how useful a piece of information would be to an adversary.

talks.title: Losing Our Reality: How Deepfakes Threaten Businesses and Global Markets
talks.teaser: Explains how deepfake audio and video threaten business reputation and markets, and which defenses organizations can plan.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how deepfakes, synthetic audio or video built with deep learning, create risks beyond politics and celebrity content. It explains that a generative adversarial network pits a generator, which produces fake samples, against a discriminator that rejects them, so each round makes forgeries more convincing. Consumer apps and paid web services now make the tools widely accessible.

Business examples include a UK company whose CEO wired 220 million euros after a deepfake audio call impersonated the parent company's CEO. A hypothetical case imagines a fabricated video of a carmaker's chief announcing a production delay, letting an attacker profit from the resulting share drop. The speaker argues that disinformation feeds on existing beliefs, so a refutation alone falls short; it must be paired with a plausible factual replacement story.

On detection, visual artifacts and blink patterns have stopped being reliable, and the speaker sees behavioral analytics, which compare a person's habitual expressions across a whole video, as more promising. Provenance watermarks at capture face the problem of platforms re-encoding uploads. For organizations, the talk recommends consolidating official communication channels, treating a fake release as an incident in the disaster recovery plan, and building ties with news outlets that can validate video before publication. It ends by urging engagement with legislators on where satire ends and libel begins.

talks.title: Practical Use of the MUD Specification to Support Access Control in the IoT
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how NCCoE builds of the MUD standard limit IoT device traffic to approved communication profiles.
talks.summary:
The talk presents proof-of-concept builds from the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence that apply the Manufacturer Usage Description specification, RFC 8520, to control which network resources IoT devices may reach. The speakers explain the problem: many low-cost IoT devices lack strong built-in security and can be abused as pivot points or botnet members, and a typical home network lets them talk to everything. With a MUD-capable device, the device advertises a URL pointing to its manufacturer's profile file, and a MUD manager fetches and verifies the signed file before turning it into traffic rules on the router.

The architecture can be combined into one router or split across on-premises and cloud components. The first demonstration, build one, used a Cisco-based setup. It showed the switch receiving the device's URL over DHCP, the manager validating the profile and returning access control lists and VLAN placement, and a test where the approved update server loaded while an unapproved site was blocked. Build two, built around a router with a built-in manager and a mobile app, showed how a user can view MUD-capable devices and their profiles. The speakers also covered threat signaling, a separate blocklist layer that uses DNS responses and a threat API to push rules that block known malicious domains.

The main takeaway is that MUD adds a network layer on top of basic device hygiene rather than replacing it. Practitioners were pointed to the NCCoE practice guides, and manufacturers and network vendors were urged to build MUD support into their products. Build three, which adds secure onboarding, was still in progress at the time of the talk.

talks.title: API Security Exposure for Gift Card Fraud: A 15-Year-Old’s Guide
talks.teaser: Walks through building credential stuffing configs against login APIs and outlines the defenses that slow them.
talks.summary:
Tanay Deshmukh, a high school student, explains how APIs behind mobile apps and websites can expose gift card balances and subscription logins. He covers credential stuffing, SQL injection used to collect login pairs, and web scraping as the main routes attackers take, and notes that a simple gift card numbering scheme, where only the final digits change, can make valid numbers easier to guess.

The demonstration uses OpenBullet with Fiddler, a local web proxy, to build a login config for a file sharing site: capturing a post request, locating a changing token, parsing it with left and right strings, and setting a failure key check. A second example tests a mobile API through an Android emulator, where Fiddler's proxy and an installed certificate expose HTTPS traffic. A session ID returned by a start-session request is parsed as JSON, and a generated device identifier is added as a variable. Paid tools with large config libraries are also mentioned.

On defense, CAPTCHAs add delay and a per-solve cost to each automated attempt, while rate limiting caps requests from one IP address within a time window, helping separate bots from people. The speaker reported issues to affected companies' security teams and through HackerOne, sharing screenshots and offering calls. The takeaway: balance checks and mobile logins need rate limits and verification, since they often lack the protections of web logins.

talks.title: Tackling Cyber-Enabled Crime at Scale: Moving Enforcement Forward
talks.teaser: Shows how the NYPD measured and trained officers on cyber-enabled crime, and the surprising victim data that followed.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with how a typical scam report moves through US policing. A patrol officer takes the complaint, and once Bitcoin or cyber comes up, the case is often referred to federal agencies and closed locally. The speaker argues that the NYPD had no structured data on cyber-enabled crime, no agreed definition, and no standard protocol, so the problem could not be measured. Observational data from people who called the police showed that victims were not mostly the older adults the department expected, and that many never reported at all.

The 2019 pilot took a bottom-up approach. Cyber-enabled crimes were defined as traditional frauds carried out through online tools, kept separate from cyber-native intrusions. Patrol officers received a short training and a simple mobile web app with drop-down questions, and about 700 officers in one Queens region were trained within a month. Cases described included an 80-year-old woman whose wire transfer was recovered after police acted quickly, and a SIM swap ring in which 53 victims were identified over ten days. Blockchain tracing tools surfaced leads that detectives had been unable to follow.

The main takeaway was that arrests were not the goal. The pilot aimed to improve data, reduce cases closed immediately for lack of leads, and return money to victims, with about $60,000 recovered. The speaker urged agencies to stop using cyber as a catch-all, standardize terminology, consolidate fraud investigations, build victim recovery guidance, and open source the app. Scaling depends on process and people more than technology.

talks.title: OpenSSL and FIPS... They Are Back Together!
talks.teaser: Traces OpenSSL 3.0’s provider model and the renewed FIPS 140-2 validation path after years apart from mainline development.
talks.summary:
Regulated deployments kept many organizations on OpenSSL 1.0.2 because the validated FIPS object module only worked with that line, even after it lost mainstream support. The speakers recap prior FIPS modules, certificate expiry and historical-list rules, and looming transitions such as RSA key-generation requirements that can force earlier sunset unless modules are updated or algorithms move to non-approved use.

They present OpenSSL 3.0 as a full rework: providers plug in at the EVP layer so applications can pin the FIPS provider via configuration while legacy and default providers remain available. The old forked “FIPS canister” statically buried inside libcrypto gives way to a separable FIPS provider, with discussion of packaging, which TLS and PRF pieces belong inside the boundary, self-tests guided by implementation notes, and disk-based integrity checks for shared-library builds.

Roadmap material covers alpha and beta milestones toward a year-end 3.0 release, weekly design involvement by the validation lab, GitHub visibility into open work, and ACVP-driven algorithm testing before CMVP submission shortly after GA. Takeaways stress planning jumps from 1.0.2 to 1.1.1 and then 3.0, expecting API compatibility but not ABI, and using an older validated provider with newer libcrypto where needed while certification work finishes.

talks.title: The Impact of Software Security Practice Adoption Quantified
talks.teaser: Quantifies how adopting specific DevSecOps practices correlates with lower security risk across about 200 Comcast teams.
talks.summary:
This talk presents correlations between software security practices and risk outcomes for about 200 teams at Comcast. The speaker frames the practices as DevSecOps practices and stresses that the results show correlation, not proven cause, so teams should weigh them against their own context. The headline finding is that teams at the highest practice maturity showed 85% lower risk than the lowest-maturity teams, with CVSS severity weighted exponentially in the risk score.

The speaker explains how the program works. Security staff act as toolsmiths and advisors, offer self-service resources, and help teams adopt about three practices per 90-day cycle with executive sponsorship. Teams self-assess each practice on a scale running from thoughts to words, actions and culture. Only culture-level adoption tracked with lower risk; partial credit for words and actions erased the signal. Among the strongest practices were clearing high-severity findings from scanners, merging only secure code, security peer review and secure coding training. Running scans alone showed no value, and a 40-hour novice security course correlated negatively, which the speaker attributed to selection bias.

The data came from network-originated scans mapped to 158 of 195 onboarded teams, so the results carry bias and incident data is planned for later analysis. The speaker closes with an action plan: make the case for a transformation, run a gap analysis on a sample of teams, build the easy button, and bring a first team to culture within six months.

talks.title: Biometric Data: Power, Promise and Privacy Challenges
talks.teaser: Covers biometric privacy laws in the US and Europe, the security risks of biometric data, and practical steps for organizations.
talks.summary:
Three speakers, from a software company and a law firm, framed biometric data as both useful and risky. A biometric identifier cannot be changed the way a password can, so many states protect it much like a social security number. Recent cases showed the stakes: a facial recognition firm faced suits over billions of scraped public photos, and Facebook settled an Illinois class action over photo tagging for $550 million after its attempts to dismiss the claims failed.

Speakers explained that the US has no federal biometric law, but Illinois' statute allows private lawsuits with penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Europe treats biometric data as a special category that requires explicit consent. A Swedish fine against a school using facial recognition for attendance and a UK order to delete voice prints showed how regulators respond. On security, printed heads, silicone fingerprint rings and high-resolution iris images have fooled sensors, so they recommended local storage, encryption, extra factors for large transactions and deleting raw data once it is no longer needed.

Practical advice included inventorying where biometrics are used and checking consent and retention rules by jurisdiction. Using a virtual reality game that collects eye movement and pulse rate, they asked why the data is needed and urged indemnity terms in developer contracts. Children under 13 need parental consent under federal law, and the panel noted that hashing can reduce breach harm.

talks.title: The Network Is Going Dark: Why Decryption Matters for SecOps
talks.teaser: Shows how TLS 1.3 and perfect forward secrecy blind network monitoring, and which decryption options still work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shift to encrypted traffic. The speakers point out that most internet traffic is now encrypted, that TLS 1.3 hides the server certificate from passive observers, and that DNS over HTTPS hides hostnames. Perfect forward secrecy also means a stolen server private key can no longer decrypt recorded sessions.

The middle section compares options. JA3 and JA3S fingerprints are useful but easy to evade and prone to false positives, since about a quarter of the blacklisted fingerprints in one check matched legitimate browsers. Traffic analysis can reveal bulk transfers and interactivity but is often overhyped. TLS interception restores plaintext for user and BYOD traffic, yet it requires a local certificate authority and can weaken security when implemented poorly. For services you control, session key forwarding keeps end-to-end encryption intact while still allowing full packet analysis.

Jesse Rothstein recommends turning off DNS over HTTPS on managed enterprise endpoints, intercepting user traffic where needed, and forwarding session keys for local services. Joshua Northrup then described Fiserv's deployment: roughly 3,000 to 3,500 session-forwarding agents, pushed out by automation, decrypting around 6,000 PFS sessions per second across about 60 data centers. He argued that logs from vendor and open-source libraries are often incomplete, so decrypted traffic adds visibility into what applications actually do.

talks.title: I Had My Mom Break into a Prison. Then, We Had Pie.
talks.teaser: Shares physical pen test stories, including a mother posing as a health inspector, and why the human element matters in security.
talks.summary:
John Strand opens by arguing that physical penetration testing has settled into predictable routines, with customers trained to spot the same ruses, such as a fake delivery worker. He says fear-driven tests do little to help organizations improve, and that the human element deserves more attention in security work.

Strand's central example is his mother, a former school food service director who later handled finances at his firm. Posing as a health inspector, she was let into a correctional facility, completed a full inspection, and plugged USB devices into systems while the team waited for callbacks to their command servers. She reported that the site scored 82 and that the director asked how to prepare better next time. He then describes an Iowa courthouse test in which two testers were arrested after an alarm drew deputies and the authorization was unclear. Community events and remarks from the sheriff highlighted downstream effects on emergency responders and the need to clarify scope before testing.

His practical advice is to treat end users with respect, since people notice condescension, and to explain why a control matters rather than simply banning tools. He recommends becoming the security resource staff turn to, telling stories with a human angle in newsletters, running regular sessions on protecting home devices, and rewarding employees who report social engineering attempts. People in authority should not react harshly when someone respectfully questions them, and testers should carry clear, verifiable permission.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: Global Threat Brief
talks.teaser: Reviews the ransomware surge and nation-state intrusions, including IP theft, then forecasts threats and offers strategy advice.
talks.summary:
The talk sets aside detailed hacking techniques in favour of a broad review of threat activity and the speaker's strategy views. It argues that 2019 was dominated by ransomware, with families such as Ryuk and GandCrab borrowing nation-state tactics like lateral movement and wake-on-LAN to reach sleeping machines. Practical lessons include that a ransom payment can still yield a faulty decryptor and that backups which take too long to restore can push victims toward paying.

The middle section covers state actors. Pakistan, Vietnam and Iran are described as moving into intellectual property theft, with Iranian groups also linked to reconnaissance that may support kinetic attacks. North Korean groups are portrayed as financially motivated, using malicious browser plugins, cryptocurrency miners and RDP access. On China, the speaker suggests indictments disrupted several units, while the MSS now runs most operations and the Equifax breach was tied to a newer PLA unit.

The closing predictions include disruptive Iranian attacks against western targets in 2020, a renewed Russian push into intellectual property theft, and continued Chinese economic espionage despite a trade deal. Advice centres on weighing tradeoffs against a realistic threat model, assuming intrusion, and reacting faster. The speaker also argues that policy, regulation and deterrence are the industry's next frontier.

talks.title: Rethink the Way You Secure Your Organization with Intrinsic Security
talks.teaser: Argues for building security into platforms rather than bolting on point tools, with a practitioner's view from an airline.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with VMware executives arguing that rising ransomware and an overcrowded vendor landscape call for security built into platforms across networking, workloads, endpoints, identity and cloud, rather than added as separate point tools. They also cite a survey of CISOs that reported attackers shifting toward evasive techniques, a resurgence of ransomware, and weak cooperation between IT and security teams.

The main segment is a conversation with Carrie Mills, a security leader at Southwest Airlines, moderated by Patrick Morley. She explains that the airline runs both an IT environment and an operational technology side, where aircraft now have IP addresses, and that the Aviation ISAC helps airlines share lessons across that gap. She says phishing remains hard because some staff still click links and enter credentials, so basic controls must limit the damage. On platforms, she describes shrinking the number of bolt-on tools, weighing when a built-in platform feature is enough versus buying a separate product, and the difficulty of networking teams taking on security functions outside their expertise.

Her practical advice centres on relationships and visibility: build trust between infrastructure and security teams before an incident, track assets with context about their function and owners, treat vendors as partners and assess their culture during selection, and keep the board informed through regular briefings. She asks vendors to reduce agent fatigue, including on OT systems where some agents do not run, and to build security into platforms from the start.

talks.title: 10 Things I Wish Every Developer Knew about Security
talks.teaser: Ten practical lessons for AppSec teams on coaching developers, third-party risk, secrets handling, and container security.
talks.summary:
Chris Romeo, CEO of a security education company, opens by imagining developers so security-minded that the OWASP Top 10 and standalone security tools would no longer be needed. He contrasts that goal with today's reality. Surveys show developers care about security but lack time for it, and a study found vulnerable snippets in almost 200,000 Google Play Store apps that likely came from Stack Overflow. He argues that AppSec programs should be judged by how fast they fix vulnerabilities, not by bug totals or blame.

The core of the talk is ten lessons. He stresses that security is an ally rather than a blocker, and that everyone on a team owns part of it, supported by champions and coaches. Teams cannot hack themselves secure, so builders deserve as much focus as breakers, with risk-based triage for findings. He points to OWASP resources such as the Cheat Sheet Series and free tools, and notes that third-party components bring vulnerabilities from the start; one of his applications pulled in 98,000 dependencies. Further points cover shifting security left, right and outward, keeping secrets out of source control, and treating Docker and Kubernetes as platforms that need secure configuration rather than security products, plus tactical use of newer AppSec tools.

He closes by urging teams to assess where they stand on each point, starting with security culture, and to begin improving now rather than waiting for a complete plan.

talks.title: Safety Implications of Medical Device Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Traces FDA medical device cybersecurity guidance and a proposed board that weighs patient safety in high-risk vulnerability decisions.
talks.summary:
Medical devices now connect to networks and run software, so unpatched vulnerabilities can cause patient harm or give an attacker a route into a hospital network. The speakers frame device security as a shared responsibility across manufacturers, healthcare organizations, clinicians, patients and researchers, with DHS, FDA and information sharing groups helping coordinate disclosure. They trace FDA's approach from 2013, when a large disclosure of device vulnerabilities prompted pre-market guidance in 2014 and post-market guidance in 2016.

The post-market guidance asks manufacturers to consider how a malicious adversary could exploit a device, not only its intended use. It also offers reporting relief when no patient harm has occurred, the risk is addressed within 30 and 60 days, and the manufacturer actively shares information. The speakers describe MITRE's work with FDA: a stakeholder study, a CVSS scoring rubric adapted for healthcare, a playbook for fitting cyber into hospital emergency response after WannaCry, and a sandbox for validating vulnerabilities against clinical scenarios. They also outline a proposed CyberMed Safety Analysis Board, which would bring clinical and manufacturer expertise into severity decisions, and a tabletop exercise that exposed gaps such as clinician-friendly advisories and help for small practices.

The question session covered vendor remote-support connections, with a warning about devices left online after maintenance and a case where such devices were used to pull 7,000 x-rays out of a network. A security-only patch generally does not require returning to FDA for recertification unless it affects essential performance. The takeaway for practitioners is to bring patient safety context into vulnerability work, and to know which devices are exposed through inventories and software bills of materials.

talks.title: Time to Tell
talks.teaser: Walks through patching delays, Curveball, cloud metadata credential theft, and the risk quantum poses to today's encrypted data.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the argument that defenders keep falling behind on basics. Patching is slow: BlueKeep was only about 60 percent addressed on internet-facing systems eight months after disclosure, and EternalBlue remained a top network exploit nearly three years after WannaCry. Trust in core building blocks is also under strain. Curveball lets an attacker make files appear to be part of the operating system, and a SHA-1 collision that once took thousands of years of processor time can now be produced in under a minute with a public script.

The middle of the talk turns to cloud risk. A scenario follows epidemiologists who publish a dashboard through a reverse proxy to reach private resources. That same proxy can also reach the instance metadata service, which exposes credentials. The demonstration shows an attacker retrieving those credentials, confirming broad S3 access, and syncing a sensitive bucket to their own machine. The speaker notes this is one of forty-three cloud-specific techniques on MITRE's ATT&CK matrix, and argues that cloud-native configuration and default internet exposure make such mistakes easy to make.

The final section covers post-quantum risk. Adversaries may collect encrypted traffic and cloud data today and decrypt it later, so the speaker urges organizations to rank their data by sensitivity and by how long it must stay protected. He points to NIST's post-quantum algorithm work and the limited funding behind it, noting that a field of 69 candidates had narrowed to 26 after three years. Practical takeaways include moving network traffic to TLS 1.3, inventorying systems that depend on quantum-vulnerable cryptography, and building migration plans that prioritize the most sensitive, long-lived data.

talks.title: Cloud Threat Hunting
talks.teaser: Walks through a simulated AWS and Azure breach, showing which cloud logs and alerts reveal an attacker.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the Capital One cloud breach, which the company learned about months after the attacker first touched its systems, when an outside party reported stolen S3 data found on GitHub. The presenters from LMG Security argue that threat hunting, a hypothesis-driven and human-led search beyond automated alerts, would have caught the intrusion much earlier, and they note that cloud visibility is often weak in most organizations.

To test this, the team built a simulated company with AWS workloads, an S3 bucket, a deliberately vulnerable AWS environment, and Office 365 with SharePoint and email. AWS logs were streamed into Splunk through Kinesis and Firehose, while Azure audit logs were pulled in through the Microsoft management API. Default EC2 logging was off, so they had to enable CloudWatch, which added storage and compute cost. A GuardDuty alert fired after the metadata credentials were pulled, while a user agent string showing Kali Linux was treated only as a weak indicator. In Office 365, a credential stuffing attack against a weak password succeeded, and inconsistent results from the built-in GUI pushed the team toward scripted log exports. The attacker then used a compromised virtual machine to reach mail and SharePoint, where an email exposed AWS keys and a SharePoint download confirmed data theft.

The main takeaways are to test cloud detections with simulations before relying on them, to know which high-value data needs watching, to budget for logging costs, and to chain weak indicators together rather than rely on single alerts.

talks.title: Rocked to the Core
talks.teaser: A panel connects systemic foundational flaws, sector patching tradeoffs, and upstream choices that strengthen cyber resilience.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with a thread linking Heartbleed, Spectre, Meltdown, and certificate-validation bugs to long-running tradeoffs that favored speed, cost, and performance over safety. One panelist argues the industry must accept deliberate inefficiency—architectures closer to aviation-style redundancy than maximal optimization—and invest in boring low-level fixes instead of stacking fragile layers.

Operational voices describe healthcare and manufacturing realities: bill-of-materials scrutiny, network isolation for devices that cannot be patched mid-production, and cases where patching risk outweighs exposure. Others stress homogeneity amplifying blast radius, untrusted code in more places, and the limits of software-only mitigations for processor flaws. The conversation moves through cyber resilience after wake-up events, embedding security knowledge in engineering teams, Swiss-cheese architecture, and integrated technology risk frameworks that balance security with reliability and capacity.

Regulation and certification draw split views—mandates that raised bars versus gold-star economics that vendors game—while metrics need paired counters for unintended consequences. Closing guidance centers on knowing what systems contain, pushing secure development responsibility into product teams, and decomposing monolithic stacks into isolatable components even at a performance cost.

talks.title: Fear and Loathing in Cybersecurity: An Analysis of the Psychology of Fear
talks.teaser: Shows why fear-based security messages often fail and how psychology research suggests more effective awareness alternatives.
talks.summary:
Jessica Barker argues that awareness work cannot avoid talking about threats, so fear is an unavoidable emotion for audiences. She explains that fear grows when a subject feels unfamiliar or out of control, and that cybersecurity often fits that description. She introduces fear appeals and the Extended Parallel Process Model, which holds that people must see a threat as real, see it applying to them, and believe a practical response will work.

Barker shows how these ideas play out. In a tetanus study, scaring students produced little action, while a campus map and a plan for reaching the health centre led to far more vaccinations. Fear can prompt quick reactions, which is why phishing works, but lasting change needs a few priority behaviours and usable tools such as password managers. Positive framing and social proof, like reporting that most staff did not click a phishing test, tend to motivate better than negative statistics. Humour aids memory but can undermine credibility. Aviation's just culture, which avoids blaming people for incidents, shows why blame discourages reporting.

In audience questions she suggested champions networks, positive messaging after a breach, and balancing empowerment with consequences for wilful negligence. For executives, she recommended peer comparisons and arriving with a concrete plan. Her takeaway is to focus on efficacy, reduce message noise, and build a positive culture so that people report incidents.

talks.title: A Forward Look at the Cyberspace Solarium Commission
talks.teaser: Commissioners preview layered deterrence, resilience priorities, and draft legislation tied to the forthcoming Solarium report.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the historical Solarium metaphor: Eisenhower’s 1953 process to reconcile competing Cold War strategies, which lawmakers echoed when standing up the Cyberspace Solarium Commission in the 2019 National Defense Authorization Act. Panelists frame the threat landscape as nation-state–led but increasingly shared with criminals and proxies, and they argue that cyberspace deterrence as practiced today is failing while still achievable if adapted to persistent offensive activity rather than nuclear-era assumptions.

They describe the commission’s forthcoming report as a blended, whole-of-nation cyber strategy—not a new agency—built around layered deterrence: shaping behavioral norms with government, industry, and allies; hardening and resilient digital infrastructure (including consequence limiting measures such as election safeguards); and imposing timely, visible costs when defense falls short. They stress executive-branch and congressional commissioners, extensive private-sector engagement, market tools like cyber insurance, prioritization of lifeline critical functions, defend forward as one instrument among many, and annexed draft bills to speed implementation. Roughly 75 recommended actions span six implementation pillars, with dozens paired to legislative language.

Practitioners hear how post-release outreach will include hearings, briefings, and sector feedback loops, plus audience concerns on funding, unified visibility for signaling deterrence, international alignment, and equitable protection when resources must be triaged. The planned March 11 public rollout is positioned as the moment to read the full recommendation set.

talks.title: JavaScript Skimmers, Formjacking and Magecart: All You Need to Know
talks.teaser: A threat researcher maps formjacking stages, incident scale, and practical steps merchants and shoppers can take to reduce risk.
talks.summary:
Payment data theft via injected JavaScript on legitimate checkout pages affects large brands and far more small merchants. Customers often notice nothing: the URL, padlock, and fulfillment look normal while card and form fields are copied in the browser and sent elsewhere. The speaker separates skimming, formjacking, and the broad use of the Magecart label, then ties the pattern to older web injects and keyloggers shifted to server-side reach.

The session follows five stages—initial access, hiding and placing the script, activation on checkout forms, harvesting fields, and exfiltration—with a staged demo that compromises a third-party visitor-counter host and poisons a shop that loads it. Telemetry from the presenter’s organization cites hundreds of thousands of blocked visits monthly, thousands of infected domains, regional spikes from supply-chain script hits, and GDPR-scale fines. Injection paths include CMS flaws, weak SSH, misconfigured storage and repos, MSP compromises, and typosquatted analytics domains. Skimmers evade analysts via obfuscation, referrer checks, devtools detection, and image-disguised payloads.

Mitigation emphasizes knowing every third-party script, hardening checkout pages, CSP and SRI where feasible, payment tokenization, monitoring, and clear abuse contacts. Shoppers get tips on alerts, disposable cards, and optional devtools during checkout. Q&A covers script blockers, vendor-hosted shops, automated browsing checks, password managers, and integrity monitoring limits when malware lives only on remote includes.

talks.title: Protect Privacy in a Data-Driven World: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how federated learning, enclaves and homomorphic encryption can train and run models without exposing private data.
talks.summary:
Casimir Wierzynski of Intel argues that machine learning services depend on increasingly sensitive personal data, and that current privacy tools fall short. Anonymization can be undone by re-identification attacks that use machine learning, and encrypted data must be decrypted while a model works on it. Multi-party trust among data owners, model owners and cloud providers is also hard to manage, so the talk looks at privacy-preserving machine learning techniques instead.

Federated learning lets institutions train a shared model without pooling raw data, but model updates can still leak information, so the speaker pairs it with Intel SGX enclaves, which provide isolation and attestation. In a brain tumor segmentation study split across institutions, a single site reached about 70% accuracy, the pooled dataset reached 86%, and federated training came close at 85.5%, though it needed more epochs to converge. For homomorphic encryption, the speaker described HE Transformer, a back end that compiles TensorFlow models to run on encrypted data with a one-line change. Reported throughput on the MNIST digit benchmark rose from on the order of one image per second to the thousands across eight papers, and a pretrained ImageNet model reached about 1500 images per second in batch mode.

The speaker concluded that no single technique solves privacy alone, but combining them can enable new use cases. He closed with homework: three papers, an open-source repository with a Docker container, and a review of which organizational machine learning tasks could run on encrypted data. In the Q&A, he noted that the HE approach requires restricted activation functions, which can be handled with multi-party computation.

talks.title: Speaking to Executives: Implementing Quantitative Risk in Cyber-Programs
talks.teaser: Panelists share lessons from applying FAIR quantitative risk analysis to win executive buy-in and fund cyber programs.
talks.summary:
This panel, moderated by Emery Csulak, looks at why cybersecurity teams often struggle to defend budgets and explain risk in terms executives understand. Panelists Joe Albaugh, Natalie Priani and Cody Scott describe their experiences adopting quantitative risk management in government and industry, with the goal of giving IT leaders a shared language with the business rather than replacing qualitative methods.

A recurring theme was the cost of over-planning. One agency spent six months designing a methodology before deciding to run one analysis every week, big or small, to build practice. Another speaker described starting with a small coalition working on a single system instead of waiting for a perfect plan, then targeting quick wins such as everyday purchase decisions and audit findings. The panel also covered tailoring vocabulary such as asset and vulnerability to match existing frameworks, and a triage exercise on a deep-space mission's data that showed the data's value and the likelihood of compromise were both low.

For practitioners, the takeaways were to define the decision a risk analysis must support, scope early work to probable scenarios rather than worst cases, and expect executives to question how the numbers were derived. Speakers said the tooling could be as simple as a spreadsheet for a small group, while larger rollouts may need a dedicated product. They closed by noting that the right mix of quantitative and qualitative methods depends on the audience and the decision being made.

talks.title: DevSecOps State of the Union
talks.teaser: A distilled playbook distills scalable DevSecOps tactics from dozens of industry talks and mature security programs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames DevSecOps as risk management under constraint: automate workflows, treat developers as customers, favor high-signal tooling, and deliberately choose what to defer. It structures advice around mindsets, near- and long-term program building, and an actionable roadmap.

Fundamentals include unified vulnerability tracking in developer workflows, risk dashboards by team and class, continuous pull-request scanning with fast actionable feedback, security linting between regex checks and heavy static analysis, asset inventory linked to cloud and code ownership, and examples such as mapping a new critical flaw across estates. The middle covers self-service security questionnaires, secure-by-default libraries and paved roads, and detection patterns that push first-line triage to users while automating analyst context and runbooks.

Longer-term themes include least-privilege automation, investing by vulnerability class using historical data to eliminate recurring work, and enforcing invariants in cloud and infrastructure. Practitioners are urged to assess current maturity, ship bite-sized measurable wins, then scale efforts with high security return and low ongoing operational cost.

talks.title: Break the Top 10 Cloud Attack Killchains
talks.teaser: Walks through ten cloud attack kill chains, from leaked keys to subdomain takeover, and the defenses that break them.
talks.summary:
This session maps ten cloud attack kill chains, adapted from the Lockheed Martin kill chain model and linked to MITRE ATT&CK, and explains how to break each one. The presenters say their frequency observations are anecdotal rather than survey data. The starting point is static credential exposure: access keys leak through public repositories, shared images, snapshots and decompiled mobile apps, and attackers may try them within minutes. Reducing static credentials through IAM roles and federation, and scanning repositories for keys, are the main defenses.

Other chains cover exposed SSH and RDP access, databases made public through open ports or platform settings, and public object storage, where object-level permissions are hard to track. The server-side request forgery chain shows how a web flaw can reach the instance metadata service and return credentials, and a recorded demo reused those credentials in another account. Moving to metadata service version two and least-privileged roles limits this. Crypto mining is spotted through egress filtering and flow logs, network attacks are constrained by least-privileged security groups set at design time, and subdomain takeover is prevented by keeping placeholder resources behind dangling DNS records.

The closing advice is to prioritize chains by environment: lift-and-shift setups face database and network exposure, while cloud-native ones face credential and novel data exposure. Controls that cover several chains should come first, since defenders only need to break one link to stop an attack.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Has a Posse
talks.teaser: A CISA director explains the agency's role in ransomware, election security and information sharing with industry.
talks.summary:
In a stage interview, CISA Director Chris Krebs explains that the agency acts as the nation's risk advisor rather than risk manager, working across federal civilian networks and bringing industry and government together. He describes a June alert on Iranian activity that combined classified intelligence, federal monitoring data and private threat-intelligence reports, shared in anonymized form to help others avoid similar intrusions.

On ransomware, Krebs advises against paying, arguing that payment validates the criminal business model, recovery keys often fail, and there is no dependable recourse afterward. For small and mid-sized businesses and state and local governments, he recommends multifactor authentication, tested offline backups and an incident response plan. After the January strike on an Iranian military leader, CISA stood up calls reaching roughly 26,000 people and pushed out Iranian TTPs mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, with detections and mitigations, while treating destructive Iranian attacks as resembling ransomware.

On elections, Krebs said risk assessments found centralized, highly networked systems such as voter registration databases to be the main exposure, and that criminals could target them for ransom. Because full security is not achievable, he recommends offline backups, practiced response plans and paper voter rolls at the precinct level, along with paper ballots that provide an auditable record. He closes by urging industry and government to work together, pointing listeners to CISA's online resources and its hiring.

talks.title: The Cryptographer's Panel
talks.teaser: Veteran cryptographers weigh AI adversarial risks, biometric regulation, privacy law, election integrity, and post-quantum preparedness.
talks.summary:
Moderated as RSA’s Human Element panel, five pioneers open on machine learning: models excel and fail unpredictably, and adversarial examples make neural networks risky for life-critical uses until the problem is better understood. The conversation turns to facial recognition in daily life—asymmetry, permanence, identification, correlation, and discrimination—and to cases where masks or mistaken matches expose brittle deployments and privacy harms beyond confidentiality alone.

The panel debates whether technical privacy tools can enable unfair outcomes, how fairness definitions collide in lending-style scoring, and what GDPR-style rights such as delisting or forgetting demand cryptographically. Shamir and others question practical erasure; Narayanan reframes delisting with scale data; Tal Rabin sketches conflicts when queries and deletions interact. Blockchain’s immutability clashes with deletion goals; Ron Rivest argues blockchain is a poor fit for voting compared with voter-verified paper ballots, risk-limiting audits, and roughly 80% paper coverage anticipated for 2020. Whitfield Diffie reflects on documented Crypto AG supply-chain compromise and ongoing end-to-end encryption policy fights without universal technical compromises.

Later threads cover quantum computing skepticism versus preparation, Princeton research showing all five tested carriers vulnerable to SIM-swap self-attacks, and two-decade reflections from AES margins to differential privacy in the census. Practitioners hear a consistent lesson: cryptography and policy rarely stand alone—human processes, carrier authentication, and institutional design determine whether math helps or hurts.

talks.title: Reality Check: The Story of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Argues the security industry must retell its story, casting boards, IT and users as active defenders.
talks.summary:
Rohit Ghai opens by framing cybersecurity as a story that shapes how people feel and act, and argues that the industry's current story is a technical contest between attackers and defenders. He describes how media coverage portrays hackers as technical sorcerers, users as gullible, and security teams as isolated techies chasing zero-days. He counters that attackers are better organized rather than better technically, that many attacks are financially motivated and rely on stolen credentials and social engineering, and that most incidents come from basic issues and unforced errors.

He then turns to burnout and roles. He cites survey findings about personal liability fears and CISOs rarely disconnecting, and argues that boards, business leaders and risk officers should act as part of the defense rather than watch from the sidelines. Using the Typhoid Mary case, he contends that IT and software makers should be held accountable for reducing attack surface, not only end users. He also argues for broader hiring, including neurodiverse people and workers across generations, and for prioritizing risk and basics such as multifactor authentication over complex tool stacks.

To change the narrative, Ghai urges the industry to share its wins as well as its losses. He points to the City of Atlanta, which declined to pay a ransom after a costly ransomware attack and then strengthened its business continuity planning, as an example that attackers can lose without defenders winning outright. He closes by calling for a story of business resilience and trust in technology, acknowledging that breaches will still happen.

talks.title: Feds Fighting Ransomware: How the FBI Investigates and How You Can Help
talks.teaser: Shows how FBI ransomware investigations work, from case teams and seizures to the outside help that supports them.
talks.summary:
FBI special agent Joel DeCapua, from the bureau's cyber division, explains what counts as a win against ransomware and the tools investigators use. Outcomes include arrests of affiliates and perpetrators, released decryption keys for variants such as GandCrab, public indictments, and seizure of criminal proceeds. Takedowns aimed at the support ecosystem included the BTCE exchange, the Scan For You counter-antivirus service and the Ex-Dedic RDP marketplace.

DeCapua presented a repeat of a 2018 wallet study using ransomware wallets the FBI has collected, tracking about $144 million in Bitcoin ransom payments. Ryuk ranked as the top variant by money raised, and most proceeds reached exchanges through intermediary hops. He said remote desktop access supplied 70 to 80 percent of initial footholds, so he urged patching, strong passwords, monitoring for lateral movement and offline backups. The FBI runs 49 open ransomware investigations, each organized by brand, with a case agent leading and a prosecutor paired to each case.

He described how the bureau depends on the security community for wallets, indicators shared before publication, and suspicious domains that can be seized or sinkholed. Companies that help are credited publicly. Listeners were pointed to InfraGuard and their local field office, and told that paying a ransom is discouraged.

talks.title: Deep Fakes Are Getting Terrifyingly Real: How Can We Spot Them?
talks.teaser: Surveys synthetic video, image, and text threats, creation methods, detection cues, and research frameworks with live classification demos.
talks.summary:
The session frames deepfakes as AI-built audio, video, and images that can mimic real people closely enough to erode trust in recordings. The presenters walk through older computer-graphics face swaps and newer generative adversarial approaches that support reenactment and expression transfer, then note why early detectors tied to blinking or head pose are losing ground as forgeries improve.

On the defensive side, they catalog vision and machine-learning options—warping cues, artifact hunting, and transfer learning from architectures such as VGG, Inception, ResNet, and Xception—and describe a McAfee pipeline that scores frames, thresholds probability at 0.5, and uses explainability so analysts see whether a model keys on meaningful facial features rather than spurious background context. A recorded Bill Hader clip illustrates frame-level fake calls aggregating to a fake video verdict.

Amanda House extends the thread to machine-generated prose: GPT-2 samples, Grover-style fake articles, and paired fake listings that mix GAN imagery with listing text. Detection discussion covers perplexity, GLTR-style likelihood profiles, Grover as detector, n-gram and TF-IDF baselines, and McAfee bi-gram graph work, with a short demo contrasting human and synthetic headlines. Closing themes stress scarce training data, industry datasets and competitions, and the need to broaden protection beyond celebrities as voice and video impersonation spread.

talks.title: Lessons from America’s Two Largest Cities on Preparing for Cyberattacks
talks.teaser: Two city officials explain how Los Angeles and New York prepare for ransomware, share intelligence and protect critical services.
talks.summary:
This panel brings together the information security chief for the City of Los Angeles and a New York Police Department intelligence lieutenant to discuss how two of the largest US cities prepare for cyberattacks. Timothy Lee describes the LA Cyber Lab, a nonprofit public-private partnership launched in 2017 that brings government, businesses and academia together. After a federal grant in 2018, the city piloted a threat-sharing platform with IBM, which launched in 2019. New York's approach grew out of ideas borrowed from Los Angeles, leading to a partnership with the FBI and the creation of New York City Cyber Command.

Gustavo Rodriguez explained that New York's CCSI effort, founded by four partners, lets city infrastructure security leaders share information daily and rehearse scenarios at an IBM cyber range. Lee outlined a ransomware playbook built on four stages: protection through layered email, web and endpoint controls plus user training; detection through log aggregation and monitoring; response centred on containment; and recovery using backups, with notification and payment decisions settled beforehand. Both speakers stressed that decisions made in advance matter because containment has to happen quickly during a live incident.

On elections, Los Angeles consolidated voting system security under LA County and applies NIST-based controls plus targeted monitoring of its most critical systems, while New York runs tabletop exercises with its Board of Elections. The panel also covered automation for handling roughly a billion daily security events, using use-case alerts and a dashboard for 89 critical assets, and the value of free federal services such as vulnerability scanning. The main takeaway was that cities gain resilience through trusted relationships, shared intelligence and regular exercises rather than any single tool.

talks.title: RSAC Innovation Sandbox 2020
talks.teaser: Pitches Mayhem, a system that autonomously finds software bugs and generates inputs proving they can be triggered.
talks.summary:
Dr. David Brumley, a former CMU professor who taught security researchers to find flaws in software, opens by arguing that manual bug hunting cannot keep up with the amount of code in use. He recalls DARPA's Cyber Grand Challenge, which asked whether fully autonomous cyber systems were possible, and says ForAllSecure entered in 2016 and won with its Mayhem system.

He contrasts the older approach, which scanned source code for risky patterns and required people to check false positives, with Mayhem. Mayhem searches a program and, when it finds a flaw, produces an input that triggers it, so each result comes with proof rather than a guess. In one demonstration on a web server, the output showed the request that would exploit the bug. He reports running Mayhem on more than 33,000 Linux applications, finding over 11,000 new vulnerabilities at about two cents of Amazon CPU time per vulnerability. Mayhem is offered on-premise, where he says 25 government organizations use it, and as a cloud service used in DevOps and supply-chain checks.

The takeaway is that autonomous testing becomes practical when every reported bug arrives with a demonstrated trigger, so teams can spend their effort on fixes instead of verification. Brumley closes by saying the results are so actionable that they are often classified, and credits the company's mix of hackers, engineers and business leaders for its approach.

talks.title: RSAC Innovation Sandbox 2020
talks.teaser: Pitches a platform that maps, fingerprints and classifies source code to reduce secret leaks and code exposure.
talks.summary:
This RSAC Innovation Sandbox pitch from BluBracket argues that source code has become a major security exposure as development moves toward distributed workflows, open-source reuse and infrastructure as code. The speaker points to credentials found in code as a growing route into systems, noting that almost 50% of all breaches in 2019 came from misuse of credentials, and says the goal is to keep code safe without breaking the developer toolchain.

The presentation describes a sequence of steps. First, the company helps customers map where their code lives, including on developer desktops and in environments run by outside contractors, and it fingerprints code to find matching signatures in public open-source projects. Detected matches become alerts that customers can act on. Second, it catalogs the infrastructure and application services that secrets and tokens protect, offers detailed analysis of them and supports active remediation. Third, customers can classify their most important code, set policies around it and block that code from leaving the organization in certain situations.

The speaker presents two products that mirror this sequence: Code Insights for visibility and Code Secure for taking the next step. The pitch closes by noting that the company's customers all started as design partners. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that visibility and classification come before enforcement, and that secrets left in repositories are a concrete risk to address.

talks.title: RSAC Innovation Sandbox 2020
talks.teaser: Shows how SaaS app configurations, permissions and third-party API connections can be scanned for leaks and control gaps.
talks.summary:
Brendan O'Connor, CEO and co-founder of AppOmni, presents the company as a finalist in the RSAC Innovation Sandbox 2020 contest. He argues that the SaaS applications most enterprises depend on are largely out of reach for security teams. API links, third-party hooks, data sharing and permission settings all live inside the provider's cloud, where network and host controls cannot see them. Each SaaS product also exposes its own set of controls, so there is no single common model to rely on.

As described, AppOmni's platform scans APIs, configurations and permissions across SaaS applications to show the current running state of an environment. It flags data leaks, failed security controls and deviations from best practice. Teams can define policies for who may access and share data and which third-party applications may connect to it. Security events and logs from different applications are aggregated and normalized, so a team gets one view of activity it previously could not see. The speaker uses a customer's reaction to illustrate how much visibility this adds.

The pitch stresses fast deployment: scanning can start within minutes, with no network changes, proxies or agents. The talk closes by citing the company's engineering team, which he says came from a cloud provider, and the security vendors, identity providers, cloud providers and Fortune 500 firms that reportedly rely on the product. The practical point for listeners is that SaaS risk has to be examined at the level of application configuration and permissions, not only at the perimeter or endpoint.

talks.title: Quick Look: You, Me and FIPS 140-3: A Guide to the New Standard and Transition
talks.teaser: Explains how FIPS 140-3 differs from FIPS 140-2 and what the transition timeline means for existing certificates.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces FIPS 140-3, the cryptographic module standard signed on March 22, 2019 that will succeed FIPS 140-2. It explains why the older standard, written around 2001, has become hard to apply to modern products such as systems on chip, nested hypervisors and cloud-based solutions. The new version is based on ISO/IEC 19790.

The middle of the session compares the two standards. It covers what happens to the finite state model, where DPA and SBA testing requirements fit, which requirements apply at each security level, and what from FIPS 140-2 has been dropped. New terms are defined, including normal versus degraded mode of operation, pre-operational and periodic self-tests, control output interfaces and end-of-life requirements. The talk also points out where the standard departs from ISO/IEC 19790, adds validation-program-specific requirements, and what becomes of the implementation guidance, which had grown past 260 pages under FIPS 140-2.

The closing part reviews the roadmap and key transition dates, what will happen to current FIPS 140-2 certificates, and whether a module can hold both a 140-2 and a 140-3 validation. The speaker closes with practical advice on planning the move and suggests questions to raise with internal teams, customers, partners and consultants. It suits organisations that need FIPS validation or have it on their product roadmap.

talks.title: New Paradigms for the Next Era of Security
talks.teaser: Argues for recovery-focused designs built on distributed, immutable and ephemeral principles over traditional CIA security.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security needs to shift from preventing and detecting intrusions toward the ability to recover from them. The speaker links the 1980s to asset management, the 1990s to prevention, the 2000s to detection and the 2010s to response, and presents the 2020s as an age of recovery. Destructive and irreversible attacks, such as ransomware, undermine recovery itself, and the speaker judges that most products on the protect, detect and respond side of the Cyber Defense Matrix do not address that gap.

To find better options, the speaker looks at recovery-oriented designs such as content delivery networks, copy-on-write, containers and serverless architectures, and extracts three paradigms: distributed, immutable and ephemeral, or DIE. Immutability makes every change stand out as an anomaly, while short-lived assets make persistence hard for attackers. Since likelihood will keep rising, the speaker argues that impact is the term to drive down. A pets-versus-cattle comparison, using uptime and illustrative 40-day and 10-day thresholds, is offered as a way to see how many long-lived systems an environment holds.

The talk later suggests keeping sensitive data on premises and sending only computed results to the cloud, using a mortgage check as a multi-party computation example. In the Q&A, the speaker presents DIE as an architecture rather than a single product, and suggests dedicated security teams for pets but integrated teams for cattle. Security is compared to brakes, which let a business move quickly.

talks.title: RSAC Unplugged 2019 Sydney: Security Governance: Building a Framework and Establishing Trust
talks.teaser: Explains how a group of Kuwaiti oil and gas companies built a shared security governance framework and maturity assessment.
talks.summary:
Dr. Reem F. Al-Shammari, CISO at Kuwait Oil Company, describes how nine oil and gas companies in Kuwait came together to agree on common security objectives and a unified governance framework. She explains the core problem: the sector is a frequent target, the companies are interconnected, and each had its own silo, budget constraints, and competing priorities. Trust grew when one company stepped forward first to share details of an attack, which encouraged others to do the same.

The middle of the talk covers the work itself. The framework is organised around four areas and 34 capabilities, mapped to a national sector strategy with its own initiatives. The assessment covered both IT and OT environments across the companies and followed six phases, from identifying objectives and crown jewels through threat scenarios, current and target states, to recommendations and a roadmap. Results were shown on a shared maturity scale from one to five, alongside an industry benchmark that leadership chose not to adopt as the target. Collaboration also produced unified awareness campaigns, a shared operations center serving several companies, and security KPIs added to executive objectives.

The closing section looks ahead. Next steps are developing an operating model for each company and defining the path to the agreed target maturity. The speaker's takeaway is to communicate and align within the company, across the sector, at national level and through regional bodies, and to share threat information so the sector can respond as one.

talks.title: The New Why of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Makes the case that cybersecurity should reframe its purpose around digital risk, with cloud sprawl and smart city examples.
talks.summary:
The session opened at RSA's APJ conference in Singapore, where Rohit Ghai argued that cybersecurity needs to revisit its purpose. He described digital technology as an accelerant that speeds up business, spreads technology into new places, turns data into fuel for machine learning, and ties supply chains closely together. In his framing, the new purpose is to enable trust in the digital world through digital risk management, because risk drives innovation and should be managed rather than avoided.

Holly Rollo then presented two examples. The first covered marketing's digital customer experience, where teams adopt many cloud services, often bought outside IT. She cited an average of 91 cloud services per enterprise, noted that teams often build shadow IT to avoid security reviews, and said that shared passwords and loose access controls are common among agencies and contractors. The second covered smart cities and nations, where connected sensors and public-private systems multiply third parties and make incident response across agencies harder.

From both examples she drew practical steps: take a holistic view of the whole environment, monitor third parties continuously, apply dynamic access controls, build a security operations center that understands business priorities, link cyber and integrated risk programs, and develop talent alongside digital transformation. Rohit closed by urging IT, security, risk and business teams to work together, with security measured by how well it minimizes business impact.

talks.title: The Five Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques and How to Counter Them
talks.teaser: Panelists review recent attack techniques, from two-factor bypass to industrial attacks, and outline countermeasures.
talks.summary:
The panel opened with how two-factor authentication can be bypassed. An attacker sitting between a victim and a real login site can proxy the session through a look-alike domain backed by a valid wildcard certificate, then replay captured session cookies in automated headless browsers. The speakers said no single control fixes this, and pointed to hardware-backed keys that bind authentication to the genuine origin, plus user awareness and close attention to unusual certificates.

The discussion then moved to highly targeted attacks and zero-day exploitation. Many compromises still come from known weaknesses such as unpatched systems and gaps in asset and software inventory. One breach example described a vulnerable framework that stayed exposed for months on machines nobody had listed. The speakers then covered supply chain compromises, from earlier third-party breaches to software updates carrying malware and watering-hole sites chosen from what employees visit. Their advice was a repeatable supplier risk framework backed by trained people.

The final section covered industrial control systems, tracing attacks on Ukrainian power grids in 2015 and 2016 and a 2017 attack on a Saudi petrochemical safety system. The lesson was that adversaries spent months learning plant operations, so defenders should watch for behaviours and tactics rather than only indicators, and treat critical systems with purpose-built engineering. The panel closed by urging the community to share lessons learned across organisations.

talks.title: Webcast: A Brief History of DevSecOps and Where We Go From Here
talks.teaser: Traces DevSecOps from lean manufacturing roots to open-source supply chain risk, and why security needs automation.
talks.summary:
The webcast opens with a remedial history for an audience that may know DevSecOps by name but not where it came from. The speakers link modern software delivery to Deming's lean manufacturing ideas and to the theory of constraints in The Goal, then to The Phoenix Project as a novel about IT. They describe how a 2009 talk about deploying to production ten times a day sparked the DevOps movement, and how DevOps Days spread from Belgium to the United States, with the first DevSecOps Days following in 2010.

Next they trace the growing focus on security. The 2016 supply chain report counted 31 billion open source downloads, and a later edition reported 146 billion. After the Equifax breach was tied to a Struts vulnerability, the speakers said download numbers for that component did not fall afterward and in fact rose. They also argued that the window between a disclosed flaw and attacks had shrunk from roughly 45 days to three days or less, so manual patching no longer keeps pace.

The closing takeaways are that security is everyone's responsibility across the pipeline, that teams should focus on the real constraint rather than optimizing isolated parts, and that managing security in complex environments without automation is effectively impossible. The speakers also contrast developer-facing tools with operations-side guardrails and note the added challenges that containers and Kubernetes bring.

talks.title: Decentralized Identity: No Promises Edition
talks.teaser: Surveys W3C decentralized identifiers, blockchain key anchoring, OIDC DID authentication, and verifiable credentials with live demos.
talks.summary:
The session opens with two contrasting motivations for decentralized identity: closing the global proof-of-identity gap affecting vulnerable populations, and revisiting decades of federated and user-centric identity movements that shaped today’s thinking. A boating metaphor frames three ways people navigate digital services—local login, outsourced cruise-ship convenience, or self-directed vessels supported by better navigational software.

The core narrative follows Alice applying for a home loan. A user agent generates keys; she registers a decentralized identifier whose document is anchored on a ledger, authenticates to the bank by proving control of that identifier rather than merely claiming a name, and obtains employment assertions from Contoso as verifiable credentials stored in a wallet or identity hub. The bank resolves issuer DIDs and verifies signatures instead of routing personal data through a bureau. Presenters unpack the W3C DID document model, resolution, why blockchains offer resilience and immutability without placing PII on-chain, and walk through three methods: Bitcoin Reference (embedding a document in a testnet transaction), uPort on Ethereum (including smart-contract identities and credential exchange demos), and Sovrin’s permissioned steward model.

DID authentication is shown as challenge–response via QR codes and HTTP, implemented with self-issued OpenID Connect so the phone acts as identity provider. The close separates mature interoperability patterns (DIDs, resolution, verifiable credentials) from work still open—transport options, pairwise identifiers, wallet portability, revocation, and key custody—with audience questions on revocation per method, FIDO-style hardware storage, and post-quantum readiness left as active community problems rather than solved promises.

talks.title: Election Hacking: Trading Malware for Votes
talks.teaser: Telemetry ties malware detection to elections and geopolitical events, outlining patterns defenders monitor in national campaigns.
talks.summary:
Kenneth Geers presents roughly two and a half years of analysis on Comodo’s worldwide malware telemetry, on the order of two to five million unique detection events per day from installations across nearly every country. His core argument is that major political, military, and diplomatic moments act as magnets for cyber activity: inauguration clusters among the US, Russia, and China; anniversary spikes in China; worm detections when US officials threatened Iran; and sharp rises after allied expulsions of Russian diplomats in Croatia.

He walks through election and referendum case studies—from Burundi and Norway to Russia, Turkey, Sierra Leone, Colombia, and others—showing recurring patterns of unwanted applications and adware ahead of voting, then worms and trojans as activity intensifies. In US data he highlights Ohio during a tight statewide contest and, before the 2018 midterms, swing states outpacing non-swing states in detection volume, with varied malware types including ransomware in New Jersey. Across about forty-five elections in a six-to-eight-month window, he estimates roughly a third had their highest spike within a few days of the electoral event.

Practitioners should treat headline news as a lens on logs, recognize a loose kill-chain ordering in national-scale campaigns, and plan incident response and legal steps without over-trusting attribution. He closes by urging teams doing malware analysis to pair technical depth with strategic intelligence tradecraft, since ordinary enterprises often sit in the path of nation-state collection infrastructure.

talks.title: Developing Key Performance Indicators for Security
talks.teaser: Shows how to set program goals and controls first, then build measurable security KPIs leadership can use.
talks.summary:
James Tarala opens by citing a recent blog post that questioned the security metrics being promoted at the conference, and he says he wants a practical, honest discussion instead. He argues that boards and executives, prompted by high-profile breaches, want to understand risk posture, yet teams often jump straight to KPIs without first setting goals, a program charter and documented security controls. He recommends getting leadership to define the charter, with goals drawn from laws, contracts and recognized standards.

Using multifactor authentication as an example, he explains that a KPI only makes sense once leadership has decided the control is worth doing. He separates a measure, a plain quantity such as the share of applications using MFA, from a metric, which judges whether that number is good enough. Teams can begin with simple yes-or-no attestations and later automate data collection from their tools. He then applies Six Sigma levels to a case where 10 percent of assets are missing from an inventory, which he says reaches sigma level two, and argues that leadership should pick an acceptable level rather than aim for perfection. The CIS Controls, with prepared measures and tool mappings, are offered as a free starting point.

For organizations new to this, he suggests focusing first on CIS Controls one through six at sigma level three, reporting progress back to leadership, and he expects a realistic program to take three to five years.

talks.title: Why the Role of CISO Sucks and What We Should Do to Fix It!
talks.teaser: Examines the stress, burnout and business pressures facing CISOs, and practical ways peers can support one another.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both security executives, open with the pressures that wear down security leaders: a workload that runs around the clock with no clear end point, boards that expect quick fixes, shifting regulation, and a role that has moved from technical expert to business leader. They tie the turnover problem to workforce research, citing a large gap in open positions and reports that roughly a third of senior practitioners are burning out or walking away. They also say many CISOs self-medicate, an estimate they consider conservative.

The middle of the talk turns to what leaders can do. Gary Hayslip describes how building relationships with legal, finance, development and marketing helped him earn trust and frame security as a service to the business and its customers. Both speakers argue for mentors inside and outside cyber, peer groups they call tribes for candid support, and speaking up through writing, podcasts and volunteering to strengthen the community.

They close by stressing personal health and balance across work, family and faith, along with hobbies unrelated to security. Their final message is to educate policymakers, advocate for the profession, and leave a stronger program and community for the people coming up behind them.

talks.title: How I Learned Docker Security the Hard Way (So You Don’t Have To)
talks.teaser: Recounts a legacy app's move into Docker, a breach through an unauthenticated Docker API, and the hardening steps that followed.
talks.summary:
Paul Asadoorian, who says he is not a Docker expert, describes moving an internal Python application that produces the Security Weekly podcast from bare metal into containers. He split the web server, application server and database into separate containers, used a private registry, Jenkins and Docker Compose, and later moved the system to AWS. The goals were repeatable environments, faster updates and independence from operating system upgrades that had broken production.

The central case is the breach. A Docker API was reachable without a password while Jenkins used it to push releases, and an attacker dropped a rogue container onto the host and began pulling files. Inspecting the binaries and uploading them to VirusTotal showed a basic DDoS payload with no sign of targeting. The warning about the exposed API had been easy to miss, and the controls described in Docker's documentation had not been turned on.

His recommendations cover hardening Docker and authenticating its API, mapping which components trust one another, stripping unneeded software from images and scanning images before deployment. He also covers runtime protection, comparing kernel-level plugins with lightweight hooks built into the container, along with a secrets manager for API keys and standardizing on one tool per function. He closes by urging developers, operations and security to make these trust and configuration decisions together.

talks.title: Defining a Cyber-Risk Appetite That Works
talks.teaser: Defines actionable cyber risk appetite through loss scenarios, dual thresholds, crown-jewel focus, and ongoing KRI and KPI alignment.
talks.summary:
Many organizations publish cyber risk appetite statements that read as vague labels such as medium-low, offer little clarity, and rarely change how leaders decide or prioritize security work. The session opens by separating risk appetite—the line executives want to manage toward—from tolerance, the guardrails and behaviors that keep operations near that line. Common published appetite language is critiqued for being unrealistic, hard to act on, or even legally awkward when compliance is impossible.

The core method is pragmatic rather than purely economic at first. Practitioners pick one loss scenario the business actually cares about, set a severity threshold (for example, a count of customer records at risk), then define a probability threshold for that severity within a fixed horizon. Qualitative terms like very low gain meaning through explicit control criteria on crown-jewel assets and privileged, internet-facing systems, including limits on exploitable conditions and remediation time frames. The approach can later bridge to quantitative models where organizations already measure risk in dollars.

Once defined, appetite drives alignment work: inventory crown jewels, shrink obvious exposures such as production data in non-production environments, fix exploitable conditions, and sustain alignment with decision boundaries, education for privileged staff, KRIs tied to assets and threats, and KPIs on CMDB accuracy, detection coverage, patching, and audit closure. Reporting can summarize quarter-over-quarter status per scenario for boards. The closing guidance is to socialize one scenario with executive stakeholders—not security alone—gain support within weeks, implement over months, and expand only after the first appetite works.
