talks.summary:
NIST speakers Naomi Lefkovitz and Kevin Stine introduce the Privacy Framework the agency is drafting as a voluntary tool for identifying, assessing, managing and communicating privacy risk alongside an organization's missions. They position it as jurisdiction and technology agnostic, sitting beneath legal compliance so it can also cover concerns that go beyond what the law requires. The session recaps the process so far, from an October workshop in Austin to a request for information that drew about 80 responses and a published analysis.

Feedback from that request shaped the outline. Respondents asked for compatibility with laws and international standards, common and accessible language, and a living, risk-based, outcome-based design that could stand on its own without the Cybersecurity Framework. The proposed core keeps five functions (identify, protect, control, inform and respond), extends protect to cover techniques such as de-identification, and adds guidance on privacy risk management that builds on NIST IR 8062. Profiles let each organization select outcomes based on its own risks, and the tiers were adapted to address workforce and ecosystem roles rather than acting as a maturity model.

The presenters closed by asking the audience to review the outline, join the May workshop in Atlanta and point out where informative references are thin, since those gaps will go into a roadmap for further work. They said they aim to finish the framework within about a year. In audience questions, they explained that GDPR-style requirements can map to outcomes, such as the ability to delete data, rather than prescribed implementation steps.

talks.title: Attacking Machine Learning: On the Security and Privacy of Neural Networks
talks.teaser: The session explains adversarial evasion of neural networks and practical ways to pull memorized training secrets from queryable models.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a guessing game that shows modern image classifiers matching human judgment on ordinary photos, then reverses the story with tiny perturbations that leave pictures looking unchanged while labels flip—for example a golden retriever classified as guacamole or a stop sign read as a speed-limit sign. The speaker extends the same evasion idea beyond vision to audio that humans hear as music but models treat as speech commands, including demonstrations that could drive a phone to open a website without the owner noticing.

On the security side, the talk walks through how adversarial examples are built, including efficient gradient-based perturbations and black-box attacks against production classifiers by training a local surrogate. A case study from ICLR 2018 reports that seven of nine evaluated defenses broke quickly while only adversarial training held up, and even that defense is costly, slow, and only partially reliable on small images. The privacy half covers memorization: models can regurgitate training faces, leak text seen in systems like translation services, and reveal inserted secrets such as social security numbers after hundreds of likelihood queries, using an improved graph-based extractor. An exposure metric inserts random canaries to compare memorization against accuracy tradeoffs.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that machine learning adds evasion and data-leakage risks rather than removing them. The speaker recommends probing deployed models with adversarial tests, measuring memorization with exposure, and applying differentially private stochastic gradient descent when strong privacy guarantees matter, while layering non-ML checks where mistakes would hurt.

talks.title: Mechanical Backdoors in Cold War Encryption Machines
talks.teaser: Declassified archives expose how Swiss cipher maker Crypto AG sold mechanically weakened devices under a secret NSA arrangement.
talks.summary:
The presentation traces mechanical cipher technology from ancient substitution schemes through Enigma and Boris Hagelin’s Crypto AG rotor and pin-and-lug designs. As Cold War customers adopted stronger models such as the CX-52 and TC-55, U.S. cryptologists worried some machines might resist timely decryption.

William Friedman’s visits to Switzerland and trip reports—preserved in the Marshall Foundation collection—describe a long-running gentleman's understanding. Friendly buyers could receive operational guidance that preserved solvability, while restricted sales and reporting limited exposure to adversary states. When roughly 52,000 pages were released around 2015, inconsistent redactions across duplicate copies let researchers reconstruct much of the arrangement, a line of inquiry the speaker pursued while studying a purchased TC-55. The narrative continues through embassy traffic, the Hans Bühler ordeal in Iran, espionage disclosures, and later Crypto AG ownership turmoil.

Practitioners are urged to treat bulk declassification as a disclosure risk, vet cryptography vendors like any other supply-chain dependency, prefer well-reviewed public algorithms over bespoke crypto, and mine historical cases because modern backdoor dynamics echo decades-old bargains.

talks.title: Lift and Shift, Don’t Lift and Pray: Pragmatic Cloud Migration Strategies
talks.teaser: Compares rearchitect, refactor and rehost options for moving existing workloads to the cloud, and the anti-patterns to avoid.
talks.summary:
Rich Mogull argues that moving existing workloads into a hyperscale public cloud is often rushed under hard deadlines, such as data center exit dates, and that published guidance on doing it securely is thin. He defines lift and shift broadly, covering any move from on-premises to a major cloud provider. He warns that moving systems without changing their controls often leaves them less secure, less reliable and less agile than before.

He compares three approaches. A rearchitect example covered a fraud analytics pipeline that swapped an SFTP server for object storage and used event-triggered batch instances in a private subnet with no internet access. His refactor example was his own content site, which moved its database to a managed service, stored files in object storage, ran the blog in an auto scaling group, and sat in an isolated account. He says rehosting is only defensible without alternatives, and should be temporary with a backup plan.

His roadmap starts with mapping application dependencies, then isolating environments into separate accounts, fitting the network to the application with least-privilege rules, and locking down identity per account. It continues with native security tools, managed services that decouple components, shared logging and incident response, guardrails, infrastructure as code, and an expiration date for the migrated system. He closes with anti-patterns such as one big account, flat networks and over-permissive rules.

talks.title: A General Introduction to Modern Cryptography
talks.teaser: A multi-hour primer explains how web commerce uses keys, ciphers, certificates, and hashes, plus quantum and election security angles.
talks.summary:
The session frames why the open internet behaves like untrusted postcard mail, then walks through Kerckhoffs’s principle, proper key entropy, and why passwords fail offline attacks. It contrasts stream and block ciphers—including why stream reuse and malleability make RC4-style designs fragile—and covers ECB weaknesses versus cipher-block chaining before returning to an online purchase scenario.

Asymmetric tools follow: modular exponentiation, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, RSA trapdoors, man-in-the-middle risks, digital signatures, certificate authorities, nonces, and how TLS negotiates a hybrid session with agility and forward secrecy. Optional depth touches randomness failures, elliptic-curve caution, Shor and Grover impacts, NIST post-quantum competition, hash definitions and SHA families, proof-of-work blockchains, and why ledger forks and mining concentration weaken trust assumptions.

Practitioners should favor vetted block modes, authenticated channels, fresh ephemerals, strong hashes, and planned algorithm migration. The closing election segment argues blockchains mismatch centralized voting, urges risk-limiting and end-to-end verifiable audits over internet voting, and shows how encrypted tallies can preserve ballot secrecy while allowing public verification.

talks.title: Security and Privacy Challenges for IoT
talks.teaser: Maps privacy and physical safety risks of connected devices, then previews an IoT hub and device-awareness tools.
talks.summary:
Jason Hong defines the Internet of Things as computation, sensing and wireless networking woven into everyday objects, from smart watches to smart toilets. He argues it is not just the old privacy and security problem repackaged, and outlines four challenges. The first is intimacy: smartphones already reveal sleep, location and habits, and connected devices will expose more, fueling intrusive advertising, breaches and accidental sharing.

The second is physical safety, such as ransomware that locks someone out of a smart lock or shuts off heat in winter, and the worst case of attacks on autonomous vehicles or implanted medical devices harming many people. Third is device awareness: he recounts an Airbnb guest who found a hidden camera only afterward, and presents a small sensor prototype whose machine learning infers door state and occupancy. Fourth, unexpected behavior: a room of Google Glass wearers all took photos after one voice command, and devices sharing the physical world may interact in unpredictable ways.

Remedies span better operating systems, networking, languages, user experience, developer support, best practices, and laws or insurance requirements for manufacturers. The team is building an open-source IoT hub that works like a smarter Wi-Fi router, relying on simple device metadata such as update locations and expected destinations, and blocking remote logins with default credentials. Cheap lights or speakers would also reveal a device's location and camera status on request. He closes by warning that there will be few second chances.

talks.title: Evolution of AI-Bot Swarming Intelligence with Robots
talks.teaser: Surveys how swarming AI bots and mobile security robots could join physical and cyber defenses for offices and cities.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that mobile robots carrying cameras, microphones and other sensors could work alongside human guards, for example in schools or on office and parking-lot patrols. He compares this to police dogs that work with a handler and extend what a person can do. In a parking-lot test, a robot-mounted camera with recognition software reportedly listed car makes, models and license plates, a job people often do by hand with a clipboard.

The middle of the talk covers swarming, meaning many simple agents coordinating toward a shared goal, as seen in bee colonies, ant colonies, flocks of birds and human construction crews. He describes research in which swarms of bots were said to probe networks, carry out machine-learning-driven intrusion attempts, move laterally and poison training data. He also points to drone and boat swarms as examples of robot coordination. Other ideas include anomaly detection on behavior represented as vectors, cognitive engines that track entity state as green, yellow or red, and scheduled Jupyter notebooks that automate validation and response steps.

To close, he says good data is the foundation for any useful model, and that IoT cameras are often forgotten by facilities, IT and security teams, so they need shared lifecycle management. He recommends automating routine analyst work, combining human judgment with machine speed in a unified workflow, and building a common security framework before robots spread widely.

talks.title: Common Security Frameworks
talks.teaser: Compares NIST and ISO security control frameworks, shows how to score risk, and explains why automation and TLS 1.3 change controls.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a security program should be aligned to business needs and managed to risk before any control framework is picked. The speaker walks through governance layers, from high-level policy down to procedures and control implementations, and a risk formula of likelihood times impact, scored consistently across assets, with confidentiality, integrity, availability and data volume weighed for impact. Several frameworks are then compared: the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, which is not required for audits and gives organizations a common language; NIST SP 800-53, which is required for FISMA and is free; and the ISO 27000 series, which suits international businesses and service providers who must show audits to customers.

The middle section covers automation and standards work. Control automation is still hard, and the speaker cites SCAP, the SUIT working group for firmware updates, MUD profiles, and YANG as partial answers, with ACME offered for automating certificate management. The talk then turns to protocol change. TLS 1.3 removes passive interception based on static RSA keys, so inspection must become active; QUIC hides most signaling information; and TCP-crypt offers unauthenticated opportunistic encryption that is not yet standardized.

The closing advice is to choose a framework that fits compliance requirements, move from an annual audit toward continuous monthly assessment, and work through a framework in sections where the largest risks sit. Automation and newer encryption standards are presented as the steps that make that ongoing management practical.

talks.title: Coding Secure Code: Best Practices, Advice for Writing Secure Code
talks.teaser: Offers business-minded advice for building security into the software lifecycle, from pipeline scanning to team culture.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why security is hard to fold into the software development lifecycle. The speaker, who has about twenty years in the industry across development, architecture, cloud and security, argues that the obstacles are often business ones: budget, hiring, pressure to ship quickly, and a security team that sits outside the engineering process. He suggests learning how the company makes money, how its teams actually work, and how to hold conversations in business terms rather than leading with the latest vulnerability.

The middle of the talk covers practical moves. He recommends that security people learn to script or code, and that when hiring engineers is not possible they build scaffolding and wrappers around existing tools to parse and feed results into databases or APIs. Security checks belong in the build and test stages, for example scanning for API keys before a build goes out. Findings should be validated before they are sent on, and filed in the tools engineers already use, such as a ticketing system or a chat channel, so fixes get scheduled. He also describes a company where most teams stopped introducing cross-site scripting issues once metrics were shared, while one team kept producing them, and how that data made the problem clear to executives.

The closing section reviews emerging categories. He is skeptical of WAFs because they sit outside the application and often cause false positives, and he sees more promise in RASP products that run inside the application and provide telemetry. He also points to automated application testing products as a way to scale repeatable penetration testing work. He ends by encouraging listeners to join communities and to treat business conversations as central to securing the pipeline.

talks.teaser: Venture partners explain how they evaluate security startups, weigh competition, and approach fundraising and scaling.
talks.summary:
This Crunchbase panel brings together two venture partners, Sarah Guo and Ariel Tseitlin, to discuss how investors find and evaluate startups, with a focus on security. One approach described starts with large technology and macroeconomic trends, maps the markets they affect, and then studies the companies serving those markets. Founders were advised to target 20 to 30 partners with relevant expertise instead of a list of a hundred firms, and to build relationships over roughly 12 to 18 months.

Competition and fundraising came next. Speakers said a crowded category is less attractive unless a team has a clear differentiator, and that investors ask the company before backing a rival. On round sizes, the panel agreed that heavy capital inflows have inflated valuations and reduced discipline, so one firm moved slightly earlier, to companies with one to five million in revenue. Scale Studio, a self-serve benchmarking tool, lets companies compare their metrics against a cohort of more than 100 companies.

The panel closed with portfolio examples: Obsidian Security in identity, a security operations software company that spread through free downloads, CyberGRX for third-party risk, Big ID for data privacy and Awake Security for network visibility. Guo said she looks for a clear vision, execution in early stages and the ability to recruit. Audience questions and book recommendations ended the session.

talks.title: Google on BeyondCorp: Empowering Employees with Security for the Cloud Era
talks.teaser: Covers Google's BeyondCorp zero-trust access without VPNs, device posture, security keys, and context-aware cloud policies.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting legacy enterprise perimeters—firewalls, VPNs, and hardware-centric access—with Google's BeyondCorp model, rooted in zero trust and refined over roughly seven years as mobile and cloud usage grew. The speaker argues that monolithic on-premises estates and static network rules no longer match distributed applications, containerized microservices, or the user experience employees expect from consumer-grade, browser-based tools.

Access decisions are framed around context-aware controls: identity, device posture and patches, geography, time of day, strong authentication beyond passwords, and encryption for data at rest and in transit. The talk walks through a layered chain of trust—from hardware roots and machine identity through binary authorization, service-level policies, telemetry, and audit—and describes an access proxy that enforces rules without routine VPN clients. Hardware security keys, automated device provisioning, Android Enterprise recommendations, and the externally offered identity-aware proxy are presented as building blocks enterprises can adopt.

A customer narrative highlights migration to managed Kubernetes, globally consistent databases, and sharp infrastructure reduction while preserving developer agility. The closing emphasis is on granular, real-time policy (including data classification APIs), ecosystem partnerships, and published BeyondCorp materials for teams planning similar transformations.

talks.title: A Conversation with Donna Brazile and Mary Matalin
talks.teaser: Two political commentators argue that collaboration across party lines and competitors is needed to keep pace with real cyber threats.
talks.summary:
This conversation brings together Donna Brazile and Mary Matalin, two political commentators with opposing party allegiances, to discuss cybersecurity from a policy and industry angle. Their opening remarks argue that the security field should not be treated as a partisan issue, and that the users of security products care most about results rather than politics.

The speakers focus on collaboration. They argue that competition in the industry can slow progress unless it is balanced by shared standards or economies of scale that let innovation move faster, and they warn that adversaries have outpaced defenders before. To show that people on opposite sides can still get things done, they recall several past periods of divided government that produced major legislation, including civil rights laws, environmental protection, a balanced federal budget, welfare reform, education reform and immigration and tax changes.

They close by describing the current period as one of political disruption and uncertainty, and by stressing that the cyber threat is real. They thank the people on the front lines who protect infrastructure and who educate organizations, both non-profit and for-profit. The main takeaway for practitioners is that relationships and open communication across divides are needed to keep pace with threats.

talks.title: Rives: The Badass Box
talks.teaser: Shares the answers attendees gave when asked what they are good at, collected in a box at RSAC.
talks.summary:
In this short closing session at RSA 2019, John Rives says it is his last year speaking at the conference after three years on stage. He thanks the attendees for their white-hat outlook and says his own work depends on theirs. He explains that he had earlier carried a box marked "better" and asked people what they would like to improve at, then reports that the answers were funny and personal.

He then repeated the exercise with a different prompt, asking attendees to name what they were already good at. The cards ranged from cooking claims, such as mac and cheese from the box and banana and chocolate pancakes, to unusual skills like returning items right before an expiry date, navigating a theme park efficiently, and claiming a sense of smell for colors. Some answers carried swagger, some were playful, and one card included a line about accepting what cannot be changed. A folded card that simply read "love notes" drew a reaction from him. He also named three people he wanted to meet after reading their cards.

He closes by saying the cards showed how many people in the room have unexpected strengths, and he wishes the audience a better RSA than they expected. The session offers no technical content. Its takeaway is a light reminder to the audience about the community around the conference.

talks.title: Engineering Trust and Security in the Cloud Era, Based on Lessons from the Early Internet
talks.teaser: Traces early internet design choices to today's cloud trust models, including zero trust, shared responsibility and encryption.
talks.summary:
This panel argues that security is largely a question of architecture and trust, and that the history of internet design explains many of today's constraints. The speakers recall the internet pioneer who regretted tying identity and location together in IP addresses, a choice that still enables denial-of-service attacks. They also cite a 1984 lecture in which a compiler back door was hidden inside its own source code, and later speculative-execution attacks on processors, to show how hard it is to trust a system all the way down to its lowest layer.

The conversation then turns to industry practice. One speaker describes retiring old server disks that held user data at Google and the difficulty of deciding whether to wipe, reuse or shred them. The panel covers the BeyondCorp zero-trust model, which moves access control to user identity and device rather than relying on a network perimeter, and the shared-responsibility split between cloud providers and their customers. Encryption at rest and in transit, the costs of encrypting at scale, and access transparency logs are presented as ways to build customer trust.

Near the end, the panel looks ahead to the growth of IoT and 5G devices, machine learning for security, confidential computing and the longer-term risk from quantum computing. Audience questions cover client-side encryption, government requests, transparency reports and participation in open standards. The main takeaway is that trust has to be earned through transparency and through designs that assume any component may fail or be hostile.

talks.title: Democratizing Cloud Security: Journey to Secure the Public Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how a company decentralized security for its public cloud fleet, covering access, secrets, scanning and incident response.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe a company's move from on-premises data centers to a public cloud, where operations became decentralized and DevOps-driven while security stayed centralized. Their answer was to decentralize security too, starting from an established baseline and building a maturity framework. Policies had to be observable, enforceable and backed by services and an exception process before enforcement.

Access ran through corporate single sign-on and short-lived credentials, with group-based authorization via an LDAP manager and a broker that maps groups to AWS roles. Long-term secrets moved into a central vault, extended with a plugin so teams managed their own paths without a super-user who could read others' secrets. A tool removed unused IAM API permissions by comparing policies against a week of usage logs. Scanning for code, images, containers and web apps was offered self-service inside CI/CD.

For monitoring, logs from cloud, network, system and DNS sources went to a central service with heartbeat checks. Operators created their own anomaly alerts, such as flagging use of their instances or secrets from unexpected users or IP addresses, which cut noise. Incident response services helped responders reach affected resources and snapshot them. The main takeaways were to involve everyone in policy-making, decentralize alert creation, build security into image pipelines and adopt controls step by step.

talks.title: The New Gold Rush: How to Hack Your Own Best Mining Rig
talks.teaser: Contrasts cryptojacking with ransomware economics, demos a stealth Monero miner build, and outlines agentless WMI fleet detection.
talks.summary:
The session frames 2018 as a shift toward malicious cryptocurrency mining, arguing that decentralized proof-of-work payouts and low prosecution risk make cryptojacking more attractive than many ransomware campaigns. The speakers recap mining pools, difficulty, and rewards, then compare miners and ransomware across damage, visibility, victim-dependent payouts versus steady pool shares, distribution (including PUAs and installers), development effort, and law-enforcement interest.

They highlight hybrid malware such as DarkGate that can mine, steal wallets, deploy remote access, or flip to ransomware when disrupted. For offense, they choose Monero and XMRig, run the payload in memory via a small Python RunPE-style loader with persistence and obfuscation, and note how quickly detection counts can drop on public scanners. Distribution paths discussed include phishing, malicious documents, and familiar document exploits.

On defense, they critique pool blacklists, IOC hunts, and naive CPU thresholds at enterprise scale, then present Miner Sweeper: WMI remote CPU telemetry, anomaly detection (e.g., in Elasticsearch), and deeper triage including process inspection and memory scans when a host looks suspicious. The closing message is that mining must burn CPU, which gives defenders a durable signal if they instrument the fleet properly.

talks.title: Do You Know Your Organization’s Top 10 Security Risks?
talks.teaser: Shows how a security team turns scattered control, incident and KPI data into a quarterly top 10 risk list.
talks.summary:
The talk lays out a five-step method for deriving an organization's top 10 security risks from data a security team already collects. The speaker argues that such a list helps focus the roadmap, guides budget requests and informs staffing, and gives a cloud example where rising vendor adoption led to a dedicated cloud security team. Governance comes first: a small dedicated team gathers inputs, oversees remediation and shares results with senior leadership, enterprise risk management and IT program management.

Next, a common risk language is built on a chosen security framework, resulting in 16 major risk categories and 30 subcategories. Risk inputs come from indicators such as incidents, exceptions and open remediation plans, from control activities including twice-yearly key control testing and monthly KPI reviews, and from external trends. Each item is tagged with a category, trended quarter by quarter, and compared when lines diverge so the team can form hypotheses and talk to data owners.

Prioritization uses a score built from impact, likelihood and control effectiveness, kept on simple scales so senior leaders can work with it. Themes are merged and a quarterly top 10 deck is reviewed by leadership. The closing advice covers executive buy-in, dedicated staff, consistent language, automation and education of data owners, and a first three months spent identifying categories and presenting what the data shows.

talks.title: Designing Effective Security UX: If It’s Not Usable, It’s Not Secure
talks.teaser: Presents practical design methods for balancing usability and security, from user context to measuring both together.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that usability and security are not opposites and should be balanced. It reviews core security goals (confidentiality, integrity, availability), privacy principles such as consent, and usability factors including efficiency, accuracy and learnability. Usable security and privacy is presented as the overlap, and a password login flow with tangled rules shows how poor design pushes people toward insecure habits.

The middle section covers five approaches: understanding user context and purpose, analysing risk with attention to accuracy and impact, and presenting it at a suitable level of detail with clear icons; reducing user burden through sensible defaults, grouped settings and inline error handling; educating users with in-line validation and impact previews; and measuring security and usability together, including attacker personas alongside user journeys. Examples include a credit score display, HTTP and HTTPS labels, one-click checkout and a streaming service's sign-out delay.

The closing plan suggests sharing these ideas with a design team, mapping users and their contexts over the first three months, then running a design thinking workshop and a validation project within six months. The overall message is that poor usability weakens protection, so both goals belong in the same design process.

talks.title: Three Things the Security Industry Isn’t Talking About (but Should Be)
talks.teaser: Argues the industry should cut its attack surface and build security into infrastructure, not chase threats.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that the security industry is failing customers, with breaches rising even as spending grows. The speaker, chief executive of VMware, says the field is too focused on chasing threats, which leaves most effort and investment in reactive work. He urges preventive investment such as hardening, patching and segmentation, aimed at reducing the attack surface.

He says so-called application awareness tools are mostly protocol analyzers that lack understanding of the application itself. He argues that modern applications, spanning legacy databases, microservices and AR/VR components, cannot be understood from wire traffic. He also says security must be built into infrastructure rather than bolted on, citing a large bank that uses about 250 security vendors and VMware's goal of fewer than 25 security products. His proposed answer is a service-defined firewall, distributed alongside each virtual machine, that learns known-good application behavior and enforces it at network and application levels.

Shannon Lietz, who leads a red team and a DevSecOps function, joined him on stage and largely agreed. She recalled a 2011 crisis when conventional controls did not help chase attackers, and argued that security features belong in developer platforms and pipelines. The closing calls to action were to put investment into reducing the attack surface, bring application teams into security work, and cut the number of security products.

talks.title: Public-Interest Tech: Bruce Schneier Interviews John "JSR" Scott-Railton
talks.teaser: Covers how a university lab tracks state-backed attacks on civil society, how it is funded, and where mobile threats are heading.
talks.summary:
The interview introduces Citizen Lab, an academically independent group at the University of Toronto that investigates targeted attacks against civil society. Its work is funded by large public foundations, and because its clients usually cannot pay, the team relies on donated and in-kind tools. The speaker notes that industry has powerful tools but often uses them for routine tasks. The lab also trains undergraduate and graduate students, some of whom move on to industry.

The conversation then turns to demand and risk. The group is swamped with requests, and it argues that its academic setting protects its independence, so its findings are read as scholarship rather than advocacy. Looking ahead, the speaker says the internet has eased communication for activists without closing the wider gap in power between citizens and states. Major platforms are widely used but not designed for high-risk users, and mobile devices that constantly emit data are a growing concern because they are harder to track and analyze.

On commercial tools that can be misused, the speaker urges developers to keep innovating but to plan for misuse early, rather than assume their original intentions will limit how a product is used. Developers should not respond defensively when misuse appears, and should engage with civil society to do better.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: Hacking Macs
talks.teaser: Live demos trace macOS delivery, escalation, credential theft, persistence, and exfil TTPs alongside practical countermeasures.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames defense as a race against intruders, introducing breakout time—the interval from first code execution to meaningful lateral movement—and comparing average speeds across tracked adversary categories, with Russian-linked actors often measured around 18 minutes. Speakers argue organizations should track detection, investigation, and remediation speed, citing a 1-10-60 minute aspiration while noting approval workflows can lag behind the fastest nation-state operators.

The core walkthrough covers macOS intrusions seen in the field, highlighting actors such as Wicked Panda targeting developers and signing certificates, and Windy Bat using custom URL schemes with Safari’s automatic zip unpacking to register malicious apps. Demonstrations include PNG-embedded bash payloads, Gatekeeper bypass via signed malware, temp-directory update races for root, DSCL-based hash extraction after older paths were restricted, launch agents and periodic cron persistence, and Spotlight-driven file discovery for theft. Each stage is paired with mitigations such as Safari download settings, patching, password-prompt awareness, EDR monitoring, keychain and SSH key hygiene, BlockBlock-style persistence alerts, and network egress controls.

Practitioners are urged to measure response metrics over time, harden Mac endpoints against techniques that still resemble decades-old Unix patterns, and use the newly released Automatic forensics collector for artifact gathering. The session closes with adversary-focused awards reinforcing speed as the dominant theme.

talks.title: The Five Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques and How to Counter Them
talks.teaser: Explains DNS hijacking, domain fronting, encrypted DNS risks and personal data exposure, along with practical defenses for each.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with Ed Skoudis describing DNS hijacking. Attackers use stolen credentials to log into DNS providers and registrars, repoint mail exchange records to their own servers, and then obtain TLS certificates by passing domain validation through the redirected email. He also covers domain fronting, where malware hides command-and-control traffic behind a trusted content delivery network and can hop across several cloud providers. Recommended defenses include two-factor authentication for DNS administrators, DNSSEC, revoking fraudulent certificates, and regularly checking DNS and certificate records with free lookup services.

Johannes Ulrich turns to encrypted DNS. DNS over HTTPS protects user privacy but removes a key signal defenders rely on to spot malicious domains, so he argues that enterprises should keep resolving names through monitored resolvers, while travelers or people who distrust their ISP may benefit from encrypted lookups. He also warns that baseboard management controllers and other embedded management components can give attackers persistent access to servers, and that these management networks need the same passive monitoring as externally facing networks.

Heather Mahalik focuses on personal exposure. Public birthdays, pet names and security-question answers can be used to reset accounts, and location tracking and third-party app access are often switched on by default. She urges users to review their provider's security checkup pages, enable two-factor authentication and use a password manager. Skoudis adds that defenders should review administrator logs for unusual accounts or login times to catch living-off-the-land activity. The takeaway is that defenders need to watch both their infrastructure and the personal information attackers can exploit.

talks.title: Future Forests: Realistic Strategies for AD Security & “Red Forest” Architecture
talks.teaser: Explains how to harden Active Directory admin paths using tiered administration and a separate administrative forest.
talks.summary:
Active Directory matters because it handles logins and administrative access, so a compromised domain controller or domain admin account can spread across a network. Under an assume-breach view, a typical attack path begins with admin rights on a laptop, which yields a shared local administrator password. That password is reused through pass-the-hash until domain admin credentials surface on an IT workstation. One widely reported incident, which forced redeployment of 45,000 workstations and 4,000 servers in 10 days, shows the damage this can cause.

The remediation steps come in order. Local administrator passwords are randomized and stored in Active Directory with Microsoft's free tool, and Credential Guard is enabled where hardware supports it. Administrators then work from privileged access workstations, either separate machines or a locked-down VM, though a hypervisor escape remains possible. A separate administrative forest with a one-way trust follows, because two-way trusts let a compromise on one side reach the other. Tiered administration then stops credentials moving downward, and time-limited, just-in-time PowerShell access reduces standing domain admin rights.

The speaker stresses that each step needs business risk decisions, such as whether admin workstations get internet access. The model does not fix weak passwords or misconfigurations that tools like BloodHound expose, and Azure has no equivalent yet. Practitioners should start with quick wins like local admin password management and admin isolation, then decide whether a full administrative forest suits their environment.

talks.title: Threat Hunting Using 16th-Century Math and Sesame Street
talks.teaser: Demonstrates finding rare machine behavior in huge networks through asset tagging and outlier counts, not attack-specific rules.
talks.summary:
Hunting in very large networks is overwhelming when hunters have only a few hours a day and indicator-based rules need constant upkeep. The talk proposes hunting for rare behavior instead, since most events on a private network are benign. It introduces the idea with the familiar spot-the-odd-one-out game, applied to groups of similar machines.

The method tags hosts by type, using sources such as Active Directory, internal wikis, and vulnerability scan inventories, then joins those tags to flow, proxy, or packet logs by IP address. Three approaches are shown. The first defines a suspicious behavior, such as POST requests with no referrer or cookies, and counts source machines per destination; domains reached by only a handful of hosts stand out, and excluding known domains reveals newly seen ones. The second compares protocols across an asset group, so one or two domain controllers using SMB or DNS when none of the others do becomes a lead. The third compares traffic characteristics per group, such as direct-IP HTTP requests or self-signed certificates on a few hosts. Real findings included a rare autorun entry that exposed custom malware and a packet capture tool running on one of 400 critical assets.

Benign causes such as misconfigured machines and help desk troubleshooting add noise that needs tuning. Look-back windows matter, with 24 hours as a starting point and a month giving more significance to rare results. The speaker recommends starting with domain controllers and pairing this with TTP-based hunting.

talks.title: RF Exploitation: IoT and OT Hacking with Software-Defined Radio
talks.teaser: Shows how low-cost software-defined radios can capture and replay wireless signals from IoT devices and car key fobs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growing number of wireless exploits and argues that many IoT and OT devices rely on radio protocols beyond Wi-Fi, such as Bluetooth, ZigBee and Z-Wave, which many security practitioners do not examine closely. It gives a short overview of radio spectrum basics, frequency and modulation, and of the hardware and software used to receive and transmit signals, including RTL-SDR, HackRF, GNU Radio, GQRX and Universal Radio Hacker.

The speakers walk through the phases of an RF attack: gathering information from FCC IDs, identifying the frequency and modulation, then transmitting. They demonstrate a simple replay attack and explain its limits, since a captured fixed code can only be reused when the signal never changes. They then describe the Dallas siren hack, in which 156 sirens were triggered, and car keyless entry attacks, including a relay device that cost $22 and a roll-jam technique built from about $30 of parts.

The closing section covers wider internet of radio threats such as rogue cell towers, rogue Wi-Fi hotspots, keyboard dongle sniffing and jamming, along with the regulatory limits on transmitting. The speakers advise practitioners to analyze and reverse engineer what their own devices transmit, to avoid relying on security by obscurity, and to note that encryption is often impractical on small devices, so some vendors add noise to each transmission instead.

talks.title: A View from the Front Lines of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Traces two decades of cyber threats, from early government intrusions and cybercrime to nation-state attacks on critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a decades-long view of cyber intrusions, beginning in the mid-1990s when attackers used public exploits against Unix servers and most activity looked like government-on-government contact. The speaker traces how Windows NT servers and databases holding credit card data pulled in financially motivated crime, how a 2000 worm forced emergency patching at a bank, and how 2013 hacktivist activity first revealed a link between geopolitics and attacker behavior.

Sandra Joyce, senior vice president of threat intelligence, then reviews 2018. Median global dwell time fell from 416 days in 2011 to 78 days, though most incidents still start with legitimate credentials. She covers North Korea's APT37, which grew more capable and began exploiting zero-days, and APT38, which used espionage skills to steal hundreds of millions from banks. Iran's APT39 focused on individuals in telecoms and travel, while China's APT40 shifted toward military and dual-use technology tied to the Belt and Road initiative. Russia's Sandworm group reached the safety systems of an industrial plant with Triton, and NotPetya showed how destructive malware can spill far beyond its target.

To close, the speakers expect more destructive attacks with collateral damage, a growing gap between offense and defense, and a push for rules of conduct between nations. They also expect the internet to split along data sovereignty and privacy lines, which defenders will need to plan for.

talks.title: From Dystopia to Opportunity: Stories from the Future of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Connects ransomware, exposed devices and bug bounty law to how hackers and regulators can build public trust in technology.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a dystopian 2025 scenario of hijacked drones, ransomware and cloud cryptojacking, then argues that hackers and lawmakers can shape whether people trust digital technology. It recalls WannaCry hitting hospitals and German train stations, the VPNFilter router malware, a chipmaker's halted production, and NotPetya spreading through an accounting software update in Ukraine. A Chilean bank wiper, used to cover fraudulent SWIFT transfers, shows how a loud attack can hide theft elsewhere.

Next the talk turns to exposure. Shodan is used to find internet-facing devices, including an Innsbruck cable car control system that researchers reported to a national emergency response team, and Mirai botnet devices that relied on default passwords. California's IoT law, effective in 2020, bans default passwords on connected devices sold there. Attacker tooling is covered too: PowerShell running in memory, and AutoSploit, which links Shodan with Metasploit. A DARPA contest for autonomous hacking closes the section.

Last, the talk makes the case for friendly hackers. It cites bug bounty programs, including the 2016 Hack the Pentagon program whose first valid report came after 13 minutes, and a 2017 Justice Department guidance document on collaborating with researchers. It also covers the hack-back idea, which remains legally unclear under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, and the FTC's view that lacking a disclosure process can be unreasonable. Practitioners are urged to publish a vulnerability disclosure policy with clear terms, and to ask vendors how a tool helps users make better decisions.

talks.title: The Role of Security Technologists in Public Policy
talks.teaser: Argues that technologists must join public policy debates, since technology now shapes law and society.
talks.summary:
Bruce Schneier opens by arguing that computer security has become a public policy issue, and that the technical understanding needed to write good policy is largely missing from the debate. He revisits the decades-long fight over access to encrypted communications, from the Clipper chip to smartphones, and points to the Apple versus FBI dispute and the DMCA debate as cases where policymakers and technologists talked past each other.

He defines public interest technologists as people who combine technical expertise with a focus on the public good, and he describes where they are needed: congressional staff, federal agencies, NGOs, academia, companies and the press. He uses supply chain security as an example, noting that where chips are made, where software is written and how updates and distribution work all matter, and that a US-only iPhone would cost far more. He lists other open policy questions, including vulnerability disclosure, election security, IoT safety and algorithmic fairness, and describes a shortage of talent, unmet demand and poor marketplaces for this work.

In the question period he compares the field to public interest law, suggests that careers can be short stints or part-time, and notes that the EU's GDPR and California's IoT password rule show how strong laws can reach global products. He closes by urging technologists to accept that their work has moral and political dimensions and to help build the policy tools the coming decades will require.

talks.title: Weaponization of the Internet
talks.teaser: A panel weighs how platforms, intelligence, and policy can curb manipulated discourse without silencing legitimate debate.
talks.summary:
The conversation treats coordinated manipulation of open networks as a security challenge that can damage democracies more visibly than many traditional breach scenarios. Participants trace how influence operations intensified on social platforms, why defenders once focused on the wrong indicators such as account intrusions instead of scaled advertising and amplification, and how virality can outweigh accuracy in what media and voters amplify.

Representatives from large platforms explain why they prioritize suspicious behaviors over raw content, using automated removal of short-lived fake accounts alongside human teams that study sophisticated actors. They break problems into content, identity, and amplification; note overlap among conspiracy networks, extremism, and state-sponsored campaigns; and discuss transparency measures, political ad disclosure, and data sharing for outside research. Intelligence and policy voices add that adversaries blend automation with handcrafted personas, that a large share of election-related conversation can be inauthentic, and that faster government-industry collaboration plus labeling of bots or inauthentic media may matter as much as platform rules alone.

Practitioners should model these campaigns as fast-evolving tradecraft, add friction to manipulative behaviors without choking legitimate debate, and treat public digital literacy and clear authenticity expectations as part of a national response—not a problem solvable by content bans alone.

talks.title: The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation: One Year Later
talks.teaser: Panelists review GDPR's first year, covering early fines, breach notification volumes, implementation costs and US state privacy laws.
talks.summary:
Five panelists looked back on the first year of the EU General Data Protection Regulation, in force since May 2018. The session opened with a chief information officer's view that the rules brought all cost and little benefit. Lawyers on the panel pushed back, arguing that most firms gained something useful, starting with learning what personal data they held and where it went.

Enforcement was discussed through cases and numbers. A roughly 50 million euro penalty against Google in France followed complaints from privacy advocacy groups. By the end of January 2019, regulators had received about 41,000 breach notifications under the 72-hour rule and had at least 250 investigations open, most of them shared between authorities. Panelists said the cases tended to target plain security failures, such as a known vulnerability left unpatched. In the US, California's privacy law was described as borrowing from the GDPR, with several other states following.

For practitioners, the panel stressed data mapping, due diligence on service providers, and contracts with vendors. Because the GDPR asks only for "reasonable and appropriate" security, speakers pointed to ISO standards and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and to documenting why controls fit the sensitivity of the data. Public privacy notices must also match internal practice. The takeaway was that the regulation largely formalises good data stewardship.

talks.title: Data Breach or Disclosure: A Quantitative Risk Analysis
talks.teaser: Dollar-based scenario modeling reveals why steady accidental disclosures can outrank rare theft in annualized cyber risk.
talks.summary:
Cyber risk programs exist to shrink uncertainty so executives can choose controls with clearer trade-offs. The session opens with familiar qualitative matrices, including NIST-style ratings that often label external client data theft as high likelihood and high impact while accidental disclosure looks equally likely but only moderate impact, which steers investment toward breach prevention.

The core walkthrough uses a fictional Widget and Co with roughly ten thousand client records, about one hundred million dollars in revenue, and a security budget near one hundred thirty thousand dollars. Two narrowly scoped cases are compared: criminals exploiting a default database password versus staff emailing one client's data to the wrong recipient. Documented assumptions, adversary economics, FAIR-style loss forms, frequency bands with confidence, and Monte Carlo simulation produce annualized and maximum dollar losses. Qualitative ordering inverts: theft still drives the worst single event, but monthly operational mistakes dominate yearly exposure, especially when PCI-related billing data rides on email.

Practitioners hear concrete treatment paths—detection, containment, response, and insurance for rare theft; removing sensitive email practices and stronger preventive controls for accidents—plus sensitivity analysis tying spend to outcomes and leadership reporting that pairs annualized risk with one-time maximum loss.

talks.summary:
The session opens with a physical social-engineering engagement in Switzerland to stress that people, not only technology, enable breaches. It then walks through ten infrastructure shortcuts that excite offensive testers, each tied to customer pentest experience.

Demonstrations include downloading payloads via certutil and DNS TXT records, bypassing application control with a 2018 scheduled-task privilege escalation, extracting IIS certificate passwords from the registry, ARP spoofing on flat networks, SMB relay without signing, infecting writable shares and trojaned Sysinternals downloads, cleartext TDS traffic injection to create SQL logins, unloading Sysmon via FLTMC, and dumping service-account passwords from misconfigured services.

The close urges short-term configuration reviews beyond periodic pentests, medium-term internal testing and incident readiness, and long-term hardening around unknown code execution, exploit prevention, and monitoring whether security agents truly remain loaded and effective.

talks.title: The Cryptographers’ Panel
talks.teaser: Cryptography pioneers debate lawful access, consumer privacy rules, election evidence, and paths from theory to deployed systems.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the RSA Conference mathematics award to Tal Rabin for distributed protocols, threshold cryptography, and signature innovations, then convenes a long-running panel of field leaders after a recorded message from Adi Shamir, who could not obtain a U.S. visa to attend. Whitfield Diffie, Paul Kocher, Shafi Goldwasser, Tal Rabin, and Ron Rivest respond to Australia's Assistance and Access Act, contrasting exceptional access mandates with the risk that mandated or secret backdoors harm legitimate users and leak like weapons-grade exploits.

Discussion turns to whether GDPR and California privacy law will change business models or remain a cost of doing business, and how cryptography might audit surveillance at scale using zero-knowledge and multi-party techniques. Panelists describe threshold-based complaint aggregation, Ron Rivest's advocacy for paper ballots and risk-limiting audits over blockchain hype, and technical strains on cryptocurrency including inexpensive majority attacks and brittle smart-contract deployments.

They close on hardware side channels, missing security metrics beside performance, NIST threshold-crypto standardization, homomorphic encryption nearing commercial use, and the need for understandable, evidence-based trust rather than blind faith. Takeaways stress decades-long adoption cycles, post-quantum readiness, voting diligence in 2020, and wider deployment of mature tools such as password-authenticated key exchange, threshold signing, and encrypted cold storage.

talks.title: The FBI: At the Heart of Combating Cyberthreats
talks.teaser: The session covers FBI enforcement against blended threats, industry partnerships, lawful-access debates, and election-influence defenses.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with the FBI director’s assessment after roughly eighteen months in office: cyber threats now span multinational crime groups, foreign intelligence services, insiders, and activists, with victims and techniques ranging from business email compromise to ransomware. He cites recent enforcement actions tied to Chinese ministry hackers, Iranian SamSam operators, a multi-continent BEC sweep, North Korean activity from Sony through WannaCry, and Russian GRU targeting anti-doping bodies, and highlights “blended threats” where states enlist criminal hackers.

He argues the bureau’s domestic law enforcement and counterintelligence mandate, nationwide field presence, cyber action team, joint task forces, twenty-four-hour watch floor, overseas legal attachés, and technical capabilities give it a distinctive role beside agencies such as Cyber Command and DHS. He stresses that most U.S. critical infrastructure sits in private hands, so pre-incident relationships and information sharing are essential, citing a case where industry tips helped stop a military kill list aimed at ISIS.

The discussion also covers encryption and lawful access without conceding a desire to weaken crypto, ongoing Russian influence operations ahead of 2020, scaled Chinese counterintelligence risk, and why public indictments matter for anonymity and travel risk. It closes with recruitment appeals and metrics on applications, selectivity, and low attrition.

talks.teaser: Explores how the same AI that strengthens cyber defense can arm criminals, deepfakes, and adversarial attacks against models.
talks.summary:
The session frames cybersecurity’s AI moment through older debates about fire, flight, and strong encryption: the same capability can protect or harm, and the underlying technique is morally neutral math. The opening argues that machine learning can improve detection, scale analytics, and ease staffing pressure, while warning that open data and cheap models also lower the bar for abuse.

A dialogue between McAfee executives walks through concrete demonstrations. Public crime records train a classifier that predicts arrest outcomes, mirroring how attackers might rank targets. A separate model highlights machines predicted as easiest to exploit. They show a deepfake built from public remarks, discuss AI-generated phishing at spearphishing scale, and cover adversarial machine learning—from perturbed images that fool classifiers to evasion against spam and malware models.

The close contrasts defensive promise with fragility and false-positive cost, citing the 1983 Soviet missile false alarm as a lesson in human judgment over automation. Practitioners should adopt AI for defense but plan for offensive use, social manipulation, and model evasion, keeping skilled oversight in the loop rather than treating outputs as fully contextual understanding.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Tips, Tools and Techniques for Your Professional Toolbag
talks.teaser: Rapid-fire tour of free and low-cost security tools for testing, investigations, administration and daily work.
talks.summary:
Ron Woerner opens from a budget-first view: most teams cannot buy expensive products, so he runs a fast tour of free tools he uses in consulting for small and mid-sized businesses and in teaching students. He begins with the human layer, pointing to free awareness materials from national programs, then shows how search engines and web archives keep an organization's public history visible long after pages change.

The middle of the session covers hardening and inventory. He points to NIST and CIS guidance, STIG guides for locking down systems, and Nmap for finding what is on a network. Internet-exposure search services reveal exposed devices and services, and SSL Labs grades a site's TLS setup; he once checked a law firm's client portal, which did poorly. On Windows he demonstrates Autoruns and Process Explorer, the Windows Subsystem for Linux, and Chocolatey for keeping systems patched. Wireshark serves as evidence that traffic is encrypted during an audit. For investigation and testing he covers Spiderfoot for OSINT, the Social-Engineer Toolkit, OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite for application testing, and 7-Zip with AES-256 for sending files.

He closes with career advice: education, certifications and hands-on experience together open jobs, with CyberSeek mapping roles and the Cybersecurity Canon offering book recommendations. His takeaway is to try one or two of the tools in a home lab, revisit the list in a few weeks, and share any tools he missed.

talks.title: Welcome: Solving Our Cybersecurity Talent Shortage
talks.teaser: Frames the cybersecurity talent shortage through diversity, burnout and mid-career attrition, and sets up the seminar's panels.
talks.summary:
The seminar opens with welcome remarks that tie the cybersecurity talent shortage to diversity, inclusion and equity. The speaker describes how she was struck by data showing women's share of computing occupations falling from 34% of the workforce during her graduate school years to 18%, and how that prompted her to ask why it was happening and what should be done about it.

The remarks then cover the format of the four-hour morning program. Companies will share how inclusion efforts work inside their own organizations, an expert panel will present, and a separate segment will address burnout. Floor questions are limited, and attendees are encouraged to speak with the presenters during the breaks. The speaker names burnout, pay equity and women leaving the profession mid-career as issues the industry has to tackle.

She also reflects on about two decades in the field, starting around 1998 when there were even fewer women, and on how early career experiences built a thick skin that she hopes newer professionals will not need. She closes by encouraging attendees to join the other diversity-focused sessions during RSA week, and offers to mentor and talk with anyone who wants to continue the conversation.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2019
talks.teaser: Explains how a platform runs analytics on encrypted data via homomorphic encryption, so collaborators need not trust each other.
talks.summary:
The pitch starts from a problem: organisations hold data they cannot analyse alone, but sharing it requires trust that the speaker says recent privacy scandals and rules such as GDPR have eroded. The company's Duality Secure Plus platform is presented as a way to collaborate without that trust, using homomorphic encryption to compute on information that stays scrambled. Data owners can encrypt records and send them to model owners, or model owners can encrypt a model and run it on the data owner's premises.

To show practicality, the speaker cited a genomic analysis competition where the team reported beating IBM by three orders of magnitude, plus use cases such as banks using third-party fraud models and healthcare groups analysing clinical genomic data together. When judges asked for proof, the answer was that the encrypted layer is open source, the open-source base was validated, and a standards effort involving IBM and Microsoft is underway.

For a proof of concept, the suggested steps are to confirm that encrypted results match clear-text results, then test which aggregates and models the platform handles. The product is sold as an API with ready-made building blocks, and the speaker said more of the library may open to the wider community later. The practical takeaway is that the claims can be checked against plain-data results before committing.

talks.title: Security Foundations
talks.teaser: Gives newcomers an overview of attacker motives, shifting regulation, and the human factors that shape today's security decisions.
talks.summary:
Hugh Thompson, program chair of the RSA Conference, opens this introductory seminar for attendees who are new to security or moving into it from another field. He uses a trip to a Bali monkey forest, where visitors who gave in to aggressive monkeys were singled out, as a metaphor for modern attackers, who study people and gather data to find the targets most likely to give in.

He then outlines how the environment has shifted. New privacy rules across many countries create audit pressure and constant change. Employees now use personal devices and free cloud tools outside IT control, most web traffic is encrypted, and flat networks give way to finer-grained access. On the attacker side, criminal groups operate like well-run companies, with personalised phishing, synthesised executive voices in payment fraud, and a focus on administrators and cloud operators whose accounts carry the most access.

He closes with economic principles: most attackers want something rather than being evil, costly breaches usually stem from simple mistakes, people make poor choices when security adds friction, and attackers exploit the weakest point. He also raises open questions about showing security's value to boards, measuring risk, and separating compliance from actual security. He urges attendees to challenge long-held assumptions, using the steering-wheel-and-airbag example to show how controls change.

Reserve-a-seat is distinguished from favorites: one reserved seat per time block, queues opening thirty minutes early, and standby chances for popular rooms. She highlights innovation programming at the Marriott, including sandbox pitches, a new venture-style launch event, early-stage exhibitors, hands-on sandbox villages, a closed CISO program, scholar and college outreach, and post-event synced audio with slides.

The operations portion returns to expo scale, briefing-center demos, an on-site security operations display, sponsor perks packs, receptions, split evening socials, and an expo pub crawl. Practical tips cover comfortable shoes, weekend badge pickup, hydration, and expo planning. Live chat questions address meeting spots, prayer space, seat timing, guest tickets, luggage check, dietary requests, skill labels on labs, and ancillary events off the official schedule.

talks.title: Privacy Essentials for Security Professionals
talks.teaser: Introduces privacy terminology, major US, Canadian and EU laws, GDPR changes and privacy-by-design principles for security staff.
talks.summary:
Todd Fitzgerald, a CISO and author, opens by arguing that security officers need working knowledge of privacy. He shows how security priorities shifted from compliance checklists toward data management, and traces privacy back to an 1890 Harvard Law Review article that framed it as an individual's claim to seclusion.

The middle section maps the legal landscape. The US relies on sectoral laws such as HIPAA and COPPA rather than one overarching statute, while the EU moved from its 1995 directive to the 2016 GDPR, which adds 72-hour breach notification, fines of up to 4% of revenue or 20 million euro, and data protection officers. He walks through the OECD's eight principles, from collection limitation to accountability, as the foundation for many privacy laws, and explains personal data, sensitive data, controller versus processor roles, privacy policies versus notices, and opt-in versus opt-out consent. A connected doll protected by a trivially guessable password illustrates weak privacy design, and a connected dinosaur toy shows how unclear data handling can be.

He closes with the seven privacy by design principles and advises attendees to meet their privacy officer or legal team, read the relevant laws, and consider IAPP certifications for deeper study.

talks.title: Virtual Session: Blockchain Security: An Improvement or a Nightmare?
talks.teaser: Weighs whether blockchain improves or weakens security, focusing on wallets, private keys and enterprise use cases.
talks.summary:
The session asks whether blockchain helps or hurts security. The presenters, both from the Hyperledger project at the Linux Foundation, first explain the underlying idea: an append-only record copied across a peer-to-peer network and kept consistent through consensus, with each block linked to the previous one by a hash so that altering history is detectable. They contrast this with traditional centralized access control, where an administrator or access list decides who can read a resource, and with capability-style access, where holding a private key grants the right to act.

The middle of the talk looks at wallets and exchanges. Wallets are described as hard to use and often little more than a graphical layer over raw keys, while centralized exchanges have suffered large server breaches that exposed stored keys. The speakers argue for better documentation, interfaces that resist misuse, and APIs that refuse calls made out of order. They also point to a curated, configurable cryptography library as a standard that could help. They warn that smart contracts written in Turing-complete languages will contain flaws, and that distributed networks remain open to denial-of-service attacks.

The closing part covers enterprise adoption, comparing permissioned and public networks and walking through examples in healthcare claims, supply chain tracking and identity-based access. The takeaway is that blockchain adds new attack surface rather than removing old risks, and that key management, staff training and operating procedures decide whether a deployment is safe.

talks.title: Adventures in Open Banking: Understanding OAuth and OpenID Client Ecosystems
talks.teaser: Traces how UK open banking adopted OAuth and OpenID Connect, and the standards gaps its security profiles exposed.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why interoperable identity standards matter and how the EU's Payment Services Directive 2 required banks to open their APIs to licensed third-party fintechs. It walks through the roles the European Banking Authority defined and the UK's push by its nine largest banks to deliver open banking on a tight deadline. The speaker explains why OpenID Connect was chosen over bare OAuth: OAuth leaves token formats undefined, while OpenID Connect standardizes ID tokens and supports certification testing.

The security requirements went beyond typical deployments and pushed standards bodies in three areas: mutually authenticated TLS for client authentication, signed request objects to convey transaction context, and transitive trust at scale. For the third, the talk covers how dynamic client registration under RFC 7591 lets software register with many banks automatically. It also describes how the UK's software statement assertions had to be mapped onto the protocol schema, which created edge cases around redirect URIs and key sets.

The closing section lists open problems, including headless operation without a browser, binding tokens to the transport channel, and building an industry-wide profile. The practical advice is to stop sending user passwords on every API call, and to avoid storing long-lived client secrets by using signed client assertions, so that a client's key never travels over the wire.

talks.title: Mind the Air-Gap: Exfiltrating ICS Data via AM Radios and Hacked PLC Code
talks.teaser: Shows how malicious ladder logic on a Siemens PLC can leak data from an air-gapped network via radio emissions.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, David Atch (introduced as David Ash / Devan David Atch), VP of Research at CyberX, demonstrates how attackers can exfiltrate sensitive data across an air-gap in operational technology (OT) and industrial control system (ICS) environments. While air-gapped industrial networks isolate critical physical processes from the internet, sophisticated attackers often breach these environments (via rogue USBs, compromised contractor engineering laptops, or supply-chain update poisoning such as NotPetya or Dragonfly's Havex malware). Once inside, attackers need reconnaissance data—such as device inventories, network schematics, and ladder logic—to design impactful physical attacks. To extract this information without relying on the physical return of infected hardware, the researchers developed a software-only technique that turns standard programmable logic controllers (PLCs) into radio transmitters.

### Key Topics
- **OT Attack Lifecycle and Reconnaissance:** Attacking industrial networks requires precise knowledge of proprietary protocols, safety systems, and process control logic before physical disruption can be executed.
- **Inherent PLC Characteristics:** PLCs feature hardware I/O, configuration storage, and control routines written in languages like ladder logic. They lack antivirus solutions or standard forensic APIs, making malicious code modification persistent and difficult to inspect.
- **Air-Gap Covert Channels:** Drawing on historical radio emission research such as TEMPEST and the open-source System Bus Radio project, the study explores electromagnetic emissions naturally radiated by electronic controller hardware.

### Technical Details
- **Target Hardware and Execution Environment:** The research evaluated Siemens PLCs. The attackers inject custom ladder logic into an Organizational Block (OB). Organizational blocks execute continuously and run alongside existing ladder logic without interrupting active industrial processes.
- **Modulating Electromagnetic Signals:** The researchers analyzed the controller's baseline RF emissions between roughly 300 kHz and 400 kHz. While mathematical routines, Ethernet cable manipulation, and network packet sniffing did not yield controllable RF modulation, copying large memory buffers (`memcpy`) consistently induced a detectable frequency shift.
- **Transmission Protocol and Demodulation:** By alternating between executing massive memory copies (representing a binary '1') and idling (representing a binary '0'), the PLC code modulates radio frequency emissions. The ladder logic routine initiates transmission with a dedicated synchronization pattern to allow a receiver equipped with a Software-Defined Radio (SDR) and antenna to identify the transmission start, isolate the optimal low-noise frequency via correlation algorithms, and decode the payload.
- **Performance:** In bench testing, the team achieved an exfiltration rate of 1 byte per second over distances up to 1 meter, noting that higher-gain antennas and refined filtering algorithms could extend range and throughput.

### Takeaways and Defenses
Host-based endpoint protections do not exist for most legacy PLCs, and password or physical keylock protections can often be circumvented once an engineering station is compromised. Defending against these covert channels requires continuous passive network monitoring to detect anomalous behaviors, such as unauthorized ladder logic uploads, unexpected network scanning or ping sweeps initiated by controllers, and the appearance of unrecognized devices on the control network.

talks.title: CCleaner APT Attack: A Technical Look Inside
talks.teaser: Dissects how a compromised build environment slipped a multi-stage backdoor into signed CCleaner releases.
talks.summary:
This talk walks through the 2017 CCleaner attack from the perspective of Avast, which was in the middle of acquiring CCleaner's maker when the intrusion happened. Attackers replaced C++ runtime libraries on the build server, so a payload was linked into signed CCleaner 5.3.3 desktop and 1.7.0 cloud builds. The modified releases reached about 2.3 million PCs, and roughly 28 days passed before anyone noticed.

The first stage contained only command-and-control code, with a hard-coded IP address and a domain generation fallback. Only about 40 machines received a second stage, which was delivered by dropping patched copies of existing DLLs into service-loading locations and storing shellcode in registry binary keys. That stage fetched the address of its next server through GitHub and WordPress profiles used as steganographic channels. Analysis of the recovered command-and-control database, found on a backup server, showed how victims were chosen by a domain list in a PHP script. On the CCleaner maker's own network, the investigators found the third-stage ShadowPad toolkit, which had entered through TeamViewer and a keylogger that captured build-server credentials.

The speaker closed with three lessons: secure the build infrastructure, make cyber due diligence a priority in acquisitions, and recognise that valid signatures undermine allowlisting for security software. Attribution pointed toward a likely state-sponsored Chinese group, based on timing, comments and target selection, though the speaker noted this was not hard evidence.
