talks.title: Red Team vs. Blue Team on AWS
talks.teaser: Walks through an AWS account attack from a single read-only key to a database, then shows how to block each step.
talks.summary:
The talk stages a red team versus blue team exercise in an AWS account built from default tutorials, including a WordPress site, a Lambda function and an RDS database. The attacker starts with one read-only key, the kind that can sit in a developer's CLI configuration. Read access alone is enough to map open subnets and security groups, then find a Lambda function whose code location URL exposes its source, including database credentials. A public WordPress site with open outbound rules is identified as the way in.

The defensive half covers least privilege: a base IAM role that only lets users manage their own password and MFA device, with each duty in a separate role that requires an MFA token and issues short-lived credentials. Secrets move from code into EC2 Parameter Store under IAM control, and secret scanning and pre-commit hooks keep keys out of Git repositories. Network fixes include a three-tier layout with tight ACLs and security groups, while CloudTrail events feed a Lambda function that flags off-hours role assumptions.

The closing section adds detection and edge protection with GuardDuty, AWS Config, CloudFront and a load balancer in front of the application. The takeaways are that read-only access can still be damaging, cloud APIs make reconnaissance easy, and monitoring everything is the baseline.

talks.title: From “No Data” to “Drowning in Data”—It’s Time for a Reality Check
talks.teaser: Cyber risk quantification needs calibrated models and clear data quality, not endless telemetry or perfect actuarial tables.
talks.summary:
Organizations often claim they lack enough data to measure cyber risk quantitatively, yet every prioritization choice already rests on implicit measurements—usually informal high, medium, and low judgments with no stated confidence. The speaker frames data as a tool for reducing uncertainty in a dynamic landscape where resources are finite, comparisons require metrics, and historical information decays at different rates across threats, assets, controls, and loss types.

The middle of the talk contrasts abundance and scarcity: security telemetry and data lakes can overflow while scenarios such as malicious privileged insiders remain almost data-free. Quality matters more than volume—through calibrated expert estimates, explicit uncertainty ranges, and simple matrices for specificity versus guesswork, and for recency versus volume of hard data. Raw telemetry, scan results, pen tests, and threat feeds gain meaning only through models; weak or proprietary models can invert priorities, as illustrated with widespread severity scoring approaches, informal mental models, and familiar framework pitfalls.

Practitioners are urged to tie metrics to decisions (for example, where unpatched vulnerabilities rank against identity, logging, or awareness programs), scope analyses carefully, and distinguish practice frameworks from true risk measurement. References include FAIR for structuring questions such as phishing scope and loss magnitude, plus guidance on scrutinizing vendor quantification claims. The close argues that waiting for perfect datasets blocks progress; honest uncertainty communication and steadily better data and models are the realistic path forward.

talks.title: Passwords and Fingerprints and Faces—Oh My! Comparing Old and New Authentication
talks.teaser: Compares password habits with fingerprint, face and FIDO-based login, and what enterprises should consider.
talks.summary:
Jackson Shaw, an identity management veteran, opens by describing what passwords still cost organizations: help desk resets, frequent breach notices, and staff writing credentials down. He cites a figure that 63% of breaches involved weak, default or stolen passwords, and recalls how attackers in the Sony incident reached sensitive files through an ordinary user account.

He then reviews newer options. Fingerprint and facial recognition on phones keep a mathematical representation of the biometric in the device's secure enclave rather than a stored image. He quotes error rates of about one in 10,000 for a passcode, one in 50,000 for a fingerprint, and one in a million for facial recognition. He also covers the drawbacks: cuts or wet fingers interfering with fingerprint sensors, the need for positive enrollment, the older gummy-bear spoofing research, and 3D-printed masks. He describes FIDO as a public key standard that resists phishing and man-in-the-middle attacks, along with risk-based authentication, push-to-approve prompts, and hardware such as TPM chips.

He closes by arguing that biometrics and FIDO are reaching a tipping point, while passwords will remain for a long time. His practical advice is to identify critical applications that would benefit from push or biometric approval, to test biometric or token-based replacements for password reset flows, and to ask software vendors whether they support FIDO and platform face authentication.

talks.title: Mining Botnets Reemerge, Bringing Shifts into the Threat Landscape
talks.teaser: Dissects three cryptocurrency mining botnet families, covering their spread, command traffic and evasion changes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how cryptocurrency mining botnets have grown and changed, using three case studies. The first family began as an information stealer and was reworked into a miner that spreads through removable drives and checks in with its command server using beacons. Over time its operators moved from public mining pools to a private pool and rewrote its scripts in AutoHotkey, so each copy had a different hash.

The second family spreads through Facebook: it loads a browser extension into Chrome and sends a file to the victim's friends by message. Its command server mostly acts as a download repository for components and does not issue tasks. The third is a coin miner sold on underground markets, with features such as silent mining, scheduled-task persistence, and repacking to evade antivirus detection. The presenters note that buyers often ask for spreading features, which sellers tend to resist.

For defenders, the presenters suggest watching for unexplained fan noise and high CPU use, protecting cloud accounts that attackers could use to launch mining instances, and running regular phishing awareness training. They also recommend monitoring that produces actionable threat intelligence, backed by a practised incident response plan that learns from each attack.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show: Artificial Intelligence APJ Style
talks.teaser: Panel segment pairs an interview with robot Sophia and demos of fooling image, audio and face recognition systems.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with host Hugh Thompson describing how his six-year-old chatted with Siri, a story he uses to show how easily people attribute human qualities to technology. The humanoid robot Sophia, from Hanson Robotics, then joins for an interview about her travels, her view that machines and people are complementary, and how her emotions are simulated. Asked whether she could be hacked, she said anything can eventually be hacked, though her closed, proprietary software makes it less likely.

Dr Ayesha Khanna then discusses adopting AI in business. She advises defining a business problem before choosing AI, and gives examples from financial services, where alternative data is used to build credit profiles for the unbanked, and from urban transport. She urges non-experts to learn the basics and question model outputs instead of treating AI as a black box. Mahmood Sharif, a PhD student at Carnegie Mellon University, then explains adversarial machine learning, covering evasion and poisoning attacks. He shows images with small perturbations that a classifier labels wrongly with high confidence, an audio clip that a voice assistant interprets as a location query, and eyeglass frames designed to make a face recognition system identify him as someone else.

The closing remarks argue that security professionals should advocate for safe and careful AI adoption rather than simply blocking projects.

talks.title: Security Maturity Drives Growth and Innovation
talks.teaser: Reframes security as a business enabler, tying basic hygiene, monitoring and crypto choices to revenue, cost and public trust.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by tracing how security professionals have been viewed over time, from obstacles to slow projects, to a necessary evil handled through yearly compliance audits, to today's role as an enabler. The core argument is that security should be pitched in the terms leaders already use: businesses care about increasing revenue or decreasing cost, and governments about economic output and citizen wellbeing.

Several examples make this concrete. A password burden is reframed as an efficiency case for single sign-on, backed by helpdesk reset costs. Biometric checks at airports are presented as a faster, more pleasant experience that draws travellers and their spending. Facial recognition at cash machines is described as cutting fraud remediation costs and as able to refuse a withdrawal when a second person appears to be coercing the customer. For cryptocurrency, the question of whether an organisation should accept it becomes a risk-versus-reward decision, because stolen identities in crypto carry no bank-style recourse. The speaker also notes that a single attack can now affect many locations and people at once.

The talk closes on citizen data: sharing health records enables early prevention, but breaches erode the willingness to share. The takeaway is that security leaders in business should protect the core and understand the drivers they support, while those in government should make sure citizens feel secure enough to engage with digital services.

talks.title: Android Malware Trends on a Global Scale
talks.teaser: Surveys regional Android malware trends from a large user base, covering lockers, aggressive ads, bankers and downloaders.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Android malware trends across a worldwide user base of tens of millions, where infection rates typically sit between four and five percent. Metrics count unique pairs of detections and users, so a device infected repeatedly is counted once. The presenters sort threats into nine categories, including lockers, aggressive ads, bankers, downloaders and rooters, and focus on four of them.

Regional comparisons form the core of the talk. Bankers grew sharply, tripling in Australia and doubling in Europe over the period, while rooters declined almost everywhere. North America saw lockers take up a large share of detections, and aggressive ads rose in most regions. Africa and Asia were analysed together, with downloaders forming a big share in Africa, and Russia was treated separately because bankers are a large part of its detections. Each category is illustrated with its typical behaviour, from ad pop-ups using overlay permissions to ransomware posing as media players and bankers intercepting one-time passwords in SMS.

The closing advice covers users, developers and app stores. Users should install apps only from trusted sources, keep patches current, question unusual permission requests such as device administrator access, and run antivirus. Developers should vet third-party code, encrypt traffic and request only the permissions an app needs, while stores should publish and enforce guidelines. Sharing threat data with the security community is encouraged.

talks.title: A Real-World Example of Using Network Behaviour to Detect Cyber-Compromise
talks.teaser: A bank's multi-year story shows how NetFlow scoring and correlated telemetry improve SOC hunts without treating ML as a silver bullet.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by framing advanced threats that slip past signatures and IPS thresholds, and argues that rich network metadata plus machine learning can spotlight kill-chain behaviors when prevention alone fails. The first arc follows PathScan, a NetFlow-driven scoring capability built with Los Alamos National Laboratory: low per-flow risk scores combine into alerts for reconnaissance, lateral hops across sensitive roles, and data staging, illustrated with a benign regional printer test that still merited review.

The middle covers scaling pains and platform growth. Telemetry meant for operations was dropped under pressure; reverse DNS and DHCP context lagged; VoIP and non-production networks flooded analysts. Testing and red-team replays train the models to treat repeats as normal. The program widened into an advanced cyber analytics lake ingesting dozens of sources via Flume and Kafka, storing billions of daily events for analytics and forensics, prioritizing use cases with MITRE ATT&CK, and feeding credential-behavior betas aligned with Apache Spot concepts.

The close highlights SOC analysts hunting C2 by contrast—bursty, referrer-poor proxy patterns versus everyday browsing on default Empire implants—and practical takeaways: invest in data quality and lineage, partner with vendors iteratively, build analyst playbooks and automation rather than alert dumps, and treat behavioral analytics as an evolving capability, not a cure-all, while adversaries adopt similar techniques.

talks.title: Top 10 Ways to Make Hackers Excited: Shortcuts That Were Not Worth Taking
talks.teaser: Live demos expose recurring architecture shortcuts that let attackers amplify DNS, steal secrets, and relay Windows authentication.
talks.summary:
The session frames a recurring pattern from enterprise penetration tests: organizations invest in visible controls yet leave familiar misconfigurations that make offensive work straightforward. The speaker walks through a curated set of shortcuts—disabled or permissive host firewalls, weak egress rules, and protocols that amplify traffic—then shows how easily DNS reflection can degrade services inside a lab network, along with mitigations such as response rate limiting on Windows DNS.

Demonstrations move into credential exposure on Windows: service account passwords in the registry, IIS application pool identities protected only by DPAPI, and hash extraction from NTDS.dit to spot password reuse across standard and privileged accounts. Without flat segmentation, ARP spoofing captures cleartext traffic; the talk explains SMB/NTLM relay mechanics, enabling SMB signing as the primary control, and walks through relay tooling even when the live chain stutters. Further segments cover unencrypted SQL Server TDS traffic combined with network positioning to inject administrative commands, unloading Sysmon mini-filter drivers while services still appear healthy, abuse of interactive logons on servers, absent application control, risky outbound paths, legacy protocol settings, blind trust in monitoring products, weak service account hygiene, and unvetted third-party utilities.

Practitioners should treat the list as a pentest-aligned checklist: assume these issues appear in production, validate egress and segmentation, enforce signing and encryption on core protocols, prefer group managed service accounts, and test whether defenses remain effective when drivers or agents are tampered with—not merely whether dashboards show green status.

talks.title: The Blurred Lines between Cybercrime and Statecraft
talks.teaser: Explores how nation-state tradecraft bleeds into cybercrime and outlines defenses beyond malware-centric security models.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a threat landscape where nation-state actors, financially motivated criminals, hacktivists, and others reuse one another’s techniques rather than staying in separate buckets. Citing Asia-Pacific economic impact estimates and high-profile incidents such as WannaCry, NotPetya, SWIFT-focused banking attacks, and targeted ransomware against cities and public-safety organizations, the speaker argues that “trickle-down” leakage of government-developed capabilities keeps exposing organizations of every size and sector.

The middle of the talk contrasts headline fixation on malware and zero-days with adversary goals and living-off-the-land methods. Examples include harvesting NTLM hashes through SMB-backed web lures, Word remote templates, credential-focused actors such as the Duke cluster, InstallUtil-based AppLocker bypass research later adopted by Chinese adversaries, and chained use of certutil, expand, and csvde for download, decompression, and Active Directory enumeration. Ransomware and cryptocurrency mining campaigns illustrate how reused exploits and scripts can evade many prevention products.

Practitioners are urged to operationalize threat intelligence beyond indicators of compromise, hunt for behavioral combinations and indicators of attack, tighten authentication and monitoring around legacy Windows features, and design for speed. Referenced benchmarks include multi-day average detection and response times, sub-two-hour lateral movement breakout windows, and a one–ten–sixty detect-investigate-contain aspiration, plus off-site logging so destructive actors cannot erase the evidence needed for response.

talks.title: Transparent Orchestration: The Visibility to Act
talks.teaser: Argues for building security into redesigned cloud applications, with a demo of one console for visibility, alerts and response.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an analogy: a child who uses a smart TV and a single voice command to reach her favorite show, with several vendors working together. The speaker contrasts that with enterprise IT, where systems built up incrementally over decades have different architectures and security teams add separate tools after the fact. The cost is high: many products, hardware, developers and specialists, plus multiple agents that each collect the same network, file and process data.

The speaker argues that organizations redesigning applications for the cloud can build security in from the start, joining development, operations and security teams. A demonstration showed a cloud security console where a vulnerability assessment was turned on for virtual machines with one click and findings appeared later in the same place. A rule could block an exposed port on a vulnerable machine and send a Slack message. A concept chatbot then answered questions about cloud account counts, resource totals and control failures, and posted results to a Slack channel.

The speaker described three kinds of orchestration: deployment, monitoring and response. Response, the ability to act on what is visible in one place, is the goal the others lead to. The closing point is that collecting data once, cutting the number of agents and building instrumentation in early gives security the visibility it lacks, and that now is the time to act.

talks.title: GDPR: A Global View
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how GDPR shapes data mapping, vendor contracts, enforcement and cross-border transfers worldwide.
talks.summary:
The panel, moderated by Trevor Hughes of the IAPP, framed the GDPR as the successor to Europe's 1995 data protection directive, which predated smartphones and social media. The regulation took effect in May 2018 and applies extraterritorially, so organizations outside Europe can fall under it when they serve people in the EU. With fines of up to 4% of global turnover, panelists said senior executives had begun paying attention, though survey results showed only about a fifth of companies claimed compliance.

Panelists described the operational work. An insurance and reinsurance company said locating personal data and tracing its flows was the hardest task, and data processing agreements now reach down supply chains to vendors and subprocessors. Accenture used GDPR as a global baseline, layering privacy controls onto existing security controls and adopting tools for impact assessments and supplier due diligence. A TrustArc representative pointed to growing demand for data discovery and mapping tools, and for assessing risk to individuals' rights, a subjective test with little guidance so far. A survey of Japanese organizations found only 7% prepared for the 72-hour breach notification deadline.

Regulators were already handling thousands of complaints, and panelists expected them to ask for evidence of records, assessments and incident handling, with good faith treated as a mitigating factor. Future concerns included new technologies such as IoT and machine learning, and cross-border transfer mechanisms under legal challenge that Brexit would complicate further. The closing message was that security and privacy teams should share a common language and build integrated data governance and risk management.

talks.title: Our Biggest Bet Yet
talks.teaser: The presentation frames negativity bias in security, cites breach-cost research, and urges three industry force multipliers.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting headline fear with real gains, from phone encryption to harder boardroom questions for security leaders, and argues that lasting improvement in a complex field requires patience and deliberate large investments rather than quick fixes.

Drawing on a long-running Ponemon breach-cost study, the talk highlights rising global losses and long mean times to spot and contain incidents, framing shorter detection and containment as direct savings. It introduces three “force multipliers”: augmented intelligence that speeds analyst research (including efforts to teach machines cybersecurity knowledge and broader machine learning uses), security orchestration through incident playbooks and practiced coordination, and immersive cyber-range exercises that stress leadership under pressure.

The closing call is for open collaboration—integrated vendor tools, shared threat intelligence, and academic partnerships—alongside public-good efforts such as open threat-sharing platforms and privacy-focused DNS. The aim is for practitioners to get smarter, respond faster, and work together at scale despite attacker sophistication and staffing gaps.

talks.title: The Impact of Autonomous Security in Today’s Threat Landscape
talks.teaser: Links rising cloud and phishing risk to autonomous detection, unified telemetry, and automated remediation for overloaded security teams.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with well-known breach patterns—phishing-driven travel-data theft in Japan, large-scale DDoS outages, and an eighty-million-dollar Bangladesh bank heist—to frame why manual defenses struggle as digital footprints, IoT, mobile access, and multi-cloud SaaS expand. Executives face simultaneous pressure to cut cost, run systems around the clock, and avoid regulatory and reputational harm when sensitive data leaks.

A KPMG-linked survey of four hundred fifty global security practitioners highlights cloud event management as the top headache: most respondents treat more than half of cloud-held data as sensitive, yet large majorities see policy violations and unpatched known vulnerabilities. The talk cites alert volumes near seventeen thousand events per week per enterprise, with only a small fraction investigated, plus a skills gap projected into millions of unfilled roles. Autonomous security is described as ingesting and normalizing telemetry from users, devices, and applications, applying machine learning for anomaly detection, and triggering rule- or AI-driven responses such as privilege reduction during suspected impersonation.

Implementation guidance stresses a single consolidated view across on-premises and multi-vendor cloud estates, real-time analysis, and a full prevent-detect-respond-predict lifecycle with adaptive, cross-environment sharing. Brief customer examples touch seasonal workforce identity in Japan and education-sector access in Korea. The close points practitioners to the Oracle–KPMG cloud threat report and trial cloud security services rather than technical walkthroughs.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Silver Linings
talks.teaser: Argues that cybersecurity is improving, and urges defenders to build on focused basics, fast adoption and teamwork.
talks.summary:
The keynote, given at an RSA Conference in Singapore, argues that the security field is improving and that defenders should build on what already works rather than chase headlines. Using a cycling team's approach of pursuing many small gains instead of one breakthrough, the speaker argues that the sector should keep managing risk in business terms and get the basics right. Patching is the example given: the speaker ties the WannaCry outbreak to an unpatched vulnerability and points to wider multi-factor authentication adoption as progress.

The middle section covers speed and collaboration. The speaker says new technology reaches the mainstream faster than security professionals learn to handle it, and cites an RSA study that measured the lag for biometrics, cloud computing and machine learning. A rowing analogy makes the case that defence needs both the security team and outside groups such as business leaders, policymakers, regulators, IT leadership and universities. Regional data protection laws and national cybersecurity agencies are offered as signs of that wider effort.

The closing turns to the clouds. The speaker points to suspected under-reporting of incidents in the region, economic losses of 1.75 trillion dollars in 2017, equal to 7% of regional GDP, and the risk that a failure in technology could erode public trust in it. The talk ends by urging the audience to avoid both recklessness and complacency and to keep building on the progress already made.

talks.title: Incident Response in the Cloud
talks.teaser: Shows how to adapt incident response and forensic evidence collection to cloud providers, logs, and automation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with survey results showing that respondents most often struggled to perform response and forensic work they could do in-house, mainly because logs and artifacts were missing. Traditional IR skills still carry over to the cloud, but pulling logs out of providers, centralizing them and automating collection are harder. Provider contracts, including how law enforcement access is handled and which logs are exposed, should be settled before an incident.

For preparation, the speaker recommends a dedicated, tightly scoped account for the response team, write-once storage for evidence with verifiable attributes, and a pre-approved quarantine network policy that can be attached to a misbehaving asset. For detection, the talk points to billing alarms, identity and access management activity, resource creation by unexpected principals and unusual regions, while filtering out the large volume of descriptive, read-only API calls. Containment means tagging suspicious instances and moving them to an isolated network rather than cutting them off at once.

Forensics is more awkward: disk snapshots can be copied and attached to a cloud-hosted SIFT workstation, but memory and packet capture are much harder because the hypervisor and network layers are hidden. The speaker points to the ThreatResponse suite and a detailed guide for memory acquisition. For eradication, instances should be treated as disposable and rebuilt, and the talk closes by urging teams to automate with provider APIs and playbooks and to run game-day exercises.

talks.title: The Bottom of the Barrel—Scraping Pastebin for Obfuscated Malware
talks.teaser: Shows how a Python scraper finds obfuscated malware hidden in Pastebin pastes and decodes it for analysis.
talks.summary:
Patrick Colford, a security analyst at Cisco, explains how Pastebin, a text-sharing site founded in 2002, is abused to hide obfuscated malware alongside legitimate content such as code and fan fiction. He notes that anonymous posting, free hosting and pastes that delete themselves after a set time make it attractive to attackers.

To find this material, the team built Fiercecroissant, an open-source Python scraper that flags non-word patterns such as long runs of characters, then decodes the matches from base64, hex, binary, ASCII, and PHP or Visual Basic wrappers. Decoded executables are run in a sandbox, and the contacted domains are added to a block list. The team reported 2,230 domains contacted by the malware, about 800 blocks as of November 2017, and 2,695 base64 pastes matching its criteria, with further hits in hex, PHP, binary, ASCII and image formats. The scraper also catches harmless content such as game ROMs, so results need careful review.

The talk also profiled three Pastebin users. One posted defacement scripts and web shells, another shared disclosures of backdoors and remote file inclusion tutorials, and a third's pastes included a Bitcoin miner and a Trojan, with three of five pastes deleted. The speaker advised corporate teams to scrape Pastebin for malware and credential leaks, consider blocking it if there is no legitimate business use, and follow peers' research as attackers adapt.

talks.title: There’s No Such Thing as a Cyber-Risk
talks.teaser: Shows security teams how enterprise risk techniques like FAIR and scenario analysis can frame cyber risk in business terms.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security programs struggle to win over the business because they describe work through tools and techniques rather than business outcomes. Evan Wheeler proposes borrowing methods from enterprise and operational risk management. Risk is defined as the potential that a threat exploits a weakness and harms an asset, with uncertainty built in. Enterprise risk sorts concerns into macroeconomic, strategic and operational buckets, and cyber has no outcome category of its own.

Loss event analysis looks at past incidents and sizes their impact across loss categories borrowed from FAIR, merged down to five. Existing approval limits and recovery time objectives can supply dollar tolerance ranges. Scenario analysis runs as a scoped workshop that lists assumptions and exclusions, keeping external and insider scenarios apart. Examples include deleting an Active Directory domain and a ransomware scoping. Comparing a data theft case, about 150K maximum single loss and about 45k annualized, with an accidental disclosure case, 10k maximum and 450k annualized, suggests insurance suits the first and mitigation the second.

The talk also covers risk and control self-assessment, which maps business processes to risks and controls, and separates control assessment from control testing. Inherent and residual risk show how preventive and detective controls shift frequency or impact. Top-down scenarios are reconciled with bottom-up asset inventories to explain differences. The closing advice is to state risks in business terms from the start rather than translating them at the end.

talks.title: How the Best Hackers Learn Their Craft
talks.teaser: Describes capture-the-flag pipelines, gamified challenges, and deliberate practice used to grow world-class competitive security teams.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by distinguishing creative hackers from criminals and asking how elite practitioners reach that level. He points to figures such as George Hotz and Richard Zhu, then describes Carnegie Mellon’s Plaid Parliament of Pwning and sustained DEF CON wins as evidence that talent can be cultivated deliberately rather than discovered by accident.

The core of the session treats capture-the-flag events as a curriculum. Jeopardy-style boards introduce skills from cryptography through exploitation; PicoCTF scales that model to high school students with a story-driven game. Three principles anchor the design: staged deliberate practice instead of throwing novices into live attack-defense arenas, self-directed research when stuck, and room for unconventional solutions judged by flags rather than prescribed write-ups. Walk-throughs cover beginner puzzles, reverse-engineering stack layouts, a Dutch team’s unexpected PHP zero day at hack.im, and implementation-side timing attacks against deployed RSA in 2003. Attack-defense formats appear as a capstone where strategy, weak-target selection, and reflection matter.

Closing themes stress measuring talent through funnels such as PicoCTF’s participation and solve-rate curves, refreshing university teams every four years, and having alumni design the next challenges. Practitioners are urged to embed CTFs in training, partner with experienced problem authors, or use open contests, then treat strong solves as a fair filter before interviews. Questions extend the model to talent that does not enroll at CMU, PPP’s dominance, diversity in game design, and why foundational offensive skills support defense.

talks.title: Building a Security Awareness Ambassador Program
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a volunteer security ambassador network that scales awareness, with motivation, onboarding and metrics guidance.
talks.summary:
Lance Spitzner, director at the SANS Institute, explains why many security awareness programs struggle to scale. Staff are often part-time, audiences are varied, and teams run out of fresh ideas. He frames awareness as a control for managing human risk and says culture shifts slowly, through repeated changes in behavior over years.

He proposes a volunteer ambassador network embedded across the organization. Ambassadors are typically non-technical peers who commit about four hours a month for at least a year. They can localize materials, present, survey colleagues and report back, and often reach staff faster than communications departments. Motivation comes from recognition and career or skills benefits, while enabling ambassadors requires training, a peer forum and resources. Time, rather than budget, is the main constraint.

For rollout, he advises starting with five to ten ambassadors for three to six months, dedicating roughly half a full-time person to run it, and tracking hours spent per ambassador so growth requests can be sized. Onboarding should include manager approval, training and a first month of introductions, with an alumni status for those who step back. Metrics should move from participation counts to impact measures such as incidents and reporting rates, and pilots should begin in receptive departments.

talks.title: A Framework to Effectively Develop Insider Threat Controls
talks.teaser: Lays out a five-step framework for identifying insider threats to critical assets and building and testing controls.
talks.summary:
The talk from CERT's National Insider Threat Center addresses how an organization can decide which insider threat controls to build and how to tell whether they work. The presenters draw on insider incident data collected since 1996 and survey results showing that about half of organizations report an insider incident in a typical year. They illustrate the stakes with three cases: an engineer who took over $1 billion in technology before joining a foreign competitor, a security director who altered a lottery's random number generator with a rootkit so accomplices could win over $14 million, and a contractor who kept access after termination and discharged 800,000 liters of raw sewage.

The framework runs in five steps: identify critical assets tied to the organization's mission, establish a control baseline using existing standards such as NIST SP 800-53, fill gaps in that baseline, measure control effectiveness, and continuously improve. Controls are sorted into preventive, detective, corrective, recovery, deterrent and compensating functions, and the presenters stress that tools support a program but cannot replace one. Using their IT system sabotage model, built from about 200 cases, they show how behavioral and technical precursors map to observables and then to specific controls.

For measurement, they suggest coverage metrics, true and false positive rates checked against ground truth, and impact measures such as prevented actions and shorter investigation times. Testing methods include tabletop exercises with insider scenarios, penetration tests that begin from authorized access, and synthetic threat data inserted into operational datasets. The session closes by noting that the threat landscape shifts with mergers, layoffs and new technology, so controls need periodic reassessment.

talks.title: Into the Web of Profit: Tracking the Proceeds of Cybercrime
talks.teaser: Follows how cybercrime revenue moves through online markets, cryptocurrency and banks, and the laundering methods used.
talks.summary:
The talk treats cybercrime as an economy rather than a single kind of business. The speaker argues that a central reason criminals act is what they earn, so the research set out to trace where those revenues go, especially how they are laundered. Criminal activity is described as a linked set of actors, some technical, some providing support or infrastructure.

The speaker challenges the idea that cybercrime is mostly drug sales on Silk Road-style marketplaces. Illicit pharmaceutical sales, including opioids and fentanyl, are presented as a much larger online category, and marketplaces trading company data and intellectual property are described as increasingly important. Cryptocurrency is shown as one laundering channel among several. The speaker says it is not yet the main tool, and points to older methods such as money transfer services and mixed physical and digital routes. A figure of about $80 billion laundered through cryptocurrency, mostly tied to Europe, is given as an example.

In the question and answer, the speaker explains that the estimates rely only on the most reliable public sources, which means many categories were left out. The work is framed as a baseline to be refined with more data. Banks are discussed as conduits: the global laundromat case and a Wells Fargo case are cited, and offshore accounts opened online without documentation are highlighted as a weak point. The practical takeaway is that mapping cybercrime as an economy helps show how money flows, and that reducing its revenue is a goal alongside protecting data.

talks.title: The Untold Story of 8200: A Launching Point for Women in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Former Unit 8200 alumnae share how military training launched their cybersecurity careers and what keeps women from advancing.
talks.summary:
The panel, moderated by Avivah Litan, starts from a gap: only about 11 percent of cybersecurity professionals are women, a figure that has stayed flat for years, while women make up 55 percent of soldiers in Unit 8200, Israel's signals intelligence unit. The three former members describe how the unit recruits from high school and screens for analytical ability, decision-making and leadership rather than coding skill, and how junior members were given real responsibility early on, such as presenting their expertise to senior commanders.

The discussion then turns to networking. The unit's alumni network gives women immediate credibility in rooms where they are often the only woman, but the speakers agree that the gap widens at senior levels. They point to bias in everyday workplace communication, such as jokes that make colleagues feel small, and to women's reluctance to self-promote. A cited 2016 figure showed women earning less than men at every level, and the panel argues that salary transparency is one of the few objective measures of inequality.

Practical advice centers on taking ownership: start a side project that others have not explored, bring it to a manager, and find a mentor, formal or informal. The panel also urges organizations to give real projects and a seat at the table to people who do not fit the usual profile, including women who have not yet considered security, to ease the talent shortage.

talks.title: Building and Selling Your Security Strategy to the Business
talks.teaser: Shows how to build a risk-based security strategy, win business buy-in through workshops, and report progress with dashboards.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how to build a security strategy from the ground up and then present it to business leaders. The presenter, who moved from government service into a director security role and later became a chief security officer, argues that the strategy should be grounded in the organization's key risks. That gives a way to set priorities, defend the budget, and be open about which risks the organization is choosing to accept.

The approach has three parts: a risk framework, business buy-in, and a control framework, supported by tooling. Risk scenarios were gathered across departments, about 500 at the first pass, consolidated to about 100, and then focused on 30 by department. Each scenario was ranked on impact, likelihood and confidence. Annual workshops with department heads took about two hours each, using magnetic boards and printed impact and likelihood guides. Controls were mapped to requirements and then to risk scenarios, and a dashboard showed the most critical and most deficient controls. A second speaker described a simpler spreadsheet version built for a regional bank, scoring 149 sub-controls across 20 families on a 1 to 4 maturity scale covering definition, implementation, automation and reporting.

In closing, the presenter advised keeping the program simple enough for executives to follow without dumbing it down. A small team with technical, risk and pragmatic skills was recommended, along with starting from an established framework rather than building one from scratch. Establishing a baseline was described as a roughly three-month effort, with control mapping taking six months or longer.

talks.title: Quick Look: Operationalised Risk Modeling Using the Data Breach Repository
talks.teaser: Outlines how VERIS and DBIR incident patterns support benchmarking, use-case gaps, tabletop exercises, and risk-based security investments.
talks.summary:
Many organizations face an overload of risk data sources and struggle to tie external breach intelligence to their own priorities. The session introduces Verizon’s Data Breach Investigations Report and companion materials, built from years of global incident contributions and organized through the VERIS taxonomy so events can be recorded with consistent attributes about actors, assets, and actions.

The discussion splits operational use into technical and strategic tracks. On the technical side, the corpus supports visualizing incidents, closing detection gaps, prioritizing vulnerabilities attackers actually exploit, and validating controls. Strategically, industry and regional views inform tabletop exercises, initiative planning, and spending before a major breach occurs. Since 2014, nine recurring incident patterns help enterprises compare their sector, reduce noise, and invest where patterns hit hardest. The Data Breach Digest adds responder narratives and attack–defend cards that map sophistication, timelines, motives, tactics, and victim profiles for rehearsal.

Recommended starting steps include classifying internal incidents with VERIS, benchmarking against DBIR statistics, and using digest scenarios to improve response over time. The speakers stress detection and response over prevention alone, broader visibility inside and outside the perimeter, and data-centric protection. They note that roughly half of actors resemble organized crime and a meaningful share are state-linked, and invite organizations to consume or contribute to the open reporting program.

talks.title: Women: The Answer to Tech's Talent Shortage | Reshma Saujani | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Explores the U.S. computing job gap and frames bringing more women into tech as a one-generation fix through culture and policy.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with visits to New York City public schools, where computer science and robotics classes were crowded with boys aspiring to follow famous tech founders, while girls were largely absent. That observation frames a workforce crisis: on the order of 500,000 open computing jobs compared with fewer than 40,000 computer science graduates in the United States in the prior year, contrasted with hundreds of thousands of engineering graduates in China. The speaker argues that high-paying engineering roles can embody the American dream, with six-figure salaries cited as an example, and that expanding women's participation is the practical answer to the talent shortage—especially where pay disparities between male and female engineers are small yet women's representation in technical roles has fallen.

The middle of the talk traces history and culture. Ada Lovelace is cited as the first programmer. Through the 1980s, gaming camps and CS classrooms were far more gender-balanced than today. The decline is tied to personal computers marketed in ads as toys for boys, so many boys gained early hands-on experience while girls often did not, and to film stereotypes of isolated male programmers that repelled girls from identifying with the field. A recurring theme is that girls are socialized toward perfection while boys are pushed toward bravery, shaping who persists in technical paths.

The close centers on urgency and measurable programs. Culture and thoughtful policy could accelerate change within years rather than decades. Girls Who Code is described as having reached 90,000 girls across all fifty states, with alumni choosing computer science majors at fifteen times the national rate and Black and Latina alumni at sixteen times that rate. The speaker warns employers that this pipeline will soon be unavoidable when hiring technical talent.

talks.title: Call for a Unified Transatlantic Digital Cybersecurity Strategy | Andrus Ansip | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Argues that EU and US should align cyber standards, certification and incident sharing to deter attackers together.
talks.summary:
Andrus Ansip, who was prime minister of Estonia in 2007 and now works on building a digital single market at the European Commission in Brussels, opens by framing 2007 as a watershed moment for his country. Drawing on that experience, he argues that no nation can succeed alone and that rapid, informal exchange of information is essential. He stresses that the EU and US partnership underpins security and prosperity on both sides of the Atlantic.

The core of the talk is a call for a transatlantic approach to cyber deterrence. Ansip points to the EU's proposed certification scheme for cybersecurity products and services as a possible basis for discussion, with the aim of aligning standards on both continents. He also suggests that common security standards for Internet of Things devices could set global norms, and that detailed sharing of cyber incident information would help prevent future attacks. His warning is that an attack on Europe today could reach the United States tomorrow.

He closes with artificial intelligence, a technology already spreading worldwide that raises questions of cyber security, privacy, ethics and fundamental liberties. He calls for shared principles governing how AI is developed and deployed, and says those principles are needed now. The talk is a political appeal rather than a technical briefing, and it refers to privacy arrangements between the two sides as part of the wider relationship.

talks.title: Crisis Management Exercise: How to Respond to a National Cyber-Crisis | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Runs a tabletop exercise simulating a national cyberattack on critical infrastructure and how government and industry respond.
talks.summary:
This RSA Conference 2018 session is a tabletop crisis exercise built around a simulated scenario in which a hostile state strikes critical infrastructure in the United States, with fatalities reported in Los Angeles. The exercise is meant to show where the national response is strong and where it has gaps, and it is framed around how officials would handle a large-scale digital attack.

Several lessons come out of the discussion. Participants argue that a serious cyber event stops being only a cyber problem once it crosses a certain threshold, and then it fits into the same emergency pathways the government already uses for other catastrophic risks, such as nuclear incidents. Attribution is treated as central to threat response, and leaders cannot wait for perfect evidence before acting. Officials also described the difficulty of deciding when and how much to tell the public, weighing the risk of unnecessary fear against giving people the information they need to make risk-based decisions.

Private companies sit at the center of the picture. Because the adversary has shown a willingness to hit non-governmental targets, businesses need to be engaged early and prepared, and every step of the response should try to limit the impact on them. Much of the work falls to state and local authorities and the private sector rather than the federal government, and industry is seen as a source of solutions as well as a potential victim. The practical takeaway is to plan coordination across levels of government and with companies before an incident occurs.

talks.title: Keeping the Cloud Secure: A New Approach to Enterprise Security | Jennifer Lin | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Argues that enterprise data can move to the cloud securely with default encryption and tighter controls on access.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how organizations can move their most sensitive data into the cloud without giving up the controls they rely on. The speaker notes that many customers have spent years manually de-identifying data before they were willing to store it off-premises, and that concerns about zero-day threats shape policy discussions. Security is presented as a provider-side baseline rather than a project each customer must build alone.

Several platform practices are described as examples. Data is encrypted both at rest and in motion, and web traffic has moved from plain HTTP to HTTPS, so every browser session runs over TLS. The speaker says this same baseline is being offered to cloud customers, so enterprise administrators can set their own policies while users keep real-time sharing and browser-based access. Once a service has confirmed that a user is allowed to reach a dataset, the platform can also work to stop that data from being exfiltrated.

The final point is that data gravity changes the problem. After data is in the cloud, the question becomes how people access it, so a tighter security posture can be applied to individual transactions, such as a SQL query, instead of giving every request the same response. The speaker argues that the stored data is also more secure as a result, and that users no longer have to manage infrastructure or set up VPN clients. The takeaway is that cloud adoption supports innovation and agility for both developers and consumers.

talks.title: Live Simulation: A Medical Device Hack and Patient Codes | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: A live clinical drill shows how a compromised infusion pump can trigger a patient emergency and shake clinician trust in connected care.
talks.summary:
The segment opens with concern that connected healthcare technology is outpacing the ability to secure it, citing an estimate that most U.S. hospitals employ no dedicated cybersecurity staff. Viewers are told the exercise rests on laboratory work where researchers showed vulnerabilities in medical gear, and that a physician volunteer will run a case without knowing the cyber angle in advance.

The scenario follows a simulated patient receiving continuous IV medication for atrial fibrillation. During treatment the infusion pump suddenly delivers the full bag at once; the patient becomes hypotensive and bradycardic and undergoes a code. Organizers explain that the pump’s firmware was reversed and could be abused to force a rapid bolus—the same failure mode just witnessed.

The closing asks clinicians to weigh how much they depend on bedside devices when compromise could harm patients, not only privacy. Practical next steps include reading a taskforce report, sharing an ABC Nightline piece, joining related volunteer efforts, and spreading tabletop or summit-style simulations across states.

talks.title: Sneak Peek: Hacking Exposed - Melting Down Memory | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Surveys live InstallUtil abuse tied to Cloud Hopper-style intrusions and outlines hunting signals when application whitelisting is bypassed.
talks.summary:
The segment ties recent Chinese-linked intrusion activity to command patterns seen in the Cloud Hopper reporting against technology firms. Attackers leaned on signed Microsoft ecosystem utilities to sit deep in compromised infrastructure, including InstallUtil-driven execution that can slip past strict allow-list programs when the underlying binary is trusted.

A concrete pattern mirrors an earlier demonstration: adversaries compile payloads on their side and drop a file whose name is largely cosmetic—what matters is that InstallUtil will run the embedded logic even under full whitelisting. The speaker walks through operational countermeasures, stressing that InstallUtil is uncommon on typical user endpoints and should raise suspicion when it appears outside developer contexts.

Detection guidance centers on fragile but useful hunting leads, such as InstallUtil invocations with lock-the-console style flags that reduce logging visibility. The closing argument warns against treating whitelisting as a silver bullet: misconfigured exception directories and abuse of legitimate utilities remain practical bypass paths, so hunts should combine command-line telemetry, utility prevalence, and hash-aware coverage rather than policy complacency.

talks.title: The Fight Against Social Media Weaponization | James Foster & Kenneth Geers | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Shows how social media enables deception and information operations, and what organizations can do to protect themselves.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that social media has become a main channel for communication, now bigger than email and text messaging combined, and that people carry it everywhere on their phones. The speakers describe how platforms are drawing new digital borders in place of geographic ones, with communities and nations increasingly formed around particular platforms. They tie this to a growing tension between a person's online identity and their offline self.

Looking ahead, the speakers expect AI to make bots and social engineering look more convincing over time. They point out that social media suits false flagging, deception and information operations, and that governments already rely on it as a new norm. Their prediction is that within ten years, people will see different platforms and real-world leaders being mistaken for one another. They also note that rules already cover cloud, web, mobile apps and email, but social media has not caught up.

For organizations, the practical advice starts with basics: write a policy, enable two-factor authentication, audit access and count the administrators on each account, and establish whether accounts are personal or corporate. Staff should be trained, and standards should be communicated clearly and often. Finally, social media data should be fed into the security operations center alongside other sources, since these accounts are gateways into the organization.

talks.title: Cybersecurity is Failing at Two Things: Patching & Authentication | Bruce Schneier | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Explains why IoT patching and device authentication are failing as connected cars, cities and appliances multiply.
talks.summary:
Schneier opens by describing a world where nearly everything is a computer, from cars and medical devices to drones, thermostats, power plants, weapon systems and whole smart cities. He contrasts ordinary software failures, which cost data, with embedded failures, which can cost lives, and argues that once physical consequences are involved, security has to be judged differently.

The first area he says is failing is patching. Phones and laptops stay reasonably secure because large vendor teams build them carefully and ship fixes quickly. Cheap embedded products such as DVRs and home routers are built on thin margins, often offshore by third parties, and have no dedicated security staff. For those devices, replacing the hardware is effectively the only update path. He notes that appliances can stay in homes for a decade or more, and a refrigerator for 25 years, and says the industry has no clear method for maintaining systems that old.

The second is authentication. Today a person pairs a device with their phone once, such as linking a car over Bluetooth, but the number of things that need to trust each other is about to grow into the hundreds or thousands, and nobody can be present for every pairing. Hubs and phones acting as pass-through controllers may work in a home, he says, but he doubts they will scale to smart cities or large organisations. He closes by tying these problems to his forthcoming book on autonomy, automation and physical agency.

talks.title: GDPR’s Information Security Requirements - What Exactly is ‘Appropriate’?
talks.teaser: Unpacks what GDPR Article 32's 'appropriate' security means in practice, and how regulators judge it after a breach.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the security duty in Article 32 of the GDPR, which asks organisations to apply suitable technical and organisational safeguards to personal data. John Elliott opens with a few legal examples to show that statutes rarely give clear-cut answers, including a case where a man who killed his mother tried to inherit her estate. He then goes through the factors the article names: the state of the art, the cost of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the risk to people's rights and freedoms.

To judge risk, he proposes combining the harm to each individual, how likely that harm is, and how much data is held into a population-level risk for a system, borrowing ideas from public health. He suggests setting a baseline security hygiene level for the whole organisation, with stricter controls for systems holding sensitive data. Responsibility splits in two: the organisation decides beforehand, and the regulator judges afterwards. In one breach case, a large, well-resourced company ran years-old operating system and web software, used the same root password across systems, and kept encryption keys in plaintext on the same file system as the encrypted data. The regulator rejected its submission, and the bar was framed as depending on the organisation's size.

He recommends aligning with recognised standards and outcome-based guidance, since regulators will measure against them, and notes that what counts as appropriate changes over time. The closing questions asked how the company had passed a payment card audit despite these gaps.

talks.title: Data Integrity: The Elephant Threat in the Room
talks.teaser: Privacy, legal and security experts discuss what data integrity means, why it is hard to detect, and how to govern it.
talks.summary:
This RSA panel looks at data integrity, the question of whether information stays accurate, correct and trustworthy, and how it differs from confidentiality and availability. The panelists, coming from privacy, legal, regulatory and security backgrounds, argue that the word is often confused with personal honesty. They walk through examples ranging from a bank teller skimming small amounts from customer deposits over many years, to children being issued social security numbers that had already been compromised. A recurring point is that detecting integrity loss is hard without a trusted source of truth to check against.

The lawyers describe real cases where data integrity failures led to regulatory settlements and class action lawsuits. They advise that controls should be designed around the expected outcome of each data process and documented in a business plan, rather than bought as compliance checkboxes. Governance was another major thread: panelists favored a clear owner for data, such as a chief data officer, and executive buy-in from finance leaders who must fund the work. They also noted that models producing data products like credit scores complicate verification, and that GDPR obligations can lay groundwork for an integrity program.

In closing, each panelist gave one takeaway. These included deciding what the organization can afford to lose, combining proactive design with the ability to recover after an integrity attack, reusing existing tools to measure and document data, and reviewing NIST guidance on integrity resources.

talks.teaser: Walks through common Ethereum smart contract flaws, from reentrancy and delegate calls to integer overflow, with code examples.
talks.summary:
Abraham Kang, a senior director of software at Samsung, gives an overview of security pitfalls in blockchain smart contracts, using Ethereum as the main example. He divides the problem into three areas: the platforms the contracts run on, the web applications that build transactions for the chain, and the contract code itself. Contract objects are replicated across miners, and any caller can invoke public methods in any order, which changes how developers need to reason about them.

Much of the talk walks through contract-level mistakes using code examples. Methods are public by default when no access specifier is given, and a delegate call runs in the caller's context, so a called library can drain the caller's balance. Using tx.origin for authentication can be spoofed through an intermediate contract. Updating balances after an external send enables reentrancy, as in the DAO case. Other cases include miner control over block timestamps, transaction ordering that lets a miner raise a price before a buy, a fallback function that blocks an auction refund, and an integer underflow in a burn function tied to the Monero Gold token.

The session closes with a review exercise in which the audience finds the flaws in a sample contract: missing access specifiers, a misnamed constructor, state updated after a send, and an underflow. The practical takeaways are to update balances before external calls, to check exactly what any called contract does, and to verify the visibility and types of every method.

talks.title: Network Monitoring Is Going Away...Now What? TLS, QUIC and Beyond
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how TLS 1.3 and newer encrypted transports limit network monitoring, and what enterprises can do instead.
talks.summary:
A panel of four security experts examined how stronger session encryption is reducing what network monitoring can see. Speakers traced the drivers: privacy, human rights and pervasive surveillance on the internet, plus compliance, intellectual property and customer data protection inside enterprises. TLS 1.3 removes static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman key exchange, so network appliances can no longer decrypt traffic passively, and it hides more of the handshake. Zero round-trip resumption was flagged as a replay risk that loses forward secrecy, so one round trip suits sensitive applications better.

QUIC runs over UDP with TLS 1.3 built in, and some institutions block it. TCP crypt encrypts TCP while leaving headers readable, using opportunistic security without authentication, and was expected to standardize within about a year. Other options included IPsec with group keying and multi-party protocols under an IETF effort. For operations, ACME was recommended to prevent certificate-expiry outages, and endpoint posture work was noted. Panelists disagreed on the short term: enterprises need visibility now, while others argued TLS 1.2 remains usable and that network-based decryption creates a target.

NIST said its guidance still favors TLS 1.3 and forward secrecy, and an IETF server-to-server opt-in idea was not adopted. The takeaways were to check whether endpoint and application logs are adequate, press vendors for the telemetry you need, deploy TLS 1.3 on internet sessions, and consider terminating sessions at the edge so internal management stays workable.

talks.title: Identity-Based Security and Privacy for the Internet of Things
talks.teaser: Examines how identity and access management can secure IoT devices, from legacy hardware to phone-based authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how identity and access management must be extended for Internet of Things devices, both legacy and new, and how users' phones could make authentication smoother. The speaker proposes a 15-layer model and argues for one consistent identity layer across verticals, protocols and platforms.

Incident case studies anchor the argument. Attackers fed fake readings into a platform that accepted data from any device and never checked users, while a 2016 thermostat firmware bug left holiday homes at risk of burst pipes because no one controlled update authorisation. A car owner relying on cloud-linked access was locked out in the desert. Default credentials and open ports fed botnets. A Zigbee lighting protocol shared one signing key, so leaked firmware could spread between bulbs. An early smart speaker's open debug port allowed firmware replacement, a TPM key-generation flaw made private keys guessable, and a clock-scaling attack extracted keys from a secure processor.

The speaker argues that an IoT platform is largely an identity and access management system, with gateways checking device messages, registries holding device and user attributes, and application gateways serving data to apps. Lifecycle questions matter too: update authorisation chains, sessions between devices and cloud services, and when devices stop receiving updates or change owners. Proposed remedies include trusted execution environments where secure elements are too costly, FIDO metadata and Android key attestation to prove genuine hardware, and directories such as LDAP. Lightweight session checks are preferred over heavy public-key use to save battery.

talks.title: The Long Road to Identity on the Blockchain
talks.teaser: Traces how Bitcoin's ledger ideas were adapted for identity, questioning where consensus and attributes truly fit.
talks.summary:
Steve Wilson opens by tracing Bitcoin back to its origins as a political response to the financial crisis. He argues its real technical contribution was agreement on the order of transactions, which removes the need for an umpire to stop double spending. Features such as open participation, pseudonymity and full transparency, he suggests, do not carry over easily to other settings, and the idea of trustlessness needs careful reading.

He then follows later designs that add permissions, configurable consensus and conventional security controls, naming projects such as R3, Hashgraph and the Hyperledger family, along with managed cloud services. For identity, he argues that attributes matter more than identity itself, and he examines one case, a Utah company's Plenum algorithm, which is built around verified claims and a governance model. He also questions many refugee identity projects, saying they solve a problem that may not exist. Consensus, he stresses, should be about something specific.

For anyone evaluating vendor claims, he recommends repeatedly asking what problem is being solved and what exactly is being agreed, checking key management first, and bringing legal and process owners into proofs of concept early. He notes that reading from a ledger is generally faster than writing, but leaves performance questions open.

talks.title: Inside Cloudbleed
talks.teaser: Traces Cloudflare's memory-leak bug from the HTML parser overrun to crisis response and lessons learned.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts Cloudbleed, a bug in Cloudflare's edge network that leaked fragments of server memory into HTTP responses. John Graham-Cumming, the company's CTO, explains how the flaw sat in an HTML parser used by three features: email obfuscation, HTTPS rewriting and server-side excludes. When a page ended with a broken attribute, the parser ran past the end of its buffer and emitted adjacent memory, which could contain cookies, tokens and internal keys. The leak was stopped in under an hour by switching off features with feature flags, while one older feature without a flag needed an emergency deployment.

The middle of the talk covers the cause and the aftermath. The parser was generated from a tool and had run for about six years without problems until a migration to a new parser changed how the final buffer was flagged, exposing the overrun. Cached copies of leaked pages in search engines had to be chased down across many providers. Disclosure came six days after the report, and the company phoned affected customers for about two weeks. Later log analysis showed the leak had run for months, and core dump counts had jumped the day the new software shipped without anyone acting on it.

The final part looks at the wider fallout. Crashes that seemed impossible were traced to a microcode erratum on one Intel processor generation, and a microcode update removed them. The speaker's takeaways are to keep a timed incident record, put a kill switch behind every feature, treat warnings and crashes as defects, measure crash rates, and move away from C where possible. He argues that transparency with customers and researchers preserved trust.

talks.title: Work: An Essential Part of the American Dream | Margot Lee Shetterly | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Explores how pioneering women in computing offer a playbook for bias, persistence, and lasting change in STEM.
talks.summary:
The speaker asks why the story of women who advanced early computing resonated so strongly, and ties that question to how Americans define themselves through work. She contrasts her upbringing among scientists with a broader history in which computing was treated as women’s work: women were hired as sub-professionals, ranked above clerical staff but below male engineers, and often paid less even when doing comparable technical jobs.

Those experiences are framed as practical guidance rather than fairy-tale inspiration—challenging bias, handling difficult colleagues, refusing accept no, and holding expectations high. The women she describes were exceptional yet ordinary contributors whose aim was to fit in through talent, not to stand out because of difference, illustrating group progress over time instead of lone “first and only” narratives.

She closes by noting how today’s larger pool of women in technical fields builds on that groundwork, and argues that this history can support enduring structural change in computing, engineering, and science despite lingering obscurity around some workplaces.

talks.title: What Online Games Can Teach Us about The Future | Jane McGonigal | RSAC 2018
talks.teaser: Links immersive future simulations to gaming labor trends and a provocative wage-play forecast for adapting to automation.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces first-person futures, immersive exercises that place people inside possible tomorrows—from everyday surveillance gadgets to stranger economic shifts—so they feel what change might mean rather than treating forecasts as abstract headlines. She ties that mindset to neuroscience: vividly imagining a future engages brain regions linked to personal relevance and environmental scanning, which can counter the habit of assuming the next decade will resemble the present and help people spot weak signals sooner.

She cites longitudinal organizational research suggesting companies that practice structured future immersion showed stronger profitability and growth years later, then walks through labor-market findings on young men spending less time in paid work while devoting large shares of new leisure to video games, with reported gains in mood, health, and social connection. That pattern is framed against automation pressure on manual jobs and the enduring human appeal of play, including esports and the limits of watching machines outperform people.

The close sketches wage play: free-to-play economies that subsidize most players to keep elite spenders engaged, using a lottery-style minimum-wage thought experiment around a favorite game. Listeners are invited to carry that first-person lens forward and watch for economic and cultural signals that paid play could scale.

talks.title: Virtual Session The Five Most Dangerous New Attacks: The Rest of the Story
talks.teaser: Panelists outline emerging attack trends, from exposed cloud data and cryptojacking to hardware flaws and safety system malware.
talks.summary:
This follow-up session extends a keynote on the year's most dangerous new attacks, with three panelists answering audience questions. Ed opens with cloud-hosted development assets, where private code marked public, secrets committed to repositories, and misconfigured Amazon S3 buckets have exposed large volumes of records. Recommended defenses include a data asset inventory with a dedicated data curator and pre-commit scanners that block keys and passwords. He also warns that stolen data can be deanonymized by correlating it with other sources, citing the Netflix Prize and IMDB ratings.

Johannes Ulrich describes attackers shifting from selling stolen data to hijacking server CPUs for cryptocurrency mining. One campaign hit about a thousand PeopleSoft servers and earned roughly $150,000. Warning signs include high CPU load, traffic to mining pools and heat, but attackers now cap CPU use and proxy pool connections to avoid detection. He also points to hardware flaws such as Rowhammer, Spectre and Meltdown, and advises isolating critical workloads on dedicated hardware and encrypting data at rest.

James Lyne examines TRISIS, malware built to disable a safety instrumented system, the last line of defense against physical damage in industrial plants. He argues that industrial control security trails mainstream computing by about 15 years, and warns that compromised sensors could feed false data to central systems. The panel closes with advice to share information, mentor young people in security, and focus defenses on the highest-risk attacks.

talks.title: SDN and Security: A Marriage Made in Heaven. Or Not.
talks.teaser: Explains SDN models and weighs whether centralized controllers make networks more or less secure, with quarantine examples.
talks.summary:
Chuck Black opens by saying his goal is to give listeners enough background to judge software-defined networking claims themselves. He traces how networking moved from distributed devices toward separating the control plane from forwarding, and how early OpenFlow work gave way to vendor API, overlay and automation approaches. He sorts these models along a spectrum, from reactive OpenFlow, where unknown packets go to the controller, to proactive flows, API-based control and data center overlays.

The security part asks whether SDN is secure and whether it can make a network safer. Reactive OpenFlow carries more risk because packets sent to the controller can be abused for denial of service, such as floods of new MAC addresses. Applications on a controller must be certified and authenticated before they run, and a compromised one could take the controller down. Centralizing policy keeps edge devices simple and easier to protect, while redundant controllers add resilience. For mitigation, suspicious traffic is sent to an analysis system, then the user's access to sensitive data is closed, the user is moved to a quarantine network, or the user is blocked.

Closing advice: build redundant controllers and links, secure communication between devices and controllers, and protect the controller itself. In Q&A, certificates on both client and server, plus trust services that verify devices and users, were offered as the main safeguards.

talks.title: WiFi Security: The Details Matter
talks.teaser: Walks through 802.11 authentication, encryption and the four-way handshake, and explains how the KRACK weakness arose.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how security works in 802.11 wireless LANs and why the KRACK weakness was possible. It argues that many Wi-Fi attacks happen at public hotspots rather than inside the enterprise, and that user policies alone rarely keep staff off them. Authentication and encryption at layer two are presented as the core focus, with monitoring treated as an add-on.

Authentication is covered first: open system authentication as a null step, pre-shared keys where a passphrase feeds an algorithm, and 802.1X with EAP, which keeps a port closed until keying material exists. Encryption moves from WEP's RC4 design through TKIP as a transitional fix to CCMP with AES in WPA2. The four-way handshake is examined message by message, showing that a wrong passphrase stalls at message three. The pairwise transient key's parts are then outlined, with the TK protecting unicast traffic.

KRACK is described as a key reinstallation attack made possible by retransmitted message three, carried out with an alternate-channel man-in-the-middle setup. The presenter argues the flaw dated back to the 2004 ratification and that time favors attackers. Closing advice: verify patches and configuration on existing gear, buy only equipment with a WPA2 certification issued after the November 2017 update, add dedicated Wi-Fi monitoring, and consider how client devices are protected at hotspots.

talks.teaser: Tours free tools and built-in Windows utilities for helping family and colleagues with everyday security and IT problems.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar situation: many attendees are the unofficial tech support for relatives. The presenter shares a personal set of free tools and techniques kept on a thumb drive, gathered over many years. Tools are treated as neutral, and attendees are urged to test them in a virtual machine or lab first.

Early sections cover public web research: Google's cached pages and advanced search, and the Wayback Machine, which is used to view an archived university site from 2002 that the presenter had permission to examine. Windows material includes Sysinternals Autoruns and Process Explorer for disabling startup entries and stubborn processes, a God Mode folder that collects control panel tasks, and PowerShell. Privacy and browsing tools include NoScript and a cookie editor, while OS Forensics, 7-Zip with AES-256 encryption, and Nmap and a phone network scanner cover forensics, file protection and home network checks. For small organisations, PDQ Inventory, Ansible and Ninite address inventory and patching.

The question-and-answer period addressed older relatives who write passwords in a notebook, kept by trusted family so accounts can be reached in an emergency. The closing answer was that a simple, practical method may beat a complicated one. The presenter urged attendees to try a few tools, share what they find and pass along other tools worth adding.
