The speakers open with Murphy’s Law not as fatalism but as a prompt to ask what could go wrong before harm happens. They connect that mindset to medical product security at GE Healthcare, where teams run similar questions daily inside a security development lifecycle, alongside safety practices such as MRI exclusion zones.

They walk through a threat modeling lifecycle: vision (assets, environments, dependencies), building a data flow diagram with processes, external entities, flows, and trust boundaries, then identifying threats and turning mitigations into engineering work items early in design and again after design drift. They contrast a generic web stack with hypothetical imaging and anesthesia architectures, noting repeating medical building blocks, protocols like DICOM and HL7, and industry-specific concerns beyond STRIDE, including system abuse and patient safety.

The demo centers on Microsoft’s free Threat Modeling Tool: extending default stencils and threat rules for medical components yields far more generated considerations than a software-only template. They describe a pending GitHub pull request, urge collaborative sessions with architects and developers, and close with practical next steps to download the tool, try the template, refine it, and build industry-specific variants.

talks.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly of the Ultrasonic Communications Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Near-ultrasonic beacons enable cross-device tracking; the session maps ecosystem risks, live attacks, and standards-based mitigations.
talks.summary:
Researchers from University College London and UC Santa Barbara survey near-ultrasonic communication as a growing alternative to familiar wireless links. Interest intensified after cross-device tracking products encoded advertisement beacons in television audio while companion apps listened continuously on phones, prompting regulatory attention and a notable vendor's retreat from the United States market. The presenters outline legitimate uses—from stadium light shows and IoT pairing to Google's AudioBytes and Nearby frameworks—while stressing that proprietary beacon formats and rush-to-market apps often treat security as an afterthought.

Attack models stay practical: attackers inject or replay inaudible beacons with ordinary smartphones, as shown when retail reward apps were gamed by sharing recorded tones online. A staged Tor scenario demonstrates how a hidden service page can leak identity and location when a nearby phone forwards decoded beacons to a provider backend, and how administrative data requests can expose subscribers. Additional techniques corrupt advertising profiles or merge a victim's device fingerprint with an attacker's hardware through co-location and replay.

A structured review highlights proximity assumptions that fail, undocumented cryptography, and Android's broad microphone access. Short-term defenses include frequency-split permissions and browser extensions that block emissions above 18 kilohertz, though the speakers argue for industry standardization, careful threat modeling, and skepticism about bespoke stacks—especially where air-gapped environments might still leak data over sound.

talks.title: How Automated Vulnerability Analysis Discovered Hundreds of Android 0-days
talks.teaser: Shows how program analysis and fuzzing uncovered hundreds of Android kernel driver and bootloader vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Giovanni Vigna, a professor at UC Santa Barbara, presented work from his lab on automated and semi-automated vulnerability analysis of Android phones. He described Android as effectively a Linux system whose drivers are added for many different chipsets and vendors, and said driver code is often written under time pressure by developers who are not security specialists. Citing the view that most bugs sit in drivers rather than the core kernel, the team focused on drivers and on bootloaders.

For drivers, the group built Dr. Checker, which combines pointer and taint analysis to follow untrusted user input through driver code and flag unsanitized uses. Across about 3.1 million lines from several chipset vendors, it produced roughly 5,000 warnings, around 3,000 of which were confirmed, leading to 158 bugs and a reported precision of 78 percent. A second tool, DIFUZE, extracted the interface structures behind ioctl calls and fuzzed them with correctly formatted but unusual values, uncovering 36 zero-days that included arbitrary read and write primitives.

For bootloaders, the threat model assumed an attacker with root who tries to persist below the operating system by modifying data the boot chain reads from writable storage. A bootloader analyzer combining symbolic execution and dynamic analysis tracked that data flow and reported 36 alerts, seven of which were real bugs, one already known and rediscovered automatically. The talk closed by urging vendors to invest in driver security; the tools are open source and findings went through responsible disclosure.

talks.title: Value-At-Risk: Decision-Making in Cybersecurity Investments
talks.teaser: Presents a Value-at-Risk model that turns cyber threats into financial loss figures to guide where and how much to invest.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with the 1987 stock market crash, when financial firms struggled to explain their losses, and compares that to organisations unable to explain breaches. The core problems are limited budgets, endless threats and difficulty showing executives what cyber spending is worth. A cited survey found 32% of respondents challenged to defend their investments.

Value-at-Risk expresses cyber risk as potential financial loss over a set period. Practitioners first identify threats, vulnerabilities and assets, including intangible ones such as customer data and brand value. The figure multiplies expected loss, probability and frequency. In a worked example of 500,000 customer records exposed through weak privileged access control, an expected loss of $116.3 million, a 10% probability and one event every three years gave a value at risk of about $0.6 million. Cutting probability to 3% and frequency to 0.2 with a $3 million investment shows the benefit. Two further scenarios, insider theft and exploitation of a known vulnerability, were compared to rank priorities. Gordon-Loeb research suggests spending no more than a third of value at risk.

Probability can come from industry breach data, Monte Carlo simulation, Delphi techniques or staff judgement. Lessons include keeping the model simple, testing assumptions, tailoring it to your environment, and asking vendors for the value at risk before buying. Barriers are missing data, limited analysis resources and gaining buy-in.

talks.title: Fighting Malware with Graph Analytics: An End-to-End Case Study
talks.teaser: Shows how a word-graph view exposes dictionary-based malware domains, and how ego-nets help flag network anomalies.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that when relationships matter more than individual attributes, a graph is the better representation. Its main case study is domain generation algorithms (DGAs), which let malware find a command-and-control server by querying generated domains. Character-based classifiers handle random-looking names, but dictionary-based DGAs that combine ordinary words defeat them.

The speaker builds a graph where each word pulled from a domain is a node, and words sharing a domain are linked. Legitimate domains yield an organic structure with popular and rare hubs, while dictionary DGA words form a consistent, machine-made pattern. Components are described by structural features such as average and maximum node degree, then labelled by a classifier. Malicious components reveal the malware's word dictionary, which can flag future domains. In an experiment with under 1% DGA domains (about 120k benign against 1,000 DGA), models trained on two dictionaries were tested on a third across three rounds. There were zero false positives, all malicious words were caught in two rounds and 90% in one, and a random forest baseline did worse.

The second part covers simple anomaly detection with ego-nets, the neighbourhood around a node. Star-shaped ego-nets can indicate robotic spam accounts, near-cliques can flag groups of suspiciously similar tax forms, and a dominant edge can point to stolen or cloned credit cards. Community detection is recommended for exploring unlabelled data, using NetworkX and a free visualization tool. The takeaway is to model data so its structure becomes visible, and to combine graph methods with traditional ones for better accuracy and fewer false positives.

talks.title: Google and Microsoft Debut: Replacing Passwords with FIDO2 Authentication
talks.teaser: Demonstrates passwordless FIDO2 sign-in on Android, Windows and security keys, showing how public key login resists phishing.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the scale of the password problem: a 2016 study tied 81% of breaches to passwords and found one in 14 phishing attacks succeeded. The presenter argues the replacement must reduce user effort rather than add steps, so one-time codes are treated as replayable bearer tokens. FIDO credentials instead use public key cryptography, where a private key stays on the device and is released only after a local check such as a PIN, fingerprint, face scan or key touch. The server stores the public key and verifies a signed, per-site challenge.

The live demonstrations ran on pre-production builds. A purchase on Android in Chrome was approved with a fingerprint through the web authentication API, and a checkout on Windows 10 in Edge used face recognition. A bank login then used a USB security key as a second factor across Edge, Firefox and a Chromebook, with the same key registered to one account. Afterward, the speakers explained that domain-bound keys stop a fake site from reusing a signature, and that revocation happens on the server.

The main takeaway for relying parties is to look for certified server products, read the architecture overview on the alliance site, and ask vendors when they will add support. The Q&A also covered limits: keys cannot be copied between devices, and support for on-premises Active Directory was still on a roadmap.

talks.title: Hacking Closed Networks
talks.teaser: A veteran tester shows why air-gapped networks often are not, with real paths into power grids, ICS, and naval systems.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with naval accident coverage where experts dismiss cyber risk because warships use closed networks. The speaker contends that ignorance and the expense of isolation do not stop motivated attackers, and that assets valuable enough to segregate attract equal attacker investment.

Most “closed” environments erode through convenience bridges, vendor links, rogue connections, unpatched gear, and field diagnostics. The talk walks through CERT warnings on Russian ICS watering holes, the creep from dual workstations to full internet access, power-capacity markets tied to production, the Target vendor path, WannaCry on isolated MRI systems, adaptive persistent threat teams (breach, staging, exfiltration), a 2008 power-company phishing exercise, grid overlap reporting, the Maroochy sewage incident, Stuxnet-style supply-chain delivery, contractor breaches, and short penetration-test stories where a cellular bridge stayed live for months.

The close stresses that protection alone fails without detection, that perfect security claims are hollow, and that operators should verify whether segregated networks are truly isolated and run architecture assessments over months. A closing disclaimer separates documented real incidents from unsponsored naval-vessel hypothetics.

talks.title: Lost in the Ether: How Ethereum Hacks Are Shaping the Blockchain Future
talks.teaser: Walks through major Ethereum smart contract heists, from the DAO to Parity wallets, and the lessons for developers.
talks.summary:
Marc Laliberte of WatchGuard Technologies opens with a primer on cryptocurrency and Ethereum. He contrasts Bitcoin's input and output model with Ethereum's account state, and explains the Ethereum Virtual Machine, Solidity contracts and gas fees. A sample token contract and the CryptoKitties application show how contract code and data live on the chain, and why functions that default to public matter.

The core of the talk walks through named incidents. The DAO investment fund was drained through a reentrancy flaw in its withdrawal logic, with roughly 3.6 million ether taken, and the community responded with a hard fork. Several initial coin offerings were hit by account and website compromises: a hijacked Twitter account pointed Insurex buyers to an attacker's wallet, an altered website address diverted CoinDash funds, and reused breach credentials exposed Enigma's systems. The Parity multisig wallet failed when an initialization function lacked an access specifier, letting attackers take ownership, and a later library self-destruct locked funds. The talk also covers bug bounty programs, phishing databases, fork debates and Verge's 51 percent attack through timestamp spoofing.

For developers, the main takeaways are to be careful with external calls and to set visibility explicitly on every function. For analysts, bug bounty programs offer paid research, and contract code should be tested on a test network before anything is deployed. The closing Q&A touched on proof of stake versus proof of work and the concentration of mining power in ASIC hardware.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show: Dr. Dawn Song
talks.teaser: Shows how crafted perturbations and modified signs can trick vehicle vision and face models while staying nearly invisible to people.
talks.summary:
The segment opens by framing adversarial machine learning as studying what happens when attackers tamper with training data or inputs to a classifier. The guest describes standard computer vision as expecting natural images, then explains that an adversary can add tiny perturbations humans barely notice yet steer the model toward arbitrary wrong labels. Hugh Thompson ties that risk to production uses such as autonomous vehicles and platforms that classify or tag large volumes of images.

A side-by-side driving demo contrasts an ordinary stop sign with a physically altered one. On the unmodified side the detector keeps treating the sign as a stop instruction; on the adversarial side it misreads the sign and the overlay shows continued travel at highway speed. The researcher outlines an optimization-based method that picks perturbations strong enough for real-world objects and robust as distance and viewing angle change, so misclassification persists from far away through close approach.

The conversation shifts to related work on deceiving facial recognition with eyeglass frames, including a recreated demonstration where specialty glasses flip identity scores between two people with high reported confidence. The guest agrees that despite deep learning’s progress, many questions about why models behave as they do remain open, and that adversarial study clarifies limits and informs defense. The exchange closes without a hands-on lab, emphasizing consequence for safety-critical perception pipelines.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show: Dr. Kate Darling
talks.teaser: Explores how people form emotional bonds with lifelike robots and why design and empathy matter as AI spreads.
talks.summary:
Dr. Kate Darling, a researcher at the MIT Media Lab, joins a conversation about the emotional attachments people form with robots and AI. She starts with Pleo, a small toy dinosaur robot whose lifelike design makes it easy to treat as alive, and notes that people are primed by science fiction and biology to attribute agency and intent to moving physical things. The discussion also covers a child who speaks lovingly to a voice assistant, and people who name Roomba vacuums and feel bad when they get stuck.

Darling argues that design shapes how much people engage, and that expectations matter. A chatbot that passed a Turing test did so by posing as a 13-year-old boy from Ukraine, which lowered what judges expected of its English and understanding. She pushes back on building AI to imitate humans, suggesting instead the history of domesticated animals as a model: systems that complement human skills and act as partners rather than replacements.

Darling closes with a workshop in which participants were asked to mistreat the dinosaur robots, which upset many of them. Follow-up experiments found a link between people's natural empathy and their willingness to harm a robot, even knowing it is a machine. Her takeaway is that the way people treat these systems, even when they feel nothing, could shape future choices and ethical questions as the technology spreads.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show: Dr. Sebastian Thrun
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for The Hugh Thompson Show: Dr. Sebastian Thrun.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this session of *The Hugh Thompson Show* at RSA Conference, host Hugh Thompson interviews Dr. Sebastian Thrun, founder and president of Udacity, CEO of Kittyhawk, and founder of Google X. Rather than focusing solely on worst-case failure modes or dystopian 'Skynet' narratives common among security professionals, the discussion examines the transformative, optimistic potential of artificial intelligence (AI). The conversation highlights AI as a force amplifier for human intellect, the societal shifts accompanying automation, the future of work, and the irreplaceable nature of human soft skills like empathy and creativity.

### Key Topics
- **Democratizing Education:** Thrun outlines Udacity's mission to double global GDP by democratizing access to education worldwide, partnering with tech leaders like Google and Facebook. Thompson announces a $50,000 scholarship donation from RSA Conference toward Udacity's newly launched cybersecurity Nanodegree.
- **Historical Parallels and Automation:** Drawing a comparison to the Industrial Revolution and the steam engine—which shifted farming from employing the vast majority of people to under two percent today—Thrun argues that modern repetitive office tasks (from data entry to document discovery) will be taken over by AI.
- **Human Augmentation and Brain Prosthetics:** Rather than replacing humanity, AI is positioned as a cognitive prosthetic that eliminates mundane labor and frees humans to focus on creative, high-value problem-solving.
- **Essential Future Skills:** As repetitive and analytical tasks automate, Thrun emphasizes that curiosity, a growth mindset, grit, teamwork, and social-emotional skills will become the most valuable attributes in the workforce.
- **The Role of Security Professionals:** Thompson concludes by noting that security professionals must understand technological failure modes preemptively so they can champion and safely guide the adoption of transformative technologies.

### Technical Details
- **Deep Learning in Healthcare:** Thrun references a Stanford study where deep learning was trained on 129,000 body images to detect skin cancer, achieving diagnostic accuracy on par with or better than top board-certified dermatologists.
- **High-Leverage Software Development:** As an example of modern technological leverage, Thrun cites WhatsApp scaling to over one billion users with a team of roughly 50 people before its acquisition by Facebook.

### Takeaways
- Automation should not be viewed as human obsolescence, but as relief from repetitive work, enabling reallocation of human effort toward empathetic and creative roles (e.g., teaching, nursing, and innovation).
- Mindsets characterized by humility, rapid iteration, admitting errors, and continuous learning are critical differentiators for entrepreneurs and technologists.
- Cybersecurity experts have a dual responsibility: to anticipate and mitigate the vulnerabilities of AI systems while actively facilitating their societal benefits.

talks.title: The Hugh Thompson Show: Artificial Intelligence
talks.teaser: Covers adversarial attacks on vision systems, emotional bonds with robots, and how AI may reshape work and skills.
talks.summary:
Host Hugh Thompson opens this closing RSAC session on artificial intelligence with a light segment, pitting himself against an anonymized smart speaker in a quiz, then frames the discussion around AI's emergent behaviors, its potential and its limits.

Dr. Don Song explains adversarial machine learning, where attackers tamper with training data or with the inputs a model classifies. He shows a video in which a physical stop sign, modified with a crafted perturbation, is still misread by a vision system as the car approaches it, and he describes earlier research in which printed eyeglass frames fooled a facial recognition engine into matching one person to another. Kate Darling then discusses how people attach feelings to robots, citing a toy dinosaur robot and a workshop where participants mistreated such robots, with reluctance to cause harm tracking people's natural empathy. She argues that designers should build AI to supplement human skills rather than imitate people.

Sebastian Thrun argues that past automation freed people from farming and then from repetitive office work, and that deep learning now matches specialists on tasks such as diagnosing skin cancer. He expects creativity, empathy, curiosity and teamwork to become more valuable as routine tasks are automated. Thompson closes by urging security professionals to understand how AI systems can fail and to help steer them toward good outcomes.

talks.title: Rives: Decoding Infosec Jargon
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Rives: Decoding Infosec Jargon.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At the RSA Conference, guest speaker Rives delivers a lighthearted, comedic monologue exploring his experience as an industry outsider trying to navigate and decipher cybersecurity jargon. Observing the unique culture, acronyms, and terminology used by attendees, Rives highlights how everyday civilian perspectives clash with specialized industry language.

### Key Topics
- **Industry Acronyms and Misinterpretations:** Rives discusses his confusion around terms like "SOC"—noting a speaker named Rohit who mentioned an RSA Academy in Singapore providing hands-on experience in a real SOC—which sounded literally like footwear to an outsider. He also riffs on the word "InfoSec," humorously guessing it might be one-sixtieth of an "info minute," a data transfer rate, or the awkward pause required when explaining a cybersecurity job to a civilian.
- **Humorous Civilian Re-definitions:** Several common technical terms are given comedic civilian translations. "Two-factor authentication" is redefined as checking a t-shirt visually and then sniffing it before deciding it is clean enough to wear. A "pseudo-random number" is likened to calling an ex-partner late at night and pretending the call was an accident. "Loadable kernel modules" are compared to microwavable popcorn, and "keylogger" is interpreted as the most critical lumberjack in a logging crew.
- **Industry Buzzwords and Concepts:** The speaker notes ubiquitous buzzwords such as "GDPR," which he repeatedly heard without knowing the formal definition, humorously noting people discuss it with frustration as if referring to an unpopular acquaintance named Kevin. He touches on looking up terms like "Smurf attack" (which led to humorous imagery involving Smurf characters), "hash value" (joking about drug measurements and college hobbies), "bad actor" and "threat actor" (associating them with film acting and movies like *Billy Madison*), and "honey monkey."

### Technical Details
Because this presentation is a comedic opening monologue rather than an engineering or threat-analysis session, it lacks formal technical architecture or deep technical detail. The transcript explicitly mentions specific security concepts and phrases—such as SOC, InfoSec, two-factor authentication, pseudo-random numbers, GDPR, loadable kernel modules, Smurf attacks, hash values, keyloggers, bad actors, threat actors, and honey monkeys—purely as subjects of observational humor and creative misinterpretation.

### Takeaways
The talk serves as an entertaining reminder of how insular cybersecurity vocabulary can sound to non-practitioners. Through observational humor, it illustrates the gap between specialized security terminology and civilian understanding, closing with Rives thanking the audience for the new vocabulary.

talks.title: Our Biggest Bet Yet
talks.teaser: Explains how IBM Security sees AI, automation and open threat intelligence sharing as force multipliers for defenders.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens on a sense of optimism about progress in security, pointing to stronger built-in encryption in operating systems and databases and to CIOs who now ask detailed questions about ransomware and malware. The speaker frames IBM's history of big bets, citing the IBM Q quantum computer, Watson Health's oncology work, and the decision to train Watson for Cybersecurity to reason like a security analyst.

The talk then proposes three force multipliers. The first is AI, which the speaker says can cut false positives in source code scanning by 98 percent and can learn over days and weeks which insiders or stolen credentials behave abnormally. The second is orchestration and automation, illustrated with an airline crew working from a written run book during an emergency. IBM built a lab in Boston where customers, including lawyers, HR and communications staff, rehearse breach responses, and the speaker stresses that leadership and clear commander's intent matter as much as the tooling.

The third is open collaboration. IBM opened decades of threat intelligence to partners and customers for free, donated a domain and related DNS research to Packet Clearing House for a clean DNS service, and opened its platform so outside developers could build apps, with more than 100,000 downloads from around 50 vendors. The takeaway for practitioners is to combine AI, rehearsed and automated response, and open sharing to multiply what a team can do with limited staff.

talks.title: Rives: Spoken Word History of RSA
talks.teaser: Charts a playful spoken-word history of the RSA Conference and the security debates it has hosted since 1991.
talks.summary:
This piece is a short, rhyming spoken-word retelling of the RSA Conference's history, framed as a two-minute tour starting in 1991. It opens with the founders behind the RSA name and describes the first gathering, which drew fewer than fifty people and felt more like a discussion than a formal event.

The narration then moves through the years, using each as a stage for a debate. In 1995 the Clipper Chip proposal and its government backdoor drew resistance, and the piece suggests the proposal was defeated, though not by one group alone. Later stops include 2011, when the hacktivist group Anonymous was debated as either a social movement or an anarchist plot; 2014, when Edward Snowden was cast as a traitor or not; and 2016, when Apple and the FBI faced off over access to encrypted devices.

The closing section ties these disputes to the present, referencing election-related cyber threats and Facebook's 2018 testimony on data collection. The piece ends on April 18, 2018, welcoming the audience to the conference's Wednesday sessions. Its takeaway is that the security debates raised at each year's event have grown more complicated over time.

talks.title: How Do I Get My Company to Ditch the Firewall
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of How Do I Get My Company to Ditch the Firewall.

talks.title: Attention Agents of Change: Are You Ready for Your Next Mission?
talks.teaser: A keynote frames rising cyber and AI risks, then urges automated analytics, human-machine teamwork, and bolder talent pipelines.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by comparing today’s fears—authoritarian control, criminal abuse of networks, and unchecked AI—to the cultural weight of Orwell’s 1984 and modern fiction such as Black Mirror, especially stories where helpful technology becomes a weapon through social media and design flaws. The speaker argues that engineers carry ethical duty for what they ship, and that global connectivity gave adversaries speed, reach, and anonymity beyond traditional crime.

Looking forward, trust and operational complexity—not only routing scale or transistor density—will define whether the Internet keeps growing safely. The proposed path pairs automation with human judgment: behavioral analytics and shared intelligence to counter evasive malware, retrospective and real-time insight, and predictive models meant to stop attacks before impact. Automation is treated as necessary because criminals already automate, while people still supply wisdom and intuition.

The closing mission calls for growing talent amid near-zero unemployment and millions of unfilled roles, citing ideas such as a cyber ROTC-style scholarship pipeline, expanded hands-on lab programs with universities and startups, and deliberate diversity so the field draws from the whole population. The talk ends where it began: machines may amplify control, but humans must break conformity and act as agents of change.

talks.title: Remarks by the Honorable Kirstjen Nielsen, Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security
talks.teaser: Sets out the Homeland Security view on systemic risk, collective defense and resilience, plus a Q&A.
talks.summary:
Kirstjen Nielsen, then Secretary of Homeland Security, opened her RSA keynote by arguing that digital, personal and physical security are merging, which makes cyber risk everyone's concern. She described the threat as worsening, citing the 2017 Equifax breach, a ransomware outbreak in more than 150 countries, and projected annual cybercrime costs of six trillion dollars by 2021.

She then previewed five areas needing new approaches. Systemic risk matters because shared dependencies such as GPS and payment systems can cascade into energy, water and health services. Collective defense, she said, depends on sharing threat information, citing an automated indicator sharing program and a financial-sector analysis center formed by banks in 2016. Federal help should be voluntary and aimed at market failures, such as cheap products built without security. Resilience means systems keep running and fail gracefully, as the Atlanta attacks showed. Deterrence means consequences for hostile actors.

In the Q&A, she said governments and companies need shared norms for cyber conflict, that offensive options were a matter for interagency talks, and that the government should consult firms before issuing alerts or sanctions. She closed by urging attendees to share threat data, build security in from the start, and recognize that individuals share responsibility for their own security.

talks.title: The Cryptographers’ Panel 2018
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Cryptographers’ Panel 2018.
talks.summary:
## Overview

This panel at RSA Conference 2018 featured cryptography legends Ron Rivest (MIT), Adi Shamir (Weizmann Institute), Whitfield Diffie, Paul Kocher, and Moxie Marlinspike, moderated by RSA CTO Zulfikar Ramzan. The discussion covered the state of cryptography, security challenges, and emerging threats facing the industry.

## Key Topics

**Elections and Democratic Security**
Rivest highlighted election security as a top concern, noting that the Department of Homeland Security designated elections as critical infrastructure. The panel emphasized that while two-thirds of voters now use paper ballots, cybersecurity vigilance on voting systems remains critical.

**Cybersecurity Research Rigor**
Shamir expressed concern about the lack of precision in cybersecurity research compared to cryptography. Cryptography has precise definitions and proofs; cybersecurity lacks formalization and theoretical grounding. The field needs to move from qualitative to quantitative analysis.

**Spectre and Meltdown**
Paul Kocher detailed the discovery of Spectre vulnerabilities. At a conference, colleague Mike Hamburg mentioned speculative execution flaws, giving Kocher "a bad feeling" that processors were silently making errors. Kocher independently discovered the exploit; simultaneously, Google researchers found the same vulnerability through a different angle (examining CPU cache contents). The discovery revealed that processor design textbooks essentially teach how to build vulnerable fast processors. Challenging embargo situations arose since hardware vulnerabilities affect multiple stakeholders (Intel, ARM, chip makers, device makers, cloud providers, end users) across long supply chains.

**Post-Quantum Cryptography**
Adi Shamir reported on the NIST post-quantum cryptography workshop: 82 initial proposals were submitted, 64 remain after withdrawals. Three main categories emerged: lattice-based (26 proposals), coding theory (19), multivariate (9), and hash-based (3). Key findings: most schemes operated in milliseconds to hundreds of microseconds; key/signature sizes typically 1-10 kilobytes. Shamir noted NIST faces difficult selection within their three-year timeline and cautioned that public-key cryptosystems historically require 15 years of analysis before wide adoption (RSA took until early 1990s; elliptic curve until early 2000s). Hash-based schemes and McEliece (since 1978) offer well-tested alternatives.

**Quantum Computing Progress**
Whitfield Diffie reported Microsoft's VP claims of a first qubit by year-end and a topological qubit quantum computer within five years, though researchers distanced themselves from these predictions. Quantum progress has been incremental: systems reached 20-72 qubits, but no measurable application advances beyond theoretical demonstrations have occurred.

**Blockchain Hype**
The panel characterized blockchain as "security pixie dust." While blockchains offer decentralization, public access, and immutability, they fail catastrophically on scalability, throughput, and latency. They are poor fits for voting (which requires secret ballots and central administration). However, one legitimate application emerged: using blockchain to timestamp digital signatures before quantum computers arrive, ensuring long-term signature validity. Rivest noted similar hype cycles with symmetric algorithms and public key cryptography; surety.com (1994, Stewart Haber and Scott Stornetta) built blockchain-like systems that never commercialized.

**Performance vs. Security Tradeoffs**
Paul Kocher emphasized that processors, operating systems, and compilers have been optimized for speed over 50 years with security as a secondary concern. The technology industry must recognize that security is now a multi-trillion-dollar problem, whereas performance gains yield marginal value by comparison. Systems require redesign with security as the primary objective.

**Encryption Backdoors and Exceptional Access**
Moxie Marlinspike stated simply: "once everyone has access, it's not exceptional anymore." The panel discussed Apple hosting iCloud data for Chinese users in China with encryption keys held domestically. Paul Kocher noted that technologists don't know how to "magically let the good guys break it and the bad guys stay out." A European Commission report strongly argued that backdoors and master keys are bad for encryption for security—not privacy—reasons. Russia's Supreme Court demanded Telegram provide keys; Telegram refused and was declared illegal in Russia. Iran took similar action. Marlinspike observed that had Telegram encrypted all data end-to-end from the start, refusing government demands would be logically easier.

**Data Privacy and Corporate Incentives**
The panel examined Facebook's Cambridge Analytica data breach and GDPR. Marlinspike framed Facebook as analogous to Exxon: indispensable yet despised. The company profits from data collection and surveillance; protecting user data directly conflicts with business interests. GDPR imposes fines of 4% of worldwide revenue for violations and mandates privacy by design, privacy by default, encryption, and data deletion rights. However, Marlinspike cautioned GDPR's consent-focused approach may entrench Facebook's monopoly since most users cannot refuse Facebook without losing internet access.

## Technical Details

- Spectre exploitation code was discovered through basic processor textbook material.
- Post-quantum key sizes manageable: 1-10 kilobytes vs. "several tens of gigabytes" for expanded RSA approaches.
- Hardware patch complexity: Spectre/Meltdown mitigations use LFENCE/CSDB instructions but are slow; comprehensive tool support remains lacking.
- Quantum timelines: incremental progress only; no evidence that 49-72 qubit jumps solved any meaningful problem beyond RSA-breaking speculation.

## Takeaways

1. **Silver Linings**: Election security focus is improving (two-thirds paper ballots); semiconductor designers investing in better hardware. Cryptographic algorithms like AES-256 have negligibly low break probability; solid crypto hardware design is achievable.

2. **Systemic Challenges**: Complexity grows exponentially; defending all attack surfaces simultaneously becomes untenable. Vendors profit from insecurity; regulation (GDPR, election audits) may be necessary.

3. **Long-Term Perspective**: Job security for security professionals is guaranteed; the fundamental problems remain unsolved for decades.

4. **Design Philosophy Shift Needed**: Systems must prioritize security over speed; bifurcate systems (e.g., ARM's big.little for power) with security variants. Privacy and cryptography technology form infrastructure for a desired world.

5. **International Convergence**: Multiple governments legislating against encrypted systems without backdoors reveals a collision between technical reality and political demand, with no technical solution available.

talks.title: The Five Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques, and What's Coming Next
talks.teaser: Panelists from SANS trace emerging attacks, from cloud data leaks and crypto mining to hardware flaws and industrial safety malware.
talks.summary:
Ed Skoudis focused on data theft. Teams now keep code and datasets in cloud repositories and storage buckets, and misconfigured ones have exposed millions of records at large companies. He urged organizations to track data assets, not only servers, and to use secret-scanning tools and cloud monitoring. He also showed how anonymized datasets can be re-identified when joined with other sources.

Johannes Ulrich described attackers who skip data theft and install cryptocurrency miners on compromised servers, including business systems, where the miners can stay hidden for long periods. Defenders can look for sustained high CPU use and connections to known mining pools. He then raised hardware flaws, comparing them to earlier network trust problems, and recommended encrypting data at rest and using hardware memory-encryption features as they mature.

James Lyne described criminal forums offering to build industrial control malware, including code aimed at a safety system that guards against critical failure. He argued that industrial environments lack the exploit mitigations common in mainstream computing and that attacks on sensors would be especially hard to detect. The panel closed with calls for vendors to ship secure defaults and for experts to mentor young people.

talks.title: Raise the Bar and Make an Impact
talks.teaser: A leadership keynote urges the industry to rethink hiring, vendor trust, and collective defense using workforce and trend data.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by rejecting the familiar RSA narrative of ever-worse breaches, vendor sprawl, and acronym fatigue, arguing that repeating the same approach yields the same poor outcomes. Long dwell times, unfilled roles, and products not built with security in mind mean the field may be widening gaps rather than closing them. He frames a thought experiment: one year to redesign anticipation, defender economics, system knowledge, diverse teams, and accountable vendors.

The middle ties global cooperation, rising penalties, and measurable inclusion gaps—only about 11% women in cybersecurity versus far higher shares in adjacent tech roles—to concrete pipeline efforts. He highlights Girls Go CyberStart, Women in Cybersecurity (WISSS), and large corporate scholarship programs, then pivots to trust: buyers should demand secure development and credible incident response, with differentiation already appearing in provider relationships.

Closing with industry statistics—Internet reach, ransomware scale, insecure IoT growth, and cybercrime costs—he warns that inaction invites regulation like GDPR and sector rules. Practitioners should pick from ten proposed actions: know systems better than attackers, sponsor careers, reset vendor expectations, and demand explicit trust, while bridging silos among security, IT, government, and citizens before external forces set the agenda.

talks.title: At the Edge of Prediction: A Look Back to the Future of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Traces lessons from past industrial revolutions to frame what cybersecurity must protect as technology merges with human life.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with a conversation with a science fiction writer on a long flight, which leads the speaker to the series Altered Carbon and its idea that the line between technology and humanity is disappearing. The speaker argues that cybersecurity should work like a compass, taking direction from where other fields are heading rather than following a fixed map.

Several examples follow. A robotic naval vessel built for ocean surveillance shifts the risk from physical harm to digital attack, raising questions about denial of service or misinformation fed into its analytics. A research project for hyper-local food production depends on networked robotics and sensors, so a cyber siege becomes a concern. A brain-computer interface effort lets a paralyzed veteran move his arm through recorded neural signals and stimulation. Historical parallels follow: a 19th-century gold theft that used wax key copies, electricity theft answered by a deliberate power surge, and the arrival of computer crime, leading into the current fourth revolution of combined biological, physical and digital systems.

The closing argument is that defenders need faster, self-defending and self-healing platforms, and must answer who is responsible when a human or a machine takes an action. Security teams have moved from asking to be included to being the agenda, and the speaker urges them to act as guardians of innovation. Perspective, empathy, creativity and humor will become scarce, which makes diversity and inclusion central to the work.

talks.title: OPERATION: Dateline
talks.teaser: Draws on airline hijacking and airport security history to argue that cybersecurity needs cultural priority across organizations.
talks.summary:
McAfee chief executive Chris Young opens with the history of aircraft hijacking, from the peak of 1970, when 24 hijackings occurred out of 5.1 million airline departures and arrivals, through the 1973 introduction of passenger and baggage screening. He then traces the security changes that followed 9/11, along with the shoe bomber, the liquid explosives plot and the underwear bomber, each of which prompted new rules for travelers.

He maps those lessons onto cybersecurity. Ransomware, crypto-jacking, the Mirai botnet and the Meltdown processor flaw are presented as threats that keep morphing and combining into new forms. He argues that security is still treated as a sidebar in many boardrooms, and he cites a Verizon breach report finding that nearly 40% of breaches are still driven by insider issues such as targeted phishing and unplugged-by-chance USB keys.

His main point is that the fix is cultural. Organizations need to make security part of their mission and leadership priorities. As examples, he describes MGM training hotel staff on how security relates to their roles and New York City's NYC Secure initiative, which helps residents use public Wi-Fi more safely. He closes by asking attendees to bring that priority back to their own offices, whether in government, the private sector or consumer work.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Silver Linings
talks.teaser: Keynote urging the security community to focus on its wins, using sports lessons on basics, anticipation and teamwork.
talks.summary:
Rohit Ghai, president of RSA, opens the 2018 RSA Conference by arguing that the community's wins rarely make headlines and deserve more credit. He frames three silver linings drawn from sports and business. The first is that consistent winners master fundamentals rather than chasing silver bullets, which means knowing the business context and network, using the NIST cybersecurity framework, quantifying cyber risk in dollars, and patching known vulnerabilities after a costly ransomware attack.

The second is a quicksilver pace of defense: anticipate attackers and fast-moving technology. New technology is both a weapon and a target, and the gap between mainstream adoption and security know-how has shrunk, from about eight years for biometrics to three for cloud computing. He highlights friendlier security tools with visualization and chat-based response, and the 3DS 2.0 payment standard, which aims to cut user friction while still stopping fraud.

The third is teamwork inside and outside the boat, drawing on rowing, where trust and communication decide results. He calls for collaboration among business leaders, policymakers, regulators, universities and users, and argues that diversity is essential to getting security right. He acknowledges real dark clouds, including breaches hitting public companies' earnings and eroding trust in technology, and closes by urging attendees to build on the silver linings.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2018: ShieldX
talks.teaser: Shows how ShieldX discovers cloud assets, groups them with machine learning, and enforces agentless microsegmentation.
talks.summary:
ShieldX is presented as a cloud security platform for organisations running highly virtualized data centers and multi-cloud environments. The pitch cites Alaska Airlines, a customer that adopted a multi-cloud architecture, and argues that the traditional security controls companies rely on fit poorly in the era of cloud computing.

After installation, the product discovers a company's assets and uses machine learning to place them into groups, which are then combined to express the company's security intent. Containerized microservices carry out the core functions, and the platform orchestrates them to enforce that intent without agents, adjusting automatically as the environment changes. Deep packet inspection supports microsegmentation and brings a range of security controls into one console, aimed at stopping east-west lateral movement inside the network.

The speaker says the company has been granted a first system pattern and has about 20 more in the pipeline, and claims the platform can handle terabits of deep packet inspection. The argument is that any enterprise moving to the cloud should use controls of this kind, which the speaker frames as a multi-billion dollar opportunity.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2018: Fortanix
talks.teaser: Runtime encryption inside Intel SGX enclaves keeps data in use private without rewriting existing applications.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a familiar gap: applications remain exposed while they run, and piling defensive tools onto ever more complex infrastructure still does not deliver dependable protection. The speaker argues for accepting that complexity and separating security from the underlying stack, then introduces a platform meant to provide deterministic protection from the application runtime through the operating system to the core, including against privileged insiders such as root users.

The core idea is runtime encryption for data in use, analogous to how organizations already protect data at rest and in transit. The approach relies on Intel SGX to execute workloads inside isolated secure enclaves, reportedly without rewriting existing applications, inside a portable security envelope that travels with the workload. The pitch also mentions supporting components such as persistent storage, trusted networking, and authorization, more than ten pending patents, broad application support, and modest performance overhead. A privacy-oriented example describes inferring personality traits from user messages while keeping correspondence private even against memory inspection, illustrated with messages involving Elvis Presley and J. Edgar Hoover.

The close emphasizes commercial momentum: dozens of customers securing containers, keys, and machine-learning datasets, partnerships with Intel and IBM to deliver the capability in public cloud, and positioning the technology as enabling safer compute and collaboration. Practitioners hear a product narrative centered on enclave-based isolation rather than a step-by-step technical walkthrough.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2018: BluVector
talks.teaser: Pitches a network threat detection product that scores live traffic and sends uncertain events to analysts.
talks.summary:
The presenter, who says they have spent 20 years in the industry, argues that the growing pile of security tools, alerts and dashboards has left analysts cutting and pasting between consoles instead of investigating. The pitch positions BlueVector as a system that works the way an analyst does, handling the steps of finding, verifying, adding context to and sorting advanced threats.

Walking through the design, the presenter explained that BlueVector analyzes live network traffic, with a partner integration with Gigamon supplying the feed. Traffic moves from a collection engine into detection engines running in containers, most of them proprietary. A probability engine then scores each event. High-scoring events can be contained automatically through tools such as Carbon Black or a firewall, while mid-range events go to a threat hunting workbench. There, logs from before and after the event, detection data, intelligence lookups and sandbox results are gathered so an analyst can make the call.

To close, the presenter listed the company's differentiators: self-adapting algorithms developed over ten years, a granted patent for machine learning in zero-day malware detection, and DHS SAFETY Act designation. The company claims customers can become 400% more efficient, and it plans to reach the market mainly through partners and the middle market, as technology inside MDR services. For practitioners, the takeaway is the argument for automated scoring and triage to reduce analyst workload, though the talk offered no independent results to test that claim.

talks.title: Virtual Session: Know Before You Go, Your RSA Conference 2018 Game Plan
talks.teaser: Maps the campus, registration, reserve-a-seat scheduling, expo halls, and major social events for first-time and returning attendees.
talks.summary:
RSA Conference leaders walk virtual attendees through what to expect on site in San Francisco, starting with the four-venue campus: Moscone North, South, and West plus the Marriott Marquis. They cover single-location registration in Moscone West, photo ID requirements, bag size limits, construction wayfinding staff in blue shirts, and a new mobile app for agendas, maps, polls, and personal schedules.

Britta Glade explains how to choose among hundreds of speakers and session formats, including peer-to-peer discussions capped at thirty people, hands-on learning labs with tight enrollment limits, keynotes with overflow viewing, and the reserve-a-seat system that holds a place until ten minutes before start. Linda Gray Martin details expo logistics with roughly six hundred fifty exhibitors, perks packs for full pass holders, Innovation Sandbox and early-stage startup areas, the hands-on sandbox, RSAC on Demand for remote colleagues, RSA Conference TV and Broadcast Alley, and evening social programming from welcome receptions through the closing bash.

Practical takeaways emphasize planning the week like a game plan: reserve seats early for popular labs and peer sessions, build backup choices when rooms fill, use shuttle and BART guidance for hotels, expect slide-plus-audio recordings after the event for missed talks, and pace food, walking, and sleep across a crowded week. Q&A clarifies loyalty lounge eligibility, one lab and one peer-to-peer reservation per attendee, CPE scanning, spouse badge rules, overflow rooms, and last year’s attendance above forty-three thousand.

talks.title: Quick Look: Agile and Continuous Threat Models
talks.teaser: Previews a one-day, team-wide method for threat modeling inside agile and continuous integration workflows.
talks.summary:
This short preview introduces agile and continuous threat modeling, an approach meant to fit threat modeling into fast development cycles. The speaker argues that security has to keep pace with development, operations and attackers. She connects the agile manifesto values, such as collaboration over enforcement and responding to change, with continuous ideas like ongoing ideation, continuous integration and deployment, and continuous evolution of threats and security.

The method is delivered as a one-day workshop for the whole DevSecOps group, including engineers, architects, developers, testers, operations staff and administrators. The first two steps, which take roughly an hour and a half to two hours, cover security background, goals and exercises, because not everyone on the team is a security expert. The third step is a threat model of the product, tool, application or service the team is responsible for. In the fourth step, the team reviews the findings together and assigns a risk ranking and an owner to each action item.

The main takeaway is that building security in is every person's responsibility, not a task for an outside security architect who forces practices on the team. The speaker presents this as a culture change. The exercises are only outlined here, and the full version of the session is offered at the RSA conference.

talks.title: Quick Look: Hacking Closed Networks
talks.teaser: Explains why isolated networks still face serious compromise paths through insiders, diagnostics gear, and supply-chain targeting.
talks.summary:
The preview opens with public reassurance after the USS John McCain collision that naval systems on closed networks cannot be hacked, and argues that belief breeds the worst security outcomes because defenders stop hunting while adversaries treat costly isolation as a sign of valuable targets.

It walks through recurring failure modes: air-gapped networks that were never truly closed (including power-sector findings after earlier grid presentations), exposed wireless or physical connections exploited in operational incidents, insider theft and sabotage, planted cellular or modem bridges, malware delivered through diagnostic and maintenance tooling, iconic supply-chain cases such as Stuxnet and contractor targeting, and reported compromises or extortion against critical infrastructure abroad.

The speaker stresses that creativity, not topology, limits attack options, and that practitioners must inventory diagnostics exposure, stray access points, insider abuse, and development channels rather than assuming closure equals safety. Detailed countermeasures are deferred to the full RSA session; this segment is meant to frame why that deeper treatment matters.

talks.title: Quick Look: It’s Time to Kill the Pentest
talks.teaser: Argues that most pen tests waste money and proposes testing controls and breach response instead.
talks.summary:
Adrian Sanabria argues that the typical penetration test delivers little value for what organizations pay. Much of the budget goes to running a vulnerability scanner, validating a handful of its results, and writing up a long report by hand. Many engagements exist because compliance requires them, and organizations that lack the maturity to act on findings often see the same issues reappear year after year, sometimes with artifacts left behind from earlier tests.

Sanabria proposes a replacement aimed at foundational controls, where the pen test sits last on the CIS Top 20. The alternative checks whether existing controls actually work, measures how well the organization detects and responds, and simulates common breach events such as credit card theft. Sampling and automation keep the work short. He says it can be done in under three hours, or about an hour with refinement, which leaves time to help clients build the controls they need.

The Target breach serves as an example of alerts that were generated but never acted on, the kind of gap a basic assessment should catch. Sanabria's takeaway is that penetration tests suit mature security programs, while most organizations should spend their budget on fundamentals and on the people and processes that respond to threats.

talks.title: Virtual Session: The 5 Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques, and What's Coming Next
talks.teaser: Reviews predicted attack trends across IoT, cloud data exposure, cryptocurrency theft and industrial control systems.
talks.summary:
This SANS panel revisits its earlier predictions of attack techniques and looks at how they have played out. Ed Skoudis starts with Internet of Things devices and their cloud back ends. He argues that smart toys and connected lights hold sensitive personal data in vendor clouds, that smaller providers are likely targets, and that default credentials and basic web flaws in device hubs keep feeding botnets. His advice covers separate accounts for controlling IoT devices, firmware updates, checking each device's wireless features, and watching children's use of smart toys. He then turns to credentials and private keys pushed to public code repositories and to exposed cloud storage buckets, recommending asset inventories, pre-commit secret scanners, two-factor authentication and regular review of access logs.

Johannes Ullrich covers cryptocurrency theft. He describes wallet files left on public web servers with weak passwords, Ethereum nodes whose JSON-RPC interface has no authentication, exchange breaches, payment QR codes swapped on compromised sites, and browser-based miners. Because cryptocurrency transactions cannot be reversed, he advises keeping offline wallet backups and enabling two-factor authentication on exchanges. He also flags weak random number generation in Android wallets as a source of guessable keys.

Michael Assante closes with industrial control systems. He describes the Crash Override modular framework aimed at power grid protocols and wormable SMB campaigns that reached operational networks. He argues that an air gap is a myth, since remote access, backups and historians all cross into control networks, and that attackers can send valid-looking protocol traffic. Defenders should monitor control networks for abuse that looks legitimate.

talks.title: Dame Stella Rimington - Do Your Best
talks.teaser: A former MI5 Director General explains that a boss's real job is putting the right people on the right work and resourcing them.
talks.summary:
Dame Stella Rimington opens by saying she cannot be out in the field running operations herself, because she has staff who do that work and do it better than she could. That raises what she calls the classic management question: what a boss is actually for.

Her answer is that a leader is not there to carry out the operational work. The job is to make sure the people doing it are well chosen and focused on the correct tasks, and that they have the resources they need to finish their work. To illustrate, she recalls being warned that the IRA was about to bring in a large lorry bomb, with no clear timing, port or target. She passed the warning to the Prime Minister, John Major, whom many people ridiculed, and she admired how he responded, saying he did exactly the right thing.

The takeaway for a practitioner is that leadership in a security service comes down to setting direction, choosing capable people, equipping them, and knowing when to act on warnings that arrive with incomplete information.

talks.title: The Future of Cybersecurity in the Age of Exponential Change
talks.teaser: A keynote contrasts exponential attacker growth with linear defenses and argues for abundance through AI, blockchain, and resilience.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing modern life through exponential change, citing Moore’s Law, storage and network growth, genome sequencing, and successive technology waves from PCs and the internet through mobility and social media. It notes conservative forecasts of tens of billions of connected devices and argues that while computing and connectivity keep accelerating, cybersecurity outcomes have not kept pace.

The core problem described is asymmetry: threats such as hacking, malware, social engineering, and mobile abuse rise exponentially, while many industry responses stay linear—point products, scarcity thinking, and reactive fixes. Internet-of-things risk is portrayed as growing faster than published attack statistics, with much offensive research staying hidden until incidents surface. The speaker then pivots to “abundant” enablers: blockchain scale and trust models, peer-to-peer hash power with concentration risks, quantum computing’s threat to legacy public-key encryption and the need for post-quantum cryptography, and artificial intelligence fed by cheap storage and rising compute for network-scale security rather than rack appliances.

The closing argument favors resilience over endless reaction to nation-states and criminals. Practitioners are urged to adopt exponential, abundance-minded approaches—AI operations, smart-city and e-government foundations, and forward-looking crypto—instead of hoping linear incident response can out-innovate adversaries.

talks.title: Digital Transformation and the New Role CISOs Need to Play
talks.teaser: Explains how CISOs can tie security work to business value and speak the board's language during digital transformation.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the pressure digital transformation places on security teams: faster delivery, more connected devices, cloud and container sprawl, and acquisitions that bring unfamiliar environments into the core network. The speaker, drawing on a past role as CISO of a financial services technology provider, argues that CISOs must move beyond running a security program in isolation and create measurable business value. That means describing risk in the financial terms that boards and business leaders use.

To make the point, the speaker describes a business question about customer journeys that the company could not answer at first. Leadership consolidated budgets across operations, infrastructure, security and application development into one integrated monitoring solution. It traced client connections through load balancers, web servers, application logic, databases and fraud analytics, and resolution time for issues dropped by 70 to 80%. Separately, the company placed information security officers inside more than 50 business units with a product-quality goal. Static, dynamic and pipeline testing were built into development, which cut product defects by 50% and resolved 80% of them within the same development cycle. Analytics built on weekly operational baselines let the team alert on unusual activity and reduce administrative accounts.

The talk closes with three imperatives the speaker gave the team: speed, agility and visibility. Alongside people, processes and tools, these goals let a CISO answer a board's question about whether the company has been breached, and keep answering it over time.

talks.title: RSAC APJ - Interview with Jacques Villeneuve
talks.teaser: Formula One champion Jacques Villeneuve explains how team trust and risk calls in racing parallel security decisions.
talks.summary:
This short interview from the RSA Conference Asia Pacific and Japan features Jacques Villeneuve, a Formula One world champion, speaking with conference general manager Linda Gray Martin. The conversation opens with how a driver and team shape a race car together. Villeneuve explains that the driver feels the car through the steering wheel, while engineers hold engine and telemetry numbers the driver cannot sense, so that data is mostly reviewed after the car returns to the garage. He notes that a human driver is not a robot, so the same numbers do not suit everyone, and that radio messages during a race can either ease a long stint or distract a driver.

The middle of the interview covers risk. Villeneuve describes risk as a constant calculation of possible gain against what might be lost, with an answer that changes with timing and mood. Drivers and pit-wall engineers see the same risk differently, so teams prepare strategies for many scenarios while keeping their minds open to situations nobody planned for. Mutual trust, where the team backs the driver and the driver believes in the team, is presented as essential to taking risks at all.

In the closing question, Martin asks how this approach to managing risk applies to an audience making critical security decisions every day. Villeneuve links the two through stress and through the fact that risk affects other people, not only the individual. The takeaway for practitioners is that deciding how much risk to accept, and on whose behalf, depends on context and on shared trust within the team.

talks.title: Best Practices and Proactive Strategies to Mitigate Cyberthreats
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how to frame cyber programs around threats, board concerns, litigation and insurance.
talks.summary:
The presenter, chief security officer at CenturyLink, argues that security leaders should move from technical, solution-focused work to threat-focused cyber risk management. Boards now judge cyber issues through litigation, regulatory disclosure, customer trust and insurance, so security programs need to explain their decisions in those terms. The talk sorts programs into reactive, proactive and predictive groups and urges planning for emerging practices, because attackers quickly defeat established ones.

To illustrate the threat landscape, the speaker walks through recurring attack types: ransomware, extortion-style denial-of-service, phishing of employees and malicious insiders. Several cases serve as lessons. The Target breach came through a vendor, which points to supply chain risk, and the Sony attack showed how attackers who obtain administrator credentials or patch-management access can disable security controls. For insiders, the speaker notes that people usually show concerning behavior for a long time before acting, and that organizations often lack training, reporting paths and investigators to act on it.

The closing advice is practical. Keep policies, procedures and evidence of a working program, since they may be examined in court. Maintain a documented, tested data breach response plan with assigned roles, and expect that the response and recovery will be judged more heavily than the breach itself. Vet vendors, run phishing tests that resemble current news, and apply stronger controls to high-value staff and systems.

talks.title: Virtual Session: GDPR without the Hype
talks.teaser: Explains the core GDPR principles, data subject rights and controller duties, and how IT teams can start preparing.
talks.summary:
This session sets out to cut through the hype around the EU General Data Protection Regulation and explain what it actually asks of organisations. The speaker, a privacy and security risk specialist who stresses he is not a lawyer, starts with the background: the regulation replaces a 1995 directive, applies the same way in every EU member state and the wider European Economic Area, and reaches non-EU organisations that offer goods or services to people in the EU. Only three of its 99 articles deal directly with security, so the talk concentrates on the principles, the rights individuals hold, and the duties placed on controllers.

The principles cover lawfulness, transparency, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation and accountability. Data subjects can request access, portability, correction and erasure, and can object to processing or to significant automated decisions, generally at no charge and with a response due within a month. Article 32 asks for security measures suited to the risk, but the speaker argues that risk should be judged by the harm to individuals rather than to the organisation. He also covers the penalty tiers of up to 20 million euros or 4 percent of global turnover, and the 72-hour window for notifying regulators of a breach.

For preparation, he recommends confirming applicability with legal counsel, identifying which people and data types are involved, mapping data flows, and deleting data that is duplicated or no longer needed. Other steps include a risk register and remediation plan, privacy impact assessments for in-flight projects, records of processing, and a tested incident response plan. The takeaway is that compliance is a business change touching many teams, not a product purchase, and that it should be built into everyday processes.

talks.title: Quick Look: Changing Data Protection: Heading towards a Blockchain-Operated Future
talks.teaser: Shows how blockchain's immutable ledger can timestamp and verify data protection objects, using a production notary service.
talks.summary:
The talk traces blockchain through stages, from a cryptocurrency base to a platform for smart contracts and then toward a decentralized web. The speaker describes public ledgers as a way to see every transaction and prove it existed, and sketches smart contracts that run conditional logic automatically without intermediaries. Possible uses in e-government, telecoms and IoT are mentioned, but the speaker frames these as early, with contract security and execution speed still open issues.

The core case study is Acronis Notary, a trusted timestamping service already in production. Users can hash any file, email, website or log, receive a certificate, and later show that the object existed at a given time. Because writing every object to a blockchain would hit throughput limits, the service batches hashes into a Merkle tree and anchors only the root hash on the chain. Each certificate, delivered as a PDF, links an object to that root, so verification can be done with an open-source tool even if the service is unavailable.

The closing section previews the decentralized web, where oracles would approve or reject actions and even parts of legal decisions. The speaker presents this as a high-level concept that is still early. For practitioners, the takeaway is that an immutable ledger with public timestamps can add an authenticity layer to backups and stored data, though the talk stayed at an overview level.

talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting widespread industry fear with a hopeful view of hackers as protectors of a connected world, anchored in a widely viewed talk that drew nearly two million viewers and ongoing outreach from researchers and tinkerers who want to contribute but feel mistrusted.

The core argument targets fear, uncertainty, and doubt: when alarmist claims arise, practitioners should slow down, separate what has happened from speculation, and communicate clearly. Trust and safety—not secrecy alone—should guide the field, with emphasis on reliable devices underpinning daily life. Organizational reputation hinges less on whether flaws surface than on response, remediation, and honest engagement when disclosures or stunts occur. Individuals are urged to insist on safer products for their households even without enterprise authority.

The close recaps three commitments—demand trustworthy devices, replace fear with facts, and collaborate with hackers—and points listeners toward an annual free international gathering in Tel Aviv each June, including a regional B-sides event.

talks.summary:
This follow-up webcast revisits a 2017 RSA Conference keynote on emerging attack methods, with SANS presenters answering questions the original session could not cover. Ed Skoudis starts with ransomware, suggesting DNS sinkholing to block the lookups malware uses to fetch components, and a Windows file share as a honeypot to catch intruders. For IoT, he advises changing default passwords, turning off Telnet and HTTP, and keeping devices off remote access.

Michael Assante focuses on industrial control systems, where firmware-driven communication devices were made to stop working at scale. His advice covers inventorying devices and management interfaces, checking for published default credentials, and rehearsing how to isolate control networks within about two minutes. Johannes Ullrich addresses weak randomness on embedded devices, which can lead to reused encryption keys, and recommends checking container images before use and locking down NoSQL databases left open without passwords.

James Lyne described reverse engineering inexpensive IoT cameras, some of which fell in under 15 minutes using basic techniques because older Linux and Android builds lacked modern exploit mitigations. He pointed to commoditized ransomware kits sold with marketing material, and to destructionware when payment addresses vanish. Closing advice stressed simple controls, a system-of-systems view, and the Center for Internet Security critical controls as a basis for budget plans.

talks.title: An Astrophysicist Reads the Newspaper: Dr. Neil deGrasse Tyson Explores Our World
talks.teaser: A famed scientist links exoplanet hunts, laser sail propulsion, and global element discovery on the periodic table.
talks.summary:
The session opens with an astrophysicist’s newspaper-style tour of headline science rather than security minutiae. He points to a newly reported Earth-sized exoplanet in the habitable zone of the Sun’s nearest stellar neighbor, credited to the European Southern Observatory, as the kind of discovery that reshapes how people picture worlds beyond our own.

He then sketches a breakthrough-propulsion thought experiment: concentrate laser power on a lightweight sail so radiation pressure might push a craft to a large fraction of the speed of light, shrinking the practical distance to nearby stars. From there he pivots to the periodic table, especially synthetic elements creeping toward an island of stability in the 120-proton range, and notes that naming rights follow discovery. Institutions in Russia, the United States, and Japan now share that lineage; historical U.S. dominance shows up in transuranics such as americium, californium, and berkelium, while a country-flag view of the chart makes the shift toward international credit visually obvious.

He ends on the noble gases—chemically aloof elements whose label, he jokes, echoes British class distinctions—and thanks the audience. For security practitioners the payload is perspective: audacious goals channel ingenuity, and exploration costs fall when diverse teams compete and collaborate on shared frontiers.
