talks.title: Solving Cybersecurity in the Next Five Years: Systematizing Progress for the Short Term
talks.teaser: Makes the case that rapid, resilient IT change can move security toward a solved state within five years.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether cybersecurity can be solved within five years and uses car safety as its model of a solved state. In that state safety is a basic expectation, threats are removed before they happen, and remaining harm declines as older vehicles leave the road. The speaker then traces enterprise IT decade by decade. In the 1980s the problem was asset inventory, in the 1990s it was viruses and insecure configurations answered by antivirus and firewalls, and in the 2000s it was alert overload met with SIEM tools and security operations centers. The 2010s brought incident response and risk management, and the speaker argues each era applied old fixes to new problems.

For the 2020s the speaker argues that recovery is the central challenge, because destructive attacks and ransomware can cause harm that prevention and detection cannot undo. Solutions that help recovery, such as immutable infrastructure, cloud services and declarative policy defined as code, also make persistence hard for attackers when environments are rebuilt often. The speaker suggests the business already moves faster than attackers, so security should enable faster change and reduce shadow IT. Static deception traps are criticized because attackers can spot the elements that never change.

The practical advice is to identify which decade your organization's security resembles, have red teams simulate destructive attacks, find resilient design patterns and encourage their adoption, and invest in know-how over new products. The speaker accepts that legacy systems and cultural change will take time, and invites counterarguments.

talks.title: Why Johnny STILL Can’t Encrypt
talks.teaser: Traces persistent encryption usability failures and argues for policy-oriented data APIs evaluated at decryption time.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits the lineage of “Why Johnny Can’t Encrypt,” from the 1999 PGP usability study through later repeats showing little improvement despite industry growth and stronger demand for encryption. It argues that blaming unmotivated or careless users no longer fits survey evidence from thousands of IT and risk professionals who now prioritize key management and data protection.

A programmer’s path through PKCS#11 illustrates the core failure mode: critical algorithm, mode, and key-handling choices are pushed onto people who only want a simple outcome, often after reading enormous standards documents. Binding security policy at encryption time—especially via long-lived symmetric keys—locks in decisions that should stay flexible when boards, custodians, or access rules change. Analyses of PKCS#11 option interactions and key-lifecycle standards such as KMIP show how complexity and combinatorics recreate the same mistakes at the API layer, sometimes enabling key extraction from tokens that should never expose plaintext keys.

The closing case is for data-security and policy-oriented APIs evaluated at decryption time, aligned with modern dynamic data and compliance needs. Practitioners are urged to describe use cases in business terms rather than crypto jargon, match protection to data value without overwhelming option menus, and participate in standards work so vendors stop shipping crypto-first interfaces that feel usable but remain unsafe.

talks.title: A Clear View: Cybersecurity by the Numbers
talks.teaser: A bank, an insurer and a ratings firm debate replacing gut-feel security calls with quantitative risk numbers.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with the reactive state of many security teams, which often respond to each new vulnerability or headline as it appears. The moderator asks whether predictive analysis and numeric measures could let organisations plan ahead instead. The Barclays panelist describes building a holistic security function that merges cyber and physical security and feeds HR, security and log data into a common analytics platform.

The cyber insurance panelist explains that the market has grown quickly from a small base, and that underwriting is effectively a series of bets on which firms will be breached. With a portfolio of roughly 25,000 clients, the insurer can price its overall book within 10 to 20 percent, though allocating risk to individual companies is harder. The ratings panelist describes scores on a 250 to 900 scale, updated continuously from data gathered from outside, and argues that third-party risk stems from information asymmetry. An audience member challenged the common impact-times-probability formula. The panel acknowledged its simplicity, and the insurer said probabilities come from claims data and are better understood as distributions than as single figures.

In closing remarks, the panelists agreed that objective, quantitative data should replace red, yellow and green labels, with uses in board reporting, third-party benchmarking, regulation and insurance. The insurer suggested that premium savings might one day help security leaders justify major investments, though the underlying data work is not finished.

talks.title: Critical Hygiene for Preventing Major Breaches
talks.teaser: Delivers prioritized hygiene controls and phased roadmaps to disrupt common credential-theft paths before domain compromise.
talks.summary:
The session frames why security leaders struggle to justify spending when boards want measurable risk reduction, and why complex, fast-moving environments let attackers reach domain admin within a day while old vulnerabilities remain exploitable. Jonathan Trull describes a personal prioritization lens that weighs attack disruption and team efficiency against business disruption when choosing controls.

Tony Sager argues defenders face too many standards and products—the “fog of more”—and must translate guidance into repeatable action. He outlines the Defender’s Challenge (decide, implement, prove) and the Community Attack Model for mapping attacker lifecycle stages to defensive options aligned with familiar framework functions.

Mark Simos explains ruining attacker return on investment by raising attack cost, breaking known playbooks first, and pairing prevention with rapid detection and ejection. The core incident pattern runs from phishing through credential harvesting and lateral movement to domain administrator access. Prescriptive first steps include privileged access workstations separating admin from daily use, unique local passwords via LAPS, then ninety-day extensions such as just-in-time privilege, just-enough administration, domain controller hardening, and behavioral analytics—organized into thirty- and ninety-day roadmaps with public implementation guidance.

talks.title: Foreign Espionage, Social Media, and the Unwitting Insider Threat
talks.teaser: Shows how foreign recruiters use social media to pull employees into unwitting insider roles and how programs can spot early signs.
talks.summary:
Bryan Krekel, a counterintelligence and insider threat manager, opens with a case from about eighteen months earlier. A foreign-linked recruitment firm sent consulting offers to roughly 300 employees through their personal LinkedIn accounts. The company spotted it only because one employee forwarded the message to information security, and staff who had listed corporate email addresses on their profiles had the approaches routed into the network. He argues these cases form a third category beyond the disgruntled or hostile insider: the unwitting insider, drawn in through paid side work with no overt request for data.

He then explains why adversaries shifted to social media. Better spearphishing detection reduced the payoff of older methods, and the 2015 Anthem and OPM breaches gave recruiters detailed personnel records to target people. Chats on personal accounts are hard for most organizations to monitor, and employees tend to trust unsolicited contact offering work. Approaches begin with flattery and questions, then move to contracts and payment for time, which can cross into export control violations unnoticed.

For defenders, he recommends a collaborative model across HR, security, legal and ethics, since network tools alone miss these conversations. Programs should identify at-risk groups for targeted awareness, offer a simple reporting path, and remind staff of conflict-of-interest and nondisclosure duties in advance. He closes by comparing this to workplace safety inspections: look for conditions that let well-meaning staff stumble into trouble.

talks.title: IEEE MACSec and NSA ESS: How to Protect Your WAN, LAN and Cloud
talks.teaser: Explains how MACsec layer-2 encryption, tightened by NSA's ESS, can isolate WAN, LAN and cloud traffic and limit lateral movement.
talks.summary:
Emil Isaakian opens with a packet capture from several enterprises, where roughly 97 percent of traffic at layer two and above was unencrypted and readable by anyone with access to the network. He argues that application-level encryption such as OpenSSL leaves the link layer exposed, and that flat networks let an attacker who gets in move laterally and map every device.

He walks through MACsec, the IEEE link-layer encryption standard, covering its frame transformation, the integrity check value that binds headers to the payload, and the anti-replay window. Key agreement through MKA, with EAP-TLS for initial authentication, distributes the keys that peers use. He then describes ESS as an NSA layer on top of MACsec that removes legacy options, keeping GCM with 64-bit packet numbers, adds support for provider bridged networks through CTAG and STAG tag handling, and offers a fixed-rate transmission mode and a tunnel mode that hides MAC addresses.

For deployment he suggests encrypting site-to-site and hybrid cloud links first, then placing printers, cameras and other IoT devices into separate connectivity associations so they cannot reach the wider network. He notes that encrypting switches are only now arriving and that monitoring tools need a mirror port inside the encrypted group. His closing advice is to start by capturing your own network traffic and to move from blacklisting devices toward whitelisting by design.

talks.title: Containers: The Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde of Security
talks.teaser: Maps container isolation limits and shows how shift-left image policy, automation, and least privilege improve security.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames containers as a deployment model built from layered archives pulled through registries and started by an engine on a shared host kernel. Unlike virtual machines, processes run natively with namespace and cgroup segmentation, which speeds DevOps but leaves security teams facing opaque images, weak legacy scanning, immutable filesystems that resist in-place patching, and host networking that hides relationships between workloads.

A live-style walkthrough shows how mounting the host root into a container running as root can alter the host password file, illustrating why user namespaces and platform defaults matter even when newer fixes exist. The speaker catalogs operational risks from hub-sourced images, misconfiguration, privilege escalation, resource exhaustion, enlarged blast radius, and sparse accountability when containers are discarded without durable logs.

The second half reframes adoption as leverage: secure base images, approved registries, signing, and CI-time checks on packages and run-as-root settings; automated pipelines to rebuild and roll out patched images at scale; and preventive microservice hardening that strips unused tools attackers rely on. Practitioners are urged to locate existing container use, avoid blanket refusal, align dev and ops through image policy and pipeline visibility, and insist on familiar controls such as segmentation, WAFs, and testing while participating early in the lifecycle.

talks.title: Psychology of an Eastern European Cybercriminal: Mindset Drives Behavior
talks.teaser: Threat intelligence on vetted underground figures links lifestyle, gangster rap, and ideology to better anticipation of attacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that defenders over-focus on malware and indicators while misreading Eastern European cybercriminals as unreachable caricatures. Drawing on law enforcement and intelligence experience, it contrasts strong technical tradecraft with weak understanding of why actors target Western banks and retailers while largely avoiding former CIS states.

Two vetted-forum personalities anchor the narrative: Ink, described as a forum godfather who arbitrates disputes and doxes rule-breakers, and Radamont, tied to a popular ransomware kit, JavaScript loaders, and bulletproof hosting. Analysis of Ink’s underground rap is used to illustrate bank botnet habits, despair, and dreams of legitimizing illicit gains. Sleeping patterns and daily rhythms are framed as predictive intelligence beside command-and-control activity.

The talk traces how elite criminals once treated ransomware as intellectual death and botnet waste, then shifted after the Hollywood Presbyterian incident and healthcare payments. Radamont’s affiliate infrastructure and hosting choices are tied to preemptive blocking, while Ink’s coaching and bans shape forum culture. The closing message is to embed in criminal chatter, marry social intelligence with technical defense, and disrupt operations so actors waste time instead of only chasing fresh IOCs.

talks.title: Developing Useful Metrics
talks.teaser: Explains how the GQIM framework links security measurements to business goals and sharpens existing program metrics.
talks.summary:
Security leaders often receive long reports full of green indicators while day-to-day operations still feel broken. The presenters argue that measurement should start from business and program objectives, not from whatever data is easiest to count, and they distinguish raw measures from metrics that put those measures in decision-making context.

They introduce GQIM—goal, question, indicator, metric—as a repeatable derivation method adapted from NASA’s GQM approach at Carnegie Mellon’s SEI, with an added indicator step between questions and combined metrics. Dave Tobar walks through each stage from high-level resilience or cybersecurity objectives down to goals, effectiveness-oriented questions, concrete indicators to collect, and ratio- or trend-based metrics, using incident-management goals as a running example. Lisa Young applies the same template to familiar hygiene numbers such as unpatched machines, reframing them around exploit risk and time from patch release to application, and to user access commensurate with role for insider-threat concerns.

Practitioners are urged to audit current metrics for the decisions they actually inform, involve sponsors and stakeholders, start with a small set, and iterate. The session also touches on peer benchmarking limits, metric gaming, and resources from Douglas Hubbard and Lance Spitzner, while slides and templates are offered for reuse after the conference.

talks.title: Charting the Course to GDPR: Setting Sail
talks.teaser: Explains GDPR obligations for security teams, from mapping personal data to encryption, audit trails and breach response.
talks.summary:
The session gives a high-level introduction to the EU General Data Protection Regulation and a starting point for organizations preparing before its May 2018 effective date. The speaker outlines the main points: stronger rights for data subjects, reach beyond Europe to any organization handling personal data of people located there, a 72-hour breach reporting window, and fines of up to 4% of annual turnover for privacy violations. A five-phase readiness model runs from assessment through design, transformation and operation to conformance, where organizations must produce evidence that they complied.

The middle presents tips for security teams. Start by identifying where the riskiest data sits, then build a data map by finding identifiers first, since data that cannot be linked to a person is not personal data. Track processing with audit trails that scale to cloud providers, and set up workflows for access, correction, deletion and transfer requests. Pseudonymization and encryption help when keys are managed centrally. Breach handling needs a rehearsed playbook and a full forensic trail.

In the audience questions, the speaker described how deleting data from very large SAP systems is often impractical, and suggested audit trails and restricted access as compensating controls. For mixed production and corporate data, the speaker said clients often apply the same controls to everything rather than separate it. The closing advice is to appoint coordinators in each business unit, run a readiness assessment against current practices, and draw on privacy professional bodies.

talks.title: Client-Side Encryption without Knowing Its Limits Is a Ticking Time Bomb!
talks.teaser: Maps client-side encryption limits, property-preserving scheme leaks, and threat models teams must plan beyond ciphertext alone.
talks.summary:
Cloud and SaaS adoption pushes sensitive data outside the corporate perimeter, making data breaches a recurring top concern. Client-side encryption keeps keys on the client or proxy so providers and intruders see ciphertext, but encrypting before upload breaks ordinary server features such as search and deduplication.

The presentation walks through homomorphic encryption as impractical for responsive workloads, then focuses on property-preserving schemes used in industry: deterministic encryption for equality, searchable encryption for keyword search, and order-preserving encryption for ranges. Examples span encrypted relational databases including Microsoft Always Encrypted, onion-layer encryption inspired by CryptDB on BigQuery, and the Mylar experimental stack for Meteor where keys stay in the browser.

Against snapshot passive, persistent passive, and active adversaries, many deployments leak via plaintext columns, metadata, misapplied deterministic encryption on non-unique fields, dense order-preserving fields, and long-lived access patterns—research cited recovery of large shares of patient attributes and clustering from queries alone. Practitioners should inventory schemes in use, layer defenses, encrypt metadata and auxiliary fields, align scheme choice with data cardinality, and assume encryption alone does not equal a secure system.

talks.title: Continuous Authentication and Distributed Session Management
talks.teaser: Reviews SSO logout options and hashgraph-synced session stores for verifiable global logout and continuous authentication.
talks.summary:
Enterprise single sign-on makes initial login straightforward, but reliably ending every application session at once remains hard. The presentation separates authentication sessions at the identity provider from shorter- or longer-lived application sessions, then walks through why administrators need a dependable global logout after terminations, device loss, or elevated risk, and how that requirement intensifies when continuous authentication replaces arbitrary timeouts.

Front-channel logout depends on the browser visiting each application's logout endpoint, often via iframes or redirects, without proof that every session actually ended. Back-channel logout lets the identity provider call applications directly but struggles to correlate user identifiers to sessions without shared, verifiable state. The speaker reviews IDP polling as an OpenID Connect-oriented proposal and its limits for scaling, availability, and non-browser clients, then introduces a replicated session database beneath the identity layer, synchronized with distributed consensus so each relying party can validate sessions locally.

That shared channel also supports session extension, suspension, and propagating changing certainty scores from continuous authentication. Requirements for legal-grade timestamps, denial-of-service resilience, immutable audit, and efficient throughput are mapped against leader-based replication, proof-of-work blockchain, and hashgraph, with hashgraph highlighted for federations of mutually untrusted members. Practitioners are urged to define use-case requirements first, then select consensus technology rather than defaulting to blockchain for every identity problem.

talks.title: Expanding Your Blue Team by Creating Security Culture
talks.teaser: Shows how rewarding employees for reporting phishing builds a human detection layer that catches what technology misses.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that employees should be treated as a source of defense rather than only as a weakness. It cites survey results in which security leaders credited employees with uncovering breaches more than any other internal process or technology, and asks why organizations invest so little in them. Phishing runs through the talk as the running example. When someone clicks a link, the speaker distinguishes three outcomes: the person does not notice, does not care, or reports it.

The speaker criticizes phishing programs that judge success only by click rates, since test difficulty varies and repeated campaigns eventually get clicked. Planning for failure means measuring reporting instead. A target of about 20 percent reporting is proposed, so that enough people flag suspicious messages for the incident response team to act. An anecdote describes an internal red team whose custom malware was reported quickly during phishing tests, making further attacks too costly to continue.

To raise reporting, the talk recommends building positive relationships before an incident, aiming for five positive interactions for every negative one, and using points, recognition and small rewards. Automated acknowledgements and faster triage kept staff engaged, and reporting rose 350 percent in the first six months, along with more false positives. Practical advice includes a single clear reporting channel and pre-announcing legitimate mass emails. The main takeaway is to reward reporting early, before it is needed.

talks.title: RSAC TV: Prakhar Pandey Interview
talks.teaser: A scholar outlines payment-focused research meant to weaken demand for booter and DDoS-for-hire services.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with an NYU computer engineering master’s student describing work on network security and ways to deter booter and DDoS-for-hire operations by tracing how they get paid. The core idea is to follow the money: many of these services accept PayPal, Bitcoin, and a handful of smaller wallets, and removing familiar options such as PayPal appears to reduce willingness to pay compared with Bitcoin alone, because cryptocurrency adds overhead, verification steps, and user anxiety.

Even when operators relaunch after takedowns, disrupting preferred payment rails is framed as a way to squeeze incentives rather than expect permanent shutdowns. The scholar reflects on a first RSA Conference visit, meeting prominent researchers and industry leaders, and the value of mentorship beyond formal academics when moving toward an industry career.

Advice that resonated emphasizes owning one’s career, working hard, and helping others. After presenting a research poster and gathering expert feedback, the plan is to continue the payment-focused cybercrime work and promote an RSA cyber safety program aimed at children.

talks.title: No More Security Empires: The CISO as an Individual Contributor
talks.teaser: A case study shows how a CISO without direct reports scales security via frameworks, RACI, and cross-functional champions.
talks.summary:
The speaker contrasts centralized “security empire” models with an alternative where the CISO acts as an individual contributor with no direct reports. Drawing on roles at fintech, large e-commerce, and a B2B payments company near nine hundred employees, he outlines organizational patterns from fully centralized teams to duplicated unit-level security functions and the engagement failures that often follow.

At AvidXchange he aligned the program with COSO risk principles, ISO frameworks, the CIS Critical Security Controls, and NIST Cybersecurity Framework. A simple red-yellow-green gap assessment and enterprise threat model fed a three-year, risk-prioritized roadmap that also elevated low-probability/high-impact risks and chronic nuisances such as phishing. Rather than hiring a large core team, he mapped synergies—Splunk monitoring, HR’s learning platform, development interest in quality—and used a RACI matrix to spread accountability across infrastructure, DevOps, software, HR, and other roles for roughly ten equivalent FTE without those people reporting to him.

Practitioners hear how he funded controls through business pain points, board interest, and partner demands; mentored contributors while defining what and why and leaving how to owners; and kept a reversible plan B to recentralize. Results after about ten months include strong ownership, faster progress, integrated privacy work, and a partner-ready story despite one full-time security headcount. Takeaways emphasize influence over empire-building, peer relationships with the CIO, and pushing commodity execution to the teams that already run the systems.

talks.title: Privacy Enhancing Technologies Work—But Can Anyone Use Them?
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh whether privacy-enhancing technologies work in practice and why users and organizations struggle to adopt them.
talks.summary:
A panel discussion opened with a speaker from NIST explaining the agency's work on a privacy engineering program and framing the question of who can actually use privacy enhancing technologies. Each panelist first defined the term. One described Firefox features such as tracking protection, cookie blocking and container tabs. Another, from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, showed Privacy Badger, which reveals the third-party domains on a web page so users can decide what to block, and Let's Encrypt, which made HTTPS certificates easy for small sites to obtain.

The middle of the session turned to whether privacy should be built into software by design or added as standalone tools. Panelists argued that a user who does not know a tool exists will never install it, so protections belong in the products people already use. They said people underestimate how much data is collected, and gave an example of separate public datasets that become revealing when combined. Tor's locked-down mode and ordinary browsing were described as two extremes, and Brave's shields and Firefox's private browsing were cited as ways to let users choose per site. Transparency about back-end data handling and legal protection, compared with Europe's GDPR, were also raised as needed controls.

In audience questions, panelists said a company's business model strongly shapes how far it will protect data, and that trust and reputation give companies a reason to limit collection. The takeaway was a layered approach that combines usable tools, privacy-minded design, clear policy and public pressure on companies.

talks.title: Privileged Access Management—Unsticking Your PAM Program
talks.teaser: Explains how to move a stalled privileged access management program forward through process, adoption and collaboration.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a working definition of privileged access management (PAM), covering administrator rights, special application permissions and shared accounts that carry business risk, and argues that identity has replaced the network perimeter. Several cases show the stakes. A South Carolina breach exposed a taxpayer database through a backup account, which was not encrypted at rest. A shared local admin password let an attacker push a script that wiped about 30,000 PCs in roughly an hour. Spear-phishing targeted IT staff who had advertised their email administration on LinkedIn.

The practical core covers vaulting, where a user checks out a credential for a time-boxed session and it is rotated afterwards, and session management, where the session is recorded and the user never sees the password. Scripts can fetch credentials at run time. Adoption began with roughly 50 lunch sessions over a year, then inventories built with business owners, risk-based prioritisation and testing before production. Onboarding through the development lifecycle and linking to the configuration management database closed gaps.

Keys to success were fault-tolerant, separately powered deployments, senior leadership support and process before tooling. Challenges included clashes with admin tools, out-of-band accounts, cloud connectivity, custom applications and service accounts with unknown owners. The main takeaway is to treat PAM as governance, not a product purchase, and to start with hygiene and vaulting.

talks.title: Tomorrow's Cyber-Risk Analyst
talks.teaser: Contrasts ad-hoc risk ratings with measurable analysis and outlines skills, hiring gaps, and steps toward mature cyber risk programs.
talks.summary:
Jack Jones argues that most organizations perform risk assessment—collecting concerns and control gaps—but almost never true risk analysis that quantifies what matters and supports prioritization. Audience polls and consulting experience frame a industry dominated by high-medium-low judgments, weakly defended top-ten risk lists, and mental models rather than structured measurement. He positions FAIR as an open standard alternative and describes executive pressure for answers in dollars and loss exposure instead of color charts.

The session defines tomorrow's cyber risk analyst as a cross-functional role: gather threat, control, and business impact data; communicate patiently; apply basic probability; and think critically through complexity and uncertainty. Illustrations include triaging hundreds of scanner findings to a handful that matter, winning mid-cycle budget with a few hundred thousand dollars versus multi-million best practices, PCI encryption trade-offs, and cutting SOX control volume through analysis-backed choices.

Closing themes cover talent shortages as FAIR adoption grows, university programs such as San Jose State, skepticism toward vendor "risk" scores, and regulatory movement toward quantitative analysis. Practical next steps include assessing organizational maturity, engaging the FAIR Institute and related communities, reading recommended foundational books, and sponsoring education—so leaders can staff credible analysts even if they do not perform the work themselves.

talks.title: Wireless Sensors’ Power Consumption and IoT Security
talks.teaser: Explores how monitoring wireless sensor power draw with machine learning can flag anomalies that point to IoT security threats.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the constraints of IoT security. Small sensors have limited compute and storage, many devices cannot be upgraded locally and rely on the manufacturer for updates, and gateways sit between field devices and the cloud or core systems. The speakers describe an edge-to-cloud view covering onboarding, monitoring, gateways and identity. They use a recent large attack on connected home devices as an example of how a compromised endpoint can spread through a network and take a long time to contain.

The core idea is to correlate the power consumption of wireless sensor nodes with security threats. The proposal is to build a power profile for each node that records minimum, maximum, peak and idle draw, then use machine learning to learn normal behaviour and raise an alert on deviations, such as a sensor that may have had unauthorised firmware injected. A security layer would gather trust scores for each device and decide whether to allow, block or flag it for extra checks. The speakers said vendor-supplied profiles and ACPI power information could help build the baseline, and they discussed latency, battery-powered sensors that report only once an hour, and fake data sent by genuine devices.

The work was presented as a proof of concept, with the speakers noting it was not yet a finished system. The practical takeaways are to treat power telemetry as an extra signal alongside existing controls, to feed it into edge management tools, and to build security into the device design rather than adding it afterwards.

talks.title: The Future of Privacy
talks.teaser: Traces privacy from ancient stories to modern data use, arguing that technology keeps renegotiating it.
talks.summary:
Trevor Hughes, president and CEO of the International Association of Privacy Professionals, argues that privacy is a basic part of being human. Drawing on artworks and old stories, he traces it from the Adam and Eve account of shame and vulnerability, to an 1890 law review article prompted by portable cameras, to Jeremy Bentham's panopticon, where people who feel watched change how they act.

Each era of new technology brought claims that privacy was dead. Hughes credits Alan Westin's 1967 book with defining informational privacy, and links Alan Turing's work to the data revolution. He compares Facebook reaching two billion users in about twelve years with Christianity's spread over more than 2,000 years, and describes a widening gap between technology and the norms, laws and policy meant to respond to it. A story of Diana and Actaeon illustrates the long-standing consequences of violating privacy, and he argues that privacy gives people room to be different, which fuels innovation.

He rejects the idea that privacy is dead, describing it instead as an ongoing negotiation, and cites an IBM example in which neonatal data analysis helped save lives. His practical takeaway is that legal compliance alone is not enough. Anyone who makes decisions about data should understand how privacy concerns arise, spot issues early, and raise them within their organisation.

talks.title: Reversing the Year: Let’s Hack IoT, Ransomware and Evasive Payloads
talks.teaser: Walks through rooting a cheap CCTV camera from its firmware, then dissects a ransomware sample's settings and payment traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a collection of cheap internet-connected devices bought for research, mainly a CCTV camera, and argues that much IoT weakness is basic rather than exotic. The speaker scans the camera live, finds an open Telnet service and a web interface whose default login was already publicly known, then works through the firmware. Strings and binary searches reveal a hard-coded root password, a password file that can be pulled out of the device, and a web archive password embedded in the code.

A command injection path in a backup feature lets the speaker leak the stored password hash. That hash is protected with DES, which he cracks in a few minutes with John the Ripper, and the resulting credentials give a root shell in under 20 minutes. He notes that such devices often run old Linux kernels without modern exploit mitigations and use outdated crypto and libraries, so a basic firmware review would expose many of these flaws.

The second half turns to ransomware. Using a 2016 sample and a configuration panel found on an onion site, he shows default settings left unchanged, a delayed registration screen, timed deletion of files if the ransom goes unpaid, and a payment flow whose Bitcoin balance check can be intercepted on the network. He contrasts this with newer samples that use proper cryptography, and warns that disappearing payment channels leave victims with destructive rather than payable ransomware. The takeaway is to fix basic IoT security while devices are still simple, and to prepare backups before an infection.

talks.title: Managing Cyber-risk: Unlocking the Mystery of the Boardroom
talks.teaser: A Fortune 500 director lays out how boards weigh cyber risk, work with CISOs, and judge whether security programs deserve trust.
talks.summary:
The session opens from the practitioner side: corporate boards are increasingly focused on cybersecurity, yet most security leaders rarely see how directors think, organize committees, or prioritize risk. Dr. Ron Sugar, a former aerospace CEO and long-serving public-company director, frames governance as three enduring duties—leadership, strategy, and risk—and places cyber risk inside enterprise risk management alongside financial, geographic, and operational threats.

He describes how breach headlines and geopolitical cyber operations pushed boards to invite CISOs into audit, risk, or compliance forums, and why effective programs must be treated as business risks, not isolated IT projects. Sugar emphasizes CEO tone-setting, federated organizations gaining central authority, twice-yearly substantive briefings, immediate escalation when incidents emerge, and private audit-committee sessions modeled on Sarbanes-Oxley practice so security leaders can speak candidly.

The conversation closes with audience questions on phishing awareness for executives, insider and privileged-access risk, investing in people over tools, career incentives for CISOs, and using frameworks plus independent assessments to give directors verifiable comfort without punitive “gotcha” reviews. The through-line for practitioners is communication, courage to escalate material issues, and metrics boards can grasp without drowning in technical detail.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed NextGen
talks.teaser: Live demos strip user-land hooks, abuse USB network gadgets on locked PCs, flash rogue BIOS, and target production voting hardware.
talks.summary:
The session chains several live offensive demonstrations framed around limitations of user-land hooking on modern Windows. After PatchGuard pushed security products into user mode, malicious code can enumerate loaded modules, compare hooked DLL sections against on-disk clean copies, and restore unhooked images in milliseconds—blinding antivirus, EDR, and similar tools that depend on hooks. A browser exploit delivers proof-of-concept unhooking and arbitrary code execution despite a tier-one product on the victim; the same chain fails when the initial exploit is blocked.

A Poison Tap-style Raspberry Pi presents itself as a gateway, captures DHCP traffic from a locked workstation, and injects JavaScript into refreshed non-TLS pages to pull down further exploits and ransomware. Firmware work walks through email-delivered droppers, privilege elevation, signing bypass, and system management mode access to overwrite UEFI on an updated Windows 10 system with Device Guard and secure boot—ending in an early-boot lock and bricked platform. Ransomware-as-a-service economics are noted briefly as a plausible payload.

The closing scenario targets a fielded voting terminal booting from attacker-controlled compact flash in a PCMCIA carrier, relying on weak update authentication and static keys recoverable by reverse engineering. Physical presence at the machine is required, but slots are unsecured and the attack grants full box control. Recommendations stress authenticated BIOS flashing, enabling platform protection features vendors often ship disabled, Chipsec checks, and not trusting user-land visibility alone.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: Real-World Tradecraft of Bears, Pandas and Kittens
talks.teaser: Demonstrates intrusion tradecraft attributed to Russian and Chinese actors, from shortcut lures to WMI persistence.
talks.summary:
This session, presented by CrowdStrike's leaders, is framed as an awards show walking through intrusion stages attributed to Russian bear and Chinese panda actors. The examples are drawn from real cases, and the presenters cite about 30 billion events per day across 176 countries as the scale of their visibility.

The initial access cases start with a bear-attributed shortcut file that hides its .lnk extension and carries a PowerShell loader, an encoded payload and a decoy Word document. Its layout is built with a script that pads the target to a fixed length so offsets stay predictable. The panda lure instead relies on a macro in a Word document that launches PowerShell, which needs no exploit but requires users to enable macros. For privilege escalation, a bear UAC bypass spoofs Explorer's command line and plants a DLL in System32, while a panda kernel zero-day was reported to Microsoft in 2015 and later reappeared at a customer. Persistence included a bear WMI event subscription that ran a payload at each interactive logon, and a panda service DLL that ran inside a shared service host.

Exfiltration examples were a bear method that archives files with makecab and mounts OneDrive over SSL with net use, and a panda habit of using RAR. Suggested countermeasures include showing hidden extensions through registry or group policy, blocking Office macros, limiting admin rights, upgrading to the final Windows Creators Update, auditing WMI and PowerShell activity, and using EDR to watch archiving tools. Several demos were skipped for time.

talks.title: Ted Schlein and Michèle Flournoy on the Future of Security and Defense
talks.teaser: A former Pentagon policy official and a security investor discuss Russia, surveillance oversight, and national cyber resilience.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with Russia's hacking of the Democratic National Committee and the wider campaign Flournoy links to Georgia, Ukraine and Estonia. She argues the United States has no settled cyber doctrine for responding to a consequential attack on public institutions, and that federal civilian agencies lack the resilience the military has built. Public-private partnerships and the movement of skilled people between industry and government are presented as the fix.

The conversation then turns to process. Flournoy says the National Security Council needs a disciplined way to bring dissent and risk assessments to the president, and that intelligence agencies must give unwelcome analysis without fear of retribution. On surveillance, she describes a report with more than 60 recommendations, centered on the Section 702 reauthorization due at year end, and suggests publishing collection categories and rough scale without exposing sources. She also faults the immigration executive order for alienating Iraqi and Muslim partners fighting extremists.

On defense acquisition, she argues the Pentagon builds rather than buys, that continuing resolutions block long-term planning, and that staff need training and incentives to use new authorities. Her closing scenarios include escalation with China, a collapse of the Iran deal, and an India-Pakistan crisis involving tactical nuclear weapons. The takeaway is that basic hygiene matters even for smaller organizations, and that resilience matters more than perfect defense.

talks.title: Protecting People and Content from Threats Already on the Inside
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders should focus on people and their intent, since threats already sit inside networks.
talks.summary:
Forcepoint CEO Matt Moynahan opens by arguing that the security industry must change its focus. Customers report that risks feel more severe while vendors meet their needs less well, and he argues that people are the constant in this shifting landscape. He describes how any employee can move from trusted insider to malicious or compromised insider depending on personal pressures, and he frames malware as largely a matter of impersonation: the real challenge is determining which identity an intruder has taken once inside.

He cites company research showing that fewer than one in three respondents felt they got their money's worth from cybersecurity spending, and that fewer than half expected more technology to solve the problem. A separate sample of enterprises reported critical data on removable media, mobile and BYOD devices, and private and public clouds. Drawing on Thomas Kuhn's ideas about confirmation bias and on military thinking, he argues that defenders should assume an intruder is already inside. He lays out a continuum of intent, from a distressed employee to an outside attacker, and says CISOs should understand workforce behavior while treating staff as partners.

He closes with crowdsourcing, pointing to the Boston bombing investigation, where public photos and videos helped identify suspects, and suggests employees could opt in to help protect their organizations. His takeaway is that technology is not magic, and that focusing on people, their intent and their behavior is the way to remain relevant.

talks.title: The Cyber-Circus: What the Rise of Hacking Everyday Things Means for All of Us
talks.teaser: Examines how hacks on medical devices, cars and webcams shape public trust, media hype and how companies work with researchers.
talks.summary:
Keren Elazari opens with the rise of hacking everyday connected things in 2017, from baby monitors and cars to insulin pumps and pacemakers, and asks whether well-meaning researchers could help makers ship safer devices. She presents hackers as a kind of immune system for connected life and recalls Barnaby Jack's demonstration of remotely triggering an insulin pump, which was followed by regulatory warnings to medical device makers.

The middle of the talk contrasts several cases. A coordinated disclosure by Jay Radcliffe with Johnson & Johnson ended in a software update, while St. Jude Medical's dispute with MedSec, which worked alongside a short-selling firm, showed how badly a disclosure can go. The remote takeover of a Jeep led to a recall of more than a million vehicles, and Tesla responded by signing firmware updates and recognising top researchers. Mirai then showed how default credentials on webcams and routers could power a large denial-of-service attack, and Elazari questioned media fear-mongering and the spread of fear, uncertainty and doubt.

She closes with practical steps: people should treat the devices in their homes as their own responsibility by changing default passwords and demanding safer products, fact-check alarming claims, and watch efforts such as FTC competitions on update mechanisms, the I Am The Cavalry group and bug bounty programs. Her takeaway is that how vendors respond to researchers matters as much as the flaws themselves.

talks.title: RSAC TV: Jeremy Rowley Interview
talks.teaser: Explores how cryptography and certificate management can shore up IoT devices, from risk assessment to healthcare settings.
talks.summary:
In this short interview, Sean Sposito of the Christian Science Monitor talks with Jeremy Rowley of DigiCert about securing Internet of Things devices. Rowley's starting advice is to run a risk assessment on each device first, to learn what data it sends, how that data is used and where it goes. From there, organizations should authenticate and encrypt communications and protect their integrity in transit.

The conversation moves through recent device incidents, including compromised home automation systems and CCTV cameras, and a pacemaker case in which the stock was shorted. Rowley argues that cryptography has moved beyond large RSA 2048-bit web certificates and can now reach low-power devices, including RFID tags, with small signatures and automated provisioning. Code signing, device certificates for encrypted links, and user or device credentials all have roles. In healthcare, he describes infusion pumps where cryptography should authenticate the remote controller, encrypt traffic and confirm the pump's integrity, while patient data and hospital operations face ransomware risk.

Rowley describes DigiCert's automated provisioning platform, which manages credentials from issuance through renewal and revocation, because security needs to change over time. His closing advice for defenders is to assess devices and their data, get the board to treat security as part of the product from design time, deploy PKI, and involve security professionals throughout the device lifecycle rather than relying only on tools.

talks.summary:
Overview: Tim Wilson is editor-in-chief and co-founder of Dark Reading.com, the IT industry's most widely-read online community for computer security. In this role, Wilson is responsible for managing the site, assigning and editing much of the content, and writing breaking news stories. Wilson also directs the content behind Dark Reading's webcasts, digital issues, and the Dark Reading University program, and is a contributor to UBM's Black Hat and Interop events. Wilson has been recognized

Key Topics: three times as one of the top cybersecurity journalists in the U.S. in voting among his peers held by the SANS Institute. In 2011, Wilson was named one of the 50 Most Powerful Voices in Security in research conducted by SYS-CON Media. Prior to joining Dark Reading.com, Wilson was the business editor for Network Computing, one of the industry's leading communities on IT infrastructure and networking. A veteran of the IT industry, Wilson has spent 20 years as a journalist, including eight years as a top editor and reporter for CMP Media's InternetWeek (originally called Communications Week). As executive editor of DataTrends Publicat

Takeaways: four industry newsletters on the subject of data communications, edited several others, and wrote a half-dozen books on the topic. Wilson also has served as an industry analyst with two globally-recognized IT consulting firms: Decisys Inc. (now part of Gartner) and Enterprise Management Associates.

talks.title: RSAC TV: Matt Moynahan interview
talks.teaser: Argues that insider risk is a people problem, and that defenders should focus on user intent and behavior.
talks.summary:
This interview with the chief executive of a security company, hosted by a news content strategist, looks at why defenders keep trailing technology change. The guest argues that defenders consistently lag behind shifts such as cloud and apps, which gives attackers the edge. He says the constant is people, because enterprises run on staff who handle intellectual property and critical data, and that the perimeter can no longer be treated as a dependable boundary.

The insider mindset comes next. Rather than relying on walls and antivirus, the guest suggests assuming that someone inside the organization may be able to take data, including well-meaning employees who have been compromised. Defenders should model what each user, partner or customer needs to do their job, then flag behavior that departs from that baseline. He describes pairing data leakage prevention with an understanding of human intent, and frames the gap as focused data on how people handle critical content rather than sheer volume. Asked about attackers abusing Google services for command and control, he pointed to prevention informed by intent.

The discussion closes with the distinction between malicious insiders, staff compromised by nation-state actors, and accidental leaks, all of which depend on intent and behavior that change over time. For advice to security leaders, he urged CISOs to focus on people rather than infrastructure, assume that anyone touching the network is already inside it, and lock down access to what each entity needs. He noted that data now flows fastest from enterprises to clouds and mobile devices, so that flow cannot be pulled back.

talks.title: Planning for Chaos
talks.teaser: Links chaos and ripple effects to business-driven security through risk science, vendor discipline, and incident plans with real resources.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with a ripple metaphor—from the invention of public-key cryptography through today's hyper-connected world—and argues that cyber and physical shocks propagate far beyond the first incident. Examples range from election-related breach discourse and the 2011 Japan earthquake–tsunami–Fukushima chain to concerns about remotely compromised vehicles and consumer devices amplifying distributed attacks.

The speaker defines business-driven security as connecting technical controls to business outcomes, names the "gap of grief" when executives hear jargon instead of impact, and uses humor to show why security and business leadership must work as one venture. Three practices follow: treat risk as a science with consistent frameworks such as FAIR or bow-tie analysis and disciplined what-if thinking; simplify what you control by consolidating dozens of vendors and integrating tools with business context; and plan for uncontrollable chaos with incident response built on availability of real resources, budget authority, and cross-functional collaboration—not wish lists.

The close ties chaos to growth, collaboration, diversity, and mentorship—including scholar programs—and a short on-stage dialogue with Michael Dell on CEOs prioritizing security risk, IT becoming business technology, and optimism around secure digital transformation.

talks.title: The Dridex Swiss Army Knife: Big Data Dissolves the APT and Crime Grey Area
talks.teaser: Traces how the Dridex crime group grew from Zeus-era roots into rented malware and APT-style intrusions.
talks.summary:
This talk from a Fox-IT product director follows the criminal group behind Dridex from its roots in the Game Over Zeus era. It explains how a gang that lost its peer-to-peer botnet after law enforcement action rebuilt around new malware, keeping the money laundering network, fake companies and bribery contacts its predecessors had built. Dridex is presented as rented crimeware, with operator groups paying for access to its infrastructure.

The middle section covers how the group used data gathered from infected machines. Stored behavioral data let operators find bookkeeping PCs and admin machines at smaller companies, which were then moved into separate botnets. Operators watched victims for weeks to learn their pay schedules, then used remote access and a fake software-upgrade prompt asking for a smart card PIN to approve a single high-value transfer. In some intrusions, attackers moved sideways with Metasploit and stayed hidden for months, a pattern the speaker described as overlapping with APT tradecraft.

The closing argument is that criminals now face little financial risk, since their costs shifted from capital spending to operating costs, and their targets now include any company with a few dozen staff. Laundering that once needed a thousand money mules now needs only a handful of fake companies, the speaker said. The practical advice is to revisit Dridex detection rules and prepare for these hybrid intrusion patterns.

talks.title: Effective Application Security Testing for DevOps
talks.teaser: Covers placing application security tests in DevOps pipelines so they stay fast and only report valid issues.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that DevOps adoption is coming whether or not security teams welcome it, and that security can gain from its traits. Frequent, traceable changes improve auditability, the heavy automation DevOps requires is something security teams need anyway, and closer work between development and operations creates chances for security to take part. The speaker advises security to follow where the organization is heading, meet DevOps teams in their own tools and processes, and embed controls into those practices rather than bolting them on.

Within a continuous integration and delivery pipeline, application security tests are split into synchronous checks that gate a build and asynchronous ones that report later. The speaker names two priorities: report only valid issues, because false positives will get security removed from the process, and run fast. He also covers trade-offs. Tuning to cut false positives can reduce coverage, and testing only changed code can miss valid vulnerabilities. Pass criteria should be realistic. Blocking only new critical or high findings is more acceptable in a legacy application with many existing flaws than demanding zero. Results belong in the defect tracking or change management systems developers already use, not in PDF or spreadsheet reports.

The talk closes with practical steps: take a development manager to lunch, learn their tools and process, and find out where DevOps initiatives are underway. Then pilot application security testing in one pipeline to learn lessons, and build a plan for an enterprise-wide rollout.

talks.title: Delivering Effective Security Outcomes
talks.teaser: Outlines how cloud-scale analytics and turnkey integrations shorten detection and response to rebalance defense against commodity attacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing every breach as an economic tax and recalling a longtime imbalance: attackers need only one success while defenders must cover every gap. Two commodity incidents illustrate the point—a municipal transit ransomware case driven by scripted scanning and a massive DDoS event built from compromised internet-facing IoT gear—alongside forecasts of tens of billions more connected devices, denser encrypted traffic, and harder east-west visibility.

Rather than asking boards whether the organization is “secure” at a moment in time, the speaker argues for measuring whether security posture stays effective through continuous blocking, segmentation, access control, and especially paired improvements in time to detection and time to response. Automation remains elusive because stacks sprawl across dozens of non-interoperating vendors—APIs shift integration burden to customers—and because “artificial stupidity” from missing context breeds disruptive false positives.

The closing case treats cloud compute, storage, and shared intelligence as a security state machine: correlate hashes and behavior globally, orchestrate policy once, and push outcomes to email, web, and endpoint controls together. Practitioners are urged to evaluate products by how they unlock analytics in the cloud and ship ready integrations, and to press vendors toward that bar so automated response can scale with device growth.

talks.title: Security Implications of Non-Financial Uses of Blockchain Technology
talks.teaser: Surveys non-payment blockchain uses like land records and smart contracts, and the people and ecosystem risks around them.
talks.summary:
Thomas Keenan, a professor at the University of Calgary, opens by separating Bitcoin from the blockchain beneath it. He describes the blockchain as a public ledger of transactions in which each block carries a hash linking it to the previous one, so tampering gets detected by validators. He then lists why businesses like it: direct ownership, fast settlement, low cost, programmability through smart contracts, and proof that a transaction occurred.

He moves on to non-financial uses. A German firm aims to verify artworks and stop unauthorised numbered copies. A Honduran project to move land titles onto a blockchain failed because of people rather than technology. Walmart tests tracing of food products, a sneaker maker uses it against counterfeits, and an IBM example has a washing machine ordering its own supplies. A Finnish project explores shipping containers that reroute cargo. He also sketches automated death processes that freeze accounts, pay insurance and settle taxes. On risk, he covers 51% attacks by colluding mining power, citing a New York Times report that four Chinese mining pools handled over 70% of Bitcoin transactions. He also shows that blockchain is pseudonymous rather than private, since IP addresses, address reuse and change outputs can reveal links.

He concludes that the core technology's risks are manageable, while wallets, exchanges such as Mt. Gox and the people who run systems are the real danger. His practical advice is to buy a small amount to learn the process, follow developments, and move non-critical business processes onto a blockchain first.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Roadmap: Global Healthcare Security Architecture
talks.teaser: Shows how a large healthcare IT firm used the NIST framework to turn tool sprawl into a prioritized security architecture roadmap.
talks.summary:
The speaker, chief security architect at a large healthcare IT company, explained how his organization used the NIST Cybersecurity Framework to build a security architecture and roadmap. The starting point was sprawl: an inventory across business units found roughly 130 products from seven vendors, bought reactively in response to compliance demands, vendor pitches and new vulnerabilities, with little governance or refresh planning. When management asked whether the extra tools had improved posture, the team had no clear answer.

The team adopted NIST because it is a respected baseline and a flexible guideline rather than a checkbox exercise. They tailored it into their own domain architectures, such as network, identity and access management, and application and data. Each domain was checked so that its capabilities spread across protect, detect and respond, could integrate with the others, and fed lessons from detection back into prevention. Threat modeling and risk analysis set priorities. A current-state map showed little visibility or control over cloud and SaaS use, which drove a cloud-first future-state design. Identity controls were applied to about 100 of the most sensitive applications, and the findings were condensed into six to eight key initiatives alongside a push to consolidate vendors.

The main takeaway was that NIST worked well as a risk-based foundation when treated as a guideline. The speaker suggested that teams evaluating it spend about a week judging fit, then three to six months analyzing their current environment and defining a future-state roadmap. In the Q&A, the discussion covered adaptive authentication, limiting access from unmanaged devices and staffing shortages as practical obstacles.

talks.title: Cyberwar in 2020
talks.teaser: Forecasts how cyberwar, geopolitics and digital governance may evolve by 2020, linking connectivity, deterrence and transparency.
talks.summary:
Kenneth Geers looks about three years ahead to predict how cyberwar and digital politics may develop by 2020. He argues that global connectivity has linked citizens across borders while governments struggle to keep pace. He sees political hacking and information operations as major disruptions, and suggests that social media makes tight information control in closed states hard to sustain, possibly fuelling uprisings similar to the Arab Spring. Corruption in Ukraine contrasts with Estonia's e-government model, which he presents as a template for transparency and accountability.

On technology, he names biometrics for authentication and virtual reality in gaming as trends to watch, and calls blockchain the most exciting technology for government, since it could keep a durable record of budgets, financial transactions and salaries. On international affairs he argues that deterrence is hard to establish, that espionage and sabotage fall under very different legal authorities, and that the EU and NATO offer the strongest venues for treaties limiting cyber espionage. He notes that tanks, ships and aircraft are networked computers, so militaries will hack in peacetime to prepare for war.

He closes by considering law enforcement powers, comparing the shock of a chess champion losing to Deep Blue with what surveillance might allow if authorities could see into homes and bodies. He admits that the next decade is hard to forecast and that technologies nobody anticipates will change the picture.

talks.title: IoT: End of Shorter Days
talks.teaser: Uses a resold connected car still linked to its old owner's app to argue for better access revocation in IoT.
talks.summary:
Charles Henderson, Global Head of X-Force Red at IBM, opens with a story about a convertible he owned. The car was connected to a mobile app that controlled navigation, climate, location and remote features. He sold it to a dealership after doing what he considered a thorough reset, including a factory reset and clearing the Bluetooth and garage door opener pairings. Hours later the old car was still listed in his app, and it stayed there for years. He describes how that leftover access could have let someone honk the horn, unlock the car, or steal it.

He then explains what went wrong and why. Automakers are paid on the first sale, so there is little incentive to manage a car remotely after that. Ownership changes are hard for manufacturers to see, and these devices offer no clear account management or alerts showing who has access. He compares this to the mobile phone industry, which established a reliable factory reset process that protects personal data at resale, and argues that carmakers need the same, along with education for used car lots that buy back and resell vehicles.

He closes with the steps he recommends. Standards, whether government-backed, industry-created or independent, are needed, but they must be paired with user training so owners know to find and use factory reset. Used car buyers should ask about connected features before purchase, and both new and used owners need to know how to shut off remote access when a car changes hands. He stresses that awareness among owners matters most.

talks.title: Adventures in Underland: What System Stores on the Disk Without Telling You
talks.teaser: Shows which Windows disk artifacts keep traces of past activity, from search indexes and prefetch files to DPAPI-protected secrets.
talks.summary:
Paula Januszkiewicz walks through places in Windows where the operating system keeps data that users rarely see or think to delete. She starts with browser cache from a private browsing session, which still gets written to disk, and then moves to the Windows Search indexing database, an 11 GB file that she copies through a shadow copy and opens in a free viewer. It can reveal files that were indexed even after they were deleted.

Other artifacts follow. Prefetch files record which programs ran and when, and in one incident a customer used them to find the first machine that ran CryptoLocker. The Remote Desktop bitmap cache can be parsed to rebuild screens seen during a session, and jump lists show which files were opened in each application. She also shows that NTFS timestamps can be changed, so metadata alone is not reliable. Using the file's cluster location, she recovers a deleted executable and its digital signature, and notes that small files under about 700 bytes can remain in the MFT after deletion.

The last section covers DPAPI, where the master keys that protect saved passwords depend on the user's password hash and, in a domain, on a domain backup key. She decrypts a KeePass database in a demo to show the exposure. Her takeaways are that domain members should not rely on Windows account protection alone for secrets, that a master password combined with a key file kept outside the system is safer, and that Sysmon is useful for monitoring which processes run.

talks.title: Auditors in the Cloud: Audit Risk and SaaS Applications
talks.teaser: Explains how auditors and security teams can bring unmanaged SaaS applications under control without slowing business adoption.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about a CISO at a lending organisation who, during a budget-driven maturity review, found a serious controls gap. Business units were signing up for SaaS applications on their own, IT did not know about them, and the company was also replacing core on-premises systems. The speaker argues that security should come before audit and compliance, and that auditors should act as enablers who help the business adopt cloud services safely rather than as keepers of a checklist.

The middle of the talk turns to practical steps. The first is a current inventory of every application in use, including the ones the business adopted without IT, followed by an inventory of existing security capabilities to identify residual risk. For vendors, the speaker recommends asking cloud-specific questions, with the Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix as a starting point. Teams should also check what their infrastructure provider already offers, such as audit logs and alerting, and whether each SaaS application exposes an API that can send events to a SIEM. Identity-as-a-service platforms and federated single sign-on can add visibility and control with less friction.

In the question-and-answer segment, the speaker suggests that cloud firewall needs can be met with security groups when the intent of the control is kept in mind, and that data loss prevention in SaaS is mostly detective, so access management matters more. The takeaway is to be honest in self-assessments, survey each application's capabilities before accepting risk, and treat audit as a consultative role.

talks.title: Briefing the Board: Lessons Learned from CISOs and Directors
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn how successful CISOs frame cybersecurity strategy and metrics so boards trust leadership and enable the business.
talks.summary:
Security leaders frequently struggle when presenting cybersecurity to corporate boards. The speakers describe a year-long series of working sessions that brought CISOs and directors together to separate hype from practice and capture what actually lands in the boardroom.

The first half stresses that winning programs convince business and IT peers to act, not only run technical controls. Boards expect strategy tied to digitization, consistent metrics comparable over time, and language about business enablement and efficiency—not feature lists or fear. Audio from directors and CISOs reinforces that boards are not budget ATMs; they defer to a few technology-savvy members and increasingly gate funding for initiatives that ignore cyber risk. Examples include trending vulnerability closure rates, mean time to detect under 24 hours and mitigate under 36 hours, and cases where security funding produced faster partner onboarding, cheaper incident handling, or SDL improvements with peer benchmarks.

The closing guidance reframes the briefing goal: leave directors confident in the CISO’s judgment, not literate in acronyms. Presentations should drop jargon, avoid startling the room without a plan, reuse meaningful charts quarterly, and never ambush the CEO or CIO. Practitioners should harvest operational metrics, elevate those that show business impact, and use organizational transitions to drive near-term wins they can report upward.

talks.title: Hacker's Perspective on Your Windows Infrastructure: Mandatory Check List
talks.teaser: Offensive demos map reflective loaders, domain DPAPI key abuse, and SMB relay against typical Windows deployments.
talks.summary:
Large Windows environments hide misconfigurations that external and insider attackers hunt systematically. The session argues that almost every operating-system action leaves traces, while default Event Viewer views still miss much of what ETW-capable monitoring can record, and urges defenders to replay one demonstrated technique at home against their own estate.

Live segments cover a reflective PE loader that repackages tooling such as Mimikatz so signature- and behavior-based antivirus largely ignores it, then cached domain logon credentials altered offline through recovery-console access. Exporting the domain backup key from a domain controller enables decrypting user DPAPI master keys and secrets such as browser passwords without local admin on the workstation. An SMB relay demo chains Metasploit handlers with relay scripts so NTLMv2 challenges captured on a noisy LAN—often within five to fifteen minutes—yield interactive access, including migration into svchost.

Closing guidance targets NetBIOS reduction, Kerberos-friendly service principal names, optional SMB signing, and code execution prevention on sensitive systems including domain controllers, plus domain-admin oversight, local admin password management, and constrained PowerShell use. The practical message is that antivirus and default caching assumptions rarely stop these paths once an attacker understands the victim’s controls.

talks.title: Hello False Flags! The Art of Deception in Targeted Attack Attribution
talks.teaser: Examines how planted false flags such as fake personas, stolen certificates and decoy malware mislead attribution efforts.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that attributing targeted attacks is hard, partly because analysts often lack formal training and because public reports teach attackers which clues researchers rely on. Compile times, debug paths, targeting, infrastructure, shared code and reused keys can all be faked, so each indicator has to be treated as fallible.

Their cases show deception in practice. Cloud Atlas left Spanish document metadata, Hindi and Arabic strings and altered system clocks before compiling, and it sent investigators a decoy Chinese payload in place of its real second stage. Wild Neutron hit large tech firms, law firms and extremist forums, which undermines targeting as a signal. Lazarus used short-lived hacktivist fronts, and APT28 ran personas such as CyberBerkut and a fake Fancy Bears hack team. Duqu 2 carried a string tied to the APT1 handle Ugly Gorilla, Tiger Milk was signed with a certificate stolen for Stuxnet, and Turla pushed a Chinese-origin stage two onto a machine it knew responders were examining before removing its traces.

The takeaways separate needs by audience. Threat intelligence supplies historical context that incident response cannot. Private organisations usually need country, motivation or cluster-level attribution, governments need individuals for sanctions, and journalists should ask for the evidence behind a claim. Producers should prioritise actionable indicators, and attribution-driven hack-back is risky.

talks.title: Why Cyber-Training Is Key, and How to Do It Right
talks.teaser: Weighs degrees, certifications, CTFs and online courses as routes into cyber work amid a workforce shortage.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short video in which a penetration tester compromises a local reporter's and a volunteer's computers using a spoofed text and a crafted link. The speaker argues that public understanding of cyber risk still lags behind physical security, and that the workforce gap makes training a pressing problem. He points to a recent executive order calling for a review of cyber training, and to the CyberSeek job-data tool as an effort to measure the shortage.

The middle of the talk surveys skill areas, from secure software engineering and malware analysis to security research and data science. He notes that the deeper roles demand top-tier expertise that takes years to build. He then reports conversations with educators, military instructors and practitioners. Views differ: some favour formal computer science education, others stress passion, mentorship, hands-on degrees or career changers moving in sideways. Several described the security operations center as an entry point for people retraining from other fields, and warned that trainers who project arrogance teach less than patient ones.

He concludes that no single path fits everyone and that a mix works best: college or equivalent for foundations, short targeted programs for employers, online courses, capture-the-flag events, conferences and social media for continuing learning. He encourages listeners to try an online class or a CTF, and to give back to the people who helped them along the way.

talks.title: EU Data Privacy: What US Orgs Need to Do Now to Prepare for GDPR
talks.teaser: Breaks down GDPR fines, consent, breach reporting and data rights, and what US organizations should check before the deadline.
talks.summary:
The talk explains what the EU General Data Protection Regulation means for organizations outside Europe that handle personal data of EU residents. Chris Zoladz starts with the penalties, which can reach 4% of global top-line revenue or 20 million euros, whichever is greater, and argues that business leaders need those figures to take compliance seriously. The rule applies wherever the company is based, replaces the 1995 data protection directive and takes effect in May 2018.

The obligations get most of the attention. Consent must be explicit and separate from long terms and conditions, and children under 16 need verifiable parental or guardian consent, an age member states may lower to 13. Individuals can request access, correction, erasure and data portability, which is hard when records sit in many systems. Breaches must be reported to regulators within 72 hours and sometimes to affected people. Article 32 on security is brief and leaves reasonable measures open to interpretation, naming encryption and pseudonymization as examples. Data protection impact assessments are required for new systems, controls need periodic testing, and vendors and cloud providers remain the company's responsibility.

For practitioners, the talk recommends agreeing on one definition of personal data, mapping data flows including shadow IT, and separating EU records where possible. It also urges documented request handling, an incident response plan, and early budgeting, since calendar budgets may already be set. Zoladz cited a survey where only 37% of respondents said they were fully compliant with the security and breach requirements.

talks.title: A Field Guide to Insider Threat Helps Manage the Risk
talks.teaser: Maps insider threats into nine attack types and thirteen threat agents, then shows how to prioritize and manage them.
talks.summary:
Tim Casey, a senior strategic risk analyst at Intel, presents the Insider Threat Field Guide, a model his analyst team built over a nearly year-long research project. It identifies nine ways an insider can affect an organization and 13 kinds of people or entities that can be one, and maps known incidents to at least 60 distinct threat vectors. Casey argues that the problem reaches well beyond the stereotypical spy or dishonest accountant.

Casey walks through the categories. Partners and suppliers can be either hostile or non-hostile, since they may be breached or may be fronts built to steal intellectual property. He also describes an "outward sympathizer", an insider who uses company systems to act against an outside party, which can draw legal attention to the organization. Among attack types, accidental leak, data exfiltration and opportunistic theft are explained. Terrorism is left out as a label because its impact spans several categories that each need separate mitigation. In a food producer example, product alteration and sabotage are ranked as the most catastrophic and tackled first.

Casey recommends using the guide to open discussions with IT, security, HR and legal, to make an initial assessment, and to record incidents in consistent categories so trends can be reported to stakeholders. The model can be tailored, such as adding a threat agent for staff who snoop in patient records or splitting espionage into economic and military types. In the Q&A he notes that quantified incident data is scarce and presents the guide as a first version open to feedback.
