talks.title: Building a Healthy Organization: The Last Great Competitive Advantage
talks.teaser: Explores why organizational health amplifies technical skill and presents tactics for building aligned, trustworthy leadership teams.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that security organizations need two foundations to succeed: operational smarts (strategy, technology, metrics) and organizational health. Most leadership time goes to the measurable “smart” side, while confusion, politics, low morale, and wasted effort often trace to neglect of the “healthy” side. He defines health as clarity about success and failure, reduced politics, genuine morale for top performers, and better productivity and retention.

He introduces four disciplines: a behaviorally and intellectually aligned leadership team, ongoing communication of clarity, and systems that reinforce stated values. The session then walks through vulnerability-based trust, productive ideological conflict, commitment with buy-in, peer accountability, collective results, and the “team number one” idea—that the team you serve on should outrank the team you lead.

For practitioners, especially in fast-moving security environments, the takeaway is that technical excellence cannot compensate for misaligned teams, “meetings after the meetings,” or decisions shut down by rank. Building health is simple in concept but hard in practice; progress starts with leaders modeling vulnerability, agreeing on conflict norms, and bringing real conversations back into the room.

talks.title: Hacking Blockchain
talks.teaser: A security consultant surveys famous exchange and smart-contract breaches plus quantum risks to elliptic-curve keys used on public ledgers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames blockchain as another computing shift where trust assumptions failed before, then walks through ledger basics: blocks, proof of work, consensus, and the promise that transactions are hard to reverse. Most failures described are not protocol miracles gone wrong but weak wrappers—exchanges that never touched the chain, missing two-factor authentication, sloppy operations, and buggy smart contracts.

Case studies span the early Bitcoin stack bug, Mt. Gox losses tied to admin access and transaction malleability, cold-wallet bypass after infrastructure reboots, the DAO recursive split draining Ether, payment processors hit via social engineering, mobile wallet theft, Bitfinex multisig mistakes, node and denial-of-service angles, and a successful large-scale majority hash-power attack. The speaker stresses testing implementations, not only buying blockchain branding.

The closing arc ties Satoshi’s impractical-to-reverse line to elliptic-curve signatures exposed when addresses are spent, Shor’s algorithm on quantum hardware, and hash-based options such as Lamport signatures plus initiatives like Open Quantum Safe. Practitioners are urged to question whether data must be immutable, prioritize high-criticality financial apps, use testers with real blockchain experience, and plan post-quantum migration before ecosystems become too large to refactor.

talks.title: Regulating the Internet of Things
talks.teaser: The presentation links IoT growth to physical-world harm and outlines why government regulation may become unavoidable.
talks.summary:
Bruce Schneier opens by treating the Internet of Things as sensors, cloud “smarts,” and actuators that together form a distributed, world-scale robot with real-world leverage. He argues that as ordinary objects become computers, computer security becomes universal security, with integrity and availability failures outweighing classic confidentiality worries—from DDoS’d thermostats and SCADA abuse to cascaded account takeovers and Mirai-scale botnets built on unpatchable DVRs.

He distills five recurring lessons: insecure software, dangerous extensibility, complexity, non-composable interconnections, and scaled “class breaks.” Cheap embedded gear lacks phone-like patch ecosystems, so buyers and sellers ignore externalized risk much as pre-regulation food or auto safety. That forces a collision between “get it right the first time” physical regulation and agile software update culture, seen in ATMs on old Windows, certified medical gear that cannot patch, and contrasting Chrysler recalls versus Tesla overnight fixes.

Near-term vendor checklists abound but lack adoption; markets and collective-action gaps will not close the gap alone. He surveys regulatory levers (standards, liability, labeling, procurement), European momentum, and a U.S. need for holistic authority across agency silos, while warning that fear-driven bureaucracy could mirror post-9/11 overreach. Courts, torts, and disasters will likely precede thoughtful statutes. He closes urging technologists into policy roles—public-interest career paths, insurance as an informed proxy, certification debates, and conscious limits on connectivity—plus brief Q&A on global enforcement when insecure devices remain abroad.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2017: RedLock
talks.teaser: Pitches an automated cloud security tool that discovers workloads and scores risk so analysts know what to fix first.
talks.summary:
RedLock pitches a cloud security product aimed at the gap between raw cloud logs and actionable priorities. The speaker opens with a statistic about how quickly cloud workloads change, arguing that collecting logs alone does not help a security team. The product discovers a cloud environment automatically by pulling data through dozens of provider APIs, covering network traffic, resource configurations and user activity.

Because that data still has gaps, the platform applies data science to fill in missing pieces. It also ingests inputs such as vulnerability management tools, SIEM systems and threat intelligence feeds. The goal is to give a junior SOC analyst the context needed to see which risks matter most and what to respond to first. Risk is scored in a way the speaker likens to credit scoring in finance, so environments can be ranked for prioritization.

As an example, the speaker describes an Amazon EC2 instance being used as a database that was found communicating with an unknown malicious IP address. The platform attaches context to that finding and quantifies its risk. The talk closes by noting the product has seen over 3.5 petabytes of network traffic, with the speaker expressing enthusiasm for where the product is heading.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2017: Veriflow
talks.teaser: Explains how a network-wide predictive model checks every change against intent to catch segmentation errors and outage risks.
talks.summary:
The pitch starts from the problem of network complexity. The speaker says enterprise networks are growing harder to manage as cloud, hybrid cloud, virtualization, SDN and containers spread, while changes arrive faster. They cite a figure that 80% of outages and vulnerabilities trace in part to human factors, and argue that securing networks device by device is no longer enough.

The company borrows its approach from formal verification, the mathematical checking used for medical devices, microprocessors and NASA's Mars rovers. Its product pulls low-level data plane state from each device, normalizes it into one functional representation, and builds a network-wide predictive model. That model predicts possible data flows without inspecting live traffic. The result is then compared against the network's intended behavior, which the speaker says is drawn from a best-practice library, analytics algorithms and a programmable API.

The talk lists several use cases. Verification can expose errors in network segmentation and microsegmentation that would otherwise go unnoticed, and it can flag changes likely to cause an outage. The product also covers continuous compliance, dynamic mapping and rapid incident response. The takeaway for practitioners is to verify each network change as part of the normal workflow rather than relying on device-level checks alone.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2017: Baffle
talks.teaser: Shows a startup's encryption-as-a-service that keeps database data encrypted while SQL operations still run.
talks.summary:
Baffle pitches an encryption-as-a-service offering aimed at a gap in enterprise security: many organisations run a mix of databases, each with its own processes and key handling, and encryption is hard to adopt. The speaker cites a figure that of 5.9 billion records lost since 2013, only 4% were encrypted, meaning most stolen data was unusable to attackers. The stated goal is to keep sensitive information inside the application and never exposed outside it.

The product has two parts. Baffle Shield is a SQL-layer database proxy that stays transparent to the application, and Baffle Manager handles key management along with compliance and audit reporting. The speaker calls the core innovation the separation of keys and encrypted data, which never sit on the same compute instance, achieved with secure multi-party computation. The talk claims all SQL operations work on encrypted data and that no application code changes are needed.

As a demonstration, a retail customer's transaction database protected by Baffle was queried by a Tableau application run by a data scientist. The speaker said the analyst could see every operation performed while the data never appeared in the clear in the database's memory or on disk. The takeaway is that encrypted data can be processed in untrusted compute environments without rewriting applications.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2017: Claroty
talks.teaser: Shows how industrial networks with non-IP devices can be made visible and monitored for abnormal controller commands.
talks.summary:
This is a short company pitch for an industrial security product. It opens with the stakes: networks that run power plants, factories, data centers and other infrastructure depend on industrial IoT, and disrupting them could deny essential services to millions. The speaker points to recent attacks on Ukraine and to criminal groups already active against these networks. These environments are a blind spot for security teams because about half of their nodes are not IP-based, and conventional IT tools cannot read the proprietary industrial protocols.

The middle section explains why these networks are easy to abuse. Attackers often need no sophisticated exploit; they can send legitimate industrial controller commands that IT security tools would not flag as suspicious. The product, as described, maps both IP and non-IP devices and monitors their communication in real time, down to individual valves and sensors. Its deep packet inspection engines parse dozens of open and proprietary protocols, and it builds a granular baseline model to catch deviations and anomalies that could affect safety or security.

The closing points concern outcomes and business traction. The alerts are meant to give InfoSec staff and industrial engineers shared context so they can resolve issues together. The speaker cites partners including Cisco, Accenture and Rockwell, Fortune 500 customers across eight verticals, several seven-figure deals, and all of this within the company's first year of sales. The practical takeaway is that industrial networks need protocol-aware visibility of non-IP assets, because standard IT tooling leaves them largely unseen.

talks.title: Sweating the Small Stuff on a Global Scale
talks.teaser: Examines how small data flaws, home IoT recruits, and joint threat programs must scale together against global adversaries.
talks.summary:
The session opens by contrasting sensational yearly security headlines with the urgency needed when similar scenarios actually unfold, using the 2016 U.S. election as a case where stolen emails, leaked data, and misleading headlines shaped public decisions. The speaker argues that integrity of the small inputs feeding big analytics matters as much as protecting systems themselves, pointing to autonomous fleets processing enormous daily data volumes where falsified telemetry could target traffic models rather than individual vehicles.

A growing attack surface story leads to the connected home: consumer devices that organizations rarely design into enterprise defenses, yet that can harm neighbors and employers when weaponized. The talk recounts large-scale denial-of-service campaigns built from home routers, cameras, and monitors, then describes an internal experiment where a disguised DVR honeypot on an open network was taken over in just over one minute, illustrating how quickly new unprotected gear joins active botnets.

The closing arc rejects any single fix—policy, vendor gadgets, or home hardening alone—and urges industry-wide cooperation modeled on coordinated teamwork. Examples include an open threat-sharing communications fabric, a multi-vendor ransomware victim assistance effort, and a formal alliance among major security vendors with expanded leadership. Children’s recorded concerns about hacking and driverless cars frame the final appeal to treat granular risks seriously so collective outcomes improve.

talks.title: How to Break the Internet
talks.teaser: Surveys publicly exposed buckets and databases that leaked voter rolls, utility assets, and legal records without any stolen credentials.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames “breaking the internet” as the steady stream of sensitive data left open on public services without authentication. The speaker describes becoming a breach hunter after a personal privacy scare, then walking through finds where insurance records, dating-app profiles, nonprofit accounts, and massive voter-registration files sat on open Amazon storage or MongoDB instances. Reporting paths matter as much as discovery: state officials and company executives sometimes urge silence, while the speaker argues that unprotected public endpoints are fair to access and compares them to traveling an open road.

Case studies span fitness and dating platforms, AARP registrations, U.S. and Mexican voter databases tied to vendors and political entities, and assistance to law-enforcement inquiries that treated the work as lawful. Later examples include a California utility’s exposed asset-management inventory, a sanctions-screening database leaking through an unauthenticated CouchDB, predictable filename exposure on a presidential campaign site, and law-firm files revealing discrepancies in a jail-death investigation.

The close highlights still-unpublished finds involving defense-linked research materials, police roster and expense data, and ongoing disclosure conversations. Practitioners should treat “staging” or test labels as irrelevant when real people’s data is involved, notify affected parties when institutions stall, and assume nation-state adversaries could exploit roadmaps such as power-grid asset lists.

talks.title: RSAC TV: Chenxi Wang Interview
talks.teaser: Discusses why security needs more women and a broader image, plus container baselines and IoT security standards.
talks.summary:
In this RSA Conference video interview, Chenxi Wang speaks with a host about why information security struggles to attract women. She argues that the field's image, a hooded hacker in a dim room, pushes people away, and suggests framing the work around social impact instead. She notes that the share of women graduating in computer science has fallen since the 1980s, and that the problem appears in academia as well as industry.

The second half covers cloud and container security. Wang explains that containers package a single function as a unit, which makes it easier to build a reliable behavioral baseline for anomaly detection. Baselines are hard to build for monolithic applications, which change constantly and produce many false positives. She adds that containers are still early, with new transient workloads moving first while large enterprise applications lag behind.

On Internet of Things security, Wang argues the industry first needs agreed minimum viable security standards, with ecosystem controls, regulation and supply chain measures to keep failing products off the market. She notes that the track record is poor, since change usually follows harm. She contrasts harmless spam from smart refrigerators with the Mirai attack that took down part of the internet, and warns that connected devices could eventually put lives at risk.

talks.title: Quick Look: Hacking Exposed NextGen
talks.teaser: Live demos show endpoint hook bypasses, rogue USB implants, BIOS takeover from documents, and practical voting machine result forgery.
talks.summary:
The session positions “next generation” threats as attackers expanding how they probe and exploit everyday technology across the economy. It follows the Hacking Exposed Live format: four attack storylines, each meant to be demonstrated live and explained step by step.

The first segment, Captain Unhooking, argues that antivirus, EDR, DLP, sandboxing, and similar products depend on hooking user mode and kernel activity to see or block behavior—and that a known but rarely shown live bypass can defeat essentially all of them. The second, Boys and Tap, describes a Raspberry Pi device on USB that can compromise a Windows host—even when locked—route traffic through the device, and deliver arbitrary payloads (including via Metasploit) for full remote control, ransomware, or backdoors.

The third covers BIOS as early boot “god mode”: a malicious Word document could alter firmware, reboot, and demand payment, crypto-lock, wipe, or brick the machine. The fourth reviews market U.S. election voting equipment and a simple walk-up takeover that could fabricate candidates, vote totals, or entire results—the speaker stresses illustrating feasibility, not claiming a specific breach occurred. Takeaways span endpoint control assumptions, physical USB trust, firmware persistence from office documents, and the gap between public confidence and practical voting-system attack surface.

talks.title: Quick Look: IoT End of Days
talks.teaser: Highlights blind spots in IoT security after resale, from connected cars to home automation hubs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a gap the security industry and device makers routinely overlook: almost all IoT marketing and testing targets the first owner, while little attention goes to what happens after provisioning ends. Charles Anderson describes how selling a connected vehicle pushed him to wipe personal data, factory-reset the head unit, and work with the dealer on physical keys—steps that protected him as the original owner but exposed how narrow that mindset is.

That resale experience became the impetus for research begun around 2016 into the full lifecycle of internet-connected things, not only automobiles. The same pattern appeared across home automation, smart hubs, and other IoT categories: heavy investment at the front of ownership and weak long-term strategy once devices are transferred or resold.

Practitioners should treat IoT as non-disposable assets that change hands and plan security across the entire lifecycle, including backend ownership changes, not just initial setup and mobile app hardening questions such as provisioning, passwords, session management, and remote control features.

talks.title: Quick Look: Hacker's Perspective on Your Windows Infrastructure: Mandatory Check List
talks.teaser: Shows how Windows stores credentials and how offline access and domain keys can expose them to attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk examines where Windows stores credentials on disk and how an attacker with local or offline access can recover them. A boot key in the system hive protects LSA secrets, such as service account passwords. A live demo elevated to SYSTEM and pulled a test service account's password from its configuration. The second focus was cached logon data, which the speaker argued is not really a set of plain credentials.

Data Protection API secrets, such as browser-saved passwords, are wrapped with master keys tied to the user's password hash and a domain backup key. In an offline demo booted from installation media, cached credentials were dumped and overwritten with a new value. The user could still log on with that password, but the saved browser passwords could no longer be decrypted. Private keys taken from domain controller memory then let the speaker re-encrypt the master key container with a chosen hash and recover the browser passwords again. A domain admin could do the same and reach every such secret in the domain.

The practical advice was to protect domain controllers and their backup key, enforce credential hygiene for privileged accounts, and consider BitLocker against offline access. Sysmon was recommended for recording which processes run on servers.

The talk opens with the Ghost Army, a World War II unit whose inflatable tanks and loudspeaker sounds misled German forces about the Normandy landings. The speaker argues the same idea of deception fits network defense. They cite three reasons breaches succeed: blind spots in the side streets of a network, a focus on attacker tools that are easy to swap, and alert floods that bury real signals under false positives.

Using the pyramid of pain, the speaker contrasts easily changed indicators such as hashes and IP addresses with techniques, tactics and procedures at the top, which are costly for attackers to change. Decoys and planted credentials let defenders watch how an intruder behaves, since anyone who uses the bait gives themselves away. Layered widely, this raises the chance of detection and makes operating harder for attackers.

For a practical path, the speaker suggests starting with gaps in current defenses, such as placing a honeypot in every VLAN while a planned sensor rollout is still pending. Next, map critical assets with penetration testers and place tripwires along the routes an attacker would take. Test that model against past and public incidents, refine it, then expand from a small network segment over about six months. The maturity path runs from detect, to detect and deflect, to defeat, where deception alerts trigger automated response such as isolating an endpoint.

talks.title: The Effects of the Digital Age
talks.teaser: Connects augmented reality, social media and trading to sustainability, marginalization and geopolitical security pressures.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with crowds chasing Pokémon Go creatures in Central Park as augmented reality: people immersed in a global data layer while the physical world already feels bleak. The speaker frames the internet as the greatest invention in human history, yet notes that seriousness in politics and daily life pushes many toward trivial or escapist digital experiences instead of confronting reality head-on.

Against that backdrop, the talk contrasts how 20th-century thinkers such as Darwin, Freud, and Marx only became fully legible around mid-century with a 21st century whose economic and political structures are still taking shape and whose “authors” remain unclear. Metadata for the session also points to social media mobilizing rebel support, high-frequency commodities trading, and youth growing up highly connected but lightly physical, alongside wider global security and geopolitical risk—the live remarks stay at this strategic level rather than technical detail.

The close argues that the internet will keep evolving whether society welcomes it or not. Progress depends on collective thinking, focus, and commitment—now easier because of connected work—for the poor, the marginalized, and children being born today, with an appeal to marshal genius and effort at scale.

Overview: Bruce Schneier is an internationally renowned security technologist, called a "security guru" by the Economist. He is the author of 14 books -- including the New York Times best-seller "Click Here to Kill Everybody" -- as well as hundreds of articles, essays, and academic papers. His influential newsletter "Crypto-Gram" and blog "Schneier on Security" are read by over 250,000 people. Schneier is a fellow at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society at Harvard University; a Lecturer in Pu

Key Topics: blic Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School; a board member of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, AccessNow, and the Tor Project; and an advisory board member of EPIC and VerifiedVoting.org.

talks.title: Virtual Session: How to Explain Cybersecurity to the Board Using a Simple Metaphor: FIRE
talks.teaser: Uses the Great Fires of London and Chicago to show how fire safety logic can explain cyber controls to boards.
talks.summary:
The session argues that executives and board members have little time and usually limited technical background, so security concepts land faster when they are explained through a familiar analogy. The speaker chooses fire, because most people learn basic fire behaviour and how to respond to it at a young age. Fire is presented as an opportunistic threat that needs only one weak point to spread and keeps going until nothing is left to consume.

To ground the comparison, the talk walks through the Great Fire of London in 1666 and the Great Fire of Chicago in 1871. In London, densely packed timber buildings, wooden water pipes and a decision not to create firebreaks let the blaze burn for days. In Chicago, better stone construction was undermined by wooden sidewalks, tarred roofs and a wooden pumping station, and the response was already worn down by earlier small fires. Each case is mapped to prevention, detection, response and recovery, with lessons on segmentation gaps, late detection, known weaknesses left unfixed, safes that failed under heat, and unreliable attribution.

The closing argument is that fire safety works because controls are tested continuously at a high maturity level, so failures are found before an attacker finds them. The speaker suggests presenting new security spending as a sprinkler or extinguisher, using everyday examples in the office to make a point, and framing a breach for the board around what happened, how it affects the business, and what the organisation learned. A short Q&A covers board metrics, baseline frameworks and breach reporting.

talks.title: Are You Ready for a Breach?
talks.teaser: Lays out a centralized breach response framework, covering triage, investigation, remediation and the stakeholders needed to run it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the view that cybercrime is now a routine business risk, so a breach is a question of when, not if. The speaker cites a 2015 global information security survey in which 14% of respondents had no incident response capability and only 7% had a robust program involving third parties and law enforcement. He notes that attackers often target people through phishing, theft and human error, and that a Verizon report showed attackers moving faster than defenders can discover them.

The middle covers how breaches are understood and handled. Serious intrusions can run for weeks or months, with criminals quietly exploring systems, stealing data and sometimes holding it for later sale, so the full damage may not be clear right away. The speaker proposes a central response framework of six components: information security, insurance, public relations, business continuity, compliance and litigation, run by a leader with legal, compliance and technology experience. The workflow moves through preparation, identification and containment, investigation, remediation and follow-up, which covers reporting, insurance claims and long-term security recommendations. Regular drills are presented as a way to build the muscle memory needed under pressure.

Roles discussed include working with the CFO, auditors and counsel on financial and disclosure questions, a compliance officer for privacy, a corporate security officer liaising with law enforcement, and the chief information security officer's team scoping, containing and eradicating the threat. The closing takeaways are to accept cybercrime as the new normal, get the basics right by knowing crown jewels and entry points, stay situationally aware to detect breaches, and run an enterprise-wide breach management program.

talks.title: How to Build a World-Class Network Defence Organization
talks.teaser: Explains how to build a security organization through a shared framework, tuned detection tools, and analytical hiring.
talks.summary:
Chris Coryea, a cyber intelligence services manager at Lockheed Martin, opens with a focus analogy and frames three myths that hold commercial security teams back: framework, technology, and people. He draws on his company's own experience, which uses the Cyber Kill Chain as a common methodology for analysing attacks and turning them into mitigations across the enterprise.

On frameworks, he describes a Fortune 500 financial services firm whose capable staff worked from different playbooks. Training leadership on the same processes let the firm correlate attacks to specific threat actors. One actor that returned in May struck eight times in 2012 and six times in 2013, so the firm moved from reacting to predicting. On technology, a large US electric utility had bought a full vendor suite and left it at default settings, so three or four tools fired on the same incident. Custom signatures built from the defenders' own findings helped, as did a capability matrix that compared tools against the kill chain and threat landscape. In that matrix, a 500K product blocked only two advanced threats, while a 75K product covered 75% of them.

On people, an oil and gas company needed to hire 30 analysts for three SOCs within 18 months. The speaker argued that an analytical mindset matters more than a computer science degree, so he screened candidates with problem-solving interview questions and looked at internal architects and DBAs. He also said retention depends on ongoing training and rotating challenges rather than pay alone. The closing message is to keep focus on what matters rather than reacting to every distraction.

talks.title: Security in the World-Sized Web
talks.teaser: Explores how connected sensors, cloud services and autonomous systems form a world-sized robot, and why policy must catch up.
talks.summary:
Bruce Schneier argues that mobile devices, cloud computing, Internet of Things hardware and autonomous systems are merging into one vast network that senses, thinks and acts on the physical world. He uses cars as an example: once a vehicle is a networked computer, the main threats shift from data confidentiality to integrity and availability, because a compromised car can put lives and property at risk. He describes three trends shaping this environment. Large systems move power between governments, corporations and individuals. Attackers currently hold the advantage, since they need only one flaw while defenders must cover the entire surface. And attackers gain scale, so the best-resourced adversary matters more than the average one.

He contrasts two security paradigms: the careful, standards-driven approach used for dangerous physical things such as cars, medical devices and aircraft, and the fast-patching approach common in computing. As these worlds collide, he says the problem is as much about law, economics and psychology as technology. Government agencies organised in silos struggle to regulate general-purpose devices that cross traditional boundaries, so he proposes a central body for computer systems. He argues governments will become involved regardless, so the real choice is between smart and poor regulation.

Looking ahead, Schneier expects connectivity to peak before people make more deliberate decisions about what to connect, comparing this to nuclear power after the accidents of the 1970s and 1980s. His practical points include layered defences, compartmentalisation and redundancy, laws that hold regardless of the underlying technology, and closer collaboration between technologists and policymakers.

talks.title: Business-Driven Perspectives
talks.teaser: Argues that security strategy should be driven by business impact, using the Fosbury flop as an analogy for changing perspective.
talks.summary:
Amit Yoran, president of RSA, argues that security teams need a sharper perspective on the problems they face. He uses Dick Fosbury's high jump as an analogy: when soft landing mats appeared, Fosbury changed his technique and was first to exploit the new setup. The point is that organizations must change how they think, not only what they buy.

To make the case, he cites Gartner's projection that 60% of enterprise security budgets would go to rapid detection and response by 2020, up from under 10% in 2014. RSA's own APJ research found over 70% of organizations reported a successful intrusion in the past year, and 90% were dissatisfied with how fast they detect and investigate attacks. He says boards now ask about the business impact of a breach, so security must connect to continuity, intellectual property and reputation. Signature tools, logging and SIEM products are not enough, and advanced analytics needs visibility and skilled people, since there are no magic solutions.

He closes by urging the audience to keep asking why, look for anomalies and conflicts with their assumptions, and build programs tied to business needs. He reminds listeners that their work matters to organizations, customers and families, even when red tape makes it hard to see.

talks.title: Digital Citizenship - Strategies for Parenting the "Always-On" Generation
talks.teaser: Offers parents practical ways to talk with kids about gaming, screen time, sleep and online behavior instead of banning devices.
talks.summary:
This parenting session urges adults to stay curious about children's online lives rather than fearful of them. The speakers, who work with families and schools, describe shifting from a directing role toward an advisory one as children grow. They suggest asking whether an app or game opens a child's world or narrows it, since no single screen-time limit suits every family. Their Minecraft examples show children learning about griefers and allies, reporting bad behavior and intervening against hateful chat, so a favourite game can start a useful conversation.

The middle section looks at tethering and modelling. Parents are often absorbed in their own devices, and children described trying to win their attention back. The speakers say children copy adults more than they listen to lectures, so they recommend device-free family zones such as the kitchen table. They also raised appearance pressure from edited images and the need to help young people question what products are selling, plus sleep loss from late-night phone use. Suggestions include charging devices outside bedrooms, putting them away an hour before bed, and writing a family media agreement together.

The closing message is that banning a tool rarely fixes the problem. Instead, parents should address the behavior the tool exposes, such as swearing, sexualized images or lack of eye contact. Traditional values like the golden rule still apply online, and the speakers encouraged treating a child's online and offline life as one world.

talks.title: Top Three Online Threats: What Can Harm Our Kids?
talks.teaser: A training director groups online dangers to youth as strangers, friends, and self, urging dialogue over reliance on monitoring apps.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a clinical perspective on why minors are poorly equipped to manage online risk: bodies mature earlier while the prefrontal cortex—the seat of judgment and impulse control—may not finish developing until near age twenty-five. That gap matters when youth self-produce intimate images, often in response to romantic pressure, and need remediation paths such as Canada’s NeedHelpNow cyber tip line.

Lance Bitsner, training director at Securing the Human, structures the afternoon around three threat classes: strangers (sexual predators and sextortion, with law enforcement as a key ally), friends (cyberbullying and relationship fallout that police may lack bandwidth to address), and children themselves (oversharing, bullying others, inappropriate media, excessive screen time, and piracy). He adds grandparents and relatives as a fourth loosening of household rules.

Across categories he argues harm is emotional and reputational, rooted in communication rather than bytes. Technology can assist but cannot replace parenting; risks evolve from ages six through fifteen; vigilance should target behaviors, not brand-name apps; and adults must model the boundaries they expect. The promised thread for the rest of the program is that better communication is both the core problem and the practical remedy.

talks.title: The Seven Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques, and What's Coming Next
talks.teaser: Surveys emerging attack trends, from PowerShell post-exploitation and Android flaws to Xcode backdoors and ransomware.
talks.summary:
The session opened with shifting attacker goals. Ed Scotis said targets now include government background records and fingerprints, not just credit cards, and that extortion malware threatens to expose browsing history to a victim's contacts. He then covered PowerShell Empire, a free post-exploitation framework, and defenses such as PowerShell 5 logging, the antimalware scan interface and constrained mode.

The middle of the talk covered mobile and supply-chain cases. The Stagefright flaws showed how Android patches pass slowly through OEMs and carriers, so staying on a current Android version and enforcing updates through mobile device management were advised. Xcode Ghost, a trojanized development environment that put a backdoor into iOS apps which then passed Apple's review, was tied to the trust-the-compiler problem. Johannes Ulrich then described the 2015 Ukrainian power grid attack, where operator desktops, VPN credentials and serial-to-Ethernet converters were hit, and a denial-of-service against the customer hotline amplified the outage.

Johannes also raised reused libraries, default passwords on Raspberry Pi devices, and ransomware moving onto servers, with monitoring of file renames as one countermeasure. The Q&A covered backups, whitelisting and whether to pay ransoms. The takeaways were to inventory software and libraries, test IoT devices before purchase, and treat air gaps as high-latency connections.

talks.title: Sophisticated Attacks vs. Advanced Persistent Security
talks.teaser: Argues that breaches labeled sophisticated were often preventable, and shows how detection and containment limit losses.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that breaches labeled sophisticated are often the result of basic security gaps. Araceli Gomes and Ira Winkler review several recent incidents. A vendor selling tools to law enforcement was itself breached after a weak password gave access to a flat network. A tax agency's authentication relied on credit-report data that criminals could also obtain, and fraudulent returns went unnoticed for a long time. An online dating service had SQL injection flaws and stored passwords without encryption. A healthcare provider was compromised through a watering hole attack, and stolen administrator credentials without multi-factor authentication went undetected for nine months.

The middle section argues that these failures were mainly in detection and reaction, not only prevention. Recurring gaps include poor network segmentation, missing allowlisting, unmonitored critical systems and weak awareness. The speakers favor assuming that controls will fail and planning around that, using kill-chain analysis to engage before an adversary reaches its objective, and prioritizing extrusion prevention, meaning keeping data from leaving, over intrusion prevention alone.

For practitioners, the takeaway is to build a program covering protection, detection and reaction, to identify valuable assets and likely threats, and to feed incident response results back into strategy. Budgets should follow a deliberate risk tolerance and potential-loss estimate rather than whatever is available. The talk closes with a 90-day check on whether an organization has a security program or only a protection program.

talks.title: The Future of Privacy
talks.teaser: Traces privacy from Roman art and 1890s cameras to smartphones and big data, arguing it is renegotiated rather than dead.
talks.summary:
Trevor Hughes, president and CEO of the IAPP, frames privacy through art, starting with a Roman Venus sculpture that shows privacy as a basic human concern. He moves to a Vermeer painting of a private letter and to the 1890 Brandeis and Warren essay, written after portable flexible-film cameras changed how photos were taken. Each new technology, he argues, brought cries that privacy was dead, while social norms and laws were renegotiated.

He then turns to today's pressures: smartphones linked to dozens of apps and many data relationships, big data that makes specific consent hard, and connected devices with no screen for notice. Drawing on Bentham's Panopticon, he argues observation changes behavior. He cites GDPR fines of up to 4% of global turnover and three cases that were not clearly illegal when launched: Google's Street View collection of unencrypted Wi-Fi data, Uber's GodView monitoring tool, and Target's pregnancy-predicting marketing.

His takeaways: compliance alone is not enough, so organizations should build privacy accountability and privacy by design into products, drawing on frameworks from OMB, NIST and others. Privacy touches HR, marketing and product teams, not just legal. Security professionals should walk over and talk to their privacy colleagues, and everyone who handles data should build privacy skills.

talks.title: Cryptoparty: An Introduction to Secure, Usable Encryption Tools for All
talks.teaser: A hands-on tour of everyday encryption tools, from password managers and disk encryption to VPNs and private messaging.
talks.summary:
The session frames widespread confusion about encryption and the need to know where privacy tools appear in daily computing. It opens with foundational habits: strong security underpins privacy, shared secrets cannot be taken back, and regular software updates close common gaps.

The walkthrough splits personal protection from communications with others. For solo use, the presenter covers password managers, full-disk encryption on phones and desktops, VPNs on untrusted networks, HTTPS Everywhere, Tor, and zero-knowledge cloud storage. For shared secrets, the material touches PGP and fingerprints, ProtonMail, OTR, the EFF secure messaging scorecard, Signal, and Wickr, including practical identity verification and the limits of interoperable encrypted chat.

Closing guidance prioritizes quick wins—password hygiene, patching, then full-disk encryption, a chosen end-to-end messenger, and VPN use on open Wi‑Fi—before nudging family or colleagues toward the same steps and trying encrypted email once for practice.

talks.title: Securing Large-Scale Socio-Technical Systems
talks.teaser: Explores why connected socio-technical systems create new security risks, and why policy and regulation must keep pace with them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at large socio-technical systems, the mixtures of software, people and institutions that now run everything from chip-and-pin authentication and eBay-style reputation systems to predictive policing and electronic voting. The speaker argues that growing scale, speed and reach change the kind of threats involved, not just their size. Systems are increasingly opaque and brittle, and failures in integrity or availability can cause physical harm rather than only data loss.

The middle of the talk frames security as an arms race that technology keeps tilting. Loosely organised groups adopt new tools fastest, while large institutions gain most once they master them. Attackers keep an edge because they need only one way in, and the gap between a new attack and a workable defence widens as change speeds up. Since attacks scale, a few capable people can now cause damage that once took many, so rare extreme cases dominate the concern.

The talk argues that policy matters as much as engineering. Economic incentives reward features over security, and existing rules are split across agencies with narrow jurisdictions, leaving gaps such as misuse of personal data unless a company breaks its own privacy promises. The speaker proposes a holistic regulatory body and design choices like distributed systems, local data limits and devices that keep working offline. The takeaway is that policymakers and technologists must work together before a major failure forces the issue.

talks.title: Machine Learning and the Cloud: Disrupting Threat Detection and Prevention
talks.teaser: Shows how Microsoft applies machine learning to cloud-scale logs to rank alerts and flag anomalous logins and DevOps activity.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why rule-based alerting struggles at Microsoft's cloud scale, where tens of petabytes of logs are generated daily and Azure Active Directory authenticates about 1 billion logons each day. Analysts receive hundreds of separate alerts and cannot tell which ones matter, dashboards add noise, and triage outcomes are rarely fed back into the rules.

The speaker explains how machine learning can combine signals from different event streams into one ranked alert that states why it was raised, and how answers from analysts and users can feed back into the model. Three applied examples follow. In DevOps anomaly detection, hashed API features and PCA with random projection made an otherwise infeasible computation practical, and the model flagged a red team's compromised service account calling APIs it had never used before. For geo-anomaly login detection, a simple rule based on the last ten locations produced a 28% false positive rate, so the approach was replaced with a reachability model built from the login histories of similar users, combined with travel speed. A customer phishing case showed a suspicious login from Nigeria that was visible in their own logs. A dashboard demo of Azure AD risk signals closes the technical section.

The takeaways are to pair data scientists with security analysts, collect logs from many sources, and obtain labelled attack data from honeypots and red team exercises, since models cannot be validated without real attacks. Public datasets and cloud machine learning services are suggested as places to start.

talks.title: The Awesome Truth about Hackers
talks.teaser: Reframes hacker stereotypes and shows how curiosity-led training builds teen cyber safety through control, not prohibition.
talks.summary:
Popular news stories often label password reuse, stolen credential lists, and social engineering as hacking, which distorts what skilled explorers actually do. The presentation contrasts those cases with a mindset built on trial, creativity, persistence, and learning from failure without aiming to harm. Hacker High School is offered as a structured outlet: it explains how systems work, supports parental and community context without replacing them, and treats hacking as an open-ended learning process comparable to science but without a fixed experiment scope.

Cyber safety for teenagers is framed around control rather than long lists of prohibitions. Narratives and hands-on exercises cover privacy choices, vetting apps, tracing where data goes, and using network visibility tools so young people can decide what to share. Examples range from physical lock picking to an Ikea-parts cart build, emphasizing resourcefulness across careers. The talk also notes adolescent brain traits—ego, peer recognition, and weak innate risk sense—and argues critical thinking must compensate when schools suspend students who proudly report findings such as SQL injection.

The closing message is that nurturing legitimate skill paths produces capable citizens instead of passive users, while harsh criminal penalties can exceed those for comparable physical acts. Curriculum materials tie to the OSSTMM security testing standard. Adults are urged to work through lesson one themselves, discuss exercises with young people, engage schools and parents, and spark early curiosity with locks and picks where appropriate.

talks.title: Key 2016 Cybersecurity Trends
talks.teaser: Surveys recent cybercrime trends, from dark web card markets and phishing experiments to macro malware and weak app security.
talks.summary:
James Lyne opens by arguing that users, and the security industry itself, hold on to advice long after it stops being good. He then describes a dark web marketplace where stolen credit cards, email accounts and RDP credentials are sold. Cards are pulled after a fixed period or discounted as they lose value, and RDP pricing tracks the privilege level on offer.

The middle of the talk covers a three-month experiment in which a social engineering tracker sent well-crafted and deliberately poor scam emails to a couple of thousand people. Badly written lures still caught many recipients, and a payment-advice scam drew 304 victims. Document-based malware followed, with macro decoys that walked users through disabling their security settings, and lower-volume campaigns aimed at specific languages, sectors or regions.

Lyne then turned to connected devices, describing a translation app that, inside China, revealed a hidden third-party app store offering pirated applications on non-jailbroken iPhones. Analysis of 1002 applications found 306 using TLS without certificate pinning, and some shipped Twitter API keys that exposed direct messages. He closed by urging organisations to disable macros where they are not needed, and warned that user trust in devices runs ahead of the protections behind them.

talks.title: The Power of a Network Defender’s First Principles
talks.teaser: A framework maps network defense to first principles, uniting prevention, detection, eradication, and intelligence around material risk.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting incremental security improvements with first-principles reasoning, using analogies from mathematics and entrepreneurship. He argues that decades of reactive tooling left enterprises with complex, expensive defenses that adversaries still bypass through gaps between products and processes.

He defines shared terms for network defenders, adversary playbooks, campaigns, and risk prioritization, then proposes a defender semantic tree. The trunk is preventing high-risk material impact to the organization. The limbs are threat prevention that turns indicators of compromise into controls along the attack lifecycle, detection through IOC hunting and abnormal-behavior analysis, eradication that feeds new findings back into prevention and mitigates impact, the irreducible trinity requiring all three operational pillars together, and intelligence plus community sharing to scale adversary understanding.

The close recaps trunk and limbs and urges practitioners to treat the framework as coherent fundamentals rather than another point solution. Audience members are pointed to a companion white paper for depth and invited to challenge the model directly.

talks.title: Defense in Depth Is Dead, Long Live Depth in Defense
talks.teaser: Argues that layered point products fail against advanced attacks and proposes six integrated domains for security.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that defense in depth no longer keeps pace with advanced attacks. The speaker lists three pressures: cloud, mobile and IoT assets that appear on networks unseen, a projected shortage of one to one and a half million security professionals by 2020, and an average breach detection time of over 200 days. He then traces the history, from antivirus on desktops to perimeter firewalls and then detection, noting that SIM platforms, built for compliance reporting, found fewer than 1% of advanced attacks. Two flaws stand out: point products at different layers are not connected, and the tools are owned by separate groups that do not collaborate.

The proposed alternative replaces layering with integration across six domains. They cover discovering every asset, assessing the state of owned devices, monitoring network activity, analyzing data to prioritize threats, responding with workflow and notifications for teams without a dedicated SOC, and protecting assets through automated patching, configuration changes or isolation. Protection is presented as the slowest domain to mature, since it depends on trusting that automated actions will not disrupt the network.

The talk closes with six self-assessment questions about visibility, context and decisive action. A no on the visibility questions points to better discovery and analysis, a no on context points to monitoring, and a no on action points to response and protection. The takeaway is to build integrated depth rather than add another point product.

talks.title: Gone in 15 Minutes: Losing Your Privacy While Standing in a Crowd
talks.teaser: Shows how shoulder surfing plus simple people lookups can expose travelers and commuters to immediate harm in crowded public places.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with vivid, firsthand observations from New York subways, airports, and rush-hour platforms: benign phone use and casual screen glare can reveal names, employers, financial details, travel plans, and routines within minutes. The speaker emphasizes that he stopped short of exploiting what he saw, using those stories to highlight how distraction and phone addiction make shoulder surfing common and under-discussed compared with long-term online data leaks.

The middle frames immediate physical-world privacy as a distinct risk from data already on the web. News examples of online stalking are cited, then attention turns to who might act—curious bystanders, opportunists, or deliberate abusers—with no special training required. "Tools of the trade" are mostly a phone plus widely available personal-data aggregators and everyday sites such as Facebook, LinkedIn, Whitepages, and Google Maps, given only a name, company, and rough location. Drawing on intelligence-collection experience, the speaker outlines a simple chain: identify a target, get close, decide what to take, capture it, and optionally execute—while noting most incidents may stay invisible because attribution rarely connects dots.

Closing guidance covers reducing aggregator exposure (including DMA opt-out, with limits as data respreads), practical screen discipline in public, richer awareness training beyond device theft, and role-playing scenarios at work and home so family and employees understand the risk. The recurring takeaway is that security audiences often grasp the problem, but people outside the field are routinely surprised.

talks.title: Hacking Healthcare
talks.teaser: Shows how connected hospital devices on flat networks can threaten patient health, and outlines a phased security blueprint.
talks.summary:
Paul Dant of Independent Security Evaluators argues that hospital security should center on patient health, not only patient records. The talk grows out of earlier research on mobile and connected devices. The speaker notes that medical devices share the same weak assumptions and outdated software as other connected gear. Threat modeling is the starting point: list the system's assets, identify threats, and weigh an attacker's cost against the reward, counting time as a resource.

Over about two years, the research team worked with roughly a dozen hospitals, mostly in the Baltimore and Washington area. Patient monitors often sat on a very flat network with little segmentation. After quickly joining that network, the researchers achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on a monitor. With the patient's sensors removed, they replayed cached vitals, which could suppress alarms for a patient in distress. Separately, patient check-in kiosks could be broken out of kiosk mode and used to pivot into internal networks.

The proposed blueprint starts within 30 days by treating information security and IT as peer organizations and enumerating assets with assigned values. Within 60 days, organizations should build a security plan, followed by a security assessment covering people, process and technology. The main takeaway is that these gaps are business failures that leadership must address.

talks.title: Hiring the Unhireable
talks.teaser: Argues that arbitrary hiring rules keep capable security candidates out, and urges valuing honesty and periodic re-vetting.
talks.summary:
Winn Schwartau opens with his own early career, describing how he was turned away by AT&T over a colour-vision test and by IBM over his appearance. He argues that security hiring rejects capable people for arbitrary reasons, and that the field keeps saying it cannot find enough talent while screening out anyone who does not fit a narrow standard of appearance and behaviour.

He makes the case for hiring people whose traits fall outside conventional HR norms, including those on the autism spectrum or with ADHD-type profiles. He holds up candidates who have failed as especially valuable, using live rock concert production as an example of learning from things going wrong. He argues against routine drug testing, and describes his son, recruited by the NSA as a teenager, whose treatment-related problems pushed him off that path. He proposes that managers profile candidates only for deception, and that trusted staff be re-vetted periodically. He cites the Ames and Hansen espionage cases as examples where static checks missed changing circumstances. He also criticises degree requirements and tax-related obstacles to clearances.

He concludes that organisations need to adapt their cultures to make room for unusual talent, much as they adapted buildings for people with physical disabilities. He says leadership must push HR and legal departments to loosen these rules, and compares the effort to the Marshall Plan and the Manhattan Project.

talks.title: Doomsday: A Probabilistic Analysis of Cyber-Dominance and Implications on Life
talks.teaser: Survey findings and incident cases show how weak segmentation and staffing leave energy and water operators exposed to paralyzing attacks.
talks.summary:
The presenters frame critical infrastructure as the utilities and systems daily life depends on, then argue that aging assets, internet-connected retrofits, and weak political attention combine into what they call an epic fail for national cybersecurity posture. They cite a third-party survey across healthcare, water, energy, and transportation showing low confidence, scarce resources, and limited preparedness, including figures such as one in five respondents doubting detect-and-respond ability, seventy-three percent failing to protect sensitive internal networks adequately, and half lacking a dedicated security team.

They walk through real and hypothetical threats: Iranian access linked to the Ryeberg Dam floodgates, repeated compromises of electric and industrial control environments, Ukraine’s BlackEnergy blackout affecting roughly seven hundred thousand people, and discovery of the same malware variant on U.S. power-grid systems. A fictional Eastern utility illustrates dangerous connectivity, with sixty percent bridging corporate networks to process control and ninety-two percent allowing outside-in access to those controls, enabling a spear-phishing path to grid shutdown and prolonged recovery without manual intervention.

Regulatory gaps dominate the closing argument. Only the electricity sector has mandatory, enforceable standards through NERC, while other sectors rely on voluntary frameworks. Capitol Hill discussion of a cyber-national mission force lacks operational detail, and most respondents report thin budgets, training, and near-term patching plans. Practitioners are urged to stay informed, understand attack surface, and push proactive hardening before adversaries already inside choose to strike.

talks.teaser: A Hollywood panel traces how CSI: Cyber was born and what entertainment can teach everyday viewers about cybercrime.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by asking whether a CSI spin-off focused on cybercrime could steer a new generation toward information security careers and broader literacy about digital risk. The creator describes choosing cybersecurity for a fourth series after conversations with a cyber psychologist about cybercrime culture, framing online crime as the next frontier rather than another city-based procedural.

He recounts outreach to U.S. intelligence and law-enforcement agencies, who repeatedly asked that storylines nudge viewers toward simple habits such as adding numbers to passwords and installing updates. Cast members contrast acting and writing with the grind of real defensive work, arguing viewers are unlikely to reject basic hygiene because a drama exists.

The discussion closes with gratitude toward practitioners who protect identities, money, and safety, and an acknowledgment that television can spotlight the field without replacing the expertise of people in the room.

talks.title: Safety Issues in Advanced AI
talks.teaser: Surveys why superintelligent AI could pose control and existential risks, and what research directions might address them.
talks.summary:
Nick Bostrom opens by arguing that the modern human condition is an anomaly rather than a stable endpoint, and that the largest existential risks are likely to come from human activity. In his view, the most plausible route to a radically different future runs through superintelligent machines that could surpass people across most intellectual tasks.

The middle of the talk traces AI history from hand-built expert systems to machine learning, credits both faster hardware and better algorithms for progress in games such as chess and Go, and reports an expert survey whose median estimate for human-level machine intelligence fell around 2040 to 2050. He then explains why controlling a far smarter system is hard: goals specified imperfectly can be pushed to extremes, as in the King Midas story and the paperclip maximizer example, and a capable system may deceive or seek resources. Scalable control methods that keep working as capability grows are the central challenge.

In the final part he surveys research directions, including inverse reinforcement learning, toy models of how control fails, imitation of human experts as a route to bootstrapping, and architectures that constrain what each module can do. He concludes that the field is only beginning to turn these worries into concrete research problems, and that early investment could shape how the technology arrives.

talks.title: The (Inevitable?) Decline of the Digital Age…
talks.teaser: Links eroding digital trust to productivity risk and urges prevention platforms, automated threat sharing, and education.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames the digital age as infrastructure society treats as invisible, then contrasts expected productivity gains with a subtler risk than one-off catastrophes: gradual loss of trust as breaches touch personal and institutional life. A banking thought experiment illustrates how perception alone could trigger runs and financial turmoil even when underlying assets are intact, tying trust to privacy debates, military cyber priorities, and board-level reputation concerns.

The speaker argues security is woven through technology and society like fabric, amplified by cloud, mobility, data aggregation, and IT–OT convergence. Declining compute costs lower attackers’ barriers, so defenders need leverage by raising the cost of successful attacks—not only in dollars but in legal and national consequences.

Three leverage themes close the talk: prevention-oriented next-generation platforms that simplify networks and automate response; threat sharing measured by speed from unknown to known threats, automated distribution, and automated ingestion; and continuous cyber education for employees, citizens, and children, including a permanent youth exhibit at the San Jose Tech Museum and a proposed mobile version across California.

talks.title: Turning the Tables: Radical New Approaches to Security Analytics
talks.teaser: Explains why security alerts drown in false positives and how memory-driven analytics could help SOCs detect threats faster.
talks.summary:
Fink argues that attackers need only one opening while defenders must protect every layer of the enterprise, so prevention alone is no longer enough. He cites breaches at Anthem, the IRS, Saudi Aramco and Sony, some of which involved no malware, and says recovery has to happen in minutes rather than weeks. His proposed approach builds integrity checks from the supply chain up through firmware and the operating system, with a recovery image kept in a protected part of the hardware.

On the operations side, he describes a security operations center that collects 2.5 billion events a day across 10 global sites. He uses the base rate fallacy to show why rare events produce floods of false positives: a detector that is 99.9% accurate, applied to one bad packet in 100,000, still misclassifies about 100 good packets and leaves most alerts false. His DNS case study cut roughly 15 billion daily packets to about 150 million by dropping benign traffic, then correlated 50 to 100 events over longer periods to find about 50 infected machines a day with almost zero false positives.

Fink closes with a memory-driven research architecture, which he proposes as the basis for a security machine. He compares current SIM systems, handling about 50,000 events per second and five minutes of data, with a projected 10 million events per second and 14 days of analysis on 640 terabytes of main memory. His takeaway is that security must be built into every layer of the IT stack and that detection and response must run at machine pace, not human pace.

talks.title: The Cryptographers' Panel
talks.teaser: The panel weighs FBI access demands, vendor resistance, backdoor failures, and quantum threats to public-key systems.
talks.summary:
The session opens with congratulations to Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman on the ACM Turing Award, then turns to how they might use the prize’s platform and funds—cryptography history research on one side and peace, sustainability, and nuclear-risk work on the other.

Moderated questions drive most of the hour. Panelists explore intelligence agencies, academia, and industry as uneasy partners, then argue the safety tradeoffs when courts or Congress might force vendors to weaken product security. Views diverge on the Apple–FBI dispute over unlocking a single work-issued phone versus setting precedent for compelled assistance, including signed malicious apps. Moxie Marlinspike outlines those distribution risks; others stress strong encryption, lawful-process limits, and legislation as the right venue.

Discussion turns to Juniper’s Dual EC-related changes as a lesson that “nobody but us” backdoors can be hijacked, possibly harming U.S. networks. Quantum computing prompts debate over NSA post-quantum guidance, Snowden-budget hints at modest agency progress, and skepticism about timing and standards control after NIST’s credibility hit. SHA-1 collision progress and browser deprecation of weak certificate signatures illustrate improving ecosystem response. Closing notes highlight detection when crypto assumptions break, hardware isolation, uncertain post-quantum algorithm readiness, and optimism for end-to-end encryption in mainstream messaging.

talks.title: Excellence in Information Security
talks.teaser: A security leader accepts an industry award and thanks his family, colleagues and employer.
talks.summary:
This is the acceptance speech for the RSA Conference Award for Excellence in Information Security, which recognizes a practitioner for an outstanding security program or initiative. The winner opens by thanking the conference and the judging committee, and says the honor feels humbling after a career spent in security. He describes his recent role at ADP, which he joined six years ago after leaving EMC, protecting a business with well over $12 billion in revenue. He presents the work as a life's mission and hopes to pass his training and experience on to a new generation of leaders.

He then credits his family, including his wife of 25 years, for supporting the travel, long hours and constant vigilance the job demands. He says they love him more for that commitment, which he treats as a calling he takes on every day.

He closes by thanking ADP's leadership, employees and security, risk and privacy practitioners for letting him think and act boldly. He names three priorities: protecting clients, protecting shareholders and serving the economies the company works within. He ends by expressing excitement about a global community of practitioners that gains momentum by sharing, innovating and executing.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: Bastille
talks.teaser: Shows how sensor-based monitoring finds risky IoT and radio devices in enterprise airspace, with data center examples.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the point that Internet of Things devices are already in most workplaces, and that many of their wireless protocols were never hardened against attack. The speaker argues that cheap software-defined radios have made radio-frequency hacking easier, and that detection tools for these signals were lacking until recently. As an example, the speaker cites a mouse-dongle flaw announced the week before, which lets an attacker up to 500 feet away take over certain keyboard dongles and send keystrokes to the host.

The company's answer is a combination of sensors and software that gives an enterprise situational awareness of its IoT devices and its airspace. The speaker describes a data center visit where the customer insisted its wireless environment was locked down. On the first day, the team found an unconfigured Zigbee device that could have let someone shut down the chillers, and an unconfigured Bluetooth device that served as an input path to the mainframe, so a keyboard brought into range could issue commands.

The final highlight is the RF persona. A person's headset, fitness tracker and phone each carry radios that move through a building together, so the system can recognise them as one persona. Enterprises use this to follow people around a site, and the speaker showed an example of mapping where people were located in a building. The practical takeaway is that unmanaged wireless devices are a blind spot, and continuous RF monitoring can expose them.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: Prevoty
talks.teaser: Presents a runtime protection product that analyzes injected input by its language structure rather than by patterns.
talks.summary:
The speaker from Prevoty argues that pattern-matching defenses are a zero-sum game for protecting applications. Using a browser pop-up as an example of injected content, they point out that people cannot easily see what a malicious string will do, and that signature-based tools leave the question of its real effect unanswered. The challenge they describe is understanding how malicious data added through HTTP parameters or SQL queries behaves inside a particular application.

The company's answer is a technology it describes as a language-based approach, which reads input through its syntax and semantics. In a SQL example, the system derives facts about the query, such as whether it forms a tautology or a contradiction, without anyone writing a rule for that case. The speaker reported a benchmark in which their product was 30 times faster than competing pattern-matching technologies. The product is a runtime security tool that attaches to containers and runtimes, with support for databases such as MySQL and Oracle and for Java, .NET and Ruby on Rails. The speaker said it has been deployed for several years at Fortune 100 customers running workloads in physical data centers and in the cloud.

The talk closes by claiming that application security travels with the application through its development lifecycle, and mentions a team of 30 and ecosystem partner announcements planned for the year. The takeaway for practitioners is to judge injected input by what it actually does in context, rather than by whether it matches a known pattern.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: Menlo Security

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: ProtectWise
talks.teaser: Shows a cloud-based network recorder that keeps full traffic history so threats can be searched retroactively.
talks.summary:
Gene Stevens, co-founder and CTO of ProtectWise, presents the company, which was founded in Denver, Colorado in 2013 and has 55 employees. He argues that the current security architecture has failed: complex threats unfold over long periods, collecting and correlating data is expensive, and existing tools react to incidents rather than anticipating them.

He describes the company's product as a DVR-style platform for network security that continuously records activity. Lightweight software can be deployed on any network segment, and it captures and optimizes traffic before sending it to the ProtectWise cloud. There the data is indexed, so analysts can search back quickly over long periods. A detection suite runs in real time, combining signatures, reputation, machine learning classifiers and behavior analytics, and it is enriched with threat intelligence. Results are exposed through APIs and a visualizer that gives operators a view of the situation.

Because the platform is multi-tenant, it can correlate patterns across customers. The main point for a practitioner is that keeping a full, searchable record of network activity lets a team re-examine earlier traffic when new indicators emerge, instead of relying only on what was flagged at the time.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: SafeBreach
talks.teaser: Shows how a platform replays hacker breach methods continuously to reveal security gaps before attackers exploit them.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who says he spent 20 years as a CSO, describes a recurring frustration: he could never get a clear answer to whether his defenses would stop a real intrusion. Outside experts, pen testers and red-team exercises gave only a point-in-time view, were hard to scale, and were risky to run in production. He argues that attackers do not follow the defenders' rules and need to succeed only once, so defenders need a way to test continuously.

The product, from SafeBreach, simulates hacker breach methods across the full attack chain on networks, endpoints, mobile devices and cloud instances. Its playbook holds thousands of discrete actions, from downloading and running an exploit kit or deploying malware on an endpoint to communicating with a command-and-control server, propagating across the network and executing a payload. Simulators run in pairs as ongoing scenarios, showing the likely impact of a future attacker and where the gaps are. Users can then pick the step to mitigate in order to break the chain, without needing to fix everything.

The closing part covers the market case. The speaker says spending on validation services, which are manual by nature, keeps growing. He claims a proof of concept can run in one day with results in a few minutes, and that the company already has paying customers in production. The takeaway is that offensive techniques can be turned into continuous validation to give defenders back the advantage.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: Vera
talks.teaser: Shows a startup that wraps enterprise data in encryption and policy controls that follow it beyond the perimeter.
talks.summary:
Vera, a startup presenting in the 2016 Innovation Sandbox contest, pitched a way to protect enterprise data wherever it travels. The core idea is to move the security perimeter onto the data itself instead of the network around it. Data is encrypted first, then access is governed through identity standards such as SAML and OAuth, so the organization decides who can open a file regardless of where it sits.

The pitch then turned to controls after a file is opened. The speaker described restricting actions such as copying, pasting, printing and granting access to others, and tracking what happens to a file at a granular level. Policies can be changed in real time, and access can be revoked at any moment, even for copies that have left the company's own systems. Customers ranging from Fortune 100 firms to small and medium businesses were cited as examples.

The closing argument was that the product needs no change in user behavior and no agents, and works across apps and devices. The takeaway for practitioners is that data-centric controls can follow files beyond the perimeter, though the talk gave no technical detail on how this was implemented.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2016: Versa
talks.teaser: Presents a software-defined approach that moves branch office security functions onto virtualized, centrally managed platforms.
talks.summary:
The pitch starts from branch offices, where enterprises and service providers increasingly send cloud application traffic straight to the internet for a better user experience. That opens a new attack surface, so the speaker argues that branch security needs to be rethought. The speaker cites analyst predictions of a 500% increase in threats originating from the branch.

The current branch setup relies on many proprietary appliances, each with its own management and configuration system, which are hard to integrate and add complexity and errors. The proposed alternative converts these appliances into virtualized security functions running on white-box hardware, which the speaker says improves agility and lowers total cost of ownership. A single management system provisions branch devices with zero-touch provisioning, and an analytics system gives network-wide security intelligence instead of separate device views. This matches a software-defined security model that moves from per-box management to policy-based, network-wide control.

Security functions can run on premises, in the cloud, or split between the two without changing the service. The speaker reports 50 proofs of concept and six telcos in production with managed services in the first year after release. The closing points are a flexible distributed architecture, integrated networking and security, zero-touch provisioning, and centralized monitoring, with lower cost and greater agility. For practitioners, the takeaway is separating security functions from dedicated hardware and managing them centrally across branches.
