talks.title: Quick Look: SaaS Attacks Happen: How Cloud Scale Changes the Security Game
talks.teaser: Explains how Office 365 uses automation and data scale to limit human access and protect hosted customer data.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a shift in responsibility. Once an organization's data and the functions built on it move to a cloud service, the provider becomes a partner in keeping that data reliable, protected from attackers, and under the customer's control. The speaker argues that the scale of cloud operations can be turned into a security advantage rather than being treated only as a risk.

The first example is automation. Office 365 uses smart diagnosis and self-healing so that code handles recovery and routine fixes while people make the decisions. Manual access is kept away from production machines: an operator runs a controlled, hardened script that receives its own narrowly scoped, temporary permission. Tight machine lockdowns then allow only defined execution and communication paths across the data centers, which reduces the surface for errors or misuse. The second example is data scale. Office 365 is described as holding more than an exabyte of physical storage across more than 100 data centers, and the provider can obscure which server holds which tenant's data, so that only code can map it. Intelligence about a malicious actor gathered from one account can be applied to protect all users.

The closing message is that customers remain the decision makers while the cloud service does the heavy lifting of running operations. For practitioners, the takeaway is to ask how a cloud provider limits human access, automates operations and isolates customer data, rather than assuming those controls sit outside their concern.

talks.title: Quick Look: How to Explain Cybersecurity to the Board Using a Simple Metaphor: FIRE
talks.teaser: Compares historic city fires with cyber defence to explain prevention, detection and recovery to senior managers.
talks.summary:
John Elliott explains how he came to use fire as a metaphor when briefing senior managers and boards on cybersecurity. The idea grew out of a manager asking why prevention was still needed if attacks could be caught inside a network. Elliott points out that people already share common sense about fire, from childhood warnings to office extinguishers and fire drills, which makes the comparison easy for non-specialists to follow.

Two historic city fires form the core of the comparison. The Great Fire of London in 1666 started in a bakery, was noticed late when someone smelled smoke, and burned for three days through wooden, tightly packed buildings, destroying about 1,300 homes. In Chicago, a fire started when a cow knocked over a lamp in a milking parlour and spread on the wind from roof to roof. A single wooden pumping station failed, and residents' safes, supposedly fireproof, left their valuables charred.

Elliott maps fire controls onto security ones. Fire detectors correspond to detection, sprinklers to automatic response like an intrusion prevention system, and insurance plus continuity planning to recovery. The lessons include avoiding flammable construction, leaving firebreaks, detecting quickly during the first critical hour, and the danger of poor management. He closes by arguing that insurers and regulators drove fire standards, and expects security to face similar demands through questions about asset value and security posture.

talks.title: Quick Look: Crypto 101: Encryption, Codebreaking, SSL and Bitcoin
talks.teaser: Introduces basic cryptography concepts, from encryption keys and signatures to TLS and Bitcoin.
talks.summary:
Ben John of HBS Lab gives a beginner-level primer on cryptography. He frames security as the absence of harm and names confidentiality and integrity as the core properties that cryptographic tools provide. Encryption is presented as a process where a secret key makes a message easy to decrypt for the holder and very hard for everyone else, with the algorithm kept public and widely reviewed.

The middle section covers asymmetric cryptography, where a public key encrypts and a related private key decrypts, so strangers can exchange secrets without first sharing a key. The same key pair supports digital signatures: a private-key signature proves origin and integrity, and certification authorities vouch for identities through digital certificates. The talk also stresses that keys need unpredictable randomness, which modern CPUs help supply by harvesting noise from the chip. TLS serves as a worked example, using public-key exchange to set up a session, symmetric encryption for bulk traffic, and certificates to confirm a website's identity.

The closing example is Bitcoin, described as a decentralized currency that runs on consensus rather than a central authority, with transactions signed by the sender and proof of work used to add new coins. The speaker notes that the blockchain prevents double spending but does not explain it in detail. Practitioners leave with a clear picture of the basic building blocks: keys, signatures, certificates and good randomness, and how they combine in everyday secure communication.

talks.title: Cyberwars in the Middle East: What Corporations & Governments Need to Do About It | RSA Conference
talks.teaser: Argues that companies and governments must invest in defence and regulation, using the Stuxnet and Aramco attacks as warnings.
talks.summary:
The keynote, given at the first RSA Conference in Abu Dhabi, argues that Gulf states are both more capable and more exposed because they are so heavily connected. It treats the Stuxnet operation against the Natanz enrichment site as an early real cyber conflict, describing centrifuges that were damaged while control room displays showed normal operation. It then covers the Iranian response: a wiper attack that erased 30,000 endpoints at Aramco, and a DDoS campaign that took online banking offline at major US banks despite large security budgets.

The middle section draws lessons from these episodes. Governments, it argues, have favoured offensive capability over defence, as shown when US banks asked for help and were told to handle the attack themselves. Corporate boards wrongly assume their own government will protect them, and Sony Pictures was attacked by North Korea. Losing power, water and banking could set a society back to a far more primitive state, and terrorist groups may be the next threat to infrastructure in the region.

The closing recommendations call for international arms control talks on cyberspace, since the Budapest Convention on cybercrime lacks teeth. They also call for regulation that sets security goals for banks, energy and water firms and then audits them, citing the Bank of England's plan to test banks with its own hackers. Existing technologies such as continuous monitoring and segmentation could block most attacks, and practitioners are urged to carry this message to their leaders.

talks.title: Lance Spitzner - "Show Me How You Use It”
talks.teaser: Offers parents practical ways to talk with children about online accounts, mobile devices and staying safe.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's experience of securing his own children's online lives. A young child showed him a new site and game he had joined, and an adult had filled in the child's name, home address, age and phone number during sign-up. That made him realise that protecting kids is not limited to the home, since they also spend time at relatives' houses, at school and at the library.

The central argument is that education matters as much as technology. When parents ask how to monitor their children, he suggests taking on the role of a clueless parent and asking kids to show how they use the apps they rely on, such as Instagram. This gets children talking and lets parents see what they actually do. For phones and tablets, he describes a household routine: devices go onto a central charging station before bed, children use strong passcodes, and location tracking is enabled so a lost device can be found or wiped remotely.

The takeaway is to start talking about security early, because younger children are more likely to listen and adopt secure habits. As kids get older, parents have less control over where they go and which technology they use, so an open, two-way conversation becomes the main safeguard.

talks.title: Children Deserve Protection - CyberSafety for Kids | RSA Conference
talks.teaser: A survivor recounts online grooming and urges parents to educate themselves and children while using guidance and monitoring tools.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes growing up as a typical teenager whose social life moved online until friends-of-friends connections led to conversations with strangers. She explains how a predator posed as a friend and used grooming—telling her what she wanted to hear—before she left home on New Year's Day 2002 to meet him. She recounts captivity, abuse, and a moment when she believed she would be killed, followed by FBI and law enforcement entering the house, removing a chain from her neck, and freeing her.

After rescue, she links the experience to absent internet safety education in schools and began speaking to students at fourteen. The Alicia Project expanded to reach parents, teachers, and law enforcement. She argues that talking to children alone is insufficient: parents must learn alongside kids, watch for behavioral changes such as withdrawal, and accept that monitoring software on computers and mobile devices can document warning signs despite privacy concerns.

She frames cyber safety dangers as real and ongoing, promotes structured cyber safety education, and closes with practical calls to educate, guide children with tools, and treat protection as every child's right.

talks.title: Securing Today's Online Kids - Cyber Safety for Kids | RSA Conference
talks.teaser: Maps online threats to kids from strangers, peers and themselves, and how parents can respond with education and rules.
talks.summary:
This RSAC webcast, part of its cyber safety effort during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, is aimed at parents. The speaker argues that children now have constant access through many devices, that parents have no earlier experience to pass on, and that the aim is protecting people rather than data. He sorts the main threats into three groups: strangers, such as predators, sextortion and hacked game accounts; friends and peers, including cyberbullying, where police often cannot help; and children's own behaviour, such as oversharing or harassing others.

The core message is that education matters more than technology, because filters stop working once children leave the house. Parents are advised to keep an open two-way dialogue, let children teach them about their apps, and adopt a no-consequences rule so kids feel safe asking for help. Practical household steps include a shared family computer in an open room, a central charging station for phones overnight, and rules that devices stay on and get answered. Grandparents' homes and school-issued devices can bypass those rules. Home DNS filtering with OpenDNS covers only the home network, and monitoring tools differ between Android and iOS. Behaviour matters more than any single app.

In the Q&A, the speaker advised not replying to a bully and using school or platform safety channels, and suggested that open school Wi-Fi may call for talks with the school and local police. The closing advice was to channel a curious child's interest in hacking into capture-the-flag contests and coding courses, and to keep talking as kids grow.

talks.title: Quick Look: Cyber Security Awareness for Executives | RSA Conference
talks.teaser: Shows how to plan a cyber awareness program for executives, from tailoring briefings to mapping organizational risk.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how to run a cyber security awareness program for senior executives. The speaker argues that cyber risk now affects every business, so leaders need enough understanding to back the organisation's security strategy. Because sectors, company sizes and individual executives differ, the speaker recommends learning each person's needs before planning delivery, and treating the program as a long-running effort that evolves over time.

The content covers device hygiene explained in plain terms, and the threat landscape, including the threat actors that might target the company's most valuable data. Intelligence can come from open sources, vendors, government contacts, critical infrastructure bodies and sector peers. The speaker also recommends keeping a record of incidents and how they were handled, so lessons survive staff changes. The core is organisational risk: estimating the impact and cost of losing particular data, with a risk assessment, a gap analysis of current defences and metrics that link investment to risk reduction.

The closing section highlights the benefits. Leadership support from the top makes a security strategy stronger, since cyber is a business risk and not just an IT issue. Informed executives make better decisions on data protection and respond more confidently to a breach, which tends to bring backing and investment for security requests. Employees who protect their own data at home and at work also strengthen the organisation's overall posture.

talks.title: Getting Ahead of Cybercrime
talks.teaser: Argues that firms should assume breach, drill for it, and treat cybersecurity as a business-cycle and boardroom issue.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a show of hands on recent breaches and argues that every organisation should expect to be breached. Rather than putting all resources into prevention, teams should prepare, train and drill to detect and contain intrusions. A quote from a global energy CEO about fending off 50,000 attacks a day illustrates how the topic has moved into boardrooms, where executives now take ownership.

Press headlines and breach-notification rules distort the picture, since countries that require disclosure show more reported breaches, and a sector-wide breach tends to raise attention across peers. A survey from late 2014 found 56% of respondents doubted their organisation could detect a sophisticated attack, and 43% expected security budgets to stay roughly flat. The speaker argues security spending should follow business events such as mergers, acquisitions and market entry rather than being treated as finished once.

Roadblocks include weak fundamentals such as patching, budget spent on the wrong things, skills shortages used as an excuse, and poor coordination between industry, government and the military. The closing point is that security should be framed around enabling society as technology dependence grows, not only around innovation or profit.

talks.title: The Game Has Changed
talks.teaser: A keynote shifts leaders from perimeter fixation to visibility, identity, and intelligence that exposes long intrusions.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting physical identity with fragile virtual credentials, then argues that even well-resourced enterprises armed with next-generation controls still lose money, secrets, and sensitive data while intrusions run for months or years. The speaker rejects prevention-only thinking, compares stale perimeter-centric security to outdated postal business models, and notes that signature-driven monitoring and SIM aggregation rarely surface advanced threats.

Five adaptation themes follow: accept that determined adversaries will breach defenses; pursue deep visibility from endpoints through networks and cloud, including full packet capture and endpoint assessment, and avoid rushing incident cleanup before the full campaign is understood; treat identity as the primary control where credentials and privileged abuse dominate real breaches; combine external and internal threat intelligence with time for analysts to learn normal behavior; and prioritize limited resources using business-critical risk.

The close insists the gap is mindset, not missing tools—visibility, authentication, intelligence, and risk systems already exist—and challenges the audience to change how security operations think before sailing further with obsolete maps.

talks.title: Quick Look: Security Risks in SDN and Other New Software Apps
talks.teaser: Surveys software risks in SDN, mobile devices, connected cars and legacy systems, with a look back at OWASP Top 10.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at security risks in software-defined networks (SDN), which separate the control plane from the data plane so that network behaviour is run by software. The speaker argues that this shifts the risk: with no physical topology to rely on, the controller and its applications must be trusted completely. A threat map of the controller, switches, control plane and management layers shows how an attacker could fake traffic flows, exploit switch vulnerabilities, isolate administrators, carry out man-in-the-middle attacks and hide from intrusion detection.

The second part widens the view to mobile and other connected software. Phones now have server-like processing power, large apps make it easy to hide malware, and connected cars can be reached through phones. Older software remains a live problem as well, with examples including Shellshock in Bash, unsupported Android and Windows XP systems still running in embedded devices, and unpatched Flash and QuickTime. A revisit of the OWASP Top 10 shows that input validation, buffer overflows and error handling still matter years after the list was first published.

The closing message is that solutions exist for phones, IoT and SDN, but they depend on vigilance and disciplined management of software, including timely patching and retiring unsupported systems.

talks.title: State of Cybersecurity: 2015 Findings and Implications
talks.teaser: Presents ISACA and RSA's global survey results on threats, skills shortages, training and how enterprises respond.
talks.summary:
Robert Stroud, international president of ISACA, presented the key results of a global cybersecurity survey run jointly by ISACA and RSA in January. More than 1,500 RSA and ISACA constituents took part, and just under 700 completed it. Most respondents were from North America, financial services was well represented, and about 66% held a role in cybersecurity.

On threats, financial gain was the leading motivation for attackers, while disruption or denial of service still affected about a quarter of respondents. Malware and phishing remained the most common attacks, cited by nearly two-thirds. Training was widespread, with 87% of organisations running awareness programmes, yet the talk noted that organisations with training reported more human-dependent incidents. Twenty-six percent did not know whether attacks had made them more vulnerable, and 83% expected to be attacked in 2015.

The skills findings were the most pointed. Respondents rated their staff's business understanding at 72% but their technical ability at 46%. Roughly a third of organisations took about three months to fill security roles and another third took six months or could not fill them at all. Security most often reported to the CIO (59%), budgets were largely stable or rising, and almost 80% said their boards cared about cybersecurity. The session closed by pointing to ISACA's CSX certificate and career resources, with the message that cybersecurity is everyone's business.

talks.title: Never, Ever, Give Up
talks.teaser: A marathon swimmer recounts repeated failed attempts to swim from Cuba to Florida before finally completing the crossing at 64.
talks.summary:
The talk follows Diana Nyad's long effort to swim from Cuba to Florida, a crossing of about 110 miles. She first tried in 1978 and was stopped after 42 hours in rough seas. After turning 60 she made several more attempts that also ended short. She describes the obstacles she faced, including the Gulf Stream pushing swimmers far off course, sharks, box jellyfish, cold water, and limited nutrition, along with a sports scientist's view that no one could finish.

The middle of the account covers her fifth attempt. The first night brought jellyfish stings, seawater, and constant vomiting into her mask. On the second day her support team saw her drifting too close to the boat and in poor condition, and told her to lift her goggles and look ahead. She had resisted that advice in earlier tries because a sealing problem could end a swim. This time she saw the lights of Key West rather than the sunrise she had expected, and she reached the beach there.

She ends by describing herself as unwilling to quit and unwilling to let others decide what is possible. Her closing message urges listeners to keep pursuing their own dreams. For a general audience, the talk's takeaways are persistence through repeated failure, the value of a support crew who can correct course, and not accepting predictions of impossibility. It is a motivational talk rather than a technical one.

talks.title: Future Crimes: Why Cyber Was Only the Beginning
talks.teaser: Surveys how interconnected technology widens future criminal risk, from online black markets to drone-enabled abuse and hijacked devices.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames today's cybersecurity challenges as an early chapter in a longer shift: as connectivity and new gadgets spread, adversaries gain fresh ways to profit and harm. It opens with large-scale online criminal commerce, citing the Silk Road case and the scale of illicit revenue attributed in court filings, alongside services that commodify violence for a stated price.

The middle of the talk argues that offending is moving beyond keyboards into physical space. Examples include aerial platforms used for voyeuristic live streaming, contraband delivery over prison perimeters, and demonstrations that even official unmanned aircraft can be compromised. The speaker stresses that none of this is an argument against technology itself, but illustrates a running contest between builders who improve lives and actors who weaponize the same advances.

The close is a call to action for practitioners and founders in the audience. Rapid tech adoption can lift billions out of poverty, extend health and learning, yet each new capability needs deliberate safeguards. The takeaway is that informed builders and entrepreneurs are positioned to shape defenses before the next wave of "future crimes" arrives.

talks.title: Stop Selling and Start Marketing Your Information Security Program
talks.teaser: Shows how treating staff as heroes and borrowing marketing tactics can make security awareness campaigns engaging.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by questioning why security awareness programmes rely on posters, short articles and computer-based training. The speaker compares this with public health campaigns against smoking, which took generations to shift habits, and argues that staff keep doing risky things, such as plugging in unknown USB sticks, because they have work to get done. The speaker suggests borrowing from advertising, which sells lifestyles rather than products, and treating staff as trusted clients and heroes rather than as fools.

The campaign was built around a branded persona, "Restricted Intelligence", a brand the organisation licensed for two years and then made its own. Films featuring recurring characters such as the boss, the intern and the sensible colleague were released over time, and the security training was rebranded to match. Life-size character cutouts appeared around the office, advice sheets were written for use at home as well as at work, and the team sponsored local events such as Chinese New Year so staff became familiar with the brand. Staff also began decorating the cutouts and photographing themselves with them, which the speaker welcomed.

The reported results include general incidents falling by two-thirds over the latest three months compared with the same period earlier, a result the speaker acknowledged runs against the expectation that reported incidents would rise. One lesson came from a joke certificate with a deliberate computer error, which generated confusion and extra calls because staff had not been told to expect the humour. The closing advice is to review your own programme, make it work for your organisation, and keep the momentum going.

talks.title: General Alexander: Life After the NSA
talks.teaser: A former NSA director traces his path from West Point to a cybersecurity startup, plus views on surveillance oversight.
talks.summary:
Ted Schlein, a Kleiner Perkins partner, interviews retired Army General Keith Alexander, former NSA director and founder of US Cyber Command, about life after government service. They begin with his decision to attend West Point and his rise through the military. A key story covers a Defense Department network incident, where about 1500 pieces of malware were found and a new defense system was built and running within 24 hours.

Alexander then addresses the public debate over data collection. He describes a real-time gateway used in Iraq to detect insurgents, and explains that bulk metadata programs were reviewed by federal judges on the FISA court, Congress and the administration. He recounts how a civil liberties critic who was given a briefing later praised the agency's integrity. On information sharing, he argues that companies need classified briefings and liability protection, and that offensive cyber tools remain a policy decision.

On the business side, he explains that Ironnet aims to give network defenders real-time visibility by combining behavioral analytics with firewall and log data, because no single company can see an entire network. He describes learning payroll, contracts and slow customer payments, and says executives often lack technical understanding. On talent, he encourages young engineers to serve in government for a few years and calls for stronger science, technology, engineering and math education.

talks.title: Dan Geer on the Future of Security
talks.teaser: Applies Kuhn's ideas on scientific paradigms to explain why perimeter control, privacy and defense are in crisis.
talks.summary:
Dan Geer opens by asking whether cybersecurity counts as a science, using Kuhn's account of how scientific paradigms form, hold and get replaced. He explains that mature fields share a paradigm that defines which puzzles researchers solve, and he argues that cybersecurity lacks this consensus partly because it has sentient opponents, which sets it apart from physics or chemistry.

He then argues that perimeter control is in crisis because always-on connectivity and universal addressability make a defensible perimeter hard to maintain. He points to a Qualcomm Snapdragon chip with roughly 18 to 21 cores, a median estimate of 35% compound annual growth for the Internet of Things, and a parameter count he says doubles every 17 months. He applies the same reasoning to privacy, where metadata collection undermines selective revelation, and suggests that data integrity may need to take priority over confidentiality. On defense, he argues that cybersecurity tools now favor offense and that silent failure is widespread: a Verizon report found 80% of breaches were discovered by third parties, and his own survey found 65%.

He closes by considering alternatives such as moving target defense and language-theoretic security, while acknowledging that the field may not yet have undergone a true paradigm shift. He leaves the audience with the question of whether the current crisis is severe enough to justify rebuilding how security is practised and studied.

talks.title: You Can’t Stop What You Can’t See
talks.teaser: Shows how long-running intrusions evade firewalls and SIEM, and why hunting, full visibility and analytics matter.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that well-funded, long-running intrusions are getting past organizations that already run firewalls, intrusion prevention, antivirus and managed monitoring. Targeted attacks are presented as a broad category, with advanced persistent threat campaigns a smaller subset that involve long reconnaissance, fast movement after entry and periodic return visits. The case examples include a malicious DLL that relayed traffic to internal servers without any beacon, a rogue page handler that ran code whenever a POST carrying a chosen string hit a nonexistent page, a Sticky Keys replacement that gave a system-level command shell without credentials, and a web shell that tunneled RDP over an allowed web port.

The shared lesson is that these intrusions rely on existing tools and on indicators that are easy to change, so alerts built on known indicators fall short. Log-based products only see what they were configured to record, and one cited Verizon figure put SIEM detection of advanced threats at 1%. In a nation-state intellectual property case, data had been leaving for nine months, yet on-site network and endpoint visibility exposed the activity within two days. The recommendations are to combine packet capture with endpoint forensics, give analysts time to hunt proactively, learn the normal patterns of the environment, and make threat intelligence actionable.

The talk closes with the value of studying published breaches and using analytics to flag outliers, such as a login from an unusual country on a new device with atypical session length. The speakers stress that technology alone will not close the gap; people need time to investigate.

talks.title: The Six Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques and What's Coming Next
talks.teaser: A veteran panel surveys six emerging attack patterns, from staged breach leaks to targeted ICS delivery, with practical defense guidance.
talks.summary:
The session follows an annual SANS-style threat briefing format: three specialists each present dangers observed over the prior year, while the moderator collects written audience questions for a long closing Q&A.

Ed Skoudis opens with the shift from monolithic breach dumps to dribbling stolen data in stages, using Sony as the anchor example and urging tabletop exercises that assume unknown scope and escalating daily disclosures. He traces Windows credential attacks from LAN Manager and NTLM through pass-the-hash into Kerberos, describing pass-the-ticket harvesting, golden tickets after domain controller compromise, and silver tickets that evade broader logging, tied to widespread tooling such as Mimikatz 2.0. He finishes on Internet of Things growth: unmanaged BYOD-style gear, weak toys and appliances, and inexpensive planted devices like keyboard emulators and rogue wireless kits.

Johannes Ullrich treats encryption as both fragile protection and an attack enabler, from poor TLS on unmaintained embedded gear to ransomware that prices victim data above resale value, backup appliances being encrypted, and long-running server encryption before key removal. He contrasts volumetric reflection floods with modest application-layer denial of service and describes manipulated web analytics scripts that weaponized ordinary browsers against GitHub during a firewall-related campaign.

Mike Assante covers industrial control systems, noting most plant incidents still come from non-targeted malware on removable media while newer campaigns customize exploits, abuse engineer trust, poison downloads and vendor sites, and probe internet-exposed controllers. He ties BlackEnergy and HAVEX modules to OPC reconnaissance, cites reported physical damage at a German steel furnace, and urges OT-side firewall ownership, jump-server discipline, monitoring, and cyber-informed hazard analysis before true ICS payloads spread.

Practitioners should plan for staggered breach publicity, credential and Kerberos hygiene, IoT discovery, ransomware scenarios that include backups, and ICS delivery paths treated as deliberate adversary work rather than accidental infection alone.

talks.title: Hugh Thompson and Guests
talks.teaser: Explores how attackers and breach victims experience emotions and outlines mental habits that help security teams recover more clearly.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing security as a human problem on every side of an attack, using a vivid personal anecdote about panic, perceived danger, and lasting avoidance after a frightening incident. That story sets up why the industry talks little about emotional fallout when organizations or individuals are compromised.

A pre-recorded conversation is referenced as context before a psychiatrist discusses why people hack—contrasting professional criminals, code-driven curiosity, and approval-seeking behavior—and highlights loneliness, detachment, and impaired social decision-making as recurring psychological themes. On the victim side, the discussion covers violation, anxiety, uncertainty, amygdala-driven poor risk judgments, paranoia, and hypervigilance, including how uncertainty can bias people toward expecting the worst.

Organizational missteps receive attention, especially habitual debriefing that may reinforce trauma instead of forward movement. The guest introduces a five-step mental resilience approach—chunking time horizons, managing intrusive thoughts, reality and control checks, and attentional shift toward solutions—and argues that teams should practice these skills alongside legal and HR readiness, treating personal freedom and anxiety management as part of serious incident preparation.

talks.title: Make the Internet Less Scary
talks.teaser: Lays out online risks facing young children and urges security professionals to volunteer their skills to keep kids safe.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an eight-year-old girl on a tablet, wondering how to choose a password and how to answer an avatar that messages her. The speaker cites figures on young children's contact with strangers online: one in eight third-graders has had an online conversation with a stranger, and one in ten of those children was asked about the private parts of their bodies. He adds that by tween age a child may spend more than half of their waking life online, and that 58% of peers don't think social media posts will affect their future.

He contrasts that with his own childhood, when his social network was a school playground and messaging meant a touch-tone phone. With his children he teaches boundaries about who they talk to and what they share, treating every conversation as permanent, asking before posting someone else's photo, choosing good passwords, and keeping communication open so they know whom to ask for help. He points to the Cyber Safety Village at the conference, where more than 3,000 people checked in, and to ready-made material from nonprofit partners that volunteers can use with kids.

He closes with more numbers: 65% of eight-to-14-year-olds have been involved in cyberbullying, 49% say they were the bully, and only 6% of parents knew. He urges security professionals to bring these facts to schools, churches and libraries, and to offer their time and skills to help kids in their communities stay safe online.

talks.title: Security on Offense
talks.teaser: Uses baseball analytics to prioritize attack campaigns, automate routine alerts, and shift skilled staff to offensive hunting.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a trust crisis in cybersecurity: soaring spend, investment, and vendor innovation have not kept pace with adversaries, and hard work is mistaken for outcomes. The speaker uses the Oakland Athletics Moneyball narrative—revaluing overlooked metrics like on-base percentage—to argue that security already has abundant data and tools but lacks reframed questions and disciplined follow-through.

The middle brings Oakland Athletics vice president and general manager Billy Beam on stage for a structured interview. He describes challenging entrenched scouting bias, hiring outsiders such as Paul DePodesta, leaning on Bill James–style analysis, removing emotion from decisions, iterating processes even after wins, and accepting organizational turnover while staying within budget constraints. Parallel lessons cover probabilistic mapping of malware and alerts to campaigns that matter, stack-ranking response, and resisting endless IOC chasing without organizational context.

The close urges practitioners to treat roughly ninety-eight percent of inbound noise as handled by architecture and automation, then dedicate human talent to hunting the remaining high-value two percent. SIEM usage should shift from inbox-style alert triage toward reference intelligence. The takeaway is cultural: measure value, embed attacker-campaign context in tools and processes, and sustain the courage to operate differently—not merely acquire more data.

talks.title: Enhancing Cloud Trust
talks.teaser: Explains how moving to the cloud shifts trust, control and transparency, and which vendor features respond.
talks.summary:
The talk looks back at Microsoft's trustworthy computing effort, which dates back 13 years, and argues that its three pillars of security, privacy and reliability still hold. As workloads move to the cloud, customers also want appropriate control over their environment and transparency into what the provider does. The speaker recalls the older model in which vendors built technology, customers secured it, and attackers exploited supply chain, code flaws, misconfiguration and social engineering. Since a 2007 keynote on trusted stacks, the threat has grown more destructive, which has pulled boards into security decisions.

Shared cloud infrastructure creates trust problems in both directions: the provider must protect its fabric from tenant virtual machines, while customers want protection from the provider's administrators. Several concrete measures were presented. Hardware roots of trust, TPM-signed credentials and Windows Hello aim to reduce reliance on passwords, and TPM 2.0 gives governments crypto agility. Hardware security modules and customer-held key revocation in Office 365 give customers control, and BitLocker on desktops lets retired drives be discarded safely. Just-in-time and just-enough administration, with customers in the approval chain and access logs exposed, address privileged access.

The closing argument is that market demand drives security investment, while governments fill the gaps the market will not cover. The speaker concludes that cloud providers must offer technically enforced trust boundaries, control and transparency so that customers' faith is grounded, and that consolidating security in the cloud can help small businesses without dedicated IT staff.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2015: SentinelOne
talks.teaser: Explains how behavior-based endpoint agents aim to catch evasive malware and replace traditional antivirus products.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that organisations spend heavily on security yet successful attacks keep happening. Malware still performs the same core actions, but authors keep changing evasion methods to get past signature scanners and sandbox analysis. Because malicious code must eventually run on the endpoint, the argument is that protection belongs there.

The approach described is next-generation endpoint protection built on real-time behavioural analysis. An agent builds a live execution context for each process, effectively a storyline of related processes and events, and anti-exploitation engines target the techniques malware uses across its lifecycle. Mitigation is automated and works even when a device is offline. The same endpoint telemetry supports indicator search and real-time forensics, and coverage spans Windows, Mac, Android, iOS and some Linux. The speaker announced an extension to the company's EDR product that aims to replace traditional antivirus by handling known and legacy threats as well as advanced ones.

In the questions that followed, the speaker acknowledged that some malicious code has to run before it can be stopped, though most detections happen at early stages and remediation is being added. A kernel-level agent that observes everything raised concerns about the platform security model, and the answer was that the data goes only to administrators who otherwise lack that visibility. Each endpoint works on its own, since malware behaviour can be spotted on the machine itself without cross-device correlation. The practical takeaway is to focus on how malware behaves over its lifecycle rather than on specific binaries or signatures.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2015: Fortscale
talks.teaser: Explains how machine learning on existing login logs scores insider risk by comparing each user to their history and peers.
talks.summary:
Idan Tendler presents Fortscale's user behavior analytics product, aimed at insider threats. He opens with two figures: 82% of attacks coming from outside the enterprise and 88% of attacks from within use user credentials. The approach analyzes authentication logs such as login, SSH and VPN records, plus logs from proprietary applications, that are already collected in a SIEM or Splunk. For each employee the system builds a baseline of normal behavior and compares that user against their own history and against their peers, since a developer should resemble other developers.

The product produces a risk score for users whose behavior looks abnormal, and gives analysts drill-down investigation tools and dashboards. It runs on-premises on top of Splunk and adds context from Active Directory, HR systems and sometimes travel systems. Tendler said most of the findings at Fortune 1,000 customers were not stolen credentials but misuse by insiders. Examples included nosy administrators, employees about to be terminated who probed sensitive servers even when they failed, and call center representatives who opened sensitive customer data in CRM applications. He argued the differences are a fully machine-learning approach rather than rules, and flexibility to work with any authentication or access log.

In the question period, he said the current scope stops at visibility into risky users, with policy and prevention planned for later. Role context such as admin or developer status feeds the peer comparisons, and the company keeps its focus on the security team rather than HR. The one requirement for customers is that the relevant logs already sit in a SIEM or Splunk. For practitioners, the takeaway is that insider risk can surface from existing authentication data when each user is measured against both their own history and their peer group.

talks.title: 2015 Quick Look: The Little JPEG That Could (Hack Your Organization)
talks.teaser: A live demo shows polyglot JPEG profile uploads bypassing checks for remote code execution on a government web server.
talks.summary:
The session revisits a real-world intrusion against a government agency where attackers started from the public internet, abused a web server upload feature, and eventually took the whole domain. The presenter focuses only on the first hop: compromising the outward-facing web server through profile photo uploads.

The demo follows attacker logic on a Microsoft-based stack. Straight uploads of active server pages fail content validation, not just extension checks. Renaming extensions fails for the same reason. The breakthrough is a file that still parses as an image while the server treats readable metadata or embedded content like HTML or executable markup. Using exiftool-style metadata editing, the speaker injects a redirect toward command execution, then chains a weak rule that only looks for “.jpeg” in the filename—allowing names such as jpeg.aspx—plus an encoded PowerShell payload that pulls an interpreter into memory without touching disk. A listener connection confirms shell access on the target.

The closing point is operational: a mundane profile upload on an internet-facing app can become full server compromise and a bridge toward internal SQL servers and domain-wide impact when filters trust image magic bytes but execution paths still honor polyglot content.

talks.title: 2015 Quick Look: Pass-the-Hash II
talks.teaser: Shows how hardware-backed virtualization keeps Windows credentials out of reach of pass-the-hash attacks, even against NTLM.
talks.summary:
A development lead on the Windows security team at Microsoft presents a session on stopping credential theft and pass-the-hash attacks with hardware-based virtualization. The approach is built on Isolated User Mode, a hypervisor-enforced boundary in which only signed operating system code runs. The problem it targets is that device drivers run in the kernel of the high-level OS, so injected code there can reach the local security authority process and pull out stored credentials.

The speaker walks through a smart card logon. The isolated component generates key parameters for a Kerberos smart card exchange, a request that stays visible to an attacker but is useless without the key material held inside the isolated environment. The domain controller returns a ticket-granting ticket and an NTLM hash encrypted to those parameters, which only the isolated component can unwrap. Single sign-on then runs through that component, so a credential-dumping tool can reach the local security authority but has no credential it can carry to another machine. Machine accounts move from passwords to hardware-bound keys, and authentication policies bind users to specific machines. Because the component answers questions for any caller, weak operations such as MS-CHAP v2 and NTLMv1 are blocked from single sign-on to prevent brute-force inference.

The talk closes by noting that firmware, UEFI components, the small isolated stub and the hardware itself form a remaining trust boundary, one that an attacker would need a zero-day to breach. The takeaway is that NTLM and Kerberos single sign-on can keep working with existing domain controllers without leaving an extractable NTLM hash on the client.

talks.title: Latest Research on PoS Malware
talks.teaser: Traces how RAM-scraping point-of-sale malware families evolved, how stolen card data is sold, and how retailers can defend.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys point-of-sale malware that steals payment card data from memory, a technique known as RAM scraping, rather than from the magnetic stripe. The presenter follows twelve malware families discovered between 2011 and 2014, beginning with early signs of debugging tools being used on POS systems. Retail and hospitality were the main targets then, and any business that accepts cards is at risk now. Recent large retail breaches are used to show the scale of the problem.

Across the families, the speaker compares features such as keylogging, a kill command that removes the malware, a customizable builder kit, and routing stolen data over Tor. Common traits include disguising as ordinary system components, encrypting data before sending it, and relying on HTTP POST for exfiltration. Eight exfiltration methods are outlined, from fake hosted sites and Tor hidden addresses to compromised email and manual removal, and multi-stage exfiltration is described as a way to avoid triggering alerts. The talk also walks through the carding underground, where stolen cards are sold in batches and priced by brand, with bulk purchases cutting unit prices.

For defenders, the presenter recommends patching, limiting internet access on POS systems, application whitelisting, data loss prevention, deleting stored cardholder data and keeping audit logs. Discovery statistics show intrusions often succeed in minutes while detection takes weeks or months. EMV chip-and-PIN and tokenization are covered, with the warning that card data is still decrypted in memory during processing, so EMV does not stop RAM scraping. The closing questions address PCI DSS as a baseline and breach detection systems.

talks.title: United We Stand, Divided We Fall
talks.teaser: Argues that digital interdependence requires agreed norms of behavior and risk-focused, intelligence-driven security.
talks.summary:
Arthur W. Coviello opens by comparing the years before World War I with today's interconnected world. He argues that tangled trade networks and alliances turned one assassination into a global war, and that nations and companies still act as if they are independent even though they are deeply interdependent. Unlike the physical world, which has centuries of established protocols, the digital world has only about two decades of experience, leaving governments, businesses and individuals unsure of their responsibilities online.

He describes how this uncertainty is spilling into real conflict, pointing to strained relations between the United States and China after espionage indictments halted cybercrime cooperation between them. He also notes that criminal groups benefit from the resulting chaos. To bring order, he proposes four foundational principles: renouncing cyber weapons for waging war, cooperating internationally on prosecuting cybercriminals, keeping internet commerce open with intellectual property respected, and protecting personal privacy. He acknowledges that trust gaps, conflicting ambitions and the difficulty of proving attribution will make these principles hard to adopt, and that no nation should act alone.

On the defensive side, he presents intelligence-driven security as the response to an expanding attack surface. The approach starts with risk to critical data and the people who access it, rather than the network perimeter, and it calls for stronger identity checks than passwords alone. It also requires visibility into how data is used, analysis that turns signals into action, and big data controls. He closes by citing the joint anti-piracy effort of Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia in the Malacca Strait as proof that leveraging interdependence can work, and urges the audience to apply the same cooperation to the digital world.

talks.title: Keeping Up with the Joneses: How Does Your Insider Threat Program Stack Up?
talks.teaser: Benchmarks from interviews with companies show where insider threat programs stand, plus a 13-element roadmap for building one.
talks.summary:
Two presenters, one from CERT's Insider Threat Center and one from a company's insider risk program, open with real cases from CERT's database of roughly 850 incidents. One involves a departing director who copied customer files and recruited colleagues to do the same. Another involves a programmer whose logic bomb was tested in a training environment and detonated after he left. Single signals look harmless, so monitoring must connect them over time.

The research came from an INSA task force and a DHS public-private partnership. Interviews showed many companies lacked a formal program, and only five had an insider threat incident response plan. The result was a 13-element roadmap across initiation, planning, operations and reporting phases, backed by a resource guide mapping about 200 publications to each element.

Key recommendations were senior leadership support, a cross-functional team spanning HR, legal and IT, and mapping critical assets before buying new tools. Existing tools wrapped in process can flag, for example, an employee who resigns while holding access to critical data. Contractor agreements should require prompt notice when staff leave, with access removed immediately.

talks.title: New Frontiers in Security
talks.teaser: Panelists debate whether companies should go on offense, how Snowden reshaped trust, and what tools would cut alert noise.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by revisiting a 1998 warning about threats to national infrastructure and asks whether the field has improved since then. The panelists agree that progress has been slow. One argues that security lags behind technology because organizations deploy IT before securing it, which makes breaches hard to avoid. Another stresses that good security needs sustained effort rather than one-time fixes.

On offense, the panelists agree that companies should not strike back. Their reasons are that such actions are illegal, that attackers mostly want data that is already gone by the time a breach is detected, and that one company's offensive move could harm many others with similar exposure. They call for clear rules of engagement and a defined government role in deciding what counts as an attack. The Snowden disclosures came up as well, with the panelists describing damage to trust in the US government abroad, greater concern about insider threats, and the view that information sharing does not have to conflict with privacy.

Looking ahead, one panelist points to near real-time, diagnostic detection that anticipates attacks before they occur. Another asks for tools that reduce tens of millions of daily alerts to the few that matter. The panel closes by saying that talent is best attracted through a sense of purpose, open communication and certified training standards.

talks.title: Storm Advancing: Security Weathermen Forecast the Advanced Threat Landscape
talks.teaser: Security leaders debate how big data analytics, anomaly detection and automation can catch advanced threats that signatures miss.
talks.summary:
A panel moderated by an industry analyst examined how advanced threat detection is changing the security operations center and where big data analytics fits in. The analyst argued that signature-based prevention misses targeted attacks, so teams need baselines of normal behavior and anomaly detection across network traffic, endpoints, databases and user activity. The panelists, from organizations with roughly 1,500 to 5,000 employees, described their tool stacks and said their security logs had grown from about 40 gigabytes per day to more than 400 gigabytes per day.

The panelists agreed that collecting data is easy and that correlating it and staffing the analysis is hard. One organization kept its SIEM for first-level detection but used Splunk for fast retrieval, since the SIEM struggled with searches over 24 hours of device traffic. Another wired Splunk into its network so that alerts from several vendors triggered automatic isolation of workstations, cutting response from about 30 minutes to seconds. Other practices included per-endpoint VLANs to limit lateral spread, multiple sandboxes as detection rates dropped, and threat sharing with industry peers preferred over commercial feeds.

For practitioners, the takeaways were to gain visibility into the network, move toward automation because attackers already use it, and get the basics right before buying advanced tools. Panelists also suggested justifying spending with measured drops in infected machines and compliance requirements, and building staff from network engineers and in-house training while outsourcing routine tier one work. The analyst expected SIEM to persist alongside newer security analytics platforms rather than disappear.

talks.title: Security Metrics: Can They Be Effectively Measured Across the Enterprise?
talks.teaser: Panelists compare board, management, and engineering metrics and show how to link measures to business objectives.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a familiar tension: security teams can quantify almost anything, yet executives often dismiss reports as too technical or unrelated to business goals. Andrew McCullough argues that meaningful metrics must be clear, actionable, and explicitly tied to stakeholder objectives, describing a flow from business goals through risk understanding to consolidated reporting. Ivana Cojbasic structures examples by audience—boards want risk posture, initiative progress, audit remediation trends, and peer benchmarks; directors track vulnerability and patch posture, training compliance, and policy coverage; engineers need operational detail such as provisioning hygiene and internal scan findings.

Jody Brazil widens the critique: the industry lacks agreement on what to measure, and many dashboards celebrate control activity—firewall drops or raw vulnerability totals—that leaders cannot influence. A Ponemon-linked survey cited in the discussion finds most respondents want alignment with business objectives but far fewer achieve it, and many avoid reporting failures. The panel distinguishes numbers from true metrics by measuring against stated objectives, such as mean time to patch against a seven-day policy, and discusses combining threat, vulnerability, and control data to trend exposure rather than isolated tool outputs.

Practical guidance closes the session: engage each constituency to learn what they value, match reporting depth to the role, invest in realistic timelines, and recalibrate as goals shift. On ROI, most panelists treat security as assurance and efficiency rather than revenue return, while noting frameworks like FAIR and external benchmarking approaches as partial answers to “what good looks like.”

talks.title: Where in the World is xn--80atbrbl6f.xn--p1ai?
talks.teaser: Researchers map how internationalized domain names enable homographic phishing, malvertising, and botnet DGAs from large-scale web logs.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why DNS still carries ASCII while the web moved to Unicode, then walks through punycode and how clients expose either Unicode or xn-- forms in browsers, Office, PDF readers, and mobile. Adoption in the speakers’ filter data climbed from a handful of domains in 2003 to thousands after the spec stabilized, yet third-party malicious lists barely flagged IDN URLs until automated evil-site harvesting surfaced tens of thousands of examples.

The middle catalogs deception modes: homographs, brand-looking punycode tails, blended phishing stories, log-sourced spoofs of major brands and regional sites, and how encoding hides repetitive Russian-label patterns analysts need decoded. Unicode block mismatch counting surfaces suspicious multilingual mashups tied to exploit kits, credential phishing, traffic-driving botnets, Facebook codec scams, and multilingual malvertising rings. Russian Cyrillic TLD traffic dominates; mobile SMS fraud jars cluster on the same infrastructure. A long-running xn--pn-- pattern looks like an IDN DGA with sparse resolution and broad customer reach, still unresolved.

Practitioners should expect continued growth as new gTLDs expand the playground, monitor both encoded and decoded forms, reject blanket blocking based on skewed prevalence stats, hunt xn-- variants of brands, and tune gateways and SIMs to flag block-mismatch domains rather than ignoring punycode outright.

talks.title: The Boy Who Played with Fusion
talks.teaser: Follows a teenage fusion builder's nuclear projects, from cargo scanning and medical isotopes to a buried reactor design.
talks.summary:
Nuclear physicist Taylor Wilson opens with his background, saying he has worked in nuclear science since about age 10. He describes building a fusion reactor in his garage at 14 and presents energy as the foundation of nearly every modern problem, from electronics and transport to clean food and water.

The first project he covers is a low-cost detector for nuclear material aimed at the millions of cargo containers entering the country each year. Existing scanners can cost more than a million dollars, so he designed a cheaper system that replaces helium-3 with water as the active detection medium. He also shows a prototype for producing medical isotopes used in PET scans, which could lower scan costs and make imaging possible in places where short-lived isotopes could not previously be supplied.

Turning to energy, Wilson argues that fusion power may arrive within his lifetime, but that current nuclear power still has problems with cost and remote accident risk. He outlines a factory-built small reactor design buried underground, with a reactor module that runs for decades without refueling and a removable power module for maintenance. He says the design could cost about half of current nuclear power and can also deliver heat for producing water. He closes by describing science as exploration.

talks.title: iOS Security: The Neverending Story of Application-Security
talks.teaser: Shows how malicious iOS configuration profiles grant remote control, how they can be hidden, and how MDM traffic can be abused.
talks.summary:
Adi Sharabani and Yair Amit of Skycure argue that iOS remains a hard target for malicious apps, yet configuration profiles sit outside the app sandbox and get little scrutiny. Profiles control settings such as proxies, VPNs and certificates, so an attacker who persuades a user to install one can route traffic and read encrypted sessions. The lures discussed include free-content sites, Wi-Fi portals that require a profile, and malicious service providers.

A live demonstration showed a phone redirected to a page that prompted a profile install, after which the attacker could steer the browser and expose a logged-in Facebook session. The speakers then described a flaw that let a profile stay active while the profile list showed none, which they had reported to Apple and expected to be fixed in iOS 7.1; technical details were withheld. The second part examined mobile device management, where the device's check-in channel to the MDM server was not certificate pinned. In a demo, the attacker altered a server response to list installed apps and then sent an erase-device command, though the attack depended on waiting for the admin's push notification.

The closing advice was to keep devices updated, review the installed profile list, and have organizations enforce OS updates and network-based protection on phones. MDM vendors were urged to verify client certificates and work with Apple on the pinning problem.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: Day of Destruction
talks.teaser: A chronological tour of disk wipers and ransomware leads into live demos that brick laptops through corrupted ACPI firmware updates.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a historical survey of attacks meant to ruin machines rather than only steal data, from early Unix resource exhaustion through the Chernobyl virus’s attempt to reflash BIOS, Stuxnet’s industrial sabotage, sophisticated and crude wipers tied to Iran, North Korean destructive campaigns against South Korea, and the evolution of encrypt-and-extort schemes from the 1989 PC Cyborg virus through CryptoLocker’s timed key destruction. Shamoon receives a recorded walkthrough: timed activation, rapid file overwrite including a political image, MBR wipe, and an unbootable recovery screen mirroring thousands of endpoints in 2012.

The narrative then argues that most “destructive” incidents are really disruptive because backups and reimaging restore operations, whereas signed BIOS and supply-chain abuse still leave recovery paths. The speakers sketch a worst-case corporate morning—badge readers, HVAC, phones, and recovery plans all dead—and pivot to attacking PC firmware at scale. They catalog updatable peripherals, explain why ACPI embedded controllers matter for power and thermals, and show reverse-engineered Apple SMC updates abused after a fake security-patch lure. One demo spikes CPU load past 100°C with fans disabled; another reflashes SMC until the laptop cannot power on at all.

Closing material stresses firmware signing across chips, not just BIOS, and introduces CrowdResponse for Windows collection: process and directory sweeps with signature checks and hashing, plus per-process Yara memory scanning demonstrated catching Shamoon before the wipe finishes. They forecast more hacktivist and nation-state interest in irreversible system loss and urge detection during malware dormancy windows.

talks.title: Hacking Exposed: The Art of Deterrence
talks.teaser: Live demos trace a phished PDF through POS RAM scraping, then explore deterrence moves and math-based controls that block the same paths.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing Hacking Exposed-style work as equally about strong countermeasures as about understanding attacks. A staged corporate network demonstration walks from a payroll-themed malicious PDF and remote shell on an administrator host through credential theft, discovery of point-of-sale systems, deployment of Dexter-style memory scrapers, and exfiltration of card data to a command-and-control panel observed in Wireshark and the attacker console.

The middle shifts to the art of deterrence: disrupting adversaries, raising cost, and—with heavy legal warnings—a walkthrough of identifying a carding-oriented C2, exploiting weak PHP and SQL in the panel, dumping operator credentials, uploading a payload that clears stolen card logs, and misattributing activity to a rival group. The speakers also recap familiar perimeter, endpoint, and outbound detection measures, including simple HTTP post indicators, and introduce botnet panel weaknesses they plan to disclose responsibly.

The close contrasts signature-heavy detection with a mathematical, feature-based classification approach trained on known good and bad samples. The same protections are shown blocking redeployed POS malware and neutering the original PDF delivery path. Audience questions probe historical anomaly detection noise, attacker motivation, and whether polymorphic malware can be separated with enough labeled data.

talks.title: We Are All Intelligence Officers Now
talks.teaser: Shows how cheap sensing, data retention and digital dependence shrink the room to opt out, and what individuals can do.
talks.summary:
Dan Geer argues, speaking for himself, that cybersecurity has become an occupation rather than a profession because the rate of change is too fast. He describes risk as transitive: when something you depend on fails, you inherit its risk. He suggests that society's attack surface may be growing faster than defenders' tools and skills, and he compares the question of who should report, observe or act on breaches with public health reporting rules and neighborhood watch duties.

The middle of the talk focuses on observability. Storage is now cheaper than deletion, traffic analysis reveals more than message content, and everyday objects such as connected street lights, cars and wearables can sense and identify people. He notes that free services make users the product, that most security products are dual use, and that other people's photos and data can expose someone who never opted in. He also questions government digital identity schemes, automatic updates and ISP-level inspection, asking who holds the data and who can act on it.

He closes by saying that opting out is becoming harder and that individual choices are shaped by the people around them. His suggested response is practical misrepresentation: keeping several digital identities, reducing one's footprint, and keeping control over when data is sent. He urges those who collect data not to drive the cost of opting out to zero, and frames the trade-off between convenience, security and liberty as a choice that is still open.

talks.title: How Artificial Intelligence Prevents Fraud
talks.teaser: Covers real-time behavioral AI, smart agents, and layered checks that spot card fraud and retail breach patterns faster.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens on how artificial intelligence already supports security in retail and financial services, not as speculation but through large-scale production systems. The guest describes a vendor focus on real-time decisions measured in milliseconds, with experience across major banks, card networks, and extensive merchant populations, processing on the order of a billion transactions per month.

A central thread is detecting compromise sooner than traditional waiting periods of weeks. The approach assigns each payment card a “smart agent” so instruments can be compared for synchronized suspicious shifts after a visit to a compromised store. That model is contrasted with population clustering and manually written fraud rules, which fail when every customer behaves differently. Prevention instead follows individual behavior for cardholders, merchants, and devices, including novel fraud patterns not yet catalogued.

The discussion closes on a four-layer holistic model: behavioral device identification, cross-channel endpoint behavior, merchant-level monitoring, and breach detection tied to stolen card activity. Consumers gain stronger protection without necessarily sacrificing privacy when behavior is modeled anonymously. The speaker frames twenty-fourteen as an inflection year for artificial intelligence amid major corporate investment, arguing that as more industries become software-driven, intelligence embedded in those systems becomes the long-term direction.

talks.title: Power of Continuous Threat Protection
talks.teaser: FireEye leaders argue signature-based defenses fall short and outline a detect-to-fix model after the Mandiant deal.
talks.summary:
This recorded interview from RSA 2014 features FireEye's Dave DeWalt and Kevin Mandia, questioned by Tom Field. They argue that attackers have become more sophisticated and that layered defenses built on signature-based detection share the same weakness, so one successful bypass can defeat the whole stack. They cite an average of 243 days from infection to discovery, followed by 32 days to remediate, and say the goal is to shorten both.

The speakers describe a threat spectrum that runs from opportunistic intrusions to criminal groups and nation-state actors, with destructive attacks as the main worry. They say people are now the easiest entry point, since spear-phishing email lures staff into compromising themselves. Their answer is to hunt for compromise rather than rely only on purchased products, and to detect quickly, with compromise confirmed within about ten minutes as an aspirational target. Detection has to be paired with response and remediation.

They walk through the capabilities behind that model: intrusion prevention, endpoint detection and response to confirm which alerts involve compromised hosts, and a Threat Analytics Platform that correlates events with intelligence to show which ones matter. They close with managed defense, offered at tiers from alert triage to full monitoring, and explain how the Mandiant acquisition added incident response and automated remediation. The practical takeaway is that products and people need to be combined.

talks.title: 2014 Fraud Prevention: 2 Key Steps
talks.teaser: Explains why big data analytics and stronger, continuous authentication are key steps for banks to head off fraud.
talks.summary:
This interview with Gartner analyst Avivah Litan, conducted around RSA Conference, looks at what banks should prioritize to prevent fraud. Litan argues that big data analytics lets institutions combine data from every banking channel and spot early warning signs faster than before. She describes one institution whose analytics staff saw a fraudulent wire transfer forming and stopped it, while noting that legacy platforms make enterprise-wide analytics hard to deploy.

On authentication, Litan says larger institutions should move toward continuous behavioral authentication, watching how customers and employees navigate systems and use endpoints over time instead of trusting a single credential. Smaller banks can get a less costly version by binding a user's identity to a mobile phone through a credential and, ideally, a biometric.

The conversation also covers the threat landscape: criminal groups building closed malware that is not shared with other criminals, social engineering aimed at call center staff, and insider risk that extends to contractors and software updates in the supply chain. Litan also points to the growing use of managed threat intelligence services. Her broader point for practitioners is that technology alone is not enough, since siloed teams cannot act well on data they do not share.

talks.title: Cybersecurity in India
talks.teaser: Surveys India's cybersecurity challenges, from new digital users and banking oversight to outsourcing risk and skills shortages.
talks.summary:
In this interview, Tom Field talks with a director of the Data Security Council of India about the country's security landscape. The council was created by an industry association as a separate body to cover security and privacy across sectors such as banking, telecom, manufacturing and critical infrastructure. Its work includes awareness and education, a security and privacy framework that Indian companies are adopting, policy support for government, chapters in ten cities, and cyber labs in eight police premises where officers are trained at several levels.

The discussion covers several pressures. Rapid growth in mobile connectivity and digital finance is bringing first-time online users into the formal economy, and protecting them is a new concern. Geography makes India a target for adversaries, so critical infrastructure such as power generation has become a government priority. The IT and BPO sector handles sensitive data and personal information for clients abroad, which creates outsourcing concerns but also a market for security services. Banking is described as a leading sector for security implementation under detailed rules from the central bank, and the government is working to formalise collaboration among banking CISOs.

On regulation, the Information Technology Act is presented as a comprehensive framework that other countries use as a benchmark. On workforce, a government study cited a need for about 500,000 people over the next four to five years. The response combines formal university programs with informal training channels and a goal of exporting skills and services. The main takeaway is that developing security skills is treated as a central priority for government, industry and educational institutions.

talks.title: How to Fight Targeted Attacks
talks.teaser: Argues that predictive defenses, insight into who clicks what, and real-world phishing training beat reacting after breaches.
talks.summary:
In this video interview recorded at RSA, Kevin Epstein of Proofpoint discusses findings from a targeted attacks survey run with Information Security Media Group. He argues that many organizations act only after an attack has surfaced, often when an employee notices something wrong, and that defenders should aim to stop attacks earlier. Phishing is singled out as the most worrying route in, since email now follows people onto mobile devices and attackers can aim lures at specific individuals.

On the technology side, Epstein pointed to deeper inspection of malware on the way in, such as sandboxes that run suspicious files rather than relying only on signatures. He also described scanning websites for precursors, like an obfuscated redirect with no legitimate purpose, so an attack can be blocked before any malware is present. For the human factor, he said staff need training and feedback, whether the clicks come from a test or a real incident, and he supported organizations running phishing tests on their own employees.

Epstein's closing advice was that organizations should focus on two things: predictive defense that stops attacks before they land, and insight into who is clicking what, so that compromises can be found and fixed in days rather than weeks. Classroom sessions and policies have a place, but he argued that realistic exercises are the most effective form of training because staff must decide on the spot whether to open or click something.

talks.teaser: Maps Syrian Electronic Army propaganda hacks and offers defender steps for domain locks, MFA, and phishing awareness.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames the Syrian Electronic Army as low-technology yet highly effective propagandists whose impact comes less from advanced malware than from social media defacement, registrar and DNS manipulation, and relentless spear phishing against people who hold Twitter, Facebook, and similar credentials.

Tracing activity from early Facebook spam and page defacements through international incidents—including high-profile media accounts and the AP Twitter message that briefly shook markets—the speaker walks through representative chains such as the Melbourne IT reseller compromise that redirected DNS for major news outlets. Attack flows include tailored Outlook and webmail lures, CEO or regional-manager pretexts, reuse of stolen passwords on corporate social accounts, harvesting of Google Apps data, and patience with sleeper credentials.

For practitioners, the closing emphasis is operational: lock domains at registrars, enforce multifactor authentication, train staff on link inspection especially on mobile devices, run awareness programs that broadcast suspected lures quickly through non-email channels, assume broad compromise after a hit, reset passwords across email and social properties, watch for delayed re-entry, and review login logs for anomalous geography.

talks.title: Crypto for Constrained Devices -- A Talk with Whitfield Diffie
talks.teaser: Covers lightweight cryptography for wearables and IoT devices, the NSA's Simon and Speck ciphers, and validation hurdles.
talks.summary:
Recorded at RSAC, this conversation between Whitfield Diffie and SafeLogic CEO Ray Potter looks at cryptography for constrained devices such as wearables, sensors and connected home gear. It opens with the NSA's release of the Simon and Speck lightweight ciphers. Diffie recounts a 2011 briefing he gave to the agency on an earlier lightweight design called Hummingbird, and says he never suspected the NSA of building in weaknesses. He compares the designs' trade-offs: Simon's combining functions are cheap compared with a table lookup, while Speck's modular adder suits both software and hardware.

Potter then describes the problems SafeLogic faced building cryptographic modules for these devices. Space and footprint are tight compared with phones, and power draw matters as much as gate count. Proof-of-concept bulk encryption tests showed little speed gap between Simon, Speck and AES-128. The bigger obstacle was validation: federal and healthcare customers ask for FIPS 140 validation, which Simon and Speck could not receive, so standards-based AES was judged worth any small performance cost. Diffie added that the core problem is implementation more than algorithm.

The discussion then turns to threats. Potter cites a surgeon recording a procedure on Google Glass, where patient data stored on the device must be encrypted under HIPAA, and connected thermostats that could reveal whether a home is empty. Diffie points to implanted medical devices and to wireless links in cars, such as brakes and tire pressure sensors. He notes that radio once made cryptography essential in the First World War and is doing so again. Both fear a serious incident will arrive before the industry plans for constrained-device security, so the talk aims to raise awareness and build crypto in from the start.
