talks.title: Project 2020: Preparing Your Organization for Future Threats ... Today
talks.teaser: Summarizes an ICSPA-backed futures exercise on technology-driven crime, scenario planning, and organizational readiness steps.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits Project 2020, a multi-year initiative begun in 2012 with ICSPA, Trend Micro, and European law enforcement partners. The goal was to look eight years ahead at how advancing technology might create new vulnerabilities and criminal opportunity, far beyond the industry’s usual one-year prediction cycle.

After baselining the threat landscape and emerging technologies, the team built three narrative scenarios: Kinako as a second-generation digital native, shifts in how small firms operate as global cloud collectives with bartered skills and agile supply chains, and the fictional nation South Silvania, where telecom and content provision sit in private cloud infrastructure classed as critical national infrastructure. The talk ties these stories to trends such as filtered “content service” experiences, cyber insurance, security scoring for partners and countries, internet regionalization, and an envisaged international cyber criminal court, plus risks from scramblers, cloud-scale denial of service, identity hijacking, and attacks on perception and infrastructure.

The speaker argues many forecasts already aligned with real-world developments and closes by urging practitioners to read the full report and share the message beyond the security community, including through a short web series aimed at a broader audience.

talks.title: Intelligence Driven Security
talks.teaser: Shows how grouping adversaries by their tools, infrastructure and habits can focus defenses on likely attackers.
talks.summary:
Adam Meyers, of CrowdStrike, argues that an enterprise intrusion is better treated as an adversary problem than a malware problem, because every implant and command-and-control setup traces back to people who built and run it. He separates adversaries into targeted attackers, who gain a foothold, escalate privileges and move laterally toward goals such as disruption or theft of intellectual property, and opportunistic "spray and pray" attackers, who use exploit kits and compromised sites to harvest credentials or borrow machine resources. He notes that criminals have begun to adopt the targeted playbook.

Attribution, in his view, depends on habits that adversaries repeat. Examples include reused passwords, mutex names and favorite registry keys, domain registration patterns, implant configurations and build times, delivery infrastructure, and reused exploit chains and shellcode. Overlapping command-and-control infrastructure can link campaigns that look unrelated, and one zero-day was traced back through its supply chain to an earlier criminal group using the same exploit. He cautions that PlugX, long assumed to belong to one actor, was used by several groups, so a single indicator can mislead. He also walks through sector views for financial institutions, naming groups by animal-based labels and noting that nation-state actors often keep business hours.

The practical takeaway is to feed this intelligence into existing controls such as IDS, firewalls, DNS monitoring and host-based detection, rather than relying on out-of-the-box products that generate noise. Intelligence can also shape penetration tests, where an assessor uses the tools and procedures of the adversaries most likely to target the organization and measures how well detection holds up.

talks.title: Internet of Things... Promising but Let's Not Forget Security Please!
talks.teaser: Surveys the security challenges of Internet of Things devices, from exposed sensors and smart meters to device lifetime and identity.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by arguing that small networked chips are now built into appliances, meters, vehicles and industrial equipment, so security professionals need to understand them. The speaker lists the threats: worms that hit general-purpose operating systems, script kiddies and organised crime, and nation-state attackers. A search engine for internet-connected devices is used to show how easily a temperature sensor and control panels can be found, some with no password protection. Denial of service and physical harm to people are raised too, with a transport incident and a dam incident cited as examples.

The middle section looks at what sets these networks apart from ordinary IT. Devices can stay in service for decades, outlasting the cryptographic algorithms they ship with, which raises the question of post-quantum options. Unique device identity is often unnecessary, since group membership and location may be enough for a room of sensors. Shared access networks mean one misbehaving application can disrupt others, and mobile devices need constant position tracking. Smart meters can leak usage patterns, and a previous study showed how sampled electricity consumption could reveal which TV channel was being watched.

To close, the speaker explains that how often a device reports determines how quickly a stolen unit is noticed, and that cheap hardware allows redundancy so losing one sensor matters less. The talk stresses that IoT risks vary widely and should be handled one slice at a time, and that the field is still a work in progress. The network itself may be a useful place to enforce security for these devices.

talks.title: Cyber Security Canon: You Should Have Read These Books by Now
talks.teaser: Presents a curated cybersecurity reading canon and spotlights five foundational books every practitioner should know.
talks.summary:
The presenter outlines a year-and-a-half project to define a cybersecurity canon using three criteria akin to literary canon debates: works that represent the field, are widely regarded as genuine landmarks, and reflect high quality from authors who understand the subject. He proposes twenty books for community consideration rather than a fixed syllabus, and aims to keep the conversation going with annual updates and voting.

Five titles receive the deepest treatment. We Are Anonymous captures hacktivism around 2010–2011, the HB Gary Federal compromise, LulzSec’s fifty-day campaign against twenty-five companies, and Sabu’s informant role leading to mass arrests. Confront and Conceal explains U.S. and Israeli policy behind Olympic Games and Stuxnet as a milestone nation-state cyber strike on Iranian enrichment infrastructure. Kingpin traces Max Butler’s conquest of carding forums and the FBI investigation that followed. The Cuckoo’s Egg follows Clifford Stoll’s late-1980s hunt for state-sponsored intruders at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, highlighting enduring intelligence-versus-law-enforcement tensions. Cryptonomicon is recommended as ambitious fiction linking early computing, cryptography, and hacker culture.

Additional mentions span cyberpunk novels, cybercrime thrillers, and CERT guidance on insider risk as largely organizational rather than purely technical. The session closes with pointers to online reviews, audience suggestions for the canon, and bookstore discounts on listed titles.

talks.title: Mobile App Privacy: Gone in 6 seconds
talks.teaser: Shows how a Trojan app and a rooted phone can lift account tokens from popular mobile apps and reuse them on another device.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how much private data apps on a phone can give up once an attacker gets onto the device. The presenter lists the ways access can happen: a lost phone, a tampered charging station, and most commonly a Trojan app delivered to the victim. Many phones run older platform versions, and rooting makes the risk worse because it exposes the whole device to other apps.

The live demo used a Trojan version of a popular game, sent by email and installed on a rooted test phone. Once it ran, it pulled the account database and app tokens from the device and uploaded them to a server. The presenter then imported that data onto a clean device, which came up signed in to Gmail, calendar, GitHub, Salesforce and other Google services. The copied tokens got past the two-factor check because they already proved the session. Beyond the demo, the presenter said similar token extraction worked on other apps, including a home alarm app, medical apps and dating apps, and that mail gateways did not flag the sample.

The takeaways are practical. Keep the platform updated, avoid rooting or jailbreaking unless you know the risks, and install apps only from reputable stores. If a phone is lost, remotely wipe it rather than relying on a lock screen. Review account activity logs and the list of devices signed in to your accounts, since copied tokens used on another device are rarely visible there. The presenter argued that the mobile industry is still behind in vetting apps.

talks.title: Beginners Guide to Reverse Engineering Android Apps
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Beginners Guide to Reverse Engineering Android Apps.
talks.summary:
Overview: Practice finding flaws in real Android apps in this fun, CTF-style hands-on workshop, and you will be ready to avoid making security errors in your own apps. Android apps are very easy to unpack, analyze, modify, and repack; partly because of the open nature of the system, and partly because most companies neglect basic security measures. In this workshop, participants will hack apps from Wells Fargo, Microsoft, Lyft, WhatsApp, Whole Foods, IBM, Harvard, Progressive, the Indian government, and o

Key Topics: ther large organizations. We will find insecure network transmissions, broken cryptography, improper logging, and pervasive lack of binary protections. We will also analyze the way iOS apps use network transmissions, and observe serious vulnerabilities in iOS apps from major companies. We will analyze Android internals in details, using the Drozer attack framework to inspect and manipulate intents to exploit insecure activities and content providers. We will perform a protection level downgrade attack on an Android 4.3 device, removing security protections from the Twitter app. All class materials are freely available on the Web, and will rem

Takeaways: ies were reported to the affected companies long ago, where appropriate. Equipment: participants must bring a laptop that can run VirtualBox machines. The host system can use Mac OS (best), Linux (OK) or Windows (usable but limited). We will use free Android emulators and a Kali virtual machine. They will be available as free downloads, and also locally on USB sticks.

talks.title: It's a Jungle Out There: The Security State of CMS Platforms
talks.teaser: Tracks vulnerable WordPress plugins over time and how attackers hunt them, ending with advice for site owners.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from a company that builds source code scanners, explains why the team turned to WordPress plugins. WordPress is the most widely used content management system, its plugin marketplace holds tens of thousands of add-ons, and nothing is checked before a plugin goes live. Low barriers to publishing combined with broad exposure made plugins a clear security concern.

The team scanned the top 50 plugins for several high-risk flaws, including SQL injection, cross-site scripting, request forgery and path traversal. About 30% were highly vulnerable at first. After notifying three vendors, one of them the company behind WordPress itself, a rescan in June still found about 20% of the plugins unfixed. A separate check of leading e-commerce plugins found seven vulnerable, together representing roughly 10 million downloads. The speaker then cited a follow-up report from Akamai that counted nearly 43,000 attacks against WordPress plugins in a single week, spread across 66 plugins. The talk walked through how an attacker could exploit many sites at once by pairing vulnerable plugins with search-engine queries, or target one site by listing the plugins it runs.

The closing advice covered three points. Ask your plugin marketplace how it vets submissions, whether through scanning, manual review or sandboxing. Keep plugins updated to the fixed versions. Set an internal standard so IT approves any WordPress site before staff deploy one. The speaker also argued that plugins distributed through wordpress.com benefit from a security review that wordpress.org lacks.

talks.title: Security Career Pro Tips
talks.teaser: Covers resumes, personal branding, online presence and working with recruiters for people building security careers.
talks.summary:
Jeff Combs, a recruiter with over 13 years of security hiring experience, starts with resumes. He says recruiters spend about six seconds on a first read, so a resume must map directly to the role, state concrete work instead of buzzwords, and cut padding that distracts the reviewer.

Next he covers professional maturity and personal branding. Calling yourself a ninja or pirate reads as juvenile, and candidates should present themselves as someone who solves business problems. He suggests rehearsing a career story aloud, explaining past decisions, results and where you are heading, since that is what interviewers want to hear. He also warns that LinkedIn profiles, search results and social media are checked, and that a single careless post can be used to screen someone out.

In the question round he advises focusing on the core problems a hiring team is trying to solve, using open source research to learn about the company, rather than claiming to cover every area of security. For people who are not job hunting, he recommends staying aware of roles and building a network by helping peers, so a future move does not start from zero. He also explains that hiring companies pay recruiters a percentage of first-year salary, so candidates should never pay one to represent them, and that reputation carries weight in a small industry.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2014
talks.teaser: Pitches a software-based threat detection platform that scales across cloud, on-premises and hybrid environments.
talks.summary:
Cypher presents a distributed software platform, built in about two and a half years, for catching the threats that matter most to each environment. It rests on three pillars. Detection actively interrogates suspicious objects to separate real malice from false positives and to reveal what an adversary is after. Actionable intelligence plugs into the existing infrastructure mesh rather than forcing its way into current tools.

Coverage comes from software sensors that run on premises, in cloud, in hybrid setups, or follow users on or off the network. The speaker contrasted this with appliances, which leave blind spots, and cloud-only tools, which miss metadata needed to infer intent. Pricing follows aggregated bandwidth rather than appliance count, and a REST API lets the platform push mitigations back into a customer's environment.

In the Q&A, the speaker explained that every unique object seen in an environment is run, alongside millions of malicious and clean samples, through machine learning to correlate metadata, and that abstracted intelligence can be shared with other organizations. Encrypted sessions are handled by partners who embed collectors in their appliances for SSL interception. Agentless device coverage comes from a model that turns network anomalies into techniques.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2014
talks.teaser: A behavioral analytics platform pitch shows how unified compliance data cuts SEC inquiry cost and helps officers spot insider human risk.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by shifting attention from network-centric security to people-centric risk. The speaker argues that compliance and security face disruptive cost and complexity when officers must pull communications, transactions, and physical security data from many silos to answer regulators; a medium-sized financial institution’s SEC inquiry workflow is described as a tangle of consultants, lawyers, and disconnected sources.

Red Owl Analytics introduces a platform that ingests multiple streams, normalizes them into one model, applies enrichment and statistical modeling of behavior over time, and offers interfaces to search, monitor, and explore. Near-term value is framed as labor savings; longer term, better discovery of harmful insider behavior. The company targets financial services first, then any domain with human reputation or balance-sheet risk, and notes growth from four to fifteen customers amid a Series A raise.

Judge questions highlight product lessons: customers use the tool to clear innocent employees faster, not only to pursue bad actors; integration relies on a small set of common fields such as originator, timestamp, participants, context, topic, and content; and false positives remain a human judgment problem—the system aims to empower analysts rather than replace them.

talks.title: Innovation Sandbox 2014
talks.teaser: Shows how the Optic platform scores, deduplicates and shares threat indicators inside vetted communities and SIEM tools.
talks.summary:
Colby DeRotif, chief technology officer of ThreatStream, pitches Optic, a threat intelligence platform for enterprise and government security teams. The talk explains that it gathers indicators from hundreds of sources, normalises and consolidates them, then adds context, relevance and severity scores using algorithms and community data.

Indicators are pushed to platforms such as ArcSight, Splunk and QRadar through prebuilt connectors, together with correlation instructions so the data can be used immediately. Operations teams then watch for activity matching those indicators. Members vote indicators up or down and share them in trusted subcommunities, and invitations let peers at other organizations join. An example given was an analyst tracking a watering hole campaign who submits a domain, giving a team on another continent the same visibility.

In the Q&A, DeRotif said duplicates are removed centrally and indicators seen from several sources are treated as more valuable, so customers receive one record per indicator type. Points and reputation are used to encourage members who prefer to receive rather than share. Vetting rejects free webmail sign-ups and includes a phone call with each applicant plus checks of professional profiles. The takeaway is a vetted sharing model meant to make indicators actionable inside existing operations.

talks.title: Little Bets: How Breakthrough Ideas Emerge from Small Discoveries
talks.teaser: Explains how small, affordable experiments and embracing failure lead to breakthrough ideas, with examples from HP and Pixar.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that breakthrough ideas rarely arrive as complete plans. The speaker points to companies such as YouTube, eBay, PayPal and Google, which all began with different aims, and suggests that schooling and management reward having the answer in advance. A single PowerPoint slide used for Army strategy in Afghanistan serves as an example of planning that breaks down in unfamiliar territory.

The middle section contrasts conceptual innovators, such as Mozart, with experimental innovators, such as Beethoven, who worked through draft after draft. It describes a former Agilent CEO who worked at HP, whose large-market initiatives all failed, and the HP 35 calculator, which market research predicted would not sell. After a prototype impressed a stranger on a flight, HP built 1,000 units and was selling a thousand a day within five months. The talk also covers managers weighing expected gains against entrepreneurs weighing what they can afford to lose, comedian Jerry Seinfeld testing new material in small clubs, and Pixar's storyboard reviews and plussing technique. Carol Dweck's research on fixed and growth mindsets rounds out the argument.

The closing section recounts how Pixar began as a hardware company, how the short films Luxo Junior and Tin Toy kept it going under Steve Jobs, and how Tin Toy won an Academy Award. The takeaway for practitioners is to make small, affordable bets, define in advance what you can lose, and expect most of them to fail while learning from each one.

talks.title: Hugh Thompson and Guests
talks.teaser: A session links behavioral analytics and growing digital histories to privacy risk, hiring ethics, and limits on forgetting data.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a vacation anecdote about wild monkeys that learn which visitors surrender food, framing a move into behavioral analytics and what richer data might infer about aptitude, pairing, or trust. The first interview covers grit as passion plus perseverance for long goals, a short self-report scale used at West Point, and why traditional whole-candidate metrics fail to predict who leaves. The speaker describes résumé follow-through scoring—multi-year commitments and visible advancement—that predicted teacher retention and student score gains without asking grit questions directly, and discusses faking, honesty incentives, deliberate practice, organizational culture, and learning from failure.

The second interview argues predictive uses of online and fused data are nearer than many assume, with behavioral signals already embedded in advanced security products. Examples include identifiers and casual facts that later become keys to identity or inference, poor de-identification under data fusion, cheaper storage than selective deletion, and formal undecidability of perfect erasure or airtight control rules.

The close contrasts resilient security with theater, breach-notification tort models versus impossible prevention mandates, and a charge to question precedent as the threat landscape shifts.

talks.title: State of the Hack: One Year after the APT1 Report
talks.teaser: Revisits the APT1 report a year on, tracing the PLA unit's behavior and drawing lessons on breach response and disclosure.
talks.summary:
The talk looks back a year after Mandiant published its 2013 report on APT1, the group it linked to PLA Unit 61398. The presenter starts with a 2012 intrusion into the New York Times and the public response to a newspaper's claim that the Chinese military was responsible. The company chose to publish evidence instead of relying on assertions. The report covered about 60 pages, roughly 3,000 indicators of compromise, and 141 victim companies across around twenty industries.

The presenter walks through the evidence behind the attribution. Of 2,672 intrusions, about 97% of the IP addresses traced back to Shanghai, and about 97% of the remote desktop sessions were set to a mainland Chinese character set. Online résumés from people who claimed past work with the unit were also cited. After publication, the group stopped using the exposed infrastructure, but new command-and-control infrastructure and new victims appeared, so the presenter describes a temporary pause rather than an end to the activity. Diplomatic and information-sharing efforts had little visible effect.

The closing section draws broader lessons from years of incident response. Attackers have the advantage because defenders must protect many systems while an intruder needs only one. Targeting people has replaced targeting perimeter systems. Organizations that learn of breaches and move from alert to fix quickly limit the damage, and the presenter urges defenders to test how they would be broken into. Disclosure rules and many stakeholders make responses harder, and a victim mindset tends to fade over time, leading to vigilance fatigue as staff leave and attention drops.

talks.title: The New Model of Security
talks.teaser: Cisco leaders outline a visibility, threat awareness and action model for securing Internet of Things devices at scale.
talks.summary:
At RSA Conference, Cisco's Christopher Young talks with Cisco chief strategy and technology officer Padmaschery Warrior about securing the Internet of Things. Warrior presents IoT as the next phase of internet evolution, pointing to roughly 10 billion connected devices today and about 50 billion expected by 2020. She argues that personalized services force a balance between locking systems down and keeping them usable.

Warrior proposes a three-part model: visibility, threat awareness and the ability to act. She compares the needed visibility to air traffic control, tracking every device, user and data flow in real time. Devices should not be trusted by default, so identity and context need constant verification. For threat awareness, she cites a Cisco annual security report in which every sampled corporation had connections to known malicious destinations, and she says indicators of compromise are underused. On action, she warns that bureaucratic processes and limited staff can slow response.

Open-source work comes up through OpenAppID, an application identification and control technology starting with detectors for about 1,000 applications. A community-based IoT Security Grant Challenge offers prize money for up to six winning security blueprints. Young adds that the industry has about a million security experts against billions of devices, so shared, community-driven approaches are needed. Practitioners should focus on visibility, threat awareness and fast action.

talks.title: Stop Looking for the Silver Bullet: Start Thinking Like a Bad Guy
talks.teaser: Frames cybercrime as a specialized marketplace and urges shifting budget toward intelligence, people, and business-critical apps.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting how defenders chase matching adversary tools with how criminals actually operate: as participants in a marketplace that sells profiles, access, maps, and stolen data while rewarding specialization across a five-stage attack lifecycle from research through exfiltration or destruction.

Despite heavy industry spending and strong blocking at the perimeter, breach counts and costs still rose, which the speaker attributes to a structural imbalance—defenders must be right every time while attackers need only one success. Research cited from the prior year showed roughly 86% of security budgets going to blocking infiltration, while newer work with the Ponemon Institute identified security intelligence (people, process, and technology) as the step yielding about 21% better return per incremental dollar, with adopters saving on average about $4 million more than peers. Assessments across dozens of companies found SOC-style capabilities averaging maturity two out of five, with compliance-focused programs often missing their own bars.

Recommendations emphasize reducing over-investment in point products, training people and processes, protecting what the business cares about (especially applications), and sharing threat intelligence that is fast, actionable, contextual, and exchanged via open standards so it integrates into existing environments.

talks.title: The FBI and the Private Sector: Closing the Gap in Cyber Security
talks.teaser: The FBI director explains how the bureau plans to partner with private companies on cyber threats.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker's first months in the director role, spent meeting state, local and industry partners to learn what they need from the bureau. The central problem is that companies often hold back from reporting intrusions. They fear government access to their networks, reputational damage, competitors learning of a breach, and liability. Reporting is also hard because there is no unified system, and it is unclear which federal body handles which kind of cybercrime.

The speaker described the bureau's current response. Its focus is on high-level intrusions, large botnets, state-sponsored hackers and global criminal syndicates. Cyber task forces operate in each of its 56 field offices, a national joint task force places several federal agencies at one table, and legal attache offices handle differences in law between countries. Agents are also embedded with police in several cyber hotspots in Europe. New tools were presented: a malware repository and analysis system that returns reports on submitted samples, an unclassified version planned for partners, a real-time channel for reporting intrusions, and fast alerts that push specific attack data to internet providers so they can block compromised nodes.

The speaker asked field office leaders to build one-to-one relationships with industry contacts rather than relying only on existing partnership groups. He argued that security and privacy are not a zero-sum trade-off and called for intelligence to be shared at machine speed under legal safeguards. For practitioners, the takeaway is to know your local FBI office contacts before an incident and to share indicators and context early.

talks.title: The Cryptographers' Panel
talks.teaser: Veteran cryptographers weigh NSA fallout, standards trust, research trends, and where deployed systems still fail.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a year shaped by large breaches and intelligence disclosures, with panelists reflecting on trapdoors in national standards, tampering with NIST guidance, and the breadth of parallel collection methods. They debate ethical red lines, cyber warfare limits, whistleblowing, and whether mathematics held while attackers bypassed endpoints and implementations.

Each participant highlights research they find notable, from censorship-resistant protocols and acoustic RSA key recovery to NSA’s Simon and Speck algorithms and counter-cryptanalysis that can flag collision-built certificates such as those tied to Flame. The conversation turns to IETF-led protocol encryption, perfect forward secrecy tradeoffs, conservative algorithm choices, slow PKI migrations, and homomorphic encryption’s promise versus today’s performance gap.

Closing threads cover Bitcoin’s centralization and hash power, password and IoT fragility, consumer privacy versus convenience, memorial remarks for departed colleagues, cryptonationalism, and the economic backlash on U.S. technology vendors after global surveillance concerns.

talks.title: Finding a Path Forward in an Increasingly Conflicted Digital World
talks.teaser: A keynote ties the RSA–NSA trust crisis to missing digital norms and four principles for nations and industry to pursue.
talks.summary:
The address opens at RSA Conference 2014 by placing the industry again at a crossroads reminiscent of 1990s fights over cryptography export, key escrow, and privacy. The presenter explains how RSA shifted from dominating encryption products to backing community-driven standards through bodies such as ANSI, X9, and NIST, including support for an elliptic-curve random-number approach adopted in 2006 and later withdrawn from products when NIST issued new guidance. He acknowledges long-standing defensive collaboration with the NSA’s IAD while arguing that blending intelligence collection with standards work erodes trust, endorsing clearer separation of roles and updated cryptographic standard-setting processes.

Stepping back, he argues that cheap, valuable information has collided government, business, and individual agendas without mature digital norms, risking loss of trust in the internet for commerce, research, and communication. He proposes four international principles: rejecting cyber warfare, cooperating against cybercrime, protecting lawful online commerce and intellectual property, and safeguarding individual privacy, framed with parallels to arms-control precedents and Kennedy’s 1963 American University speech.

For practitioners, the closing emphasis is on collective industry action alongside governments: convening stakeholders as with expanded financial-sector sharing models, articulating consequences of inaction, and advancing intelligence-driven security—analytics, identity for mobile and cloud, automated response, and risk management—so policy ideals are backed by deployable capability.

talks.title: Conundrums in Cyberspace: Exploiting Security in the Name of, well, Security
talks.teaser: Frames government surveillance and cyber conflicts as balancing problems, using actors, objectives, actions and impacts.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a theme from an earlier keynote: governments hold four overlapping roles online, as users, protectors of users and the internet, exploiters of vulnerabilities, and seekers of data. Public surveillance disclosures made those tensions concrete. A mid-1990s case involving AOL records and a French investigation shows how data stored in other jurisdictions complicates investigations.

The presenter then outlines Microsoft's principles in three areas. On security, the company says it plays defense rather than offense, builds no back doors, and flags malware regardless of its source. On privacy, it hands over data only under court orders naming specific accounts and would contest bulk demands. On transparency, it opens source code to governments, publishes reports on law enforcement requests, and gives customers notice where appropriate. A forensics tool example shows how one action can be framed in opposite ways in public.

To organize the problem, the presenter splits cyber threats into four categories, each needing its own strategy: cybercrime, economic espionage, military espionage, and cyber warfare. Judging any activity means walking through actors, objectives, actions and impacts, illustrated with airport scanners, the surveillance disclosures and Stuxnet, whose effects reached PCs worldwide that needed patches. The talk closes by urging listeners to reject objectives that are wrong and to weigh impacts, so society can judge the next disclosure.

talks.title: Survival Isn't Mandatory: Challenges and Opportunities of DevOps
talks.teaser: Argues that security teams should join DevOps early, using deployment data and Netflix's failure-testing practices as examples.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that DevOps, the joining of development and operations, changes how fast software reaches production, and that security professionals should engage with it now. Developers are rewarded for causing change and operations staff for preventing it, and the talk cites survey figures showing about 30 times more frequent deployments and 50% fewer failures among DevOps adopters, regardless of company size.

Controlling change comes first: knowing what assets exist and which changes are good is presented as the base for any anomaly detection. Netflix's Chaos Monkey, which switches off production instances on purpose, is offered as an example of deliberately testing failure. The Rugged Software movement is tied to a proposed security monkey that would surface SQL injection flaws early. One financial services example reported moving from quarterly releases to 46 changes per month while cutting its failure rate from 17% to 4%.

The closing part urges security staff to move upstream, use feedback loops, and build tooling that flags bugs when they are introduced. The speaker sees the meeting of developers and security as a rare chance that may not return for decades, so the audience should join DevOps and shape it rather than let it pass.

talks.title: Data-Driven Security - Where's the Data?
talks.teaser: Shows how security teams can use metrics like patch half-life and exploitability data to prove progress to management.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that information security lacks the accepted metrics finance uses, which makes it hard for security programs to show progress to management and technical peers. The speaker contrasts this with a CFO whose all-hands presentation consistently wins attention, then points to the US Department of State. There, a security score was calculated for each machine, rolled up to department level and shared internally, so departments could compare results. Within a year the organization's risk score fell by roughly 90%, and temporarily raised costs on critical vulnerabilities drove fast patching.

The main metric discussed is half-life, the time it takes to address half of the vulnerabilities in a network. For critical vulnerabilities it was 30 days in 2003, 29 days in 2009, and is now around 25 days overall, with clear differences by industry. Finance and service organizations were at 21 to 24 days, while health care and manufacturing sat at 38 and 51 days. Internet Explorer's half-life was 16 days, which the speaker tied to well-managed patching. Breach data correlated with vulnerabilities suggested that exploitability is a better guide than severity: a random fix reduced breach probability by about 2%, a CVSS 10 fix about 4%, and fixing vulnerabilities with known exploits about 30%.

Other examples reinforced the point. A customer with a 30-day patch target found that its rate dipped whenever new networks were added without clear ownership, so ownership was identified as the key factor. A company that tracked malware alerts saw detections drop after deploying a tool that ran users as standard accounts, and an Australian organization saw detections stay high after application whitelisting, which it attributed to attackers mutating malware. The speaker closed by proposing a shared, vendor-neutral platform under the Trustworthy Internet initiative for publishing monthly half-life benchmarks, and asked the audience for data, since it already sits in logs and scanners.

talks.title: Using Big Data to Fight Banking Fraud
talks.teaser: Explains how banks can use big data and predictive analytics to spot account takeover and fraud before damage occurs.
talks.summary:
At RSA Conference 2013, Tom Field of Information Security Media Group interviews Terry Austin, president and CEO of Guardian Analytics, about using big data and analytics against banking fraud. Austin argues that perimeter protections no longer stop evolving threats, and that predictive analytics applied to network, application and user-interaction data can spot risk before damage occurs, whatever the attack method. He points out that many financial firms outsource their technology and lack large in-house fraud and security teams, so they need a consolidated view of information and the expertise to act on it.

Austin describes attackers as organized and technically advanced. He says automated threats such as the High Roller banking Trojan have given way to combinations of automated and manual activity. Denial-of-service attacks are used as a distraction, and fraudsters increasingly cover their tracks or misdirect responders after an incident. His point is that anticipating attacks puts defenders in a far better position than reacting to them.

Guardian Analytics started with a fraud prevention product for online banking built on big data and predictive analytics. Over the past year it added a mobile banking solution and an ACH payment system that analyzes the full payment flow, with a wire system planned soon. Austin says about 250 financial institutions now rely on the platform, which he frames as a foundation for their strategic growth as well as their protection.

talks.title: Criminal Education: Lessons from the Criminals and their Methods - Dan Lamorena
talks.teaser: Explains how criminal markets split up attacks, and why published standards leave defenders predictable.
talks.summary:
He opens by contrasting the classic gunslinger bank robbery with today's version, where criminals can reach thousands of ATMs remotely and stay anonymous. He uses a recent case in which about $45 million was withdrawn in a few hours after attackers altered withdrawal limits at an Indian debit card processor and took account and PIN data for crews in 26 countries. Such operations, he notes, take years of planning and split the work among specialists.

He describes how defenders look predictable because they follow published standards such as PCI and ISO, and how roughly 3% of IT budgets goes to security, mostly spent meeting those requirements. He walks through a typical attack: researching staff on social media, a fake restaurant follow-up email carrying malware, access points sold to a buyer, and slow mapping of systems before data leaves. He also points to application and mobile weaknesses, a detection time of 416 days, and breaches usually reported by third parties.

His recommendations are to spend across the whole attack chain rather than mostly on blocking, train employees, apply big data analysis to spot anomalies, use data loss prevention and encryption, and rehearse breach response. He compares the two related heists, about $5 million and $40 million, and argues that intelligence shared between the victims could have stopped the second. He closes by urging attendees to share intelligence with their peers.

talks.title: James Pang
talks.teaser: Describes how Interpol's digital crime centre links national investigators and private partners against transnational cybercrime.
talks.summary:
This keynote at RSA Conference Asia Pacific 2013 treated cybercrime as a transnational problem that no single country can handle alone. The speaker noted that countries differ in how much priority they give it within national security, and that investigations are often slowed by the time needed for mutual legal assistance requests. Interpol was presented as an organisation working at the intersection of crime and technology, with tools and services used by its 190 member countries.

The central section described Interpol's approach through three processes: networking, leveraging and harmonising. The Interpol Digital Crime Centre was described as a way to build networks between national cybercrime investigators and public and private sector stakeholders, and to test and develop new technologies and tools for law enforcement use. Partnerships with industry and regional bodies were also outlined as part of that work.

A worked operation was used to show the results. Actionable cyber intelligence let several law enforcement authorities carry out simultaneous operations with prosecutors, with 47 houses searched across 19 cities in 5 countries and IT equipment seized for later analysis. The closing message was that cybercrime affects law enforcement as well as the public and private sectors, and that shared intelligence and capacity building are needed. The practical takeaway for practitioners was that cross-border coordination and information sharing are the main levers.

talks.title: If Only We Would Look - Nawaf Bitar
talks.teaser: Argues for deception and digital fingerprints to catch attackers earlier and track them more precisely than IP addresses.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that signature-based defenses such as antivirus, IPS and web application firewalls act only after an attack has already started, so data center security needs a different approach. The speaker turns to wartime deception, describing the inflatable tanks and fake audio used to mislead German planners before the 1944 Normandy invasion, and asks how similar ideas could protect systems at the reconnaissance phase.

Deception could present attackers with fabricated pages and files, so any interaction with them marks them as hostile, and fake data can cost an automated attacker hours of wasted effort. Tracking them precisely is the harder problem. The speaker recalls the Bertillon system, whose 1905 mistaken identity case involving William West showed the risks of relying on measurements, and notes that IP addresses are easy to evade and can block whole countries, as when Qatar was cut off from Wikipedia. Digital fingerprints built from many device traits, such as screen resolution, browser version and installed fonts, could identify a device even when some traits are hidden.

The final section argues that identifiers must be shared across enforcement points. A 1969 Houston murder went unsolved for 34 years until a national fingerprint database, IAFIS, produced a match within five hours of the print being entered. The takeaway is to track attackers precisely and share what is learned, so that one attacker does not become a repeat attacker.

talks.title: We Were Hacked: Here's What You Should Know
talks.teaser: Victims of high-profile account takeovers explain how linked recovery flows let attackers seize their digital lives.
talks.summary:
Two people who were targeted in high-profile intrusions describe how their accounts were taken over. Matthew Prince, co-founder of Cloudflare, explains how attackers used relay-service phone calls, a purchased Social Security number and a redirected voicemail to pass carrier checks. They then used Google's phone-based account recovery to reach his personal email and corporate account. A flaw let that recovery path bypass two-step verification, and the intruders redirected a customer's website to their own social feed within about ninety minutes.

Mat Honan, a writer for Wired, describes a separate chain. Attackers added a card to his retail account by phone, used its last four digits to reset his Apple account, then used his backup email to take over Gmail and Twitter in roughly half an hour. They deleted his Google account and remotely wiped his devices. His last backup was two years old, so his photographs were lost until a costly data recovery service restored them. Both speakers stress that each service was secure alone, but the links between services created new weaknesses. They also interviewed some of the teenage attackers, who were motivated more by notoriety than money.

The advice is practical. Companies should explain clearly what victims must do after a breach, such as checking mail forwarding rules and removing unfamiliar app authorisations. Prince says Cloudflare disclosed its incident openly and did not appear to lose customers. Individuals should avoid using one email address as a universal login, pick a less guessable recovery address, and enable every extra authentication option offered, since providers can often add protections when asked.

talks.title: Webcast: Link by Link: Crafting the Attribution Chain
talks.teaser: Walks through how analysts link technical breadcrumbs and human clues to attribute threat actors, and why misattribution is risky.
talks.summary:
This webcast, presented by Will Graschado of RSA's SMC business unit, looks at how analysts build an attribution chain, the linked evidence that connects a cyber attack to the people or group behind it. It starts by noting there is no universal definition of attribution, and that some organisations care more about who the actor is than how they are classified, while others take the opposite view. Ideas from psychology, such as explaining why someone acts, are used to frame the discussion.

The middle section focuses on the breadcrumbs attackers leave behind, such as IP addresses, command and control infrastructure, domain registrations and file hashes. Graschado argues that no single data point settles attribution; analysts must combine pieces and watch for repeated signatures over time. He separates technological from human attribution and lists questions to ask: who acted, why, how, from where, and what the infrastructure shows. He warns that a machine's location does not reveal the actor, since attackers often compromise systems in other regions, and that misattribution can harm innocent parties. The Q&A covers cloud forensics with network packet capture, big data analysis, and whether confidence percentages are useful, with the speaker preferring near-certainty. The APT1 report serves as an example of combining human and open-source intelligence.

The takeaway is to gather and corroborate several linked data points across investigators before naming an actor, weigh the risks of publishing attribution, and leave retaliation to law enforcement and government.

talks.title: Webcast: Mitigating the Top Human Risks
talks.teaser: Shows how to identify top human risks and build an awareness program that changes behavior, not just compliance.
talks.summary:
The talk treats people as another operating system that organizations rarely secure. Spitzner argues that people misjudge risk, overfearing vivid threats like shark attacks and underestimating everyday ones. He compares the odds of dying from a shark, about 250 million to one, with vending machines, about 112 million to one, which he says claim three to four lives a year.

He then presents an early list of top human risks developed with the Critical Security Controls consortium, starting with phishing, password reuse, outdated systems, removable media and oversharing on social networks. He stresses that organizations should adapt the list to their own needs. Misconceptions get attention: awareness is one control among several, not a failure when some staff still click, and staff who report incidents act as a human sensor. Technical and privileged staff need targeted training, and content should show how safe habits help at home, since people forget material quickly and need regular reinforcement.

For practical steps, he recommends a maturity model with five levels, a project charter, and a steering committee of volunteers who help shape the program. Planning should answer who, what and how, with a phased rollout that starts with employees. Behavior should be measured with monthly phishing assessments, framed as support rather than punishment, with management told only about repeat failures. Where privacy rules limit individual tracking, anonymous link-click counts can serve instead. The talk closes with free resources, including a roadmap poster, templates and a monthly newsletter.

talks.title: Criminal Education - Art Gilliland
talks.teaser: RSA Conference US 2013 Keynote details Criminal Education - Art Gilliland.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about the speaker's daughter asking whether good guys or bad guys win, and uses that question to frame a case for studying adversaries rather than only hardening defenses. The speaker argues that defenders are predictable because their capabilities follow compliance standards and budget cycles, while attackers adapt quickly. The figures cited include 94% of breaches being reported to the organization by a third party, intruders remaining inside for an average of 416 days before discovery, remediation time growing by 71 percent, and 84% of breaches exploiting application-layer vulnerabilities.

The speaker describes the criminal ecosystem as a market with specialists: one group builds target profiles, another sells initial access, and others map the environment and extract data. Cheap services are part of the picture, with botnet access rented for $18 a day and a Zeus kit priced at about $7,000 on average. A kill-chain style model is used to walk through the stages. The speaker notes that around 86% of security spending goes to blocking the adversary at the entry stage, about five times as much as all the other stages combined.

The recommended response is to build capabilities at each stage, especially finding intruders after they get in but before they steal data, protecting sensitive data, and remediating faster. The speaker suggests combining internal data with external sources, cloud data, employee sentiment and access patterns to spot malicious insiders, and scanning criminal networks for stolen information. The closing challenge is for the industry to share security data in a central, cloud-based big data platform so defenders can match the speed at which attackers share intelligence.

talks.title: Building and Securing Aadhaar - Srikanth Nadhamuni
talks.teaser: Walks through building India's Aadhaar biometric ID system and the privacy and security choices made around it.
talks.summary:
Srikanth Nadhamuni, who led the technology side of India's Aadhaar program, explains why the government built a national identity for its 1.2 billion residents. Welfare subsidies were being drained by duplicate and fake ration cards, so the system needed biometrics to make sure each person is enrolled only once. Enrollment captures demographic fields, ten fingerprints, iris scans and a photo, and each new record is compared against the entire database before a random number is issued. Iris was added as a second biometric because worn fingerprint ridges in rural workers often fail to capture.

The technical walkthrough covers a back end built mostly on open-source components, including Hadoop, MySQL, Java and ZooKeeper, running on commodity blade servers. Three separate biometric vendors are used so that suspected duplicates can be re-checked by the others, and transaction volume is shifted toward whichever vendor performs better. On privacy, the number carries no personal details, data is encrypted at the source, operators sign each enrollment with their own fingerprint, raw biometrics are not stored in the clear, and authentication returns only a yes or no answer.

The talk closes with the societal case: a farm worker losing a large share of his wages to travel costs and moneylenders because no bank existed in his village. Aadhaar-linked micro ATMs run by village shopkeepers are presented as a way to bring banking locally. The speaker argues the system should be an identity platform that banks and insurers can build on, and that its human impact is what sets it apart.

talks.title: RSA Conference Europe 2012 Keynote
talks.teaser: Frames security as a way to keep defectors rare enough that strangers can cooperate and trust each other.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker tracing the many people he trusted in a single morning, from pilots and drivers to food suppliers, and argues that this everyday trust is what lets society function. He separates personal trust, based on knowing someone's intentions, from the thinner trust of dealing with strangers, which is really about expecting them to follow social norms.

The central model treats every cooperative system as open to defectors who profit by free-riding, and security as the means of keeping their numbers down to an acceptable level rather than to zero. He lists four societal pressures that push people toward cooperation: morals, reputation, laws and institutions, and security systems. A coffee-box experiment, where a picture of eyes behind the box raised honesty payments, illustrates how reputation cues alone change behaviour. He notes that morals fade with distance, while reputation can travel through language.

Technology, he argues, upsets the balance because attackers adopt new tools quickly while institutions take years to catch up, a gap that widens during fast change. He points to credit scoring and online feedback systems as examples where technology helped reputation scale. He closes with cautions: defectors will always exist, more security can hurt cooperation, and some defection is needed for social change.

talks.title: RSA Conference Europe 2012 Keynote
talks.teaser: Shows why security should tailor protections to how different people judge risk, using a bird story and insurance pricing examples.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that security is moving from guarding endpoints and networks toward recognising that people differ in how they judge risk. The speaker opens with a story about a bird that got loose on a flight to London. Two colleagues reacted very differently: one worried about the bird, the other saw a way someone could sneak something onto an aircraft. He calls this a "bird test" for how people read risky situations, such as a certificate error.

He argues that current safeguards are generic, so people who do not think about risk are set up to fail. Good protection, he suggests, should resemble a gymnastics spotter who knows the athlete, rather than a stranger who gives false positives and misses real falls. He then turns to insurance: car premiums now depend on personal answers, and his father's hurricane cover in the Bahamas is priced by house elevation because surge causes the most damage. A MacBook Air support plan example shows a vendor failing to price the service by the buyer's real risk. He also warns that personalised phishing is becoming cheap to produce and that people are easy to research before a first meeting.

He closes with the steering wheel analogy: the hand position taught for decades became dangerous once airbags arrived. He urges attendees to test long-held assumptions about perimeters and lockdown, and to assess risk so the business can adopt new technology rather than simply saying no.

talks.title: Webcast: Large Scale Cloud Forensics
talks.teaser: Explores acquiring and analyzing evidence in large multi-tenant clouds across jurisdictions, with a proposed forensic architecture.
talks.summary:
Sam Curry and Edward Haletky frame why forensic investigations in large cloud environments are so hard. They start with a 2011 case in which FBI seizure of one hosted environment shut down a company and also took offline about twenty to thirty smaller tenants that had no link to the crime. The speakers use that example to set out the core problems: collecting data without disrupting uninvolved customers, respecting tenant boundaries and the privacy laws of each jurisdiction, and avoiding broad collection that pulls in data an investigator has no right to examine.

They describe current practice as taking everything, with warrants that target an IP address that may front thousands of servers, and disk replication whose integrity courts have questioned. They then propose three principles. The first is a cloud version of Locard's exchange principle, which assumes an intruder always leaves traces. The second is a unique identifier that follows each virtual machine and its related files, logs and snapshots through clones and migrations. The third is an external, common time source, because guest clocks can drift. Analysis is treated as a big-data problem, requiring storage that preserves chain of custody and tools that can query mixed data such as disk, network, logs and memory images. Memory analysis may also help recover encryption keys without relying on suspects.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to plan for forensics before an incident, involve legal counsel early, and press cloud vendors on acquisition support. The speakers say they are prototyping an initial acquisition kit and a more advanced analysis lab, and they invite collaboration from technical, legal and policy people.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 -- The Psychology of a Cyber Predator; Decoding the Deviate Mind
talks.teaser: Explains how cyber predators exploit basic human needs online and offers practical signs and habits to reduce grooming risk.
talks.summary:
The session opens by arguing that defense starts with understanding who online abusers are and how digital channels amplify lying, stalking, and coercion. It defines a cyber predator as someone who psychologically or physically victimizes others through technology, citing extreme cases such as a California attacker who accessed hundreds of homes via webcams and used intimate images for sextortion, alongside broader patterns like cyberbullying and large-scale financial fraud compared with traditional bank robbery losses.

The core framework maps criminal motivation to unmet human needs drawn from Schindler and Tony Robbins–style models: love and connection, significance, certainty, variety, growth, and contribution. The speaker contends that offenders chase these needs behind a screen—through chat, scams, power plays, identity play, and escalating “wins”—and that meeting even two needs intensely can fuel addictive behavior tied to a compelling future, whether quick cash or long-running schemes.

Recognition and avoidance close the talk. Predators are said to profile victims’ needs and groom accordingly, as in a romance fraud targeting a divorced professional asked for thousands before a promised visit. Practical guidance stresses instinct, skepticism toward offers that feel too good, vetting contacts and references, limiting shared personal data, and refusing in-person meetings with suspicious online relationships.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 -- Human Hacking Exposed: 6 Preventative Tips That Can Save Your Company
talks.teaser: Six practical measures help organizations spot persuasion-based attacks and train staff against phishing and pretext scams.
talks.summary:
Organizations face adversaries who pair technical skill with deception aimed at employees. The presenter defines social engineering as any influence that leads someone to act, often against their interests, and points to high-profile 2011 breaches and phishing trends as evidence that the human layer dominates many intrusions. A simple help-desk password pretext that fooled most IRS testers in a legal pen test illustrates how cheap attacks still succeed.

Six preventative habits anchor the session. Teams should stay current on real attack methods, run awareness that feels personal rather than generic compliance training, and teach staff how small disclosures enable dumpster dives and physical access. Patching matters because outdated PDF and browser stacks invite exploit-led social pitches. Written playbooks for terminations, suspicious calls, and suspected phishing reduce chaotic responses, as shown when a dismissed worker wiped thirteen servers and backups without offboarding rules.

Social engineering assessments should be targeted and actionable, not thick reports for their own sake. Working backward from audit gaps lets leaders focus training where people fail—phone elicitation versus email—so effort matches actual weakness. The closing message is pragmatic: perfect immunity is unrealistic, but raising the bar makes the organization a harder target than peers who remain easy prey.

talks.title: Art Coviello interviews former Prime Minister Tony Blair at RSA Conference 2012
talks.teaser: A former prime minister discusses political leadership, social media's revolutionary force and how technology reshapes government.
talks.summary:
Art Coviello, RSA's executive chairman, interviews former prime minister Tony Blair live at RSA Conference 2012. Coviello first asks where political leadership will come from when partisan bickering dominates. Blair names two pressing challenges: steadying the economy and handling the fallout from the Arab uprisings, which he expects to have large but unpredictable effects on security. He also points to the rise of China as a new geopolitical order. He argues that politics should move past old left-and-right categories and renew a shared sense of national purpose, confident in core values while applying them to a changed world.

On social media, Blair calls it a revolutionary force that can create waves of opinion with great intensity, but he stresses that protest is not the same as government, which needs difficult, evolutionary decisions. He says the technology has a liberating effect and must be handled with respect for its power. Asked whether he is optimistic, he says he is by nature, and that technology will solve many problems, though politicians face the challenge of deciding how to apply it. He adds that he would design education, health care and government differently if starting today.

Asked about his future, Blair says he does not rule out another role in public life but wants each morning to bring a sense of purpose and motivation beyond himself. Coviello closes by thanking him and calling that view both unselfish and optimistic.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 Keynote - The Hugh Thompson Show
talks.teaser: Examines cognitive bias, political framing, and targeted messaging so defenders can see how human choices start breaches.
talks.summary:
The session argues that many major data breaches begin not with exotic technology but with a person’s choice—to open an attachment, follow a link, or accept a risky shortcut. The host connects that pattern to an era of profiling and tailored online experiences, asking whether personalized framing can steer decisions the way a friend coaching a car salesman or an attacker might.

Author Dan Gardner describes unconscious “system one” versus deliberate “system two” thinking, illustrating anchoring, the availability heuristic, and confirmation bias amplified by search engines and big data built on revealed preferences. He points to metacognition—pausing to question where a gut reaction came from—as a practical counterweight, even when statistics say a feared outcome is rare.

Pollster Dr. Frank Lutz shows how word choice reshapes reactions in live audience tests and relates political mugging-scam email tactics to personal, urgent calls to action. He urges security leaders to sell peace of mind, protection, and preemptive preparedness rather than sensational threat language, and to instill confidence when communicating value upward. The program closes with a call for practitioner-driven innovation after a difficult year for trust in the industry.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 Keynote - Protecting Business in the New World Order
talks.teaser: Shows how security can enable business growth through data dispersal, QR code access and continuous authentication.
talks.summary:
Mike Denning, general manager of security at CA Technologies, opens with short video skits. One shows a restrictive company where a locked-out employee loses access after his phone is wiped; another shows a firm that lets staff bring their own devices and still recovers their data. The framing is that security should enable business, since users route around controls that block them.

Dr. Carrie Gates of CA Labs then covers the enabling technologies. Data dispersal splits a file into pieces spread across machines, providers and countries, so any k of them rebuild it and one compromised holder sees only a fraction. Context-based keyword analysis helps classify corporate data on personal devices, and QR codes can authenticate a user and provision access in real time, such as a conference room. Geolocation can feed risk scores for each transaction.

The closing section covers continuous authentication, which checks typing rhythm, mouse use and browsing habits over time. Gates noted the research so far involved 80 people, while CA has 14,000 people, so scaling and cross-device behavior remain open, and government funding supports the work. Anomaly detection aims at insider threats, where someone with legitimate access uses it for the wrong reason. Denning's takeaway is that security teams must keep pace with the business and work alongside users.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 Keynote - Combating Threats in the Cyber World
talks.teaser: Outlines the FBI's view of top cyber threats, from terrorist use of the internet to state espionage and criminal syndicates.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with a New York case in which a stolen iPhone was traced through the Find My iPhone app to a suspect's sock, showing technology as both a target and an investigative tool. It then traces how crime has moved online since a 2000 denial-of-service attack, describing terrorist groups that publish magazines and social media accounts, plotters of a 2010 Times Square attempt who used web cameras, file sharing and proxy servers, state-sponsored intruders who seek intellectual property, and profit-driven groups that sell stolen access.

In response, the speaker described cyber squads in each of the 56 field offices, a national task force of 18 agencies organised into threat-focused cells, and legal attaché offices abroad. Two cases were highlighted: the Core Flood botnet, which infected an estimated two million computers and was rerouted to FBI-controlled servers, and Operation Ghost Click, a click-fraud ring that generated more than $14 million in illegal fees, infected 4 million computers and led to six Estonian nationals being charged.

The main message is that defenders must share information with law enforcement and with each other. The speaker cited companies collaborating on email authentication, the InfraGuard partnership, which has grown to more than 85 chapters and 47,000 members, and a case in which a member's tip helped identify 100 US banks hit by unauthorised ATM withdrawals. The advice is to assume breach, limit the data at risk, separate mission-critical information and build systems that help catch attackers rather than only withstand them.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 The Great Cipher Mightier Than the Sword
talks.teaser: Recounts how the Rosignol family's Great Cipher guarded France for Louis XIV and why the code keys disappeared after his death.
talks.summary:
The presentation traces a French cryptographic tradition nicknamed the Great Cipher, passed down as sons and grandfathers in the Rosignol line kept the work alive across generations. During Louis XIV's youth, that system shielded royal and state communications while the throne was still vulnerable. Under Cardinal Richelieu's successor Mazarin, the same lineage supported the young monarch's transition from a child king toward the absolutist "Sun King" era, with the cipher woven into how power was exercised and secrets were kept.

The middle of the talk stresses continuity: the method was not a one-off invention but something refined from one generation to the next, carrying institutional memory and tactical options that had accumulated over centuries. That framing treats strong encryption as a strategic asset comparable to conventional force—a cipher that could matter as much as arms in great-power politics.

Practitioners are left with a cautionary historical arc. When Louis XIV died, the keys to the code were lost, undercutting whatever operational advantage the cipher had provided. The takeaway is that long-lived cryptosystems depend on key stewardship and succession planning, not only on algorithmic strength; losing material after a regime change can erase capability as thoroughly as breaking the math.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2012 Keynote - Lock it Down or Free it Up?
talks.teaser: Argues that the network can enforce security without forcing a choice between locking systems down and freeing users up.
talks.summary:
Christopher Young, Cisco's senior vice president for security, opens by describing the tension security teams face between locking systems down and freeing users up. He points to employees who use personal devices, personal email and cloud file-sharing, and argues that security is often seen as cumbersome. He recalls a virtual desktop rollout in call centers, where many terminals starting antivirus at the same moment during shift changes caused storms that could take a center offline. His lesson is that applying an old security model to a new architecture fails.

He then turns to healthcare, where doctors and staff bring their own devices, desktops are delivered over the network, and IPv6 gives equipment its own address. He cites Cisco estimates of over 8 billion smart handheld devices by 2016 and mobile data traffic rising to 18 times current levels. He also reports that enterprise users averaged 339 malware encounters per month, with one third of that malware being zero-day. In his view, the network is the place to enforce security, using global reputation data from email and web traffic, NetFlow visibility into traffic between devices, and context-aware access based on who, what, where, when and how a device connects.

His application example lets a hospital permit some uses of Facebook or YouTube in the break room while blocking risky ones near the emergency room. He closes by arguing that visibility and context-based enforcement let organizations say yes to users while still protecting them. He leaves the IPv6 transition risks for a future session.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2010 - Practical Return-Oriented Programming
talks.teaser: Explains how return-oriented programming reuses existing code to bypass DEP, demonstrated with the Aurora Internet Explorer exploit.
talks.summary:
Dino Dai Zovi explains return-oriented programming, a way to exploit memory corruption bugs without injecting new code. Instead of running attacker-supplied code, the exploit returns into short instruction sequences already in executable memory, including shared libraries, and chains them into gadgets that perform higher-level operations such as writing a chosen value to a chosen location. Blocking malicious code is therefore not enough to stop malicious computation.

He then shows that DEP and ASLR make exploitation harder but not impossible. A return-oriented exploit needs a stack pivot that moves the stack pointer into attacker-controlled data. Without full ASLR, permanent DEP offers little protection, since modules that do not opt in give predictable addresses. As a worked example he covers the Aurora Internet Explorer bug, a reference counting error that leaves a stale pointer after a heap block is freed. Heap spraying and a forged vtable lead to a stack pivot, a return sled and then the payload, which he says works on IE8 across Windows XP SP3, Vista and Windows 7.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that malware may already use these techniques against DEP-enabled processes, so analysts need to recognize ROP payloads. Vendors should assume that vulnerabilities lead to code execution rather than rely on DEP and ASLR to make them unexploitable. He recommends restricting what applications can do, through privilege reduction such as low integrity on Windows Vista and 7, sandboxing, and approaches such as virtualization.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - How to Recruit Spies on the Internet
talks.teaser: Explains how spies identify and recruit insiders through social networks, using case studies of blackmail, ego and money.
talks.summary:
Ira Winkler argues that social networking is not new, recalling Usenet posts from the early 1990s that let him profile companies. He separates operatives, who recruit, from agents, the insiders who already hold access and are manipulated into passing information along. Bradley Manning and the Russian illegals case serve as examples of people who looked unremarkable yet were susceptible or well placed to gather information.

The middle of the talk covers why people become susceptible: money, ideology, ego and coercion, often in combination. A former intelligence officer he knew recruited a contractor's analyst through small favours and rising payments, so the man never realised he was passing information to a foreign operative. Winkler also describes a blackmail case in which an attacker used hacked email accounts to extract further material, and a bachelor party photo that a cousin tagged online, causing family fallout. A class exercise in which students compiled dossiers on themselves showed how much exploitable detail they had published.

He closes with practical advice. Public records, group memberships and certifications let an adversary build targets, and fake profiles can attract real contacts quickly. Training, in his view, should focus on what makes employees personally vulnerable, because that exposure carries over to the company. Strategy matters more than policy alone.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - From White Hat to Black - The Curious Case of Cybercrime Kingpin, Max Vision
talks.teaser: Follows a former white hat hacker's slide into payment card fraud and the undercover sting that ended his run.
talks.summary:
The talk traces Max Vision, a computer security researcher turned cybercriminal, from his late-1990s white hat work to his criminal career. He wrote a program that exploited a BIND flaw to patch government systems, but he also left rootkits on them, and he was tracked down and charged after those rootkits reported back to him. After prison he struggled to find work, and a former bank robber began funding him to hack for profit.

Working from hotel rooms in San Francisco, the pair used Wi-Fi scanning and known exploits to get into small banks and credit unions. The stolen magnetic stripe data, known as dumps, was sold through underground carding forums. Max lured carders with a fake offer of free American Express data that infected anyone who clicked, and he later breached restaurant point-of-sale systems, collecting 1.1 million card numbers. The speaker explains why the card verification value stored on the stripe made dumps far more valuable than plain card numbers.

The story ends with an undercover FBI agent who ran a rival forum, Dark Market, and a long cat-and-mouse contest that led to Max's arrest and a 13-year sentence. The takeaway is that magnetic stripe data was the real prize for criminals, while the card numbers printed on the face of a card were worth much less to them.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - Hacking Exposed - Exploiting the Cloud and Virtual Machines
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how attackers pivot from a cloud guest VM to the host, and how to limit that risk.
talks.summary:
The speakers define cloud computing as a delivery model built on dynamically scalable, often virtualized resources, and frame the session around its risks. They outline threats such as account hijacking, data leakage, malicious insiders, weaknesses in shared technology and insecure APIs. Co-residency is the central concern: tenants share CPU, memory, network and firmware, so a compromised neighbour can become a route in.

The demonstrations follow an attack chain. A free account on a hosted blogging service lets the attacker slip a PHP script past the upload filter by disguising it as a JPEG, giving a foothold on the web server. From there, a netcat shell and an uploaded remote access tool are used to exploit a print spooler flaw, the one tied to Stuxnet, and reach a neighbouring database guest with administrator rights. A VMware graphics vulnerability (CVE-2009-1244), weaponized in the Canvas tool, is then used to break out of the guest and take over the host. A bonus MOF technique runs code without user action.

For defenders, the speakers recommend prompt patching, hardening systems, controlling who can reach them, and using private hypervisors where possible. They also stress watching outbound DNS and other traffic for command-and-control channels, moving toward application whitelisting so unapproved code cannot execute, correlating logs, and using decoy address space to catch anomalous traffic.
