talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - The Seven Most Dangerous New Attack Techniques, and What's Coming Next
talks.teaser: Practitioners hear how social platforms, in-memory theft, IPv6 pivoting, and embedded gear widen breach paths, plus mitigations that matter.
talks.summary:
The session frames seven worrisome attack trends drawn from large breach responses and penetration testing. Social networks become the main lure layer: impostor pages, in-group link challenges, and surveys that trick friends into answering password-reset style questions for someone else. Defenders are urged to run awareness around social leakage, register official company presences, and watch what employees expose.

A central theme is that filesystem and wire encryption does not stop memory scraping. Processed data sits in cleartext in RAM, and attackers use frameworks to inject in-process interpreters, regex-hunt secrets, and even alter tools such as SSH clients in memory to pivot outward. Separately, compromise over IPv4 often jumps to IPv6 neighbors because many internal controls ignore v6; default client stacks and tunnels widen that gap. Stuxnet illustrates trickle-down militarized malware—stolen signing keys, multiple zero-days, and kinetic SCADA effects—while maturing software pushes crime toward applications and physical hardware, including smart meters and bus-level key extraction.

Johannes Ulrich extends IPv6 planning gaps, browser-history-driven scams, automated research for targeted phishing, and DNS logging as a cheap choke-point control. Cloud questions stress provider management-plane breach over guest escape, customer-side encryption, and data placement discipline. Q&A covers remote firmware backdoors, mobile parity with PCs, limits of virtualization against RAM theft, and closing calls for basics, telemetry sharing, and growing skilled staff.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - Update on DNSSEC: A Discussion with the Experts
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss DNSSEC adoption after root signing, covering overhead, cache poisoning, certificate trust and rollout advice.
talks.summary:
This panel looked at where DNSSEC adoption stood after the root zone was signed. The panelists framed it as one building block for DNS security, with the aim that users reach the site they expect when they click a link. They acknowledged early setbacks, including two top-level domains dropping out of DNSSEC before returning.

The middle of the discussion covered technical and operational concerns. One panelist dismissed bandwidth worries, noting that DNS amplification predates DNSSEC and that the main extra costs were memory, bandwidth and CPU, estimated at roughly a factor of five. The source port randomization fix for cache poisoning was described as a stopgap, while DNSSEC gives cryptographic assurance that an answer is genuine. Others discussed using the signed namespace for authentication across organizations, and contrasted the certificate authority model, where one speaker cited over 1,500 intermediate CA certificates able to sign for a company, with delegated trust in DNS. A quantum computing answer said RSA and elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman would be badly damaged, while conventional ciphers would only lose effective key length.

For organizations, the advice was to turn on DNSSEC validation on resolvers for zones already signed, add browser plug-ins, and check registrar and DNS software support before .com is signed. Root and registry levels were described as essentially free, with registrar service pricing varying. Secondary servers can use either their own keys or uploaded keys, linked by DS records. The panel closed by saying the next step is building tools that read signed data back out, and that adoption was encouraging.

talks.title: RSA Conference 2011 - The Psychology of Risk: Why Understanding Human Behavior is Essential
talks.teaser: Empirical studies on risk homeostasis reveal why awareness training, engineering controls, and penalties often fail in security programs.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens from prior work on formal risk assessment, noting that identical inputs can yield different conclusions and asking what happens in human psychology before the process starts. Everyday examples—from smoking and driving after drinking to skipping flossing—frame risk homeostasis theory: people hold a subjectively acceptable level of risk and adjust behavior to restore that equilibrium, including taking more risk when they feel too safe.

The middle of the session maps levers that raise or lower accepted risk—advantages and costs of risky versus cautious choices—and ties them to information security tradeoffs such as shortcutting change management or bearing compliance overhead. Engineering, education, and enforcement approaches are tested against evidence: Atlanta driver training with extensive hours produced more accidents in the fullest training group; Munich taxis with anti-lock brakes showed no accident reduction but faster driving; motorcycle and citation crackdown studies showed little lasting effect. Reactance is introduced as active resistance to coercive rules.

The close favors lowering perceived compliance burden and rewarding cautious behavior, citing a fleet reward program that cut at-fault accidents sharply at modest cost. For security programs aimed at employee choices rather than direct network attack, practitioners are urged to favor simple policies, collaboration, flexibility, and opt-outs over punishment-heavy models that may not shift equilibrium risk.

talks.title: Conference 2011 Keynote - The Department of Defense, Active Cyber Defense, and the Secure Zone
talks.teaser: Outlines the US military's move from static network defense to active defense and a proposed Secure Zone.
talks.summary:
General Alexander's keynote explains how the Department of Defense is changing its approach to protecting military networks and, by extension, the wider nation's infrastructure. He opens with the rapid growth of online data and social platforms, then points to disruptive attacks against Estonia, Georgia and other countries as the reason for urgency. He describes about 15,000 DoD networks that are scanned more than a million times a day, with malicious email attacks above 20,000 a month.

He traces the 2009 creation of US Cyber Command, which merged two existing commands into one organization that reached full operational capability in October 2010. He argues that a static defense, such as the Maginot Line, cannot hold against an adaptive adversary. Active defense means hunting for adversary malware inside networks, watching the boundaries, and providing early warning. A 2010 agreement between the Defense and Homeland Security departments, with NSA support, set up liaison roles and shared responsibilities.

Next he presents the Secure Zone idea, extending protection from military systems to critical infrastructure through public-private partnership, with industry handling sensitive signatures and information flowing in both directions. He insists that civil liberties and privacy must be protected alongside security. He closes by calling for better situational awareness, public demand for secure technology, and stronger STEM education. His takeaway is that defending cyberspace is a team effort across government, industry and allies.
